### [1] [Pre-training, Reasoning, Benchmarking: X-ray Report Generation on CheXpert Plus Dataset](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08813)
*Xiao Wang,Yuxiang Zhang,Dan Xu,Yuehang Li,Shiao Wang,Bo Jiang,Yaowei Wang,Yonghong Tian,Jin Tang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper establishes a comprehensive benchmark for X-ray radiology report generation (RRG) on the CheXpert Plus dataset and proposes MambaXray-PRB, a novel framework using multi-stage large-model pre-training and multi-modal Chain-of-Thought reasoning to improve report generation performance and model interpretability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The field of X-ray image-based RRG faces bottlenecks due to insufficient standardized benchmarks and inadequate domain adaptation of generic large models. The newly released CheXpert Plus dataset lacks baseline implementations and evaluation results, hindering standardized training, quantitative evaluation, and fair comparison among algorithms.

Method: The paper proposes MambaXray-PRB framework with three successive phases: (1) self-supervised auto-regressive modeling, (2) X-ray-report contrastive learning, and (3) post-training optimization for reasoning and report generation. The framework incorporates multi-stage large-model pre-training and multi-modal Chain-of-Thought reasoning to enhance both performance and interpretability.

Result: Extensive experiments on IU X-ray, MIMIC-CXR, and CheXpert Plus datasets validate the effectiveness of MambaXray-PRB for radiology report generation. The benchmark provides a reliable comparative foundation for identifying state-of-the-art approaches.

Conclusion: The benchmark addresses the lack of standardized evaluation on CheXpert Plus, while MambaXray-PRB demonstrates that combining multi-stage pre-training with multi-modal Chain-of-Thought reasoning can significantly improve both the quality of generated radiology reports and model interpretability in the paradigm of large models.

Abstract: X-ray image-based Radiology Report Generation (RRG) constitutes a critical research direction within medical artificial intelligence, with great potential to alleviate clinicians' diagnostic workload and shorten patient waiting periods. Despite substantial advances over recent years, the field faces evident bottlenecks stemming from insufficient standardized benchmarks and inadequate domain adaptation of generic large models. Notably, the newly released CheXpert Plus dataset is provided without accompanying baseline implementations and evaluation results, which impedes standardized training, quantitative evaluation and fair comparison among follow-up algorithms. To mitigate this limitation, we establish a comprehensive benchmark encompassing prevailing X-ray report generation models and Large Language Models on CheXpert Plus. This benchmark delivers a reliable comparative foundation for upcoming methods and enables researchers to rapidly identify state-of-the-art approaches within this domain. Beyond benchmark construction, we rethink X-ray RRG under the paradigm of large models and propose a novel framework termed MambaXray-PRB. Our framework improves report generation performance and enhances model interpretability via multi-stage large-model pre-training and multi-modal Chain-of-Thought reasoning. The pipeline consists of three successive phases: self-supervised auto-regressive modeling, X-ray-report contrastive learning, and post-training optimization for reasoning and report generation. Extensive experiments on IU X-ray, MIMIC-CXR, and CheXpert Plus datasets validate the effectiveness of MambaXray-PRB for radiology report generation. The source code of this paper is available on https://github.com/Event-AHU/Medical_Image_Analysis

</details>


### [2] [Autonomous Driving Research Requires a Community-Driven Data Paradigm](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08825)
*Jinsu Yoo,Zanming Huang,Katie Z Luo,Zheda Mai,Qiyuan Wu,Bharath Hariharan,Mark Campbell,Wei-Lun Chao*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: The paper argues that autonomous driving research suffers from a fragmented data paradigm where 600+ datasets remain underused due to limited visibility, incompatible protocols, and benchmark incentives favoring a few dominant datasets. The authors propose a collaborative, community-driven data paradigm to improve dataset discovery, reuse, integration, and evaluation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The field of autonomous driving remains far from achieving universal robustness (anywhere, anytime, for anyone). The authors posit this gap is not merely a modeling problem but stems from the prevailing data paradigm - reliance on a few benchmark datasets with limited spatial and scenario coverage, despite the existence of many diverse datasets.

Method: The authors analyze the current state of autonomous driving datasets, identifying fragmentation, limited visibility, incompatible protocols, and benchmark incentives as key barriers. They outline principles for a community-driven data paradigm and present an early implementation.

Result: The paper identifies that over 600 autonomous driving datasets exist across nearly 50 countries, but most remain significantly underused. The dominant datasets receive disproportionate attention due to benchmark incentives, while diverse and underexplored data remains underutilized.

Conclusion: The authors call for collaboration across academia and industry to transform fragmented datasets into shared community infrastructure through a collaborative data paradigm. This would improve dataset discovery, reuse, integration, evaluation, and lower barriers for new contributors, ultimately advancing the goal of anytime-anywhere autonomy.

Abstract: Autonomous driving has made remarkable progress, with recent AI advances enabling commercial deployments that are reshaping urban mobility. Yet the field remains far from its universal social promise: autonomous systems that can operate robustly anywhere, anytime, for anyone. We posit that this gap is not merely a modeling problem, but a problem of the prevailing data paradigm. Current research relies heavily on a few benchmark datasets with limited spatial and scenario coverage, even though the community has collectively produced over 600 autonomous driving datasets across nearly 50 countries. However, this abundance has not translated into broad research impact: most datasets remain significantly underused due to fragmentation, limited visibility, incompatible protocols, and benchmark incentives that concentrate attention on a few dominant datasets. We therefore argue that autonomous driving research requires a collaborative, community-driven data paradigm. Such a paradigm would improve the discovery, reuse, integration, and evaluation of diverse datasets; make underexplored data easier and more rewarding to study; and lower the barrier for new contributors. We outline its key principles, illustrate an early realization, and call for collaboration across academia and industry to transform fragmented datasets into shared community infrastructure for anytime-anywhere autonomy.

</details>


### [3] [PanoPed: Beyond Bounding Boxes for Sim-to-Real Panoramic Pedestrian Tracking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08826)
*Qinfeng Zhu,Weiguang Zhao,Yunxi Jiang,Anh Nguyen,Lei Fan*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: PanoPed is a sim-to-real benchmark for pedestrian tracking on full-sphere panoramic cameras, addressing the limitation that planar bounding boxes cannot fully describe a person's location on a sphere. The benchmark includes synthetic (108K frames) and real (28K frames) data. Sextant, a lightweight 0.035M parameter angular localization head, achieves state-of-the-art results by improving MOTIP from 47.30 to 49.49 HOTA and generalizes well from synthetic to real data without fine-tuning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Full-sphere panoramic cameras enable 360° tracking, but traditional planar bounding boxes fail to uniquely determine a person's spherical center and angular extent. The ERP (equirectangular) rectangle cannot uniquely map to spherical coordinates, necessitating a new approach for angular localization on the sphere.

Method: 1) Created PanoPed benchmark with synthetic (PanoPed-S, 108K frames from fixed/quadruped/drone cameras) and real (PanoPed-R, 28K frames) data with annotations. 2) Proposed Sextant, a plug-and-play angular localization head with ~0.035M parameters that reuses a frozen detector, maintains identity consistency, and requires no extra image encoder. 3) Leveraged the detector's visual query which carries information about spherical location.

Result: Sextant achieves best results on PanoPed-S: improving MOTIP from 47.30 to 49.49 HOTA with gains on all 8 test sequences. When transferring from synthetic to real data without fine-tuning, Sextant improves MOTIP and HAT by 0.96-1.14 HOTA, benefiting every real sequence. HAT+Sextant scores best among systems without additional localization image encoder.

Conclusion: The spherical localization problem requires angular measurement approaches rather than planar bounding boxes. Sextant provides an effective, lightweight solution that generalizes well from simulation to real-world deployment, making it practical for fixed cameras, legged robots, and drones equipped with panoramic cameras.

Abstract: Full-sphere panoramic cameras let fixed monitoring systems and mobile robots track people in every direction, but a planar bounding box does not fully describe where a person is on the sphere. We introduce PanoPed, a sim-to-real benchmark for pedestrian tracking on the full sphere. PanoPed-S contains 108,000 frames from fixed, quadruped-mounted, and drone-mounted cameras, with synchronized masks, depth, camera poses, and 3D pedestrian states. PanoPed-R adds 28,002 real frames from fixed cameras, 16,247 of them densely annotated. We find that an ERP rectangle cannot uniquely determine the spherical center and angular extent of the visible person, while the detector's visual query still carries information about them. Inspired by the sextant's use of angular measurements to locate objects, we propose Sextant, a plug-and-play angular localization head with only about 0.035M parameters. It reuses a frozen detector, keeps track identities unchanged, and needs no extra image encoder. Sextant gives the best result in our PanoPed-S test comparison, raising the strongest baseline, MOTIP, from 47.30 to 49.49 HOTA, with gains on all eight test sequences. Without fine-tuning on real data, the same synthetic-trained heads improve MOTIP and HAT by 0.96-1.14 HOTA on real video, and both seeds improve every real sequence. HAT+Sextant scores best among the compared systems that add no localization image encoder.

</details>


### [4] [MoR-MLLM: Mixture of Recursions for Efficient Multimodal Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08830)
*Pengcheng Zheng,Chaoning Zhang,Jiaxin Yan,Sihan Cao,Jianwei Zhang,Xudong Wang,Jiaquan Zhang,Jewon Lee,Tae-Ho Kim,Yang Yang,Heng Tao Shen*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: MoR-MLLM introduces adaptive per-token recursion to reduce computational and memory demands of Multimodal Large Language Models by dynamically adjusting recursive depth based on token complexity, using a three-stage MoR-Tuning strategy and entropy-regularized loss.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multimodal Large Language Models suffer from high computational and memory costs, and existing lightweight approaches use static sparsity/depth allocation that cannot adapt to the semantic complexity of each token.

Method: 1) Adaptive per-token recursion based on MoR framework to dynamically adjust recursive depth; 2) Three-stage MoR-Tuning strategy for stable training of recursive sparsity; 3) Entropy-regularized loss to encourage diverse routing distributions.

Result: Greatly reduces training memory and computation complexity while retaining high performance on various vision-language tasks compared to recent advanced tiny MLLMs.

Conclusion: MoR-MLLM effectively addresses the computational efficiency bottleneck of MLLMs through adaptive computation allocation, achieving a favorable trade-off between efficiency and performance.

Abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have demonstrated remarkable reasoning capabilities across vision and language tasks. However, their massive computational and memory demands hinder real-world deployment. While recent efforts reduce costs by employing lightweight language backbones, existing paradigms remain computation-dense due to their static sparsity and depth allocation, which cannot adapt to the semantic complexity of each token. To this end, we propose MoR-MLLM, a computation-sparse MLLM based on the recent Mixture-of-Recursions (MoR) framework. MoR-MLLM introduces adaptive per-token recursion, allowing the model to dynamically adjust its recursive depth and allocate more computation to visually or linguistically challenging tokens while skipping redundant operations for simpler ones. To stabilize the training of recursive sparsity in multimodal settings, we further design a three-stage MoR-Tuning strategy and an entropy-regularized loss to encourage diverse routing distributions. Extensive experiments show that compared with recent advanced tiny MLLMs, our proposed MoR-MLLM can greatly reduce the training memory and computation complexity while retaining high performance on various vision-language tasks.

</details>


### [5] [VCR-Bench: A Modular Open-Source Benchmark for Video Classification Robustness](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08936)
*Maksim Plinskiy,Aleksandr Gushchin,Sergey Lavrushkin,Dmitriy S. Vatolin,Anastasia Antsiferova*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: VCR-Bench is a modular open-source benchmark framework for standardizing video classification robustness evaluation, addressing the lack of standardized benchmarks in video adversarial robustness that exists in contrast to well-established image classification benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While image classification robustness has several benchmarks, video classification lacks comparable standardized benchmarks. The temporal dimension in videos introduces additional complexities (temporal sampling, perturbation budgets, metric aggregation) that lack direct analogues in image settings. Current video robustness research is scattered across incompatible implementations, making results hard to reproduce and analyze.

Method: VCR-Bench provides a unified framework with standardized components: video loading, classifier wrappers, adversarial attacks (14), defenses (10), perceptual metrics, configuration presets, and result logging. The benchmark evaluates 30 video classification models on Kinetics-400 subset using metrics including clean accuracy, attack success rate, perceptual quality, runtime, and memory usage.

Result: VCR-Bench currently integrates 30 video classification models, 14 adversarial attacks, and 10 defense wrappers under a common evaluation protocol. The framework is released with documented installation, reproducible run presets, component-extension interfaces, and scripts for reproducing results.

Conclusion: VCR-Bench addresses the reproducibility and standardization gap in video classification robustness research by providing a comprehensive, modular benchmark framework that enables fair comparison across different models, attacks, and defenses.

Abstract: Robustness of image classification has several benchmarks, but their video counterparts are absent. In video classification temporal dimension introduces additional degrees of freedom for adversarial attacks, defenses, and preprocessing. Temporal sampling, perturbation budgets, and metric aggregation also interact in ways with no direct analogue in the image setting. Therefore, robustness for video classifiers is studied across scattered, incompatible implementations, making reported numbers hard to reproduce and analyze. We introduce VCR-Bench, a modular open-source benchmark framework that standardizes video loading, wrappers for classifiers, adversarial attacks and defenses, perceptual metrics, configuration presets, and result logging. VCR-Bench currently integrates 30 video classification models, 14 adversarial attacks, and 10 defense wrappers under a common evaluation protocol. We evaluate representative video classifiers, attacks, and defenses on Kinetics-400 subset, reporting clean accuracy, attack success rate, perceptual quality, runtime, and memory usage. VCR-Bench is released with documented installation, reproducible run presets, component-extension interfaces, and scripts for reproducing the reported results at https://github.com/msu-video-group/vcr-bench.

</details>


### [6] [SPW-Nav: A Streaming Panoramic World Model for Language-Guided Navigation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08941)
*Yunheng Liu,Ziqi Cai,Siqi Yang,Yimu Wang,Minggui Teng,Jiaming Tan,Shuchen Weng,Erwin Wu,Kaipeng Zhang,Boxin Shi*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: SPW-Nav is a streaming panoramic world model that generates one minute of 2K 360-degree video in real time from a single panorama, guided by language movement instructions. It interprets instructions as camera motion within previously generated panoramas.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing panoramic generators follow predefined trajectories, and interactive world models operate through low-level actions in perspective views. There is a need for language-guided panoramic video generation that supports interactive 3D scene exploration, virtual reality experiences, and embodied agent training.

Method: SPW-Nav employs three key techniques: (1) Spherical rotation decoupling applies rotation exactly on the sphere; (2) Pose-aligned conditioning keeps translation inputs bounded over long streams; (3) A multi-term memory with a few-step generator continues the scene as instructions change. The model also uses SPW-NavSet, a dataset of panoramic videos with camera trajectories and verified instructions.

Result: SPW-Nav outperforms prior panoramic generators in camera-following accuracy and video quality, and supports on-the-fly instruction switching.

Conclusion: Language-guided streaming panoramic world models can effectively generate high-quality 360-degree video in real time by interpreting movement instructions as camera motion, enabling interactive applications in VR and embodied agent training.

Abstract: Language-guided panoramic video generation benefits various downstream applications, such as interactive 3D scene exploration, virtual reality experiences, and embodied agent training. Existing panoramic generators follow predefined trajectories, and interactive world models act through low-level actions in perspective views. We propose SPW-Nav, a streaming panoramic world model that understands movement instructions and streams one minute of 2K 360-degree video in real time from a single panorama. SPW-Nav interprets each instruction in the previously generated panorama as camera motion. Spherical rotation decoupling applies rotation exactly on the sphere, pose-aligned conditioning keeps translation inputs bounded over long streams, and a multi-term memory with a few-step generator continues the scene as instructions change. We also build SPW-NavSet, panoramic videos with camera trajectories and verified instructions. Driven by language, SPW-Nav outperforms prior panoramic generators in camera-following accuracy and video quality, and supports on-the-fly instruction switching.

</details>


### [7] [StableGrasp: Reconstructing Physically Stable Human Hand Grasps from Single Images](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09195)
*Han Jiang,Etienne Vouga,Qixing Huang,Georgios Pavlakos*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: StableGrasp is a differentiable simulation-based optimization framework that reconstructs physically stable human grasps from single RGB images by explicitly separating visual hand pose from control targets, jointly optimizing both through kinetic energy minimization in a differentiable simulator while maintaining visual consistency and geometric plausibility.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reconstructing physically stable human grasps from single RGB images is challenging because existing methods either model only visual hand geometry without physics considerations or rely on less plausible physical modeling, limiting the physical validity of resulting grasps.

Method: The method explicitly separates visual hand pose from control targets (which determine grasping forces), and jointly optimizes hand geometry and control by minimizing kinetic energy of the grasp in a differentiable simulator, while regularizing hand geometry to preserve visual consistency and geometric plausibility.

Result: The reconstructed grasps are substantially more stable under rigorous physical simulation while remaining visually consistent with input images and geometrically plausible. The approach produces far more stable grasps than alternative hand-control strategies.

Conclusion: StableGrasp can benefit visual-only grasp reconstruction pipelines by turning their outputs into physically stable grasps, providing a bridge between visual-only methods and physically valid grasps.

Abstract: Reconstructing a physically stable human grasp from a single RGB image is challenging because physically modeling grasps is itself difficult, and the problem requires estimating not only a visually constrained hand pose but also a control target that stabilizes the grasp. Existing methods either model only visual hand geometry without considering physics, or rely on less plausible physical modeling, which limits the physical validity of the resulting grasps. In this paper, we present StableGrasp, a differentiable simulation-based optimization framework that explicitly separates the visual hand pose from the control target that determines the grasping forces. Our method jointly optimizes hand geometry and control by minimizing the kinetic energy of the grasp in a differentiable simulator, while regularizing the hand geometry to preserve visual consistency and geometric plausibility. The reconstructed grasps are substantially more stable under rigorous physical simulation, while remaining visually consistent with the input images and geometrically plausible. Experiments show that our approach produces far more stable grasps than alternative hand-control strategies, benefiting visual-only grasp reconstruction pipelines by turning their outputs into physically stable grasps.

</details>


### [8] [One-Slide Calibration of Pathology Foundation Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08944)
*Ming Ren Hou,Tianyi Huang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: SlideRuler is a method that corrects scanner-induced shifts in pathology foundation model embeddings by using intra-slide regions as internal controls and a transfer map learned from paired rescans, enabling calibration from a single scan while keeping the foundation model fixed.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Scanner variation in digital pathology causes inconsistent representations of the same tissue across different imaging systems, limiting the reliable use of frozen pathology foundation models across scanners.

Method: SlideRuler uses regions within a slide as internal controls to estimate acquisition-induced shifts, learns a transfer map from paired rescans, and applies calibration from a single scan at inference while keeping the foundation model fixed. A source-anchored variant is also proposed.

Result: Learned transfer reduces mean target-to-source embedding distance by 16.3-38.5% relative to raw embeddings. Positive same-slide contribution is observed across all four evaluation settings, including scanner holdout. The source-anchored variant reduces source-feature displacement by 47.7-83.6% relative to learned transfer while retaining most alignment gain.

Conclusion: SlideRuler offers a path toward more consistent use of frozen pathology models across imaging systems by drawing calibration information from the slide itself, enabling reliable deployment across different scanners.

Abstract: Scanner variation changes how pathology foundation models represent the same tissue. We introduce SlideRuler, which uses regions within a slide as internal controls to estimate and correct acquisition-induced shifts in other regions. A transfer map learned from paired rescans enables calibration from a single scan at inference while keeping the foundation model fixed. Across two encoders and five SCORPION scanners, learned transfer reduces mean target-to-source embedding distance by 16.3-38.5% relative to raw embeddings. Comparisons with unrelated same-scanner controls reveal a positive same-slide contribution across all four evaluation settings, including scanner holdout. A source-anchored variant reduces source-feature displacement by 47.7-83.6% relative to learned transfer while retaining most of its alignment gain. By drawing calibration information from the slide itself, SlideRuler offers a path toward more consistent use of frozen pathology models across imaging systems.

</details>


### [9] [StyleFields: Multi-Scale AdaIN-Modulated Implicit SDFs for Coarse-to-Fine 3D Shape Reconstruction and Editing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09200)
*Ehsan Garaaghaji,Nicolas Talabot,Pascal Fua,Doruk Oner*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: StyleFields is a DeepSDF-based architecture for high-fidelity 3D reconstruction that enables controllable geometric style mixing, combining coarse structure of one object with fine-scale details of another using depth-aware modulation via multi-level Adaptive Instance Normalization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enable controllable geometric style mixing in 3D reconstruction without requiring part labels or adversarial training, and apply it to practical automotive aerodynamics optimization.

Method: Depth-aware modulation: inject latents via multi-level Adaptive Instance Normalization at several decoder depths, supervise matching auxiliary heads with a coarse-to-fine schedule while gradually growing network depth. Uses learned surrogate drag predictor as differentiable objective for optimization.

Result: StyleFields delivers faithful reconstructions, convincing cross-instance hybrids, and consistent gains in ablations over injection depth and supervision granularity. Enables targeted edits of global form or surface details by freezing complementary latent stream.

Conclusion: StyleFields offers a simple, effective recipe for controllable implicit reconstruction and downstream performance-driven design for automotive applications.

Abstract: We introduce StyleFields, a DeepSDF-based architecture for high-fidelity 3D reconstruction that enables controllable geometric style mixing: the coarse structure of one object can be combined with the fine-scale details of another. The core idea is depth-aware modulation: instead of a single global code, we inject latents via multi-level Adaptive Instance Normalization at several decoder depths, and supervise matching auxiliary heads with a coarse-to-fine schedule while gradually growing network depth. This aligns early layers with global shape and later layers with high-frequency detail, achieving content-style decoupling without part labels or adversarial training. StyleFields delivers faithful reconstructions, convincing cross-instance hybrids, and consistent gains in ablations over injection depth and supervision granularity. We further demonstrate a practical application in automotive aerodynamics: a learned surrogate drag predictor serves as a differentiable objective to optimize reconstructed cars, allowing targeted edits of global form or surface details by freezing the complementary latent stream. StyleFields offers a simple, effective recipe for controllable implicit reconstruction and downstream performance-driven design.

</details>


### [10] [RACER: Reflective Agent Coupling Query Interpretation and Tool-Based Retrieval for Frame Selection in Long Video Understanding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08954)
*Yiyang Huang,Yitian Zhang,Yizhou Wang,Jianglin Lu,Qihua Dong,Hailing Wang,Huimin Zeng,Mingyuan Zhang,Yun Fu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper proposes RACER, a training-free reflective agentic framework for long-video frame selection that decomposes the task into query interpretation (by a lightweight Vid-LLM) and evidence localization (by an embedding model), forming a reflection loop to iteratively improve frame selection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Frame selection for long videos is challenging because it requires retrieving relevant frames distributed across segments from a large candidate pool given complex queries. Existing approaches face two key gaps: Query Comprehension Gap in similarity-based methods and Interpretation-Selection Gap in judgment-based methods.

Method: RACER decomposes long-video frame selection into: 1) Query interpretation driven by a lightweight Vid-LLM that reformulates complex queries into sub-queries making implicit requirements explicit; 2) Evidence localization supported by an embedding model serving as retrieval tool; 3) A reflection loop where retrieved frames are fed back to the Vid-LLM for sub-query refinement, iteratively improving query interpretation and frame selection.

Result: Experiments across multiple benchmarks show that RACER consistently improves long video understanding. Notably, RACER achieves effective frame selection even with limited-capability components, demonstrating that agentic integration enables these components to enhance more capable Vid-LLMs.

Conclusion: The agentic integration of a lightweight Vid-LLM for query interpretation and an embedding model for retrieval effectively addresses the Query Comprehension Gap and Interpretation-Selection Gap, achieving improved long video understanding without requiring training, and showing that even limited-capability components can enhance more capable Vid-LLMs through proper integration.

Abstract: Video large language models (Vid-LLMs) excel at diverse video-language tasks by reasoning over selected frames. However, frame selection for long videos remains challenging, as it requires retrieving relevant frames distributed across segments from a large candidate pool given complex queries. This paper investigates dominant approaches to long-video frame selection from a task-decomposition perspective, identifying two key challenges: the Query Comprehension Gap in similarity-based methods and the Interpretation--Selection Gap in judgment-based methods. To address them, we propose RACER, a training-free reflective agentic framework that decomposes long-video frame selection into query interpretation driven by a lightweight Vid-LLM and evidence localization supported by an embedding model serving as a retrieval tool. Specifically, the Vid-LLM is responsible solely for reformulating the complex query into sub-queries that make implicit information requirements explicit, mitigating the Query Comprehension Gap. Meanwhile, the retrieval tool leverages these sub-queries to localize relevant evidence, relieving the Vid-LLM of direct frame selection and thus addressing the Interpretation--Selection Gap. Finally, the retrieved frames are fed back to the Vid-LLM for sub-query refinement, forming a reflection loop that iteratively improves query interpretation and frame selection. Experiments across multiple benchmarks show that RACER consistently improves long video understanding. Notably, RACER achieves effective frame selection even with limited-capability components, demonstrating that agentic integration enables these components to enhance more capable Vid-LLMs.

</details>


### [11] [KASALv2: Fully Automatic 3D Rotational Symmetry Classification and Axis Localization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09534)
*Mengxin Zhang,Yulin Wang,Chen Luo,Yongzhe Li,Yijun Zhou*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper presents a fully automatic framework for detecting and analyzing 3D rotational symmetry in objects, addressing the limitation of manual/semi-automatic symmetry annotation. The method identifies symmetry types, rotational orders, and localizes symmetry axes across all eight canonical 3D rotational symmetry types, with a texture-aware extension to handle appearance-induced order reductions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current symmetry annotations for 3D objects require manual or semi-automatic methods with predefined types/orders, limiting scalability. Rotational symmetry is an important prior in 6D pose estimation for improving accuracy and supporting symmetry-aware evaluation, but lack of automated annotation tools hinders this application.

Method: The framework consists of: (1) Localizing a dominant high-order symmetry axis through analysis; (2) Inferring rotational order via self-consistency analysis; (3) Reconstructing complete symmetry structure under hierarchy-guided formulation; (4) A texture-aware extension that models appearance-induced reductions in rotational order while preserving axis orientations.

Result: 94.75% accuracy on 438 symmetric objects in the Google Scanned Objects (GSO) dataset. When used as priors for training FoundationPose (a 6D pose estimation method), accuracy improved by up to 0.9% across five BOP (BOP Challenge) datasets.

Conclusion: The automatically estimated rotational symmetry priors successfully improve downstream 6D pose estimation performance, demonstrating the practical value of this automatic symmetry detection framework for computer vision applications.

Abstract: Rotational symmetry is an important prior in 6D pose estimation, improving pose accuracy and supporting symmetry-aware evaluation. However, current symmetry annotations for 3D objects remain largely manual or semi-automatic, often requiring predefined types or orders, which limits scalability. This work introduces a fully automatic, reference-free framework for symmetry-type classification, rotational-order identification, and full-axis localization across all eight canonical 3D rotational symmetry types. The method localizes a dominant high-order axis, infers its rotational order through self-consistency analysis, and reconstructs the complete symmetry structure under a hierarchy-guided formulation. A texture-aware extension further models appearance-induced reductions in rotational order while preserving axis orientations. Experiments on idealized and real-world datasets demonstrate strong accuracy and generalization, achieving 94.75% accuracy on 438 symmetric objects in GSO. Training FoundationPose with these priors improves accuracy by up to 0.9% across five BOP datasets, showing that automatically estimated rotational priors improve downstream 6D pose estimation. Code is available at https://github.com/WangYuLin-SEU/KASAL.

</details>


### [12] [S2Tok: Streaming 3D Gaussian Reconstruction with Persistent Spatial Tokens](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08978)
*Fang Li,Jiraphon Yenphraphai,Quentin Herau,Depu Meng,Yihan Hu,Tianshuo Xu,Narendra Ahuja,Wei Zhan*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: S2Tok is a feed-forward framework for streaming 3D reconstruction that maintains a size-adaptive, persistent scene state using latent spatial tokens. It distinguishes between updating existing representation and expanding to new content, using a spatially informed transformer for integration and a learned admission module for selective expansion.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Streaming 3D reconstruction requires a persistent scene state that can incorporate new evidence and remain renderable as observations arrive. While latent spatial tokens offer a promising representation, it was previously unclear how to maintain them online from uncalibrated image streams, where each observation may revisit known regions or reveal new content.

Method: S2Tok uses three key components: (1) A spatially informed transformer that integrates each incoming observation with persistent scene tokens, (2) A learned admission module that selectively expands the representation to limit redundant storage, (3) A hierarchical decoder and Gaussian head that converts the evolving state into non-pixel-aligned 3D Gaussians for novel-view rendering without caching previous frames.

Result: Experiments across four benchmarks demonstrate competitive streaming rendering quality with compact Gaussian representations.

Conclusion: Latent spatial tokens can serve as a persistent computational state for online 3D reconstruction, combining learned scene updates with explicit Gaussian rendering. The approach achieves competitive quality while maintaining a compact representation.

Abstract: Streaming 3D reconstruction requires more than a sequence of geometric predictions: it requires a persistent scene state that can incorporate new evidence and remain renderable as observations arrive. Latent spatial tokens offer a promising representation for this purpose, but constructing them from an image collection leaves open how to maintain them online, where each observation may both revisit known regions and reveal new content. We introduce S2Tok, a feed-forward framework that maintains a size-adaptive, persistent scene state from uncalibrated image streams. Its central idea is to distinguish updates to the existing representation from selective expansion. A spatially informed transformer integrates each incoming observation with the persistent scene tokens, while a learned admission module selectively expands the representation to limit redundant storage. A hierarchical decoder and Gaussian head convert the evolving state into non-pixel-aligned 3D Gaussians, enabling novel-view rendering without caching previous frames. Experiments across four benchmarks demonstrate competitive streaming rendering quality with compact Gaussian representations. These results support latent spatial tokens as a persistent computational state for online 3D reconstruction, combining learned scene updates with explicit Gaussian rendering.

</details>


### [13] [Zero-Shot Brain MRI Inpainting with 2.5D Unconditional Flow Priors](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08983)
*Arnela Hadzic,Franz Thaler,Simon Johannes Joham,Martin Urschler*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A zero-shot brain MRI inpainting framework using 2.5D unconditional flow priors that processes axial slice triplets autoregressively to synthesize healthy tissue in pathological regions while maintaining volumetric consistency across all planes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard 3D inpainting approaches are computationally prohibitive, while efficient 2D slice-wise methods suffer from severe inter-slice discontinuities. Traditional models also require conditional training with task-specific learning of masked inputs.

Method: A 2.5D flow matching model learns the joint distribution of adjacent axial slice triplets, modeling healthy brain anatomy while excluding pathological regions from the loss. At inference, the model processes input triplets autoregressively along the depth axis using the Restora-Flow solver to constrain the unconditional prior with input masks. An ensemble of multiple stochastic reconstructions is averaged for the final prediction.

Result: The method achieves SSIM of 0.816 ± 0.112, MSE of 0.007 ± 0.005, and PSNR of 22.923 ± 4.343 on the BraTS 2026 Inpainting Challenge validation set, resolving structural discontinuities of 2D baselines while maintaining volumetric consistency.

Conclusion: The 2.5D zero-shot approach effectively balances computational efficiency with volumetric consistency, synthesizing plausible healthy tissue across axial, sagittal, and coronal planes without requiring task-specific training.

Abstract: Generative inpainting of brain MRI volumes is essential for synthesizing healthy tissue in pathological regions, improving the accuracy and reliability of automated downstream brain analysis applications such as image registration, brain extraction, and segmentation. However, standard 3D approaches are computationally prohibitive, while efficient 2D slice-wise methods suffer from severe inter-slice discontinuities. Furthermore, traditional models rely on conditional training, requiring task-specific learning of masked inputs. We propose a zero-shot brain MRI inpainting framework utilizing 2.5D unconditional flow priors to capture spatial context along the superior-inferior axis without the overhead of full 3D convolutions. During training, our flow matching model learns the joint distribution of adjacent axial slice triplets, modeling the manifold of healthy brain anatomy while explicitly excluding pathological regions from the loss function. At inference, the model processes the input triplets autoregressively along the depth axis. We employ the Restora-Flow solver to constrain the unconditional prior using the input mask, achieving accurate zero-shot inpainting. Evaluations show our 2.5D strategy resolves the structural discontinuities of 2D baselines, synthesizing plausible healthy tissue while maintaining volumetric consistency across the axial, sagittal, and coronal planes. As a final step, we generate and average an ensemble of multiple stochastic reconstructions to form the final prediction. Quantitative results benchmarked on the official BraTS 2026 Inpainting Challenge validation set demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed approach, yielding an SSIM of 0.816 $\pm$ 0.112, MSE of 0.007 $\pm$ 0.005, and PSNR of 22.923 $\pm$ 4.343. Code is available at https://github.com/imigraz/brats2026-inpainting.

</details>


### [14] [Personalize at Test Time: Learning User Preferences for Image Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09015)
*Jiamu Bai,Jiaming Hu,Yanhong Wu,Zellux Wang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper proposes a method to learn personalized reward models for diffusion models directly from users' historical image preference pairs. The approach uses an autoencoder to compress visual attributes into 50 preference dimensions, then represents each user's preferences as a linear combination of these dimension scores, with user-specific weights estimated via the Bradley-Terry model. This enables data-efficient personalization from sparse feedback while keeping the diffusion model frozen during inference.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Aligning diffusion model outputs with individual user preferences is challenging due to the difficulty of accurately modeling diverse user preferences from limited feedback. Existing approaches rely on labor-intensive manual annotations or computationally expensive vision-language models, limiting scalability.

Method: 1) Use an autoencoder to compress hundreds of visual attributes into 50 attribute-anchored preference dimensions; 2) Train an evaluator to score images along these dimensions; 3) Represent each user's preferences as a linear combination of the shared dimension scores; 4) Estimate user-specific weights by maximizing likelihood of observed pairwise preferences under the Bradley-Terry model; 5) Use learned personalized rewards to guide image generation at inference time while keeping the diffusion model frozen.

Result: The approach achieves approximately 77% held-out pairwise preference prediction accuracy and improves the alignment of generated images with individual user preferences on real-user preference data.

Conclusion: The proposed formulation reduces per-user adaptation to optimizing a low-dimensional weight vector, enabling data-efficient personalization from sparse feedback. This approach successfully personalizes diffusion model outputs without requiring manual annotations or heavy computational costs.

Abstract: Diffusion models can generate high-quality images, yet aligning their outputs with individual user preferences remains challenging. A key bottleneck is accurately modeling diverse user preferences from limited feedback. Existing approaches often rely on labor-intensive manual preference annotations or vision-language models (VLM) to extract preference information from user interaction histories, introducing substantial annotation or computational costs that limit scalability. We propose an approach that learns personalized reward models directly from users' historical image preference pairs. First, we use an autoencoder to compress hundreds of visual attributes into 50 attribute-anchored preference dimensions and train an evaluator to score images along these dimensions. We then represent each user's preferences as a linear combination of the shared dimension scores, estimating the user-specific weights by maximizing the likelihood of their observed pairwise preferences under the Bradley-Terry model. This formulation reduces per-user adaptation to optimizing a low-dimensional weight vector, simplifying optimization and enabling data-efficient personalization from sparse feedback. The learned personalized rewards guide image generation at inference time while keeping the diffusion model frozen. Experiments on real-user preference data show that our approach achieves approximately 77% held-out pairwise preference prediction accuracy and improves the alignment of generated images with individual user preferences.

</details>


### [15] [Beyond Explanation: Debugging Medical Imaging Models via Concept Intervention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09031)
*Samrajya Thapa,Daniel J. Quest,Timothy L. Kline,Carrie L. Langstraat,Emanuel C. Trabuco,Wei Le*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A plug-and-play framework for concept-based interpretation and refinement of medical imaging models, using BioMedCLIP-aligned single-modality encoders to build Concept Bottleneck Models (CBMs) that enable concept-level interventions for model diagnosis and improvement.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Medical imaging models operate as black boxes, limiting interpretability and systematic debugging. There's a need for interpretable frameworks that can isolate causal from spurious correlations, validate insights with domain experts, and enable targeted model refinement.

Method: Align a single-modality encoder to BioMedCLIP to construct a Concept Bottleneck Model (CBM). The framework enables: (1) concept-level interventions to isolate causal vs. spuriously correlated concepts, (2) domain expert validation of insights, and (3) counterfactual sample generation for guided fine-tuning. Evaluation on Mayo Clinic ultrasound dataset and CheXpert 5x200 chest X-ray dataset.

Result: Concept intervention enables reliable model diagnosis while maintaining or occasionally improving predictive performance via guided fine-tuning.

Conclusion: The framework provides practical value for controlled, interpretable refinement of clinical deep learning models, bridging the gap between black-box performance and interpretable healthcare AI.

Abstract: Medical imaging models often operate as black boxes, limiting interpretability and systematic debugging. We introduce an easy-to-use, plug-and-play framework for concept-based interpretation and model refinement. By aligning a single-modality encoder to BioMedCLIP, we construct a Concept Bottleneck Model (CBM) that enables concept-level interventions. These interventions allow us to isolate causal versus spuriously correlated concepts, validate insights with domain experts, and generate counterfactual samples for targeted fine-tuning. We evaluate our framework on a Mayo Clinic ultrasound dataset and the CheXpert 5x200 chest X-ray dataset. Results demonstrate that concept intervention enables reliable model diagnosis while maintaining, and occasionally improving predictive performance via guided fine-tuning. Our findings highlight the practical value of this framework for controlled, interpretable refinement of clinical deep learning models.

</details>


### [16] [Shape-Bayes: Bayesian Inference of Structured Shapes under Visual Ambiguity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09032)
*Mani Kumar Tellamekala,Tosh Brown,Michel Valstar*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Shape-Bayes is a probabilistic framework for human face shape regression that combines uncertainty-aware visual perception with Bayesian shape reasoning. It dynamically weights visual evidence against geometric priors to infer structurally valid shape posteriors, addressing the brittleness of deterministic regression under ambiguous or incomplete visual evidence.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deterministic regression for shape inference is brittle when visual evidence is ambiguous or incomplete. Under severe occlusions, deterministic models exhibit structural collapse, predicting incoherent shapes or reverting to generic averages. This necessitates a probabilistic approach that can handle uncertainty while maintaining structural integrity.

Method: Shape-Bayes comprises three components: (1) a base model predicting noisy landmarks alongside distilled aleatoric uncertainties; (2) a lightweight Transformer encoding observations into an adaptive prior over a PCA shape manifold; (3) a differentiable Bayesian solver computing closed-form posteriors by balancing noisy predictions against this prior.

Result: Shape-Bayes achieves an absolute improvement of up to ~34% IDR over state-of-the-art deterministic models, reduces relative error by up to 12.5%, and yields highly calibrated uncertainty bounds, establishing a new state-of-the-art for robust 2D face shape regression under severe occlusion.

Conclusion: By guaranteeing complete structural integrity through Bayesian inference, Shape-Bayes successfully addresses the limitations of deterministic regression. The framework provides robust shape inference even under severe occlusions while producing well-calibrated uncertainty estimates.

Abstract: Perceiving structured shapes, such as human faces, from pixels is an inherently ambiguous task in real-world conditions. Yet, shape inference is largely posed as a deterministic regression task predicting fixed spatial coordinates. We find that deterministic regression is brittle when visual evidence is ambiguous or incomplete; under severe occlusions deterministic models exhibit structural collapse, predicting incoherent shapes or reverting to generic averages. To address this, we introduce Shape-Bayes, a probabilistic framework that couples uncertainty-aware visual perception with Bayesian shape reasoning. Rather than forcing point estimates, Shape-Bayes dynamically weights visual evidence against geometric priors to infer a structurally valid shape posterior. Demonstrated on human face shape regression, a rigorous testbed featuring complex non-rigid deformations and strict anatomical constraints, Shape-Bayes comprises: (1) a base model predicting noisy landmarks alongside distilled aleatoric uncertainties; (2) a lightweight Transformer encoding these observations into an adaptive prior over a PCA shape manifold; and (3) a differentiable Bayesian solver computing closed-form posteriors by balancing the noisy predictions against this prior. By guaranteeing complete structural integrity, Shape-Bayes achieves an absolute improvement of up to ~34% IDR over state-of-the-art deterministic models. Simultaneously, it yields highly calibrated uncertainty bounds and reduces relative error by up to 12.5%, establishing a new state-of-the-art for robust 2D face shape regression under severe occlusion. The project page is at https://shape-bayes.github.io.

</details>


### [17] [GUARD: Geometric Uncertainty-Aware Point Cloud Denoising and Segmentation for Robotic Hard Disk Drive Disassembly](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09068)
*Zuoxu Wang,Xiao Liang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: GUARD is a geometric uncertainty-aware framework for robotic disassembly that distinguishes reliable component geometry from scanning artifacts in point clouds. It combines a multi-scale geometric transformer with a multi-bandwidth random Fourier feature Gaussian Process to estimate per-point geometric uncertainty, improving HDD point cloud segmentation mIoU from 0.7739 to 0.8318.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reliable robotic disassembly requires distinguishing genuine component geometry from scanning/reconstruction artifacts. Structured ghost artifacts in HDD point clouds can resemble valid components locally but remain inconsistent with overall geometry, causing semantic predictions to receive plausible labels despite unreliable underlying geometry. Semantic prediction confidence alone cannot establish geometric reliability.

Method: GUARD performs point filtering and segmentation within a single forward pass by modeling geometric representation reliability. It combines: (1) multi-scale geometric transformer for feature extraction, (2) multi-bandwidth random Fourier feature Gaussian Process for per-point geometric uncertainty estimation, and (3) predictive entropy to suppress unreliable measurements while preserving informative structures.

Result: On 2,745 real HDD point clouds, GUARD improves PointNet++ segmentation mIoU from 0.7739 to 0.8318. On manually annotated ScanNet samples, geometric uncertainty achieves corrupted-point detection F1 score of 0.7931, compared with 0.2212 for predictive entropy. Additional experiments on ShapeNetPart and ScanNet demonstrate robustness across corruption types, point-cloud domains, and segmentation backbones.

Conclusion: The work demonstrates the value of distinguishing geometric reliability from semantic confidence in 3D point cloud analysis. It reveals a tradeoff between artifact suppression and preservation of informative structures. GUARD contributes a reliability-aware approach to interpreting imperfect 3D measurements for component identification in robotic handling applications.

Abstract: Reliable robotic disassembly requires part-level representations that distinguish genuine component geometry from scanning and reconstruction artifacts. In point clouds of hard disk drives (HDDs), structured ghost artifacts can resemble valid components locally while remaining inconsistent with the overall geometry, allowing erroneous measurements to receive plausible semantic labels. This creates an engineering information problem: semantic prediction confidence alone does not establish whether the underlying geometry is reliable. We propose \textbf{GUARD}, a geometric uncertainty-aware framework that performs point filtering and segmentation within a single forward pass by modeling the reliability of learned geometric representations. GUARD combines a multi-scale geometric transformer with a multi-bandwidth random Fourier feature Gaussian Process to estimate per-point geometric uncertainty, complemented by predictive entropy to suppress unreliable measurements while preserving informative structures. Evaluation on 2,745 real HDD point clouds shows that GUARD improves PointNet++ segmentation mean intersection over union from 0.7739 to 0.8318. Additional experiments on ShapeNetPart and ScanNet examine robustness across corruption types, point-cloud domains, and segmentation backbones. On manually annotated ScanNet samples, geometric uncertainty achieves a corrupted-point detection F1 score of 0.7931, compared with 0.2212 for predictive entropy. The results demonstrate the value of distinguishing geometric reliability from semantic confidence and reveal a tradeoff between artifact suppression and preservation of informative structures. GUARD contributes a reliability-aware approach to interpreting imperfect 3D measurements for component identification and subsequent robotic handling. Project website: https://001-wang.github.io/GUARD_Point_denoiser/.

</details>


### [18] [OverLay++: Dense-Overlap Layout-to-Image Generation Dataset](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09071)
*Shivansh Aggarwal,Shresth Grover,Divyansh Srivastava,Haiyang Xu,Bingnan Li,Xiang Zhang,Ethan J. Armand,Chuan Li,Jianwen Xie,Zhuowen Tu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: OverLay++ is a large-scale Layout-to-Image dataset with ~500K images containing dense, overlapping object annotations and rich per-object captions. It addresses the bottleneck that existing datasets lack complex object interactions, which limits current methods' ability to handle scenes with many overlapping and interacting objects.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing Layout-to-Image methods struggle with complex scenes containing many overlapping and interacting objects. The authors identify training data as the key bottleneck: current datasets lack examples with dense, complex object interactions needed to train robust models.

Method: The dataset generation pipeline is designed to produce dense, overlapping object annotations with rich per-object captions. The dataset contains approximately 500K images with an average of 6.6 objects per image, and includes detailed captions for each object that are over six times longer than in existing datasets.

Result: OverLay++ achieves 1.67 times higher annotation density than existing datasets and provides object captions over six times longer. When used for training, state-of-the-art Layout-to-Image methods show consistent improvement across multiple benchmarks and faster convergence, demonstrating the importance of dense, overlap-aware, and caption-rich supervision.

Conclusion: Dense, overlapping, and caption-rich supervision is crucial for controllable image generation. The OverLay++ dataset addresses a critical gap in training data for Layout-to-Image tasks, enabling models to better handle complex real-world scenes with multiple interacting objects.

Abstract: Layout-to-Image generation has made substantial progress in spatial and object-level control. However, existing methods still struggle with complex scenes containing many overlapping and interacting objects. We argue that training data is a particular bottleneck: existing datasets lack examples with dense, complex object interactions. To address this gap, we introduce OverLay++, a large-scale Layout-to-Image dataset with structurally complex scenes. OverLay++ contains approximately 500K images with an average of 6.6 objects per image, exceeding existing datasets by 1.67 times in annotation density. Beyond annotation density, OverLay++ provides rich semantic detail with object captions over six times longer than in current datasets. Our dataset generation pipeline is simple and produces dense, overlapping object annotations with rich per-object captions. Across multiple benchmarks, state-of-the-art Layout-to-Image methods trained on the OverLay++ dataset show consistent improvement and faster convergence, demonstrating the importance of dense, overlap-aware, and caption-rich supervision for controllable image generation.

</details>


### [19] [DISRQAD: Diffusion Image Super-Resolution Quality Assessment Dataset and Benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09077)
*Nikita Kukuzei,Artem Borisov,Evgeney Bogatyrev,Khaled Abud,Egor Chistov,Dmitriy Vatolin*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Summary generation failed


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Motivation analysis unavailable

Method: Method extraction failed

Result: Result analysis unavailable

Conclusion: Conclusion extraction failed

Abstract: Diffusion-based image super-resolution (SR) can create visually plausible detail that is not supported by the low-resolution input. We introduce DISRQAD, a subjective-quality dataset and diagnostic benchmark for this setting. It contains mean opinion scores (MOS) for 14,000 SR outputs from ten diffusion and four non-diffusion methods, spanning four low-resolution degradation conditions and x2/x4 upscaling. We evaluate 51 standard full-reference and no-reference metric configurations and 11 adapted variants. Agreement with MOS is substantially weaker on diffusion outputs: the strongest standard no-reference baseline reaches 0.431 SRCC on diffusion SR versus 0.813 on non-diffusion SR. As a case study in benchmark use, a pruned and distilled Q-ReAlign-mini student reaches 0.496 SRCC on diffusion SR. DISRQAD measures perceived output quality, not faithfulness to the input; it enables analysis of metric behavior across generator families and input conditions. Our findings reveal a substantial gap in the assessment of diffusion-based SR and provide a basis for developing quality models sensitive to diffusion-specific artifacts.
