### [20] [Anaximander: Interactively Running Geospatial Deep Learning Models on Any Compute Backend](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09085)
*Satej S. Soman,Akram Zaytar,Girmaw A. Tadesse,Gilles Q. Hacheme,Muhammad S. Danish,Inbal Becker-Reshef,Rahul Dodhia,Juan Lavista Ferres*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Anaximander is an open-source system that enables seamless deployment and comparison of deep learning models on satellite imagery within GIS environments, supporting multiple model sources and compute backends through a unified QGIS plugin interface.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Remote sensing practitioners face high friction when applying deep learning models to satellite imagery in GIS, due to incompatible model formats and varying compute environments (local workstations to cloud services). Each evaluation requires custom deployment, tiling, and georeferencing code, discouraging systematic model comparison despite its operational importance for tasks like field delineation, crop monitoring, and disaster response.

Method: Anaximander provides an inference server backend that loads models from multiple sources and serves them on any accessible compute backend with session management and model caching. It pairs with a QGIS plugin that handles tiling, result reassembly, georeferencing, and real-time per-tile status visualization. An additional UI path injects layer legends as prompts into vision-language models.

Result: The system was demonstrated in a code-free side-by-side comparison of three heterogeneous models on an agricultural field delineation task: gpt-image-1 via cloud API, Segment Anything Model 3 (SAM3) on a remote GPU, and DelineateAnything on a local CPU.

Conclusion: Anaximander enables systematic comparison of diverse deep learning models across different compute environments without custom coding, addressing a critical gap in remote sensing workflows. The inference backend and protocol are open-source.

Abstract: Applying deep learning models to satellite imagery from within geographic information systems (GIS) remains high-friction for remote sensing practitioners. Models arrive in incompatible formats and target different compute environments, from local workstations to serverless cloud services. As a result, every evaluation demands custom deployment, tiling, and georeferencing code before a single prediction reaches the analyst's map. This friction discourages systematic comparison in a domain where model choice directly affects operational outcomes such as field delineation, crop monitoring, and disaster response. We present Anaximander, an open-source system that unifies model source and compute location choice behind one interactive interface. The system's backend is an inference server that loads models from multiple commonly-used sources and serves them on any accessible compute backend. The server provides session management and model caching, and streams results back per tile. The backend is paired with a QGIS plugin that drives tiling, result reassembly, georeferencing, and real-time per-tile status visualization. An additional user-interface path injects layer legends as prompts into vision-language models. We demonstrate the system in a code-free side-by-side comparison of three heterogeneous models on an agricultural field delineation task: gpt-image-1 via a cloud API, Segment Anything Model 3 (SAM3) on a remote GPU, and DelineateAnything on a local CPU. The inference backend and protocol are open-source and available at https://github.com/microsoft/nxmndr.

</details>


### [21] [SPLATIFY: Reproduce, Discover, Innovate! From Papers and Ideas to Trainable 3DGS Code](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09116)
*Seemandhar Jain,Keshav Gupta,Manmohan Chandraker*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: SPLATIFY is a multi-agent framework that automates the conversion of 3D Gaussian Splatting papers into trainable gsplat-based implementations, reducing development time from weeks to minutes and achieving up to 2.4 dB PSNR improvement through compositional discovery.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The rapid growth of 3DGS research demands significant reimplementation effort before building on existing work, and generic paper-to-code methods fail for this specialized domain.

Method: Five innovations: (1) Context-free grammar with modular templates for gsplat, (2) Fork-aware citation recovery + Graph-of-Thought synthesis + RAG-guided retrieval + visual feedback, (3) Knowledge-driven compositional improvement, (4) Interdisciplinary method discovery from physical priors, (5) SPLATIFY-Bench evaluation across 30 papers.

Result: Matches expert implementations on papers without public code, reduces development time from weeks to minutes, improves PSNR by up to 2.4 dB, and demonstrates novel methods for volumetric nebula rendering and scientific domains.

Conclusion: SPLATIFY successfully automates 3DGS paper implementation through architectural constraints and compositional reasoning, enabling both faithful reproduction and novel scientific discoveries.

Abstract: The rapid growth of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) research demands significant effort to reimplement papers before building on them. We introduce SPLATIFY, a multi-agent framework that converts 3DGS papers into trainable gsplat-based implementations, where generic paper-to-code methods and frontier models fail. SPLATIFY achieves this through five innovations: (1) A context-free grammar for gsplat over a modular method template with extension points for losses, densification, rendering, and optimization, constraining synthesis so generated code satisfies gsplat's architectural invariants by construction. (2) Architectural elements for faithful reproduction: fork-aware citation recovery retrieving component-level code at function-level granularity, Graph-of-Thought synthesis in topological dependency order, RAG-guided in-context example selection from over 20 verified implementations, and visual feedback combining PSNR-guided regeneration, Gaussian-level structural checks, and VLM-driven patching. (3) Knowledge-driven compositional improvement that autonomously finds weaknesses and composes complementary regularizers, losses, and densification strategies to improve upon original results. (4) Interdisciplinary method discovery where agents retrieve physical priors from outside the 3DGS literature and compose them with rendering knowledge to produce methods for previously unaddressed scene types. (5) SPLATIFY-Bench, an evaluation framework across 30 diverse 3DGS papers. On papers without public code, SPLATIFY matches expert implementations while reducing development time from weeks to minutes, and through compositional discovery further improves PSNR by up to 2.4 dB. We additionally demonstrate novel methods for volumetric nebula rendering and other scientific domains, synthesized entirely by SPLATIFY.

</details>


### [22] [TopoCurve: Geometry-Aware Topology Reasoning via Bézier Curves in Autonomous Driving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09118)
*Mihai Bogdan Deaconu,Laura Dioşan*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: TopoCurve is a geometry-driven architecture for 3D topology reasoning that models lanes as endpoint-fixed cubic Bézier curves, enabling continuous geometry with exact endpoints and analytically defined directionality. It achieves 50.6 OLS on OpenLane-V2, establishing new state-of-the-art among end-to-end camera-only methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current methods model lanes as discrete polylines, lacking smoothness, analytical tangent directions, and global spatial support for attention, while providing sparse topology supervision. This work aims to address these limitations through a structured parametric lane representation.

Method: TopoCurve models lanes as endpoint-fixed cubic Bézier curves enabling continuous geometry. The method encodes endpoint distance and tangent alignment with multi-scale Fourier features injected into the topology head. Sampled curve points serve as geometry-aligned references for deformable cross-attention spanning the full lane. Parallel curve-anchored attention branches provide diverse predictions for one-to-many topology supervision, forming a tightly coupled cascade where representation enables geometric reasoning, guides feature aggregation, and supports denser supervision.

Result: TopoCurve achieves 50.6 OLS on the OpenLane-V2 benchmark without any post-processing, establishing a new state-of-the-art among end-to-end camera-only methods, and outperforms all existing approaches on endpoint detection (56.8 vs. 52.6 on DET_p).

Conclusion: The parametric curve representation successfully enables geometric reasoning, guides feature aggregation, and supports denser supervision, demonstrating that grounding topology reasoning in structured parametric lane representation significantly improves performance over discrete polyline-based methods.

Abstract: Topology reasoning jointly detects 3D lanes and traffic elements from multi-view images and infers their structural connectivity. Current methods model lanes as discrete polylines, lacking smoothness, analytical tangent directions, and global spatial support for attention, while providing sparse topology supervision. We propose TopoCurve, a geometry-driven architecture for 3D topology reasoning grounded in a structured parametric lane representation. Lanes are modeled as endpoint-fixed cubic Bézier curves, enabling continuous geometry with exact endpoints and analytically defined directionality. We exploit this shared curve geometry across the entire pipeline. Endpoint distance and tangent alignment are encoded with multi-scale Fourier features and injected into the topology head. Sampled curve points serve as geometry-aligned references for deformable cross-attention spanning the full lane. Parallel curve-anchored attention branches provide diverse predictions for one-to-many topology supervision. These components form a tightly coupled cascade where representation enables geometric reasoning, guides feature aggregation, and supports denser supervision. TopoCurve achieves 50.6 OLS on the OpenLane-V2 benchmark without any post-processing, establishing a new state-of-the-art among end-to-end camera-only methods, and outperforms all existing approaches on endpoint detection (56.8 vs. 52.6 on DET_p).

</details>


### [23] [Depth-to-RGB: Repurposing a Frozen Depth Estimator for Geometry-Guided Compositing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09125)
*Sanghyun Jo,Chae Yeon Lim,Donghwan Lee,Sihyun Kim,Soo Ye Kim,Kyungsu Kim*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: The D2R (Depth-to-RGB) framework addresses reference-based object compositing by predicting composite depth for scenes not observed in RGB inputs. It uses reference-conditioned corrections to a frozen depth estimator, with encoder features of paired completed scenes as supervision targets. The method significantly outperforms 15 baselines across multiple metrics, including a 43.7% reduction in AbsRel and 55% reduction in CLIP distance on category-disjoint and unpaired benchmarks respectively.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reference-based object compositing inserts/replaces objects using background, reference image, and 2D mask. However, these inputs leave the completed scene's geometry implicit, which can distort object structure or alter the surroundings. This work aims to predict composite depth for unobserved scenes to improve geometric consistency.

Method: The D2R framework predicts composite depth by learning reference-conditioned corrections to a frozen depth estimator using encoder features of paired completed scenes as targets. The unchanged decoder maps corrected representations to scene depth, while a separately trained renderer holds depth fixed during RGB synthesis. The key innovation is encoder-feature supervision rather than decoded-depth supervision.

Result: Encoder-feature supervision reduces OOD Stage-1 AbsRel by 31.4% relative to decoded-depth supervision. D2R leads 12 open-source and 3 closed-source baselines in estimator-derived geometry and photometric quality. On category-disjoint data, D2R reduces AbsRel by 43.7% and improves PSNR by 2.4 dB. Across three unpaired benchmarks, D2R leads identity metrics and reduces mean CLIP reference cosine distance by 55% relative to the strongest baseline.

Conclusion: The D2R framework successfully addresses depth prediction in reference-based object compositing through reference-conditioned corrections and encoder-feature supervision. It demonstrates superior generalization beyond training categories and strong performance across paired and unpaired benchmarks, establishing new state-of-the-art results across 15 baselines.

Abstract: Reference-based object compositing inserts or replaces an object using a background image, a reference image, and a 2D compositing mask. These inputs guide appearance and placement but leave the completed scene's geometry implicit, which can distort object structure or alter the surroundings. Our Depth-to-RGB (D2R) framework predicts composite depth for a scene not yet observed in the RGB inputs. It learns reference-conditioned corrections to a frozen depth estimator using encoder features of paired completed scenes as targets. The unchanged decoder maps the corrected representation to the intended scene's depth, which a separately trained renderer holds fixed during RGB synthesis. Under matched architecture and training, encoder-feature supervision reduces OOD Stage-1 AbsRel by 31.4% relative to decoded-depth supervision. We also introduce AnyInsertion++ with paired in-distribution and category-disjoint splits to evaluate generalization beyond compositing training categories. The complete D2R system leads 12 open-source and 3 closed-source baselines in estimator-derived geometry and photometric quality on both paired splits. On category-disjoint data, D2R reduces AbsRel by 43.7% and improves PSNR by 2.4 dB over the matched RGB baseline. Across three unpaired benchmarks, D2R leads both identity metrics and reduces mean CLIP reference cosine distance by 55% relative to the strongest baseline. Project page: https://shjo-april.github.io/Depth2RGB/

</details>


### [24] [RDGSplat: Render-Dedicated Geometry for Novel View Synthesis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09173)
*Zhijie Zheng,Xinhao Xiang,Jiawei Zhang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: RDGSplat is a framework that improves novel view synthesis in 3D foundation models by decoding a second rendering-dedicated geometry from a frozen model, without altering the original metric predictions. It uses duplicated decoders optimized under photometric supervision and a pose-conditioned adapter.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current 3D foundation models render views that fall short of the geometry they recover. Existing methods fix this by updating backbone weights, which discards the metric predictions the model was built for and must be repeated for every new backbone.

Method: 1) Render-Dedicated Geometry Decoding: Duplicates pretrained decoders and optimizes them under photometric supervision alone. 2) Target-Pose Conditioned Adapter: Reformulates the representation those decoders read, conditioned on target camera pose rather than target image.

Result: Improves novel view synthesis across three feed-forward backbones on four benchmarks. On RE10K, WM2.0 increases from 20.918 to 24.266 dB while training 205.5M added parameters against a frozen 1.4B backbone, with depth and pose predictions unchanged.

Conclusion: RDGSplat successfully improves rendering quality while preserving the original metric predictions by using a dedicated rendering geometry decoded from a frozen 3D foundation model.

Abstract: 3D foundation models enable efficient novel view synthesis by carrying a Gaussian head on the representation they already use for reconstruction. However, the views they render fall short of the geometry they recover, because that geometry is estimated under a metric objective and never scored on how it renders. Recent methods alleviate this by updating the backbone weights, but they thereby discard the metric predictions the model was built for and must be repeated for every new backbone. To this end, we propose RDGSplat, a framework that decodes a second geometry dedicated to rendering from a frozen 3D foundation model, leaving its metric predictions intact. In particular, we devise Render-Dedicated Geometry Decoding, which duplicates the pretrained decoders and optimizes the duplicates under photometric supervision alone. Then, a Target-Pose Conditioned Adapter is introduced to reformulate the representation those decoders read, conditioned on the target camera pose rather than the target image. Extensive experiments show that RDGSplat improves novel view synthesis across three feed-forward backbones on four benchmarks, with every pretrained weight frozen. On RE10K, it raises WM2.0 from 20.918 to 24.266\,dB while training 205.5\,M added parameters against a frozen 1.4\,B backbone, and the depth and pose the same model predicts are unchanged.

</details>


### [25] [One Frame, Full Heartbeat: ECG-Free 4D Cardiac Cine MRI Synthesis via Radial-Decomposed Flow Matching](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09185)
*Shiyi Wang,Ruochen Sun,Xiang Li,Peirong Liu,Fangxu Xing*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: PhaseFlow3D is a deep learning framework that synthesizes a complete 4D cine cardiac MRI sequence from a single end-diastolic 3D volume without ECG gating. It uses a phase-conditioned rectified flow model with physics-informed radial contraction decomposition to generate cardiac motion trajectories.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard cine CMR acquisition requires ECG gating and repeated breath holds, which are challenging for many patients. Current visual synthesis methods lack accuracy for quantitative clinical metrics like ejection fraction (EF) and ventricular volumes. The paper aims to generate temporally consistent, anatomically accurate 4D cardiac sequences from a single 3D snapshot.

Method: PhaseFlow3D represents the cardiac cycle as a piecewise linear phase anchored at end-diastolic (ED) and end-systolic (ES) time points. It uses: (1) A phase-conditioned rectified flow model in latent space to generate motion trajectories, (2) Radial Contraction Decomposition that combines physics-informed radial contraction with an image-conditioned residual for rotation/out-of-plane motion, and (3) Direct warping of the ED volume to generate each frame, bypassing VAE decoding.

Result: On the combined ACDC and M&Ms benchmark, PhaseFlow3D achieves: lowest EF mean absolute error, the only positive left-ventricular volume-curve R², and best distributional quality. Ablations confirm each component's contribution. Downstream evaluations show utility for segmentation, pathology classification, label propagation, and myocardial strain analysis.

Conclusion: PhaseFlow3D successfully synthesizes clinically accurate 4D cardiac sequences from a single 3D volume without ECG. It outperforms existing methods on EF accuracy and volume curve quality, while enabling downstream clinical applications including segmentation, classification, and strain analysis.

Abstract: Cine cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) captures the cardiac cycle as a four-dimensional (4D) sequence, but standard acquisition requires electrocardiogram (ECG) gating and repeated breath holds. Visual realism alone does not establish accurate patient-specific ejection fraction (EF) or ventricular volumes. We present PhaseFlow3D, a generative framework that synthesizes a complete 4D cine sequence from a single end-diastolic (ED) three-dimensional (3D) volume without ECG. To capture asymmetric systolic and diastolic dynamics, it represents the cardiac cycle as a piecewise linear phase anchored at ED and end-systolic (ES) time points. At inference, a population-level canonical template supplies this phase without patient-specific temporal information. A phase-conditioned rectified flow model generates a cardiac motion trajectory in latent space. Radial Contraction Decomposition converts each latent state into a 3D displacement field, combining a physics-informed radial component for centripetal myocardial contraction with an image-conditioned residual for rotation and out-of-plane motion. Each frame is generated by directly warping the ED volume, bypassing variational autoencoder decoding. On the combined ACDC and M&Ms benchmark, PhaseFlow3D achieves the lowest EF mean absolute error, the only positive left-ventricular volume-curve $R^2$, and the best distributional quality among compared methods. Ablations confirm each component's contribution. Downstream evaluations demonstrate the utility of the synthesized sequences and displacement fields for segmentation, pathology classification, label propagation, and myocardial strain analysis.

</details>


### [26] [R-CNN-Based Chess Position Recognition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09191)
*Paras Govind,Ognjen Arandjelović*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper presents an R-CNN-based framework for recognizing chess game positions from a single 3D board image. The method combines piece recognition (using modified Faster R-CNN) with board geometry estimation (using Mask R-CNN keypoint detection) to reconstruct the complete chess position.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Performing chess position recognition from a single 3D board image is challenging because it requires predicting the board's position and orientation relative to the camera, square occupancy, and piece types (including color) simultaneously.

Method: The framework uses two independent components: (1) For piece recognition - adapt Faster R-CNN with class-weighted objective and deeper classification head, operating directly on input images with alternative hypotheses refined using constraints on piece counts and square occupancy. (2) For board detection - introduce octagonal arrangement of 8 boundary keypoints predicted using Mask R-CNN keypoint head, providing redundant correspondences for homography estimation and encoding board orientation.

Result: On synthetic dataset: piece detection mAP increased from 61.59% to 90.14% with modifications; 97.11% of predicted board keypoints within 1% of image diagonal; using ground-truth piece boxes with predicted homographies gives correct square assignments for every test position; complete framework recovers 76.61% of test positions exactly and 96.49% with at most one incorrect square.

Conclusion: The proposed R-CNN-based framework with independent piece recognition and board geometry estimation components effectively recognizes chess positions from single 3D images, achieving high accuracy in position recovery when combining both components.

Abstract: Performing chess game position recognition solely from a single image of a three-dimensional board requires predicting the position and orientation of the board relative to the camera, the occupancy of squares and the piece type, which includes its colour. We propose an R-CNN-based framework with independent components for piece recognition and board geometry estimation, whose predictions are combined to reconstruct the position. For piece recognition, we adapt Faster R-CNN using a class-weighted objective and a deeper classification head. The detector operates directly on the input image, retaining alternative piece hypotheses that are subsequently refined using constraints on piece counts and square occupancy. For board detection, we introduce an octagonal arrangement of eight labelled boundary keypoints, predicted using the keypoint head of Mask R-CNN. These provide redundant correspondences for homography estimation and encode board orientation. The estimated homography maps representative points from the piece boxes to an 8x8 grid. On a synthetic dataset, the modifications to piece detection increase mean average precision from 61.59% to 90.14%. Of the predicted board keypoints, 97.11% are within 1% of the image diagonal of their labelled targets. Using ground-truth piece boxes with the predicted homographies gives correct square assignments for every test position. The complete framework recovers 76.61% of test positions exactly and 96.49% with at most one incorrect square.

</details>


### [27] [Do Vision Models Learn Physical Constraints or Rendering Shortcuts? A Counterfactual Benchmark for Grounded Physical Consistency](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09205)
*M. Moein Esfahani,Sepehr Salem,Mohammed Alser,Vince Calhoun*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper introduces a physical plausibility diagnosis system for image editing, detecting violations of scene physics (shadows, reflections, support, surface response, occlusion) in edited images. The authors create a synthetic benchmark of 5,500 images using Mitsuba 3 renderer and evaluate three VLM baselines, achieving 64.0-67.8% macro-F1, but performance drops significantly under distribution shift.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern image editing models can produce images that violate physical laws (missing shadows, failed reflections, floating objects). There is a need to automatically diagnose these physical plausibility violations, including detection, classification, localization, and explanation.

Method: The authors create a counterfactual benchmark using Mitsuba 3 to generate 5,500 images from 500 scene families. Each family contains one clean image and ten matched violations across five categories (shadows, reflection, support, surface response, occlusion). They evaluate three VLM baselines (LLaVA-1.5-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL3.5-8B) on category classification, affected region localization, and explanation tasks.

Result: On the 1,650-image synthetic test set, the baselines achieve 64.0-67.8% category macro-F1. A key finding is that LLaVA-1.5-7B's performance drops from 64.0% to 40.8% under intervention shift, revealing that in-distribution accuracy partly reflects rendering artifacts and counterfactual construction cues rather than true physical reasoning.

Conclusion: Current VLM baselines can achieve moderate performance on physical plausibility diagnosis but rely heavily on distribution-specific cues. The benchmark reveals a significant generalization gap, highlighting the need for models that genuinely understand physical relationships rather than exploiting rendering artifacts. The synthetic benchmark provides valuable training and evaluation data with ground truth labels, masks, and explanations.

Abstract: Modern image editing models can satisfy a text instruction while breaking the physics of the edited scene. A new object may cast no shadow, a mirror may fail to reflect visible geometry, or an object may float above a surface that should support it. We study physical plausibility diagnosis, detecting whether an edited image violates scene physics, naming the violation type, localizing the affected region, and explaining the failure in language. We introduce a counterfactual benchmark whose controlled synthetic component uses Mitsuba~3 to generate 5,500 images from 500 scene families. Each family contains one clean image and ten matched violations involving shadows, reflection, support, surface response, and occlusion. The renderer pipeline provides category labels, affected-region masks and boxes, scene metadata, and explanation targets. We use LLaVA-1.5-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, and InternVL3.5-8B as diagnostic baselines rather than proposed methods. On a 1,650-image synthetic test set, the adapted baselines reach 64.0--67.8\% category macro-F1 on standard held-out scenes. For LLaVA-1.5-7B, category macro-F1 falls from 64.0\% on the standard split to 40.8\% under intervention shift. This gap shows that high in-distribution accuracy partly reflects cues tied to rendering and counterfactual construction.

</details>


### [28] [A Deterministic Evidence Layer for Vision-Language Autism Screening from Naturalistic Home Video](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09217)
*Wenqi Li,Mindi Ruan,Chuanbo Hu,Shuo Wang,Xin Li*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper addresses instability in using Vision-Language Models (VLMs) for Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) screening from home videos. The authors发现VLMs在temperature~0时16-37%的clip预测标签在不同运行间变化，原因是serving stack而非模型本身。他们提出一种"grounded perception"方法：冻结VLM让其生成带有时间戳和术语标签的事件表，然后使用确定性评分器进行决策。在43个家庭自由游戏视频上达到AUC 0.851，86%准确率，且74.4%的clip在每次运行中标签一致（vs 零样本基线60.5%）。


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: ASD早期诊断受限于专业观察者的可及性。VLMs可以从视频描述儿童行为，但预测不稳定——在temperature~0时，16-37%的clip在不同运行间改变预测标签。问题根源在于serving stack而非模型本身。解决这一稳定性问题对实际临床应用至关重要。

Method: 1. 冻结VLM，将决策移出模型；2. 使用"grounded perception constraints"：VLM生成事件表（时间戳、术语标签、触发因素、反面证据）；3. 文本-only阶段对每行进行年龄校准；4. 确定性的weight-of-evidence评分器求和并分层为风险类别；5. 决策可分解为每特征的命名贡献，可从保存的表重新评分。

Result: 在43个家庭自由游戏视频上：- AUC: 0.851 ± 0.012；- 准确率: 86.0%；- F1: 71.8；- 74.4%的clip在每次运行中标签一致（零样本基线60.5%）；- 零样本基线标记9/31个正常发展为ASD，而本方法在每次运行中未标记任何正常发展为ASD。

Conclusion: 通过冻结VLM并使用确定性评分器替代原有决策机制，可以显著提高ASD筛查的稳定性和准确性。grounded perception约束通过确定性评分器阅读是性能提升的关键。Ablation验证了这一归因。

Abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is diagnosed through specialist observation of a child's social behavior, and access to that expertise is the bottleneck for early identification. Vision-language models (VLMs) describe a child's behavior from video well; the verdict drawn from the description is unstable: at temperature~0, across eight pipeline configurations on one backbone, 16--37\% of clips change their predicted label between repeated runs, and the cause lies in the serving stack. We keep the VLM frozen and move the decision out of the model. Under our grounded perception constraints the VLM writes an event table of timestamped, glossary-labeled events that names the eliciting press and logs counter-evidence; a text-only stage age-calibrates the confidence of each row; a deterministic weight-of-evidence scorer sums it into an evidence total and stratifies it into a risk category, so every decision decomposes into named per-feature contributions and can be re-scored from the saved table. On 43 caregiver-recorded, protocol-free home free-play clips of preschool children, the pipeline reaches AUC $0.851 \pm 0.012$, 86.0\% accuracy, and F$_1$ 71.8 over three runs. It labels 74.4\% of clips correctly in every run (60.5\% for the zero-shot baseline) and flags no typically developing clip in every run (9 of 31 at zero-shot). An ablation on the same backbone attributes the gain to the grounded perception constraints read through the deterministic scorer.

</details>


### [29] [PVSync: A Unified Lip-Sync Expert for Timing and Articulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09223)
*Kevin Stephen,Varun Menon,Timo Mertens,Nikita Drobyshev*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: PVSync is a unified model for audio-visual synchronization estimation and phoneme-level articulation scoring. It combines window-level contrastive learning with viseme-based alignment objectives to evaluate lip-sync quality in talking-head videos without manual annotations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Lip movements can match speech timing without matching the actual spoken sounds. Existing methods like LSE-C have limited correlation (0.34) with human rankings of lip-sync quality. There was a need for a unified model that can both estimate temporal offset and evaluate articulation quality at the phoneme level.

Method: PVSync uses two complementary objectives: (1) window-level contrastive learning for synchronization estimation, and (2) phoneme-level articulation scoring that aligns audio and video embeddings of the same viseme class across clips. Viseme labels are automatically derived from forced-aligned transcripts, eliminating the need for manual annotations. The model was evaluated on offset-corrected videos from 13 talking-head video generation models and on an automatically constructed benchmark from held-out speech.

Result: PVSync achieves a Spearman correlation of 0.83 with human rankings of lip-sync quality, significantly outperforming LSE-C's 0.34. It distinguishes viseme-matched from mismatched audio-visual pairs with an ROC AUC of 0.91. PVSync also outperforms SyncNet and MTD-VocaLiST in temporal offset recovery on held-out in-the-wild clips.

Conclusion: PVSync successfully combines audio-visual offset estimation and phoneme-level articulation scoring in a unified model. Its automatic viseme labeling approach and strong performance on multiple benchmarks (0.83 correlation with human rankings, 0.91 ROC AUC) demonstrate its effectiveness for evaluating lip-sync quality in generated talking-head videos.

Abstract: Lip movements can match the timing of speech without matching the spoken sounds. We introduce PVSync, a unified model for audio-visual offset estimation and phoneme-level articulation scoring. PVSync combines window-level contrastive learning for synchronisation with a phoneme-level articulation objective that aligns audio and video embeddings of the same viseme class across clips. Visemes group phonemes with similar visible articulation. Viseme labels are derived automatically from forced-aligned transcripts, without manual annotations. On offset-corrected videos from 13 talking-head video generation models, PVSync matches human rankings of lip-sync quality more closely than LSE-C, achieving a Spearman correlation of 0.83 versus 0.34. On an automatically constructed benchmark from held-out speech, PVSync distinguishes viseme-matched from mismatched audio-visual pairs with an ROC AUC of 0.91. PVSync also outperforms SyncNet and MTD-VocaLiST in temporal offset recovery on held-out in-the-wild clips. Code and benchmark data will be released upon acceptance.

</details>


### [30] [Pooling Representation Autoencoders for Efficient Diffusion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09242)
*Ramón Calvo-González,Youssef Saied,François Fleuret*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: PoolDINO introduces a learned affine pooling operator to reduce token density in Representation Autoencoders, achieving 3.7x-9.0x throughput gains through 4x-16x token compression while maintaining comparable generation quality under internal guidance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Representation Autoencoders (RAEs) generate images from pre-trained visual features but suffer from expensive generative modeling due to dense token grids. The key insight is that local feature correlations exist, suggesting neighboring tokens can be merged without significant quality loss.

Method: PoolDINO is a learned affine pooling operator that merges neighboring tokens. It is trained jointly with the RGB decoder while preserving the standard two-stage RAE procedure (no separate feature auto-encoder needed). This approach leverages local feature correlations to reduce token density.

Result: On ImageNet-256: (1) 4x token compression retains comparable generation quality under internal guidance; (2) 16x compression trades some quality for greater efficiency; (3) At 100 sampling steps, latent-sampling throughput increases by 3.7x (4x compression) and 9.0x (16x compression) relative to unpooled baseline; (4) Classification and dense prediction evaluations show weaker performance on other tasks while maintaining comparable guided generation quality.

Conclusion: Token compression via learned pooling enables efficient RAE generation with significant throughput gains. However, there is a tradeoff: the approach prioritizes generation efficiency over other vision tasks (classification, dense prediction), indicating that optimized generation quality may not coexist with strong performance across all vision benchmarks.

Abstract: Representation Autoencoders (RAEs) generate images from pre-trained visual fea- tures, but their dense token grids make generative modeling expensive. Motivated by local feature correlations, we introduce PoolDINO, a learned affine pooling operator that merges neighboring tokens. Training the pooling operator jointly with the RGB decoder preserves the standard two-stage RAE procedure without a separate feature auto-encoder. On ImageNet-256, 4x token compression retains comparable generation quality under internal guidance, while 16x compression trades some quality for greater efficiency. At a fixed budget of 100 sampling steps, latent-sampling throughput increases by 3.7x and 9.0x, respectively, relative to the unpooled baseline. Classification and dense prediction evaluations show that comparable guided generation quality can coexist with weaker performance on other tasks.

</details>


### [31] [Adaptive Visual Token Reduction for Accelerated Image Understanding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09252)
*Seyoung Jeong,Jong Pil Yun,Sang Jun Lee*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: ReFIT is an instruction-guided visual token reduction framework for efficient LVLM inference that preserves spatially structured information through Relevance-Guided Window Reshaping (RWR) and Instruction-Guided Token Refinement (ITR), achieving improved accuracy and reduced computational cost on VQA benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing visual token reduction methods either prune individual tokens or use fixed-size cropping, which loses spatially structured information like horizontally or vertically elongated text. Meanwhile, processing high-resolution images requires substantial computation.

Method: ReFIT consists of two components: (1) RWR captures instruction-relevant regions by adapting to their spatial characteristics, and (2) ITR further removes unnecessary visual tokens while preserving relevant information.

Result: Experiments on four VQA benchmarks demonstrate that ReFIT improves answer accuracy while reducing computational cost. Qualitative results show effective localization of relevant regions and removal of unnecessary visual information.

Conclusion: ReFIT successfully addresses the limitation of existing methods in preserving spatially structured information while achieving both accuracy improvement and computational efficiency in LVLM inference.

Abstract: Large Vision-Language Models achieve strong VQA performance, but processing high-resolution, information-rich images requires substantial computation, motivating visual token reduction. However, existing methods often prune individual tokens or rely on fixed-size cropping, limiting their ability to preserve spatially structured information such as horizontally or vertically elongated text. To address this limitation, we propose ReFIT, an instruction-guided visual token reduction framework for efficient LVLM inference. ReFIT consists of Relevance-Guided Window Reshaping (RWR) and Instruction-Guided Token Refinement (ITR), where RWR captures instruction-relevant regions by adapting to their spatial characteristics, while ITR further removes unnecessary visual tokens. Experiments on four VQA benchmarks demonstrate that ReFIT improves answer accuracy while reducing computational cost, and qualitative results demonstrate its effectiveness in localizing relevant regions and removing unnecessary visual information.

</details>


### [32] [PhyDiCT: Plug-and-Play CT Reconstruction from Sparse X-Rays via Differentiable Rendering and Strong Priors](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09253)
*Weicheng Dai,Shantanu Ghosh,Kayhan Batmanghelich*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: PhyDiCT is a training-free framework that reconstructs 3D lung CT images from few X-ray projections by combining a differentiable physics-based forward model (Beer-Lambert law) with a text-conditioned diffusion model as a prior. The method uses Split Gibbs sampling to guide the diffusion process toward solutions that satisfy both projection fidelity and anatomical coherence.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reconstructing 3D CT images from limited X-ray projections is highly ill-posed due to volumetric information loss. Existing methods either require extensive training or fail to leverage the physics of image formation.

Method: The framework integrates: (1) a differentiable physics-based forward model grounded in Beer-Lambert law, (2) a text-conditioned diffusion model as a training-free prior, (3) Split Gibbs sampling to jointly optimize projection fidelity and prior consistency, and (4) a test-time refinement step for enhanced anatomical coherence.

Result: PhyDiCT outperforms existing plug-and-play diffusion and fully trained reconstruction approaches on public 3D CT datasets, achieving 7.5% improvement in SSIM compared to full training methods.

Conclusion: Combining a strong generative prior with the underlying physics of image formation substantially improves reconstruction quality, enabling high-quality 3D CT reconstruction from limited projections without requiring model fine-tuning.

Abstract: Reconstructing 3D Computed Tomography (CT) images from a few X-ray projections is a highly ill-posed inverse problem due to the loss of volumetric information. We propose PhyDiCT, a training-free framework that integrates a differentiable Physics-based forward model, grounded in the Beer-Lambert law, with a text-conditioned Diffusion as a strong prior to reconstruct 3D lung CT images. We refer to our approach as training-free since the prior model is used without fine-tuning, and our goal is to steer the denoising procedure to generate samples consistent with X-ray observations. We guide the diffusion generation using Split Gibbs sampling to jointly optimize for projection fidelity (reward) and consistency with prior knowledge. Also, we introduce a test-time refinement step that enhances image realism and anatomical coherence. We extensively evaluate our method on publicly available 3D CT datasets using both perceptual and semantic metrics, demonstrating that it surpasses existing plug-and-play diffusion and fully trained reconstruction approaches. Our findings highlight that combining a strong generative prior with the underlying physics of image formation substantially improves reconstruction quality, e.g., 7.5\% improvement on SSIM compared to full training methods. Code will be released at https://github.com/batmanlab/PhyDiCT.

</details>


### [33] [Hardware-aware Calibrated Clustered Attention for Efficient Visual Geometric Transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09274)
*Weitian Wang,Shubham Rai,Cecilia De La Parra,Akash Kumar*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper presents blockwise clustered attention (BC attention) to accelerate the Visual Geometry Grounded Transformer (VGGT) for 3D scene reconstruction. The method addresses the latency bottleneck caused by global attention layers with extremely long sequences by limiting clustering to neighborhood blocks and introducing calibration techniques to reduce clustering errors.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: VGGT is the first model to jointly infer camera poses, depths, and dense geometry in one pass for 3D scene reconstruction. However, its joint inference mechanism requires global attention layers with extremely long sequences, causing significant latency bottleneck that limits practical deployment on GPUs.

Method: The proposed blockwise clustered attention (BC attention) limits query clustering within HW-friendly neighborhood blocks to reduce computation overhead and data movement between on-chip and off-chip memory. Two additional techniques are introduced: (1) hashing hyperplane calibration method and (2) threshold-based error compensation method to reduce clustering errors efficiently.

Result: Experiments on GPU show calibrated BC attention accelerates global attention layers by 2.10-2.63× and the whole backbone by 1.77-2.35× with negligible loss (1%) for large scenes. With small performance loss (< 5%), it achieves 2.26-2.87× latency improvement on attention layers and 1.90-2.55× on backbone.

Conclusion: Blockwise clustered attention successfully addresses the latency bottleneck in VGGT's global attention layers while maintaining high accuracy. The method enables practical deployment of VGGT on GPUs for 3D scene reconstruction tasks.

Abstract: The Visual Geometry Grounded Transformer (VGGT) marks a significant leap forward in 3D scene reconstruction, as it is the first model that directly infers all key 3D attributes (camera poses, depths, and dense geometry) jointly in one pass. However, this joint inference mechanism requires global attention layers with extremely long sequences that causes a significant latency bottleneck. In this paper, we propose blockwise clustered attention (BC attention) to accelerate the global attention layers in VGGT. By limiting the clustering within HW-friendly neighborhood blocks, BC attention reduces the computation overhead of query clustering as well as the costly data movement between on- and off-chip memory. This enables BC attention to scale to long sequences and deliver practical latency improvements on GPUs. Moreover, we introduce a hashing hyperplane calibration method and a threshold-based error compensation method to reduce clustering errors efficiently, which is a bottleneck in the current clustered attention mechanism. Overall, our experiments on GPU demonstrate that calibrated BC attention accelerates the global attention layers by 2.10-2.63$\times$ and the whole backbone by 1.77-2.35$\times$ with negligible loss (1%) for large scenes. With a small performance loss (< 5%), calibrated BC attention further achieves a 2.26-2.87$\times$ latency improvement on the global attention layers and a 1.90-2.55$\times$ improvement on the backbone.

</details>


### [34] [EM-SNN: Efficiently Modulated Spiking Neural Network for Remote Sensing Image Dehazing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09275)
*Jie Shao,Jiaqi Ma,Wenwen Min,Beihang Song,Ning Chen,Youfa Liu,Jun Wan*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: EM-SNN is a spiking neural network designed for remote sensing image dehazing that uses threshold-modulated neurons and structural modulation to overcome limitations in recovering fine details caused by haze-induced signal attenuation and discrete spike thresholding.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Spiking neural networks offer energy efficiency advantages but have limited application in remote sensing image dehazing due to the coupling between haze-induced high-frequency attenuation and discrete spike thresholding, which suppresses weak responses and limits recovery of edges, textures, and fine details.

Method: The proposed EM-SNN integrates two key components: (1) a statistics-driven Threshold-Modulated Leaky Integrate-and-Fire (TM-LIF) neuron that adaptively compensates for haze-induced contrast compression, and (2) a Spike Sobel Modulation (SSM) module that enhances structural cues and reduces depth-wise attenuation during spiking feature propagation. These components jointly modulate activation scales and structural representations while preserving event-driven sparsity.

Result: EM-SNN achieves competitive dehazing performance on HRSD, RICE, RRSHID, and SateHaze1K datasets while consuming only one quarter of the energy of the strong ANN baseline SFRDP-Net.

Conclusion: EM-SNN successfully addresses the core challenge of spiking dehazing models by maintaining energy efficiency (1/4 of ANN baseline) while achieving competitive performance on multiple remote sensing dehazing benchmarks, demonstrating the viability of SNNs for practical image dehazing applications.

Abstract: Although spiking neural networks (SNNs) provide an energy-efficient alternative to artificial neural networks (ANNs), their application to remote sensing image dehazing remains limited. A key challenge arises from the coupling between haze-induced high-frequency attenuation and discrete spike thresholding. This interaction suppresses weak responses and fundamentally limits the recovery of edges, textures, and fine details in spiking dehazing models. To address this challenge, we propose the Efficiently Modulated Spiking Neural Network (EM-SNN), a dedicated spiking framework tailored to remote sensing image dehazing. EM-SNN integrates a statistics-driven Threshold-Modulated Leaky Integrate-and-Fire (TM-LIF) neuron to adaptively compensate for haze-induced contrast compression, together with a Spike Sobel Modulation (SSM) module that enhances structural cues and reduces depth-wise attenuation during spiking feature propagation. By jointly modulating activation scales and structural representations, EM-SNN improves dehazing performance while preserving the inherent event-driven sparsity of SNNs. Experiments on HRSD, RICE, RRSHID, and SateHaze1K demonstrate that EM-SNN achieves competitive dehazing performance while consuming only one quarter of the energy of the strong ANN baseline SFRDP-Net.

</details>


### [35] [Why VLMs Miss Small Objects, and When Zooming In Is Safe](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09313)
*Junzhe Shi,Yuan Gan,Shida Jiang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper investigates why vision-language models (VLMs) struggle with small objects in large images, develops a theoretical framework based on two key quantities (S = visual tokens per object side, L = content per call), and evaluates whether local decomposition remains a viable approach. The authors derive limits on VLM performance, test predictions on ~177,000 requests across 797 images, and find that decomposition can maintain or improve recall without penalties.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Vision-language models often fail to detect small objects in large images. The authors seek to understand: (1) what fundamental limits VLMs, (2) which limits can be overcome with better models, and (3) whether classical local decomposition still has a future despite increased token budgets in modern VLMs.

Method: The authors built a theoretical framework using two quantities: S (number of visual tokens across an object's side) and L (content a call must cover). They derived mathematical limits on VLM performance based on these quantities, then tested predictions empirically on ~177,000 requests across 797 images including drawings, floor plans, natural and synthetic images. They evaluated 8 different VLMs with 40 orderings.

Result: Theoretical results: (1) A W×H image with N tokens gives objects of side m at most m×√(N/(WH)) tokens per side; (2) Doubling token budget N only increases largest S by 41%; (3) Seeing an image at the S an object needs costs at least S² tokens. Empirical results: (1) None of 40 predicted orderings were violated on controlled images; (2) On drawings, 61/89 implied orderings hold significantly and 4 fail (all for OpenAI models with more pixels than default); (3) On construction drawings, decomposition never significantly lowered recall and raised it by up to 0.28.

Conclusion: Local decomposition still has a future under specific conditions: splitting an image cannot lower recall if no view zooms out relative to the whole image and views overlap by one object. A simple rule approaches the theoretical cost bound as images grow. The approach is particularly effective on technical drawings like construction plans, where it can significantly improve recall without penalties.

Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) often miss small objects in large images. We ask three questions: what limits them, which of these limits better models can remove, and whether the classical way of handling large images, local decomposition, still has a future. We answer them with a theory built on two quantities of the image interface: S, the number of visual tokens across an object's side, and L, the content a call must cover. The limits: a W x H image sent whole within N tokens gives an object of side m at most m*sqrt(N/(WH)) tokens per side. Doubling the token budget N therefore raises the largest S a whole image can reach by only 41%, and seeing an image at the S an object needs costs at least order S^2 tokens whatever the model. If recognition improves gradually with S, any search strategy, zoom agents included, obeys a recall-cost frontier. What better models can change: the S an object needs and how much one call can carry, measured in bits per object found; the coverage cost remains. Decomposition: yes. Assuming only that more tokens per object and less content per call do not hurt on average, splitting an image cannot lower recall if no view zooms out relative to the whole image and views overlap by one object. Neither part of this condition can be dropped; we bound the cost of every such decomposition, and a simple rule approaches the bound as the image grows. We test the theory in about 177,000 requests on 797 images. On controlled images, none of 40 orderings predicted for 8 VLMs is violated. Checked after the fact on drawings, floor plans, natural and synthetic images, 61 of 89 implied orderings hold significantly and 4 fail, all for OpenAI models given more pixels than their default path. On construction drawings the rule never significantly lowered recall relative to the whole image and raised it by up to 0.28. Code and data: https://github.com/shijunzhe/vlm-small-objects

</details>


### [36] [SAREO-FM: Decoupled Semantic Supervision for SAR-EO Foundation Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09317)
*Jeonghyeok Do,Munchurl Kim*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: SAREO-FM is a multimodal fusion method that combines Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) and Electro-Optical (EO) imagery by using separate token streams: modality tokens for masked reconstruction and learnable semantic queries guided by a vision foundation model. This design allows semantic and reconstruction supervision to operate independently while maintaining interaction within a shared encoder.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: SAR and EO provide complementary observations - SAR enables day-and-night, weather-resilient sensing while EO provides rich appearance and fine-grained semantic cues. Existing methods force a single token stream to serve two distinct roles, which is suboptimal. The goal is to leverage both modalities effectively while maintaining strong unimodal transfer capabilities.

Method: The method uses two separate token streams: (1) Modality tokens that preserve how each sensor observes the scene through masked reconstruction, and (2) Learnable semantic queries that capture what the scene contains under guidance from a pretrained vision foundation model (VFM). These queries are jointly encoded with SAR and EO tokens, allowing queries to acquire modality-grounded semantic context while modality-token outputs remain targets for masked reconstruction. The model is pretrained on the million-scale SAR-1M corpus.

Result: SAREO-FM achieves strong unimodal transfer for both SAR-only and EO-only inputs, while delivering substantial gains from joint SAR-EO observations on tasks that benefit from complementary sensing.

Conclusion: The separate token stream design effectively assigns semantic and reconstruction supervision to different pathways while preserving their interaction within the shared encoder, enabling both strong unimodal performance and effective multimodal fusion.

Abstract: Synthetic aperture radar (SAR) and electro-optical (EO) imagery provide complementary observations: SAR enables day-and-night, weather-resilient sensing, whereas EO provides rich appearance and fine-grained semantic cues. We introduce SAREO-FM, which avoids forcing a single token stream to serve two distinct roles: modality tokens preserve how each sensor observes the scene through masked reconstruction, while learnable semantic queries capture what the scene contains under guidance from a pretrained vision foundation model (VFM). By jointly encoding these queries with SAR and EO tokens, the queries acquire modality-grounded semantic context, while the modality-token outputs remain the explicit targets of masked reconstruction. This design assigns semantic and reconstruction supervision to separate token streams while preserving their interaction within the shared encoder. Pretrained on the million-scale SAR-1M corpus, SAREO-FM achieves strong unimodal transfer for both SAR-only and EO-only inputs, while delivering substantial gains from joint SAR--EO observations on tasks that benefit from complementary sensing.

</details>


### [37] [VIS-Ground: Video Interactive Storytelling with Contextual Grounding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09326)
*Bingxuan Li,Yiwen Song,Xueqing Wu,Yanzhou Pan,Yang Li,Kuang Su,Jingyun Liu,Sebastian Ko,Huan Zhang,Tong Zhang,Nanyun Peng,Tomas Pfister,Yale Song*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper addresses interactive video storytelling where viewers can steer video content. The key challenge is that viewer requests have latent dependencies on both source materials and current video state, which may not be explicitly stated. The authors propose VIS-Ground, a framework that transforms heterogeneous inputs into executable constraint models through structured context abstraction, generation constraints induction, and constrained video generation. The method achieves 10.3 points improvement over baselines across three video generation backbones.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing interactive video generation systems focus on following viewer instructions, while source-grounded methods focus on aligning with external narrative or knowledge sources. However, the fundamental question of what context a generation model should ground on during interactive continuation, and how to transform heterogeneous unstructured inputs into such grounding context, remains underexplored.

Method: VIS-Ground employs three main components: (1) Structured Context Abstraction to recover grounded states and cross-context dependencies from heterogeneous inputs; (2) Generation Constraints Induction to project relevant dependencies into candidate-specific constraints; (3) Constrained Video Generation to enforce these constraints through planning, verification, revision, and rendering.

Result: VIS-Ground consistently achieves the highest overall composite score across three video generation backbones, reaching an average absolute improvement of 10.3 points over the strongest per-backbone baselines. Gains are observed across both narrative and knowledge grounding scenarios.

Conclusion: The proposed contextual grounding framework successfully transforms heterogeneous input context into executable constraint models for video generation. Remaining challenges include dependency extraction accuracy and faithful realization during video rendering.

Abstract: Video interactive storytelling enables viewers to actively steer how a video unfolds. However, once we allow viewers to intervene during generation, a new challenge arises: The viewer's request can have latent dependencies on both the grounding source and the current rendered video state. These dependencies may not be explicitly stated in any individual input, but emerge only when the source, rendered history, and new viewer intent are considered jointly. Existing interactive video generation systems primarily emphasize following viewer instructions, while source-grounded video generation methods focus on aligning generated content with an external narrative or knowledge source. This leaves a fundamental question underexplored: What context should a generation model ground on during interactive continuation, and how can heterogeneous, unstructured inputs be transformed into such grounding context? In this work, we formulate contextual grounding as the process of transforming heterogeneous input context into an executable constraint model for video generation. To address this challenge, we introduce VIS-Ground, which performs Structured Context Abstraction to recover grounded states and cross-context dependencies, Generation Constraints Induction to project relevant dependencies into candidate-specific constraints, and Constrained Video Generation to enforce these constraints through planning, verification, revision, and rendering. Across three video generation backbones, VIS-Ground consistently achieves the highest overall composite score, reaching an average absolute improvement of 10.3 points over the strongest per-backbone baselines. Detailed analysis further shows gains across both narrative and knowledge grounding, and reveals remaining challenges in dependency extraction, and faithful realization during video rendering.

</details>


### [38] [Visual Jev Rewards: Reference-Bound Verification for Multi-Subject Image Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09328)
*Baoteng Li,Wenzhuo Wu,Kongming Liang,Zhanyu Ma*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper introduces reference-bound Visual Jev rewards for multi-subject image generation, which verify whether requested attributes, actions, and relations hold for specified reference subjects. The method uses a Qwen3.5-4B verifier with binary supervision to generate training signals, achieving a GPT-5.4 composite score improvement from 41.78 to 52.50 on a 897-task MICo-Bench subset.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current rewards for multi-subject image generation fail to verify whether the correct subjects participate in requested interactions—subject presence alone is insufficient to establish that the requested condition holds for the specified reference identities.

Method: The approach constructs fixed questions offline, trains a Qwen3.5-4B verifier with binary supervision, and reads Yes probabilities directly from its language-model head. The mean of these probabilities supplies a GRPO reward while retaining individual judgments for inspection. Training used 200 MICo-150K tasks with 30 updates.

Result: The framework raises GPT-5.4 composite score from 41.78 to 52.50 on a manually selected 897-task MICo-Bench subset; direct 27B rewards yield 51.84. However, offline human evaluation does not establish a statistically significant advantage over direct scoring.

Conclusion: The study provides an initial implementation and evaluation of Visual Jev as a reference-bound reward for multi-subject image generation, though further validation is needed to demonstrate significant advantages over direct scoring methods.

Abstract: Multi-subject image generation requires rewards that verify whether requested attributes, actions, and relations hold for the specified reference subjects. Subject presence alone does not establish that the correct subjects participate in a requested interaction. We present reference-bound Visual Jev rewards that turn these visual decisions into generator training signals. Each subject-related question receives a positive label only when the requested condition and the relevant reference identities hold jointly. We construct fixed questions offline, train a Qwen3.5-4B verifier with binary supervision, and directly read Yes probabilities from its language-model head. Their mean supplies a GRPO reward while retaining individual judgments for inspection. Using 200 MICo-150K training tasks and 30 updates, the framework raises a GPT-5.4 composite score from 41.78 to 52.50 on a manually selected 897-task MICo-Bench subset; direct 27B rewards yield 51.84. Each reward is tested in one GRPO run, and offline human evaluation does not establish a statistically significant advantage over direct scoring. The study provides an initial implementation and evaluation of Visual Jev as a reference-bound reward for multi-subject image generation.

</details>

### [40] [CRT-HMAR: Causal Requirement Tracing-Guided Hierarchical Multi-Agent Regulation for Open-Task-Aware Infrared-Visible Image Fusion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09330)
*Zengyi Yang,Shuai Yuan,Zhong-Cheng Wu,Juan Cheng,Huafeng Li,Yu Liu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: CRT-HMAR proposes a causal requirement tracing-guided hierarchical multi-agent regulation framework for open-task-aware infrared-visible image fusion. It addresses the limitation of existing methods that struggle to generalize to unseen tasks by introducing task-specific semantic preference mapping and adaptive requirement-customized image fusion through collaborative agents.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing IR-VIS image fusion methods are typically tailored to seen tasks within a fixed task set and cannot generalize to unseen tasks, restricting applicability in real-world open-task scenarios where the downstream task is unknown or changes dynamically.

Method: The framework introduces: (1) Causal Requirement Tracing Task Localization mechanism that maps task-specific semantic preferences into image-level causal requirement maps by intervening in key image information and observing task-network response variations; (2) Requirement Analysis Agent to aggregate task-specific requirement knowledge; (3) History-Analysis Multi-Objective Balancing mechanism; (4) Task-Level-Correction Conflict Mitigation mechanism. These components form a hierarchical regulation chain of "requirement interpretation - task balancing - conflict mitigation".

Result: Extensive experiments on open-task scenarios involving five downstream tasks demonstrate that CRT-HMAR significantly improves generalization to unseen tasks while maintaining performance and balance of seen tasks.

Conclusion: CRT-HMAR shifts IR-VIS image fusion from task-oriented modeling toward requirement-oriented modeling, promoting its extension from closed-task settings to real-world open-task scenarios.

Abstract: Infrared and visible (IR-VIS) image fusion integrates complementary multimodal information into a single fused image to support downstream vision tasks. However, existing methods are typically tailored to seen tasks within a fixed task set and struggle to generalize to unseen tasks, which restricts their applicability in real-world open-task scenarios. To address this issue, this paper proposes CRT-HMAR, a Causal Requirement Tracing-Guided Hierarchical Multi-Agent Regulation Framework for open-task-aware IR-VIS image fusion. CRT-HMAR introduces a Causal Requirement Tracing Task Localization mechanism, which actively intervenes in key image information and observes task-network response variations to map task-specific semantic preferences into image-level causal requirement maps. Based on these maps, a requirement analysis agent aggregates task-specific requirement knowledge to adaptively guide requirement-customized image fusion. Moreover, CRT-HMAR incorporates History-Analysis Multi-Objective Balancing and Task-Level-Correction Conflict Mitigation mechanisms, jointly constructing a hierarchical regulation chain of "requirement interpretation - task balancing - conflict mitigation". Through multiple collaborative agents, CRT-HMAR dynamically regulates key processes including open-task requirement modeling, multi-task balanced optimization, and gradient conflict mitigation. Extensive experiments on open-task scenarios involving five downstream tasks demonstrate that CRT-HMAR significantly improves generalization to unseen tasks while maintaining the performance and balance of seen tasks. Overall, CRT-HMAR shifts IR-VIS image fusion from task-oriented modeling toward requirement-oriented modeling, promoting its extension from closed-task settings to real-world open-task scenarios.

</details>


### [41] [TileSkipper: Region-Adaptive Tile Pruning for 3D Gaussian Splatting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09343)
*Jingxing Li,Yongjae Lee,Deliang Fan,Abhay Kumar Yadav,Cheng Peng,Rama Chellappa*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: TileSkipper is a method that optimizes 3D Gaussian Splatting rasterization by assigning static per-Gaussian contribution cutoff policies, achieving 1.088×-1.238× speedups with minimal PSNR loss (-0.007 to -0.023 dB) across 13 scenes from standard datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Tiled 3D Gaussian Splatting rasterizers currently use a single scene-wide contribution cutoff for tile enumeration, but different content has varying sensitivity to support truncation. This one-size-fits-all approach leads to suboptimal performance.

Method: TileSkipper selects static per-Gaussian cutoff policies for frozen checkpoints. It uses calibration renders to measure candidate pair savings and an isolated-removal distortion proxy accounting for front transmittance and background color. Cutoffs are allocated across 64 Gaussian groups, with policies accepted only after complete renders on disjoint selection views. The exported policy uses one byte per Gaussian with no parameter updates, additional kernel, or per-frame inference required.

Result: Across 13 scenes from Mip-NeRF 360, Tanks & Temples, and Deep Blending: 1.088× speedup at standard resolution, 1.238× at 3840-pixel width, with -0.007/-0.023 dB mean PSNR change. Six integrations with opacity-aware bounds yield 1.009×-1.121× compiler-only speedups. Shows modest gains over scene-global calibration and parity with per-Gaussian control.

Conclusion: TileSkipper provides a practical, zero-overhead optimization for 3D Gaussian Splatting that achieves significant speedups with minimal quality loss. The method is orthogonal to existing optimizations and can be combined with opacity-aware bounds for compounded benefits.

Abstract: Tiled 3D Gaussian Splatting rasterizers often use one scene-wide contribution cutoff for tile enumeration, although content differs in its sensitivity to support truncation. TileSkipper selects a static per-Gaussian cutoff policy for a frozen checkpoint. Calibration renders measure candidate pair savings and an isolated-removal distortion proxy that accounts for front transmittance and background color. The method allocates cutoffs across 64 Gaussian groups and accepts policies only after complete renders on disjoint selection views. The exported policy uses one byte per Gaussian, with no parameter updates, additional kernel, or per-frame policy inference. Across 13 scenes from Mip-NeRF 360, Tanks & Temples, and Deep Blending, a fixed-policy AccuTile sweep gives dataset-macro speedups of $1.088\times$ at standard resolution and $1.238\times$ at 3840 pixels wide, with $-0.007/-0.023$ dB mean PSNR change. Six integrations with existing opacity-aware bounds yield $1.009\times$--$1.121\times$ compiler-only speedups. For four ports from $3σ$ rasterizers, we separately attribute the prior exact-bound transition and our incremental gain. Matched-quality ablations show modest gains over scene-global calibration and parity with per-Gaussian control; the standalone comparison with AdaGScale is regime-dependent.

</details>


### [42] [Do Image Editors Follow Depth-Dependent Blur and Aperture Response? A Rendered-Ground-Truth Pilot Audit](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09344)
*Zhihan Chen,Yuhuan Zhao,Yijie Zhu,Xinyu Yao,Mengcong Ren,Yuchen Sun,Yunqing Chen*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper audits two AI image editors (Gemini 3.1 Flash Image and GPT-image-2.5) to determine if they produce physically accurate blur effects that follow thin-lens optics when asked to simulate wide apertures like f/1.4. The authors find that neither editor produces accurate depth-of-field effects - they fail to properly scale blur with aperture changes and show compressed depth blur ratios compared to a ground-truth Blender renderer.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to address a gap in evaluating AI image editors: while they claim to simulate shallow depth of field (like photos taken at f/1.4), no prior work systematically checks whether their blur follows actual thin-lens physics. Existing evaluations check blur monotonicity or vision-language judgments, but not the two key properties (aperture scaling and depth blur ratios) separately at known depths.

Method: The authors use a controlled experimental approach: (1) Create Blender Cycles scenes with true thin-lens DOF as an "oracle" baseline, (2) Apply identical blur-width estimation to both oracle and AI editor outputs, (3) Test 24 texture scenes in three-panel geometry with preregistered depth and aperture indices, (4) Test black-box interventions varying qualitative wording vs aperture numbers, (5) Test both center-focus and near-focus layouts to detect depth compression.

Result: Key findings: (1) f/1.4-to-f/2.8 width ratios show AI editors produce 0.99-1.18 vs oracle's 1.98-2.13 - blur barely increases with wider aperture, (2) Near/far blur ratios are 1.18-1.25 (Gemini) and 0.97-1.05 (GPT-image) vs oracle's 1.69-1.82 - depth blur is compressed, (3) Qualitative wording changes blur 2-10x while aperture number changes only 1.1-1.3x, (4) No f-number wording meets the "followed" criterion, (5) Depth compression appears in all layouts tested, (6) Scalar metrics incorrectly give high scores to synthetic editors with compressed proportions.

Conclusion: The conclusion is that current AI image editors do not follow thin-lens optics for depth of field simulation. They fail to properly scale blur with aperture changes and produce compressed depth blur ratios. The authors recommend that future evaluations check aperture scaling and depth blur proportions separately at known depths, and that developers should aim for physically accurate DOF rendering rather than just "aesthetic" blur.

Abstract: General image editors are asked to make a photo look as if it were taken at f/1.4, yet it is rarely checked whether the blur they add follows thin-lens optics. A physical aperture edit spreads blur across depth in thin-lens proportions and changes the blur when the aperture changes; prior evaluations check blur monotonicity, sharpness-trend correlation, effective-aperture error, or vision-language judgments, and none we found reports the two properties separately at known depths. In this pilot audit of two editors (Gemini~3.1 Flash Image and GPT-image-2.5) we compare against a rendered oracle: Blender Cycles scenes with true thin-lens depth of field, one blur-width estimator applied identically to oracle and editor outputs, and preregistered depth and aperture indices. In 24 texture scenes rendered in one three-panel geometry, accepted and measurable panels show f/1.4-to-f/2.8 width ratios, $\barσ_{1.4}/\barσ_{2.8}$, of 0.99--1.18 against 1.98--2.13 for the oracle, and ratios of pooled median Gaussian-equivalent near/far blur widths of about 1.18--1.25 (Gemini) and 0.97--1.05 (GPT-image) against 1.69--1.82. Preregistered black-box interventions show that qualitative wording changes blur strength by roughly 2--10 times, whereas a request for 2 versus 6 px changes it 1.1--1.3 times and no tested wording of the f-number meets the registered ``followed'' criterion. The depth compression appears in the original and reversed centre-focus layouts; with the focus on the near panel, the available-panel depth index reaches the registered threshold, and the aperture response stays attenuated in every layout tested. Scalar metrics adapted from published ones give oracle-like scores to synthetic editors whose proportions are compressed.

</details>


### [43] [Closing the Loop on Contrail Avoidance with Satellite Verification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09363)
*Spandan Ghose Chowdhury*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper addresses contrail detection from satellite imagery using a small diffusion model (8.4M parameters). The model achieves 0.476 PR-AUC, outperforming DeepLabV3+ (0.414) and MedSegDiff (0.119). The study reveals three key insights: input resolution is critical, simple data augmentation (flips/rotations) significantly improves performance, and pretraining on contrail shapes causes harmful false positives due to the model learning to paint thin strokes on empty scenes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Contrails (ice clouds from aircraft) contribute significantly to aviation's warming effect. While rerouting flights that produce them could reduce this impact, satellite confirmation that contrails never formed is technically challenging due to their narrow width (1-2 pixels), rarity (0.18% of pixels), and similarity to natural cirrus clouds.

Method: The researchers built a small diffusion model with 8.4M parameters, trained on a single GPU. They conducted controlled ablation studies to identify which components contribute to detection performance. They compared against DeepLabV3+ baseline and adapted MedSegDiff, and tested the effect of doubling input resolution on the CNN.

Result: The diffusion model achieved 0.476 PR-AUC, outperforming DeepLabV3+ (0.414) and MedSegDiff (0.119). Doubling the input resolution of the CNN brought it to parity (0.499, p=0.07). Key findings: (1) input resolution matters more than architecture design, (2) simple flips and rotations more than double accuracy, (3) pretraining on contrail shapes is harmful - precision collapses to 1% while recall-based metrics still appear excellent.

Conclusion: Three transferable lessons: (1) check input resolution before designing new architectures, (2) simple data augmentation (flips/rotations) matters more than architectural choices, (3) pretraining on the target task can be counterproductive - the model learns to paint contrail-like strokes everywhere. Precision-based metrics are essential to detect such failure modes.

Abstract: Contrails are the thin ice clouds that aircraft leave behind. They cause a large share of aviation's warming, and rerouting the few flights that produce them could avoid much of it. However, an avoided contrail only counts if a satellite can confirm that it never formed, and this check is hard: contrails are one to two pixels wide, cover only 0.18% of pixels, and look very similar to natural cirrus. We build a small diffusion model (8.4M parameters, trained on one GPU) that detects them, and we run a controlled study to find out which components matter. The model reaches 0.476 PR-AUC, compared with 0.414 for a DeepLabV3+ baseline and 0.119 for an adapted MedSegDiff. Doubling the input resolution of the CNN brings it to parity (0.499, p=0.07). Three lessons apply beyond contrails. First, check the input resolution before designing a new architecture. Second, simple flips and rotations more than double accuracy and matter more than any architectural choice we measured. Third, pretraining the model on contrail shapes is harmful: the model learns that thin strokes appear everywhere and paints them onto empty scenes. Precision collapses to 1% while recall-based metrics still rate the degraded model as excellent, and no threshold or guidance heuristic repairs this failure.

</details>


### [44] [Unified Multi-plane Autoregressive Diffusion for 3D Multi-contrast MRI Synthesis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09376)
*Yejee Shin,Geonhui Son,Jinglu Wang,Minwoo Jung,Yan Lu,Dosik Hwang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: MPAD is a latent diffusion framework for synthesizing missing MRI contrasts from acquired ones, using efficient 2D operations to achieve full-volume 3D synthesis while preserving volumetric coherence through plane-wise autoregressive synthesis with inter-plane priors.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Acquiring complete MRI contrast sets is time-intensive and uncomfortable for patients, necessitating synthesis of missing contrasts from existing ones. This is inherently a 3D problem requiring anatomical coherence across axial, sagittal, and coronal planes, but full 3D models are computationally impractical.

Method: A 3D autoencoder compresses MRI scans into isotropic 3D latent representations. A 2D diffusion model reconstructs masked latent slices conditioned on source-contrast slices and unmasked target-contrast slices.
