Inference uses plane-wise autoregressive synthesis: slices are generated autoregressively in random order within one plane orientation for intra-plane continuity, then propagated as conditioning priors to orthogonal planes for inter-plane consistency.

Result: MPAD reduces training and inference FLOPs by 7x and 3x respectively compared to 3D latent diffusion baselines, while also lowering inference time and peak memory consumption. Experiments demonstrate superior performance in generating high-fidelity 3D volumes and supporting one-to-many translation within a single unified model.

Conclusion: MPAD successfully balances computational efficiency with volumetric coherence, achieving state-of-the-art performance in MRI contrast synthesis through an innovative plane-wise 2D approach that maintains 3D anatomical integrity.

Abstract: Acquiring a complete set of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) contrasts is time-intensive and uncomfortable for patients, despite the diagnostic value of multi-contrast imaging. This motivates synthesizing missing contrasts from those already acquired, which is an inherently 3D problem requiring anatomical coherence across axial, sagittal, and coronal planes. However, fully 3D generative models are often impracti- cal under computational resources that scale cubically with volume size. We propose a unified Multi-Plane Autoregressive Diffusion (MPAD), a latent diffusion framework that achieves full-volume 3D synthesis using efficient plane-wise 2D operations while preserving volumetric coherence. A 3D autoencoder first compresses MRI scans into an isotropic 3D la- tent representation. A 2D diffusion model is then trained to reconstruct masked latent slices of the target contrast, conditioned on both source- contrast slices and unmasked target-contrast slices. During inference, we introduce plane-wise autoregressive synthesis with inter-plane priors. Slices are generated autoregressively in random order within one plane orientation to maintain intra-plane continuity, then propagated as con- ditioning priors to orthogonal plane orientations to enforce inter-plane consistency. Compared to 3D latent diffusion baselines, MPAD reduces training and inference FLOPs by 7x and 3x, respectively, while also lowering inference time and peak memory consumption. Experiments on multiple datasets demonstrate that MPAD achieves superior perfor- mance, generating high-fidelity 3D volumes and supporting one-to-many translation within a single unified model.

</details>


### [45] [PPCAR-Net: Projection-Refined Parametric 3D Coronary Artery Reconstruction from Sparse X-ray Angiographic Views](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09383)
*Yu Ren,Hwee Kuan Lee,Tat-Jen Cham,Jonathan Yap,Khung Keong Yeo*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: PPCAR-Net is a projection-refined parametric coronary artery reconstruction network that directly predicts branch-structured centreline-and-radius representation from sparse angiographic views, without explicit point matching, triangulation, or intermediate volume generation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Sparse-view 3D coronary reconstruction has limitations: cross-view correspondence and triangulation methods are vulnerable to vessel overlap and foreshortening, while volumetric prediction followed by vascular-graph extraction does not directly provide centrelines and radii.

Method: The method uses: 1) A coarse predictor combining frozen VGGT features with learned branch queries to estimate branch presence, B-spline centreline trajectories, and dense radius profiles; 2) Projection-guided geometry and radius refiners that sample local evidence from input views and apply residual corrections learned with 3D supervision. Evaluation is on simulated angiographic masks from CT-derived coronary anatomy.

Result: PPCAR-Net produces better connected artery reconstructions, achieves strong centreline accuracy (particularly for RCA), maintains competitive volumetric overlap, and enables real-time reconstruction with 121 ms inference time.

Conclusion: The approach successfully reconstructs coronary arteries from sparse views with high fidelity, offering a practical solution for real-time clinical applications.

Abstract: Sparse-view 3D coronary reconstruction commonly relies on cross-view correspondence and triangulation, which are vulnerable to vessel overlap and foreshortening, or on volumetric prediction followed by vascular-graph extraction, which does not directly provide centrelines and radii. We introduce PPCAR-Net, a projection-refined parametric coronary artery reconstruction network that directly predicts a branch-structured centreline-and-radius representation without explicit point matching, triangulation, or an intermediate volume. Given a variable number of segmented views, a coarse predictor combines frozen VGGT features with learned branch queries to estimate branch presence, B-spline centreline trajectories, and dense radius profiles. Projection-guided geometry and radius refiners then sample local evidence from the input views and apply residual corrections learned with 3D supervision. We evaluate representation fidelity and sparse-view reconstruction quantitatively and qualitatively. On simulated angiographic masks generated from CT-derived coronary anatomy, PPCAR-Net produces better connected artery reconstructions and achieves strong centreline accuracy, particularly for RCA, while maintaining competitive volumetric overlap. Coarse-to-fine inference takes 121 ms, enabling real-time reconstruction.

</details>


### [46] [Quantifying Volumetric Risk: Class-Aware Asymmetric Weighted Conformal Prediction for 3D Medical Image Segmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09392)
*Shadi Alijani,Fereshteh Aghaee Meibodi,Homayoun Najjaran*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: The paper proposes Class-Aware Asymmetric Weighted Conformal Prediction (CA-WCP) to address uncertainty quantification in 3D medical image segmentation. The method handles distribution shift by combining latent-space density-ratio weighting with class-specific asymmetry factors derived from false-positive and false-negative rates. It achieves valid coverage while reducing interval width by 8-14% compared to symmetric methods, and can be integrated with LLMs for uncertainty-conditioned clinical reports.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Foundation models like MedSAM are deterministic and lack calibrated uncertainty under distribution shift. Existing conformal prediction methods are typically 2D and assume symmetric error distributions, failing to capture class-specific biases in 3D multi-class segmentation. This limits reliable clinical diagnostics where understanding prediction uncertainty is critical.

Method: CA-WCP combines latent-space density-ratio weighting for covariate shift with directional quantiles for lower and upper volume bounds. Each bound is scaled by a class-specific asymmetry factor derived from validation-set false-positive and false-negative rates. The method retains weighted-exchangeability marginal coverage guarantees for every class.

Result: On BraTS 2020 (brain tumor segmentation) and a synthetic multi-organ CT benchmark under covariate shift, the 95% Clopper-Pearson interval for observed coverage contains the nominal 90% level for every semantic class. Interval width is reduced by 8-14% relative to symmetric weighted conformal prediction. The method also enables uncertainty-conditioned radiology reports via LLM integration.

Conclusion: CA-WCP provides distribution-shift-aware uncertainty quantification with theoretical coverage guarantees while reducing prediction interval width. The integration with multimodal LLMs for clinical communication bridges the gap between statistical uncertainty quantification and interpretable clinical reporting, potentially improving clinical decision-making under distribution shift.

Abstract: Reliable volumetric segmentation is critical for clinical diagnostics, yet foundation models such as MedSAM remain deterministic and lack calibrated uncertainty under distribution shift. Existing conformal prediction methods offer statistical guarantees but are frequently applied in 2D and assume symmetric error distributions, so they do not capture the class-specific biases that arise in 3D multi-class segmentation. We propose Class-Aware Asymmetric Weighted Conformal Prediction (CA-WCP), which combines latent-space density-ratio weighting for covariate shift with directional quantiles for the lower and upper volume bounds, and scales each bound by a class-specific asymmetry factor derived from validation-set false-positive and false-negative rates. We prove that CA-WCP retains the weighted-exchangeability marginal coverage guarantee for every class, and we evaluate it on 3D brain tumor segmentation (BraTS 2020) and on a synthetic multi-organ CT benchmark constructed under covariate shift. On both benchmarks the 95\% Clopper--Pearson interval for the observed coverage of CA-WCP contains the nominal 90\% level for every semantic class, while interval width is reduced by 8--14\% relative to symmetric weighted conformal prediction. We further encode the calibrated intervals into structured prompts for a multimodal large language model to produce uncertainty-conditioned radiology reports, linking distribution-shift-aware uncertainty quantification to interpretable clinical communication.

</details>


### [47] [One Frame, Full Heartbeat: ECG-Free Cardiac Cine MRI Synthesis via Phase-Conditioned Flow Matching](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09397)
*Shiyi Wang,Ruochen Sun,Peirong Liu,Xiang Li,Fangxu Xing*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: PhaseFlow is a unified generative framework for synthesizing full cardiac motion sequences from cine CMR data without ECG dependency. It estimates cardiac phase from LV area curves and uses a rectified flow model with diffeomorphic displacement fields to generate temporally consistent frames with high physiological fidelity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard multi-frame CMR acquisition depends heavily on ECG gating and repeated breath-holds, which poses challenges in uncooperative populations, resource-limited settings, and temporally corrupted datasets. Existing synthesis methods either rely on explicit ECG signals or employ deformable registration without physiological constraints, failing to faithfully reproduce clinically relevant dynamic metrics such as ejection fraction (EF) and ventricular contraction magnitude.

Method: PhaseFlow estimates a non-linear cardiac phase signal directly from the input sequence via a segmentation-derived left-ventricular (LV) area curve, capturing the asymmetric dynamics of systole and diastole without any ECG dependency. At inference, this phase signal is provided by a pathology-specific template. A rectified flow model conditioned on the phase and slice position synthesizes the full cardiac motion trajectory in the latent space, decoded into a diffeomorphic displacement field that warps end-diastole pixel intensities directly.

Result: On the ACDC benchmark, PhaseFlow achieves superior physiological fidelity and image realism, with best LV volume curve R², structural similarity (SSIM) and generative quality (FID) among all baselines.

Conclusion: PhaseFlow successfully addresses both limitations of prior methods: ECG dependency and lack of physiological constraints. Ablation studies confirm that each proposed component contributes measurably to the overall performance. The method represents a significant advancement in ECG-free cardiac motion synthesis with high clinical relevance.

Abstract: Cine cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) analysis relies on multi-frame sequences capturing the full cardiac cycle. However, standard multi-frame acquisition depends heavily on electrocardiogram (ECG) gating and repeated breath-holds, posing challenges in uncooperative populations, resource-limited settings, and temporally corrupted datasets. Existing methods that synthesize full cardiac sequences either rely on explicit ECG signals to parameterize myocardium function, or employ deformable registration without physiological constraints, failing to faithfully reproduce clinically relevant dynamic metrics such as ejection fraction (EF) and ventricular contraction magnitude. We present PhaseFlow, a unified generative framework that overcomes both limitations. PhaseFlow estimates a non-linear cardiac phase signal directly from the input sequence via a segmentation-derived left-ventricular (LV) area curve, capturing the asymmetric dynamics of systole and diastole without any ECG dependency. At inference, this phase signal is provided by a pathology-specific template, informing phase-specific frame generation. A rectified flow model conditioned on the phase and slice position synthesizes the full cardiac motion trajectory in the latent space, decoded into a diffeomorphic displacement field that warps end-diastole pixel intensities directly, eliminating the reconstruction blur often accompanying the variational autoencoder. On the ACDC benchmark, PhaseFlow achieves superior physiological fidelity and image realism, with best LV volume curve $R^2$, structural similarity (SSIM) and generative quality (FID) among all baselines. Ablation studies confirm that each proposed component contributes measurably to the overall performance.

</details>


### [48] [TiTok: Audio-Visual LLM for Multi-Segment Temporal Grounding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09408)
*Eunji Shin,Dahyun Choi,Seungyeon Jo,Yejin Hong,Jiyoung Lee*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: TiTok is an audio-visual LLM that localizes multiple temporal event segments in untrimmed videos for a given query. It addresses the count miscalibration problem in audio-visual models through Time Token Interleaving (TTI) for precise boundary prediction and decoupled multi-segment-oriented rewards for reinforcement learning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Visual-only models miss complementary acoustic cues, while existing audio-visual models fail to calibrate the number of events (count miscalibration). This limits the ability to reason over audio-visual evidence and predict multiple segments accurately.

Method: TiTok introduces: 1) Time Token Interleaving (TTI) method that injects special time tokens into the audio-visual stream to align input-side temporal perception with output-side temporal prediction; 2) Decoupled multi-segment-oriented rewards for RL (global, local, count, precision, and format rewards) optimized with Group reward-Decoupled Normalization Policy Optimization (GDPO); 3) CountF1 metric to quantify count miscalibration.

Result: TiTok achieves 65.7 mIoU and 0.58 CountF1 on the UnAV-100-based evaluation protocol, establishing state-of-the-art performance.

Conclusion: TiTok effectively addresses the count miscalibration problem in audio-visual multi-segment grounding through TTI and decoupled RL rewards, achieving superior performance over existing methods.

Abstract: Audio-visual multi-segment grounding (AV-MSG) in untrimmed videos, reasoning over audio-visual evidence and predicting multiple segments for a query, is a fundamental problem but remains challenging. Visual-only models overlook complementary acoustic cues, while audio-visual models often fail to calibrate the number of events - a phenomenon we refer to as count miscalibration. We present TiTok, an audio-visual large language model (AV-LLM) that localizes an arbitrary number of temporal event segments for each query. For precise boundary prediction, we introduce the Time Token Interleaving (TTI) method, which explicitly injects special time tokens into the audio-visual stream to align input-side temporal perception with output-side temporal prediction. We further propose decoupled, multi-segment-oriented rewards for reinforcement learning, consisting of global, local, count, precision, and format rewards, optimized with Group reward-Decoupled Normalization Policy Optimization (GDPO). To assess the performance on AV-MSG, we establish a new UnAV-100-based evaluation protocol, and propose the CountF1 metric for quantifying count miscalibration that overlap metrics fail to capture. TiTok reaches 65.7 mIoU and 0.58 CountF1, achieving state-of-the-art performance. Our code is available at this link.

</details>


### [49] [trACT: temporal revelation Airborne Camera Trap](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09417)
*Oliver Bimber,Rakesh John Amala Arokia Nathan,Mohamed Youssef,Vinayak Lal Bhatnagar,Ralf Berger,Klaus Hackländer*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: trACT is a lightweight, real-time aerial robotics framework for autonomous consumer drones that enables effective remote monitoring and surveillance in challenging environments by using Temporal Max Pooling (TMP) to transform subtle movements into robust encodings, combined with self-supervised motion anomaly detection to isolate targets from background motion, and motion prediction with gimbal-stabilized optical zoom verification for precise target tracking.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Remote monitoring and surveillance using drones are frequently impeded by severe environmental and thermal clutter, dynamic vegetation, target camouflage, and system latency. The authors drew inspiration from birds of prey that hover and stabilize their vision to isolate subtle ground motion.

Method: The system integrates: (1) Temporal Max Pooling (TMP) - a low-level signal processing method that transforms imperceptible movement across a rolling integration window into robust value and time encodings; (2) self-supervised motion anomaly detection to isolate target motion from background environmental motion (caused by wind gusts and drone drift); (3) motion prediction combined with automated gimbal-stabilized optical zoom verification; and (4) equitable multi-target verification balancing.

Result: Extensive real-world field experiments in densely forested wildlife habitats and surveillance scenarios demonstrate that trACT successfully bridges the gap between wide-area aerial monitoring and precise, autonomous target verification under challenging operational conditions.

Conclusion: trACT provides an effective solution for autonomous target verification in challenging environments, successfully combining wide-area aerial monitoring with precise target tracking capabilities using consumer drones.

Abstract: Effective remote monitoring and surveillance using drones are frequently impeded by severe environmental and thermal clutter, dynamic vegetation, target camouflage, and system latency. Drawing inspiration from the hunting strategies of birds of prey that hover and stabilize their vision to isolate subtle ground motion, we introduce trACT (temporal revelation Airborne Camera Trap), a lightweight, real-time aerial robotics framework designed for autonomous consumer drones. The system integrates Temporal Max Pooling (TMP), a low-level signal processing method that transforms imperceptible movement across a rolling integration window into robust value and time encodings, with self-supervised motion anomaly detection to isolate target motion from background environmental motion caused by wind gusts and drone drift. To overcome mechanical and processing delays, trACT combines motion prediction with automated gimbal-stabilized optical zoom verification and equitable multi-target verification balancing. Extensive real-world field experiments in densely forested wildlife habitats and surveillance scenarios demonstrate that trACT successfully bridges the gap between wide-area aerial monitoring and precise, autonomous target verification under challenging operational conditions.

</details>


### [50] [Spatial Latent Reasoning for Embodied Reference Understanding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09418)
*Ling Li,Jianhui Zhong,Wei Liu,Zheng Jiang aand Yuxuan Liu,Jingyu Li,Zhidong Deng*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: The paper proposes Spatial Latent Reasoning (SLR), a framework for pointing-gesture visual grounding that structures intermediate supervision around an ordered sequence of geometric and visual states. It introduces parity pooling for constructing visual targets and achieves significant improvements on EgoPoint-Ground and YouRefIt benchmarks across multiple VLM backbones.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Pointing-gesture visual grounding requires connecting hand geometry with visual identity and extent of referred objects. The central challenge is how to organize complementary geometric and visual cues into useful intermediate supervision for continuous latent reasoning.

Method: The proposed SLR framework structures supervision around an ordered sequence of states: (1) a spatial ray state supervised by fingertip position and pointing direction, followed by (2) four states aligned with target-region features. Parity pooling is introduced to construct visual targets by applying polyphase grouping to average region tokens on four interleaved spatial supports. All states are generated recurrently during both training and inference, with auxiliary annotations required only during training.

Result: On EgoPoint-Ground, SLR improves mIoU over same-backbone supervised fine-tuning by 2.8, 17.5, and 21.1 percentage points on Qwen3.5-4B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, and Qwen3-VL-8B respectively, with improvements on both hard subsets. On YouRefIt, it achieves 77.6% precision at IoU 0.5, a 5.2 percentage point margin over the reported state of the art. Ablations support joint geometric and visual supervision and favor parity pooling over three alternative pooling operators.

Conclusion: The results support task-structured supervision for continuous pointing grounding. The framework demonstrates that organizing geometric and visual cues into structured intermediate supervision significantly improves performance across multiple VLM architectures.

Abstract: Pointing-gesture visual grounding requires connecting hand geometry with the visual identity and extent of a referred object. A central challenge for continuous latent reasoning is how to organize these complementary cues into useful intermediate supervision. We propose Spatial Latent Reasoning (SLR), a framework that structures this supervision around an ordered sequence of geometric and visual states. A spatial ray state is supervised by fingertip position and pointing direction, followed by four states aligned with target-region features. To construct the visual targets, we introduce parity pooling, which applies polyphase grouping to average region tokens on four interleaved spatial supports. All states are generated recurrently during training and inference; auxiliary annotations are required only during training. On EgoPoint-Ground, the framework improves mIoU over same-backbone supervised fine-tuning by 2.8, 17.5, and 21.1 percentage points on Qwen3.5-4B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, and Qwen3-VL-8B, respectively, with improvements on both hard subsets. On YouRefIt, it achieves 77.6% precision at IoU 0.5, a numerical margin of 5.2 percentage points over the reported state of the art under differing evaluation protocols. Ablations support joint geometric and visual supervision on the standard and similar-object sets, and favor parity over three alternative pooling operators on the standard set. These results support task-structured supervision for continuous pointing grounding. We will release the code and supporting materials.

</details>


### [51] [Event-Aligned Visual Action Reasoning for World Action Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09427)
*Xiaomeng Yang,Yushu Wu,Yi Gao,Yuhao Lei,Xuan Zhang,Pu Zhao,Yanzhi Wang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper introduces an event-aligned visual action reasoning framework for World-Action Models (WAMs) that organizes visual foresight around interaction events rather than predefined temporal intervals. The key contributions include: (1) event-aligned visual-action supervision that generates visual context focused on task-critical state changes, and (2) an execution validity head that identifies valid portions of predicted action sequences to avoid redundant actions during chunked inference.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing WAMs structure visual imagination according to predefined temporal intervals without explicitly accounting for the different roles of task-critical interactions and connecting transitions. The authors argue that effective visual foresight should align directly with task-relevant interactions and their corresponding reasoning demands, rather than using uniform temporal segmentation.

Method: The paper proposes two key innovations: (1) Event-aligned visual-action supervision - organizes visual-action prediction around interaction events, generating event-aligned visual context in each imagined rollout with detailed reasoning around critical events and coarser progression through connecting transitions; (2) Execution validity head - identifies the valid portion of each predicted action sequence to avoid redundant actions during chunked inference.

Result: The method achieves a 10.26 percentage point improvement in DOMINO success rate over baseline and competitive performance on RoboTwin 2.0. It also demonstrates successful transfer from DOMINO Level 1 to Levels 2 and 3 without target-level adaptation.

Conclusion: The event-aligned visual action reasoning framework effectively shapes visual reasoning granularity according to underlying interaction dynamics. The approach shows strong cross-level transfer capability, suggesting that learning event-aligned reasoning at one difficulty level can generalize to more complex tasks without additional training.

Abstract: World-Action Models (WAMs) utilize future visual prediction as an intermediate reasoning process to guide action generation. However, existing WAMs typically structure visual imagination according to predefined temporal intervals, without explicitly accounting for the different roles of task-critical interactions and connecting transitions. We argue that effective visual foresight should align directly with task-relevant interactions and their corresponding reasoning demands. To this end, we introduce an event-aligned visual action reasoning framework that organizes visual-action prediction around interaction events. Through event-aligned visual-action supervision, WAM learns to generate event-aligned visual context in each imagined rollout, placing greater emphasis on critical state changes that inform action generation. This shapes the visual reasoning granularity according to the underlying interaction dynamics, with detailed reasoning around task-critical events and coarser progression through connecting transitions. Furthermore, we introduce an execution validity head that identifies the valid portion of each predicted action sequence, avoiding redundant actions during chunked inference. Experiments demonstrate a 10.26 percentage point improvement in DOMINO success rate over baseline and competitive performance on RoboTwin 2.0. It also transfers from DOMINO Level 1 to Levels 2 and 3 without target-level adaptation.

</details>


### [52] [SkillCycle: Co-Evolving Agent Policies and Skill Banks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09430)
*Ling Li,Qiuyu Shen,Zheng Jiang,Qinwei Ma,Yuxuan Liu,Zhidong Deng*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: SkillCycle is a framework that co-evolves agent policies and skill banks through a feedback loop, where token-level contextual differences locate rules for inspection while interaction outcomes guide edits to their content. It achieves 74.74% success rate and 88.37 score on WebShop without inference-time skill inputs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: When language agents internalize external skills, their capabilities change, making existing rules potentially redundant, misleading, or insufficient. This creates a coupled problem of learning from skills while simultaneously adapting the skills that supervise further learning.

Method: SkillCycle alternates between two phases: (1) policy learning with a fixed skill bank and router, and (2) rule revision with a frozen policy. Candidate edits undergo both rule-level and whole-bank environment comparisons before guiding the next learning cycle. The framework gives distillation feedback a dual role - token-level contextual differences help locate rules for inspection, while interaction outcomes guide edits to their content and applicability.

Result: On WebShop with a 3B model: 74.74% success rate and 88.37 score without inference-time skill inputs, representing 0.73% and 3.96% relative improvements over SOTA. In Cycle 3 ablations on ALFWorld and WebShop, no-skill success rates improve by 10.18% and 18.11% relative to static skill bank, and by 2.41% and 2.50% relative to single bank update.

Conclusion: Continually revising skill guidance as the agent's capabilities change helps transform external skills into policy capabilities that require no skill inputs at inference, demonstrating the value of co-evolving policies and skill banks.

Abstract: Internalizing external skills changes a language agent's capabilities and, with them, the value of its remaining guidance: rules can become redundant, misleading, or insufficient for newly encountered decisions. This creates a coupled problem of learning from skills and adapting the skills that supervise further learning. We introduce SkillCycle, a framework for co-evolving agent policies and skill banks through a feedback loop between skill internalization and rule revision. Our central contribution is to give distillation feedback a second role: token-level contextual differences help locate rules for inspection, while interaction outcomes guide edits to their content and applicability. SkillCycle alternates between two phases: policy learning with a fixed skill bank and router, and rule revision with a frozen policy. Candidate edits undergo rule-level and whole-bank environment comparisons before they guide the next learning cycle. On WebShop, SkillCycle with a 3B model achieves a success rate of 74.74% and a score of 88.37 without inference-time skill inputs, representing relative improvements of 0.73% and 3.96% over the state-of-the-art (SOTA) model, respectively. In Cycle 3 ablations on ALFWorld and WebShop, SkillCycle's no-skill success rates improve by 10.18% and 18.11% relative to a static skill bank, and by 2.41% and 2.50% relative to a single bank update, respectively. These results show that continually revising skill guidance as the agent's capabilities change helps transform external skills into policy capabilities that require no skill inputs at inference. We will release code, configurations, skill banks, and evaluation protocols.

</details>


### [53] [Controllable Crowd Generation through World-Model Planning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09438)
*JunGyu Lee,Jisu Shin,Seunghyun Shin,Hae-Gon Jeon*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Ctrl-CWM is a multi-agent Controllable Crowd World Model that integrates crowd generation with run-time control by adapting world-model planning principles to crowd simulation. It consists of an encoder (learns human motion dynamics from trajectory prediction), actor (proposes displacements), critic (evaluates trajectories), and planner (selects actions). The method can adapt to new user-specified objectives without retraining.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing crowd simulation methods rely on predefined control settings and have limited flexibility in accommodating new user-specified objectives. Applications like robot navigation, autonomous driving, and urban planning require crowds to adapt to environmental changes and user objectives, but current approaches cannot easily introduce new control objectives at runtime.

Method: Ctrl-CWM consists of four components: (1) Encoder that learns human motion dynamics through trajectory prediction on real-world pedestrian videos, then frozen to preserve dynamics; (2) Actor that generates imagined crowd trajectories through repeated state updates using the learned representation; (3) Critic that evaluates imagined crowd trajectories; (4) Planner that combines critic scores with user costs to select actions. The system learns human motion dynamics first, then uses repeated planning to advance the simulated crowd while allowing additional user costs to introduce new control objectives without retraining.

Result: Ctrl-CWM outperforms the state-of-the-art method on most crowd realism and collision metrics. It successfully adapts crowd behaviors to user-specified objectives introduced during simulation. Evaluations were conducted under varied agent arrival conditions and run-time control across avoidance and attraction scenarios.

Conclusion: Ctrl-CWM provides a flexible framework for controllable crowd simulation that can adapt to new user objectives without retraining. The world-model approach successfully integrates crowd generation with run-time control, achieving superior performance in crowd realism and collision metrics compared to existing methods.

Abstract: Crowd simulation plays a central role in robot navigation, autonomous driving, and urban planning. For these applications, realistic simulation requires crowds to adapt their behavior to environmental changes and user objectives. However, existing methods that rely on predefined control settings have limited flexibility in accommodating new user-specified objectives. To address this limitation, we propose Ctrl-CWM, a multi-agent Controllable Crowd World Model that integrates crowd generation and run-time control. Our key idea is to adapt the world-model principle of planning using imagined futures to crowd simulation. To this end, Ctrl-CWM consists of an encoder that learns a representation of human motion dynamics, an actor that proposes pedestrian displacements, a critic that evaluates imagined crowd trajectories, and a planner that selects actions. We first learn human motion dynamics through trajectory prediction on real-world pedestrian videos and then freeze the encoder to preserve them. Using this representation, the actor generates imagined crowd trajectories through repeated state updates, and the planner combines the critic's scores with user costs to select actions. Repeated planning advances the simulated crowd, while additional user costs introduce new control objectives without retraining. We extensively evaluate crowd generation under varied agent arrival conditions and run-time control across avoidance and attraction scenarios. Ctrl-CWM outperforms the state-of-the-art method on most crowd realism and collision metrics, and adapts crowd behaviors to user-specified objectives introduced during simulation. The project page is available at https://jungyu0413.github.io/Ctrl-CWM

</details>


### [54] [InscriptionOCR: A Dataset and Method for Understanding Inscriptions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09439)
*Jaidev Sanjay Khalane,Akbar Ali,V. N. Prabhakar,Shanmuganathan Raman*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: An end-to-end AI framework for analyzing ancient Ashokan Brahmi inscriptions, featuring image restoration, OCR, transliteration to Roman script, and neural machine translation from Prakrit to English, accompanied by two new datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The degraded nature of ancient inscription imagery and the lack of standardized digital resources for Ashokan Brahmi script (3rd century BC) pose significant challenges for automated processing and computational analysis of historical documents.

Method: The proposed pipeline processes low-quality stone inscription images through four stages: (1) image enhancement/restoration, (2) Brahmi script character recognition via OCR, (3) transliteration to Roman script, and (4) neural machine translation from Prakrit to English.

Result: Two new datasets were created: (i) InscriptionOCR Dataset - the largest publicly usable Brahmi OCR dataset with over 200,000 character images across approximately 600 classes, and (ii) a bilingual Prakrit-English parallel corpus with over 2,000 sentence pairs for NMT training.

Conclusion: The proposed framework and datasets will facilitate future research in ancient script analysis, low-resource OCR, and digital epigraphy by providing the first comprehensive AI pipeline for Brahmi inscription interpretation.

Abstract: Ancient script image restoration is a fundamental problem in computer vision, as it directly affects the reliable analysis and interpretation of historical documents and inscriptions. Ashokan Brahmi is an ancient script extensively used during the reign of Emperor Ashoka in the 3rd century BC, primarily for inscriptions in Prakrit. These inscriptions, including major and minor rock and pillar edicts, constitute a valuable yet largely unexplored source of data for computational analysis. The degraded nature of inscription imagery and the lack of standardized digital resources pose significant challenges for automated processing.
  We present an end-to-end AI-based framework for understanding ancient inscriptions that encompasses image enhancement, optical character recognition (OCR), transliteration, and neural machine translation (NMT). The proposed pipeline processes low-quality images captured directly from stone inscriptions, performs image restoration and Brahmi script character recognition, maps the recognized characters to the Roman script, and finally translates the resulting Prakrit text into English. We also introduce two new datasets: (i) InscriptionOCR Dataset: the largest publicly usable digital OCR dataset for Brahmi script to date, consisting of over 200,000 character images across about 600 classes, and (ii) a bilingual Prakrit-English parallel corpus comprising over 2,000 sentence pairs for NMT. We believe that the proposed framework and datasets will facilitate future research in ancient script analysis, low-resource OCR, and digital epigraphy.

</details>


### [55] [Mixture of Layers: Dynamic Layer Routing for Visual Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09440)
*Jeonghwan Kim,Sofia Stoica,Jiwan Chung,Ansel Blume,Hyeonjeong Ha,Zhenhailong Wang,Xin Luna Dong,Heng Ji*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: MoL is a query-adaptive layer routing mechanism for MLLMs that dynamically selects and aggregates features from intermediate vision encoder layers based on the input text query, achieving significant improvements on fine-grained visual reasoning tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current MLLMs rely only on final or penultimate vision encoder representations using fixed aggregation rules, making visual abstraction largely query-agnostic. This limits access to fine-grained visual cues such as small objects, spatial details, text, and subtle visual attributes that are present in intermediate layers.

Method: Mixture of Layers (MoL) - an instruction-conditioned layer routing approach at the visual patch level. Given a text query, MoL predicts routing probabilities over vision encoder layers and performs top-k sparse aggregation over selected hidden states at image level, patch level, or through hybrid routing. This enables query-adaptive access to layer-specific visual features for fine-grained visual reasoning.

Result: Substantial performance improvements across 7 fine-grained visual reasoning tasks: +18.9% on V* (overall accuracy), +4.5% on HRBench4K, and +16.3% on CharXiv compared to baseline MLLMs, without using multi-resolution inputs, multiple vision encoders, or additional patch tokens.

Conclusion: MoL represents a significant advancement in multimodal learning by enabling query-adaptive access to layer-specific visual features. The approach demonstrates that intermediate vision encoder layers contain valuable fine-grained information that static pooling methods discard. By dynamically routing to relevant layers based on the text query, MoL achieves substantial performance gains across multiple fine-grained visual reasoning benchmarks without increasing computational overhead through higher resolution inputs or additional vision encoders. The analysis of layer receptive fields provides important insights into why layer-wise sampling is effective - different layers encode different abstraction levels suitable for different reasoning tasks.

Abstract: Pre-trained vision encoders contain layer-wise visual representations that differ in spatial granularity, semantic abstraction, and sensitivity to local details. However, most Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) rely on only the final or penultimate vision encoder representations or fixed aggregation rules, making visual abstraction largely query-agnostic and limiting access to fine-grained cues such as small objects, spatial details, text, and subtle visual attributes. In this work, we propose Mixture of Layers (MoL), an instruction-conditioned layer routing approach at the visual patch level that dynamically aggregates query-relevant latent representations from intermediate vision encoder layers. Given a text query, MoL predicts routing probabilities over vision encoder layers and performs a top-k sparse aggregation over selected hidden states at either the image level, patch level, or through a hybrid routing mechanism. In doing so, MoL enables query-adaptive access to layer-specific visual features for fine-grained visual reasoning. Our experiments across 7 fine-grained visual reasoning tasks demonstrate substantial performance improvements, especially across fine-grained visual grounding and understanding tasks such as +18.9% improvement on V* in overall accuracy, +4.5% on HRBench4K, and +16.3% on CharXiv compared to the baseline MLLMs, without resorting to multi-resolution inputs, simple interleaving of multiple vision encoders, or increasing the number of patch tokens. We study vision encoders' receptive field scales across different layers and their sampling behaviors to provide an in-depth analysis of why layer-wise sampling is helpful, demonstrating that conditional visual representations are a key step towards better visual perception and reasoning in MLLMs. Our project page is available at https://wjdghks950.github.io/mol.github.io/.

</details>


### [56] [TIRA: Tumor Immune Representation Adaptation for Zero-Shot Cross-Cancer MSI and TMB Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09441)
*Dasari Naga Raju*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: TIRA is a target-free framework that adapts frozen pathology foundation model representations using spatial immune topology for cross-cancer prediction of MSI-H and TMB-H biomarkers, without requiring target-domain data during training or adaptation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current histopathological prediction models for MSI-H and TMB-H biomarkers struggle when transferred across morphologically distinct cancer types. While immune-associated spatial patterns persist across cancers, existing foundation-model-based predictors trained on single cancers don't leverage this information, limiting cross-cancer generalization.

Method: TIRA uses a topology-supervised biology representation to condition tile-level attention while pooling only morphological features for joint MSI and TMB prediction. The framework refines frozen foundation-model representations using spatial immune topology without requiring target-domain data during model development or test-time adaptation. Training was performed on TCGA-COAD+READ, and evaluation used three foundation models (UNI2, CONCH, Virchow2) across multiple datasets.

Result: With UNI2, TIRA improved zero-shot AUROC on TCGA-STAD from 0.633 to 0.766 for MSI and from 0.651 to 0.772 for TMB. The method was evaluated on CPTAC-COAD, TCGA-STAD, TCGA-UCEC, and CPTAC-UCEC, covering cross-site, cross-cancer, and combined cross-cancer-site distribution shifts.

Conclusion: Source-derived spatial immune topology improves the cross-cancer robustness of frozen pathology foundation-model representations, enabling effective zero-shot transfer of MSI and TMB prediction across different cancer types without requiring target-domain data or test-time adaptation.

Abstract: Microsatellite instability-high (MSI-H) and high tumor mutational burden (TMB-H) are clinically relevant biomarkers, yet their histopathological prediction remains challenging when models are transferred across morphologically distinct cancer types. Immune-associated spatial patterns can persist across cancers despite these morphological differences, but foundation-model-based predictors trained on a single cancer do not explicitly use this information, limiting cross-cancer generalization. To address this limitation, we propose TIRA (Tumor Immune Representation Adaptation), a target-free framework that refines frozen foundation-model representations using spatial immune topology, without requiring target-domain data during model development or test-time adaptation. TIRA uses a topology-supervised biology representation to condition tile-level attention while pooling only morphological features for joint MSI and TMB prediction. We train TIRA on TCGA-COAD+READ and evaluate it zero-shot on CPTAC-COAD, TCGA-STAD, TCGA-UCEC, and CPTAC-UCEC, covering cross-site, cross-cancer, and combined cross-cancer-site distribution shifts under UNI2, CONCH, and Virchow2. With UNI2, TIRA improved zero-shot AUROC on TCGA-STAD from 0.633 to 0.766 for MSI and from 0.651 to 0.772 for TMB. Source-derived spatial immune topology improved the cross-cancer robustness of frozen pathology foundation-model representations.

</details>


### [57] [LighTROcc: Lightweight 4D Occupancy Forecasting via Instance-Centric 3D Gaussians](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09444)
*Hwanhee Jung,SeungHyeon Kim,Inkyu Koo,Qixing Huang,Sang Ho Yoon,Sangpil Kim*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: LighTROcc is a lightweight instance-centric framework for camera-based 4D occupancy forecasting in autonomous driving. It represents movable objects using compact learned queries and predicts present and future occupancy in a single forward pass, modeling instances as anisotropic 3D Gaussians propagated via predicted displacements.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing 3D occupancy forecasting methods rely on dense voxel or bird's-eye-view representations that suffer from high computational cost (growing with resolution and prediction horizon) and lack explicit object identity maintenance, leading to poor instance consistency over time.

Method: LighTROcc uses attention-guided forward lifting combining image-space cross-attention, query-specific depth, and camera geometry to estimate 3D centers. Each instance is modeled as a mixture of anisotropic 3D Gaussians and propagated across future timesteps using predicted displacements, enabling continuous and temporally consistent occupancy forecasts in a single forward pass.

Result: LighTROcc outperforms evaluated dense and instance-wise baselines in instance-level forecasting accuracy while maintaining strong voxel-level occupancy quality on nuScenes and nuScenes-Occupancy datasets. It achieves favorable balance between forecasting accuracy and computational efficiency.

Conclusion: Compact instance-centric modeling demonstrates strong potential for camera-based 4D occupancy forecasting, offering an efficient alternative to dense representations while preserving instance consistency across time.

Abstract: Forecasting future 3D occupancy from surround-view cameras is essential for autonomous driving, yet existing approaches rely on dense voxel or bird's-eye-view representations whose cost grows rapidly with spatial resolution and prediction horizon. Because these representations do not explicitly maintain object identities, they also struggle to preserve instance consistency over time. We present LighTROcc, a lightweight instance-centric framework that represents movable objects with a compact set of learned queries and predicts present and future occupancy in a single forward pass. LighTROcc localizes each query through attention-guided forward lifting, combining image-space cross-attention, query-specific depth, and camera geometry to estimate its 3D center. Each instance is modeled as a mixture of anisotropic 3D Gaussians and propagated across future steps using predicted displacements, producing continuous, temporally consistent occupancy forecasts. Experiments on nuScenes and supplemented nuScenes-Occupancy show that LighTROcc outperforms the evaluated dense and instance-wise baselines in instance-level forecasting accuracy while maintaining strong voxel-level occupancy quality. Across different model configurations, LighTROcc achieves a favorable balance between forecasting accuracy and computational efficiency, demonstrating the potential of compact instance-centric modeling for camera-based 4D occupancy forecasting.

</details>


### [58] [From Global Alignment to Local Grounding: Zero-Shot Chinese Character Recognition with Radical Verification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09449)
*Yu-Heng Shih,Bing-Chen Wu,Tsz-To Wong,Ting-En Yen,Hong-Han Shuai,Bin-Hua Hsieh,Chien-An Chen,Yi-Ren Yeh,Ching-Chun Huang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper proposes a global-to-local two-stage framework for zero-shot Chinese character recognition (ZS-CCR). The method augments Ideographic Description Sequences (IDS) with explicit geometric priors (STG-CLIP) for high-recall global retrieval, followed by a Radical Verification Module (RVM) that performs radical-level matching to refine rankings. The method achieves 83.06% top-1 accuracy on ICDAR2013 with 2,755 seen classes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current CLIP-style ZS-CCR methods rely on single global image-IDS similarity that discards spatial layout of radicals, leading to poor generalization to unseen classes. Additionally, global matching often retrieves the correct character but fails to rank it first when characters differ only in subtle local radicals.

Method: The proposed framework consists of two stages: (1) STG-CLIP augments IDS with explicit tree-position and radical-level geometric priors, yielding a spatial-aware prototype for high-recall global retrieval; (2) RVM uses radical instances of each retrieved candidate as queries to verify whether corresponding radicals can be matched to spatially compatible regions in the input glyph. A margin-based gating rule activates RVM only when top candidates have similar similarity scores.

Result: State-of-the-art performance on ICDAR2013 benchmark under character-level zero-shot setting: 83.06% top-1 accuracy with 2,755 seen classes. Ablation studies show that explicit geometric priors and radical-level verification provide complementary improvements.

Conclusion: The combination of spatial-aware prototypes with explicit geometric priors and radical-level verification effectively addresses the limitations of global-only matching in ZS-CCR, achieving superior performance through complementary improvements from both components.

Abstract: Zero-shot Chinese character recognition (ZS-CCR) aims to recognize characters whose categories are never observed during training, and typically relies on the compositional structure shared between seen and unseen characters. Recent CLIP-style methods represent this structure with the Ideographic Description Sequence (IDS) and align it with glyph images in a shared embedding space. However, they rely on a single global image--IDS similarity that discards the spatial layout of radicals and, being learned only implicitly from seen classes, generalizes poorly to unseen ones; moreover, global matching often retrieves the correct character within the top candidates yet fails to rank it first when characters differ only in subtle local radicals. To address these issues, we propose a global-to-local two-stage framework. In the first stage, STG-CLIP augments the IDS with explicit tree-position and radical-level geometric priors, yielding a spatial-aware prototype that provides a consistent spatial description across seen and unseen categories for high-recall global retrieval. In the second stage, the Radical Verification Module (RVM) uses the radical instances of each retrieved candidate as queries to verify whether the corresponding radicals can be matched to spatially compatible regions in the input glyph. A margin-based gating rule activates the RVM only when the leading global candidates receive similar similarity scores. Experiments on the ICDAR2013 benchmark demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance under the character-level zero-shot setting, obtaining 83.06% top-1 accuracy with 2,755 seen classes. Ablation studies further show that the explicit geometric priors and radical-level verification provide complementary improvements.

</details>


### [59] [Iris-3B: Going Beyond the Latent with Pixel-Space Diffusion Training, Conversion and Fine-Tuning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09450)
*Hanqiu Li Cai,Chema Garabito*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether pixel-space diffusion models outperform latent models on downstream tasks requiring fine-grained detail. The authors pretrained Iris-3B (a 3B pixel-space transformer) and converted FLUX.2 Klein to pixel space, then fine-tuned both for depth estimation and image restoration. They found no significant advantage from pixel-space generative priors.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Pixel-space diffusion models avoid the lossy VAE encoding used in latent models, which should theoretically preserve more fine-grained detail. This paper tests whether this architectural difference translates to practical improvements on downstream tasks requiring precise detail reproduction.

Method: The authors pursued two approaches: (1) training Iris-3B from scratch through a 256→512→1024 curriculum after ablating prediction target and representation alignment at 256², and (2) converting a pretrained latent model (FLUX.2 Klein base 4B) to pixel space. Both pixel-space models and the latent FLUX.2 Klein were then fine-tuned for monocular depth estimation and 4× super-resolution on DIV2K.

Result: No significant improvement was found from pixel-space generative priors. For depth estimation, Iris-3B matched latent FLUX.2 Klein, while converted pixel FLUX.2 Klein fell behind. For 4× DIV2K restoration, neither pixel model beat latent FLUX.2 Klein, with the converted model trailing slightly. However, Iris-3B demonstrated that pixel-space pretraining scales to 3B parameters and achieves competitive text-to-image quality, matching Qwen-Image on OneIG at 1024².

Conclusion: Pixel-space pretraining does not provide significant advantages over latent models for downstream fine-grained tasks. The negative result may be due to documented failure modes and remaining confounds. Nevertheless, Iris-3B proves that pixel-space generation can scale effectively and achieve competitive quality, paving the way for future research.

Abstract: Pixel-space diffusion models avoid the lossy VAE of latent models, which suggests an advantage on downstream tasks where fine-grained detail matters. We test this claim along both routes to a pixel-space backbone. We pretrain Iris-3B, a 3B-parameter pixel-space text-to-image transformer, from scratch through a $256\to512\to1024$ curriculum, after first ablating the prediction target and representation alignment at $256^2$ to decide what to scale. We also convert a pretrained latent model, FLUX.2 Klein base 4B, to pixel space. We fine-tune both families for monocular depth estimation and for image restoration/super-resolution. We find no significant improvement from using a pixel-space generative prior. Fine-tuned for depth with one matched direct-regression recipe, Iris-3B is level with the latent FLUX.2 Klein and the converted pixel FLUX.2 Klein falls behind it, and on $4\times$ DIV2K restoration neither pixel model beats a latent FLUX.2 Klein fine-tune, the converted one trailing it slightly. We document the recipes, the failure modes and the remaining confounds behind this negative result. Nevertheless, Iris-3B shows that pixel-space pretraining with the pixel-transformer (PiT) head of PixelDiT scales to 3B parameters and to text-to-image quality competitive with latent models, matching Qwen-Image on OneIG under the official evaluators at $1024^2$. We release its weights and training code in the hope that they help pave the way for further work on pixel-space generation.

</details>


### [60] [RLHND: Video Foundation Models as Physically Grounded Hand Trackers for Robot Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09455)
*Seungjun Moon,Subin Jeon,Sangwoo Kim,Hanbyul Joo,Jinwoo Shin*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: RLHND is a video foundation model-based hand tracking model that jointly estimates hand pose and realistic tactile information (contact and force) from monocular egocentric videos, leveraging the Cosmos 3 video diffusion backbone as a feature extractor.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing hand trackers regress pose from cropped frames with limited priors on hand motion and object interaction, resulting in inaccurate and physically inconsistent estimates. Additionally, the lack of physical cues (contact and force) limits the use of human videos for robot policy training.

Method: RLHND converts the pre-trained Cosmos 3 video diffusion backbone into a deterministic clip-level feature extractor via clean-latent conditioning. For pose estimation, it predicts hand poses with anatomically plausible joint angles and allows optional conditioning on shape parameters for consistent hand shape. A separate tactile expert stream predicts dense contact and force over the hand surface. LBS-based feature spreading enables vertex-wise feature extraction without costly per-vertex attention.

Result: RLHND achieves state-of-the-art performance across various benchmark datasets for pose estimation, while also achieving state-of-the-art performance in contact and force estimation. Demonstrated utility for robot learning through retargeting results and real-world robot experiments.

Conclusion: The proposed RLHND successfully addresses limitations in existing hand tracking methods by combining pose and tactile estimation using a video foundation model, enabling more effective utilization of human videos for robot policy training.

Abstract: Recently, approaches that leverage human video datasets for robot policy training have become increasingly prevalent. However, most existing hand trackers regress pose from cropped frames with limited priors on hand motion and object interaction, resulting in inaccurate and physically inconsistent estimates. Moreover, the lack of physical cues, e.g., contact and force, limits the use of human videos for robot policy training. To this end, we propose RLHND, a video foundation model-based hand tracking model that jointly estimates hand pose and realistic tactile information from monocular egocentric videos. RLHND turns the pre-trained Cosmos 3 video diffusion backbone into a deterministic clip-level feature extractor via clean-latent conditioning, carrying its learned priors on hand motion and hand-object interaction into tracking. For pose estimation, RLHND (i) predicts hand poses with anatomically plausible joint angles and (ii) enables optional conditioning on the shape parameter to maintain consistent hand shape within the same video and even across videos recorded by the same actor. For tactile estimation, a separate tactile expert stream, trained with the pose stream frozen, predicts dense contact and force over the hand surface. We further adopt LBS-based feature spreading to enable vertex-wise feature extraction without costly per-vertex attention. RLHND achieves state-of-the-art performance across various benchmark datasets for pose estimation, while also achieving state-of-the-art performance in contact and force estimation. Moreover, we demonstrate the utility of RLHND for robot learning through retargeting results and real-world robot experiments. The code will be publicly available at https://seungjun-moon.github.io/rlhnd/.

</details>


### [61] [An Invariant Tangent-Angle Descriptor and a Band U-Net for 2D Fragment Adjacency Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09459)
*Guillaume Brouillette,Alain Goupil,Pierre-Olivier Parisé,Fadel Touré*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper improves upon a two-stage architecture for predicting adjacency between 2D fragments by replacing image-window scoring with tangent-angle profile comparison (rotation-invariant and contour-starting point agnostic), and substituting the final classifier with a band U-Net. The proposed method achieves 98% accuracy on synthetic data and AUC of 0.93 on PairingNet benchmark, significantly outperforming the original approach.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The original two-stage architecture from Beaulac's thesis used rotation-equivariant Siamese CNN with image windows, which had limitations: sensitivity to contour-starting point selection and dependence on training data. The authors aimed to create a more robust, rotation-invariant method that could work better on real-world data.

Method: 1) Replaced local image window scoring with tangent-angle profile comparison of contour windows (rotation-invariant by construction and agnostic to contour-starting point). This can be implemented as either: a) training-free likelihood ratio, or b) small 1D convolutional model trained on corresponding points. 2) Replaced final classifier (ResNet detecting partial anti-diagonal band) with a band U-Net that segments the band and classifies the pair simultaneously, extracting the shared arc along with the decision.

Result: On synthetic dataset: tangent descriptor performs as well as or better than image-window approach in all tested configurations; accuracy improved from 93-95% to 98%. On PairingNet benchmark: AUC of 0.93. Under PairingNet pair-searching protocol: Recall@10 of 0.82 on real set (vs 0.56 for original best model).

Conclusion: The tangent-angle profile approach combined with band U-Net significantly outperforms the original image-window based method. The rotation-invariant tangent descriptor is more robust and effective, achieving substantial improvements in both accuracy and recall metrics, especially on real-world data.

Abstract: This paper addresses the prediction of adjacency between pairs of 2D fragments based on their contours. We improved the two-stage architecture proposed in Beaulac's thesis, in which a rotation-equivariant Siamese convolutional neural network scores pairs of local image windows along the two contours of two fragments. The scores are gathered in an adjacency matrix in which a ResNet detects the partial anti-diagonal band that reveals the adjacency of two fragments. In the current work, we keep the pipeline and replace the local score by a comparison of tangent-angle profiles of contour windows, making it, by construction, invariant to fragment rotation and agnostic to the selected contour-starting point. These adaptations may be either a training-free likelihood ratio or a small one-dimensional convolutional model trained on corresponding points. We also replaced the final classifier by a band U-Net that segments the band and classifies the pair, so that the shared arc is obtained along with the decision. In the synthetic data set of the original thesis, the tangent descriptor performs as well as or better than the image-window approach in all tested configurations. The proposed pipeline reaches an accuracy of 98%, vs 93% to 95% for the original approach once its evaluation is corrected. We tested our pipeline, with models trained only on synthetic data, on the PairingNet benchmark, and obtained an AUC of 0.93. Furthermore, under the PairingNet pair-searching protocol conditions, our learned descriptor obtains a Recall@10 of 0.82 on the real set against 0.56 from the best model of the original paper.

</details>


### [62] [InstanceBench: Diagnosing Referential Reasoning and Target Identity in Referring Expression Segmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09478)
*Yuchen Li,Shaoyang Zhou,Yiran Wang,Ruiyi Deng,Haoyu Wang,Ziru Wei,Zhen Zhao,Luping Zhou*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: InstanceBench is a diagnostic benchmark for Referring Expression Segmentation (RES) that addresses limitations in standard evaluation by providing instance-level analysis of referential reasoning. It comprises 6,194 images with 9,264 target instances and 25,077 human-verified expressions, using target-centric expression sets (TCES) to test target preservation across different grounding paths.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard RES evaluation provides limited insight into instance-level reasoning: it does not distinguish referential logics, test target preservation across valid grounding paths, or separate target-selection from mask-generation errors. The authors needed a benchmark that can diagnose specific failure modes in RES models.

Method: The benchmark uses: (1) Target-centric expression sets (TCES) - fixing image and target mask while pairing minimal expressions with same-target variants using different cues/grounding paths; (2) A referential-logic taxonomy spanning direct target evidence, same-class selection, relational/compositional grounding, and exclusion; (3) Logic-critical construction to suppress simpler shortcuts; (4) Identity-aware metrics to measure target retention while separating selection from mask-generation errors.

Result: Across 22 native-mask RES checkpoints from 18 model families, the strongest checkpoint achieves 67.1% mIoU but only 59.6% All@0.7. Controlled interventions confirm language sensitivity. Failure decomposition shows target selection (not mask decoding) is the main bottleneck. Matched supervision on a training subset improves identity-aware performance.

Conclusion: InstanceBench enables a measure-diagnose-improve cycle: measuring target consistency across grounding paths, localizing failure sources, and evaluating targeted interventions. The benchmark reveals that current RES models struggle more with target selection than mask generation, and that language understanding is a critical factor.

Abstract: Referring Expression Segmentation (RES) links natural-language descriptions to pixel-level object masks. Yet standard evaluation provides limited insight into instance-level referential reasoning: it does not systematically distinguish referential logics, test target preservation across valid grounding paths, or separate target-selection from mask-generation errors. We introduce InstanceBench, an instance-centered diagnostic benchmark comprising 6,194 images, 9,264 target instances, and 25,077 human-verified expressions. Each target-centric expression set (TCES) fixes the image and target mask while pairing a minimal expression with a same-target variant that uses another valid cue or grounding path. A compact referential-logic taxonomy spans direct target evidence, same-class selection, relational and compositional grounding, and exclusion, while logic-critical construction suppresses simpler shortcuts. Identity-aware metrics measure target retention and set-level success while separating selection from mask-generation errors. Across 22 native-mask RES checkpoints from 18 model families, the strongest checkpoint reaches 67.1% mIoU but only 59.6% All@0.7. Controlled interventions confirm language sensitivity, while failure decomposition identifies target selection rather than mask decoding as the main bottleneck. On a controlled training subset, matched supervision improves identity-aware performance, showing that the diagnosed capability responds to targeted supervision. Collectively, InstanceBench supports a measure-diagnose-improve cycle: measuring target consistency across grounding paths, localizing failure sources, and evaluating targeted interventions.

</details>


### [63] [Gaussian Material Fields for Volumetric Multi-Energy CT Decomposition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09492)
*Jian Lin,Jiancheng Fang,Hongming Shan,Shaoyu Wang,Yang Chen,Qiegen Liu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper introduces Gaussian material fields, a novel representation for volumetric multi-material decomposition in multi-energy CT. It uses shared anisotropic 3D Gaussian primitives with independent nonnegative coefficients to represent multiple material distributions, combined with a differentiable spectral forward model and material-aware adaptive density control.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Volumetric material decomposition in multi-energy computed tomography requires representing multiple 3D material fields in a common spatial domain while retaining differences in composition and local structure. Existing methods struggle to share spatial primitives across materials without tying their coefficients, and lack adaptive capacity for material-specific reconstruction needs.

Method: The authors introduce Gaussian material fields using shared anisotropic 3D Gaussian primitives with independent nonnegative material coefficients. A differentiable spectral forward model combines Gaussian material path integrals with a calibrated basis matrix for joint optimization of spatial geometry and material composition. Material-aware adaptive density control retains material-specific refinement evidence before aggregation and adjusts local representation capacity for both extensive components and sparse details.

Result: Across 15 cases using synthesized multi-energy projections from pseudo-reference material maps, the approach improves average PSNR by 4.03 dB and SSIM by 4.96% over the strongest baseline, while reducing NRMSE by 33.45%. Material-wise comparisons and component ablations support improved recovery of localized structures, with favorable computational scaling in runtime and memory.

Conclusion: Gaussian material fields establish an explicit, adaptive representation for volumetric multi-material reconstruction, demonstrating significant improvements in reconstruction quality metrics and computational efficiency compared to baseline methods.

Abstract: Volumetric material decomposition in multi-energy computed tomography requires a representation that organizes multiple three-dimensional material fields in a common spatial domain while retaining differences in composition and local structure. We observe that spatial primitives can be shared across materials without tying their coefficients, but their local capacity must respond to material-specific reconstruction needs. We introduce Gaussian material fields, which represent multiple material distributions with shared anisotropic 3D Gaussian primitives and independent nonnegative material coefficients. The shared geometry defines a continuous spatial basis, while the coefficients determine each primitive's contribution to the individual material fields. To reconstruct this representation from multi-energy projections, a differentiable spectral forward model combines Gaussian material path integrals with a calibrated basis matrix, enabling joint optimization of spatial geometry and material composition. Material-aware adaptive density control retains material-specific refinement evidence before aggregation and adjusts local representation capacity to accommodate both spatially extensive components and sparse details. Experiments use synthesized multi-energy projections generated from pseudo-reference material maps constructed by conventional methods from publicly available CT data. Across 15 cases, our approach improves average PSNR by 4.03 dB and SSIM by 4.96% over the strongest baseline, while reducing NRMSE by 33.45%. Material-wise comparisons and component ablations support improved recovery of localized structures, while runtime and memory measurements show favorable computational scaling. These results establish Gaussian material fields as an explicit, adaptive representation for volumetric multi-material reconstruction.

</details>


### [64] [SpatialUQ: Post-Hoc Uncertainty Quantification from Spatial Consistency in Black-Box Vision Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09498)
*Md Kawsher Mahbub,Milon Biswas,Mirza Niaz Morshed,Wei Yu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: SpatialUQ is a post-hoc uncertainty quantification method for frozen clinical vision models that measures spatial consistency via Jensen-Shannon divergence between global predictions and five fixed spatial crops. It achieves 0.784 failure-detection AUC on NIH ChestX-ray14, outperforming MC-Dropout (0.664) at one-fifth the compute, with best-in-class calibration (SCE=0.049).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Clinical vision models are deployed as frozen black boxes with no access to internals, retraining, or ground truth at inference time. Existing uncertainty methods like MC-Dropout require model modification or high compute, while simple baselines like entropy lack robustness. The authors propose that trustworthy predictions should be spatially consistent across crops.

Method: SpatialUQ measures Jensen-Shannon divergence between the global prediction and the mean of five fixed spatial crops across six deterministic forward passes. The Multicrop Uncertainty Score (MUS) captures spatial inconsistency as uncertainty. A supervised fusion combines MUS with entropy, confidence, and ℓ1 distance for enhanced performance.

Result: MUS achieves 0.784 failure-detection AUC vs 0.664 for MC-Dropout (p<10^-6) at 1/5 compute. Native calibration (SCE=0.049) is best among methods above 0.78 AUC. Supervised fusion reaches 0.832, outperforming five-member ensemble (0.813). MUS scales with model quality (BiomedCLIP: 0.899 AUC, ρ=0.846). In-distribution correlation is meaningful (ρ=0.523) but breaks under severe distribution shift (VinBigData, ρ=0.027). Works well for diffuse findings but less for small focal lesions.

Conclusion: SpatialUQ provides an effective, computationally efficient post-hoc uncertainty quantification method for frozen clinical vision models. It achieves superior failure-detection performance and calibration compared to existing methods, scales with model quality, but loses reliability under severe distribution shift and for small focal lesions like nodules.

Abstract: Clinical vision models are often deployed as frozen black boxes with no access to internals, retraining, or ground truth at inference time. We introduce \textbf{SpatialUQ}, a post-hoc uncertainty method using only output probabilities. It measures the Jensen-Shannon divergence between the global prediction and the mean of five fixed spatial crops in six deterministic forward passes. The premise is simple, trustworthy predictions are spatially consistent. On NIH ChestX-ray14 (DenseNet-121, $N{=}25{,}596$), our Multicrop Uncertainty Score (MUS) reaches $0.784$ failure-detection AUC versus $0.664$ for MC-Dropout ($p{<}10^{-6}$) at one-fifth the compute, with native calibration ($\text{SCE}{=}0.049$ vs.\ $0.127$ for $\ell_1$), the best-calibrated among methods above 0.78 AUC. A supervised fusion of MUS with entropy, confidence, and $\ell_1$ reaches $0.832$, outperforming a five-member ensemble ($0.813$). MUS scales with model quality, reaching $0.899$ with BiomedCLIP ($ρ= 0.846$), while this relationship remains meaningful in-distribution ($ρ= 0.523$) but breaks down under severe distribution shift (VinBigData, $ρ= 0.027$). MUS is well-suited to diffuse findings but is less dependable for small focal lesions such as nodules. Code and experimental materials are publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/kawsher11/SpatialUQ.

</details>


### [65] [RT-DETR-World: Transferring Rich LLM Semantics to Real-Time Open-Vocabulary Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09502)
*Yupeng Zhang,Ziyi Zhao,Juntao Cheng,Sheng Wang,Ningnan Guo,Ruize Han,Liang Wan*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: RT-DETR-World is a real-time open-vocabulary object detector that leverages multi-level semantic supervision (category names, object descriptions, and image descriptions) during training to achieve strong zero-shot generalization while maintaining efficient inference through lightweight query-text matching.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing real-time OVD methods focus on vocabulary coverage but neglect rich instance semantics and scene context. Under strict efficiency constraints, compact detectors struggle to absorb these semantic cues. The authors aim to transfer rich semantics from textual descriptions during training while retaining inference efficiency.

Method: The authors propose three key innovations: (1) GroundingCapv2 with three-level supervision - category names for standard OVD, object descriptions for instance-level semantics, and image descriptions for scene context; (2) Dual-Path Description Alignment (DDA) combining a deployment-consistent MiniLM pathway with a training-only LLM teacher, where MiniLM provides query-category supervision and object-description alignment while offline teacher features supervise matched queries and global visual representations; (3) Relation-Aware Negative Relaxation (RNR) that uses teacher-derived semantic similarities to relax related negatives while preserving exact positives.

Result: The method achieves competitive zero-shot accuracy and a favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off, demonstrating that rich semantic supervision can be transferred to compact detectors without compromising inference speed.

Conclusion: The proposed RT-DETR-World successfully bridges the gap between rich semantic understanding and real-time efficiency in open-vocabulary detection by leveraging multi-level description supervision and dual-path alignment during training while maintaining lightweight inference through compact query-text matching.

Abstract: Open-vocabulary detection (OVD) recognizes categories unseen during training through textual category queries, yet achieving strong generalization with real-time efficiency remains challenging. Beyond vocabulary scaling, zero-shot generalization may benefit from reusable visual--semantic cues learned from seen data, including attributes, actions, states, and contextual relations. Existing real-time OVD methods primarily emphasize vocabulary coverage and efficient region/query--text matching; under strict efficiency constraints, compact detectors may struggle to absorb rich instance semantics and scene context. We propose RT-DETR-World, a compact DETR-style detector that transfers the rich semantics conveyed by descriptions during training while retaining lightweight query--text matching at inference. We construct GroundingCapv2 with three levels of supervision: category names for standard OVD, object descriptions conveying instance-level semantics, and image descriptions conveying object relations and scene context. These descriptions serve only as training-time semantic supervision. To help the compact detector absorb these semantics, we propose Dual-Path Description Alignment (DDA), combining a deployment-consistent MiniLM pathway with a training-only LLM teacher. MiniLM provides query--category supervision and object-description alignment, while offline teacher features supervise matched queries and global visual representations at the object and image levels, respectively. All teacher features are precomputed, and the teacher-side modules are removed after training. We further propose Relation-Aware Negative Relaxation (RNR), which uses teacher-derived semantic similarities to relax related negatives while preserving exact positives.
