Experiments demonstrate competitive zero-shot accuracy and a favorable accuracy--efficiency trade-off. The code will be released.

</details>


### [66] [TERRA: Learning Transportable Latent Actions through Temporal Effect Representation and Relational Alignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09509)
*Tianxingjian Ding,Mubarak Shah,Yu Tian*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: TERRA (Temporal Effect Representation and Relational Alignment) introduces a method for learning latent actions from visual transitions by describing transitions through compact temporal effects (net feature change + within-window dynamics). It addresses two key challenges: capturing temporal information without nuisance variation, and enabling latent reuse across different initial states via Effect-Anchored Transport (EAT).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The core tension is that latent actions face two fundamental problems: (1) temporal representation trade-offs - endpoint differences discard motion unfolding while full sequences introduce nuisance variation, and (2) reuse uncertainty - reconstruction only observes latents with their source states, leaving unclear whether latent codes remain meaningful when applied to different initial states.

Method: TERRA represents transitions using: (1) a compact temporal effect capturing net feature change, and (2) a low-order within-window dynamics component. A continuous latent is learned from this effect representation. EAT (Effect-Anchored Transport) decodes latents in other initial states and anchors the resulting effect to the observed source effect, shaping latents by what they do across contexts rather than just their source transition.

Result: TERRA with frozen linear readers predicts actions more accurately than UniVLA and LAPA-style baseline, degrades more slowly under visual distractors, and maintains faithful transported transitions as recipient context diverges. Control experiments show these gains primarily come from EAT. At matched pretraining scale, the complete system achieves 93.4% average success on LIBERO versus 91.8% for UniVLA.

Conclusion: The paper successfully addresses both fundamental questions about latent actions: temporal effects capture meaningful motion information while filtering nuisance variation, and EAT enables effective latent reuse across different initial states by anchoring effects. The approach demonstrates consistent improvements across multiple metrics and achieves state-of-the-art results on LIBERO benchmark.

Abstract: Latent actions supervise robot policies with action-like codes inferred from visual transitions, and their usefulness hinges on two questions: what a code keeps from a transition, and whether it still means the same thing when reused in a different initial state. The first is a tension in time: an endpoint difference discards how motion unfolds, while the full sequence admits nuisance variation. The second is left open by reconstruction, which only ever observes a latent together with the state it came from. We argue that both questions can be answered in the same place. TERRA (Temporal Effect Representation and Relational Alignment) describes a transition by a compact temporal effect, its net feature change together with a low-order within-window dynamics component, and learns a continuous latent from this effect. The same effect space then serves as the reference for reuse: Effect-Anchored Transport (EAT) decodes a latent in other initial states and anchors the resulting effect to the one observed at its source, so that the latent is shaped by what it does across contexts rather than only by the transition it came from. With frozen linear readers, TERRA predicts actions more accurately than UniVLA and a LAPA-style baseline, degrades more slowly under visual distractors, and keeps transported transitions faithful to the donor action as the recipient context moves farther away; a same-budget control shows that these gains come largely from EAT. At matched pretraining scale, the complete system reaches 93.4% average success on LIBERO, compared with 91.8% for UniVLA.

</details>


### [67] [LiG-DETR: Local-in-Global Reassembly in Latent Space for Aerial Object Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09511)
*Yupeng Zhang,Fangzhuo Gao,Juntao Cheng,Ziyi Zhao,Liang Wan,Ruize Han*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: LiG-DETR proposes an Efficient Global-Local Reassembly framework for aerial object detection that addresses scale and density variations by combining high-fidelity local features with global context in a unified end-to-end DETR architecture, avoiding the trade-offs between image slicing (independent processing) and feature compression (unified but degraded representations).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Aerial object detection struggles with scale variations: small objects degrade from downsampling, while medium/large objects need global context. Existing methods either use image slicing (clear local evidence but independent processing) or feature-level optimization (unified but compressed representations). The key question is how to acquire high-fidelity local evidence before feature degradation and integrate it into a unified framework.

Method: LiG-DETR uses a shared encoder to extract both global and locally magnified features, projecting them into detector feature space. Local features are reassembled according to original spatial locations to form a globally aligned local feature level. A single DETR decoder jointly decodes global and local features. Two efficiency mechanisms: (1) Context-Preserved Selective Reassembly focuses high-resolution encoding on informative regions while preserving dense feature layout; (2) Density-Aware Adaptive Query Allocation adapts decoder query budget using encoder proposal scores.

Result: Substantial gains on small and medium objects while retaining strong large-object performance, with favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-offs and improved cross-domain generalization.

Conclusion: LiG-DETR successfully integrates high-fidelity local evidence into a unified end-to-end framework, achieving improved detection across various object scales while maintaining computational efficiency and cross-domain generalization capability.

Abstract: Aerial object detection faces substantial scale and density variations. Small objects are easily degraded by downsampling and feature compression, while medium and large objects require sufficient global context. Existing methods mainly follow two paradigms: image slicing provides clearer local evidence but relies on independent crop-level prediction and post-processing, whereas feature- and query-level optimization preserves unified inference but operates on already compressed full-image representations, limiting recovery of fine-grained information. This raises a key question: can aerial detection directly acquire high-fidelity local evidence before feature degradation and integrate it into a unified end-to-end framework? To this end, we propose LiG-DETR, an Efficient Global-Local Reassembly framework that reformulates image slicing as high-fidelity local feature acquisition. A shared encoder extracts global and locally magnified features, which are projected into the detector feature space. The projected local features are reassembled according to their original spatial locations to form a globally aligned local feature level, and a single DETR decoder jointly decodes global and local features. To reduce redundant computation, Context-Preserved Selective Reassembly focuses high-resolution encoding on informative regions while preserving a dense feature layout, and Density-Aware Adaptive Query Allocation adapts the decoder query budget using encoder proposal scores. Experiments show substantial gains on small and medium objects while retaining strong large-object performance, with favorable accuracy--efficiency trade-offs and improved cross-domain generalization. The code will be released.

</details>


### [68] [OmniCam: Omni-Camera Trajectory Generation via Geometry-Grounded Pose Token Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09513)
*Zhenyang Liu,Chenjie Cao,Yisu Zhang,Xuhui Zuo,Xiangyang Xue,Yanwei Fu,Tengfei Wang,Chunchao Guo*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: OmniCam generates camera pose sequences from a single panorama and textual trajectory descriptions using an autoregressive model with geometry-grounded pose token learning, achieving significant improvements in trajectory accuracy and collision reduction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Camera trajectory control is crucial for video generation, scene reconstruction, and robotic perception. Generating trajectories from language requires understanding both scene geometry and achieving target-aware framing.

Method: OmniCam uses three key components: (1) panoramic point-cloud encoder for omnidirectional geometric context; (2) hybrid absolute-rotation and relative-translation tokenization with temporally consistent quaternion signs; (3) separate geometric and semantic conditioning streams with explicit 3D target anchor. Trained on OmniCaT dataset with 267,700 trajectories across four camera behaviors.

Result: OmniCam reduces trajectory errors by 28-47% and collision rate by 65.8% relative to GenDoP. Against best baseline: ATE reduction of 43.0% and collision reduction of 62.3%. Component ablations support geometric and target-aware conditioning approaches.

Conclusion: OmniCam effectively generates camera trajectories from language and panorama, with downstream applications in camera-controlled video generation and robotic active perception.

Abstract: Camera trajectories control viewpoint changes in video generation, scene reconstruction, and robotic perception. Generating them from language requires both scene geometry and target-aware framing. We introduce OmniCam, an autoregressive model that generates camera pose sequences from a single panorama and textual trajectory descriptions. Its geometry-grounded pose token learning combines three components: a panoramic point-cloud encoder for omnidirectional geometric context; hybrid absolute-rotation and relative-translation tokenization with temporally consistent quaternion signs; and separate geometric and semantic conditioning streams with an explicit 3D target anchor. We also construct OmniCaT, containing 267,700 trajectories across four camera behaviors. On the reported OmniCaT evaluation, OmniCam reduces trajectory errors by 28--47% and collision rate by 65.8% relative to GenDoP retrained on OmniCaT. Against the best baseline for each metric, the ATE and collision reductions are 43.0% and 62.3%, respectively. Component ablations support the use of geometric and target-aware conditioning, while downstream experiments examine camera-controlled video generation and robotic active perception.

</details>


### [69] [STRIKE: Learning Visual State Transitions for Physical World Modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09514)
*Wenbin Teng,Tianshuo Xu,Depu Meng,Yuelei Li,Quentin Herau,Yihan Hu,Yajie Zhao,Wei Zhan*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: STRIKE is a framework for physical world modeling that separates visual state transition learning from dense video generation. It uses event-aligned supervision to train an image-based transition model that predicts next scene configurations from current image, transition specification, and elapsed time. A vision-language planner predicts time transition specifications at inference, and a separately trained dynamic model generates complete rollouts conditioned on predicted states.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Physical world modeling requires predicting how interactions change a scene, not merely generating coherent motion. Existing methods may focus on generating coherent motion but fail to accurately model physical causality and state changes.

Method: 1) Construct event-aligned supervision by extracting observed states from training videos and pairing them with transition descriptions and temporal offsets. 2) Train an image-based transition model to predict next scene configuration from current image, local transition specification, and elapsed time. 3) Use pretrained vision-language planner to predict time transition specifications at inference. 4) Recursively apply transition model to produce sequence of future visual states. 5) Train separate dynamic model to generate complete rollout conditioned on predicted states and temporal locations.

Result: STRIKE shows improvements over corresponding video-backbone baselines in benchmark measures of physical consistency and manipulation-video fidelity on Physics-IQ Verified, PhyGenBench, Pisa-Experiments, and RoboTwin2.0 datasets.

Conclusion: Learned visual state transitions serve as an effective intermediate representation for physical world modeling, enabling better prediction of how interactions change scenes compared to direct video generation approaches.

Abstract: Physical world modeling requires predicting how interactions change a scene, not merely generating coherent motion. We propose STRIKE, a framework that separates visual state transition learning from dense video generation. We construct event-aligned supervision by extracting observed states from training videos and pairing them with transition descriptions and temporal offsets. An image-based transition model learns to predict the next scene configuration from the current image, a local transition specification, and elapsed time. At inference, a pretrained vision-language planner predicts time transition specifications, and recursive application of the learned transition model produces a sequence of future visual states. A separately trained dynamic model then generates the complete rollout conditioned on these states and their temporal locations. Experiments on Physics-IQ Verified, PhyGenBench, Pisa-Experiments, and RoboTwin2.0 show improvements of STRIKE over the corresponding video-backbone baselines in benchmark measures of physical consistency and manipulation-video fidelity. These results support learned visual state transitions as an effective intermediate representation for physical world modeling.

</details>


### [70] [It Is Not Seeing the Hazard: A Frozen Vision-Language Safety Score Measures Its Caption Bank](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09517)
*Samuel Tetteh,Cody Fleming*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper presents a controlled evaluation of frozen CLIP-based safety scores in reinforcement learning, questioning whether these vision-language model (VLM) signals actually detect hazards or merely respond to correlated features like prompt structure, embedding geometry, or camera viewpoint.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to address a critical gap in VLM-based safety methods: they assume that similarity to language describing danger indicates hazard perception, but this assumption remains unverified. The authors aim to determine whether these scores actually detect hazards or respond to correlated features of the scene.

Method: The authors conducted a controlled evaluation of a frozen CLIP prompt-margin safety score by: (1) applying the score to trajectories from policies that never received it, (2) matching pre-contact observations to contact-free observations with comparable hazard geometry, and (3) varying captions, encoder, and camera view. They tested across three policies, 180 episodes, and 130 isolated contact onsets.

Result: The score decreases for about twenty steps before contact. However, mechanism controls indicate the score mainly tracks resemblance to the scene shared by captions and changes with caption separation and camera view. A constant-confidence control retains the lower catastrophe-rate point estimate, suggesting policy gains do not establish hazard perception.

Conclusion: The conclusion is that VLM-based safety scores may not actually perceive hazards but rather respond to correlated features like prompt structure, embedding geometry, or camera viewpoint. The findings suggest that reported gains from VLM-based methods may not indicate true hazard perception, as the score tracks scene resemblance rather than actual danger.

Abstract: Frozen vision-language models increasingly provide safety signals for reinforcement learning. Their use assumes that similarity to language describing danger indicates the hazard itself. Yet policy return and collision rate cannot reveal whether a score detects hazards or responds to correlated features of the scene. VLM-based methods have reported gains in driving and safe-RL benchmarks by converting image-text similarity into rewards, costs, or confidence weights. Such signals promise to reduce reliance on manually designed feedback. They may also reflect prompt structure, embedding geometry, or camera viewpoint, leaving their safety meaning unverified. To address this gap, we present a controlled evaluation of a frozen CLIP prompt-margin safety score. We apply the score to trajectories generated by policies that never receive it, match pre-contact observations to contact-free observations with comparable hazard geometry, and vary the captions, encoder, and camera view. Across three policies, 180 episodes, and 130 isolated contact onsets, the score decreases for about twenty steps before contact. Mechanism controls indicate that the score mainly tracks resemblance to the scene shared by its captions and changes with caption separation and camera view. A constant-confidence control retains the lower catastrophe-rate point estimate, so policy gains do not establish hazard perception.

</details>


### [71] [ActiveLang: Active Open-Vocabulary 3D Mapping with Semantic-Uncertainty-Guided Exploration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09518)
*Liyan Chen,Hairong Yin,Huangying Zhan,Yi Xu,Raymond A. Yeh,Philippos Mordohai*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: ActiveLang is an autonomous system for active open-vocabulary 3D mapping that uses semantic-uncertainty-guided exploration and online language-feature adaptation on dual-Gaussian representations. It achieves state-of-the-art results in open-vocabulary segmentation while being more efficient than existing approaches.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Robots increasingly assist humans with diverse tasks and need both geometric and semantic understanding of their surroundings. They often operate in unfamiliar environments and take on new tasks without knowing relevant concepts ahead of time, necessitating open-vocabulary scene understanding and human-robot interaction capabilities.

Method: ActiveLang uses online language-feature adaptation on a compact dual-Gaussian representation to jointly reconstruct scene geometry, appearance, and open-vocabulary semantics. It employs an efficient planner that selects informative viewpoints based on semantic uncertainty, enabling effective mapping with modest memory overhead.

Result: Experiments on Replica and ScanNet++ datasets demonstrate substantial improvements in 2D and 3D open-vocabulary segmentation over both online and offline baselines. The system builds language-annotated 3D maps more efficiently with fewer observations and lower computational cost.

Conclusion: ActiveLang demonstrates that actively exploring scenes with semantic-uncertainty guidance enables more efficient construction of language-annotated 3D maps. The method achieves substantial improvements in open-vocabulary segmentation while requiring fewer observations and lower computational cost compared to baseline approaches.

Abstract: As robots increasingly assist humans with diverse tasks, they need both geometric and semantic understanding of their surroundings. Moreover, robots often operate in unfamiliar environments and take on new tasks without knowing the relevant concepts ahead of time. This motivates language-annotated 3D maps that support open-vocabulary scene understanding and human-robot interaction. We introduce ActiveLang, an autonomous system for active open-vocabulary 3D mapping with semantic-uncertainty-guided exploration. ActiveLang performs online language-feature adaptation on a compact dual-Gaussian representation to jointly reconstruct scene geometry, appearance, and open-vocabulary semantics with modest memory overhead. Its planner efficiently selects informative viewpoints, enabling effective mapping with fewer observations and lower computational cost. Experiments on Replica and ScanNet++ demonstrate substantial improvements in 2D and 3D open-vocabulary segmentation over both online and offline baselines, highlighting that actively exploring scenes builds language-annotated 3D maps more efficiently.

</details>


### [72] [WAPR: A Foundation Model for Wide-Angle Refinement in Unseen Object Pose Estimation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09535)
*Yulin Wang,Mengting Hu,Hongli Li,Jianghao Zhou,Chen Luo*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: WAPR is a zero-shot wide-angle pose refinement model for 6D pose estimation that handles rotational deviations up to 90 degrees, achieving fast inference (1s/frame, 25 objects/sec) and state-of-the-art performance on unseen objects using a novel SA6D dataset with rotational symmetry priors and angle-balanced loss.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Real-world applications require 6D pose estimation to be accurate, fast, and scalable to unseen objects. Existing methods struggle with wide-angle refinement (large rotational deviations) and symmetry handling for rotated symmetric objects.

Method: WAPR uses rotational symmetry priors to canonicalize symmetry-equivalent pose targets before loss computation. SA6D dataset was constructed with KASAL-assisted rotational symmetry priors for 944 GSO scans, expanded through geometry and texture augmentation into ~50K object instances and ~2M RGB-D images. An angle-balanced loss stabilizes learning across different angular ranges.

Result: WAPR achieves state-of-the-art performance on seven BOP core datasets for unseen-object 6D pose localization and detection under both fast and unconstrained inference settings, using only 12 candidate poses per object instance.

Conclusion: The combination of rotational symmetry priors, large-scale SA6D training data, and angle-balanced loss enables effective zero-shot wide-angle pose refinement for accurate, fast, and scalable 6D pose estimation on unseen objects.

Abstract: Real-world applications require 6D pose estimation to be accurate, fast, and scalable to unseen objects. This paper introduces WAPR, a zero-shot wide-angle pose refinement model that refines candidate poses with rotational deviations up to 90 degrees. With as few as 12 candidate poses per detected object instance, WAPR supports fast inference within 1 s per frame and reaches a pose-estimation throughput of up to 25 detected object instances per second. To support wide-angle training for rotationally symmetric objects, WAPR uses rotational symmetry priors to canonicalize symmetry-equivalent pose targets before loss computation. We further construct SA6D, a large-scale 6D training dataset with such priors. SA6D obtains KASAL-assisted rotational symmetry priors for 944 GSO scans and expands them through geometry and texture augmentation into about 50K augmented object instances and about 2M rendered RGB-D images. In addition, an angle-balanced loss stabilizes learning across different angular ranges by reducing the influence of uninformative large-error cases. Experiments on seven BOP core datasets show that WAPR achieves state-of-the-art performance in unseen-object 6D pose localization and detection under both fast and unconstrained inference settings. Project page: https://github.com/WangYuLin-SEU/WAPR.

</details>


### [73] [Visual Evidence Under Cross-Examination: Evaluating and Controlling Decision-Level Evidence Use in Vision-Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09550)
*Huiyao Zhang,Jin Bai,Zilong Su,Rui Guo,Chaofan Qin,Jinze Lv,Wenhui Yu,Hongfei Wang,Ye Li*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: The paper studies how visual evidence in vision-language models affects candidate predictions, introducing the concept of "candidate-bound visual contribution" where evidence should help its supporting candidate and have its effect removed when invalidated or redirected when rebinding. The authors present CROSS-Bench (28,000 decision problems) and RIVET interface to evaluate and improve evidence ownership, demonstrating that RIVET significantly improves evidence effect transfer and cross-bench accuracy by 5.70 pp across four frozen backbones.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Vision-language models increasingly use visual evidence (crops, regions, tool-produced observations) to reason, but the authors observe that an observation can influence the answer without properly benefiting the candidate it supports. This raises the question of whether visual evidence is truly "owned" by its supporting candidate or if its effect is misdirected. The motivation is to separate the utility of visual evidence from the candidate-specific destination of its effect.

Method: The authors introduce CROSS-Bench, a benchmark of 28,000 decision problems with matched invalidation and rebinding tests on a dedicated evaluation subset. They propose RIVET interface that: (1) preserves evidence identity and uncertainty, (2) composes a candidate-conditioned response, and (3) separately controls its strength. Experiments use shared-evidence settings where the same visual evidence supports different candidates across test cases.

Result: 1) Task accuracy and evidence ownership can diverge under shared-evidence experiments. 2) RIVET increases normalized effect transfer from 0.512 to 0.651 where clean evidence has a positive effect. 3) The advantage persists on common evaluation examples and across repeated decision-layer fits. 4) With evidence predicted from raw inputs, RIVET improves CROSS-Bench accuracy by an average of 5.70 percentage points across four frozen backbones, relative to models without auxiliary evidence.

Conclusion: The paper demonstrates that visual evidence utility can be separated from its candidate-specific destination. RIVET successfully redirects visual effects to their proper supporting candidates, improving both effect transfer and overall accuracy. This work provides a framework for evaluating whether vision-language models properly attribute visual evidence to their intended candidates.

Abstract: Vision-language models increasingly reason through crops, regions, and tool-produced observations. Yet an observation can influence the answer without benefiting the candidate it supports. We study candidate-bound visual contribution: valid evidence should help, invalidating its supporting relation should remove its additional effect, and valid rebinding should redirect that effect to the newly supported candidate. We introduce CROSS-Bench, a benchmark of 28,000 decision problems, with matched invalidation and rebinding tests on a dedicated evaluation subset. Our RIVET interface preserves evidence identity and uncertainty, composes a candidate-conditioned response, and separately controls its strength. Shared-evidence experiments show that task accuracy and evidence ownership can diverge. Under matched capacity and training, RIVET increases normalized effect transfer from 0.512 to 0.651 where clean evidence has a positive effect. The advantage persists on common evaluation examples and across repeated decision-layer fits. With evidence predicted from raw inputs, RIVET improves CROSS-Bench accuracy by an average of 5.70 pp across four frozen backbones, relative to the same models without auxiliary evidence. These results separate the utility of visual evidence from the candidate-specific destination of its effect.

</details>


### [74] [Gradient-Based Trajectory Optimisation over Continuous Poses for Sparse-View Cone-Beam CT](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09579)
*Linda-Sophie Schneider,Simon Wittl,Gabriel Herl,Andreas Maier*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper proposes continuous trajectory optimization for cone-beam CT, treating all source poses as continuous variables optimized jointly by gradient ascent on the scanner's kinematic manifold, incorporating soft-Tuy plane coverage, View Covariance Loss, and attenuation-aware penalties.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Fixed candidate pools in trajectory optimization prevent off-grid refinement and require new object-specific precomputation for each acquisition manifold. This work aims to develop a unified optimizer that handles various scanner geometries without discrete candidate limitations.

Method: The approach formulates trajectory optimization as a continuous gradient ascent problem on the scanner's kinematic manifold. The objective function combines three terms: (1) soft-Tuy plane coverage for complete data acquisition, (2) continuous View Covariance Loss for view distribution optimization, and (3) an analytic attenuation-aware ray-bundle penalty. The same optimizer handles circular, limited C-arm, two-axis, and freesphere parametrisations.

Result: On a Defrise flange, continuous selection recovers laminar defects invisible to circular orbit, matches discrete swap search on free sphere at sparse budgets, and outperforms it at denser budgets. Moderate elevation bands recover most free-sphere gains. Photon noise preserves ordering on the flange and compresses it on dense fuel nozzles. Prescan-planned poses executed on a robot CT bench demonstrate feasibility, though no consistent metric gain over uniform band sampling was achieved.

Conclusion: Continuous pose optimization incorporates attenuation and scanner constraints directly into sparse-view acquisition design. Selection takes seconds rather than minutes without object-specific reconstruction basis, enabling practical transfer to bounded scanner envelopes while maintaining reconstruction quality.

Abstract: Trajectory optimisation for cone-beam computed tomography (CT) determines which information sparse-view scans acquire. Fixed candidate pools prevent off-grid refinement and require new object-specific precomputation for each acquisition manifold. We make every source pose an individual continuous variable and move all poses jointly by gradient ascent on the scanner's kinematic manifold. The objective combines soft-Tuy plane coverage, continuous View Covariance Loss, and an analytic attenuation-aware ray-bundle penalty. The same optimiser handles circular, limited C-arm, two-axis, and freesphere parametrisations. On a Defrise flange, continuous selection recovers laminar defects invisible to a circular orbit, matches discrete swap search on the free sphere at the sparser budget, and leads at the denser one, with the same objective evaluated in every arm. A moderate elevation band already recovers most of the free-sphere gain at the defects, so the same optimiser transfers to bounded scanner envelopes. Photon noise preserves the ordering on the flange and compresses it on a dense fuel nozzle. Sparseprescan planning benefits from matching prescan and planned acquisition manifolds. Selection takes seconds rather than minutes without an object-specific reconstruction basis. Prescan-planned poses were executed on a robot CT bench and reconstructed in a common frame, demonstrating feasibility but no consistent metric gain over uniform band sampling. Continuous pose optimisation incorporates attenuation and scanner constraints directly into sparse-view acquisition design.

</details>


### [75] [STORK: Spatio-Temporal Observation of uterine contRactions via neural networKs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09598)
*Melissa Schween,Tristan Gottwald,Jordina Aviles Verdera,Lisa Story,Mary Rutherford,Jana Hutter*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: STORK is a multi-instance learning model for detecting uterine contractions in fetal MRI, trained with only series-level labels (weakly-supervised) and capable of recovering per-frame contraction scores without frame-level supervision.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Uterine contractions in fetal MRI are currently identified manually and discarded, limiting understanding of contraction dynamics. There was a need for an automated method to detect and analyze these contractions.

Method: STORK uses multi-instance learning with 3D spatio-temporal convolutions factorized into parallel branches across temporal hyperplanes. Per-frame embeddings combine intensity and Demons-estimated displacement fields, aggregated by linear mean-pooling head to enable post-hoc frame-level scoring without frame-level supervision.

Result: Evaluated on ~700 multi-vendor dynamic fetal MRI series, STORK achieves series-level AUROC of 95.0% and AUPRC of 94.6%, substantially outperforming 3D ResNet and ConvNeXt baselines.

Conclusion: Grad-CAM analysis reveals the model uses predictive features extending beyond the placenta into uterine tissue, providing an automated tool for richer phenotyping of uterine behavior.

Abstract: Uterine contractions in fetal MRI are typically identified manually and discarded, limiting insights into contraction dynamics. We formalize Uterine Contractile Activity Detection (UCAD) as a weakly-supervised learning problem and introduce STORK, a multi-instance learning model trained on dynamic MRI series using only coarse, series-level labels. STORK factorizes 3D spatio-temporal convolutions into parallel branches across temporal hyperplanes to capture coherent tissue motion without the cost of full 4D convolutions. Per-frame embeddings, combining intensity and Demons-estimated displacement fields, are aggregated by a linear mean-pooling head. This ensures that frame-level contraction scores can be recovered post-hoc without frame-level training supervision. Evaluated on around 700 multi-vendor dynamic fetal MRI series, STORK achieves a series-level AUROC of 95.0% and AUPRC of 94.6%, substantially outperforming 3D ResNet and ConvNeXt baselines. Grad-CAM analysis suggests that the model draws on predictive features extending beyond the placenta into the uterine tissue, offering an automated tool for richer phenotyping of uterine behavior.

</details>


### [76] [Identity-Duplication Auditing in National-Scale Neuroimaging Repositories](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09614)
*Jiheng Li,Michael E. Kim,Trent M. Schwartz,Yuhan Cui,Gaurav Rudravaram,Derek B. Archer,Timothy J. Hohman,Lori L. Beason-Held,Victoria L. Morgan,Dario J. Englot,Angela L. Jefferson,for the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative,for the BIOCARD Study team,for the Health,Aging Brain Study,:,Health Disparities,Study Team,Lianrui Zuo,Guray Erus,Christos Davatzikos,Bennett A. Landman*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: HAPPEN is a human-in-the-loop pipeline for auditing identity duplication in T1-weighted brain MRI repositories. It combines SHA-256 fingerprinting for exact-duplicate detection with supervised contrastive retrieval for near-duplicate detection, deployed on a 95,129-scan repository and validated on an independent 22,386-scan dataset.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: National-scale MRI repositories aggregate data from different studies/institutions, causing subject identifiers that were only locally unique to become globally non-unique. This identity duplication creates data leakage between training/test sets and inflates apparent performance in downstream biomedical studies. No existing method provides an end-to-end, image-based workflow for auditing this problem at repository scale.

Method: HAPPEN combines SHA-256 fingerprinting for exact-duplicate detection with supervised contrastive retrieval to identify non-identical scans that may originate from the same person. Retrieved pairs are reviewed as candidates through a locally hosted interface rather than automatically classified. The workflow was deployed on a 95,129-scan repository and assessed using 54 genetic-reference pairs. Transferability was tested on 22,386 scans at an independent institution without model retraining or image transfer.

Result: Deployment identified 1,316 exact-duplicate scan groups and 1,275 reviewer-supported near-duplicate subject groups. Of these, 56% and 82% respectively crossed dataset boundaries. All 54 genetic-reference pairs were recovered. The external team independently completed the full workflow using locally selected operating threshold and review standard.

Conclusion: HAPPEN provides an effective end-to-end solution for auditing identity duplication in large-scale MRI repositories. The method demonstrates high accuracy (100% recovery of genetic-reference pairs) and strong transferability across institutions without retraining. The high rate of cross-dataset duplicates (56-82%) confirms the significance of this problem in aggregated repositories. The human-in-the-loop approach ensures high confidence through reviewer verification.

Abstract: National-scale magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) repositories increasingly integrate data from different studies and institutions. However, subject identifiers that are valid only within individual datasets are no longer guaranteed to remain globally unique after aggregation, making it possible for the same subject to be assigned multiple identifiers, which we define as identity duplication. Such duplication can create leakage between training and test data and inflate apparent performance in downstream biomedical studies. Existing methods do not provide an end-to-end, image-based workflow for auditing this problem at repository scale. In this work, we present HAPPEN, a human-in-the-loop pipeline for auditing identity duplication in T1-weighted brain MRI repositories. It combines SHA-256 fingerprinting for exact-duplicate detection with supervised contrastive retrieval of non-identical scans that may originate from the same person. Retrieved pairs are reviewed as candidates in a locally hosted interface rather than automatically classified as duplicates. We deployed the workflow in a 95,129-scan aggregated repository and assessed end-to-end recovery using 54 genetic-reference pairs. Transferability was assessed by locally deploying the same workflow on 22,386 scans at an independent institution without model retraining or image transfer. Deployment in the study repository identified 1,316 exact-duplicate scan groups and 1,275 reviewer-supported near-duplicate subject groups. Of these groups, 56% and 82%, respectively, crossed dataset boundaries. All 54 genetic-reference pairs were recovered. The external team independently completed the full workflow using a locally selected operating threshold and review standard.

</details>


### [77] [Quasi-Binarized Autoencoders: An Architecture-Independent Information Bottleneck for Medical Image Anomaly Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09670)
*Shouhei Hanaoka,Takahiro Nakao,Atsushi Takamatsu,Takeharu Yoshikawa,Osamu Abe*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper introduces the Quasi-Binarizing (QB) layer for unsupervised anomaly detection in medical imaging. The QB layer constrains information flow between encoder and decoder by squashing latent elements to [0,1] and adding Laplace noise, making each element epsilon-locally differentially private and bounding mutual information between image and reconstruction. The resulting QBAE model achieves state-of-the-art results on MedIAnomaly benchmark (mean AUROC 0.828) and BraTS2021 (AUROC 0.911, pixel-level AP 0.838).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reconstruction-based anomaly detection methods suffer from identity mapping where networks reconstruct anomalies too well. Current solutions rely on architectural choices that cannot be quantified in bits. The authors seek a principled, information-theoretic approach to limit information flow that works across datasets without per-dataset tuning.

Method: The quasi-binarizing (QB) layer squashes each latent element into [0, 1] and adds Laplace noise of scale 1/epsilon. This provides epsilon-local differential privacy and bounds mutual information between input and reconstruction. QBAE is built by placing QB layers on every encoder-decoder path including skip connections, forming a seven-level attention U-Net with 32,768 QB elements. Noise is maintained at test time to ensure the information bound holds.

Result: On the seven datasets of MedIAnomaly benchmark, QBAE with one architecture and configuration achieves mean image-level AUROC of 0.828, the highest among methods not adapting to each dataset. On BraTS2021, it achieves AUROC 0.911 and pixel-level AP 0.838. Without input corruption, the bottleneck alone prevents identity collapse (mean AUROC 0.805 vs 0.590).

Conclusion: The QB layer provides a principled, information-theoretic approach to prevent identity mapping in reconstruction-based anomaly detection. The method achieves robust performance across multiple medical imaging datasets with a single architecture, outperforming non-adaptive methods and demonstrating the effectiveness of bounded mutual information for anomaly detection.

Abstract: Unsupervised anomaly detection, which learns only from normal images, is a central task in medical image analysis and remains an open problem. Reconstruction-based methods pass an image through an encoder-decoder network trained on normal data and detect anomalies from the residual between the image and its reconstruction. This works only if the information passed from the encoder to the decoder is limited; otherwise the network learns an identity mapping and reconstructs anomalies too. This limit is usually imposed through architectural choices, tuned per dataset, that cannot be stated in bits. We introduce the quasi-binarizing (QB) layer, which squashes each latent element into [0, 1] and adds Laplace noise of scale 1/epsilon. Each element is then epsilon-locally differentially private, and the mutual information between an image and its reconstruction is bounded by a quantity that depends only on epsilon and the number of QB elements, whatever the encoder and decoder. Placing a QB layer on every encoder-decoder path, including all skip connections, we build QBAE, a seven-level attention U-Net with 32,768 QB elements. On the seven datasets of the MedIAnomaly benchmark, QBAE with one architecture and one configuration reaches a mean image-level AUROC of 0.828, the highest among methods that do not adapt to each dataset, and the best reported results on BraTS2021 (AUROC 0.911, pixel-level AP 0.838). The noise is kept at test time, so that every reconstruction satisfies the bound. Without input corruption, the bottleneck alone prevents identity collapse (mean AUROC 0.805 vs. 0.590). Code is available at https://github.com/hanaokalog/MedIAnomalyQB.

</details>


### [78] [A Multi-Source Ultrasound Benchmark Revealing the Limits of Contemporary Self-Supervised Anomaly Detection Methods](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09677)
*Marco Riedenauer,Daniel Kienzle,Pratik Mayekar,Rainer Lienhart*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Self-supervised anomaly detection in medical ultrasound struggles to generalize across multiple anatomies; the new SADUSI benchmark reveals significant limitations in current methods, with PatchCore variants achieving the best but still limited performance (0.76-0.83 AUROC, 0.14-0.40 F1), while reconstruction-based diffusion methods perform poorly (0.56-0.72 AUROC, 0.10-0.26 F1).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current anomaly detection evaluations are limited to single anatomy or task, making it unclear whether models learn robust normal ultrasound appearance or only source-specific representations. There is a need for a diverse, multi-source benchmark to evaluate generalization across anatomical regions, views, and acquisition protocols.

Method: Introduced SADUSI benchmark - a multi-source ultrasound dataset designed to train and evaluate anomaly detection methods across diverse anatomical regions, views, and acquisition protocols. Evaluated representative self-supervised methods including reconstruction-based diffusion methods (AnoDDPM, DeCo-Diff) and feature-based PatchCore variants.

Result: Reconstruction-based diffusion methods (AnoDDPM, DeCo-Diff) achieved pixel-level AUROC of 0.56-0.72 and maximum F1 scores of 0.10-0.26, indicating limited separation of pathology from normal regions. Feature-based PatchCore variants performed better, reaching pixel-level AUROC of 0.76-0.83 but remained limited with maximum F1 scores of 0.14-0.40.

Conclusion: Broad multi-source ultrasound anomaly detection remains an open challenge. Current approaches struggle in this diverse setting. SADUSI can serve as a valuable resource for developing methods that generalize beyond anatomy-specific settings.

Abstract: Self-supervised anomaly detection is a promising paradigm for medical ultrasound, as normal images are often easier to obtain than exhaustive annotations of all possible pathologies. However, most existing evaluations are limited to a single anatomy or task, making it unclear whether models learn a robust notion of normal ultrasound appearance or only a source-specific representation. We introduce the SADUSI benchmark, a multi-source ultrasound dataset designed to train and evaluate anomaly detection methods across a broad range of anatomical regions, views, and acquisition protocols. The goal of SADUSI is to provide a diverse normal ultrasound distribution and a benchmark for visible structural anomalies that can be assessed from single images. We evaluate representative self-supervised anomaly detection methods and find that current approaches struggle in this setting. In particular, reconstruction-based diffusion methods such as AnoDDPM and DeCo-Diff achieve pixel-level AUROC values of 0.56-0.72 and maximum F1 scores of 0.10-0.26, indicating limited separation of pathology from normal image regions. Feature-based PatchCore variants perform better, reaching pixel-level AUROC values of 0.76-0.83, but remain limited with maximum F1 scores of 0.14-0.40. These findings suggest that broad multi-source ultrasound anomaly detection remains an open challenge and that SADUSI can serve as a resource for developing methods that generalize beyond anatomy-specific settings.

</details>


### [79] [What Makes Synthetic Hard Negatives Work in Vision-Language Pretraining?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09700)
*Nikos Giakoumoglou,Paschalis Giakoumoglou,Andreas Floros,Kleanthis Marios Papadopoulos,Tania Stathaki*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: The paper addresses the challenge of transferring synthetic hard negatives from unimodal self-supervised learning to vision-language pretraining. Through analysis of six representation-space synthesis strategies, the authors identify two failure modes: cross-modal constructions producing overly easy negatives, and intra-modal constructions incorporating the positive. They propose SNAP, which generates intra-modal hard negatives that avoid the positive from either modality, and find that fixing the temperature parameter improves performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Synthetic hard negatives have proven effective for unimodal self-supervised learning, but this approach cannot be directly transferred to vision-language pretraining. The authors aim to understand why existing strategies fail in the cross-modal setting and develop a solution that works for vision-language models.

Method: The authors analyzed six representation-space synthesis strategies and identified two failure modes through geometric analysis. Based on these findings, they propose SNAP, which generates intra-modal hard negatives that never involve the positive from either modality. They also found that fixing the temperature parameter (instead of learning it) improves downstream performance.

Result: SNAP is model-agnostic, requires no external generative models, and adds less than 10% training time overhead. Evaluated on CLIP and FLIP across multiple architectures and datasets, it delivers consistent improvements on zero-shot retrieval, zero-shot classification, and linear probe evaluation.

Conclusion: The geometric analysis of synthetic hard negatives in vision-language pretraining reveals specific failure modes that differ from unimodal settings. SNAP successfully addresses these issues by avoiding positives from either modality in negative construction, providing a simple yet effective approach that improves various downstream tasks without significant computational overhead.

Abstract: Synthetic hard negatives generated in the representation space have proven effective for unimodal self-supervised learning, but transferring this idea to vision-language pretraining is not straightforward. We analyze six representation-space synthesis strategies and identify two failure modes in their transfer to vision-language pretraining: cross-modal constructions that produce overly easy negatives or pull them toward the query, and intra-modal constructions that incorporate the matched positive. We also observe logit-scale saturation when training with synthetic hard negatives and a learnable temperature, and find that fixing the temperature improves downstream performance. Using this geometric analysis we propose SNAP, which generates intra-modal hard negatives that never involve the positive from either modality, avoiding both failure modes entirely. SNAP is model-agnostic, requires no external generative models, and adds less than 10% training time overhead. Evaluated on top of CLIP and FLIP across multiple architectures and datasets, SNAP delivers consistent improvements on zero-shot retrieval, zero-shot classification, and linear probe evaluation.

</details>


### [80] [Latent Watermarks under Generative Editing: A Benchmark and Analysis of Detection Survival](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09702)
*Sung Ju Lee,Nam Ik Cho*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper benchmarks 8 watermark detection methods against 5 prompt-based editors across multiple generative backbones, editing strengths, and semantic categories. It reveals that ordinary editing can inadvertently break watermark detection, and that decomposing outcomes into editing-only vs. editing+distortions reveals hidden differences between watermark methods. Clean d' (score separation) emerges as a useful diagnostic metric for predicting watermark survival.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to understand how prompt-based editing affects watermark detection in generative AI, particularly whether ordinary editing operations inadvertently compromise watermark detection without explicitly targeting the watermark. The authors seek to systematically benchmark different watermark methods against various editing techniques.

Method: The authors conducted a comprehensive benchmark testing 8 watermark methods against 5 editors across 4 generative backbones, 4 editing strengths, and 5 semantic categories. They performed edit-validity and threshold checks, separated editing from 7 subsequent distortions, conducted sequential edit experiments, and tested embedding-strength interventions. They used standardized clean score separation (d') and spatial overlap as metrics.

Result: Key findings: (1) Ordinary editing can cause latent watermark detection to fail without explicitly targeting the watermark. (2) Editing alone primarily affects Tree-Ring watermark, while added distortions expose broader detection survival differences. (3) Score separation can decline while detection rates remain near ceiling. (4) Clean d' organizes composite-survival tiers effectively, while spatial overlap adds little predictive value. (5) Higher clean separation correlates with higher post-edit separation for embedding-strength interventions. (6) In HSTR, margin contrast is positive but angular layout contrast at matched clean separation remains unresolved. (7) Method tiers remain stable under threshold recalibration.

Conclusion: The authors conclude that outcome decomposition and continuous separation metrics expose differences hidden by aggregate true positive rate (TPR). Clean d' is a useful empirical diagnostic within this benchmark, though its transfer to unseen methods is mixed. The benchmark provides a systematic framework for evaluating watermark robustness against editing attacks.

Abstract: Ordinary prompt-based editing can cause latent watermark detection to fail without explicitly targeting the watermark. We benchmark eight watermark methods against five editors across four generative backbones, four editing strengths, and five semantic categories, with edit-validity and threshold checks. Separating editing from seven subsequent distortions reveals that editing alone primarily distinguishes Tree-Ring, while added distortions expose a broader spectrum of detection survival. Sequential edits reveal a second hidden difference: score separation can decline while detection rates remain near their ceiling. Across methods, standardized clean score separation ($d'$) organizes composite-survival tiers, whereas spatial overlap adds little to predicting edit-only survival beyond clean detectability. Embedding-strength interventions in two methods link higher clean separation to higher post-edit separation. In HSTR, the margin contrast is positive, while the angular layout contrast at matched clean separation remains unresolved. Together, outcome decomposition and continuous separation expose differences hidden by aggregate TPR. Method tiers are stable under threshold recalibration at the main operating points and alternative composite weights. Clean $d'$ is thus a useful empirical diagnostic within this benchmark, with mixed transfer to unseen methods. Code and supporting artifacts are planned for a separate release.

</details>


### [81] [Enhancing Multi-Region Stylization with Interior-Guided Boundary Repair](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09706)
*Hong-Son Nguyen,Thi-Ngoc-Hanh Le*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: IGBR is a lightweight, model-agnostic method that repairs boundary artifacts in multi-region neural style transfer by using interior-guided propagation and distance-based blending, without requiring retraining.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Region-based neural style transfer enables fine-grained artistic control by allowing independent stylization of semantic image regions, but compositing these regions often leads to boundary artifacts that degrade visual quality.

Method: IGBR repairs boundary pixels using interior-guided propagation and applies inward, distance-based blending restricted to object-background boundaries to prevent inter-object style leakage. The method is derived from a region-wise constrained formulation with a closed-form solution and can be integrated into existing stylization pipelines without retraining.

Result: IGBR consistently produces plausible boundaries and outperforms prior blending techniques in boundary consistency, gradient stability, and interior preservation. The paper also introduces quantitative metrics for measuring boundary consistency, gradient artifacts, inter-object leakage, and interior preservation without requiring annotated stylized images.

Conclusion: IGBR provides an effective solution for boundary artifacts in multi-region stylization, offering a lightweight, model-agnostic approach that can be seamlessly integrated into existing pipelines.

Abstract: Region-based neural style transfer enables fine-grained artistic control by allowing independent stylization of semantic image regions. However, compositing these regions often leads to boundary artifacts, degrading visual quality. We propose Interior-Guided Boundary Repair (IGBR), a lightweight and model-agnostic method that improves boundary handling in multi-region stylization. IGBR repairs boundary pixels using interior-guided propagation and applies inward, distance-based blending restricted to object-background boundaries, preventing inter-object style leakage. The method is derived from a region-wise constrained formulation with a closed-form solution and can be seamlessly integrated into existing stylization pipelines without retraining. To evaluate efficiency of our IGBR, we introduce quantitative metrics that measure boundary consistency, gradient artifacts, inter-object leakage, and interior preservation without requiring annotated stylized images. Our experiments and evaluations demonstrate that the proposed IGBR consistently produces plausible boundaries, outperforming prior blending techniques in boundary consistency, gradient stability, and interior preservation. The code is available at https://github.com/Son-SDT/IGBR.

</details>


### [82] [DynStream: Online Streaming 4D Gaussian Reconstruction of Dynamic Worlds from Unposed Video](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09720)
*Dingwei Xian,Xiaoyu Zhou,Yajiao Xiong,Yongtao Wang,Ming-Hsuan Yang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: DynStream is a framework for streaming 4D Gaussian reconstruction from long, unposed videos that enables online reconstruction and photorealistic rendering without per-scene optimization. It processes continuous video streams within local temporal windows and incrementally aligns and fuses reconstructions into a globally consistent scene.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing methods struggle to achieve continuous processing and photorealistic rendering simultaneously for dynamic 4D scene reconstruction from long, unposed streaming videos. Feed-forward Gaussian methods are restricted to offline processing, while online point-cloud approaches cannot maintain dense geometry and high-fidelity rendering.

Method: DynStream reconstructs scenes within local temporal windows from continuous video streams and incrementally aligns and fuses these local reconstructions into a globally consistent scene. The method jointly enforces cross-window geometric consistency and models time-varying scene content.

Result: Experiments demonstrate that DynStream enables high-fidelity online dynamic reconstruction and rendering from long video streams, achieving state-of-the-art performance across diverse dynamic indoor and outdoor scenes.

Conclusion: DynStream successfully supports efficient reconstruction and photorealistic rendering over extended video streams without per-scene optimization, representing a significant advancement in online 4D scene reconstruction.

Abstract: Online reconstruction of dynamic 4D scenes from long, unposed streaming videos requires both continuous processing and photorealistic rendering, which existing methods struggle to achieve simultaneously. Existing feed-forward Gaussian methods are restricted to offline processing, whereas online point-cloud approaches struggle to maintain dense geometry and high-fidelity rendering. We present DynStream, a framework for streaming 4D Gaussian reconstruction from long, unposed videos. Given a continuous video stream, DynStream reconstructs the scene within local temporal windows and incrementally aligns and fuses these local reconstructions into a globally consistent scene, enabling online 4D reconstruction without per-scene optimization. By jointly enforcing cross-window geometric consistency and modeling time-varying scene content, DynStream supports efficient reconstruction and photorealistic rendering over extended video streams. Experiments demonstrate that DynStream enables high-fidelity online dynamic reconstruction and rendering from long video streams, achieving state-of-the-art performance across diverse dynamic indoor and outdoor scenes.

</details>


### [83] [MeshCarve: Artisan Mesh Generation with Flow Matching in Compact Latent Spaces](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09723)
*Xiyu Wang,Ruocheng Wu,Yufei Wang,Zhihao Li,Lanqing Guo,Bihan Wen*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: MeshCarve is a flow matching method for 3D mesh generation that uses hierarchical sparse transformer with VertexVAE and EdgeVAE to separately generate vertex positions and edge connections in compressed latent spaces, achieving shorter token sequences than prior works while maintaining quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior artisan mesh generation works predict face tokens autoregressively, causing slow inference. VAE-based flow matching methods suffer from reconstruction quality drops when geometry and topology are jointly encoded, especially with latent compression. Existing approaches struggle with compact joint latents and long token sequences.

Method: MeshCarve proposes: (1) Separate generation of vertex positions and edge connections via VertexVAE and EdgeVAE; (2) Hierarchical sparse transformer backbone to shorten token sequences; (3) VAEs anchor on discrete vertices rather than surface voxels; (4) Spatial-aware compression; (5) Vertex-link encoding that converts arbitrary connectivity into fixed-length per-vertex embeddings; (6) Flow matching on shortened token sequences.

Result: MeshCarve outperforms state-of-the-art autoregressive and flow matching methods on Objaverse and generalizes to Toys4K. It achieves token sequences only a fraction of the most compressed previous autoregressive and flow matching works, while being among the first mesh generation methods where every generative stage runs in spatially compressed latent space.

Conclusion: MeshCarve demonstrates that separate latent encoding of geometry (vertex positions) and topology (edge connections) via dedicated VAEs, combined with vertex-anchored tokenization and spatial-aware compression, enables efficient high-quality mesh generation. This approach sidesteps the difficulty of joint compact latent representation while significantly reducing computational overhead.

Abstract: Prior artisan mesh generation works largely predict face tokens autoregressively, which makes inference slow. Recent methods instead flow match continuous latents built by Variational AutoEncoders (VAEs), but reconstruction quality drops significantly when geometry and topology are jointly encoded, and further when the latent space is compressed. We present MeshCarve, a flow matching method that generates entirely in compact latent spaces, generating vertex positions and edge connections separately and sidestepping the difficulty of a joint compact latent. To shorten the token sequence, we propose a hierarchical sparse transformer backbone, instantiated as VertexVAE and EdgeVAE. Instead of encoding fields over the surface voxels, both VAEs anchor on discrete vertices in their latent spaces, which drastically reduces the token sequence length, and our spatial-aware compression shortens it further without costing reconstruction. VertexVAE directly encodes vertex occupancy. For connectivity, we propose vertex-link encoding, which turns arbitrary connectivity between vertices into fixed-length continuous per-vertex embeddings and recovers complex artistic topology faithfully. MeshCarve combines these VAEs with an anchor generator and flow matches on the shortened token sequences. It shows advantages over state-of-the-art autoregressive and flow matching methods on Objaverse and generalizes to Toys4K. To the best of our knowledge, it is among the first artisan mesh generation methods whose every generative stage runs in a spatially compressed latent, with a token sequence only a fraction of the most compressed previous autoregressive and flow matching works.

</details>


### [84] [Beyond Group Splits: Specimen-Level Cross-Validation and Visual Attribution for Remaining-Shelf-Life Regression in Climacteric Fruit](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09726)
*Rovhona Mudau,Jean Frederic Isingizwe Nturambirwe,Clement Nthambazale Nyirenda*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper addresses estimating remaining shelf life (RSL) of Hass avocados from images using a frozen ImageNet-pretrained visual backbone with a lightweight regression head. The key finding is that specimen-disjoint evaluation yields substantially higher error (RMSE 3.12 days) compared to observation-level evaluation (RMSE 2.37 days), demonstrating that standard evaluation protocols can give overly optimistic performance estimates. Additionally, lightweight models like MobileNetV3-Small achieve comparable accuracy to larger models like ResNet-18 while providing higher throughput.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current evaluation protocols for perishable produce shelf-life prediction can produce misleading results when repeated images from the same biological specimen are available. This leads to inflated performance estimates that may not generalize to real-world deployment where new specimens are encountered.

Method: The study uses the Hass Avocado Ripening dataset (8,834 image-RSL pairs from 426 fruits across three storage regimes). A frozen ImageNet-pretrained visual backbone with lightweight regression head is evaluated under two protocols: (1) observation-level random splits and (2) specimen-disjoint 5-fold cross-validation. Lightweight backbones (MobileNetV3-Small) are compared with heavier backbones (ResNet-18), and Grad-CAM is used for spatial attribution analysis.

Result: Observation-level evaluation yields mean RMSE of 2.37 days (SD=0.03), while specimen-disjoint evaluation yields mean RMSE of 3.12 days (SD=0.11) with R²=0.553. The per-specimen comparison confirms significantly higher error under specimen-disjoint evaluation (p<0.001). MobileNetV3-Small (0.93M parameters) achieves accuracy comparable to ResNet-18 while providing substantially higher throughput. Grad-CAM reveals differences in spatial attribution between lightweight backbones.

Conclusion: Specimen-disjoint evaluation should be standard for assessing vision models in longitudinal shelf-life prediction, as observation-level partitioning gives substantially more optimistic estimates. Lightweight models like MobileNetV3-Small are suitable for RSL estimation with better throughput, and attribution analysis provides insights into model decision-making.

Abstract: Estimating remaining shelf life (RSL) from images could provide affordable decision support for perishable produce, but evaluation protocols can substantially affect reported performance when repeated images are available from the same biological specimen. We use the Hass Avocado Ripening dataset, comprising 8,834 image-RSL pairs from 426 fruits across three storage regimes, to evaluate a frozen ImageNet-pretrained visual backbone with a lightweight regression head. Our contributions are threefold: we quantify the effect of observation-level versus specimen-disjoint evaluation, compare lightweight and heavier visual backbones under specimen-disjoint cross-validation, and examine their spatial attributions using Grad-CAM. Across ten observation-level random splits, the model achieves a mean RMSE of 2.37 days with a standard deviation of 0.03 days, whereas specimen-disjoint 5-fold cross-validation yields a mean RMSE of 3.12 days with a standard deviation of 0.11 days. The corresponding mean coefficient of determination is 0.553. A matched per-specimen comparison confirms higher error under specimen-disjoint evaluation, with a probability value below 0.001 across 426 specimens, showing that observation-level partitioning gives a substantially more optimistic estimate for this dataset and model configuration. Under specimen-disjoint evaluation, MobileNetV3-Small (0.93 million parameters) achieves accuracy comparable to ResNet-18 while providing substantially higher throughput, and Grad-CAM reveals differences in spatial attribution between the lightweight backbones. These results support specimen-disjoint evaluation and attribution analysis when assessing lightweight vision models for longitudinal shelf-life prediction.

</details>


### [85] [SoccerNet-FoulRet: Retrieving Semantically Similar Soccer Foul Videos](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09742)
*Jacobus Arthur,Ahmad Sait,Batool Hani,Merey Ramazanova,Jan Held,Marc Van Droogenbroeck,Bernard Ghanem,Anthony Cioppa,Silvio Giancola*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: SoccerNet-FoulRet is the first benchmark for semantic foul retrieval in professional soccer, addressing the problem of inconsistent refereeing decisions by enabling comparison of contentious fouls against relevant past precedents. The task retrieves semantically similar fouls based on refereeing interpretation rather than visual similarity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Refereeing decisions in professional soccer remain inconsistent because referees cannot easily compare a contentious foul against similar past cases. This lack of a systematic comparison tool leads to inconsistent rulings. The authors cast this as a retrieval problem to help referees make more consistent decisions by finding relevant precedent cases.

Method: The authors built SoccerNet-FoulRet benchmark from the SoccerNet-MVFoul dataset, containing 693 human-verified queries and category-relevance labels. They evaluated zero-shot video and vision-language embedders along with a task-specific fine-tuned baseline. The task differs from prior video-to-video retrieval by matching based on refereeing interpretation relevance rather than visual similarity or shared events.

Result: Semantic foul retrieval remains highly challenging. The strongest zero-shot model achieves under 5% HitRate@10 on human-verified precedents. While category-supervised fine-tuning improves category relevance, it transfers only modestly to precedent retrieval, indicating the difficulty of the task.

Conclusion: The authors release SoccerNet-FoulRet to establish semantic foul retrieval as an open problem. The benchmark and code are available at https://github.com/SoccerNet/sn-foulret. The study demonstrates that current vision-language models struggle with this task, highlighting the need for further research in semantic foul retrieval for sports officiating.

Abstract: Refereeing decisions in professional soccer remain inconsistent because referees cannot easily compare a contentious foul against similar past cases. We cast this as a retrieval problem and introduce SoccerNet-FoulRet, the first benchmark for semantic foul retrieval. Given a query foul, the task is to retrieve past fouls judged to be relevant precedents, regardless of camera angle, teams, or appearance. This differs from prior video-to-video retrieval, which matches clips by visual similarity or a shared event. Here, relevance is defined by refereeing interpretation. We build the benchmark from the SoccerNet-MVFoul dataset and evaluate retrieval ability of zero-shot video and vision-language embedders together with a task-specific fine-tuned baseline on 693 human-verified queries and category-relevance labels. Semantic foul retrieval remains challenging. The strongest zero-shot model achieves under 5% HitRate@10 on human-verified precedents, while category-supervised fine-tuning improves category relevance but transfers only modestly to precedent retrieval. We release SoccerNet-FoulRet to establish semantic foul retrieval as an open problem: https://github.com/SoccerNet/sn-foulret.

</details>


### [86] [Flow-of-Thought: A Framework for Visual Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09746)
*Mariia Baidachna,Nicolas Pugeault*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper introduces Flow-of-Thought (FoT), a framework that integrates visual sketches as intermediate reasoning steps to enhance spatial understanding in AI models, mimicking human mental imagery.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) and Vision Transformers (ViTs), they still underperform on tasks requiring spatial understanding. The researchers aimed to address this gap by introducing visual sketches as intermediate reasoning steps, similar to how humans use mental imagery.

Method: The FoT framework trains coordinate-aware trajectory flow fields on SO(2) group orbits and cumulative shortest paths, then freezes the learned dynamics. Same vs. different decisions are made by comparing competing generative hypotheses using foreground-weighted reconstruction energy.

Result: FoT achieves 100.0% accuracy on Tetris and 99.0% on colored shapes on locked tests. Under frozen transfer, the orbit-trained 2D flow improves over its endpoint-only control on BLINK Multi-view (72.2% vs. 63.9% on 133 public validation pairs).

Conclusion: Continuous visual traces (orbits) serve as an effective and interpretable representation for spatial reasoning in some out-of-distribution settings, supporting the use of mental imagery-like representations in AI systems.

Abstract: Mental imagery, ``seeing with the mind's eye'' is an essential aspect of human cognition. Despite rapid progress Large Language Models (LLMs) and Vision Transformers (ViTs) still underperform on tasks requiring spatial understanding. To address this, we introduce Flow-of-Thought (FoT), a framework that integrates the generation of visual sketches as intermediate reasoning steps, mimicking mental imagery in humans. We train coordinate-aware trajectory flow fields on $SO(2)$ group orbits and cumulative shortest paths, then freeze the learned dynamics; same vs. different decisions compare competing generative hypotheses using foreground-weighted reconstruction energy. On locked tests FoT reaches 100.0% accuracy on Tetris and 99.0% on colored shapes. Under frozen transfer, the orbit-trained 2D flow improves over its endpoint-only control on BLINK Multi-view (72.2% vs. 63.9% on 133 public validation pairs), supporting continuous visual traces as an effective and interpretable representation for spatial reasoning in some out-of-distribution settings.

</details>


### [87] [Diffusion-Generated Image Watermarking: A Two-Axis Taxonomy and Three Protocol-Bounded Case Studies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09755)
*Sung Ju Lee,Nam Ik Cho*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper presents a comprehensive framework for analyzing and comparing watermarking methods for diffusion-generated images, organizing approaches by insertion mechanism and signal representation, and conducting three protocol-bounded case studies while identifying attack families and evaluation protocols.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the challenge of balancing provenance signals with image quality, robustness, and computational cost in watermarking diffusion-generated images, and to provide a structured framework for systematic comparison rather than establishing universal rankings.

Method: The authors organize watermarking methods along two axes (insertion mechanism and primary signal-bearing representation), formalize a z_T-Fourier pipeline, and structure three protocol-bounded case studies examining frequency integrity, semantic persistence, and VAE-latent phase modulation. They also identify four content-level attack families and propose evaluation protocols.

Result: The paper provides: (1) a taxonomy for organizing watermarking methods, (2) three case studies revealing insights about frequency integrity/cropping, semantic imprinting without localized carriers, and single-shot VAE-latent modulation efficiency/robustness, (3) identification of four content-level attack families separate from model adaptation, and (4) evaluation protocols and testable conjectures for parameter-tuning threats.

Conclusion: Instead of establishing universal rankings, this work provides a framework for matched, protocol-aware comparisons of watermarking systems for diffusion-generated images, enabling researchers to make appropriate method selections based on their specific requirements and use cases.

Abstract: Watermarking diffusion-generated images requires balancing provenance signals with image quality, robustness, and computational cost. This work organizes methods along two axes: insertion mechanism and primary signal-bearing representation, and formalizes a representative $z_T$-Fourier pipeline for verification and identification. We then use the taxonomy to structure three protocol-bounded case studies. The first examines associations among frequency integrity, detection, quality, and cropping behavior. The second revisits persistence under seed-linked and seed-independent editing and formulates a scoped Semantic Imprinting Hypothesis without claiming a localized carrier or causal mechanism. The third studies single-shot VAE-latent phase modulation, including its efficiency, regeneration robustness, and robustness--quality operating points. Finally, we separate four content-level attack families from model/pipeline adaptation, propose corresponding evaluation protocols and testable conjectures for parameter-tuning threats, and identify additional temporal extensions for video. These analyses do not establish a universal ranking; instead, they provide a framework for matched, protocol-aware comparisons of watermarking systems for diffusion-generated images.

</details>


### [88] [PARC-Loc: Text-to-Point-Cloud Localization with Partial Assignment and Relational Consistency](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09761)
*Shengkai Ma,Zhenyu Hou,Weihua Cao*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: PARC-Loc addresses text-to-point-cloud localization in city-scale 3D maps by handling two failure modes: layout-inconsistent aliasing (repetitive objects causing false matches) and boundary evidence incompleteness (relevant instances spanning submap boundaries). The method uses Partial Assignment with Relational Consistency to jointly model hint-object compatibility and spatial relations, enabling layout-consistent submap selection and context expansion from adjacent maps.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Text-to-point-cloud localization is important for city-scale 3D navigation but suffers from two key problems: (1) repetitive urban objects inflate similarity between queries and wrong submaps, even when instance layouts violate the query; (2) query-relevant instances often span submap boundaries, leaving retrieved submaps with incomplete evidence. Existing coarse-to-fine methods fail to handle these issues effectively.

Method: PARC-Loc uses Partial Assignment with Relational Consistency (PARC) which jointly models hint-object compatibility and pairwise spatial relations while allowing unmatched elements. At the coarse stage, candidate-level assessment complements neural similarity for layout-consistent submap selection. At the fine stage, context is expanded with query-relevant instances from adjacent submaps, and PARC yields object-level matching weights guiding cross-modal attention.

Result: On KITTI360Pose, PARC-Loc improves Top-1 localization recall at 5m from 0.50 to 0.67, achieving a 34% relative gain over the strongest baseline. Experiments on CityLoc also demonstrate superiority over conventional coarse-to-fine baselines.

Conclusion: PARC-Loc successfully addresses layout-inconsistent aliasing and boundary evidence incompleteness through relational consistency modeling. The approach significantly outperforms existing methods, demonstrating the importance of considering spatial relations and handling cross-boundary evidence in text-to-point-cloud localization tasks.

Abstract: Text-to-point-cloud localization estimates a position in a city-scale 3D map from descriptions of surrounding objects. Existing coarse-to-fine methods retrieve submaps using aggregate learned compatibility and then localize within a selected submap. However, repetitive or similar urban objects can inflate the embedding similarity between the query and multiple submaps, even when the instance layout within a submap violates the query description.
