Meanwhile, query-relevant instances often span submap boundaries, leaving the retrieved submap with incomplete contextual evidence. We term these failure modes layout-inconsistent aliasing and boundary evidence incompleteness, respectively. To address them, we propose PARC-Loc, a coarse-to-fine localization framework built on Partial Assignment with Relational Consistency (PARC). PARC jointly models hint-object compatibility and pairwise spatial relations, allowing unmatched elements while favoring assignments consistent with the queried layout. At the coarse stage, its candidate-level assessment complements neural similarity for layout-consistent submap selection. At the fine stage, the context is expanded with query-relevant instances from adjacent submaps, while PARC yields object-level matching weights that guide cross-modal attention. Extensive experiments on KITTI360Pose and CityLoc show that PARC-Loc outperforms conventional coarse-to-fine baselines. On KITTI360Pose, our method improves Top-1 localization recall at 5 m from 0.50 to 0.67, achieving a 34% relative gain over the strongest baseline.

</details>


### [89] [Relational Abstractions for Spatial Reasoning with Diffusion Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09780)
*Ana Ezquerro,Ozan Özdenizci*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper addresses a key limitation of diffusion models: their inability to learn logical rules for spatial reasoning tasks. The authors propose a novel framework that combines unsupervised object discovery with relational abstractions to guide diffusion models during both training and inference. They also introduce a large-scale benchmark with four puzzle-inspired datasets for evaluating spatial reasoning in generative models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Diffusion models excel at image synthesis but struggle with structured spatial reasoning tasks that require understanding implicit logical rules. Current state-of-the-art models tend to approximate pixel-space distributions without learning the underlying reasoning constraints needed for tasks like puzzles. This limits their ability to generate images that satisfy specific reasoning conditions.

Method: The proposed framework leverages unsupervised object discovery to identify objects in images, then creates abstractions of object relations. These relational representations serve as structural primitives that enrich diffusion models, allowing them to guide the generative representation space during both training and inference phases. The approach enables conditional image generation that satisfies reasoning constraints.

Result: Relational abstractions significantly improve the reasoning capabilities of diffusion models across various complex reasoning tasks. The method enables robust generalization in out-of-distribution settings, demonstrating that incorporating object-centric representations with relational knowledge helps diffusion models learn underlying logical rules rather than just approximating pixel distributions.

Conclusion: This work demonstrates that combining unsupervised object discovery with relational abstractions can effectively address diffusion models' limitations in spatial reasoning. The proposed framework successfully enables diffusion models to satisfy structured reasoning constraints, and the new benchmark provides a valuable testbed for evaluating spatial reasoning in generative models.

Abstract: Diffusion models excel at image synthesis, but they remain limited in their ability to reliably satisfy structured spatial reasoning constraints. In conditional data distribution modeling tasks with implicit logical structure, such as puzzles defined by visible clues paired with consistent solutions, state-of-the-art generative models tend to approximate pixel-space distributions without learning the underlying logical rules required for inference. To address this limitation, we present a novel framework for spatial reasoning with diffusion models that leverages unsupervised object discovery and abstractions of object relations. We show that the relational knowledge derived from object-centric representations enriches diffusion models with structural primitives, allowing them to effectively guide the generative representation space during both training and inference, and enabling conditional image generation that satisfies reasoning constraints. Additionally, we introduce a large-scale generative spatial reasoning benchmark with four datasets inspired by human-solvable puzzles. Our results show that relational abstractions significantly improve reasoning capabilities of diffusion models on a variety of complex reasoning tasks, while enabling robust generalization in out-of-distribution settings.

</details>


### [90] [CIRSeg: Coarse-to-Fine Intensity-Robust Liver Segmentation with Source-Free Continual Test-Time Adaptation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09784)
*Ruoshi Xu,Mingqi Gao,Shengda Luo,Jingkun Chen*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: CIRSeg is a coarse-to-fine liver segmentation framework for contrast-enhanced MRI that addresses limited annotated data, intensity variations, and generalization challenges through cascaded architecture, intensity augmentation, test-time adaptation, and post-processing.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reliable liver segmentation in contrast-enhanced MRI is essential but faces challenges: limited annotated data causes overfitting; scanner/vendor-dependent intensity variations lead to poor generalization; achieving both robust global localization and precise boundary delineation is difficult; and predictions may contain isolated false-positive regions.

Method: CIRSeg combines 3D CutMix with stochastic intensity transfer (Nyul augmentation or histogram matching) for intensity robustness. Its cascaded architecture decouples low-resolution anatomical localization from full-resolution boundary refinement. Inference uses source-free test-time adaptation with confidence-filtered predictions and probability-prior regularization. Largest connected component filtering removes isolated false-positives.

Result: On CARE 2026 test set: in-domain achieves Dice 97.13% with HD95 20.18 mm; unseen-domain achieves Dice 97.93% with HD95 11.30 mm.

Conclusion: CIRSeg demonstrates consistently accurate segmentation across both in-domain and unseen acquisition settings, effectively addressing intensity variations and generalization challenges in liver MRI segmentation.

Abstract: Reliable liver segmentation in contrast-enhanced MRI is essential for quantitative hepatic assessment, treatment planning, and longitudinal disease monitoring. However, limited annotated data and scanner- or vendor-dependent intensity variations can cause overfitting and poor generalization to unseen acquisition domains. Moreover, simultaneously achieving robust global localization and precise boundary delineation remains challenging, while predictions may contain isolated false-positive regions outside the main liver component. To address these challenges, we propose CIRSeg, a coarse-to-fine, intensity-robust liver segmentation framework based on nnU-Netv2. CIRSeg combines 3D CutMix with stochastic intensity transfer using either Nyul augmentation or histogram matching to improve robustness to heterogeneous MRI intensities. Its cascaded architecture decouples low-resolution anatomical localization from full-resolution boundary refinement. At inference, source-free test-time adaptation based on confidence-filtered predictions and probability-prior regularization further improves robustness to out-of-distribution inputs. As a final deterministic post-processing step, largest connected component filtering removes isolated false-positive regions. On the CARE 2026 test set, CIRSeg achieves Dice scores of 97.13\% and 97.93\% on the in-domain and unseen-domain subsets, with corresponding HD95 values of 20.18 mm and 11.30 mm, respectively. These results demonstrate consistently accurate segmentation across both in-domain and unseen acquisition settings. The code is available at https://github.com/jingkunchen/MICCAI_CARE_2026

</details>


### [91] [UltraWorld: Learning Interactive Ultrasound World Models from Untracked Clinical Videos with Acoustic Sampling Map](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09785)
*Keke Yang,Erqi Wang,Sainan Guan,Hongliang Ren*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: UltraWorld is a self-distillation method that enables autonomous ultrasound scanning by transferring priors from clinical ultrasound videos into interactive world models without requiring real action annotations. It adapts a video foundation model into an ultrasound generator and uses synthetic action-video pairs for training, while introducing Acoustic Sampling Map (AsMap) to represent probe poses as pixel-wise 3D sampling positions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Learning action-observation relationships for autonomous ultrasound scanning typically requires synchronized video-pose pairs, which are costly to collect at scale and largely unavailable in routine clinical recordings. Additionally, modeling ultrasound's cross-sectional sampling geometry is necessary for reliable action following.

Method: 1) Adapt a video foundation model into an ultrasound generator conditioned on reference images and anatomical masks. 2) Use anatomical masks sampled along programmable trajectories through 3D anatomy to provide spatial guidance for synthesizing action-video pairs. 3) Self-distill the generator into a world model that predicts future observations from local observations and actions, without requiring anatomical masks or 3D assets at inference time. 4) Introduce Acoustic Sampling Map (AsMap) to represent probe poses and imaging settings as pixel-wise 3D sampling positions, beam directions, and depths.

Result: Improved prediction fidelity and action following. Across nine simulated closed-loop local planning episodes, UltraWorld reduces mean final distance to goal by 29% and orientation error by 38%, compared with visual servoing.

Conclusion: UltraWorld successfully enables autonomous ultrasound scanning by training world models from clinical videos without real action annotations, achieving significant improvements in planning accuracy compared to visual servoing approaches.

Abstract: World models can enable autonomous ultrasound scanning by predicting the outcomes of probe motions from local observations. Learning this action--observation relationship typically relies on synchronized video--pose pairs, which are costly to collect at scale and largely unavailable in routine clinical recordings. Reliable action following further requires modeling ultrasound's cross-sectional sampling geometry. We present UltraWorld, a self-distillation recipe that transfers priors from clinical ultrasound videos into interactive world models without real action annotations. Starting from clinical videos, we adapt a video foundation model into an ultrasound generator conditioned on reference images and anatomical masks. Anatomical masks sampled along programmable trajectories through 3D anatomy provide spatial guidance for synthesizing action--video pairs. We then use these synthetic pairs to self-distill the generator into a world model that predicts future observations from local observations and actions, without requiring anatomical masks or other 3D assets at inference time. To further improve action following, we introduce the Acoustic Sampling Map (AsMap), which represents probe poses and imaging settings as pixel-wise 3D sampling positions, beam directions, and depths. Experiments demonstrate improved prediction fidelity and action following. Across nine simulated closed-loop local planning episodes, UltraWorld reduces the mean final distance to the goal and orientation error by 29\% and 38\%, respectively, compared with visual servoing. Project Page: https://ultraworld-project.github.io/.

</details>


### [92] [Counterfactual Route Optimization for Gaussian Head Avatar Modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09791)
*Shikun Zhang,Yong Li,Yiqun Wang,Qiuhong Ke,Cunjian Chen*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A counterfactual route optimization framework for Gaussian head avatar modeling that adapts loss weights dynamically during training by evaluating short-horizon alternative optimization routes and amortizing the learned preference into a lightweight controller.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Head avatar modeling requires jointly optimizing multiple objectives (geometry, appearance, cross-view consistency) with different dominant effects. Existing pipelines rely on fixed loss weights or handcrafted schedules that cannot adapt to varying training states, leading to suboptimal optimization.

Method: The framework performs short-horizon route-restricted lookahead over geometry, appearance, and joint update routes from the same training state, evaluating outcomes under a unified utility. This counterfactual evidence is factorized into geometry-appearance preference and residual joint advantage. A lightweight controller is trained to amortize this offline evidence and directly estimate current optimization preference, applying bounded modulation to training objectives during full avatar optimization.

Result: Experiments on the NeRSemble dataset show consistent improvement over existing methods, preserving clearer local facial structures and finer details.

Conclusion: The proposed counterfactual route optimization framework effectively addresses the challenge of state-dependent optimization preference in Gaussian head avatar modeling by learning to adaptively modulate training objectives rather than relying on fixed weights or handcrafted schedules.

Abstract: Head avatar modeling requires jointly optimizing multiple objectives with different dominant effects on geometry, appearance, and cross-view consistency. However, their relative effectiveness varies across training states, while existing pipelines typically rely on fixed loss weights or handcrafted stage-wise schedules. A central challenge is therefore to identify which optimization direction is more beneficial at each training state. We propose a counterfactual route optimization framework for Gaussian head avatar modeling, which characterizes state-dependent optimization preference from the realized effects of alternative updates rather than predefined heuristic weighting. Starting from the same training state, we perform short-horizon route-restricted lookahead over geometry, appearance, and joint update routes and evaluate their outcomes under a unified utility. The resulting counterfactual evidence is factorized into a geometry--appearance preference and a residual joint advantage, separately capturing the relative preference between individual update directions and the additional benefit of coordinated optimization. We further amortize this offline evidence into a lightweight controller that directly estimates the current optimization preference and applies bounded modulation to the training objectives during full avatar optimization. Experiments on the NeRSemble dataset validate the effectiveness of the proposed design, consistently outperforming existing methods while preserving clearer local facial structures and finer details.

</details>


### [93] [Beyond Masks and Trajectories: Flow-Guided Latent Action Injection for Stable Surgical Video Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09800)
*Tsz-Yui Qin,Siyu Zhou,Chi-Keung Tang,Yuxiang Nie,Shu Yang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: FLAIR is a reference-free surgical video generation framework that learns action priors from optical flow and generates high-quality surgical videos from text prompts without requiring auxiliary visual conditions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing surgical video generation methods rely on auxiliary conditions (masks, trajectories, depth, reference videos) that require additional manual annotation or specialized acquisition, making them difficult to scale beyond small datasets. There is a need for reference-free architecture that can generate realistic surgical videos without auxiliary conditions at inference time.

Method: FLAIR learns action priors from optical flow of real surgical videos, dynamically predicts latent action representations from input prompts, and injects them into a frozen base model to generate surgical videos with improved action consistency. The method also introduces SurgActionClip-30K (a large-scale surgical vision dataset with action-centric segmented clips and structured captions) and SurgMetrics (surgical domain-specific evaluation metrics).

Result: FLAIR enables generating high-quality surgical videos using text-only inference without auxiliary conditions. Validation in SurgMetrics demonstrates its strength in alignment with human perception compared to traditional metrics.

Conclusion: FLAIR successfully addresses the challenge of reference-free surgical video generation, providing a scalable approach that produces clinically plausible motion without auxiliary conditions. The introduction of SurgActionClip-30K and SurgMetrics addresses critical gaps in datasets and evaluation standards for surgical video generation.

Abstract: Surgical video generation holds substantial potential for surgical education, simulation, and data augmentation, yet generating surgical videos with realistic and clinically plausible motion remains challenging. Most existing methods rely on auxiliary conditions, such as masks, trajectories, depth, or reference videos, to achieve visually plausible synthesis. Yet, these auxiliary conditions typically require additional manual annotation or specialized acquisition, making it difficult to scale such methods beyond small, curated datasets. This motivates the need for a reference-free architecture capable of generating high-quality surgical video without requiring auxiliary visual conditions at inference time. We propose FLAIR, a Flow-guided LatentAction Injection framework for Reference-free surgical video generation. FLAIR learns action priors from optical flow of real surgical videos, dynamically predicts corresponding latent action representation from an input prompt, and injects it into a frozen base model to generate surgical videos with improved action consistency. We further construct SurgActionClip-30K, the first large-scale surgical vision dataset comprising action-centric segmented clips and structured caption labels, addressing the persistent lack of fine-grained, action-centric surgical datasets. Lastly, we introduce SurgMetrics, the first surgical domain-specific evaluation metrics for quantifying the quality of generated surgical videos, addressing the persistent absence of clinically grounded evaluation standards in this domain. Extensive experiments demonstrate that FLAIR enables generating high-quality surgical videos using text-only inference without auxiliary conditions, and validation in SurgMetrics demonstrates its strength in alignment with human perception compared to traditional metrics.

</details>


### [94] [DisParQ: Self-Supervised Part Concepts for Interpretable Vision Foundation Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09802)
*Adam Pardyl,Siddhartha Gairola,Sukrut Rao,Adam Wróbel,Bartosz Zieliński,Bernt Schiele,Dawid Rymarczyk*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: DisParQ introduces a method to learn spatially grounded, discrete concept representations from a frozen vision-only self-supervised backbone (DINOv2) without class labels or language supervision. It uses prototype dictionaries, continuous residuals quantized into discrete attributes, and a spatial decoder for reconstruction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current concept-based vision models are limited to fixed categories or depend on language supervision. There is a need for vision-only, spatially grounded discrete concept representations that can capture variations within concepts (e.g., different types of "wheel") without relying on labels or language.

Method: DisParQ uses a frozen DINOv2 backbone and assigns each image patch to one concept from a learnable prototype dictionary (sparse activation). It learns continuous residuals to capture concept variations, then quantizes them into discrete attributes. A spatial decoder reconstructs the backbone's representation from concepts and attributes.

Result: DisParQ achieves 83.2% top-1 on ImageNet linear probing (matching DINOv2 teacher), higher concept consistency than language-aligned models, competitive fine-grained recognition, and enables cross-category part-based retrieval across 7 datasets (ImageNet, PartImageNet, Places, CUB, Cars, Dogs, Flowers).

Conclusion: DisParQ successfully learns interpretable, discrete concept representations from vision-only self-supervised learning without labels or language, achieving strong performance on recognition tasks while enabling new capabilities like cross-category part retrieval.

Abstract: Concept-based vision models represent images through an intermediate layer of human-inspectable concepts, so what a model relies on can be traced to those concepts. However, those models are often limited to fixed categories or depend on language to define their concepts. We introduce DisParQ (Discrete Parts with Quantized attributes), a method that learns spatially grounded, discrete concept representations from a powerful frozen vision-only self-supervised backbone. It requires no class labels and no language supervision. Each image patch is assigned to exactly one concept from a learnable prototype dictionary, and only a sparse subset of concepts may activate per image. To capture how each concept varies across images (e.g., the type of a "wheel"), we learn continuous residuals alongside the concepts and then quantize them into discrete attributes. A spatial decoder reconstructs the backbone's representation from the concepts and attributes alone, so successful reconstruction means that the discrete representation preserves the backbone's information. We evaluate DisParQ across seven datasets, from general recognition (ImageNet, PartImageNet, Places) to fine-grained benchmarks (CUB, Cars, Dogs, Flowers). We show that DisParQ closely matches its frozen DINOv2 teacher on ImageNet linear probing (83.2% top-1), achieves higher concept consistency than language-aligned models, remains competitive on fine-grained recognition, and enables cross-category part-based retrieval.

</details>


### [95] [Concentration, Not Uncertainty: Why Targeted Synthetic Data Doesn't Help Camouflaged Object Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09807)
*Akshat Dobhal,Sanjay Singh*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether uncertainty-guided synthetic data generation improves camouflaged object detection compared to random allocation. Across 103 training runs, uncertainty-based targeting does not outperform random allocation. The effect is explained by budget concentration rather than uncertainty targeting - any concentration rule reproduces the effect. Additionally, significant data contamination was found in CHAMELEON dataset.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Obtaining pixel-accurate masks for camouflaged object detection is slow and costly. Synthetic training images are attractive, but it remains unclear which real-image regions to target for synthetic data generation under a fixed budget.

Method: Uncertainty-guided generation strategy: (1) cluster unlabelled real images, (2) identify clusters where model is least certain, (3) allocate synthetic generation toward those clusters, (4) iteratively retrain the model. Tested across 103 training runs with five independent controls.

Result: Uncertainty-based targeting does not outperform random allocation. Targeted training sets differ from random sets, but this is explained by budget concentration rather than uncertainty concentration. Every concentration rule tested reproduces the effect, including aiming at most certain clusters. Also found 50/76 images in CHAMELEON duplicated from training data despite zero overlap reported.

Conclusion: Under a fixed synthetic-data budget, budget concentration, not uncertainty-based targeting, accounts for the observed training-set effects. The study highlights the importance of controlling for budget concentration in synthetic data generation experiments.

Abstract: Camouflaged object detection requires pixel-accurate masks, but obtaining such annotations is slow and costly, making synthetic training images an attractive alternative. Under a fixed generation budget, however, it remains unclear which real-image regions to target for synthetic data generation. We study an uncertainty-guided generation strategy that clusters the unlabelled real images, identifies clusters on which the model is least certain, allocates synthetic generation toward those clusters, and iteratively retrains the model. Across 103 training runs, uncertainty-based targeting does not outperform random allocation. Five independent controls further show that this null result is not an artifact: targeted training sets are measurably different from random sets, but the difference is explained by concentrating the generation budget rather than by where uncertainty is concentrated, as every concentration rule we test reproduces the effect and, on boundary accuracy, so does aiming at the clusters the model was most certain about. Separately, we find substantial data contamination in CHAMELEON, with 50 of its 76 images duplicated from training data despite the standard overlap check reporting zero overlap. Together, these results show that, under a fixed synthetic-data budget, budget concentration, not uncertainty-based targeting, accounts for the observed training-set effects.

</details>


### [96] [Efficient 3D Gaussian Head Avatars for Edge Devices](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09821)
*Umar Farooq,Jean-Yves Guillemaut,Adrian Hilton,Marco Volino*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A parameter-efficient generator architecture for unconditional 3D Gaussian head avatar synthesis that reduces computational complexity by 94% in FLOPs, 70% in parameters, and 81% in model size while maintaining competitive quality, enabling CPU inference and mobile browser deployment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While generative 3D Gaussian head avatars provide high-quality rendering, their Gaussian representation synthesis is computationally expensive, limiting deployment on resource-constrained and edge devices. The need for efficient avatar synthesis without dedicated GPU hardware motivates this work.

Method: The authors propose: (1) A parameter-efficient synthesis block architecture, (2) Depth-wise separable convolutions to reduce computation, (3) Retention of style-based conditioning. The approach avoids model compression or quantization post-training.

Result: The method achieves 94% FLOPs reduction, 70% parameter count reduction, and 81% model size reduction compared to the baseline, while maintaining competitive generation quality. Practical CPU inference and browser-based execution on mobile devices is demonstrated using ONNX Runtime.

Conclusion: The proposed efficient generator architecture enables 3D Gaussian avatar synthesis on resource-constrained devices without dedicated GPU hardware or application-specific software, making it practical for mobile and edge deployment while maintaining acceptable quality.

Abstract: Generative 3D Gaussian head avatars provide high-quality, efficient rendering, but synthesising the Gaussian representation remains computationally expensive, limiting deployment on resource-constrained and edge devices. We introduce an efficient generator architecture for unconditional 3D Gaussian head synthesis, based on a parameter-efficient synthesis block and depth-wise separable convolutions while retaining style-based conditioning. Our architecture reduces generator complexity without requiring model compression or quantisation. Compared with the baseline model, our approach reduces FLOPs by 94%, parameter count by 70%, and model size by 81%, while maintaining competitive generation quality. We further demonstrate practical CPU inference and browser-based execution on mobile devices using ONNX Runtime, enabling 3D Gaussian avatar synthesis without dedicated GPU hardware or application-specific software. In addition to conventional image-quality metrics, we evaluate multi-view consistency, training cost, and deployment performance. Code, trained models, and evaluation tools will be released publicly.

</details>


### [97] [UltraText Bench: A Comprehensive Bilingual Benchmark for Evaluating Visual Text Rendering in Image Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09823)
*Deyuan Liu,Yihao Hu,Jingxuan Zhang,Xingying Li,Jun Xie,Jiacheng Liu,Jungang Li,Yu Huang,Xuanyi Liu,Yue Ding,Zecheng Wang,Lei Zhao,Mingda Wang,Zhenglin Cheng,Peng Sun,Tao Lin*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: UltraText Bench is a bilingual benchmark for evaluating image generators on dense visual text generation, containing 432 prompts across 24 categories and 3 difficulty levels. It uses Q-Judger VLM to assess text fidelity, clarity, spatial quality, and scene quality, revealing significant performance variations across 24 model configurations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As short-string rendering improves, evaluation must test sustained performance across more demanding scenes with dense visual text requiring correct placement and legibility across multiple regions.

Method: 432 bilingual prompts (English/Chinese) with 4-12 text regions each, evaluated using Q-Judger vision-language model against structured references for content, placement, and visual attributes. 10 participants conducted human evaluation of automatic scores.

Result: Different models show different strengths; Z-Image-Turbo gains 3.81 clarity points over Z-Image-Base but loses 14.76 fidelity points. Qwen-Image-2512's English composite drops from 86.50 (L1) to 42.86 (L3). Performance varies significantly with workload and difficulty level.

Conclusion: The benchmark reveals that no single model excels across all evaluation dimensions; performance trade-offs exist between clarity and fidelity, and difficulty levels significantly impact results, highlighting the need for comprehensive evaluation of dense visual text generation.

Abstract: Dense visual text requires image generators to reproduce long strings across multiple regions with correct placement and legibility. As short-string rendering improves, evaluation must test sustained performance across more demanding scenes. We introduce UltraText Bench, a bilingual benchmark for prompt-only generation of dense visual text. It contains 432 prompts spanning 24 real-world scene categories and three difficulty levels, split equally between English and Chinese. Each human-reviewed prompt supplies exact strings for four to twelve text regions, paired with structured references for their content, placement, and visual attributes. We use the Q-Judger vision-language model to assess each image against the complete reference, reporting text fidelity, text clarity, spatial quality, and scene quality. Across 24 model configurations, these dimensions reveal different strengths: Z-Image-Turbo gains 3.81 clarity points over Z-Image-Base while losing 14.76 fidelity points under the reported settings. Performance also varies with workload; Qwen-Image-2512's English composite falls from 86.50 at L1 to 42.86 at L3. Ten participants took part in human evaluation of the automatic scores. Repository: https://github.com/LINs-lab/UltraText_Bench.

</details>


### [98] [MOTIF: Person-of-Interest Deepfake Detection Beyond 3DMM Coefficients](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09830)
*Giovanni Affatato,Sara Mandelli,Paolo Bestagini,Stefano Tubaro*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: The paper investigates which components of 3D Morphable Model (3DMM) coefficients carry the most signal for detecting video deepfakes of specific individuals (Person-of-Interest). It finds that shape coefficients alone recover almost full accuracy, temporal evolution adds bounded value, and the dense surface geometry (normally discarded) carries additional identity information. Based on these findings, they develop MOTIF, a visual-only detector trained only on real videos that outperforms state-of-the-art POI detectors across datasets and manipulation types.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Video deepfakes targeting specific individuals (POIs) are highly harmful. Existing detectors use full 3DMM coefficients without understanding which parts actually carry the identity signal. The motivation is to dissect what parts of the 3DMM description are actually useful for detection.

Method: The researchers held encoder, training corpus, and enrollment protocol fixed while varying only what the encoder observes. They systematically tested: (1) different groups of 3DMM coefficients (shape, texture, expression, pose), (2) temporal evolution contributions, and (3) the dense surface geometry (normally discarded). They then assembled the best configuration into MOTIF - a visual-only detector trained only on genuine videos with no manipulated video or POI-specific data.

Result: Key findings: (1) Shape block alone recovers almost all accuracy of full vector (coefficients largely redundant), (2) Temporal evolution contributes real but bounded amount, (3) Dense surface carries identity information that coefficients don't, and (4) Helps precisely where coefficients are weakest. MOTIF improves on state-of-the-art POI detectors across every dataset and manipulation in the benchmark at two quality levels.

Conclusion: The study demonstrates that 3DMM-based deepfake detection can be significantly improved by understanding which components carry identity signals. Using shape coefficients plus dense surface geometry, trained only on real videos, MOTIF achieves superior performance over existing POI detectors without requiring any fake training data or POI-specific enrollment.

Abstract: Video deepfakes targeting a specific individual, the Person-of-Interest (POI), are the most harmful ones, and, since a public figure is abundantly recorded, a detector can be built from genuine footage of that individual. Such detectors commonly describe a subject through a 3D Morphable Model (3DMM) and adopt its coefficients as a whole, so which part of that description carries the signal has never been measured. We dissect it, holding the encoder, the training corpus and the enrollment protocol fixed and varying only what the encoder observes. The groups of coefficients prove largely redundant, since the shape block alone recovers almost all the accuracy of the full vector, and their temporal evolution contributes a real but bounded amount. We further show that the dense surface the same fit returns, which these detectors discard, carries identity information that the coefficients do not, and that it helps precisely where they are weakest. We assemble the best configuration into MOTIF, a visual-only detector trained on real videos only, with no manipulated video and no POI-specific data. It improves on both state-of-the-art POI detectors in every dataset and manipulation of our benchmark and at two quality levels. Our experimental code will be released at https://github.com/polimi-ispl/MOTIF.

</details>


### [99] [ORCA: Hunting Compositional Failures in Text-to-Image Diffusion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09841)
*Arshia Hemmat,Amirhossein Vahidi,Amitis Shidani,Mohammad Vali Sanian,Hesam Asadollahzadeh,Aryan Yazdan Parast,Mohammad Lotfollahi*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: ORCA addresses text-to-image diffusion models' compositional failures (attribute binding, spatial relations, object count) by aligning diffusion transformer latents with visual encoder features through an auxiliary loss. The method uses a low-rank subspace of self-supervised visual features and a learned residual between T5 and CLIP embeddings to provide prompt-dependent visual readout signals.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Text-to-image diffusion models fail predictably on compositional prompts. While CLIP's contrastive embedding loses compositional structure and T5 was added to address this, failures persist. The authors argue this is a misalignment problem - the text encoder preserves compositional structure but in a language-modeling-shaped space rather than vision-shaped, and the denoising objective doesn't reward cross-modal alignment.

Method: ORCA aligns diffusion transformer latents with a low-rank target derived from a frozen visual encoder. The predictor's orthogonal basis is parameterized by a learned residual between T5 and CLIP embeddings, providing a prompt-dependent signal for selecting the visual readout subspace. This is implemented as a single auxiliary loss during diffusion training. The cross-modal information recoverable at a given rank is bounded by the spectral mass of the visual encoder's covariance in top components.

Result: ORCA improves FID and GenEval over both vanilla and REPA baselines at zero inference-time cost. On DiT-L/2, it achieves FID 16.65 and GenEval 0.291 at 200K steps, exceeding the strongest 400K baseline at half the training cost. Largest gains on attribute binding, spatial relations, and multi-object prompts.

Conclusion: The cross-modal alignment signal can be supplied as explicit training signal. The relevant information is concentrated in a low-rank subspace of self-supervised visual features. Supplying this alignment as an auxiliary loss significantly improves compositional capabilities of diffusion transformers while maintaining zero inference overhead.

Abstract: Text-to-image diffusion models fail predictably on compositional prompts: attributes bind to the wrong objects, spatial relations invert, and multi-object scenes lose count. Recent architectures already augment CLIP with a T5 encoder precisely because CLIP's contrastive embedding loses compositional structure, yet these failures persist. We argue the binding problem is therefore not one of missing information but of misaligned information: a text encoder preserves compositional structure, but in a representation space shaped by language modelling rather than vision, and the denoising objective does not directly reward aligning the two. We show this correspondence can be supplied as an explicit training signal, that the relevant cross-modal information is concentrated in a low-rank subspace of self-supervised visual features, and that supplying it can be folded into diffusion training as a single auxiliary loss. Our method, ORCA (Orthogonal Residual Compositional Alignment), aligns the latent of a diffusion transformer with a low-rank target derived from a frozen visual encoder, through a predictor whose orthogonal basis is parameterised by a learned residual between T5 and CLIP embeddings, which provides a prompt-dependent signal for selecting the visual readout subspace. We prove that the cross-modal information recoverable at a given rank is bounded by the spectral mass of the visual encoder's covariance in the top components. Across three diffusion-transformer backbones (DiT-B/2, DiT-L/2, U-ViT-L), ORCA improves FID and GenEval over both vanilla and REPA baselines at zero inference-time cost; on DiT-L/2 it reaches FID 16.65 and GenEval 0.291 at 200K steps, exceeding the strongest 400K baseline at half the training cost, with the largest gains concentrated on attribute binding, spatial relations, and multi-object prompts.

</details>


### [100] [Hard, Yet Reducible: Controlled Forward Transfer for Synthetic Degradation Curation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09849)
*Chunming He,Kailai Zhou,Jiaming Zuo,Hanqi Liu,Fengyang Xiao,Youwei Pang,Xiaofeng Liu,Weisi Lin,Xiaoqi Zhao*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: The paper proposes cRDG (controlled Reducible Degradation Gap) to measure the training utility of synthetic degradations for dense prediction tasks. It identifies a "correctable severity band" where synthetic degradation training yields high controlled gain. The method CRB uses cRDG to select synthetic data, improving semantic segmentation and salient object detection while preserving clean performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current methods for selecting synthetic degradations have confounding issues: the gap can shrink when clean performance deteriorates, and improvements on degraded images still credit progress that clean training would have produced. There was no proper way to measure the true generalization benefit of synthetic degradations under finite training budgets.

Method: cRDG runs two budget-matched probes from a common checkpoint: one with synthetic degradation augmentation and one with clean augmentation. The score measures the gain on held-out degraded images relative to the clean-control probe. Clean harm is measured as a separate feasibility constraint. CRB uses cRDG scores to select synthetic data without changing the predictor.

Result: cRDG reveals a "correctable severity band" where training on degradation yields high controlled gain. This band moves with the predictor, starting checkpoint, and training budget. On semantic segmentation and salient object detection, CRB improves representative predictors under matched budgets and training schedules, extends to existing data-generation pipelines, and preserves clean performance.

Conclusion: The proposed cRDG metric and CRB curation method effectively identify optimal synthetic degradations for training dense prediction models. This approach provides a principled way to select synthetic data that improves degradation robustness while maintaining clean performance, with the optimal degradation severity depending on the specific predictor, checkpoint, and training budget.

Abstract: Selecting synthetic degradations for dense prediction requires an estimate of their training utility, the generalization gain they bring under a finite training budget. Clean and degraded twins share content and labels, suggesting a score based on how much short training reduces the excess error caused by degradation. However, this gap can also shrink when clean performance deteriorates. Measuring the improvement on degraded images alone avoids that confound, but it still credits progress that the same amount of clean training would have produced. We propose the \textbf{controlled Reducible Degradation Gap} (cRDG) for regions defined by degradation type and severity. From a common checkpoint, cRDG runs two budget-matched probes that differ only in one augmentation slot, which holds either a synthetic degradation or a clean augmentation. The score is the gain on held-out degraded images relative to the clean-control probe. Clean harm is a separate feasibility constraint. cRDG reveals a correctable severity band in which training on the degradation yields high controlled gain under the available budget, and the band moves with the predictor, the starting checkpoint, and the training budget. \textbf{Curation of Reducible Bands} (\method) uses cRDG to select synthetic data without changing the predictor. On semantic segmentation and salient object detection, \method{} improves representative predictors under matched synthetic-data budgets and training schedules, extends to existing data-generation pipelines, and preserves clean performance. Code and supporting materials will be publicly released.

</details>


### [101] [DeltaSplat: Iterative Gaussian Refinement for Pose-Free Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09853)
*Chanung Park,Seunghyeon Song,Joo Chan Lee,Eunbyung Park,Jong Hwan Ko*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: DeltaSplat is a lightweight refinement module for pose-free feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting that corrects camera estimation errors by iteratively rendering Gaussians at input views and predicting per-Gaussian updates from residuals, using Plücker rays and depth as geometric priors.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Pose-free feed-forward 3DGS reconstructs scenes from sparse, unposed images but suffers from camera estimation errors that propagate into predicted Gaussians, compounding geometric and photometric inaccuracies. A 2D residual alone underdetermines the 3D correction needed.

Method: DeltaSplat introduces a dual-branch convolutional mixer that encodes per-pixel Plücker rays and rendered depth as soft geometric priors, combined with rendered residuals. Per-attribute heads decode fused features into position, opacity, and color updates. The module iteratively refines Gaussians and adds only ~2.2% parameters to the backbone while remaining fully feed-forward.

Result: On DL3DV, DeltaSplat achieves 26.64 dB PSNR in pose-free settings, improving the state-of-the-art backbone by 1.75 dB and surpassing even baselines with ground-truth cameras. Consistent gains are observed across 6-24 views and all camera regimes.

Conclusion: DeltaSplat effectively corrects camera estimation errors in pose-free feed-forward 3DGS through a lightweight refinement module that leverages geometric priors from rendered depth and Plücker rays, achieving significant PSNR improvements while maintaining feed-forward inference efficiency.

Abstract: Pose-free feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) reconstructs a scene from sparse, unposed images in a single network pass, removing the need for camera calibration and per-scene optimization. However, camera estimation errors propagate into the predicted Gaussians and compound the geometric and photometric inaccuracies of single-pass prediction. To correct these errors, we introduce DeltaSplat, a lightweight Gaussian refinement module for pose-free feed-forward 3DGS. It iteratively renders the current Gaussians at the input context views and predicts per-Gaussian updates from the resulting residuals. A 2D residual alone, however, underdetermines the 3D correction. DeltaSplat therefore conditions each update on per-pixel Plücker rays and rendered depth as a soft geometric prior. A dual-branch convolutional mixer efficiently encodes these inputs, and per-attribute heads decode the fused features into position, opacity, and color updates. The module adds only ~2.2% parameters to the backbone and remains fully feed-forward at inference. On DL3DV, DeltaSplat reaches 26.64 dB PSNR in the pose-free setting, improving its state-of-the-art backbone by 1.75 dB and surpassing even baselines supplied with ground-truth cameras; consistent gains hold across 6-24 views and all camera regimes.

</details>


### [102] [DeepTopoClustering: Unsupervised Derivation of Surface Process Taxonomy from 4D Point Clouds for Topographic Monitoring](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09860)
*Jiapan Wang,Daan Hulskemper,Mathilde Letard,Roderik Lindenbergh,Katharina Anders*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: DeepTopoClustering (DTC) is an unsupervised framework that derives a hierarchical process taxonomy from 4D point cloud data (4D objects-by-change) by transforming them into GeoMorphograms and using a convolutional autoencoder with hierarchical deep clustering. The method achieves F1=0.78 and match accuracy=0.92 at the 8-type taxonomy level, outperforming existing approaches.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: 4D point clouds from permanent laser scanning enable high-frequency monitoring of surface change in dynamic topographic environments, but existing methods cannot organize detected surface activities into meaningful process types. There is a need to derive a hierarchical process taxonomy from object-based surface activities (4D-OBCs).

Method: The framework transforms each 4D-OBC into a GeoMorphogram - a distributional sequence representing temporal evolution of topographic change within spatially bounded surface activities. A convolutional autoencoder learns latent embeddings from these GeoMorphograms, which are jointly optimized using a hierarchical deep clustering objective to organize surface activities into a hierarchy.

Result: DTC with GeoMorphograms achieves the highest agreement with expert judgment at the taxonomy level comprising eight major process types (F1=0.78, match accuracy=0.92), outperforming dimensionality reduction and conventional flat clustering. The learned taxonomy separates major erosion- and deposition-dominated activities and distinguishes finer subtypes based on change magnitude, duration, compactness, and temporal evolution.

Conclusion: DTC provides a scalable and interpretable route from 4D change detection to a data-driven, expert-supported surface process taxonomy, advancing automated knowledge derivation for understanding surface dynamics in topographic monitoring. It enables automated classification of surface processes from 4D point cloud data.

Abstract: 4D point clouds acquired by permanent laser scanning (PLS) enable accurate high-frequency monitoring of surface change in dynamic topographic environments. However, existing methods remain limited in organizing detected surface activities into meaningful process types. We propose DeepTopoClustering (DTC), an unsupervised framework for deriving a hierarchical process taxonomy from object-based surface activities, so-called 4D objects-by-change (4D-OBCs). We transform each 4D-OBC into a GeoMorphogram, a distributional sequence representing the temporal evolution of topographic change within a spatially bounded surface activity. A convolutional autoencoder learns latent embeddings from GeoMorphograms, which are jointly optimized using a hierarchical deep clustering objective to organize surface activities into a hierarchy. We evaluate the learned hierarchy using expert annotations on two 4D datasets of sandy beach sites and their combination. DTC with GeoMorphograms achieves the highest agreement with expert judgment at the taxonomy level comprising eight major process types ($F_1=0.78$, match accuracy $=0.92$), outperforming dimensionality reduction and conventional flat clustering. The learned taxonomy separates major erosion- and deposition-dominated activities and distinguishes finer subtypes based on change magnitude, duration, compactness, and temporal evolution. DTC thus provides a scalable and interpretable route from 4D change detection to a data-driven, expert-supported surface process taxonomy, advancing automated knowledge derivation for understanding surface dynamics in topographic monitoring.

</details>


### [103] [Global Average Precision for Representation Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09863)
*Bill Psomas,Mohammad Mahdi,Michalis Thomas,Danda Pani Paudel,Giorgos Tolias,Giorgos Kordopatis-Zilos*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: gSAP is a differentiable ranking loss that optimizes global average precision across all query-candidate pairs jointly, rather than per-query. It enables consistent similarity comparisons across queries, which is essential for systems using a single decision threshold. It can replace InfoNCE in supervised metric learning, cross-modal alignment, and self-supervised pretraining, achieving up to 4x improvement in retrieval at same precision.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard metrics (mAP) and losses (InfoNCE, per-query AP surrogates) evaluate performance query-by-query without considering whether similarities are comparable across queries. This is problematic for systems relying on a single decision threshold. Global Average Precision (gAP) addresses this but lacks a differentiable surrogate for training.

Method: gSAP takes a similarity matrix and binary positive matrix (same input as existing losses) and computes a differentiable approximation of global AP by considering all pairwise comparisons in the batch jointly. This enables training at low temperatures where per-query surrogates fail.

Result: gSAP improves supervised metric learning, cross-modal alignment, and self-supervised pretraining. It is the first ranking loss to replace InfoNCE in the latter two tasks. It retrieves up to 4x more positive pairs at same precision, degrades least when queries with no positives are added, and achieves higher transfer, kNN, and zero-shot classification accuracy.

Conclusion: gSAP provides a drop-in replacement for existing ranking losses that enables consistent cross-query similarity comparisons. It achieves significant improvements in retrieval performance and representation quality across multiple metric learning tasks, with particular benefits for threshold-based decision systems.

Abstract: Standard information retrieval metrics, such as mean Average Precision (mAP), assess performance one query at a time, based on how the similarities between a query and its positives compare against those with its negatives. The same holds for common representation learning losses, such as InfoNCE and per-query AP surrogates. None of them considers whether similarities are comparable across queries, which any system with a single decision threshold relies on. Global Average Precision (gAP) does, by ranking all query-candidate pairs in one list and computing a single AP. We introduce gSAP, a differentiable surrogate of gAP. It needs only a similarity matrix and a binary matrix marking the positive pairs, the same input as existing losses, so it is a drop-in replacement for them and agnostic to the encoder, the modality, and the source of supervision. Since it considers all possible pairwise comparisons in the batch jointly, it also remains trainable at low temperatures, a regime where per-query surrogates run out of gradient. Swapping it into established recipes improves supervised metric learning, cross-modal alignment, and self-supervised pretraining, where, to our knowledge, it is the first ranking loss to replace the community standard InfoNCE in the latter two. Its similarities are more consistent across queries, which drives the gains under a universal threshold. gSAP retrieves up to four times as many positive pairs as the strongest AP surrogate at the same precision, and it degrades the least when queries with no positives in the database are added. Beyond thresholding, models trained with gSAP also learn better representations, with higher transfer, $k$NN and zero-shot classification accuracy.

</details>


### [104] [Bringing BNNs to Fast Event Processing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09873)
*Paul Longour,Julien Moreau,Franck Davoine*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper explores the combination of Binary Neural Networks (BNNs) and event cameras for efficient deep learning. The authors introduce PBEV (Polar-wise Binary Event Volume), a binary representation enabling event data processing by BNNs, and demonstrate cross-modal pretraining from RGB to improve neuromorphic classification. Achieved 90.58% accuracy on N-Caltech101 with 7.5x computational savings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Both BNNs and event cameras share a core emphasis on efficiency - BNNs compress weights/activations to 1-bit reducing model size and inference cost, while event cameras offer low latency, high dynamic range, and low power by capturing asynchronous events instead of dense frames. Despite this complementary potential, the combination remains largely unexplored in literature.

Method: 1) Adapted modern deep BNN architectures to work with event data
2) Applied cross-modal pretraining from RGB data to improve classification accuracy on neuromorphic datasets
3) Introduced Polar-wise Binary Event Volume (PBEV) - a binary representation that enables event-camera data to be processed directly by BNNs

Result: Best performing BNN achieved 90.58% accuracy on N-Caltech101 classification benchmark, with 7.5x fewer operations compared to full-precision counterparts.

Conclusion: The combination of BNNs and event cameras is viable and beneficial. Cross-modal pretraining from RGB data improves BNN performance on neuromorphic datasets. PBEV represents a step toward fully binarized event-based vision systems, achieving significant computational efficiency with competitive accuracy.

Abstract: Binary Neural Networks (BNNs) enable efficient deep learning deployment on resource constrained devices with weights and activations compressed to one bit, substantially reducing model size and inference cost. Event cameras offer complementary advantages, including low latency, high dynamic range, and low power consumption, by capturing asynchronous streams of events rather than dense image frames. Despite their shared emphasis on efficiency, the combination of these technologies remains largely unexplored. This work aims at adapting and evaluating modern deep BNN architectures on event data. We also show that cross-modal pretraining from RGB data can improve the classification accuracy of BNNs on neuromorphic datasets. We introduce the Polar-wise Binary Event Volume (PBEV), a binary representation that enables event-camera data to be processed directly by BNNs and represents a step toward fully binarized event-based vision systems. Best evaluated BNN on N-Caltech101 classification benchmarks shows 90.58% accuracy with 7.5x less operations than their full-precision counterparts.

</details>


### [105] [SANet: Selective Attention Network for Infrared Small Target Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09875)
*Yingmei Zhang,Wangtao Bao,Qin Xiao,Yong Yang,Weiguo Wan,Yitao Luo,Xueting Zou,Lei Zhang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: The paper proposes a Selective Attention Network (SANet) for infrared small target detection, which addresses the challenge of detecting dim targets in complex backgrounds. SANet uses a dual-path semantic-aware module combining standard and pinwheel convolutions, spatial and channel attention mechanisms, and a selective attention fusion module to adaptively integrate multi-scale features. The method achieves state-of-the-art performance on three public benchmarks (NUAA-SIRST, IRSTD-1K, NUDT-SIRST), with IoU improvements of 1.93, 4.32, and 2.21 percentage points respectively over the second-best method.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Infrared small target detection is challenging due to the small size and weak contrast of targets, making it difficult to balance detection accuracy and false alarms. Applications include maritime surveillance and military search and rescue. Existing methods struggle with the trade-off between detecting dim targets and minimizing false alarms in complex backgrounds.

Method: The paper proposes three key components: (1) A dual-path semantic-aware module combining standard and pinwheel-shaped convolutions to preserve local spatial consistency while capturing broader contextual information; (2) Spatial and channel attention mechanisms to refine features and improve target-background discrimination; (3) A selective attention fusion module that replaces static skip connections in U-Net, using spatially varying weights to adaptively integrate features across scales and selectively enhance salient regions.

Result: SANet achieves competitive performance on three public benchmarks (NUAA-SIRST, IRSTD-1K, NUDT-SIRST) across metrics including IoU, normalized IoU, detection probability, and false alarm rate. IoU improvements of 1.93%, 4.32%, and 2.21 percentage points respectively over the second-best method.

Conclusion: SANet effectively addresses infrared small target detection through its dual-path architecture and attention mechanisms. The selective attention fusion module enables better discrimination between true targets and false alarms, demonstrating the method's effectiveness in dim-target perception, discriminative feature representation, and background suppression.

Abstract: Infrared small target detection aims to accurately identify and locate dim targets in complex backgrounds and supports applications such as maritime surveillance and military search and rescue. However, the small size and weak contrast of infrared targets make it difficult to balance detection accuracy and false alarms. This paper proposes a selective attention network (SANet) for infrared small target detection. A dual-path semantic-aware module combines standard and pinwheel-shaped convolutions to preserve local spatial consistency and capture broader contextual information. Spatial and channel attention further refine the features and improve target-background discrimination. To address the limitations of static skip connections in U-Net, a selective attention fusion module adaptively integrates features across scales using spatially varying weights. It selectively enhances salient regions and improves discrimination between true targets and false alarms. Experiments on three public benchmarks, NUAA-SIRST, IRSTD-1K, and NUDT-SIRST, show that SANet achieves competitive performance in intersection over union (IoU), normalized IoU, detection probability, and false alarm rate. Its IoU exceeds that of the second-best method by 1.93, 4.32, and 2.21 percentage points, respectively. These results support the effectiveness of SANet in dim-target perception, discriminative feature representation, and background suppression.

</details>


### [106] [FedSSMCoOp: SSM Encoders for light-weight Federated Prompt Learning for Few-shot Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09907)
*Ankita Das,Ambarish Parthasarathy,Sumohana S. Channappayya,C. Krishna Mohan*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: FedSSMCoOp is a federated few-shot image classification framework for biomedical images that uses SSM-based Vision Mamba and Cross Mamba blocks to enable multimodal learning without external LLMs, while only optimizing soft-prompt and communication-prompt updates.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current VLM approaches rely on cosine similarity for cross-modal alignment, which fails to capture token-level structure and cross-modal interactions. In biomedical federated settings, data sharing is restricted, labeled data is scarce, and statistical heterogeneity exists across institutions, making traditional approaches inadequate.

Method: The framework uses SSM-based Vision Mamba and Cross Mamba blocks for multimodal learning. It optimizes only soft-prompt and communication-prompt updates in the federated setting, eliminating the need for external Large Language Models for feature alignment.

Result: The proposed framework delivers stable performance relative to baselines and is on average 1.96 times lighter (more computationally efficient).

Conclusion: FedSSMCoOp successfully enables privacy-preserving multimodal learning for biomedical image classification in federated environments, achieving comparable performance with significantly reduced computational requirements.

Abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have shown strong performance across a wide range of downstream vision tasks, thanks to the complementary information contained in the respective domains. Despite the performance gains, most of these approaches rely on aligning these domains using the cosine similarity metric, which fails to capture token-level structure and cross-modal interactions prior to the classification stage. This is especially critical in biomedical applications under federated constraints, where data sharing is restricted, labeled data is scarce at each site, and it differs widely across institutions, leading to substantial statistical heterogeneity. To overcome this issue, we propose FedSSMCoOp, a federated few-shot image classification framework that enables multimodal learning while preserving data privacy. With the help of the SSM-based Vision Mamba and Cross Mamba blocks, and by optimizing only the soft-prompt and communication-prompt updates in the federated setting, the framework prioritizes both computation and performance. Importantly, this eliminates the need to use an external Large Language Model (LLM) for feature alignment. The framework is further trained and evaluated on various biomedical image datasets, and its performance is assessed. The proposed framework delivers stable performance relative to the baselines and is, on average, 1.96 times lighter. The corresponding script will be made available soon.

</details>


### [107] [Do Generative Priors Align with Human Naturalness Perception?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09928)
*Taiki Fukiage*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: The study investigates whether visual generative models capture human perception of image naturalness by testing 25 image/video generators using content-preserving interventions that disrupt facial configurations or illumination consistency. The generative loss landscapes reproduce human-like sensitivities (Thatcher effect, illumination responses) and strongly correlate with human naturalness judgments (r=.84 faces, r=.64 scenes), even after controlling for vision encoders and image quality metrics. However, sensitivity and human alignment dissociate along denoising schedules.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To test whether native priors of visual generative models reflect the regularities governing human perception of image naturalness, since raw single-image losses are dominated by scene content and visual complexity rather than perceptual violations.

Method: Evaluated 25 open image and video generators using directional loss differences with content-preserving, paired relational interventions that selectively disrupt facial configurations or physical illumination consistency while limiting changes in low-level image statistics.

Result: Loss differences reproduce human-like selective sensitivities: Thatcher effect on faces, shape-dependent responses to illumination inconsistencies. They reliably track continuous gradations of human naturalness judgments (r=.84 on faces, r=.64 on physical scenes) and retain unique human-aligned signals after controlling for feature distances from frozen vision encoders and standard image quality metrics. Sensitivity and human alignment decouple along denoising schedules, with alignment peaking earlier than sensitivity.

Conclusion: Learning visual probability distributions of images yields generative loss landscapes that capture distinct aspects of human naturalness perception, demonstrating that human-like naturalness judgments dissociate from generic violation detection.

Abstract: Visual generative models are trained to capture the probability distributions of natural images, yet whether their native priors reflect the regularities governing human perception of image naturalness remains an open question. Here, we probe these priors through native prediction errors across 25 open image and video generators. Because raw single-image losses are dominated by scene content and visual complexity, we evaluate directional loss differences using content-preserving, paired relational interventions that selectively disrupt facial configurations or physical illumination consistency while limiting changes in low-level image statistics. Across both domains, these loss differences reproduce human-like selective sensitivities and tolerances, capturing the classic Thatcher effect on faces and shape-dependent responses to illumination inconsistencies. Notably, these loss differences reliably track continuous gradations of human naturalness judgments across individual stimulus pairs (peaking at $r = .84$ on faces and $.64$ on physical scenes) and retain unique human-aligned signals even after controlling for feature distances from frozen vision encoders and standard image quality metrics. We also find that while overall sensitivity to these violations broadly covaries with human alignment across models, the two systematically decouple along denoising schedules, with alignment peaking earlier than sensitivity, revealing that human-like naturalness judgments dissociate from generic violation detection. Together, these findings demonstrate that learning visual distributions yields generative loss landscapes that capture distinct aspects of human naturalness perception.

</details>


### [108] [Purifying Backdoored Large Vision-Language Models by Removing Hijacked Directions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09941)
*Bojun Yang,Haochen Zhou,Zhifang Zhang,Haobo Wang,Songze Li,Lei Feng*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: OrthoPurify is a defense method against backdoor attacks in Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) that uses one-step orthogonal projection to purify backdoored model weights without retraining or inference-time overhead.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing backdoor defenses are costly, requiring either extensive retraining on clean data or per-query intervention at inference time. The authors aim to develop a more efficient purification method.

Method: The method leverages the "direction hijacking" phenomenon - where backdoor attacks divert weight update directions from task adaptation to backdoor shortcut encoding. OrthoPurify uses a pseudo-benign reference model (obtained by fine-tuning pretrained weights on a small set of clean samples) to identify hijacked directions, then removes them through a single orthogonal projection on the weight update.

Result: OrthoPurify reduces attack success rate to near zero while preserving original performance across diverse benchmarks, without retraining the backdoored model or introducing inference-time overhead.

Conclusion: OrthoPurify provides an efficient, practical defense against backdoor attacks in LVLMs by exploiting the directional nature of backdoor encoding and using minimal clean data to establish a pseudo-benign reference for purification.

Abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) are increasingly deployed in safety-critical applications, yet they remain vulnerable to backdoor attacks. Defending against such attacks remains costly, as existing methods require either extensive retraining on clean data or per-query intervention at inference time. To address this limitation, we propose OrthoPurify, a more efficient method to purify backdoored model weights via one-step orthogonal projection. Specifically, through structural analysis of backdoor weight updates, we find that the backdoor is encoded by diverting a small number of weight update directions from task adaptation to backdoor shortcut encoding, a phenomenon we term direction hijacking. However, identifying these hijacked directions requires a benign reference model, which is typically inaccessible to the defender. We show that a pseudo-benign model, obtained by fine-tuning the pretrained weights on only a small set of clean samples, provides a sufficient approximation, as the dominant update directions stabilize within the first few gradient steps. OrthoPurify uses this pseudo-benign reference to isolate the hijacked directions and removes them through a single projection on the weight update. Extensive experiments show that OrthoPurify reduces the attack success rate to near zero while preserving the original performance across diverse benchmarks, without retraining the backdoored model or introducing inference-time overhead. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/womeimingzi/OrthoPurify.

</details>


### [109] [MSU Team at the Explainable Deepfake Detection Challenge 2026: Grounded Artifact Evidence for Deepfake Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09952)
*Artem Filippov,Aleksandr Gushchin,Kirill Koltsov,Dmitriy Vatolin,Anastasia Antsiferova*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper presents a solution to the Explainable Deepfake Detection Challenge on the XPlainVerse dataset. The system combines a multi-backbone detector (DINOv3 + Mesorch features) with a Grounding-DINO-based artifact evidence mapping pipeline and uses Qwen3-VL models for explanation generation, followed by GRPO-optimized text simplification.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The proliferation of highly realistic AI-generated images necessitates detectors that are both accurate and explainable. The challenge requires not only real/fake classification but also generating complex and simple explanations grounded in visible forensic cues.

Method: The method employs a modular detection-and-explanation design: (1) Multi-backbone detector combining DINOv3 models with Mesorch manipulation-localization features; (2) Grounding-DINO-based pseudo-mask generation for weak patch-level supervision (Artifact Evidence Map); (3) Local patch-level contrastive objective for separating artifact and authenticity evidence; (4) Class-conditional Qwen3-VL for complex explanation generation; (5) GRPO-optimized text simplification model.

Result: On the full test split, the submission achieves 0.9349 detection accuracy, 0.5571 explanation score, and 0.7456 final challenge score.

Conclusion: The proposed modular approach effectively combines visual detection with explainability, achieving strong performance on both detection accuracy and explanation quality in the Explainable Deepfake Detection Challenge.

Abstract: Recent advances in generative image models have made many manipulated images highly realistic, raising the need for detectors that are not only accurate but also able to provide visual evidence for their decisions. In this paper, we present our solution to the Explainable Deepfake Detection Challenge [2] on the XPlainVerse dataset [1], where systems are required to predict whether an image is real or fake and generate both complex and simple explanations grounded in visible forensic cues. Our method follows a modular detection-and-explanation design. For the real/fake decision, we build a multi-backbone detector that combines several DINOv3 models with Mesorch manipulation-localization features, bringing together pretrained visual representations, DCT-aware cues, and multi-scale forensic information. To inject explanation evidence into the detector, we use a Grounding-DINO-based pseudo-mask generation pipeline that converts local artifact descriptions from training explanations into weak patch- level supervision for an Artifact Evidence Map. We further introduce a local patch-level contrastive objective that separates artifact and authenticity evidence in the detector feature space without requiring paired images or pixel-level manipulation masks. For language output, we use class-conditional Qwen3-VL models to generate complex explanations for fake and real predictions, followed by a GRPO-optimized text simplification model. The proposed methods were trained and evaluated on the challenge subset of XPlainVerse. On the full test split, our submission achieves 0.9349 detection accuracy, 0.5571 explanation score, and a 0.7456 final challenge score.

</details>


### [110] [Perceptually Aligned Evaluation of Style Transfer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.10003)
*Yang Deng,Eleftherios Ioannou,David Mould,Steve Maddock,Paul L. Rosin,Yu-Kun Lai*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: ASTRA introduces a framework for automatic evaluation of style transfer algorithms, consisting of ASTRA-Data (benchmark dataset with human judgments) and ASTRA-Score (learnt evaluator that predicts preference-aligned scores). The approach achieves higher correlation with human rankings than existing metrics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Style transfer lacks reliable evaluation standards: ground truth is ill-defined, and existing automatic metrics fail to reflect human preference.

Method: ASTRA-Data: benchmark image set with style transfer results and human judgments via two-stage pairwise comparison protocol. ASTRA-Score: learned evaluator predicting preference-aligned scores from content-style-stylization triplets.

Result: ASTRA-Score achieves substantially higher correlation with human rankings compared to prior metrics.

Conclusion: ASTRA establishes a robust mechanism for standardized evaluation of style transfer methods.

Abstract: Style transfer lacks a reliable evaluation standard: ground truth is inherently ill-defined, and existing automatic metrics often fail to reflect human preference. This paper introduces ASTRA (Assessment of Style TRansfer Algorithms), an approach for automatic evaluation of style transfer algorithms; it contains two components, ASTRA-Data and ASTRA-Score. ASTRA-Data consists of a benchmark image set of content and style references, a collection of style transfer results generated on the benchmark set, and user study data capturing human judgements through a two-stage pairwise comparison protocol. From these annotations, we derive ranking-based ground truth for content preservation, style fidelity, and overall preference. Based on ASTRA-Data, we construct ASTRA-Score, a learnt evaluator that predicts preference-aligned scores from content-style-stylization image triplets, enabling automatic and scalable evaluation of new models applied to the benchmark set. Experimental results demonstrate that ASTRA-Score achieves substantially higher correlation with human rankings compared to prior metrics. Overall, ASTRA establishes a robust mechanism for standardised evaluation of style transfer methods.

</details>


### [111] [Playing with Kruskal: algorithms for flat and hierarchical watershed cuts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.10012)
*Jean Cousty,Laurent Najman,Benjamin Perret,Deise Santana Maia*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper presents a comprehensive review and end-to-end pipeline for computing watershed segmentation in edge-weighted graphs, covering algorithms from graph-based image representations to hierarchical segmentation, including supervised and unsupervised variations with various seed computation methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Watersheds in edge-weighted graphs are linked to optimization problems like Minimum Spanning Tree (MST), enabling efficient algorithms for watershed segmentation. However, the literature is scattered, and there was no unified reference consolidating all watershed notions and algorithms in a compact, understandable manner.

Method: The authors review the literature on watershed segmentation and present a detailed end-to-end pipeline of algorithms. They cover: (1) graph-based image representations, (2) computation of edge weights, (3) watershed transform algorithms, (4) hierarchical watershed segmentation, (5) supervised and unsupervised versions, and (6) various seed computation methods.

Result: The paper synthesizes all watershed notions and algorithms into a unified, compact, and understandable framework. It provides a complete pipeline from image representation to final connected components of hierarchical segmentation.

Conclusion: This work serves as a reference for researchers and practitioners interested in implementing or employing the watershed segmentation framework for their specific tasks, consolidating previously scattered knowledge into a comprehensive guide.

Abstract: In the framework of edge-weighted graphs, watersheds have proven to be linked to well-known optimization problems, as Minimum Spanning Tree, which allowed the design of efficient algorithms for computing (hierarchical) watershed segmentations. In the present article, after reviewing the literature related to watershed segmentation, we present a detailed end-to-end pipeline of algorithms to compute (hierarchical) watershed segmentations, starting from the computation of graph-based image representations, up to the computation of connected components of the final (hierarchical) segmentation. We consider the several variations of watersheds, including their supervised and unsupervised versions, and the various ways of computing seeds, to name a few. For the first time, we bring together all these watershed notions and algorithms in a compact and understandable way.
