We aim at providing a reference for those interested in employing and reimplementing the watershed segmentation framework for their task at hand.

</details>


### [112] [Scalable Patch-Level Self-Supervised Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.10013)
*Maximilian Seitzer,Gabriele Trivigno,Antonín Vobecký,Seungeun Yi,Maxime Oquab,Huy V. Vo,Oriane Siméoni,Piotr Bojanowski*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: JEM (Joint Embedding Method) is a principled information-theoretic self-supervised learning algorithm that aligns patch representations across views with explicit regularization. It scales stably from 300M to 7B parameters and surpasses DINOv2 on segmentation benchmarks, outperforming DINOv3 on panoptic segmentation at 7B scale with 12x less training data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current scalable SSL methods rely on ad hoc combinations of multiple objectives and stabilization mechanisms. The authors seek to design a high-performing yet principled SSL algorithm based on the multi-view assumption, which stipulates that task-relevant content is captured by information common to different views.

Method: Starting from the multi-view assumption, the authors derive an information-theoretic objective decomposing into interpretable terms. JEM is a student-teacher method that learns by aligning corresponding patch representations across views, explicitly regularized by information and structure preservation losses.

Result: JEM trains stably from 300M to 7B parameters, being the first latent-space patch-level method demonstrated at 7B scale. It achieves strong performance on both global and dense probing tasks. On segmentation benchmarks, it consistently surpasses DINOv2. At 7B parameters, it exceeds DINOv3 on panoptic segmentation despite being trained on 12x less data without refinement stages.

Conclusion: A principled, stable SSL algorithm can be designed to learn strong visual representations, demonstrating that information-theoretic foundations can yield effective self-supervised learning without ad hoc components.

Abstract: Self-supervised learning (SSL) at scale produces powerful visual representations. However, most scalable SSL methods rely on ad hoc combinations of multiple objectives and stabilization mechanisms. Taking a step back, we ask if we can design a high-performing, yet principled SSL algorithm. Starting from the multi-view assumption, stipulating that task-relevant content is captured by the information common to different views, we construct an information-theoretic objective decomposing into interpretable terms. This derivation yields JEM, a student-teacher method that learns by aligning corresponding patch representations across views, explicitly regularized by information and structure preservation losses. JEM trains stably from 300M to 7B parameters, and, to our knowledge, is the first latent-space patch-level method demonstrated at 7B scale. Across all scales, JEM reaches strong performance on both global and dense probing tasks, on segmentation benchmarks consistently surpassing the DINOv2 algorithm, an influential foundation for today's strongest visual SSL methods. Notably, at 7B parameters, it exceeds the performance of DINOv3 on panoptic segmentation, despite being trained on $12\times$ less data without refinement stages. These results demonstrate that we can indeed design an SSL algorithm that learns strong representations, is principled and stable.

</details>


### [113] [AdSpark: A Large-Scale Dataset and Benchmark for Product-Centric Advertisement Video Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.10047)
*Zhifei Yang,Zhao Jiang,Keyang Lu,Honghe Zhu,Zheng Zhang,Jingjing Lv,Changping Peng,Ching Law,Zhen Xiao*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: AdSpark is a large-scale dataset (300K samples) and benchmark for product-centric advertisement video generation, addressing the lack of advertisement-specific datasets and evaluation frameworks in this emerging task.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Product-centric advertisement video generation is an emerging but underexplored task due to the lack of large-scale advertisement-specific datasets and comprehensive evaluation frameworks.

Method: The authors created AdSpark-300K with ~300K reference image-prompt-video triplets (real-world and synthetic subsets), with structured annotations including product identity, selling-point descriptions, creative plans, and audio scripts. They also proposed AdSpark-Bench, a diagnostic benchmark evaluating six dimensions: visual quality, product fidelity, instruction adherence, temporal coherence, audio alignment, and advertisement effectiveness.

Result: Evaluation of representative models revealed key challenges in product preservation, multi-shot storytelling, and selling-point visualization. Experiments with fine-tuned models validated the dataset's effectiveness.

Conclusion: AdSpark provides a unified dataset and benchmark for future research in product-centric advertisement video generation. The dataset will be released upon acceptance.

Abstract: Product-centric advertisement video generation aims to create promotional videos that preserve fine-grained product identity while presenting selling points through coherent multi-shot narratives. However, this emerging task remains underexplored due to the lack of large-scale advertisement-specific datasets and comprehensive evaluation frameworks. To address this gap, we introduce \textbf{AdSpark}, a large-scale dataset and benchmark for product-centric advertisement video generation, based on data from a major e-commerce platform. \textit{AdSpark-300K} contains approximately 300K reference image--prompt--video triplets, comprising a real-world subset and a synthetic subset. Each sample provides structured advertisement annotations, including product identity annotations, selling-point descriptions, creative plans, and aligned audio scripts, enabling models to learn product preservation and advertisement-oriented visual storytelling. We further propose \textit{AdSpark-Bench}, a diagnostic benchmark that evaluates generated advertisements across six dimensions, including visual quality, product fidelity, instruction adherence, temporal coherence, audio alignment, and advertisement effectiveness. Based on AdSpark-Bench, we evaluate representative models, revealing key challenges in product preservation, multi-shot storytelling, and selling-point visualization. Experiments with AdSpark-300K-finetuned models further validate the effectiveness of our dataset. AdSpark provides a unified dataset and benchmark for future research, and we will release the dataset upon acceptance.

</details>


### [114] [From Pixel to Coding: Evaluating the Figure Reproduction Capabilities of MLLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.10066)
*Zijian Chen,Zhengyu Chen,Bohan Liang,Lirong Deng,Yushuo Zheng,Yanwei Jiang,Qi Jia,Kaiwei Zhang,Wenjun Zhang,Guangtao Zhai*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: FigCodeBench is a new benchmark for evaluating Multimodal Large Language Models on figure reproduction tasks, combining visual understanding and code generation. It contains 6,194 instances across 7 functional categories and 4 programming languages, with three difficulty tiers and multi-dimensional evaluation including visual fidelity and syntactic isomorphism.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing benchmarks evaluate visual understanding and code generation in isolation, lacking assessment of their unification. Current visual code generation benchmarks rely on simplified layouts within single programming environments and fail to evaluate true unified multimodal reasoning - specifically how models can perceive complex visual structures and synthesize them into precise, executable code.

Method: The authors designed a systematic dataset construction pipeline creating 6,194 instances covering 7 functional categories and 4 programming languages. They categorized figure reproduction into three tiers with visual and code complexity modeling, targeting complex structural reasoning, varying aspect ratios, and dense geometric constraints. A multi-dimensional evaluation protocol was introduced, encompassing visual fidelity and syntactic isomorphism aligned with Mean Machine Opinion Score (MMOS) and human preferences. Experiments were conducted on 24 MLLMs including Gemini 3.1 Pro, GPT-5.4, and Kimi-K2.5.

Result: The study revealed a universal, non-linear performance cliff across different programming languages and difficulty scenarios for all models tested. A significant metric decline was observed in rigid declarative languages. The evaluation protocol aligns highly with MMOS and human preferences.

Conclusion: FigCodeBench provides a comprehensive framework for rigorously evaluating MLLMs on figure reproduction, integrating multimodal comprehension and generation. The benchmark exposes that current MLLMs still struggle with unified multimodal reasoning in visual code generation tasks, particularly as complexity increases across different programming languages.

Abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities in both visual understanding and code generation. However, existing benchmarks typically evaluate these two modalities in isolation, lacking a dedicated assessment of their unification, i.e., how a model can perceive complex visual structures and synthesize them into precise, executable code. Moreover, current visual code generation benchmarks often rely on simplified layouts within single programming environments, falling short of evaluating true unified multimodal reasoning. To bridge this gap, we propose FigCodeBench, a comprehensive framework for rigorously evaluating MLLMs on figure reproduction, integrating multimodal comprehension and generation. We first design a systematic dataset construction pipeline, resulting in a total of 6,194 instances that cover 7 functional categories and 4 types of programming languages. We further categorize figure reproduction into three tiers with visual and code complexity modeling, specifically targeting complex structural reasoning, varying aspect ratios, and dense geometric constraints. We introduce a multi-dimensional evaluation protocol, encompassing visual fidelity and syntactic isomorphism, that aligns highly with the Mean Machine Opinion Score (MMOS) and human preferences. Based on our framework, we conducted extensive experiments on 24 widely used proprietary and open-source MLLMs (e.g., Gemini 3.1 Pro, GPT-5.4, and Kimi-K2.5), where we observed a universal, non-linear performance cliff across different programming languages and difficulty scenarios for all models, and gained several insights, such as the significant metric decline in rigid declarative languages.

</details>


### [115] [Temporal Residual Bottleneck for Robust Asynchronous Collaborative Perception](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.10090)
*Melih Yazgan,Ahmed Abouelazm,J. Marius Zöllner*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper proposes Temporal Residual Prediction to address latency issues in asynchronous collaborative perception for autonomous vehicles. The method uses a pose-warped collaborator feature as an anchor and a Δt-conditioned xLSTM to extract residual temporal evidence, applying only gated corrections before fusion to avoid overwriting reliable static structures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Collaborative perception extends sensing range of autonomous vehicles, but performance degrades when shared features arrive stale or incomplete due to communication delays. Existing methods (flow-guided alignment, direct feature transport) either lack robustness under severe delays or become unreliable without accurate temporal correspondence.

Method: The method formulates asynchronous collaborative perception as temporal residual prediction. It uses a Temporal Residual Bottleneck that: (1) maintains a deterministic pose-warped collaborator feature as a conservative anchor, (2) employs a Δt-conditioned xLSTM to extract residual temporal evidence from available history, and (3) applies only gated, regularized corrections before ego-side fusion to reduce risk of overwriting reliable static structure.

Result: Experiments on DAIR-V2X and OPV2V show the method is especially effective under severe fixed/irregular delays and packet drops. On DAIR-V2X, it trades a small amount of synchronized peak accuracy for better robustness under stronger communication degradation. Direct feature transport has oracle headroom but becomes unreliable when deployed without accurate correspondence.

Conclusion: Temporal residual fusion is a practical alternative for asynchronous and incomplete collaborative perception, offering better robustness under communication degradation while maintaining reasonable accuracy.

Abstract: Collaborative perception extends the sensing range of autonomous vehicles, but its performance degrades when shared features arrive stale or incomplete. Most latency-robust methods compensate delayed collaborator features through flow-guided alignment or direct feature transport. In this work, we formulate asynchronous collaborative perception as temporal residual prediction. Our Temporal Residual Bottleneck keeps a deterministic pose-warped collaborator feature as a conservative anchor and uses a $Δt$-conditioned xLSTM to extract residual temporal evidence from the available history. A detector-facing residual bottleneck then applies only gated, regularized corrections before ego-side fusion, reducing the risk of overwriting reliable static structure when temporal correspondence is uncertain. Experiments on DAIR-V2X and OPV2V show that our method is especially effective under severe fixed/irregular delays and packet drops. On DAIR-V2X, the reported checkpoint trades a small amount of synchronized peak accuracy for better robustness under stronger communication degradation. Controlled diagnostics further indicate that direct feature transport has oracle headroom but can become unreliable when deployed without accurate correspondence. These results support temporal residual fusion as a practical alternative for asynchronous and incomplete collaborative perception. Code will be publicly released at https://url.fzi.de/8dk38.

</details>


### [116] [A Probabilistic Perspective on Wasserstein-Based Evidential Uncertainty for Out-of-Distribution Segmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.10116)
*Arnold Brosch,Abdelrahman Eldesokey,Michael Felsberg,Kira Maag*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper proposes a Wasserstein-based Evidential Deep Learning framework for out-of-distribution (OOD) detection in semantic segmentation. By replacing Euclidean objectives with Wasserstein-based ones that respect the probability simplex geometry, the method achieves better uncertainty calibration and OOD detection while requiring only a single deterministic forward pass.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Semantic segmentation networks fail when OOD objects appear during deployment, which is critical for safety-critical applications like autonomous driving. Existing methods like softmax-based confidence scores are overconfident, while Bayesian alternatives require costly repeated forward passes. EDL offers an efficient single-pass alternative but uses Euclidean objectives that encourage overconfidence rather than preserving uncertainty for unfamiliar inputs.

Method: The paper employs Wasserstein-based objectives within the evidential framework, which respect the geometry of the probability simplex. The authors study the influence of Wasserstein order on segmentation accuracy and OOD detection using both convolutional (DeepLabV3+) and transformer-based (SegFormer) architectures. Evaluation is performed on the SegmentMeIfYouCan benchmark including LostAndFound, RoadObstacle21, RoadAnomaly21, and Fishyscapes datasets.

Result: The optimal Wasserstein order is architecture-dependent: second-order objectives dominate on the convolutional backbone, while third-order objectives perform best on the transformer backbone. The framework surpasses comparable baselines on most metrics while requiring only a single deterministic forward pass.

Conclusion: Wasserstein-based evidential learning provides an efficient and effective solution for OOD detection in semantic segmentation, with the optimal order depending on the backbone architecture. This approach achieves superior uncertainty calibration and OOD detection performance compared to existing methods without the computational overhead of Bayesian alternatives.

Abstract: Semantic segmentation networks operate on a fixed set of classes and therefore fail when out-of-distribution (OOD) objects appear during deployment, a critical limitation for safety-critical applications such as autonomous driving. Reliably identifying OOD objects requires well-calibrated epistemic uncertainty, yet common softmax-based confidence scores remain overconfident, while Bayesian alternatives such as Monte Carlo dropout or deep ensembles require costly repeated forward passes. Evidential Deep Learning (EDL) offers an efficient alternative by modeling class probabilities as a Dirichlet distribution learned from a single deterministic forward pass. Existing EDL formulations rely on Euclidean objectives that push predictions towards the simplex vertices, encouraging overconfidence rather than preserving uncertainty for unfamiliar inputs. We instead employ Wasserstein-based objectives, which respect the geometry of the probability simplex, and study the influence of the Wasserstein order on segmentation accuracy and OOD detection within a unified evidential framework. We evaluate this framework on a convolutional (DeepLabV3+) and a transformer-based (SegFormer) architecture on the SegmentMeIfYouCan benchmark, including LostAndFound, RoadObstacle21, RoadAnomaly21, and Fishyscapes. Our results show the optimal Wasserstein order is architecture-dependent: second-order objectives dominate on the convolutional backbone, third-order objectives on the transformer backbone, and our framework surpasses comparable baselines on most metrics, with a single deterministic forward pass.

</details>
