# cs.SE [[Back]](#toc)

### [117] [Mitigating Uncertainty Interactions in GenAI-based Adaptive Systems: Vision, Challenges and Preliminary Guidelines](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08881)
*Karthik Vaidhyanathan,Norha Villegas,Raffaela Mirandola,Nicolás Cardozo,Ivana Dusparic,Marin Litoiu,Ralf Reussner,Gabriel Tamura*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This position paper addresses uncertainty management in GenAI-based software-intensive systems, proposing a conceptual framework that spans the full software lifecycle from requirements to runtime adaptation. It introduces a mitigation function to map uncertainty interactions to quality attributes and tradeoffs, validated through three use cases.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: GenAI components (LLMs, agents) introduce novel uncertainty sources (hallucinations, probabilistic outputs, memory staleness) that compound across system layers, requiring re-examination of existing uncertainty management frameworks.

Method: Position paper proposing an initial conceptual framework with: (1) guidelines for characterizing uncertainty interactions, (2) mitigation spanning full lifecycle (requirements, design-time, runtime), (3) mitigation function mapping interaction categories, uncertainty types, architectural tactics to quality attributes and tradeoffs.

Result: Framework applied to three use cases: LLM serving, AI-driven software operations (AIOps), and agentic cloud management.

Conclusion: Mitigation cannot be decoupled from monitoring and analysis at execution; comprehensive lifecycle approach is needed for uncertainty management in GenAI-based systems.

Abstract: Modern software-intensive systems increasingly incorporate GenAI components, including LLM and agentic subsystems, which introduce novel and compounding sources of uncertainty across system layers. The self-adaptive systems community has made significant strides in understanding and managing uncertainty. The intrinsic characteristics of GenAI, including probabilistic outputs, hallucinations, context window limitations, and memory staleness, demand a re-examination of existing frameworks and mitigation strategies for dealing with uncertainty, and especially, the interactions among uncertainty occurrences and manifestations. This position paper posits an initial conceptual framework that establishes preliminary guidelines for characterizing and mitigating uncertainty interactions in GenAI-based software-intensive systems. We argue that mitigation must be considered across the full software lifecycle, encompassing requirements analysis, design-time decisions, and run-time adaptations, which implies the unfeasibility of decoupling it from monitoring and analysis at execution. We introduce the notion of a mitigation function that maps uncertainty interaction categories, involved uncertainty types, system design characteristics, criticality, and mitigating architectural tactics to impacted quality attributes and corresponding tradeoffs. As a proof of concept, we apply the framework to three illustrative use cases: LLM serving, AI-driven software operations, and agentic cloud management.

</details>


### [118] [Psychological Safety in Software Engineering Teams: A Systematic Mapping Study of Team Processes and Performance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08896)
*Adnan Manzoor,Muhammad Azeem Akbar,Jussi Kasurinen,Muhammad Hamza,Aakash Ahmad,Abdul Razzaq*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: A systematic mapping study analyzing 112 primary studies on psychological safety in software engineering teams, examining its conceptualization, associations with team performance, contextual influences, barriers, and strengthening strategies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Psychological safety is recognized as an important factor in software development teams, but evidence remains fragmented across various dimensions. This study aims to map and synthesize the literature to provide a comprehensive understanding of psychological safety in software engineering contexts.

Method: Systematic mapping study following established software engineering guidelines. Analysis of 112 primary studies published between 2006 and June 2026 using descriptive statistics and thematic analysis across six research questions.

Result: Psychological safety emerges as a multidimensional, context-dependent, team-level construct characterized by interpersonal risk-taking, open communication, collaboration, learning, trust, and supportive interaction. It is predominantly associated with productivity, software quality, innovation, team satisfaction, collaboration, communication, and decision-making. These relationships are shaped by leadership, organizational culture, work environment, trust, and sociocultural and individual conditions. Recurring barriers include communication problems, organizational constraints, leadership issues, diversity and inclusion challenges, and workload pressures. Evidence on effectiveness and long-term sustainability of interventions remains limited.

Conclusion: Psychological safety is a multidimensional, context-dependent team-level construct associated with team interaction and performance. The study highlights the need for longitudinal, context-sensitive research on psychological safety interventions in software development environments.

Abstract: Context: Psychological safety is an important human and behavioral factor in software development teams, supporting collaboration, knowledge sharing, interpersonal risk-taking, and learning. However, evidence in software engineering remains fragmented across team processes, performance outcomes, contextual conditions, barriers. Objective: This study maps literature on psychological safety in software engineering, examining its conceptualization, associations with team performance and processes, contextual influences, barriers, and strengthening strategies. Method: We conducted a systematic mapping study following established software engineering guidelines. We analyzed 112 primary studies published between 2006 and June 2026 using descriptive statistics and thematic analysis across six research questions. Results: Psychological safety emerges as a multidimensional, context-dependent, team-level construct characterized by interpersonal risk-taking, open communication, collaboration, learning, trust, and supportive interaction. It is predominantly associated with productivity, software quality, innovation, team satisfaction, collaboration, communication, and decision-making. These relationships are shaped by leadership, organizational culture, work environment, trust, and sociocultural and individual conditions. Recurring barriers include communication problems, organizational constraints, leadership issues, diversity and inclusion challenges, and workload pressures. Although diverse practices are reported, evidence of their effectiveness and long-term sustainability remains limited. Conclusion: Psychological safety is a multidimensional, context-dependent team-level construct associated with team interaction and performance. This study highlights the need for longitudinal, context-sensitive research on psychological safety interventions in software development environments.

</details>


### [119] [Evaluating Change Point Detection Methods for Software Performance Regression Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09023)
*Diego Elias Costa,Michele Tucci,Luca Traini,Daniele Di Pompeo,Thomas Bach,Francois Farquet,David Daly,Simon Eismann,Petr Tůma,Vittorio Cortellessa,André van Hoorn*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper evaluates the effectiveness of 12 Change Point Detection (CPD) methods for identifying performance regressions in software systems. The study uses performance data from three large software systems, characterizes performance time series properties, and assesses human annotator consistency in identifying performance changes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Performance issues in software systems erode user trust, violate service-level agreements, and affect business efficiency. Software performance engineering needs robust techniques to detect performance regressions early in the development cycle. While CPD methods are widely used in other domains (finance, healthcare, performance monitoring), their effectiveness for software performance measurements has not been thoroughly evaluated.

Method: The researchers collected performance measurement data from three large software systems and characterized the unique properties of performance time series data. They conducted a large-scale annotation effort to evaluate the consistency of human annotators in identifying potential performance changes. Finally, they evaluated the accuracy of twelve distinct CPD methods in detecting potential performance changes.

Result: The abstract does not provide explicit results. It mentions that the study provides insights into the applicability and effectiveness of various CPD methods in software performance regression analysis, but specific findings are not stated in the abstract.

Conclusion: The abstract does not explicitly state conclusions. The study appears to provide a comprehensive evaluation that would help practitioners understand which CPD methods are most suitable for software performance regression analysis.

Abstract: Performance issues in software systems are a critical quality issue that can erode user trust, violate service-level agreements, and ultimately affect business efficiency. Consequently, software performance engineering has shifted its focus to developing robust techniques to detect performance regressions as early as possible in the development cycle. Performance regression analysis often relies on time series of performance measurements to detect significant changes in performance behavior. Change Point Detection (CPD) methods have been widely used to automate the identification of such changes in various domains, including finance, healthcare, and performance monitoring. However, the effectiveness of these methods for software performance measurements has not been thoroughly evaluated. In this paper, we present a comprehensive study to evaluate the effectiveness of various CPD methods on real-world software performance measurement datasets. We start by collecting performance measurement data from three large software systems and characterizing the unique properties of performance time series data. Then, we undertake a large-scale effort to annotate and evaluate the consistency of human annotators' identification of potential performance changes. Thereafter, we evaluate the accuracy of twelve distinct CPD methods in detecting potential performance changes, providing insights into their applicability and effectiveness in software performance regression analysis.

</details>


### [120] [Large-scale Repository Engineering via Agent-Native Reusable Code Primitives](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09079)
*Haibo Jin,Peng Kuang,Xucheng Yu,Jerry Wang,Dehao Wu,Haohan Wang*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: The paper introduces Code Primitives - reusable executable components with interface contracts, dependency closures, validation tests, and provenance - and LEGO, a system that uses these primitives for repository-scale code construction. The approach organizes 1,424 primitives in CodeFace and achieves significant improvements over baseline models, with LEGO raising GPT-5.6-terra's delivery score from 0.3180 to 0.5134 (+61.4%).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Building complete repositories with LLMs remains difficult because interacting modules, interfaces, configurations, tests, and dependencies must work together. Existing approaches struggle with repository-scale construction despite progress in code generation.

Method: The authors propose (1) Code Primitives - reusable components with interface contracts, dependency closures, validation tests, and provenance; (2) CodeFace - a searchable library of 1,424 validated primitives; (3) LEGO - a system that activates task-relevant primitives, integrates their adapted implementations with task-specific code while resolving cross-component constraints, and revises results against executed tests. Each primitive uses a resident LLM to assess relevance and adapt implementation to the target repository.

Result: LEGO-REPO benchmark (522 tasks, 7 domains, 22 tracks, 5 difficulty levels) shows: strongest baseline achieves 0.318 delivery score with 41.0% zero-scoring tasks; LEGO improves all 13 backbones by 0.1474 average; GPT-5.6-terra improves from 0.3180 to 0.5134 (+61.4%). Adapted primitives outperform retrieved code. GPT-OSS-20B retains 95.1% of score at 24% lower cost.

Conclusion: Code Primitives and LEGO represent a paradigm shift toward agent-native reusable components for repository-scale code construction, demonstrating significant improvements across multiple backbones and benchmarks. The approach successfully addresses the challenge of integrating interacting modules, interfaces, and dependencies in complete repository construction.

Abstract: Large language models equipped with development environments have moved code generation toward repository-scale construction, yet building complete repositories remains difficult because interacting modules, interfaces, configurations, tests, and dependencies must work together. We introduce Code Primitives, agent-native reusable executable components with interface contracts, dependency closures, validation tests, and provenance. Each primitive uses a resident LLM to assess relevance and adapt its implementation, interfaces, and dependencies to the target repository, and we organize 1,424 validated primitives in CodeFace, a searchable library for repository construction. We introduce LEGO (Large-scale repository Engineering via aGent-native reusable cOde primitives), which activates task-relevant primitives, integrates their adapted implementations with task-specific code while resolving cross-component constraints, and revises the result against executed tests. To measure construction end to end, we build LEGO-REPO, a benchmark of 522 executable reconstruction tasks spanning seven software domains, 22 capability tracks, and five difficulty levels, scored against native test suites between an empty-package floor and original-source ceiling. The strongest of 13 evaluated backbones reaches a delivery score of 0.318 and scores zero on 41.0% of tasks; LEGO improves all 13 by 0.1474 on average and raises GPT-5.6-terra from 0.3180 to 0.5134 (+61.4%). In controlled comparisons, adapted primitives outperform retrieved code supplied as context or vendored unchanged. The effect persists against independent repository agents, across three external benchmarks, and with a disjointly re-mined CodeFace; GPT-OSS-20B for adaptation and diagnosis retains 95.1% of the homogeneous score at 24.0% lower cost.

</details>


### [121] [Who Broke Me? Execution-Guided Repair of Behavioral Dependency Breaks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09267)
*Juntao Chen,Tingting Bi,Yanlin Wang,Patanamon Thongtanunam*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: BBCFixer is a repair method that identifies the root API causing behavioral breaking changes in dependency upgrades by comparing test outputs between old and new library versions, then uses that information to filter library diffs for LLM-based repair. It also introduces BBCBench, a benchmark of 100 behavioral dependency breaks in Python and JavaScript.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Dependency upgrades can break downstream projects through behavioral changes without altering library interfaces. These behavioral breaking changes are difficult to fix because: (1) failing tests don't point to the root upstream API, (2) no compiler feedback exists, and (3) the changes are often undocumented. Existing LLM-based repair methods fail because they lack upgrade evidence.

Method: BBCFixer operates in three main steps: (1) Run the failing test under both old and new library versions, (2) Rank calls whose return values differ to identify candidate root APIs, (3) Filter the library diff using the identified candidate. The evaluation uses BBCBench, a benchmark containing 100 behavioral dependency breaks in Python and JavaScript.

Result: BBCFixer raises the average pass rate by up to 17% relative to Pure Agent (which receives no upgrade evidence) and needs up to 27% fewer agent steps per successful repair.

Conclusion: BBCFixer provides an effective method to select upstream evidence behind behavioral breaks, enabling LLM agents to repair behavioral breaking changes more effectively and efficiently. The introduction of BBCBench also provides a valuable benchmark for evaluating similar repair approaches.

Abstract: Dependency upgrades can break downstream projects without changing the library interface. Such behavioral breaking changes are difficult for developers to fix, because the failing test does not always point to the root API, the upstream API that causes the break. Existing LLM-based repair methods obtain evidence for the repair from compiler feedback or library documentation. However, a behavioral break produces no compiler feedback and is often undocumented. Agents that receive no upgrade evidence also usually do not retrieve upstream evidence themselves, and most of their failed repairs do not identify the root API.
  The library diff provides useful upstream evidence, but the root API must first be identified to select the relevant part of the diff. We present BBCFixer, a repair method that runs the failing test under the old and new library versions, ranks the calls whose return value differs to identify a candidate root API, and filters the library diff with that candidate. To evaluate repairs of behavioral breaks, we further introduce BBCBench, a benchmark of 100 behavioral dependency breaks in Python and JavaScript.
  We compare BBCFixer on BBCBench with two baselines: (1) Pure Agent, an agent that receives no upgrade evidence, and (2) BDUpdater, a method that mines library documentation. BBCFixer raises the average pass rate by up to 17% relative to Pure Agent and needs up to 27% fewer agent steps per successful repair. BBCFixer thus provides a way to select the upstream evidence behind a behavioral break, so that an LLM agent can repair behavioral breaking changes more effectively and efficiently.

</details>


### [122] [Beyond FAIR: A Fitness Function Framework for Sustainable Research Software](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09580)
*Irdin Pekaric,Philipp Zech*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper extends a fitness function framework for assessing research software sustainability beyond the FAIR principles by adding environmental (resource efficiency, execution footprint) and security (dependency health, vulnerability exposure, secure configuration) fitness functions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The FAIR principles (findability, accessibility, interoperability, reusability) are widely used for software sustainability assessment but fail to address environmental responsibility and security concerns. Excessive resource consumption increases environmental costs, while insecure software creates maintenance overhead, technical debt, and barriers to reuse.

Method: The authors extend a previously proposed fitness function framework by introducing two new sets of fitness functions: environmental functions (targeting resource efficiency and execution footprint) and security functions (targeting dependency health, vulnerability exposure, and secure configuration). This creates a multi-dimensional sustainability assessment framework.

Result: A broadened framework that treats research software sustainability as a multidimensional property encompassing FAIR compliance, environmental responsibility, and long-term security, enabling more comprehensive continuous software assessment.

Conclusion: The framework provides a more complete view of sustainability by integrating environmental and security considerations alongside FAIR principles, addressing gaps in traditional software sustainability assessment approaches.

Abstract: Research software sustainability is often assessed through the FAIR principles: findability, accessibility, interoperability and reusability. While important, FAIR does not cover all relevant sustainability concerns. Research software should also be environmentally responsible and secure over time. Excessive resource consumption increases environmental cost, while insecure software creates maintenance overhead, technical debt and barriers to reuse. To this end, in this paper, we extend a previously proposed fitness function framework for sustainable research software beyond FAIR. We introduce two additional sets of fitness functions: environmental functions targeting resource efficiency and execution footprint, and security functions targeting dependency health, vulnerability exposure and secure configuration. Together, these functions broaden continuous software assessment from FAIR compliance to a more complete view of sustainability. The resulting framework treats research software sustainability as a multidimensional property that includes FAIR, environmental responsibility and long-term security.

</details>


### [123] [GRAML: Graph-Grounded Reasoning and Multi-Task Learning for LLM-Based Software Vulnerability Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09605)
*Ruohan Li,Miaoqing Tian,Haipeng Qu,Ruobing Jiang*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: GRAML is a framework that enhances LLM-based software vulnerability detection by combining graph-based structural evidence from static analysis, Tree-of-Thought-guided Vulnerability Reasoning (ToT-VR) for generating vulnerability descriptions, and multi-task training on a unified four-task dataset (Detection, Localization, Assessment, and description generation). It achieves 66.67%-68.70% F1 scores, outperforming baselines by up to 30.92%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLMs for software vulnerability detection suffer from limited performance due to insufficient use of control-flow and data-flow information. There is a need to better leverage structural program information to improve detection accuracy.

Method: 1) Static analysis on C/C++ programs to extract critical source lines and typed line relations as structural evidence; 2) Graph evidence-guided Tree-of-Thought Vulnerability Reasoning (ToT-VR) to generate vulnerability descriptions; 3) Combining descriptions with Detection, Localization, and Assessment samples into a unified four-task training dataset.

Result: GRAML achieves average F1 scores of 66.67% to 68.70% across in-distribution and six out-of-distribution datasets, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines by up to 30.92%. Ablation experiments show that ToT-VR and graph-guided vulnerability descriptions improve detection performance compared to standard Chain-of-Thought reasoning and raw Code Property Graph serializations.

Conclusion: The combination of graph-based structural evidence, ToT-VR reasoning, and multi-task training significantly improves LLM-based vulnerability detection. This approach provides practical guidance for building more reliable and secure software engineering systems using large language models.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have been widely applied to software vulnerability detection. However, their performance is often limited by insufficient use of control-flow and data-flow information. In this paper, we propose GRAML, a framework that combines graph evidence, vulnerability description generation, and multi-task training. GRAML first performs static analysis on C/C++ programs to extract critical source lines and typed line relations as structural evidence. It then uses this evidence to guide GPT-5 through the Tree-of-Thought-guided Vulnerability Reasoning (ToT-VR) process and generate vulnerability descriptions. These descriptions are further combined with Detection, Localization, and Assessment samples to build a unified four-task training dataset. We evaluate GRAML on an in-distribution (ID) test set and six out-of-distribution (OOD) datasets. The results show that GRAML achieves average F1 scores ranging from 66.67% to 68.70%, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines by up to 30.92%. Ablation experiments further show that ToT-VR and graph-guided vulnerability descriptions improve detection performance compared with standard Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning and raw Code Property Graph (CPG) serializations. These findings provide practical guidance for building more reliable and secure software engineering systems with large language models.

</details>


### [124] [A Chat Assistant for Software Exploration in a 3D Software Visualization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09901)
*Malte Hansen,Karim Issa,Wilhelm Hasselbring*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper presents a chat assistant for interactive software exploration integrated into the 3D visualization tool ExplorViz. The assistant uses LLMs combined with deterministic tool-based actions (similar to Model Context Protocol) to enable users to ask questions about software systems and trigger visualization changes through natural language. An empirical evaluation with 11 participants showed positive results for summaries/explanations and certain actions (highlighting, color themes), but mixed results for software restructuring, indicating need for stronger LLM guardrails.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to reduce interaction overhead during exploratory program comprehension tasks by enabling natural language interactions with software visualization tools, allowing users to query and manipulate visualizations through a chat interface rather than traditional manual interactions.

Method: The researchers integrated a chat assistant into ExplorViz frontend using CopilotKit libraries, combining probabilistic LLMs with deterministic tool-based actions. They conducted an empirical experiment with 11 participants evaluating perceived comprehension support and tool calls triggered by the assistant.

Result: Participants rated the assistant's generated summaries and explanations as largely correct. High usability was reported for actions like highlighting entities and creating new color themes. However, open-ended chat-assisted software restructuring showed mixed results. Overall, the assistant was perceived as usable and promising for reducing interaction overhead.

Conclusion: The chat assistant shows promise for reducing interaction overhead in exploratory program comprehension. However, stronger guardrails for the LLM and better incorporation of user feedback are needed, particularly for open-ended restructuring tasks. The approach demonstrates the potential of combining LLMs with deterministic tool-based actions in software visualization tools.

Abstract: We present a chat assistant for interactive software exploration, embedded in the 3D software visualization tool ExplorViz. The assistant builds upon current Large Language Models (LLMs) and enables users to ask questions about the currently visualized software system and trigger actions that change the visualization through natural language. We integrate the chat assistant in our ExplorViz frontend using the CopilotKit libraries such that probabilistic LLMs are combined with deterministic and tool-based actions similar to implementations using the Model Context Protocol (MCP). The chat assistant is also enabled to restructure the software system by adding, removing, or modifying parts of the software system in the visualization. An empirical experiment with eleven participants evaluated both perceived comprehension support and the tool calls that were triggered by the chat assistant. Participants rated the assistant's generated summaries and explanations as largely correct. They also reported high usability for actions like highlighting entities in the visualization and the creation of new color themes. In contrast, open-ended chat-assisted software restructuring in the visualization showed mixed results. This suggests a need for stronger guardrails for the employed LLM and better incorporation of user feedback. Overall, the assistant was perceived as usable and promising for reducing interaction overhead during exploratory program comprehension tasks. We provide a video presenting the chat assistant's use and a reproduction package of the software system that was used in our evaluation.

</details>


### [125] [Analysis and Visualization of the Linux Kernel's Software Evolution Using the City Metaphor](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09910)
*Malte Hansen,Lukas Damerau,Moritz Bugla,David Moreno-Lumbreras,Wilhelm Hasselbring*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper presents a visualization approach for the Linux kernel using the ExplorViz tool, which applies a 3D city metaphor to display software structure and evolution. The authors analyze Git commits from the Linux repository, collecting metrics like lines of code for files, directories, and commits, which can be mapped to building dimensions or displayed via heat maps.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The Linux kernel is one of the largest open source projects with over 40 million lines of code, making it extremely challenging to understand its internal structure and assess its software evolution. Existing visualization tools lack the capability to effectively represent such a massive and complex codebase.

Method: The authors developed an approach using their software visualization tool ExplorViz. They created a custom analysis service to analyze commits from the Linux Git repository. The web-based frontend uses a 3D city metaphor where metrics such as line counts are collected for each file and accumulated for directories and commits. These metrics are mapped to building dimensions or displayed via heat maps. The system includes various visualization, search, and filter options for interactive exploration.

Result: The authors present two visualizations: (1) a visualization of all files in the kernel repository, and (2) a visual analysis of the code evolution of Rust files in the Linux kernel. A demo video is available at https://youtu.be/3ODnERqD8g0.

Conclusion: The visualization approach enables effective exploration and analysis of the Linux kernel's structure and evolution, particularly for tracking the introduction and growth of Rust code in the kernel.

Abstract: The Linux kernel is one of the largest and longest-maintained open source projects in existence. With more than 40 million lines of code, understanding the kernel's internal structure and assessing its software evolution is a great challenge. In this paper, we present an approach to visualize the Linux kernel using our software visualization tool ExplorViz. We analyze commits from the Linux Git repository using a custom analysis service. The web-based frontend utilizes the 3D city metaphor for visualization of the software structure. Metrics such as the number of lines are collected for each file and are accumulated for directories and commits. Calculated metrics can be mapped to the building's dimensions or be displayed via a heat map. A wide range of visualization, search, and filter options enable the interactive exploration of the visualized data. We present both a visualization of all files in the kernel repository and a visual analysis of the code evolution of Rust files in the Linux kernel. Demo video: https://youtu.be/3ODnERqD8g0

</details>


### [126] [AgentTracer: Tracing Indirect Prompt Injection Attack through Fine-Grained Intention-Execution Alignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09935)
*Zitong Yao,Jiangrong Wu,Yixi Lin,Anrui Huang,Luoyun Zhang,Yuhong Nan*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: AgentTracer is an intent-aware tracing framework that detects and reconstructs indirect prompt injection (IPI) attack chains in LLM agents by modeling IPI as task intent drift and constructing an Intent-Driven Execution Graph to connect dispersed tool calls driven by malicious instructions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Indirect prompt injection (IPI) attacks redirect LLM agents toward attacker-intended tasks through malicious instructions embedded in external resources. Existing tracing methods only capture explicit control-flow and data-flow dependencies, missing implicit relationships among tool calls driven by malicious instructions that may lack explicit dependencies and be interleaved with legitimate operations.

Method: AgentTracer recovers implicit decision dependencies among tool calls to construct an Intent-Driven Execution Graph. It combines user requests with an operation knowledge base to build a user intent authorization space and identify intent-drift tool calls. Starting from an anomalous tool call, it performs target-based pruning and backward tracing to reconstruct the attack chain and locate the injection source and injection point.

Result: AgentTracer achieves 94.17% injection-point accuracy and 93.56% path precision in end-to-end experiments using execution logs from AgentDyn and InjecAgent combined with normal execution logs (1,800 user requests, 9,000 background tool calls). It improves injection-point accuracy over existing methods by 18 to 54 percent.

Conclusion: AgentTracer effectively addresses the challenge of tracing IPI attacks that involve implicit relationships among tool calls by treating IPI as task intent drift and using intent-driven analysis. This approach enables complete attack-chain reconstruction even when malicious tool calls lack explicit dependencies and are interleaved with legitimate operations.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents interact with external resources to complete complex user tasks, exposing them to indirect prompt injection (IPI), where malicious instructions redirect agents toward attacker-intended tasks. Since IPI is difficult to defend against in real-world environments, post-incident tracing is essential for locating the injection source and reconstructing the attack chain. However, existing tracing methods primarily capture explicit control-flow and data-flow dependencies, overlooking the implicit relationships among tool calls driven by the malicious instruction. These tool calls may lack explicit dependencies and be interleaved with legitimate operations, making complete attack-chain reconstruction difficult. In this paper, we present AgentTracer, an intent-aware tracing framework that treats IPI as task intent drift. AgentTracer recovers implicit decision dependencies among tool calls to construct an Intent-Driven Execution Graph that connects dispersed tool calls by task intent. It combines the user request with an operation knowledge base to construct a user intent authorization space and identify intent-drift tool calls. Starting from an anomalous tool call under audit, AgentTracer performs target-based pruning and backward tracing to reconstruct the attack chain and locate the injection source and injection point. To evaluate AgentTracer in the presence of noise from normal tasks, we combine execution logs constructed from successful IPI attacks in AgentDyn and InjecAgent with normal execution logs containing 1,800 user requests and 9,000 background tool calls without IPI. In end-to-end experiments, AgentTracer achieves 94.17 percent injection-point accuracy and 93.56 percent path precision. Comparative experiments show that AgentTracer improves injection-point accuracy over existing methods by 18 to 54 percent.

</details>


### [127] [Designing Collaborative AI-Driven Workflows for Scientific Software Engineering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09995)
*Akash Dhruv,Max Knobbe,Pedro Machado,Anshu Dubey*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper proposes a collaborative human-AI workflow for scientific code generation, where domain experts provide specifications while agents operate under deterministic orchestration. The approach requires human review at each stage with numerical verification against reference code. Evaluation on Fortran-to-C++ translation of a high-energy physics application shows a simple author-reviewer loop achieves comparable results to multi-agent workflows at significantly lower cost (1/3 per file).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The core challenge in scientific computing is verifying that agent-generated code is both correct and understandable to diverse teams with different areas of expertise. The authors argue that agentic AI systems are best used within collaborative team structures rather than as full automation solutions.

Method: The proposed workflow involves: (1) domain experts writing specifications and plans, (2) agents operating under deterministic orchestration to write target code, (3) numerical comparison against reference code at each stage, and (4) human review and approval required before proceeding to the next stage. The evaluation tested different orchestrators, design patterns, and models across fourteen experiments on Fortran-to-C++ translation of a large high-energy physics application.

Result: A simple author-reviewer loop with enforced limits completed a comparable number of files to a multi-agent workflow at about one-third of the cost per file.

Conclusion: Agentic AI systems are best deployed within collaborative team structures rather than as full automation. Simple human-in-the-loop workflows can achieve similar accuracy to complex multi-agent systems at significantly lower cost, suggesting that human oversight and deterministic orchestration are more important than sophisticated multi-agent architectures for scientific code generation tasks.

Abstract: Agentic artificial intelligence systems can carry out a broad range of tasks in software engineering and scientific research, from writing and translating code to running workflows for data analysis and visualization. In scientific computing, the difficulty is verifying that agent-generated code is both correct and understandable to teams whose members bring different areas of expertise. We therefore argue that these systems are best used within collaborative team structures rather than as full automation. In the workflows we propose, domain experts write the specification and plan, and agents operate under a deterministic orchestration pattern to write the target code. Each stage ends with a numerical comparison against the reference code and requires human review and approval before the next begins. We evaluate these workflows on the translation of a large high-energy physics application from Fortran to C++, running the same task under different orchestrators, design patterns, and models. Across fourteen experiments, a simple author--reviewer loop with enforced limits completed a comparable number of files to a multi-agent workflow at about one-third of the cost per file.

</details>


### [128] [AdaT$^2$: Adaptive Test Transformations for Black-Box Boundary Testing of Conversational Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.10141)
*Liting Lin,Boxi Yu,Qinghua Xu,Yuzhong Zhang,Lionel Briand,Emir Muñoz*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: AdaT² is a testing system for LLM-based conversational agents that generates boundary tests by extracting statements from agent replies and using adaptive pair selection (novelty + Bayes-UCB bandit algorithm) to choose statement-instruction pairs. It outperforms AgentEval, achieving 62.7%-83.3% valid boundary tests vs 47.7%-68.1%, and detects more seeded policy faults (all 8 in airline, 4/8 in retail vs 5 and 2 for AgentEval).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-based conversational agents must comply with policies, which define boundaries between compliant and non-compliant user requests. Testing these boundaries is challenging due to the large number of possible statement-instruction pairs and the difficulty of identifying policy violations.

Method: AdaT² extracts statements from agent replies in exploratory conversations, where each statement describes a policy condition and expected behavior. It generates plain tests from single statements and transformed tests from statement-instruction pairs (e.g., "omit one required input"). Adaptive pair selection uses novelty for choosing statements and Bayes-UCB bandit algorithm for instructions, learning from test generation success/failure and LLM judge evaluation.

Result: On τ³-bench's four domains, AdaT² achieves 62.7% to 83.3% valid boundary tests (vs AgentEval's 47.7% to 68.1%). Transformed tests add 13 to 46 explicitly defined boundaries missed by plain tests. As regression tests, AdaT² detects all 8 seeded policy faults in the airline domain and 4/8 in retail, while AgentEval (with fewer than 1/3 as many tests) detects 5 and 2 respectively.

Conclusion: AdaT² significantly outperforms AgentEval in generating valid boundary tests and detecting policy violations. The combination of statement extraction, transformed tests, and adaptive pair selection using bandit algorithms provides an effective approach for testing LLM-based conversational agents against policy compliance.

Abstract: Conversational agents based on large language models (LLMs) must comply with policies. Each condition in a policy draws a boundary between user requests, and the agent must behave differently on its two sides. We present AdaT$^2$, which extracts statements from the agent's replies in exploratory conversations with an LLM acting as the user, and uses the statements to guide boundary test generation. Each statement describes one condition and the behavior expected when the condition holds. Besides plain tests guided by single statements, AdaT$^2$ writes transformed tests guided by pairs of a statement and a test transformation instruction, such as "omit one required input". The instruction of a pair can move a test to the other side of the statement's boundary or to another boundary. The statements and instructions form far more pairs than a run can try, and many pairs are not applicable. Adaptive pair selection therefore chooses the statement of each pair by novelty and the instruction with the bandit algorithm Bayes-UCB, which learns from whether earlier pairs yielded a test and whether the agent passed it according to an LLM judge. Our benchmark counts the two sides of each boundary separately and distinguishes boundaries explicitly defined by the agent's prompt, tool code, or knowledge base from boundaries that the agent's LLM infers from domain knowledge. On four domains of $τ^3$-bench, 62.7% to 83.3% of AdaT$^2$'s tests are valid boundary tests whose expected behavior is explicitly defined, higher in every domain than AgentEval's (47.7% to 68.1%). Transformed tests add 13 to 46 explicitly defined boundaries that plain tests miss. As regression tests, AdaT$^2$'s test suites detect all eight seeded policy faults in the airline domain and four of eight in the retail domain, and AgentEval's test suites, with fewer than a third as many tests, detect five and two, respectively.

</details>


### [129] [Why Software Engineering Is Indispensable in the Age of Coding Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.10226)
*Alfonso Fuggetta*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper argues that AI coding agents actually make software engineering and software engineers more essential, not obsolete. The author contends that three inherent properties of LLMs (probabilistic generation, agnosticism, and semantic statelessness) create a structural vacuum that cannot be fixed through training alone. To address this, four knowledge levers are proposed: methodological knowledge, domain knowledge, design choices, and process choices—all requiring software engineers as methodologists, mediators, and custodians.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The author seeks to counter the narrative that AI will make software engineers obsolete. The motivation is to reframe AI as a tool that enhances rather than replaces the need for skilled software engineers, by highlighting fundamental limitations of LLMs that require human expertise to overcome.

Method: This is a conceptual/philosophical analysis paper. The author uses logical reasoning to analyze the fundamental properties of large language models and their implications for software engineering practice. No empirical experiments are conducted; the argument is built through theoretical analysis of LLM characteristics.

Result: The paper establishes that AI cannot replace software engineers due to three structural limitations of LLMs. The author proposes four "knowledge levers" that software engineers must provide to make AI-assisted development trustworthy: methodological knowledge, domain knowledge, design choices, and process choices.

Conclusion: The conclusion asserts that software engineers are not made redundant by AI but rather become more essential—serving as methodologists, mediators, and custodians who ensure AI-generated code is verifiable, trustworthy, and properly contextualized within organizational and domain requirements.

Abstract: Can AI make Software Engineering (SE) -- the discipline -- obsolete? And can it make software engineers -- the professionals -- redundant? This paper argues that the rise of capable AI coding agents makes SE and software engineers essential, not obsolete: the missing foundation without which AI-assisted development produces misleadingly plausible, unverifiable, and ultimately untrustworthy software. Three structural properties of large language models (probabilistic generation, agnosticism, and semantic statelessness) create a structural vacuum that no amount of training can eliminate. Filling it requires four knowledge levers: methodological knowledge, domain knowledge, design choices, and process choices. All four must be reified as persistent artifacts, and each requires the software engineer as methodologist, mediator, and custodian.

</details>


### [130] [TestGRAD: Evolving Test Suites via Failure Pattern Momentum for SWE-Agent Ensemble](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.10242)
*Pengfei He,Jiayuan Zhou,Shaowei Wang,Ruiqi Pan*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: TestGRAD is a framework for automatic test optimization in SWE-agent ensembles, formulated as test-space optimization that evolves executable repository test suites to distinguish competing candidate patches. It achieves 84.2% Pass@1 on SWE-bench Verified, outperforming the strongest baseline by 3.6 percentage points.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The central problem in SWE-agent ensembles is test-based selection: generating tests, executing candidate patches, and identifying the best patch. Existing test-generation methods are limited optimizers that lack an explicit loss for ensemble selection, optimize through incomplete directions (mostly creating/deleting tests), and perform one-off generation without feedback from repeated failures.

Method: TestGRAD introduces three key concepts: (1) Differential loss - provides an explicit execution-defined target where useful tests should separate candidate patches by behavior; (2) Full CRUD gradients - expands update directions from merely creating/deleting tests to reading existing test infrastructure, creating new tests, updating stale assertions, and deleting obsolete tests; (3) Failure Pattern Momentum - mines frequent failure sequences from memory to avoid repeated non-discriminative directions while compressing failure-history context.

Result: On SWE-bench Verified, TestGRAD achieves 84.2% Pass@1 with a 4-agent ensemble, outperforming the strongest baseline (80.6%) by an absolute improvement of 3.6 percentage points, while compressing failure-history context by over 100×.

Conclusion: TestGRAD successfully formulates test-based selection as test-space optimization and demonstrates that gradient descent-inspired optimization with differential loss, full CRUD operations, and failure pattern momentum can significantly improve issue resolution in SWE-agent ensembles.

Abstract: SWE-agent ensembles improve issue resolution by combining candidate patches from different agents with complementary strengths. The central problem is therefore test-based selection: generate tests, execute candidate patches, and identify the best patch. We formulate this process as test-space optimization: evolving an executable repository test suite until it distinguishes competing patches. Existing test-generation methods are limited optimizers. They usually lack an explicit loss for ensemble selection, optimize through incomplete directions that mostly create new tests or delete old ones, and perform one-off generation without feedback from repeated failures. Inspired by gradient descent with momentum, we introduce TestGRAD, a framework for automatic test optimization. TestGRAD centers on three concepts. Differential loss gives the optimizer an explicit execution-defined target: useful tests should separate candidate patches by behavior. Full CRUD gradients expand the update direction from merely creating or deleting tests to reading existing test infrastructure, creating new tests, updating stale assertions, and deleting only obsolete tests. Failure Pattern Momentum mines frequent failure sequences from memory, allowing the optimizer to avoid repeated non-discriminative directions while compressing the failure-history context. On SWE-bench Verified, TestGRAD achieves 84.2% Pass@1 with a 4-agent ensemble, outperforming the strongest baseline (80.6%) by an absolute improvement of 3.6 percentage points, while compressing failure-history context by over $100\times$.

</details>


### [131] [QuSema: Detecting Silent Bugs in Quantum Libraries via Quantum-knowledge-enhanced Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.10258)
*Yujin Song,Kaining Zhang,Qixin Zhang,Shuai Wang,Pingchuan Ma,Yuxuan Du*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: QuSema is an autonomous testing agent for quantum libraries that uses quantum semantics and documentation as a source-level semantic oracle to detect silent bugs. It operates through an agentic loop that inspects library APIs and source code, reasons about intended quantum operation behavior, identifies semantic deviations, and validates them with executable tests. Implemented for Qiskit and PennyLane, it achieved higher bug relocation rates than Claude Code and Codex on 20 historical bugs, and discovered 40 previously unknown bugs (30 silent) confirmed by developers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing quantum library testing techniques rely on failure-based or comparison-based oracles that only detect bugs when executions fail or produce incorrect outputs. This leaves silent bugs undetected, which can propagate incorrect results into experimental conclusions, simulation studies, and algorithmic designs.

Method: QuSema uses an agentic loop that: (1) inspects library API documentation and source code, (2) reasons about intended behavior of quantum operations using quantum semantics constraints, (3) identifies potential semantic deviations, and (4) generates executable tests through library APIs to validate findings. It transforms high-level behavioral mismatches into concrete, user-triggerable bug reports.

Result: On a benchmark of 20 historical silent bugs, QuSema achieved higher mean bug relocation counts than Claude Code and Codex, with DeepSeek configuration costing less than Claude Code. QuSema also discovered 40 previously unknown bugs confirmed by developers, including 30 silent bugs.

Conclusion: QuSema effectively detects silent bugs in quantum libraries by using constraints from quantum semantics and documentation as a semantic oracle, enabling autonomous bug detection without relying on execution failures.

Abstract: Quantum libraries are now critical infrastructure for quantum algorithm development, yet their correctness remains difficult to test. Existing testing techniques mainly rely on failure-based or comparison-based oracles, exposing bugs only when executions fail, violate runtime checks, or disagree with another implementation. Their applicability is limited when suitable execution-based oracles are unavailable, leaving some silent bugs undetected. Such missed bugs can produce incorrect results that propagate into experimental conclusions, simulation studies, and algorithmic designs. Here we present QuSema, an autonomous testing agent for finding silent bugs in quantum libraries. QuSema uses constraints from quantum semantics and documentation as a source-level semantic oracle to assess whether implementation logic can produce invalid outputs from valid inputs. It operates through an agentic loop that repeatedly inspects library API documentation and source code, reasons about the intended behavior of quantum operations, identifies potential semantic deviations, and validates them by generating executable tests through library APIs. Guided by quantum-domain reasoning, QuSema turns high-level behavioral mismatches into concrete, user-triggerable bug reports, enabling it to uncover non-crash defects. We implement QuSema for Qiskit and PennyLane. On a benchmark of 20 historical silent bugs, QuSema achieves higher mean bug relocation counts than Claude Code and Codex, with the DeepSeek configuration costing less than Claude Code. QuSema also discovers 40 previously unknown bugs confirmed by the developers, including 30 silent bugs.

</details>


### [132] [Using Small Language Models to Reverse-Engineer Machine Learning Pipelines Structures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.10261)
*Nicolas Lacroix,Frederic Precioso,Mireille Blay-Fornarino,Sebastien Mosser*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper evaluates whether Small Language Models (SLMs) can effectively extract ML pipeline stages from source code, addressing limitations of manual labeling and existing classifiers. The study compares SLMs against reference works using statistical tests (Cochran's Q, McNemar's, goodness-of-fit). Results show taxonomy wording significantly impacts performance, SLMs perform comparably but don't outperform other classifiers, and different classification methods yield significantly different insights into ML practices.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The constant evolution of ML (algorithms, datasets) creates diversity that makes extracting ML pipeline stages from source code challenging. Existing approaches suffer from non-scalable manual labeling or classifiers that don't adequately support the domain's diversity, limiting reliable understanding of ML practices.

Method: Confirmatory study based on two reference works: (1) Compared several SLMs using Cochran's Q test; (2) Evaluated best-performing model against reference studies via two McNemar's tests; (3) Additional Cochran's Q test examined how taxonomy definition variations affect SLM performance; (4) Goodness-of-fit tests compared ML practice insights from SLM classification with prior studies.

Result: Three key findings: (1) Taxonomy wording significantly impacts classification performance; (2) Best-performing SLM yielded good results but didn't outperform other classifiers; (3) Three classification methods led to significantly different insights with varying effect sizes when exploring data scientists' practices.

Conclusion: Limitations of existing classification methods bias understanding of ML practices. While current SLMs show promising results without prior fine-tuning, they still exhibit common limitations plus high inference costs that challenge applicability in large-scale studies.

Abstract: Context: Once defined a taxonomy of stages structuring Machine Learning (ML) pipelines (e.g. Data Preprocessing, Modeling...), extracting these stages from source code is key for better understanding ML practices. However, the diversity caused by the constant evolution of ML (e.g., algorithms, datasets) makes this task challenging. Existing approaches either rely on non-scalable manual labeling or on classifiers that do not properly support domain's diversity. These limitations call for more reliable solutions.
  Objective: We evaluate whether Small Language Models (SLMs) can leverage their code understanding and classification abilities to address these limitations, and enhance our understanding of practices in ML.
  Method: We conduct a confirmatory study based on two relevant reference works representing current limitations in the state-of-the-art. We first compare several SLMs using Cochran's Q test, then evaluate the best-performing model against reference studies via two McNemar's tests. An additional Cochran's Q test examines how taxonomy definition variations affect the SLM performance. Finally, goodness-of-fit tests compare ML practice insights from SLM classification with those from prior studies.
  Results: First, we found that the taxonomy wording significantly impacts classification performance. Second, the best performing SLM yielded good results, yet, without outperforming other classifiers. Third, the three classification methods led to significantly different insights, with varying effect sizes, when exploring practices of data scientists.
  Conclusions: Limitations of existing classification methods bias our understanding of ML practices. While current SLMs show promising results without prior fine-tuning, they still exhibit common limitations, in addition to inference high costs challenging their applicability in large-scale studies.

</details>


### [133] [When Sub-Agents Work in Parallel: The Promises and Pitfalls of Dynamic Concurrency in Long-Horizon Coding Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.10263)
*Han Li,HanHaoNing Li,Ziqian Jiang,Yiling Lou*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper investigates dynamic concurrency in coding agents through controlled experiments comparing Codex, Claude Code, and Kimi Code across 354 tasks and 2,124 executions. The study identifies 13 concurrency-specific failure modes and 28 observable patterns to determine when dynamic concurrency provides advantages in long-horizon software development.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As coding agents advance toward long-horizon development tasks, static approaches become insufficient. While model capability determines outcomes on shorter tasks, orchestration becomes central for complex development. Existing research focuses on short-task failures or predefined workflows, leaving a gap in understanding dynamic concurrency in frontier agents across task complexity.

Method: The authors conducted controlled comparisons of matched executions of three coding agents (Codex, Claude Code, Kimi Code) with dynamic concurrency enabled versus disabled. They evaluated 354 tasks spanning different complexity levels and execution horizons (2,124 total executions), examining end-to-end effects, scheduling behavior, and analyzing matched trajectories.

Result: The study identified 13 concurrency-specific failure modes and 28 observable patterns, characterizing the conditions under which dynamic concurrency provides advantages in long-horizon software development tasks.

Conclusion: Dynamic concurrency offers a promising approach to scale complex development tasks, but its effectiveness depends on specific conditions related to task complexity and execution horizon. The findings provide actionable insights for designing more robust concurrent coding agents.

Abstract: As coding agents advance from bounded software engineering tasks toward long horizon development, dynamic concurrency offers a promising way to scale complex development tasks. Under this policy, agents decide during execution whether and how to spawn concurrent sub-agents. Model capability largely determines outcomes on shorter tasks, whereas long horizon development makes orchestration central to task completion. Existing work, focused on coding agent failures on shorter tasks or collaboration in predefined multiagent workflows, offers little insight into dynamic concurrency in frontier agents across task complexity. We study dynamic concurrency as an execution policy through controlled comparisons of matched Codex, Claude Code, and Kimi Code executions with the policy enabled or disabled. Across 354 tasks and 2,124 executions spanning a range of task complexities and execution horizons, we evaluate its end to end effects and scheduling behavior, and analyze matched trajectories to characterize 13 concurrency specific failure modes, 28 observable patterns, and the conditions under which it provides an advantage.

</details>


### [134] [TaoD2C-Bench: Benchmarking MLLMs for Industrial UI Code Generation Beyond Visual Fidelity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.10374)
*Chengwei Shi,Yunnong Chen,Tingting Zhou,Qiang Lu,Shiyu Yue,Xinyuan Hu,Jianfang Ru,Liuqing Chen*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: TaoD2C-Bench is a benchmark for evaluating multimodal large language models (MLLMs) on industrial design-to-code (D2C) tasks, featuring 2,861 production designs with 97,652 annotations across four categories. It defines three evaluation tasks and reveals significant gaps in MLLMs' ability to generate UI code satisfying implementation requirements.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current MLLMs lack constraint-aware cross-modal reasoning capabilities needed for industrial UI code generation. Existing benchmarks don't evaluate MLLMs' ability to connect design images with metadata, infer implementation requirements, and realize them in code under library-specific constraints in realistic industrial settings.

Method: The authors created TaoD2C-Bench with 2,861 production designs from 17 commercial platforms, annotated with 97,652 expert labels across Component, Group, Alignment, and Position categories. They evaluated 8 MLLMs on three tasks: end-to-end UI code generation, requirement inference, and requirement realization.

Result: Evaluating eight MLLMs reveals substantial gaps in generating UI code that satisfies implementation requirements. MLLMs show distinct performance profiles in inference and realization tasks. Importantly, visual reconstruction ability does not necessarily correlate with the ability to generate code meeting implementation requirements.

Conclusion: The benchmark successfully identifies significant limitations in current MLLMs for industrial UI code generation. The release of TaoD2C dataset will support future research on improving MLLMs' constraint-aware reasoning and code generation capabilities in practical industrial applications.

Abstract: A key challenge for multimodal large language models (MLLMs) is moving beyond visual recognition to constraint-aware cross-modal reasoning. This involves combining visual cues with information from other modalities to understand elements' relationships under domain-specific rules. This challenge is acutely evident in industrial design-to-code (D2C), which converts user interface (UI) designs into code and requires MLLMs to connect design images with disorganized layer metadata, infer component and layout implementation requirements, and realize them in code under target-library constraints. However, these capabilities remain insufficiently evaluated in realistic industrial settings. To fill this gap, we present TaoD2C-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating MLLMs' ability to generate UI code that satisfies implementation requirements in industrial applications. The TaoD2C dataset consists of 2,861 production designs from 17 commercial platforms with 97,652 expert annotations across four categories: Component, Group, Alignment, and Position. These annotations distinguish required constraints from permitted implementation choices. TaoD2C-Bench defines three tasks: end-to-end UI code generation, requirement inference, and requirement realization. Evaluating eight MLLMs reveals substantial gaps in generating UI code that satisfies implementation requirements, alongside distinct performance profiles in inference and realization. We further show that MLLMs' visual reconstruction ability does not necessarily imply an ability to generate code that meets these requirements. We release TaoD2C to support research on industrial UI code generation.

</details>

### [135] [A Bayesian Mirror Architecture for Emergent Consciousness: Circular Hierarchies, Self-Manifolds, and Hybrid Event-Self Binding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08792)
*Eduardo Righi Capanema de Almeida*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces the Bayesian Mirror Architecture (BMA), a self-referential generative framework where sensory abstractions, meta-abstractions, and self-latent interact through circular recursion. The framework uses optimal-transport geometry (2-Wasserstein metric) to formulate stability and coherence, and defines a Causal Learning Regime (CLR) to diagnose learnable causal structure in the environment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors seek to establish consciousness not as an optimization objective or semantic label, but as an architectural property of systems possessing circular self-referential structure. They aim to provide a foundational mathematical framework for understanding self-representation, stability, and agency in generative systems.

Method: The framework operates over posterior beliefs in a space of probability measures equipped with optimal-transport geometry. Stability and coherence are formulated using the 2-Wasserstein metric on probability measures. CLR is defined via bounds on Wasserstein belief drift combined with an integration index. Learning proceeds via variational free-energy minimization. Basin-wise self-manifolds are identified as supports of invariant measures under local Wasserstein contractivity.

Result: BMA can exhibit multiple coherent basins rather than requiring global strict contractivity. Wasserstein epsilon-necks act as transport bottlenecks where basins decouple, yielding a unique realized continuation in a vanishing-conductance limit. This selection is interpreted as "choice" - internally determined but externally unpredictable at finite resolution.

Conclusion: Consciousness, in a restricted sense, emerges as an architectural property of systems with circular self-referential structure. Stability and agency arise from what the environment affords to learn. The framework provides a mathematically rigorous foundation for understanding self-referential cognition and potential machine consciousness.

Abstract: We present a foundational formulation of the Bayesian Mirror Architecture (BMA), a self-referential generative framework in which sensory abstractions, meta-abstractions, and a self-latent interact through circular recursion. The defining constraint is a closed update S_t <- H_{t-1}, where a hybrid event-self latent H_t binds self-representations to abstract world models and reinjects this coupling into the self-state. Consciousness, in a restricted sense, is not an optimization objective nor a semantic label, but an architectural property of systems possessing this circular structure.
  Because inference operates over posterior beliefs, BMA's intrinsic state space is a space of probability measures equipped with optimal-transport geometry. Stability and coherence are formulated in the 2-Wasserstein metric on P_2, yielding coordinate-free notions of self-stability and hybrid coherence along belief trajectories. We define a Causal Learning Regime (CLR) via bounds on Wasserstein belief drift together with an integration index capturing sustained coupling between self and world latents. CLR diagnoses whether the environment contains learnable causal structure; it is not a marker of consciousness.
  Global strict contractivity is not required: BMA may exhibit multiple coherent basins. We define self-manifolds basin-wise as supports of invariant measures under local Wasserstein contractivity. We identify Wasserstein epsilon-necks, transport bottlenecks where basins decouple, yielding a unique realized continuation in a vanishing-conductance limit. We interpret this selection as choice: internally determined yet externally unpredictable at finite resolution. Learning proceeds via variational free-energy minimization, with stability and agency emerging from what the environment affords to learn.

</details>


### [136] [Beyond Baseline Severity: Temporal and Disease-Specific Predictors of Depression Outcomes Following Mindfulness Interventions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08809)
*Muhammad Jawad Chowdhury,Sultanus Salehin,Akib Jayed Islam*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This study uses interpretable machine learning to predict depression severity (BDI-II scores) at 12 and 24 weeks following mindfulness-based interventions, using demographic, clinical, and behavioral engagement data from a multi-center longitudinal cohort. Ridge Regression performed best for 12-week predictions (RMSE=5.186, R²=0.474), while LightGBM performed best for 24-week predictions (RMSE=5.038, R²=0.525). Key findings reveal that baseline severity is the strongest predictor, short-term outcomes depend more on clinical context, and long-term outcomes are more influenced by behavioral adherence and demographics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Depression severity in patients with chronic or acute medical conditions is influenced by multiple complex factors including psychological state, demographics, clinical context, and engagement with behavioral interventions. Understanding which factors predict depression outcomes at different timepoints after mindfulness-based interventions could help personalize mental-health support and improve patient outcomes.

Method: The study analyzed a multi-center longitudinal clinical cohort using five regression models (regularized linear regression and tree-based ensemble methods). Features included demographic variables, clinical condition information, hospital-center identifiers, baseline BDI-II scores, and therapy engagement measures. Missing follow-up outcomes were addressed using model-based stochastic imputation to preserve sample size while maintaining outcome variability. Subgroup analyses examined disease-specific and hierarchical patterns.

Result: Ridge Regression achieved the best 12-week performance with RMSE=5.186 and R²=0.474, while LightGBM achieved the best 24-week performance with RMSE=5.038 and R²=0.525. Three clinically relevant patterns emerged: (1) baseline severity remains the strongest overall predictor; (2) short-term outcomes are more strongly associated with clinical and hospital context; (3) long-term outcomes show greater dependence on behavioral adherence and demographic factors. Subgroup analyses showed that predictors differ substantially across and within clinical categories.

Conclusion: Interpretable, context-aware machine learning modeling can effectively predict depression outcomes following mindfulness-based interventions. The findings support personalizing mental-health support based on baseline severity, timepoint-specific predictors (clinical context for short-term, behavioral adherence for long-term), and disease-specific patterns. This approach could help clinicians tailor interventions to individual patient needs.

Abstract: Depression severity among patients with chronic or acute medical conditions is influenced by a complex interaction of baseline psychological state, demographic characteristics, clinical context, and engagement with behavioral interventions. This paper presents an interpretable machine-learning analysis of a multi-center longitudinal clinical cohort to predict Beck Depression Inventory-II (BDI-II) scores at 12 and 24 weeks following mindfulness-based intervention participation. The study uses demographic variables, clinical condition information, hospital-center identifiers, baseline BDI-II scores, and therapy engagement measures to model short-term and long-term depression outcomes. Missing follow-up outcomes were addressed using a model-based stochastic imputation procedure to preserve the modest sample size while maintaining outcome variability. Five regression models were evaluated, spanning regularized linear regression and tree-based ensemble methods. Ridge Regression achieved the best 12-week performance with an RMSE of 5.186 and R^2 of 0.474, while LightGBM achieved the best 24-week performance with an RMSE of 5.038 and R^2 of 0.525. Beyond prediction accuracy, the analysis reveals three clinically relevant patterns: baseline severity remains the strongest overall predictor, short-term outcomes are more strongly associated with clinical and hospital context, and long-term outcomes show greater dependence on behavioral adherence and demographic factors. Disease-specific and hierarchical subgroup analyses further indicate that predictors differ substantially across and within clinical categories. These findings support the use of interpretable, context-aware modeling to inform personalized mental-health support following mindfulness-based interventions.

</details>


### [137] [Transferability and operational reliability of a Prithvi crop classification foundation model under phenological and geographic shift across three continents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08810)
*Venkatesh Kolluru,Rajat Shinde,Abdelhak Marouane,Caden Helbling,Deepak Shah,Othneil Drew,Srinivas Kolluru,Iksha Gurung,Manil Maskey,Rahul Ramachandran*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The study evaluates the out-of-distribution performance of a fine-tuned geospatial foundation model (Prithvi-EO-2.0) for crop classification across 37 events in 12 countries. Results show significant accuracy decline (0.65 to 0.40 from US to Europe), primarily due to phenological misalignment rather than spatial transfer issues. Two practical adjustments (class consolidation and window compression) can recover accuracy without retraining.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Fine-tuned geospatial foundation models (GeoFMs) pretrained on large satellite archives have shown improved crop classification accuracy and geographic transferability, but their operational performance beyond the training distribution remains poorly characterized. This study addresses this gap by evaluating the model's out-of-distribution performance.

Method: The study evaluated Prithvi-EO-2.0 across 37 events in 12 countries on three continents, validating against regional reference products. Assessment included: (1) whether model confidence indicates signal failure, (2) sensitivity to observation windows, (3) effect of coarsening class schemes, (4) robustness to band loss, and (5) cloud/shadow contamination. Monte Carlo dropout entropy was used to detect distribution shifts.

Result: Mean overall accuracy declined from 0.65 in the US to 0.40 in Europe. Accuracy collapsed when observation windows misaligned with local crop phenology, while deterministic confidence remained high. Expected calibration error increased in 7/8 paired events, with 12-51% of scenes confidently mislabeled at near-zero precision. Monte Carlo dropout entropy detected shifts in all 8 events. Consolidating 13 classes to 10 raised mean OA by 8.4 percentage points. Compressing the window toward near-real-time preserved accuracy across a 45- to 90-day plateau.

Conclusion: Fine-tuned crop GeoFMs transfer usefully only where observation windows match local growing seasons. The apparent cross-continent decline largely reflects phenological misalignment rather than spatial transfer issues. Two adjustments (class consolidation and window compression) can recover accuracy without retraining, providing operational guidance for reliable deployment.

Abstract: Fine-tuned geospatial foundation models (GeoFMs) pretrained on large satellite archives have been shown to improve crop classification accuracy and geographic transferability. However, their operational performance beyond the training distribution remains poorly characterized. We evaluated the out-of-distribution performance of a widely adopted GeoFM [Prithvi-EO-2.0] across 37 events in 12 countries on three continents and validated against regional reference products. Results indicated that the mean overall accuracy (OA) declined from 0.65 in the United States to 0.40 in Europe. Beyond accuracy metrics, we assessed five key aspects of model performance: whether model confidence indicates signal failure, sensitivity to observation windows, the effect of coarsening class schemes, and robustness to both band loss and cloud- and shadow-contamination. Accuracy collapsed when the observation window misaligned with local crop phenology, while deterministic confidence remained high. Expected calibration error increased for seven of eight paired events, and 12-51% of each affected scene was confidently mislabeled at near-zero precision. Monte Carlo dropout entropy registered the shift in all eight, indicating that much of the apparent cross-continent decline reflected phenological misalignment rather than spatial transfer. Two adjustments recovered accuracy without retraining. Consolidating 13 classes into 10, based on the model's dominant confusions, raised the mean OA by 8.4 percentage points. Compressing the window toward near-real-time use preserved accuracy across a 45- to 90-day plateau, peaking near 75 days, though arms tighter than 30 days fell about 0.11 below that plateau. Fine-tuned crop GeoFMs therefore transfer usefully only where observation windows match local growing seasons. We translate these findings into operational guidance for the reliable deployment of the released model.

</details>


### [138] [KVFetch: Temporal Prefetching for the Missing Half of KV Cache Compression](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08811)
*Linfeng Dong*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper identifies a fundamental limitation in KV cache compression methods for LLMs: current approaches only use content-based relevance for cache management, ignoring sequential/positional access patterns. This causes "sequential forgetting" where continuation tokens are lost during compression, breaking verbatim copying in tasks like RAG, code completion, and structured data extraction. The authors propose KVFetch, a training-free framework that adds a temporal recall channel to existing compressors by demoting evicted candidates to a quantized cold tier and prefetching positional successors into hot-tier slots.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to address a critical gap in KV cache compression: existing methods (score-based eviction, summary compensation, offload-and-recall) all rely solely on content relevance to the current query, ignoring the sequential/temporal nature of context access. This matters because many practical applications (RAG, code completion, structured data extraction) require the model to reproduce identifiers, field values, or code tokens verbatim from context, which fails when compression discards continuation tokens while retaining the sequence head.

Method: KVFetch is a training-free, drop-in framework that adds temporal recall to any score-based compressor through three mechanisms: (1) demoting evicted candidates to a quantized cold tier, (2) detecting active copying through a monotone read pointer, and (3) prefetching positional successors into fixed-size hot-tier slots without increasing attention cost. The key innovation is recognizing that cache supports two access modes - associative lookup by content AND sequential traversal by position - and current compressors only implement the first.
