Result: On RULER-16K under iso-budget control, KVFetch recovers verbatim copying performance from 0.8 to 78.4 and raises the 13-task average by +8.4, with gains concentrated on tasks requiring sequential access. On LongBench, where no task requires sequential access, the channel remains dormant and imposes no cost, demonstrating the approach is selective and incurs no overhead when unnecessary.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that sequential forgetting is the dominant source of quality loss under compression, and that this failure cannot be fixed by better scoring, larger budgets, summary compensation, or dynamic re-scoring. The proposed KVFetch framework successfully addresses this by adding a temporal recall channel that opens only when needed, providing significant improvements on tasks requiring sequential access while maintaining performance on other tasks. The approach is training-free and drop-in compatible with existing compressors.

Abstract: As context windows scale to tens or hundreds of thousands of tokens, KV cache compression has become essential for efficient LLM inference. Existing methods fall into three families: score-based eviction, summary compensation, and offload-and-recall. Yet all three decide what to keep or recall by content relevance to the current query. We show this shared design is structurally incomplete. A cache supports two access modes: associative lookup by content and sequential traversal by position; current compressors implement only the first. The gap matters in practice: retrieval-augmented generation, code completion, and structured-data extraction all require the model to reproduce identifiers, field values, or code tokens verbatim from the context. Under compression, content-based eviction retains the head of such a sequence but discards its continuation, causing verbatim copying to break irreversibly midway, a failure we call sequential forgetting. This failure resists better scoring, larger budgets, summary compensation, and dynamic re-scoring; it is the dominant source of remaining quality loss under compression. We propose KVFetch, a training-free, drop-in framework that opens a temporal recall channel for any score-based compressor. It demotes evicted candidates to a quantized cold tier, detects active copying through a monotone read pointer, and prefetches positional successors into fixed-size hot-tier slots without increasing attention cost. On RULER-16K under an iso-budget control, KVFetch recovers verbatim copying from 0.8 to 78.4 and raises the 13-task average by +8.4, with gains concentrating on tasks that require sequential access. On LongBench, where no task requires sequential access, the channel remains dormant and imposes no cost.

</details>


### [139] [Bounded Autonomy and Verifiable Safety for Agentic AI Enabled Automation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08815)
*Srini Ramaswamy,Deveeshree Nayak*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: BRaVeS is a bounded reasoning and safety-governance framework for AI systems that addresses epistemic drift by encoding subject-matter-expert constraints as invariant anchors, using depth-aware attention mechanisms to maintain constraint visibility, and implementing a state hierarchy that reduces autonomy as epistemic risk increases. The framework uses a Lyapunov-Bounded Consensus Framework (LBCF) to map continuous epistemic risk into discrete states and enforce safety through shielded transitions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The core problem is that agentic AI systems cannot be safely deployed in high-stakes environments using probabilistic reasoning alone. A recurring risk is epistemic drift: as reasoning deepens, system behavior may deviate from subject-matter-expert constraints for safe operation.

Method: The paper proposes: (1) Encoding SME-defined constraints as invariant anchors; (2) MoDA-Style (Mixture of Depths Attention) depth-aware access to keep anchors visible during inference; (3) SMARtAutonomy state hierarchy to reduce autonomy as epistemic risk increases; (4) LBCF to map continuous epistemic-risk signals into finite K-bag abstraction with shielded state transitions enforcing Lyapunov-style energy descent or routing to human-mediated terminal states. Evaluation uses discrete event Monte Carlo simulation with HAI 22.04 industrial-control-system time-series data.

Result: Across tested parameter-grouping strategies and thresholds, the LBCF process achieved finite-step convergence and no safety-guard violations. The results provide simulation-based evidence that bounded governance behavior can be enforced under the stated abstraction.

Conclusion: The framework shows promise for bounded governance of AI systems in high-stakes environments. Limitations include: formal convergence applies only to the finite LBCF abstraction (not the full continuous neural activation space), and evaluation is simulation-based rather than deployed transformer implementations. Future work should address deployed implementations, live human-in-the-loop validation, and broader adversarial settings.

Abstract: Agentic AI-enabled automation cannot be safely deployed in high-stakes environments on probabilistic reasoning alone. A recurring risk is epistemic drift: as reasoning deepens, system behavior may move away from subject-matter-expert constraints for safe operation. This paper presents BRaVeS, a bounded reasoning and safety-governance framework termed the Defensible Next-Gen Reasoning System (DNRS). BRaVeS encodes SME-defined constraints as invariant anchors, proposes MoDA-Style (Mixture of Depths Attention) depth-aware access as a candidate mechanism for keeping these anchors visible during inference, and uses a state hierarchy (SMARtAutonomy) to reduce autonomy as epistemic risk increases. To formalize bounded recovery, we introduce the Lyapunov-Bounded Consensus Framework (LBCF), which maps continuous epistemic-risk signals into a finite K-bag abstraction and applies shielded state transitions that enforce Lyapunov-style energy descent or route the system to a human-mediated terminal state. The formal convergence result applies to the finite LBCF abstraction under fixed thresholds and feasible-shield assumptions; it does not prove safety of the full continuous neural activation space. We evaluate the framework through a discrete event Monte Carlo simulation using HAI 22.04 industrial-control-system time-series data with synthetic noise and sensor-degradation regimes. Across the tested parameter-grouping strategies and thresholds, the LBCF process achieved finite-step convergence and no safety-guard violations. These results provide simulation-based evidence that bounded governance behavior can be enforced under the stated abstraction, while motivating future work on deployed transformer implementations, live human-in-the-loop validation, and broader adversarial settings.

</details>


### [140] [The Cost of Long Memory: State, Context, and Stability Complexity in Sequence Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08816)
*Yuheng Song*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper studies the fundamental resource requirements for sequence models to forecast accurately under long-range temporal dependence. For algebraically decaying predictive memory, the optimal forecast error decays as e^{-Θ(√r)} requiring r = Θ(log²(1/τ)) states to achieve error τ. Fractional long memory changes the geometry with 1/L decay from finite context length L, while nonlinear recurrences with contractive dynamics require exponential first-chaos envelopes and approach criticality for vanishing forecast error.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The core question is: for a specified predictive-memory law, how much state, context, or dynamical criticality is required to forecast accurately? This addresses the fundamental resource constraints in sequence modeling, particularly the "curse-of-memory" limitations.

Method: Theoretical analysis using approximation bounds, matching upper and lower bounds for exponential and finite-state modes, analysis of fractional integration geometry, and finite-sample Kullback-Leibler calculations. Experimental validation with contractive state-space, gated recurrent, and attention models.

Result: Key findings: (1) Best r-mode forecast error decays as e^{-Θ(√r)}; (2) Reaching error τ requires r = Θ(log²(1/τ)) states; (3) Fractional long memory changes geometry with exact 1/L leading order; (4) Fixed fractional strength d preserves square-log complexity law; (5) Contractive nonlinear recurrences have exponential first-chaos envelope; (6) Vanishing forecast error on algebraic target forces recurrence toward criticality (necessary but not sufficient).

Conclusion: The paper establishes the optimal resource exponent for one canonical predictive target in forecast risk, showing that the square-log state-complexity law (r = Θ(log²(1/τ))) is fundamental. Fractional long memory fundamentally alters the predictive geometry, while nonlinear recurrences must approach criticality to achieve vanishing forecast error, with statistical information geometry via KL divergence providing additional constraints.

Abstract: Long-range temporal dependence poses a resource question for sequence models: for a specified predictive-memory law, how much state, context, or dynamical criticality is required in order to forecast accurately? We study this question directly in forecasting risk. For algebraically decaying predictive memory, we prove matching upper and lower approximation bounds for exponential and finite-state modes. The best $r$-mode forecast error decays as $e^{-Θ(\sqrt r)}$, so reaching forecast error $τ$ needs $r=Θ(\log^2(1/τ))$ states or modes. Earlier curse-of-memory results establish broad limitations of stable recurrent models under different approximation notions; here both sides match for one canonical predictive target in forecast risk, which fixes the optimal resource exponent for that target. We then show that genuine fractional long memory changes the geometry itself. In particular, forecast error is measured after fractional integration, prediction from a finite context of length $L$ has an exact $1/L$ leading order, and a fixed fractional strength $d$ keeps the square-log state-complexity law. Near the short-memory boundary, we identify the relevant $d^2$ and $d^4$ scales and give a uniform constructive law in the intermediate regime. For nonlinear contextual recurrences with uniformly contractive state dynamics, we derive an exponential first-chaos envelope and an explicit necessary condition that relates forecast accuracy to the contraction margin. Vanishing forecasting error on an algebraic target forces the recurrence quantitatively toward criticality, a condition that is necessary and not by itself sufficient. Finite-sample Kullback--Leibler calculations further connect the predictive geometry to statistical information. Theorem-matched experiments with contractive state-space, gated recurrent, and attention models reproduce the state and stability predictions.

</details>


### [141] [DenoFlow: Flow Matching for SSVEP Denoising under Real Physiological Artifacts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08817)
*Zhentao He,Ziwei Wang,Dongrui Wu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: DenoFlow is a novel SSVEP denoising method that formulates denoising as a transport problem using rectified-flow. It uses a field network to learn velocity fields between contaminated and clean trials, integrating forward from observations. A classifier is trained alongside to ensure the output remains decodable. The method addresses limitations of prior approaches by avoiding direct mapping, preventing mode collapse, and incorporating downstream decoding accuracy into the optimization objective.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current SSVEP denoising methods have three key limitations: 1) they lack paired ground truth for training, 2) they risk reproducing their input (mode collapse), and 3) they are optimized solely on waveform distance without ensuring the output remains decodable for BCI tasks.

Method: DenoFlow uses a rectified-flow formulation that learns a velocity field between contaminated and clean trials instead of direct mapping. The field network is an encoder-decoder architecture that receives the contaminated trial at every layer and the path position at its bottleneck. Denoising is performed by integrating the learned field forward from the observation. A classifier is trained alongside to supervise the integrated output, ensuring decodability. To create paired training data, physiological artifacts (EMG/EOG) were injected into clean signals at controlled SNR levels.

Result: DenoFlow outperformed seven baseline denoising models on two public SSVEP datasets across five popular SSVEP decoders, in terms of both signal fidelity and downstream decoding accuracy.

Conclusion: DenoFlow successfully addresses the limitations of existing SSVEP denoising methods by reformulating denoising as a transport problem. The approach ensures the denoised output remains decodable while avoiding mode collapse, demonstrating superior performance in both signal quality and BCI classification accuracy.

Abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG)-based brain-computer interfaces (BCIs), particularly steady-state visual evoked potential (SSVEP) systems, are highly vulnerable to noise and artifacts, which severely degrade decoding accuracy. Although recent denoising approaches have shown promise, they are fitted without paired ground truth, can settle on reproducing their input, and are optimized on waveform distance alone, which says nothing about whether the output stays decodable. To address these issues, we propose DenoFlow, which casts SSVEP denoising as transport: instead of learning a direct map from a contaminated trial to a clean one, a field network regresses the velocity of the straight path between them, following the rectified-flow formulation, and denoising integrates that field forward from the observation. The field network is an encoder-decoder that sees the contaminated trial at every layer and the path position at its bottleneck, and a classifier trained alongside it supervises the integrated output. Because the observation itself is both the conditioning input and the starting point of the integration, the model never generates a trial from noise, and training reduces to regression, removing the adversarial min-max game. To obtain paired data on datasets with no ground truth, we injected physiological artifacts of the recorded electromyography (EMG) and electrooculography (EOG) signals under a controlled signal-to-noise target. Experiments on two public SSVEP datasets with five popular SSVEP decoders showed that DenoFlow outperformed seven baseline denoising models on both signal fidelity and downstream decoding accuracy. Code is available at https://github.com/wzwvv/DenoFlow.

</details>


### [142] [Just for FUNS: LLM-Guided Spatio-Temporal Graph Node Generation for Forecasting Unobserved Node States](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08818)
*Shuhao Li,Weidong Yang,Changan Liu,Wei Zhuo,Yingbo Zhou,Fan Zhang,Siqiang Luo*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: GenST is a novel framework that uses Large Language Models as semantic bridges to forecast states of unobserved nodes in spatio-temporal graphs, addressing the challenge of limited sensor network coverage by extracting semantic features from node descriptions (e.g., functional zones, road network structures).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional spatio-temporal forecasting models rely on historical observations and fail when encountering nodes without prior records. This limitation arises because sensor networks often lack comprehensive spatial coverage due to deployment costs and maintenance constraints, making the forecasting of unobserved node states (FUNS) a critical yet challenging problem.

Method: The paper proposes a two-stage generative architecture: (1) A Spatio-Temporal VAE compresses spatio-temporal dynamics into a latent space, and (2) A Generative Transformer (GenT) reconstructs future states of unobserved nodes from noise, guided by multi-modal conditions including semantic features extracted by a fine-tuned LLM, geographic coordinates, and neighborhood contexts.

Result: Experiments on six traffic datasets and two non-traffic datasets demonstrate that GenST significantly outperforms existing baselines in zero-shot prediction tasks.

Conclusion: Semantic-guided generation using LLMs as semantic bridges offers a promising approach to mitigating spatio-temporal data sparsity, showing practical potential for real-world applications in logistics, urban planning, and intelligent transportation systems.

Abstract: Spatio-temporal forecasting is a cornerstone of logistics, urban planning, and intelligent transportation systems. However, constrained by deployment costs and maintenance resources, sensor networks often lack comprehensive spatial coverage, rendering Forecast Unobserved Node States (FUNS) a critical yet formidable challenge. Conventional models rely on historical observations and typically falter when encountering nodes without prior records. To address this, we redefine the problem as a conditional generation task on spatio-temporal graphs and propose GenST, a framework that introduces Large Language Models (LLMs) as a semantic bridge, leveraging a pre-trained LLM fine-tuned to extract rich semantic features from node descriptions, such as functional zones and road network structures, to compensate for missing spatio-temporal signals. Specifically, we design a two-stage generative architecture: a Spatio-Temporal VAE first compresses spatio-temporal dynamics into a latent space, followed by a Generative Transformer (GenT) that reconstructs the future states of unobserved nodes from noise, guided by multi-modal conditions including semantics, geographic coordinates, and neighborhood contexts. Experiments on six traffic and two non-traffic datasets show GenST significantly outperforms existing baselines in zero-shot prediction tasks, demonstrating the practical potential of semantic-guided generation for mitigating spatio-temporal data sparsity.

</details>


### [143] [HydroSphere: A Framework for Governed, Self-Healing Wastewater Infrastructure](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08819)
*Prabu,Fancy C,Suresh A,Srini Ramaswamy*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: HydroSphere is a data-driven framework for real-time water quality monitoring, forecasting, treatment optimization, and fault recovery in wastewater systems. It integrates a hybrid TCN-LSTM forecasting model, PPO-based adaptive dosage optimization, and deep autoencoder-based anomaly detection, evaluated on 2.82 million measurements spanning 84 years.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Rapid industrialization and urban growth are increasing pressure on water quality and wastewater treatment systems. Conventional treatment plants rely on static monitoring and control strategies that cannot adapt to changing pollutant conditions, necessitating more intelligent and adaptive approaches.

Method: The framework combines three core components: (1) a hybrid Temporal Convolutional Network-LSTM (TCN-LSTM) model for multi-step forecasting of seven water-quality parameters; (2) an Adaptive Dosage Optimization Module using Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) reinforcement learning for chemical dosing adjustment; and (3) SHADE anomaly detection module employing a deep autoencoder for identifying sensor and process anomalies. The system is governed by tiered governance, deterministic safety bounds, and human oversight.

Result: The TCN-LSTM model achieved RMSE of 0.1417, MAE of 0.1047, and R² of 0.3596. The PPO-based dosage optimization achieved a mean step reward of 1.059 compared to 1.017 for fixed-dose baseline, though unconstrained optimization led to excessive dosing, highlighting the need for operational safeguards. The SHADE anomaly detection achieved an F1 score of 0.651 under controlled fault injection.

Conclusion: HydroSphere provides a scalable foundation for intelligent wastewater management by combining forecasting, optimization, and anomaly detection with governance mechanisms. The framework supports safer and more adaptive water infrastructure and aligns with UN Sustainable Development Goals 6 (Clean Water and Sanitation) and 13 (Climate Action).

Abstract: Rapid industrialization and urban growth are increasing pressure on water quality and wastewater treatment systems, while conventional treatment plants often rely on static monitoring and control strategies that cannot easily adapt to changing pollutant conditions. This paper presents HydroSphere, a governed, data-driven framework for real-time water quality monitoring, forecasting, treatment optimization, and fault recovery. HydroSphere is evaluated using 2.82 million water-quality measurements collected between 1940 and 2023. The framework integrates three main components. First, a hybrid TCN-LSTM model performs multi-step forecasting across seven water-quality parameters, achieving an RMSE of 0.1417, MAE of 0.1047, and R2 of 0.3596. Second, the Adaptive Dosage Optimization Module uses PPO reinforcement learning to adjust chemical dosing, achieving a mean step reward of 1.059 compared with 1.017 for a fixed-dose baseline. The results also show that unconstrained reward optimization can lead to excessive dosing, demonstrating the need for explicit operational safeguards. Third, the SHADE anomaly detection module uses a deep autoencoder to identify sensor and process anomalies, achieving an F1 score of 0.651 under controlled fault injection. HydroSphere combines these capabilities with tiered governance, deterministic safety bounds, and human oversight to support safer and more adaptive water infrastructure. The framework provides a scalable foundation for intelligent wastewater management and supports the objectives of UN Sustainable Development Goals 6 and 13.

</details>


### [144] [Task-Oriented Key-Layer KV Communication for Efficient Latent Multi-Agent Collaboration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08820)
*Dongsen Zhang,Peipei Li,Zekun Li,Wenjun Xu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: KITE is a training-free framework for task-oriented key-layer KV communication in LLM-based multi-agent systems. It shifts the objective from sender-side state fidelity to receiver-side task sufficiency by identifying a task-effective key layer using receiver trajectory distortion criterion, transmitting only the latent working memory associated with the key layer, and using the same layer for autoregressive latent reasoning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing KV-based latent communication methods in LLM-based multi-agent systems prioritize sender-side state fidelity, leading to substantial communication and computation overhead and potentially introducing redundant information. The high inference costs of natural language communication have driven interest in latent communication using model internal states, but current approaches lack task-oriented optimization.

Method: KITE introduces three key components: (1) identifies a task-effective key layer using a receiver trajectory distortion criterion, (2) transmits only the latent working memory associated with the key layer (rather than full-layer KV), and (3) uses the same layer as the entry point for autoregressive latent reasoning. This training-free framework rethinks latent communication from a task-oriented perspective.

Result: Experiments on seven benchmarks across two model families and three model scales show that compared with full-layer KV communication, KITE reduces communication volume by 28-36x, achieves up to 3x end-to-end inference speedup, and improves accuracy by up to 23.3 percentage points.

Conclusion: KITE successfully demonstrates that shifting the objective of latent communication from sender-side state fidelity to receiver-side task sufficiency can significantly improve both efficiency and accuracy. The framework achieves substantial communication and computation savings while actually improving task performance, validating the task-oriented perspective for latent communication in multi-agent LLM systems.

Abstract: Large language model-based multi-agent systems improve complex problem solving through collaboration, while latent communication directly transmits model internal states to avoid the high inference costs of natural language. However, existing KV-based latent communication methods prioritize sender-side state fidelity, leading to substantial communication and computation overhead and potentially introducing redundant information. To address these limitations, we revisit latent communication from a task-oriented perspective, shifting its objective from sender-side state fidelity to receiver-side task sufficiency. Under this formulation, we propose KITE, a training-free framework for task-oriented key-layer KV communication. KITE identifies a task-effective key layer using a receiver trajectory distortion criterion, transmits only the latent working memory associated with the key layer, and further uses the same layer as the entry point for autoregressive latent reasoning. Experiments on seven benchmarks across two model families and three model scales show that, compared with full-layer KV communication, KITE reduces communication volume by 28-36$\times$, achieves up to 3$\times$ end-to-end inference speedup, and improves accuracy by up to 23.3 percentage points.

</details>


### [145] [A Vehicle-Integrated Approach to Digital Twin Deployment for Bridges Through Drive-By Sensing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08822)
*Zihao Liu,Daigo Kawabe,Jiaji Wang,Chul-Woo Kim,Mehrisadat Makki Alamdari*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes a vehicle-integrated digital twin framework for continuous drive-by bridge monitoring, combining physics-based modeling with machine learning. The framework addresses challenges of conventional SHM by using a sensorised vehicle to recover structural information from vehicle-bridge interaction (VBI) and vehicle-road interaction (VRI) responses.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to address the growing global concern of ageing bridge infrastructure. Conventional SHM systems are costly, difficult to scale, and visual inspections are subjective. Drive-by bridge inspection offers a scalable alternative, but key challenges remain in separating bridge responses from road roughness, detecting damage under normal traffic, and generalising across diverse bridge types.

Method: The framework has three pillars: (1) Surrogate models using Fourier Neural Operator (FNO) for VBI and VRI, trained on simulated and field data for millisecond-scale inference; (2) Custom electric inspection vehicle with sensor layout and signal processing optimized through Bayesian optimization, plus unsupervised damage-assessment pipelines using adversarial autoencoders, matrix profiles, and transformers; (3) Validation through coordinated multi-site field trials in Australia and Japan.

Result: The abstract presents a framework rather than specific quantitative results. The framework unifies physics-based modeling and machine learning for continuous monitoring of bridge and road conditions, with validated pipelines and multi-site field trials.

Conclusion: The paper presents a comprehensive vehicle-integrated digital twin framework that addresses the limitations of conventional bridge monitoring approaches. The combination of FNO surrogate models, optimized sensor design, and unsupervised damage detection pipelines offers a scalable solution for continuous bridge health monitoring across diverse bridge types and traffic conditions.

Abstract: Ageing bridge infrastructure is a growing global concern, yet conventional Structural Health Monitoring (SHM) systems are costly and difficult to scale, and routine visual inspections remain subjective. Drive-by, or indirect, bridge inspection, in which a sensorised vehicle recovers structural information from vehicle-bridge interaction (VBI) and vehicle-road interaction (VRI) responses, offers a scalable alternative. However, key challenges remain unresolved, including separating bridge responses from road roughness, detecting damage under normal traffic, and generalising across diverse bridge types. This paper presents a vehicle-integrated digital twin framework that unifies physics-based modelling and machine learning for continuous monitoring of bridge and road conditions. The framework comprises three pillars. First, surrogate models of VBI and VRI are constructed using a Fourier Neural Operator that learns function-to-function mappings from operating conditions to vehicle responses. Trained on both simulated and field data, these surrogates deliver millisecond-scale inference, replacing computationally intensive full-order analyses. Second, the design of a custom electric inspection vehicle, its sensor layout, and signal processing chain are optimised through Bayesian optimisation to maximise bridge information yield while suppressing road and vehicle noise. Unsupervised damage-assessment pipelines based on adversarial autoencoders, matrix profiles, and transformer architectures have been developed and validated to process the resulting vehicle data. Third, the complete workflow is validated through coordinated multi-site field trials in Australia and Japan, covering a range of bridge types, traffic conditions, and environmental settings.

</details>


### [146] [HCPN-GCN: Scaling Hierarchical Prototype Networks with Cone Geometry for Continual Graph Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08823)
*Sammuel R. Silva,Vander L. S. Freitas,Gladston Moreira,Eduardo J. S. Luz,Rodrigo Silva*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: HCPN-GCN is a graph-aware extension of Hierarchical Prototype Networks for Continual Graph Learning that uses Graph Convolutional Networks as feature extractors and cone-based prototypes with diversity regularization to address catastrophic forgetting while reducing prototype count by 30× compared to the original HPN.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The research addresses catastrophic forgetting in Continual Graph Learning, where learning new graph tasks degrades performance on previous ones. Existing HPNs have limitations: linear feature extractors cannot exploit graph topology, and point-based prototypes lead to inefficient growth on structurally diverse graphs.

Method: The proposed HCPN-GCN replaces linear feature extractors with Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) to capture graph topology, and introduces cone-based prototypes with a diversity regularization objective to compactly model the embedding space and reduce prototype proliferation.

Result: Experimental results on six continual graph learning benchmarks show that HCPN-GCN consistently improves average classification accuracy over HPN and representative continual learning baselines while maintaining near-zero forgetting. The model learns richer class-level prototype hierarchies using approximately 30× fewer atomic prototypes than the original HPN.

Conclusion: HCPN-GCN provides a more compact and effective memory representation for continual graph learning, successfully addressing catastrophic forgetting while exploiting graph topology through GCNs and reducing prototype count through cone-based prototypes with diversity regularization.

Abstract: Continual Graph Learning (CGL) aims to incrementally learn from graph-structured data while preserving knowledge acquired from previous tasks. A major challenge in this setting is catastrophic forgetting, where learning new tasks degrades performance on previously learned ones. Hierarchical Prototype Networks (HPNs) address this problem through a prototype-based memory mechanism that avoids storing historical data, but their reliance on linear feature extractors limits their ability to exploit graph topology, while point-based prototypes often lead to inefficient prototype growth on structurally diverse graphs. In this work, we propose HCPN-GCN, a graph-aware extension of HPN that replaces the original linear feature extractors with Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) and introduces cone-based prototypes with a diversity regularization objective. The proposed design produces richer graph-aware representations while compactly modeling the embedding space, reducing prototype proliferation without sacrificing discriminability. Experimental results on six continual graph learning benchmarks demonstrate that HCPN-GCN consistently improves average classification accuracy over the original HPN and representative continual learning baselines while maintaining near-zero forgetting. Furthermore, our analysis shows that the proposed model learns substantially richer class-level prototype hierarchies using approximately $30\times$ fewer atomic prototypes than the original HPN, providing a more compact and effective memory representation for continual graph learning.

</details>


### [147] [FinVector-Market-4B: A Controlled Study of LoRA Adaptation for Structured Financial Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08882)
*Alina Khaybullina*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: FinVector-Market-4B adapts Qwen3.5-4B with rank-16 LoRA on 22,000 examples for structured financial tasks. Schema-only prompting raises JSON validity from 0% to 91.3%. Under explicit prompting, frozen model improves significantly on FinQA (14.7%→40.0%), calculator expressions (48.0%→82.7%), scenario labels (20.1%→89.5%), and implication direction (52.4%→87.2%). A post-hoc audit reveals macro-F1 decline reflects label set changes; using consistent three-class labels yields 77.4% (base) vs 83.1% (adapter). Compact domain adaptation produces substantial task-specific gains beyond format learning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The research addresses the challenge of adapting compact language models for structured financial tasks, particularly improving JSON output validity and task-specific performance beyond basic format learning. The authors investigate whether domain adaptation can produce meaningful gains under both implicit and explicit prompting conditions.

Method: Qwen/Qwen3.5-4B was adapted using rank-16 LoRA on a 22,000-example corpus for structured financial tasks. Evaluation was conducted on a 600-example benchmark under two conditions: implicit (schema alone) and explicit JSON-schema prompting. The study also includes a post-hoc policy-scoring audit to examine macro-F1 decline.

Result: Schema-only prompting raised base-model JSON validity from 0% to 91.3%. Under matched explicit prompting: FinQA exact match improved from 14.7% to 40.0%; calculator-expression correctness from 48.0% to 82.7%; scenario branch-label agreement from 20.1% to 89.5%; implication-direction agreement from 52.4% to 87.2%. Post-hoc audit using consistent three target classes showed 77.4% (base) vs 83.1% (adapter). Limitations include filing overlap and calculator-target inconsistencies affecting generalization claims.

Conclusion: Compact financial domain adaptation via LoRA can produce substantial task-specific gains beyond output-format learning, with gains bounded by the evaluated task distribution and prompt contract. The study highlights the importance of consistent evaluation metrics and notes benchmark limitations regarding generalization claims.

Abstract: FinVector-Market-4B adapts Qwen/Qwen3.5-4B with rank-16 LoRA on a 22,000-example corpus for structured financial tasks. We evaluate the base and adapted models on the same 600-example benchmark under implicit and explicit JSON-schema contracts. Supplying the schema alone raises base-model JSON validity from 0% to 91.3%. Under matched explicit prompting, the frozen scores improve from 14.7% to 40.0% for FinQA answer exact match, from 48.0% to 82.7% for calculator-expression correctness, from 20.1% to 89.5% for scenario branch-label agreement, and from 52.4% to 87.2% for implication-direction agreement. A post-hoc policy-scoring audit shows that the reported macro-F1 decline reflects a changing label set; using the same three target classes gives 77.4% for the base and 83.1% for the adapter. Filing overlap and calculator-target inconsistencies qualify the benchmark's generalization claims. The results show that compact financial domain adaptation can produce substantial task-specific gains beyond output-format learning under matched prompting, with gains bounded by the evaluated task distribution and prompt contract.

</details>


### [148] [GraphOPD: Graph-Augmented On-Policy Distillation for LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08959)
*Bohan Lin,Liyi Chen,Zhuoning Guo,Muyang Li,Qimeng Wang,Yan Gao,Yao Hu,Yudong Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: GraphOPD introduces graph-based structural augmentation to on-policy distillation for LLM agents, addressing the failure of divergence-based step selection in multi-turn settings by using environment state changes to build dependency graphs and score steps by their causal impact.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing on-policy distillation methods allocate supervision based on teacher-student divergence at each step, assuming large disagreement indicates mistakes. However, this approach fails in multi-turn agentic settings because early drift propagates to later contexts (making teacher consistent with drifted trajectories), and interchangeable steps show large but outcome-irrelevant divergences. Empirical tests show highest-divergence selection performs no better than random selection.

Method: GraphOPD builds a dependency graph from the environment's own record of state changes, identifying which steps enabled later ones. It computes a random-walk stationary distribution over this graph to score each step's structural credit, then fuses this with the divergence signal into a trajectory-relative mask to concentrate supervision on high-aptitude steps.

Result: Across three model scales and eleven baselines on ALFWorld, WebShop, and SearchQA, GraphOPD shows competitive performance throughout, improving over the strongest baseline by up to +5.8 percentage points. Executed-replay audit confirms the structural credit score tracks true causal impact far above chance, both signals are independently necessary, and the method transfers to out-of-domain tool-integrated reasoning.

Conclusion: This work demonstrates that divergence-based step selection is ineffective for multi-turn agent distillation, and that graph-based structural credit from environment state changes provides a complementary signal that identifies causally important steps. The combination of both signals outperforms either alone, establishing a new paradigm for on-policy distillation in agentic LLM settings.

Abstract: On-policy distillation post-trains large language model agents by supplying dense, step-level guidance from a teacher policy when the reinforcement-learning reward is sparse and arrives only once per trajectory. Existing instantiations allocate this guidance by the size of the teacher-student divergence at each step, on the single-turn intuition that a large disagreement marks a mistake worth correcting. Once decisions chain over many turns, that rule misfires, since an early drift enters every later context both policies condition on, leaving the teacher consistent with the drifted trajectory instead of flagging its cause, while interchangeable steps register large but outcome-irrelevant divergences. We demonstrate this on an agentic benchmark, where distilling the highest-divergence steps brings no consistent benefit over random selection. To this end, we introduce GraphOPD, the first method to bring graph-based structural augmentation into on-policy distillation for agent capabilities. It reads which steps enabled which later ones from the environment's own record of state changes, immune to the drift that corrupts the teacher-student gap, organizes them into a dependency graph, scores each step by a random-walk stationary distribution over it, and fuses that structural credit with the divergence signal into a trajectory-relative mask concentrating supervision on each rollout's highest-aptitude steps. Across three model scales and eleven baselines on ALFWorld, WebShop, and SearchQA, GraphOPD shows competitive performance throughout, improving over the strongest baseline by up to +5.8 pp. An executed-replay audit further shows that this structural credit score tracks true causal impact far above chance, that both fused signals are independently necessary, and that the same signal transfers to out-of-domain tool-integrated reasoning.

</details>


### [149] [Directed Temporal Representations for Offline Visual Control](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08960)
*Chenyang Yuan,Haoyu Wang,Zhuo Sun,Xiaoyuan Cheng*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: DTRC introduces a directed temporal quasimetric over learned control representations for goal-conditioned policy learning. It builds on frozen LeWorldModel features, calibrates distance using short-range temporal offsets, and uses bootstrapped targets and action-conditioned consistency to enable temporal reachability learning. This temporal progress signal serves as a critic for direct policy learning, achieving strong performance across 10 visual control tasks without iterative trajectory search at test time.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard predictive world models provide compact visual representations but their latent geometry is optimized for predictive similarity rather than temporal reachability, which is essential for control tasks. The authors argue that control requires a latent space where distance corresponds to temporal cost of reaching one state from another.

Method: DTRC constructs a directed temporal quasimetric over learned control representations on top of frozen LeWorldModel (LeWM) features. Three key mechanisms are used: (1) Short-range temporal offsets calibrate the distance scale; (2) Bootstrapped targets extend temporal reachability across longer horizons; (3) Action-conditioned consistency aligns the representation with local transition dynamics. The resulting distance estimates temporal reaching cost, and its change defines goal-relative temporal progress used as a temporal critic for goal-conditioned policy learning. Model-assisted targets provide additional training-time refinement under behavior-support and dynamics-agreement constraints.

Result: Across ten visual control tasks, DTRC achieves strong goal-conditioned control performance relative to planning and direct-policy baselines. Held-out diagnostics on four LeWM tasks show consistent short-range temporal calibration, task-dependent long-range and directional structure, and positive transition-level progress. Temporal supervision improves the same flow-policy parameterization across all four LeWM tasks, while the resulting policy acts directly without iterative trajectory search at test time.

Conclusion: Learning a latent geometry aligned with temporal reachability rather than predictive similarity is beneficial for goal-conditioned control. The directed temporal quasimetric approach provides an effective way to learn such geometry, enabling direct policy learning that outperforms planning-based baselines while being computationally efficient at test time.

Abstract: Predictive world models provide compact visual representations for control. Control requires a latent geometry aligned with temporal reachability rather than predictive similarity alone. We introduce Directed Temporal Representations for Control (DTRC), which learns such a geometry from offline visual trajectories on top of frozen LeWorldModel (LeWM) features. DTRC constructs a directed temporal quasimetric over the learned control representation. Short-range temporal offsets calibrate the distance scale. Bootstrapped targets extend temporal reachability across longer horizons. Action-conditioned consistency aligns the representation with local transition dynamics. The resulting distance estimates temporal reaching cost, and its change across a transition defines goal-relative temporal progress. We use this progress signal as a temporal critic for direct goal-conditioned policy learning. Model-assisted targets provide an additional training-time refinement under behavior-support and dynamics-agreement constraints. Across ten visual control tasks, DTRC achieves strong goal-conditioned control performance relative to planning and direct-policy baselines. Held-out diagnostics on the four LeWM tasks show consistent short-range temporal calibration, task-dependent long-range and directional structure, and positive transition-level progress. Temporal supervision improves the same flow-policy parameterization across all four LeWM tasks, while the resulting policy acts directly without iterative trajectory search at test time.

</details>


### [150] [On KL-Regularized Policy Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08963)
*Yifan Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: KLPO (KL-Regularized Policy Optimization) is a framework for asynchronous reinforcement learning in large language model agents that addresses the probability mismatch between inference and training by anchoring the KL regularizer at the sampler. It eliminates the need for importance weights, critics, learned normalizers, and group-of-responses sampling while maintaining unbiased gradients.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Asynchronous RL for LLM agents suffers from: (1) stale checkpoint rollouts causing distribution mismatch, and (2) probability discrepancies between the inference engine and trainer at identical parameters. Existing solutions either introduce bias (importance ratio clipping) or incur high costs (GRPO requires group of responses per prompt, which is expensive for long episodes).

Method: KLPO anchors the KL regularizer at the sampler level, enabling a closed-form Gibbs solution for the regularized improvement step. It fits the log-ratio optimality condition by least squares on the sampler's own trajectories, using sampler probabilities through log-ratios without importance weights. The method profiles out the regression intercept to replace the intractable log-partition function. For token-level policy mirror descent, gradients are computed from terminal returns via sampler-centered scores or single trajectory residual, even under stochastic tool outputs. Independent Monte Carlo estimates maintain unbiased KL term gradients.

Result: KLPO provides a critic-free update requiring only one rollout per prompt. It achieves this without learned normalizers or group-of-responses. The method also derives exact KL gaps for cheaper top-K and binary approximations.

Conclusion: SPPO, GPO, REBEL, and BPO emerge as special cases of KLPO, demonstrating its unifying theoretical framework. The approach successfully resolves asynchronous RL challenges for LLM agents while maintaining computational efficiency and theoretical soundness.

Abstract: Asynchronous reinforcement learning (RL) for large language model (LLM) agents trains one policy on trajectories generated by another: rollouts come from stale checkpoints, and the inference engine's probabilities differ from the trainer's even at identical parameters. Standard remedies either clip importance ratios, which biases the update, or, as in GRPO, sample a group of responses per prompt, which is costly when episodes are long. We propose KL-Regularized Policy Optimization (KLPO), a framework that anchors the KL regularizer at the sampler. The regularized improvement step then has a closed-form Gibbs solution, and KLPO fits its log-ratio optimality condition by least squares on the sampler's own trajectories, so the sampler probability enters through a log-ratio and no importance weights are needed. Profiling out the regression intercept replaces the intractable log-partition function with the signal's sampler mean plus a sampler-to-trainer KL divergence. For token-level policy mirror descent targets, we show that the resulting gradient can be computed from terminal returns without a critic, via sampler-centered scores or a single trajectory residual, even under stochastic tool outputs. We further prove that independent Monte Carlo estimates of the KL term keep these gradients unbiased, derive the exact KL gap of cheaper top-$K$ and binary approximations, and show that SPPO, GPO, REBEL, and BPO arise as special cases of KLPO. The result is a critic-free update that uses one rollout per prompt and requires neither a learned normalizer nor a group of responses.

</details>


### [151] [Work While They Sleep: Exploiting Evaluation Latency for Fully Bayesian Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08969)
*Gustavo Sutter,Alejandro Comas-Leon,David Holzmüller,Hao Wang,Luis Ricardez-Sandoval,Pascal Poupart,Agustinus Kristiadi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ELF-BO is a Bayesian optimization algorithm that performs fully Bayesian hyperparameter inference without incurring additional decision-time latency by exploiting the wait time during objective function evaluations. It samples from the hyperparameter posterior during evaluation and reweights samples when results arrive, achieving fully Bayesian performance with standard BO computational cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The problem addresses a key limitation in Bayesian optimization: the trade-off between uncertainty estimation quality and computational efficiency. While fully Bayesian approaches (using model averaging over hyperparameters) provide better uncertainty estimates in low-data regimes, they are computationally prohibitive. The core motivation is to make fully Bayesian optimization practical for real-world applications with expensive objective functions.

Method: The method exploits the evaluation latency (the time waiting for objective function computation) as computational slack. ELF-BO samples from the hyperparameter posterior while the objective is being evaluated, then only reweights these samples when the objective value is observed. This approach amortizes the expensive Bayesian inference over the evaluation time, eliminating it from the critical decision-time path.

Result: Across synthetic functions and real-world applications, ELF-BO matches the performance of fully Bayesian methods while maintaining decision latency comparable to or better than standard BO with point estimates. This makes fully Bayesian optimization practically viable.

Conclusion: ELF-BO successfully bridges the gap between fully Bayesian optimization (best uncertainty quantification) and standard BO (practical computational cost). By hiding the Bayesian computation behind objective evaluation latency, it achieves the best of both worlds: superior uncertainty estimates without the traditional computational penalty.

Abstract: Black-box optimization problems are ubiquitous across science and engineering, often dealing with expensive objective functions. This objective latency has two consequences during optimization: (i) the objective evaluation dominates execution time, and (ii) sample-efficient algorithms are crucial to accelerate development and avoid wasting resources. Bayesian optimization (BO) methods are the \textit{de facto} choice of planners for suggesting the next point to try. Standard BO fits the surrogate model's hyperparameters with a point estimate. Alternatively, a fully Bayesian approach uses model averaging to account for uncertainty over the hyperparameters, leading to better uncertainty estimates---useful in the low-data regime that is pervasive in BO. However, it is often prohibitively expensive and thus rarely used. In this work, we propose ELF-BO, an algorithm that uses the objective evaluation latency to headstart the computation of the next suggestion, allowing for fully Bayesian optimization without incurring substantial decision-time costs. This is done by sampling from the hyperparameter posterior \emph{while} the objective is being evaluated, only requiring reweighting of the samples once the objective value is observed. Across synthetic functions and real-world applications, we show that ELF-BO matches the performance of fully Bayesian methods while only incurring decision latency on par with or better than standard BO. Thus, ELF-BO makes fully Bayesian optimization practical in real-world use cases.

</details>


### [152] [The Best Optimizer Depends on Batch Size](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08975)
*Xingyu Dang,Kaiyue Wen,Sadhika Malladi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper challenges the common practice of benchmarking adaptive optimizers at a single batch size and using scaling rules to predict performance at other batch sizes. The authors show that scaling rules fail for the Muon optimizer, and that the optimal optimizer for language model pretraining changes with batch size even after extensive hyperparameter tuning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The machine learning community typically designs new adaptive optimizers and benchmarks them at a single batch size, assuming that scaling rules will preserve performance across different batch sizes. This work questions this assumption by investigating whether the best optimizer at one batch size remains the best at another.

Method: The authors conducted experiments in two parts: (1) testing multiple scaling rules for the Muon optimizer across various training settings, and (2) performing extensive hyperparameter tuning for language model pretraining across different batch sizes to determine which optimizer performs best at each batch size.

Result: Two key findings emerged: (1) No principled scaling rule for Muon works consistently across different training settings, and (2) The best optimizer for language model pretraining changes with batch size, even after exhaustive hyperparameter tuning.

Conclusion: The current approach to developing and evaluating optimizers—benchmarking at a single batch size and applying scaling rules—is fundamentally flawed. The assumption that the best optimizer at one batch size remains the best at another does not hold, necessitating a重新evaluation of optimizer benchmarking practices.

Abstract: A plethora of new adaptive optimizers are designed to efficiently estimate and use minibatch gradient statistics to shape parameter updates, but they are typically benchmarked at a single batch size. Hyperparameter scaling rules promise to preserve performance as batch size and gradient noise change, suggesting that the best optimizer at one batch size should remain the best at another. We challenge this approach to developing and evaluating optimizers by showing: (1) no principled scaling rule for Muon works consistently across training settings, and (2) the best optimizer for language model pretraining changes with batch size even after extensive hyperparameter tuning.

</details>


### [153] [Coding-Agent Benchmarks Should Match Their Users' Task Flows](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09633)
*Igor Slinko,Yaroslav Golubev,Sergey Titov*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses the mismatch between how coding agents are evaluated in benchmarks versus how they are actually used in practice. The authors collect 4,782 real-world agent sessions from JetBrains IDEs and find that long sessions (with ≥3 user messages) differ significantly from issue-derived benchmarks in task types and user behavior patterns. They propose SWE-TaskFlow, a method to transform issue-derived benchmarks to match target interaction distributions, and demonstrate that the interaction protocol itself is a critical but overlooked dimension of evaluation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current coding agent benchmarks use issue-derived tasks that don't reflect real-world usage patterns. The authors observed that real software engineers use coding agents for diverse task types (questions, planning, review, refactoring, execution) and switch between these types within sessions, which existing benchmarks don't capture.

Method: The authors collected 4,782 Production Sessions from JetBrains IDEs and analyzed sessions with at least three user messages (33% of sample). They compared Task Flow distributions (session lengths, task types, type-to-type transitions) across three public interaction corpora. They then developed SWE-TaskFlow, which transforms issue-derived benchmarks by using prompt splitting and verifiable repository QA to steer interactions toward a target Task Flow, with a TaskFlow Alignment Score (TFAS) for trajectory selection.

Result: The study found that long sessions differ from issue-derived benchmarks in two key ways: (1) user requests span a far wider mix of task types, and (2) users switch between types throughout sessions. Different interaction corpora exhibit markedly different Task Flows, indicating no single interaction distribution is universally realistic. Pilot experiments on 700 SWE-Bench Pro tasks showed that solving tasks sequentially in several steps approximately doubles agent cost without stable improvement in resolve rate.

Conclusion: The interaction protocol itself is an important dimension of evaluation that has been overlooked. Benchmarks should name their target use case and calibrate to measurements from it rather than assuming a universal interaction pattern. SWE-TaskFlow provides a practical approach for transforming existing benchmarks to match target interaction distributions.

Abstract: The evaluation of coding agents generally strives to be as realistic as possible. In our study, we collect 4,782 agent sessions of real software engineers in JetBrains IDEs, which we call Production Sessions. Since our subject is interactive agents, we study the sessions with at least three user messages (33% of the sample). These long sessions differ from issue-derived benchmark tasks in two ways: (i) user requests span a far wider mix of task types - questions about the project's code, planning, review, refactoring, execution - and (ii) users switch between types throughout a session. Long-session samples from three public interaction corpora exhibit markedly different Task Flows (the distributions of session lengths, task types, and type-to-type transitions), so no single interaction distribution is universally realistic: benchmarks should name a target use case and calibrate to measurements from it. We present SWE-TaskFlow, an approach for transforming any issue-derived benchmark: it preserves the verified tasks and tests while steering the interaction toward a target Task Flow through prompt splitting and verifiable repository QA, with a TaskFlow Alignment Score (TFAS) for selecting among generated trajectories. In a pilot on 700 SWE-Bench Pro tasks, solving the task sequentially in several steps approximately doubles agent cost without a stable change in resolve rate: the interaction protocol itself is an important dimension of evaluation.

</details>


### [154] [SNR-Gated LSTM-Conditioned Diffusion Model for MIMO Channel Estimation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08977)
*Jixing Zhou,Xinming Huang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A time-series conditioned diffusion model for MIMO channel estimation that leverages LSTM-based temporal dynamics and SNR-gated late-fusion to achieve accurate, low-latency channel estimation under mobility conditions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern MIMO systems require accurate and low latency channel estimation, especially under mobility where channels exhibit structured sparsity and strong temporal correlation. Existing diffusion-based methods perform per-snapshot estimation, failing to exploit temporal dynamics.

Method: 1) Train a diffusion denoiser operating in the angular domain starting from LS observations; 2) Use LSTM network to encode conditioning information over a short observation sequence for temporal dynamics; 3) Introduce learnable SNR-gated late-fusion shortcut with sigmoid gate for balanced observation fidelity and generative priors; 4) Apply DDIM-style reverse updates with SNR-adaptive truncation and step allocation for inference acceleration.

Result: The proposed method achieves consistent performance gains over existing diffusion-based channel estimation baselines while maintaining low latency through SNR-adaptive inference on time-evolving standardized channel models.

Conclusion: The time-series conditioned diffusion framework effectively exploits temporal correlation in mobile MIMO channels, with the SNR-gated fusion and adaptive inference mechanism enabling robust performance across wide SNR ranges while significantly reducing inference latency at high SNR.

Abstract: Accurate and low latency channel estimation is critical for modern MIMO systems, particularly under mobility, where channels exhibit structured sparsity and strong temporal correlation. This paper proposes a time-series conditioned diffusion framework for channel estimation that performs denoising in the angular domain. Starting from least squares (LS) observations, we train a diffusion denoiser whose conditioning information is encoded by a long short-term memory (LSTM) network over a short observation sequence, enabling the model to exploit temporal dynamics beyond per-snapshot estimation. To robustly balance observation fidelity and learned generative priors across a wide signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) range, we introduce a learnable SNR-gated late-fusion shortcut that injects the network input into the final decoding stage through a sigmoid gate with trainable center and scale. To reduce inference latency, we adopt deterministic denoising diffusion implicit model (DDIM) style reverse updates with SNR-adaptive truncation and step allocation, which significantly reduces the number of reverse diffusion steps at high SNR while maintaining strong performance in low SNR regimes. Simulations on time-evolving standardized channel models demonstrate that the proposed method achieves consistent performance gains over existing diffusion-based channel estimation baselines, while retaining low latency through SNR-adaptive inference.

</details>


### [155] [LASER: Latent Space Adjoint Matching for Support-Constrained Entropy-Regularized Offline RL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08989)
*Songyuan Zhang,Oswin So,Eric Yang Yu,Matthew Cleaveland,Peter Crowley-Dolen,Chuchu Fan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: LASER is a novel offline RL algorithm that uses latent-space adjoint matching with entropy regularization to address OOD action risks and policy collapse issues in latent-space RL. It achieves state-of-the-art performance on 40 OGBench tasks using fixed hyperparameters.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Offline RL enables policy optimization from static datasets without costly online interaction, but is bottlenecked by the risk of executing out-of-distribution (OOD) actions. Existing approaches using flow matching and constrained latent spaces suffer from policy collapse into brittle modes and exploitation of critic artifacts.

Method: LASER applies latent-space adjoint matching to achieve entropy-regularized latent-space RL with expressive flow policies while avoiding backpropagation through time.

Result: LASER achieves state-of-the-art performance on 40 challenging OGBench tasks with varying dataset qualities. It uses fixed method-specific hyperparameters across all tasks and outperforms baselines including those with task- and dataset-specific tuning.

Conclusion: Entropy regularization is essential in latent-space RL for addressing policy collapse and critic exploitation issues. LASER demonstrates robust applicability with consistent hyperparameters across diverse tasks.

Abstract: While offline reinforcement learning (RL) enables policy optimization from static datasets without costly online interaction, it remains bottlenecked by the risk of executing out-of-distribution (OOD) actions. Recent approaches mitigate this by learning a behavior-cloning policy through flow matching and then performing RL within its constrained latent space. However, naively optimizing the latent policy can easily cause the policy to collapse into a brittle mode or exploit sharp artifacts of the learned critic. In this work, we find that entropy regularization is essential in latent-space RL for addressing these challenges. We introduce LASER, a novel offline RL algorithm that applies latent-space adjoint matching to achieve entropy-regularized latent-space RL with expressive flow policies while avoiding backpropagation through time. Through comprehensive experiments on 40 challenging OGBench tasks with varying dataset qualities, we show that LASER achieves state-of-the-art performance. Notably, LASER uses fixed method-specific hyperparameters across all tasks and outperforms the evaluated baselines, including those with task- and dataset-specific tuning, which highlights the robust applicability of LASER. Project website: https://mit-realm.github.io/laser/.

</details>


### [156] [REFIT: Recognize, Fix, and Test Wearable Sensor Placement Shifts without Labels](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08991)
*Bangxun Tang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: REFIT is an input calibration method for frozen activity-recognition models that corrects sensor misplacement (e.g., watch on different wrist, sensor re-attached) without labels or retraining by fitting families of axis transforms to match training data statistics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: When users wear inertial sensors differently at deployment than in training (e.g., moving a watch to the other wrist or re-attaching a strap sensor turned), the model sees the same motion on changed axes, causing accuracy loss. Existing methods require labels or retraining to address this.

Method: REFIT describes axis shifts using families of transforms (reflections and rotations), fits each family to user's data so simple statistics match training data, selects the family that removes most mismatch, applies the best transform before the frozen model, re-estimates normalization statistics, and tests with a label-free accuracy estimate.

Result: REFIT outperforms label-free test-time adaptation methods on every dataset, restores most accuracy lost to re-attachment, and names injected shifts more reliably than a confidence-based selector. After correction over signed permutations, the estimate separates successful from failed corrections.

Conclusion: REFIT provides an effective label-free solution for correcting sensor misplacement in activity recognition models, requiring no retraining or labeled data, and can reliably detect when re-wearing is necessary.

Abstract: We present REFIT, an input calibration for frozen activity-recognition models whose inertial sensors are worn differently at deployment than in training. When users move a watch to the other wrist or put a strap sensor back on turned, the model sees the same motion on changed axes. REFIT undoes such shifts without labels or retraining. It describes them by families of axis transforms, such as reflections and rotations, and fits each family to the user's data so that simple statistics match those of the training data. The family that removes most of the mismatch names the shift. REFIT fixes the shift by applying the best member of that family before the frozen model and re-estimating its normalization statistics. It tests the fixed model with a label-free accuracy estimate and asks the user to re-wear the sensor when it is low. Experiments on real left/right sensor pairs and on real and simulated re-attachment show that REFIT outperforms label-free test-time adaptation methods on every dataset and restores most of the accuracy lost to re-attachment. It names injected shifts far more reliably than a confidence-based selector. After a correction over all signed permutations of the axes, the estimate separates successful from failed corrections.

</details>


### [157] [Algorithmic Scratchpads and Curriculum Staging for Arithmetic Reasoning in Tiny Transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09003)
*Sourabh Kasliwal*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates training small Transformers (~10.6M parameters) on multi-step arithmetic tasks using scratchpad-style reasoning. Key findings include: (1) sequence padding causes 83% gradient starvation remedied by continuous packing; (2) linguistic pretraining is essential; (3) a digit-by-digit long division scratchpad with curriculum learning boosted division accuracy from 4.0% to 86.7%; (4) multiplication remains challenging due to simultaneous multi-term summation; (5) performance collapses on unseen 4-digit operands and unbuffered training causes catastrophic forgetting.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Autoregressive LLMs struggle with deterministic multi-step algorithmic tasks like multi-digit multiplication and long division. The authors investigate the mechanics of teaching arithmetic reasoning to compact "Tiny" Transformers through step-by-step scratchpad training.

Method: Train ~10.6M parameter Transformers on synthetic data for four basic operations (+, -, *, /) using scratchpad-style reasoning. Investigate training foundations including dataloader sequence padding, linguistic pretraining, and modern architectural primitives (RoPE, RMSNorm, SwiGLU, MoE). Compare different scratchpad formulations (FOIL for multiplication vs. digit-by-digit for division) and implement a 4-stage Hierarchical Developmental Curriculum.

Result: Sequence padding creates an 83% gradient starvation artifact (40%→1% accuracy). Linguistic pretraining is essential (<=2.0% without it). Modern architectural primitives substantially improve additive reasoning. The digit-by-digit long division scratchpad with curriculum learning elevated single-digit division from 4.0% to 86.7% on a 4,000-problem held-out benchmark. Multi-digit multiplication remained challenging due to the FOIL scratchpad forcing simultaneous summation of up to nine multi-digit terms. Performance collapses to 0% on unseen 4-digit operands, and unbuffered training causes catastrophic forgetting (86.7%→0% division accuracy).

Conclusion: The success of algorithmic scratchpad training depends critically on proper scratchpad formulation—the digit-by-digit approach works for division but FOIL fails for multiplication due to excessive simultaneous computation. Key boundaries exist: performance generalizes poorly beyond training distribution (4-digit operands) and sequential training without buffering causes catastrophic forgetting. This work provides essential foundations for training compact models on deterministic multi-step reasoning tasks.

Abstract: Autoregressive Large Language Models (LLMs) frequently struggle with deterministic multi-step algorithmic tasks such as multi-digit multiplication and long division. In this paper, we investigate the mechanics of multi-step arithmetic in compact "Tiny" Transformers (~10.6M non-embedding parameters, 49.3M total) trained on synthetic data across four basic operations (+, -, *, /) unrolled as step-by-step scratchpads. First, we establish the necessary training foundations: (1) dataloader sequence padding creates an 83% gradient starvation artifact that collapses accuracy from 40% to 1%, remediated via continuous sequence packing; (2) linguistic pretraining is an essential prerequisite (<= 2.0% without it); and (3) modern architectural primitives (RoPE, RMSNorm, SwiGLU) and Sparse Mixture of Experts (MoE) substantially improve additive reasoning over baseline GPT-2. Second, we demonstrate that algorithmic scratchpad formulation directly dictates success. Introducing a deterministic Digit-by-Digit Long Division scratchpad within a 4-stage Hierarchical Developmental Curriculum dramatically elevates single-digit division from 4.0% to 86.7% accuracy on a 4,000-problem held-out benchmark. In contrast, multi-digit multiplication remained challenging: detailed error analysis revealed that while the model correctly computed single-digit sub-products and place-value zeros, our FOIL scratchpad failed because it forced a simultaneous summation of up to nine multi-digit terms in a single step without pairwise intermediate accumulation. Finally, we identify two key boundaries: performance collapses to 0.00% on unseen 4-digit operands, and unbuffered training induces catastrophic forgetting, collapsing division accuracy from 86.7% down to 0.00%.

</details>


### [158] [Input-Blind Controls Produce Substantial Oracle Headroom for Layer Programs in Multiple-Choice Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.10368)
*Yibei Guo,Rui Liu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether gains from adaptive layer-skipping program selection in language models reflect genuine benefits from the selected computation or merely artifacts of shared option order. Using 32 programs across two models and 4,413 multiple-choice questions, the authors find that input-blind control perturbations actually outperform real selected programs, suggesting the apparent gains may not be specific to the selected layer computation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors aim to distinguish between two possible explanations for gains from adaptive computation selection: (1) the selected programs genuinely provide better layer computation, or (2) the gains come from artifacts like shared option order between evaluation and test prompts. This distinction is crucial for understanding whether adaptive computation truly improves model reasoning.

Method: The study compares 32 layer-skipping and repetition programs on Qwen3-4B-Base and Llama-3.1-8B using 4,413 multiple-choice items. They compare gains from selected programs against input-blind perturbations at the same sites, re-evaluating selections on different prompts. They test multiple conditions: shared option order, rotating options, fixed letter offsets, and a supplementary generated-answer test with rewording.

Result: Control perturbations (input-blind) show 10.2-11.8 and 15.6-19.4 percentage points of headroom on Qwen3-4B-Base and Llama-3.1-8B, exceeding real programs' 9.0 and 10.1 points. Rotating options reduces headroom for both families but leaves positive real-minus-control differences of 1.4-2.3 and 3.7-4.5 points. A supplementary test shows search-selected programs keep a 26.0-point advantage after rewording, but without placebo comparison.

Conclusion: Substantial headroom can persist across prompts with shared option order without establishing a benefit specific to the selected layer computation. Neither ordering against the controls identifies that benefit. The apparent gains from adaptive program selection may largely be artifacts rather than genuine computational advantages.

Abstract: Adaptive computation aims to improve language-model inference by tailoring execution to each input. For layer programs, oracle evaluations use known answers to estimate the potential gain from this flexibility, before a practical selector is available. However, a gain from selection does not by itself explain why the chosen programs help. This study examines this distinction using 32 layer-skipping and repetition programs on two models and 4,413 multiple-choice items. The analysis compares their gains over a fixed action selected without the evaluation prompt with those of input-blind perturbations at the same sites, re-evaluating selections on another prompt. With shared option order, the controls give 10.2-11.8 and 15.6-19.4 percentage points of headroom on Qwen3-4B-Base and Llama-3.1-8B, exceeding the real programs' 9.0 and 10.1 in all three random-direction draws per model. They match answer-change rate only, and the ordering depends on the menu: in post hoc comparisons, real programs lead on Llama's repeat-only menu in every draw. A smaller KL-calibrated comparison, including an input-dependent control, favours real programs in point estimate, with inconclusive corrected tests. Fixed letter offsets produce headroom of similar scale. Rotating options sharply reduces both families' headroom, while leaving positive real-minus-control differences of 1.4-2.3 and 3.7-4.5 points; their magnitudes and statistical support depend on further adjustments and the reference. A supplementary generated-answer test finds that search-selected programs keep a 26.0-point advantage over programs selected for other problems after rewording, without a placebo comparison. These results show that substantial headroom can persist across prompts with shared option order without establishing a benefit specific to the selected layer computation; neither ordering against these controls identifies that benefit.

</details>


### [159] [Removing Information Content Does Not Certify Tamper Resistance in Open-Weight Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09004)
*Domenic Rosati,Alessa Carbo,Ali Dadsetan,Hong Huang,Matthew Young,Subhabrata Majumdar,Frank Rudzicz,Hassan Sajjad*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper challenges the common belief that removing harmful information from open-weight models (via training-data filtering or capability removal) makes them resistant to fine-tuning attacks. The authors argue that mutual information at release alone cannot certify resistance, because function-preserving reparameterizations can leave information unchanged while altering gradient descent dynamics, enabling fast recovery in certain parameterizations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The research addresses a critical security question in open-weight AI models: if we remove harmful information through techniques like training-data filtering or capability removal, can we guarantee the model remains resistant to fine-tuning attacks that restore those capabilities? This is important for AI safety and deployment of open-source models.

Method: The authors use theoretical analysis based on information theory (mutual information), differential geometry (parameter Jacobians), and gradient descent dynamics. They examine weight-data mutual information under training-data filtering and label-representation mutual information under capability removal. They also construct explicit examples to demonstrate their claims.

Result: The key findings are: (1) mutual information at release alone cannot universally certify slow recovery; (2) function-preserving reparameterizations leave information unchanged while changing gradient-descent geometry; (3) training order affects recovery time at fixed information; (4) representation-level independence can preserve the parameter Jacobian; (5) an explicit construction with zero information still recovers in one gradient step exists.

Conclusion: The missing requirement for certification is constraints on attack dynamics beyond mutual information at release. Current information-theoretic certificates are insufficient because they don't account for parameterization-dependent attack speed and training order effects. The paper identifies that certification must consider the fastest reachable parameterization and attack dynamics, not just information content at release.

Abstract: Does removing harmful information make open-weight models resistant to fine-tuning attacks? We show that mutual information at release alone cannot universally certify slow recovery. Function-preserving reparameterizations leave information unchanged while altering gradient-descent geometry, so an invariant certificate is bounded by the fastest reachable parameterization.
