We apply this principle to weight--data mutual information under training-data filtering and label--representation mutual information under capability removal. Training order can change recovery time at fixed weight--data information, while exact representation-level independence can preserve the entire parameter Jacobian. An explicit construction has both information quantities equal to zero and recovers in one gradient step. Controlled experiments illustrate order-dependent recovery and parameterization-dependent attack speed. These results identify the missing requirement for certification: constraints on attack dynamics beyond mutual information at release.

</details>


### [160] [Neighborhood Smoothing for Calibration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09020)
*Idan Horowitz,Avigdor Gal*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces graph smoothing as a train-time calibration method for neural networks, where similar predictive distributions are encouraged across neighboring samples in representation space. A regularizer (GraphCal) penalizes Jensen-Shannon divergence between neighboring samples' predictions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern neural networks are miscalibrated with overconfidence. Existing train-time calibration methods modify task losses or calibration penalties but leave neighborhood structure in learned representations underexploited. The authors aim to leverage this untapped structure for calibration.

Method: The paper proposes GraphCal, a graph-based train-time regularizer that penalizes Jensen-Shannon divergence between predictive distributions of neighboring samples in representation space. The analysis derives bounds connecting predictive divergence to local confidence variation and calibration error propagation.

Result: Across standard calibration benchmarks, GraphCal improves predictive quality. The improvement is complementary to post-hoc calibration: after temperature scaling, GraphCal achieves the lowest NLL among all evaluated train-time methods in 7 out of 8 image and tabular settings.

Conclusion: Graph smoothing over learned representations provides significant value for neural network calibration. The method is complementary to post-hoc calibration techniques, and the analysis provides conditions under which smoothing can or cannot improve calibration.

Abstract: Modern neural networks are often miscalibrated, with a tendency to overconfidence. Existing train-time calibration methods largely modify task losses or calibration penalties, leaving neighborhood structure in learned representations underexploited. We introduce graph smoothing as a general principle for train-time calibration, which encourages similar predictive distributions across neighboring samples in representation space. We analyze the effects of graph smoothing, deriving bounds that connect predictive divergence between neighboring samples to local confidence variation and to the propagation of pointwise calibration error, and characterize the conditions under which smoothing can or cannot improve calibration. In light of this analysis, we propose \modelNoSpace, a graph-based train-time regularizer that penalizes the Jensen--Shannon divergence between predictive distributions of neighboring samples. We present a thorough empirical analysis, showing that across standard calibration benchmarks, \model improves predictive quality, and the improvement is complementary to post-hoc calibration: after temperature scaling, \model attains the lowest NLL of all evaluated train-time methods in seven of the eight image and tabular settings. These findings demonstrate the value of graph smoothing over learned representations for neural network calibration.

</details>


### [161] [SPIN: Shadow Predictive Indexer for Sparse Attention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09025)
*Yao Fu,Cyrus Chang,Ritchie Zhao,Bryce Long,Yueying Li,Mahdi Kamani,Samkit Jain,Rahul Raman,Tara Safavi,Shreya Gupta,Parsa Ashrafi Fashi,Minseok Lee,Julien Demouth,Bita Darvish Rouhani*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SPIN introduces a lightweight, history-based prediction mechanism to reduce indexer overhead in sparse attention systems, avoiding the need to score the entire KV cache at every decoding step while maintaining 30-40% sparsity and improving throughput by up to 14.9%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Indexer-based sparse attention reduces attention costs by passing only important tokens to the core attention mechanism. However, the indexer must still score the entire KV cache at every decoding step, creating a significant overhead that becomes a major bottleneck as context length grows.

Method: SPIN uses lightweight, history-based prediction to identify important KV blocks, treating KV blocks and speculative decoding as first-class design and implementation considerations.

Result: SPIN achieves 30-40% sparsity while preserving task quality. In end-to-end vLLM serving, SPIN improves output throughput by up to 14.9% and reduces median inter-token latency by up to 13.2%.

Conclusion: SPIN effectively reduces indexer overhead in sparse attention systems, enabling efficient long-context and agentic inference while maintaining quality and significantly improving throughput and latency metrics.

Abstract: Indexer-based sparse attention reduces the cost of core attention by passing only a fixed, small number of important tokens to it. However, the indexer must still score the entire KV cache at every decoding step. This scoring overhead becomes a major bottleneck as the context length grows. We propose SPIN (Shadow Predictive Indexer) to reduce this indexer overhead. SPIN uses lightweight, history-based prediction to identify important KV blocks, avoiding the need to score the full KV cache at every decoding step. SPIN treats KV blocks and speculative decoding as first-class design and implementation considerations. Across extensive evaluations on long-context and agentic benchmarks, SPIN achieves 30-40% sparsity while preserving task quality. In end-to-end vLLM serving, SPIN improves output throughput by up to 14.9% and reduces median inter-token latency by up to 13.2%.

</details>


### [162] [ORACLE: Optimizer-Relative Alignment for Constrained LEarning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09040)
*Utkarsh Grover,Wyatt Mackey,Kaixun Hua,J. Morris Chang,Xiaomin Lin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces ORACLE (Optimizer Relative Constrained Learning), a novel approach to constraint handling that assesses constraint compatibility on the post-optimizer update rather than before the optimizer acts. Instead of modifying objectives or gradients, ORACLE evaluates the optimizer's realized step through joint endpoint linearization of constraint families, constructs alignment in the optimizer's geometry, bounds authority, and validates before committing.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional constraint handling methods intervene before the optimizer acts by modifying the objective or gradient. However, optimizer components like momentum, adaptive scaling, and structured preconditioning can substantially reshape the signal before it becomes a parameter update. The authors argue that constraint compatibility should be assessed on the post-optimizer update rather than the pre-optimizer signal.

Method: ORACLE evaluates the native optimizer's realized step through: (1) joint endpoint linearization of heterogeneous constraint families, (2) constructing the resulting alignment in the optimizer's own geometry, (3) bounding its authority, and (4) committing only after validation. This approach works across different optimizer geometries including Euclidean, diagonal adaptive, and structured preconditioned geometries.

Result: ORACLE improves or matches native optimizer performance in 94% of configurations across 8 PDE benchmarks with 4 optimizers. Cross-model analysis shows 92% of configurations benefit. Matched comparisons show improvements over alternative constraint-handling methods at objective, gradient, and post-optimizer levels.

Conclusion: The optimizer-relative approach to constraint handling (ORACLE) demonstrates significant advantages over traditional methods by working within the optimizer's own geometry and validating before committing. This provides a more general and effective framework for constraint handling in optimization problems.

Abstract: Constraint handling methods typically intervene before the optimizer acts, by modifying the objective or the gradient. Yet momentum, adaptive scaling, and structured preconditioning can substantially reshape that signal before it becomes a parameter update. We formulate optimizer relative constrained learning, where constraint compatibility is assessed on the post optimizer update. Building on this view, we introduce ORACLE, which evaluates the native optimizer's realized step through a joint endpoint linearization of heterogeneous constraint families, constructs the resulting alignment in the optimizer's own geometry, bounds its authority, and commits it only after validation. We evaluate ORACLE across eight Partial Differential Equation benchmarks and four optimizers spanning Euclidean, diagonal adaptive, and structured preconditioned geometries, where it improves or matches native optimizer in 94% of configurations. Cross model analysis shows the same behavior in 92% of configurations, while matched comparisons show improvements over alternative constraint-handling methods acting at the objective, gradient, and post-optimizer levels.

</details>


### [163] [Towards Financial World Modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09048)
*Humzah Merchant,Alec Guthrie,Simon Mahns,Randall Balestriero,Bradford Levy*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses financial representation learning for world models by introducing Market-1T (1 trillion observations, 2008-2025, U.S. equities at 1 Hz), developing a rigorous evaluation protocol, and systematically comparing 18 encoder-training strategies across nearly two decades of market regimes. The key finding reveals that encoders with similar predictive performance can organize market state very differently.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current financial representation learning is evaluated on individual predictive tasks using narrow datasets and single time periods, which is insufficient for building world models that support planning and decision-making over unknown future tasks. Financial world models require representations that capture market-wide conditions, asset-specific returns, liquidity, volatility, and cross-asset relationships.

Method: The authors create Market-1T dataset containing nearly 1 trillion observations across U.S. equities from 2008 to 2025 at 1 Hz resolution. They develop a rigorous evaluation protocol and conduct a systematic large-scale study comparing 18 encoder-training strategies across nearly two decades of market regimes. Representations are evaluated through both predictive utility on common finance tasks and probes of latent structure.

Result: Encoders with similar predictive performance can organize market state very differently, indicating that predictive accuracy alone does not capture the quality of financial representations for world modeling purposes.

Conclusion: This work establishes a foundation for training and evaluating financial market representations in support of world models such as DINO-WM, V-JEPA 2, and LeWM, providing benchmark datasets, evaluation protocols, and empirical insights for the research community.

Abstract: Building a world model requires a state representation useful for planning and decision-making---potentially over tasks unknown at training time. In the context of financial markets, planning and decision-making may require a model to reason about market-wide conditions, asset-specific expected returns, liquidity, volatility, and cross-asset relationships. Yet financial representation learning has largely been evaluated on individual predictive tasks, oftentimes on a single time period using comparatively narrow datasets. We address this through three primary contributions. First, we introduce Market-1T, a dataset containing nearly one trillion observations across U.S. equities from 2008 to 2025 at 1 Hz resolution. Second, we develop and implement a rigorous evaluation protocol. Third, we conduct a systematic large-scale study of financial representation learning, comparing 18 encoder-training strategies across nearly two decades of market regimes. We evaluate learned representations both by their predictive utility on common finance tasks and through probes of latent structure. We find that encoders with similar predictive performance can organize market state very differently. Collectively, we establish a foundation for training and evaluating financial market representations in support of world models such as DINO-WM, V-JEPA 2, and LeWM.

</details>


### [164] [A Self-Pruning Transformer: Extreme KV-Cache Compression with Universal Attention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09051)
*Davis Wertheimer,Haochen Shen,Ahan Gupta,Derrick Liu,Yu Chin Fabian Lim,Mudhakar Srivatsa,Raghu K. Ganti,Minjia Zhang,Naigang Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A new Universal Attention framework that replaces traditional attention mechanisms with a flexible decay-based approach, enabling adaptive KV-cache pruning while preserving RoPE embeddings and Softmax attention. Achieves 10×-25× compression with improved or maintained performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The large KV-cache size in modern LLMs creates significant barriers to efficient deployment. Existing approaches use decay-based mechanisms to prune KV-cache, but these have limited expressivity and result in simple sliding-window eviction patterns.

Method: Proposed Universal Attention - an end-to-end trainable architecture with a composite decay mechanism that captures complex key statistics and interactions. The decay mechanism acts as an adaptive pruning criterion, automatically removing tokens that contribute least to attention computation while preserving RoPE embeddings and Softmax attention.

Result: Achieves state-of-the-art 10× compression on natural language and synthetic task data while improving downstream performance compared to both state-of-the-art baselines and unpruned oracles. Demonstrates unprecedented 25× compression at length 16k with superior long-context generalization.

Conclusion: Universal Attention provides a highly expressive and adaptable attention mechanism that enables aggressive KV-cache compression without performance degradation, showing particular strength in long-context scenarios.

Abstract: The large KV-cache size of modern LLMs creates a barrier to efficient deployment. Recent work has explored replacing attention layers' RoPE positional embeddings with alternative decay-based mechanisms, which can then be used to prune KV-cache during inference. However, these decay functions have limited expressivity, and in practice devolve into sliding-window-like eviction patterns. In this work, we propose a unifying framework for complementary and novel decay mechanisms, capturing complex key statistics and interactions while preserving expressive RoPE embeddings and Softmax attention. The resulting Universal Attention is a highly expressive and end-to-end trainable architecture, whose composite decay mechanism acts as a natural, $\textit{adaptive}$ pruning criterion, removing tokens that contribute least to attention computation. Experimentally, Universal Attention achieves state-of-the-art $10\times$ compression on natural language and synthetic task data, while $\textit{improving}$ downstream performance compared to both state-of-the-art baselines and unpruned oracles. It further demonstrates superior long-context generalization with unprecedented $25\times$ compression at length 16k.

</details>


### [165] [BeatFlow-ECG: Rectified Flow for ECG Reconstruction from Indirect Wearable Signals](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09052)
*Mohamed Kamel,Sahar Selim,Walaa Medhat,Tamer Nadeem*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: BeatFlow-ECG is a conditional rectified-flow model that reconstructs single-channel ECG from synchronized PPG and inertial measurements (IMU), addressing the trade-off between ECG's rich cardiac information and PPG's ease of continuous acquisition. It uses a convolutional encoder-decoder with transformer bottleneck and explicit flow-time conditioning, incorporating motion information through IMU-derived features, motion-dependent loss weighting, and curriculum learning. The model achieves state-of-the-art results on PPG-DaLiA and WESAD datasets, outperforming deterministic, adversarial, and diffusion-based baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Continuous cardiac monitoring outside clinical settings requires signals that are both informative and practical. ECG provides rich cardiac rhythm and waveform morphology information but is difficult to acquire continuously in daily life. PPG is easier to acquire continuously but is only an indirect cardiovascular measurement and is highly sensitive to motion. This work aims to reconstruct ECG from easier-to-collect PPG and inertial measurements.

Method: BeatFlow-ECG models ECG reconstruction as conditional transport from noise to ECG using: (1) convolutional encoder-decoder with transformer bottleneck, (2) explicit flow-time conditioning, (3) IMU-derived conditioning features, (4) motion-dependent loss weighting, and (5) easy-to-hard training curriculum. Evaluated under leave-one-subject-out protocols on PPG-DaLiA and WESAD datasets.

Result: BeatFlow-ECG achieves best results among all evaluated baselines across all waveform and beat-timing metrics. On PPG-DaLiA: Pearson correlation of 0.983, R-peak F1 score of 0.946. On WESAD: Pearson correlation of 0.986, R-peak F1 score of 0.955. Compared with Conditional DDPM-1D, L1 error decreases from 0.085 to 0.062 on PPG-DaLiA and from 0.074 to 0.055 on WESAD. Additional analyses show higher correlation in fixed R-peak-relative waveform regions and lower reconstruction error across low-, medium-, and high-motion subsets.

Conclusion: BeatFlow-ECG successfully reconstructs high-quality ECG from PPG and inertial measurements, outperforming existing deterministic, adversarial, and diffusion-based methods. The incorporation of motion information through multiple mechanisms (IMU conditioning, motion-dependent loss weighting, curriculum learning) effectively addresses the motion sensitivity issue of PPG, making it suitable for continuous cardiac monitoring in daily life scenarios.

Abstract: Continuous cardiac monitoring outside clinical settings requires signals that are both informative and practical to collect during daily life. Electrocardiography (ECG) provides rich information about cardiac rhythm and waveform morphology, while wearable photoplethysmography (PPG) is easier to acquire continuously but is only an indirect cardiovascular measurement and is highly sensitive to motion. We present BeatFlow-ECG, a conditional rectified-flow model for reconstructing single-channel ECG from synchronized PPG and inertial measurements. BeatFlow-ECG models reconstruction as conditional transport from noise to ECG using a convolutional encoder-decoder with a transformer bottleneck and explicit flow-time conditioning. Motion information is incorporated through IMU-derived conditioning features, motion-dependent loss weighting, and an easy-to-hard training curriculum. We evaluate the model under leave-one-subject-out protocols on PPG-DaLiA and WESAD. BeatFlow-ECG achieves the best results among the evaluated deterministic, adversarial, and diffusion-based baselines across all reported waveform and beat-timing metrics, with Pearson correlations of 0.983 and 0.986 and R-peak F1 scores of 0.946 and 0.955, respectively. Compared with Conditional DDPM-1D, L1 error decreases from 0.085 to 0.062 on PPG-DaLiA and from 0.074 to 0.055 on WESAD. Additional analyses on PPG-DaLiA show higher correlation in fixed R-peak-relative waveform regions and lower reconstruction error across low-, medium-, and high-motion subsets.

</details>


### [166] [A Geometry-Based Capacity Theory for Finite-Feature Associative Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09056)
*Jianhai Zhang,Donghao Zhang,Pattarawut Charatpangoon,Bijoy Menon,M. Ethan MacDonald,Wu Qiu,Aravind Ganesh*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper develops a geometry-based capacity theory for Hebbian associative memory that predicts exact-key retrieval quality based on representation geometry. The theory separates retrieval interference into finite-feature noise (decreasing with feature dimension) and structural interference (determined by kernel overlap, persists in infinite-feature limit), providing fit-free predictions and identifying when increased features or redesigned representations are needed.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand and predict memory capacity in compressed finite-feature Hebbian associative memory systems, particularly how representation geometry affects retrieval quality. The key insight is that retrieval interference has two components that behave differently with increasing feature dimension.

Method: Theoretical analysis separating finite-feature noise from structural interference, using kernel overlap metrics. For correlated values, the method jointly analyzes key kernel and value Gram matrix. Validated through experiments on synthetic, visual, and medical image representations.

Result: The theory provides fit-free predictions of retrieval quality, reveals geometry-dependent capacity ceilings, predicts feature budgets for target retrieval quality, and correctly identifies when to increase features vs. change representation. Predicted retrieval curves closely match empirical behavior across all validation settings.

Conclusion: The framework directly links representation geometry to memory capacity, distinguishing between cases where performance can be improved by increasing feature budget versus cases requiring fundamental representation changes. This provides practical guidance for memory system design across different applications.

Abstract: We develop a geometry-based capacity theory for exact-key retrieval in compressed finite-feature Hebbian associative memory. For random or approximately isotropic values, retrieval interference separates into finite-feature noise, which decreases with feature dimension, and structural interference, which is determined by squared kernel overlap among stored keys and persists in the infinite-feature limit. This yields a fit-free prediction of retrieval quality, reveals a geometry-dependent capacity ceiling, and predicts the feature budget required for a target retrieval quality. When stored values are correlated, we show that retrieval depends jointly on the key kernel and value Gram matrix, and derive finite-feature approximations that account for this interaction. We validate the theory on synthetic, visual, and medical-image representations. Overall, the framework links representation geometry directly to memory capacity and distinguishes when performance can be improved by increasing the feature budget and when the representation itself must be changed. Across these settings, the predicted retrieval curves closely match empirical behavior and correctly identify changes in the preferred memory design.

</details>


### [167] [Learning Cross-Model Activation Alignments with Explicit Many-to-Many Layer Maps](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09058)
*Alina Sudakov,Guy Bar-Shalom,Fabrizio Frasca,Haggai Maron*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MATCHA is a method that learns activation alignment between different LLMs, mapping a source model's layerwise activations to a target model's. It factors the map into a layer map and a layer-shared feature map, learned jointly from prompts. The method reveals that layer correspondences are many-to-many (each target layer draws from a band of source layers) and enables transfer of activation-space interventions like steering vectors and probes between models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Understanding how two independently trained LLMs relate in terms of layer correspondence and feature transformation, as models are released at a rapid pace.

Method: MATCHA learns an activation alignment by factoring it into two components: (1) a layer map that produces an explicit target-by-source matrix identifying which source layers correspond to which target layers, and (2) a layer-shared feature map between hidden spaces. Unlike prior work that fixes layer correspondence in advance (pairing layers at similar relative depths), MATCHA learns both factors jointly from prompts.

Result: Across 42 pairs of seven models spanning three different model families, MATCHA reconstructs target activations more faithfully and substantially improves retrieval-based metrics compared to previous approaches. The recovered maps are broadly monotone in depth but consistently many-to-many: each target layer draws on a band of source layers rather than one-to-one mappings.

Conclusion: The alignment enables transfer of activation-space interventions, allowing steering vectors and probes developed for one model to be transferred to another, facilitating cross-model interpretability and intervention techniques.

Abstract: LLMs are released at a rapid pace, raising a natural question: how do two independently trained models relate, both in which layers correspond and in how features transform between them? We study this by learning an activation alignment, a map from a source model's layerwise activations to a target's. Our method, MATCHA, factors this map into a layer map, whose output is an explicit target-by-source matrix that can be extracted and inspected, and a layer-shared feature map between hidden spaces. Most of prior work fixes the layer correspondence in advance, pairing layers at roughly the same relative depth; in contrast, we learn both factors jointly from prompts. Across 42 pairs of seven models spanning three different families, MATCHA reconstructs the target's activations more faithfully and improves retrieval-based metrics substantially, w.r.t. previous approaches. The recovered maps are broadly monotone in depth but, in contrast with most previous approaches, are consistently many-to-many: each target layer draws on a band of source layers. Our alignments also enable transfer of activation-space interventions, allowing steering vectors and probes developed for one model to transfer to another.

</details>


### [168] [EDiS: Edge Disjoint Subgraph Sparsification Framework for Graph Neural Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09059)
*Sai Karthik Navuluru,Siddhartha Shankar Das,Franck Dernoncourt,S M Ferdous,Ryan A. Rossi,Nesreen K. Ahmed,Baris Coskunuzer,Alex Pothen,Lakshman Tamil,Mahantesh M Halappanavar*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: EDiS is a graph neural network (GNN) training framework that separates one-time structural extraction from per-epoch graph composition. It decomposes the graph once into cacheable edge-disjoint subgraphs, then recombines them across epochs without re-extracting structure, achieving the best performance across 19 benchmarks against 17 baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Sparse GNN training reduces computation but deciding which edges to keep is costly. Reusing one sparse graph locks training to a fixed topology, while varying it across epochs can require repeated sampling or recomputation. Existing methods either suffer from static topology or expensive recomputation.

Method: EDiS decomposes the graph once into cacheable edge-disjoint subgraphs using feature-based scores and successive maximum score covering forests. It then recombines these subgraphs into training graphs with edge-budget constraints across epochs without re-extracting structure. The framework supports alternative edge selection rules through the same composition mechanism.

Result: EDiS achieves the highest mean benchmark score (accuracy/ROC-AUC) and the lowest average rank and gap-to-best among ranked methods across 19 homophilic, heterophilic, and large-scale node classification benchmarks against 17 baselines under the same edge budget. The clearest benefits appear at tight edge budgets.

Conclusion: The proposed EDiS framework effectively addresses the trade-off between computational efficiency and topological flexibility in sparse GNN training by separating structural extraction from graph composition. The deterministic preservation of high-score cut edges under the covering-forest selector and the selector-agnostic conditional bound provide theoretical guarantees for the approach.

Abstract: Sparse GNN training reduces computation, but deciding which edges to keep can be costly. Reusing one sparse graph is cheap, but locks training to a fixed topology, while varying it across epochs can require repeated sampling or recomputation. We introduce EDiS (Edge-Disjoint Subgraph sparsification framework), which separates one-time structural extraction from per-epoch graph composition. EDiS decomposes the graph once into cacheable edge-disjoint subgraphs, then recombines them into graphs with edge-budget constraints across epochs and retention ratios without re-extracting structure. Our default construction uses feature-based scores and successive maximum score covering forests, while the same composition mechanism also supports alternative edge selection rules. We provide a combinatorial analysis of the per-epoch sampler, the composition step that draws a training graph from the cached decomposition. We show that, under the default covering-forest selector, the stored decomposition deterministically preserves high-score cut edges, and we derive a selector-agnostic conditional bound on high-score cut survival in composed training graphs. Across 19 homophilic, heterophilic, and large-scale node classification benchmarks against 17 baselines under the same edge budget, EDiS achieves the highest mean benchmark score (accuracy/ROC-AUC) and the lowest average rank and gap-to-best among ranked methods. Ablations show the clearest benefits of structural decomposition and epoch variation at tight edge budgets.

</details>


### [169] [Multi-Label Topic Assignment via LLM Distillation: A Comparative Analysis of Generative vs. Discriminative Student Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09063)
*Sourabh Kasliwal,Shubhranshu Singh*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Summary generation failed


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Motivation analysis unavailable

Method: Method extraction failed

Result: Result analysis unavailable

Conclusion: Conclusion extraction failed

Abstract: Multi-label topic assignment for user-generated content (UGC) -- including product reviews and buyer-seller conversations -- poses unique scalability challenges in large-scale e-commerce due to informal language, extreme label sparsity, and rapidly evolving taxonomies. While utilizing Large Language Models (LLMs) as labeling oracles to distill ground-truth data has emerged as an industry standard to bypass prohibitive manual annotation costs, determining the optimal, low-latency architecture for the resulting student models remains an open challenge. To address this, we conduct a comprehensive evaluation across Small Language Model (SLM) parameter scales (1B, 4B, and 8B) and architectural paradigms (causal generative versus bidirectional discriminative). Comparing generative text-to-label classifiers against discriminative baselines (DeBERTa-V3 and ModernBERT), our analysis reveals a crucial data-dependent trade-off: while discriminative models outperform ultra-lightweight generative models on structured product reviews, even the smallest 1B generative model surpasses discriminative baselines on complex, multi-turn conversational data. Furthermore, generative models maintain robust performance under massive label-set expansion (up to 112 topics) and severe long-tail distributions, whereas discriminative baselines suffer a 35% drop in Macro-F1 at scale. Finally, we detail the successful production deployment of these optimized models across both product review and conversational domains, demonstrating strict latency compliance and tangible business impact at a global marketplace scale.

</details>


### [170] [TAP: Efficient Long-Horizon Agent Pruning via Trajectory-Anchored Recovery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09074)
*Yuanzhe Li,Pengxin Wang,Yuxin Ren,Jianing Deng,Jingtong Hu,Song Wang,Jingdi Chen,Huanrui Yang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TAP is the first structural pruning framework designed for RL-trained agents operating in long-horizon tasks. It addresses the failure of existing pruning methods (designed for QA tasks) when applied to agentic models by coupling structural pruning with on-policy recovery, using teacher trajectories to guide student training while allowing autonomous response generation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-horizon agentic tasks require repeated model calls, significantly increasing inference costs. While existing methods suggest aggressive model pruning could help, methods designed for question answering tasks severely degrade performance when applied to agentic models. The authors identified two key failures: one-shot importance estimates fail to track model adaptation, and existing recovery methods (offline distillation or full-trajectory on-policy distillation) either cover only teacher prefixes or cause error compounding across turns.

Method: Trajectory-Anchored Pruning (TAP) combines structural pruning with efficient on-policy recovery. The approach: (1) Uses a frozen dense teacher to supervise the student's response prefixes, addressing training-inference mismatch while preventing student-induced deviations from propagating across turns; (2) Allows the student to generate each reasoning-action response autonomously; (3) Re-scores channels using gradients of the recovery objective on the recovered student rather than one-shot pruning, connecting iterative channel selection to the evolving policy.

Result: With 60% of FFN channels removed, TAP retains 99.2% and 88.0% of the dense 7B agents' task success rates on ALFWorld and WebShop benchmarks, respectively, while reducing GPU time per successful task by approximately 22% and 17%.

Conclusion: TAP demonstrates effective structural compression of long-horizon agents under limited recovery budget, successfully pruning 60% of FFN channels while maintaining high task success rates and achieving significant GPU time savings.

Abstract: Emerging long-horizon agentic tasks require repeated model calls, worsening the inference cost of already-costly language models. While narrow agentic tasks suggest potential for aggressive model pruning without performance drop, empirical results show existing methods proposed for question answering tasks severely degrade task performance when applied to agentic models. We trace this failure to two decisions: what to prune and how to recover. For pruning, one-shot importance estimates fail to track how the pruned model adapts. For recovery, offline distillation covers only teacher prefixes, while full-trajectory on-policy distillation causes student errors to compound across turns. In this work, we propose Trajectory-Anchored Pruning (TAP), the first structural pruning framework for reinforcement learning (RL)-trained agents. TAP couples structural pruning with efficient on-policy recovery, anchoring interactions to teacher trajectories while allowing the student to generate each reasoning-action response. A frozen dense teacher supervises the student's response prefixes, addressing within-response training-inference mismatch while preventing student-induced deviations from propagating across training turns. Instead of one-shot pruning, TAP re-scores channels using gradients of the recovery objective on the recovered student, connecting iterative channel selection to the evolving policy. With 60% of FFN channels removed, TAP retains 99.2% and 88.0% of the dense 7B agents' task success rates on ALFWorld and WebShop, respectively, while reducing GPU time per successful task by approximately 22% and 17%. These results demonstrate effective structural compression of long-horizon agents under a limited recovery budget.

</details>


### [171] [Tucker Bottleneck Attention for Multi-Dimensional Sequence Modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09090)
*Ryan Solgi,Parsa Madinei,Zheng Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TuBA (Tucker Bottleneck Attention) is a novel efficient self-attention mechanism that exploits low-rank tensor structure to achieve subquadratic computation for processing long sequences from multidimensional data. It projects hidden tensors into compact Tucker cores, performs attention on these cores, and achieves up to 66.6% computation reduction and 4.27x speedups on video prediction and weather forecasting tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard self-attention suffers from quadratic computational complexity, which limits scalability to long sequences from multidimensional data (e.g., video, weather data). Existing efficient attention methods often sacrifice global token mixing or require significant architectural changes. This work aims to develop a more efficient attention mechanism that maintains global receptive fields while reducing computational cost.

Method: TuBA employs low-rank tensor decomposition (Tucker decomposition) to project hidden tensors into compact Tucker cores. Multi-head self-attention and linear projections are performed on these compressed cores before writing updates back to the ambient space. For autoregressive tasks, the method combines bidirectional interactions within cores with causal attention across cores. The approach maintains global token mixing while achieving subquadratic complexity.

Result: On video prediction: up to 24.7% error reduction and 66.6% computation reduction. On autoregressive weather forecasting: up to 37.1% error reduction and 85.1% computation reduction. Speedups up to 4.27x. Low-rank Tucker cores outperform full-rank attention, and multi-frame generation outperforms frame-by-frame generation.

Conclusion: TuBA achieves favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-offs compared to standard and efficient attention methods and task-specific models. The low-rank tensor approach provides an effective solution for scaling self-attention to long sequences in multidimensional data applications, demonstrating that structured compression can improve both computational efficiency and prediction accuracy.

Abstract: The quadratic cost of self-attention limits scalability to long sequences from multidimensional data. We introduce Tucker bottleneck attention (TuBA), which exploits low-rank tensor structure for efficient global token mixing. TuBA projects hidden tensors into compact Tucker cores, performs multi-head self-attention and linear projections on the cores, and writes updates back to the ambient space, enabling subquadratic computation. Its autoregressive extension combines bidirectional interactions within cores with causal attention across cores. On video prediction and global weather forecasting, TuBA achieves favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-offs over standard and efficient attention and task-specific models. Compared to standard self-attention, TuBA reduces error and computation by up to 24.7% and 66.6% for video prediction and 37.1% and 85.1% for autoregressive weather forecasting, with speedups up to 4.27 times. Low-rank Tucker cores and multi-frame generation also outperform full-rank attention and frame-by-frame generation, respectively.

</details>


### [172] [FedRSPO+: A Heterogeneity-aware Algorithm for Decision-focused Federated Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09091)
*Konstantinos Ziliaskopoulos,Alexander Vinel,Jiaqi Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses decision-focused learning (DFL) in federated settings where cross-silo clients have heterogeneous objectives and feasible sets. The authors propose FedRSPO+, which uses RSPO+ (regularized predict-then-optimize) to smooth the decision map through projection, addressing the instability caused by discontinuous changes in optimal decisions from small perturbations in polyhedral problems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing DFL methods assume centralized data, while standard federated learning optimizes prediction quality rather than decision quality. The key challenge is that heterogeneity in downstream objectives and feasible sets causes discontinuous changes in optimal decisions, destabilizing client updates and aggregation.

Method: The paper proposes FedRSPO+ framework built on RSPO+, a regularized predict-then-optimize surrogate that smooths the decision map through projection. Key theoretical contributions: (1) RSPO+ upper bounds decision error and regret for regularized decisions, and under conditions, for original LP decisions; (2) Cross-client heterogeneity bounds that depend on both objective and feasible-set heterogeneity, vanish at homogeneity, and require no strong convexity. FedRSPO+ uses an annealed, modular training procedure compatible with standard federated personalization and aggregation methods.

Result: Experiments on synthetic knapsack, shortest-path, and real-world energy pricing tasks compare against prediction-only federated learning and DFL baselines under varying heterogeneity and communication budgets. Results suggest that smoothing is a useful ingredient for stable collaborative decision learning.

Conclusion: The paper provides a heterogeneity-aware foundation for federated DFL, demonstrating that smoothing through RSPO+ addresses the instability issues in heterogeneous federated settings. The theoretical bounds and experimental results validate the approach as a useful tool for stable collaborative decision learning across diverse applications.

Abstract: Decision-focused learning (DFL) trains predictive models for downstream optimization, but existing methods largely assume centralized data. In cross-silo settings, federated learning offers a natural alternative, yet standard federated methods optimize prediction over decision quality and do not address heterogeneity in downstream objectives or feasible sets. This heterogeneity is especially challenging for DFL because small perturbations in polyhedral problems can cause discontinuous changes in optimal decisions, destabilizing client updates and aggregation. We propose FedRSPO+, a heterogeneity-aware framework for decision-focused federated learning, built on RSPO+, a regularized predict-then-optimize surrogate that smooths the decision map through projection. We show that RSPO+ upper bounds decision error and regret for the regularized decision and, under exact regularization and consistent LP solution selection, for the original LP decision. We further derive cross-client heterogeneity bounds that depend on both objective and feasible-set heterogeneity, vanish at homogeneity, and require no strong convexity. FedRSPO+ uses an annealed, modular training procedure compatible with standard federated personalization and aggregation methods. Experiments on synthetic knapsack, shortest-path, and real-world energy pricing tasks compare against prediction-only federated learning and DFL baselines under varying heterogeneity and communication budgets. Results suggest that smoothing is a useful ingredient for stable collaborative decision learning and provide a heterogeneity-aware foundation for federated DFL.

</details>


### [173] [MaRK: Markov-adapted Recurrent Kernels for Dynamic Operator Conditioning in State Space Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09092)
*Syed Ibrahim Omer,Ginny Y. Wong. Xiangyu Zhao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MaRK introduces a dynamic operator-conditioning framework that maps context vectors directly into bounded modulations of frozen SSM parameters (A, B, C, D, Δ), enabling parameter-efficient fine-tuning (6.3-11M params) for transitioning from bidirectional to iterative diffusion generation. The Chebyshev variant achieves the best validation loss of 2.55.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current SSM conditioning methods operate outside the recurrent operator through input injection or activation modulation, leaving the underlying temporal dynamics fixed. This work aims to reshape the model's input-output memory kernel at each diffusion timestep by modifying the Markov parameter sequence directly.

Method: MaRK instantiates three adapter geometries (Hypernet, Chebyshev polynomial, and DCT kernels) on a frozen 111M-parameter Hydra SSM backbone. These adapters modify the Markov parameter sequence through low-rank auxiliary maps, providing parameter-efficient fine-tuning. The method also yields an analytic Affine Quadratic Stability certificate for the modulated recurrence.

Result: The Chebyshev variant achieves the strongest performance with an average validation loss of 2.55, followed by DCT (2.59) and Hypernet (3.77). Synthetic LPV recovery experiments and Markov-operator diagnostics show that MaRK recovers coordinate-invariant temporal operators under matched assumptions and produces distinct, stable timestep-conditioned memory profiles.

Conclusion: MaRK successfully enables parameter-efficient fine-tuning of frozen SSMs for iterative diffusion generation by directly conditioning the recurrence parameters. The bounded recurrence parameterization provides stability guarantees, and the Chebyshev polynomial adapter emerges as the most effective geometry for this task.

Abstract: State Space Models (SSMs) offer an efficient alternative to Transformers for sequence modeling, yet conditioning pre-trained SSMs for iterative generation typically operates outside the recurrent operator, through input injection or activation modulation. While such mechanisms expose the model to conditioning information, they leave the underlying temporal dynamics fixed. We introduce MaRK (Markov-adapted Recurrent Kernels), a dynamic operator-conditioning framework that maps context vectors directly into bounded modulations of a frozen SSM's recurrence ($A$), read-in ($B$), read-out ($C$), skip ($D$), and discretization ($Δ$) parameters. Viewed through the lens of LPV-SSM systems, MaRK induces a context-indexed family of Markov parameter sequences, allowing each diffusion timestep to reshape the model's input-output memory kernel. We instantiate MaRK on a frozen 111M-parameter Hydra SSM backbone and study three adapter geometries: Hypernet, Chebyshev polynomial, and Discrete Cosine Transform kernels. Since these adapters modify the Markov parameter sequence through low-rank auxiliary maps on the frozen backbone, parameter-efficient fine-tuning arises as a structural consequence of the adaptation mechanism itself, requiring only 6.3--11M trainable auxiliary parameters to transition from a bidirectional objective to an iterative diffusion regime. The bounded recurrence parameterization further yields an analytic Affine Quadratic Stability certificate for the modulated recurrence. Through synthetic LPV recovery experiments and Markov-operator diagnostics, we show that MaRK recovers coordinate-invariant temporal operators under matched assumptions and produces distinct, stable timestep-conditioned memory profiles. Empirically, the Chebyshev variant yields the strongest performance, achieving an average validation loss of 2.55, followed by the DCT (2.59) and Hypernet (3.77) geometries.

</details>


### [174] [Are We Really Benchmarking Forecasting Models? The Impact of Preprocessing on Time Series Performance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09096)
*Guilherme Afonso Galindo Padilha,Paulo Salgado Gomes de Mattos Neto,Rafael Menelau Oliveira e Cruz*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper reveals that preprocessing is critically overlooked in time series forecasting research. Current benchmarks use simple scaling instead of addressing nonstationarity (e.g., differencing), creating a structural bias that unfairly favors models with built-in data treatments. Through a comprehensive benchmark on 29,000 M4 time series evaluating 11 models across 16 preprocessing pipelines, the authors demonstrate that optimized preprocessing can improve forecasting performance by 27-87%, allowing simpler models to compete with complex state-of-the-art architectures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current forecasting benchmarks ignore preprocessing, using only simple scaling. This creates a structural bias favoring models with internalized preprocessing (like neural networks with built-in differencing) while obscuring the true potential of simpler architectures. The research aims to quantify this bias and demonstrate the importance of preprocessing optimization.

Method: The authors conducted a preprocessing-aware benchmark using: (1) 11 forecasting models (including both simple and complex architectures), (2) 16 reversible preprocessing pipelines (varying in scaling and differencing), (3) 29,000 M4 time series. They evaluated the effect of optimizing preprocessing per series on model performance.

Result: Preprocessing is a key driver of forecasting performance. Optimizing preprocessing per series yields gains of approximately 27% to 87% across all evaluated models. Models lacking internalized preprocessing experience the most substantial improvements. This allows simpler architectures to become highly competitive with complex, state-of-the-art models.

Conclusion: Preprocessing is a critical yet overlooked factor in forecasting research. Proper preprocessing optimization can significantly enhance model performance and reveal the true potential of simpler architectures. The benchmark provides a comprehensive metadataset to support future metalearning research on preprocessing selection.

Abstract: While established literature underscores the pivotal role of preprocessing in forecasting accuracy, this stage remains largely overlooked in current research. Modern benchmarks typically resort to simple scaling, failing to account for critical transformations required to address nonstationarity, such as differencing. This omission creates a significant structural preprocessing bias that favors models with built-in data treatments while obscuring the true potential of simpler architectures. We study this effect through a preprocessing-aware benchmark that evaluates 11 forecasting models across 16 reversible preprocessing pipelines on 29,000 M4 time series. Our results identify preprocessing as a key driver of forecasting performance. Optimizing preprocessing per series yields gains of approximately 27\% to 87\% across all evaluated models, with architectures lacking internalized preprocessing experiencing the most substantial improvements. This allows simpler architectures to become highly competitive with complex, state-of-the-art models in modern forecasting benchmarks. All resources and experimental results from this benchmark are stored in a comprehensive metadataset to support future metalearning tasks.

</details>


### [175] [Convex-Concave Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09108)
*Shripad V. Deshmukh,Yaswanth Chittepu,Dhawal Gupta,Philip Thomas,Scott Niekum*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper reveals hidden convex-concave structure in the policy learning problem by working in log-density-ratio coordinates, developing CCRL that recovers existing algorithms as special cases and enables a multi-step axis k for coupling consecutive decisions, with strong empirical performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Policy learning in reinforcement learning relies on maximizing expected return, which is notoriously non-convex. The field has largely avoided this by using convex surrogate approximations under trust-region constraints (NPG, TRPO, PPO, AWR). This paper aims to show that the problem is not actually structureless and to develop a more principled approach.

Method: The paper reformulates the policy learning problem in log-density-ratio coordinates y := log[π/π_n], transforming the exact per-iteration objective (computable via per-decision importance sampling/PDIS) into a DC-constrained DC program. This structure enables application of sequential convex programming (SCP), the standard solver for difference-of-convex problems, with convergence guarantees under mild conditions.

Result: Multi-step CCRL wins on diagnostic MDPs where credit must propagate across a horizon, with advantage growing with dependency length. It is competitive with tuned PPO on classic control tasks. On a realistic stochastic mid-horizon healthcare domain, CCRL converges markedly faster than tuned PPO to the same near-optimal survival, with an 11.3% higher area under the training curve.

Conclusion: The paper introduces CCRL (Convex-Concave RL), a novel policy learning method that leverages the DC (difference-of-convex) structure in log-density-ratio coordinates. This method recovers existing algorithms (CPI, NPG, TRPO, AWR) as special cases and provides a multi-step axis k for coupling consecutive decisions. Empirically, CCRL outperforms tuned PPO on diagnostic MDPs requiring credit propagation across horizons and achieves 11.3% higher area under the training curve in a healthcare domain while converging faster.

Abstract: Policy learning drives many of the most consequential and heavily-invested applications of reinforcement learning today. Yet the core optimization problem it rests on (maximizing expected return) is notoriously non-convex, even under a direct policy parameterization, and the field has largely responded by avoiding it: optimizing convex surrogate approximations of the return under trust-region constraints (NPG, TRPO, PPO, AWR). We show that this seemingly unstructured problem is not actually structureless. In log-density-ratio coordinates $y := \log[π/π_n]$, the exact per-iteration objective, computable via per-decision importance sampling (PDIS), is a difference-of-convex-constrained difference-of-convex (DC-constrained DC) program. This structure lets us move beyond surrogate approximations: it recovers CPI, NPG, TRPO, and AWR as special cases along interpretable axes, and it opens a multi-step axis $k$ that couples consecutive decisions. We solve the per-iteration program with sequential convex programming (SCP), the standard solver for difference-of-convex problems, and give convergence guarantees under mild conditions, bridging the difference-of-convex optimization and RL literatures. Empirically, multi-step Convex-Concave RL (CCRL) wins on diagnostic MDPs where credit must propagate across a horizon (its advantage growing with the dependency length), is competitive with a tuned PPO on classic control, and on a realistic, stochastic, mid-horizon healthcare domain converges markedly faster than tuned PPO to the same near-optimal survival, with an 11.3% higher area under the training curve.

</details>


### [176] [Breaking Adversarial Transferability in Fine-Tuned Speech Recognition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09109)
*Mojtaba Nafez,Aref Mousavi,Mohammad Ebrahim Mahdavi,Mobina Poulaei,Kiarash Kiani Feriz,Mohammad Hossein Rohban*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses a critical security vulnerability in fine-tuned ASR systems: adversarial perturbations crafted on public base models transfer to fine-tuned target models, degrading performance even when the attacker has limited (black-box) access. The authors propose TransferBreaker, a unified framework combining Base Adversarial Fine-Tuning, Latent Jacobian Regularization, and HybridGrad-AFT to suppress adversarial transfer. The framework was evaluated across three languages and four large ASR models, reducing adversarial Word Error Rate from 92.6% to 27.8%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Organizations often fine-tune publicly available pretrained ASR models and deploy them in black-box settings, assuming limited access provides protection against adversarial attacks. This paper challenges this assumption by demonstrating that adversarial perturbations from the base model transfer effectively to fine-tuned target models, posing significant concerns for safety-critical applications.

Method: The authors propose TransferBreaker, a unified fine-tuning framework with three components: (1) Base Adversarial Fine-Tuning (Base-AFT), which restricts adversarial training to base-effective perturbations; (2) Latent Jacobian Regularization, which enforces latent-space invariance by suppressing adversarially sensitive directions; and (3) HybridGrad-AFT, which improves robustness against adaptive attacks by interpolating transferable perturbations from base and target gradients. The approach is theoretically justified and evaluated across three languages and four large ASR models.

Result: TransferBreaker significantly reduces adversarial transferability. It reduces the adversarial Word Error Rate (WER) from 92.6% to 27.8%, demonstrating substantial robustness improvement against adversarial attacks on fine-tuned ASR models.

Conclusion: The assumption that limited (black-box) access provides protection for fine-tuned ASR models is fragile. TransferBreaker effectively suppresses adversarial transfer from base models to fine-tuned models, providing meaningful protection for safety-critical ASR deployments. The code is publicly available.

Abstract: Many organizations fine-tune publicly available pretrained Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) models and deploy them in black-box settings, assuming limited access provides protection. We show this assumption is fragile: adversarial perturbations crafted on the public base model transfer effectively to fine-tuned target models, severely degrading performance and posing concerns for safety-critical applications. We propose TransferBreaker, a unified fine-tuning framework that suppresses adversarial transfer by integrating Base Adversarial Fine-Tuning, which restricts adversarial training to base-effective perturbations; Latent Jacobian Regularization, which enforces latent-space invariance by suppressing adversarially sensitive directions; and HybridGrad-AFT, which improves robustness against adaptive attacks by interpolating transferable perturbations from base and target gradients. We theoretically justify all components and evaluate TransferBreaker across three languages and four large ASR models, reducing adversarial WER from 92.6 to 27.8. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/rohban-lab/TransferBreaker.

</details>


### [177] [The Deceptive Bandit Problem: Exploratory Coupling and the Fragility of Multi-Agent Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09120)
*Michael Tang,Mahmoud Abdelgalil,Jorge I. Poveda*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates security vulnerabilities in randomized exploration for bandit learning, multi-agent RL, and zeroth-order policy search. The authors show how an adversarial agent can exploit leaked signals correlated with a victim's exploration to steer learning dynamics toward a deceptive Nash equilibrium (DNE), while maintaining optimal convergence rates.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Randomized exploration is a foundational technique in bandit learning, multi-agent reinforcement learning, and zeroth-order optimization, yet the independence and privacy of exploration are typically assumed without rigorous security analysis. This work addresses this critical gap by demonstrating that exploration can be exploited by adversarial agents, with significant implications for security-sensitive applications.

Method: The authors analyze a deceiver-victim pair in the minimal two-player strongly monotone setting. The deceptive player exploits leaked signals merely correlated with the victim's exploration, coupling their exploratory actions with this information to inject an externality that shifts the steady state toward a Deceptive Nash Equilibrium (DNE).

Result: The deceptive bandit learning (DBL) dynamics converge to an arbitrarily small neighborhood of the DNE while retaining optimal convergence rates. Notably, these optimal rates are achieved while relaxing second-order smoothness conditions required in standard bandit optimization. The authors further characterize conditions under which deception strictly shifts the steady state and analyze its effect on the deceiver's cost.

Conclusion: This work establishes that exploration privacy is not merely a technical assumption but a critical security property. The introduced DNE framework provides a foundation for understanding and mitigating adversarial exploitation in multi-agent learning systems, with practical implications demonstrated through a resource-allocation game example.

Abstract: Randomized exploration is central to bandit learning, multi-agent reinforcement learning, and zeroth-order policy search, yet its independence and privacy are usually only treated as technical assumptions. We show that these properties are critical for security purposes and demonstrate how an adversarial agent can exploit privileged information on another agent's exploration. We analyze a deceiver-victim pair in the minimal two-player strongly monotone setting, where a deceptive player obtains leaked signals that are merely correlated with the victim's exploration. We show that, by coupling their own exploratory action with this information, the deceptive player injects an externality that steers the learning dynamics to a new steady state, called the deceptive Nash equilibrium (DNE). We prove that the deceptive bandit learning (DBL) dynamics converge to an arbitrarily small neighborhood of the DNE while retaining optimal convergence rates. Interestingly, our analysis attains these optimal rates while relaxing second-order smoothness conditions from standard bandit optimization literature. We characterize conditions under which deception strictly shifts the steady state and its effect on the deceiver's cost, illustrating the results in a resource-allocation game.

</details>


### [178] [Are Parameter-Efficient Fine-tuning Methods Really Different?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09122)
*Yikuan Li,Pinyan Lu,Fanghui Liu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper compares six parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods across language and diffusion models, examining their relationships to task performance, forgetting, and pretrained weight geometry. Key findings: LoRA-family methods approximately preserve pretrained geometry; restoring singular-value spectra largely preserves task performance; DoRA often outperforms LoRA in mean task scores; LoRA best limits forgetting; PiSSA incurs greater retention costs. Restoring dominant spectral components produces the largest reduction in general-text NLL or base-image drift.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to understand the methodological and functional differences among PEFT parameterizations, specifically whether spectral preservation (as in OFT) is necessary for adaptation and retention, and to evaluate geometric constraints through their functional consequences rather than preservation alone.

Method: The authors compare six PEFT methods (including LoRA-family, DoRA, PiSSA, and OFT) across language and diffusion models. They conduct intervention experiments to examine how parameterizations relate to task performance, forgetting, and changes in pretrained weight geometry. They also test whether restoring drifted singular-value spectra affects task performance.

Result: Key findings: (1) LoRA-family methods approximately preserve pretrained geometry; (2) Restoring drifted singular-value spectra largely preserves task performance, questioning the necessity of explicit geometric preservation; (3) LoRA most consistently limits forgetting at competitive performance; (4) DoRA achieves higher mean task scores than LoRA in most comparisons; (5) PiSSA often incurs greater retention costs; (6) Restoring dominant spectral components produces the largest mean reduction in general-text NLL or base-image drift.

Conclusion: The authors conclude that performance gains from different PEFT methods can be attributed to modifications in different groups of spectral components. They argue for evaluating geometric constraints through their functional consequences rather than preservation alone, and that spectral preservation itself may not be necessary for effective adaptation and retention.

Abstract: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) offers many parameterizations, yet their methodological and functional differences remain unclear. We compare six methods in language and diffusion models to examine how their parameterizations relate to task performance, forgetting, and changes in pretrained weight geometry. Motivated by the spectrum-preserving design of orthogonal fine-tuning (OFT), we first ask whether spectral preservation is itself important for adaptation and retention. We find that the selected LoRA-family methods also approximately preserve pretrained geometry, and that restoring their slightly drifted singular-value spectra largely preserves task performance, questioning the necessity of explicit geometric preservation. Beyond this, we observe that some methods exhibit distinct adaptation--retention trade-offs that vary across settings: LoRA most consistently limits forgetting at competitive performance, DoRA achieves higher mean task scores than LoRA in most comparisons, while PiSSA often incurs greater retention costs. Further intervention experiments suggest that while performance gains from different PEFT methods can be attributed to modifications in different groups of spectral components, we consistently find that restoring dominant rather than intermediate or trailing components produces the largest mean reduction in general-text NLL or base-image drift. Together, these results motivate evaluating geometric constraints through their functional consequences rather than preservation alone. Code is available at https://github.com/Kuaaannn/PEFT_methods.

</details>


### [179] [Spatial Induction Heads: In-Context Learning of Multidimensional Cellular Automata](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09124)
*Kimia Kazemian,Menghan Xu,John Thickstun,Sarah Dean*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces "spatial induction heads" to explain how transformers perform in-context learning on multidimensional data (like cellular automata) where serialization scatters spatial neighbors across distant token positions. The authors propose a two-layer gather-and-match circuit that reconstructs spatial neighborhoods and matches against prior occurrences, showing both theoretical guarantees and empirical validation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing induction head theory assumes context forms contiguous blocks, but in multidimensional data, serialization breaks this assumption by scattering spatial neighbors across distant positions. This work aims to understand how transformers overcome this "routing problem" in multidimensional cellular automata.

Method: Theoretical analysis using gather-and-match circuits: (1) Two explicit realizations of the gather operation where positional dimension depends only on local neighborhood and spatial dimension, not grid volume or trajectory horizon; (2) A matching layer implementing Bayesian counting; (3) Empirical validation with trained two-layer transformers on 1D and 2D stochastic and deterministic cellular automata, using attention pattern analysis and layerwise probes.

Result: Theoretically: positional dimension scales with neighborhood size and spatial dimension only; end-to-end circuit approximates Bayesian posterior arbitrarily closely for stochastic rules and predicts exactly for deterministic rules. Empirically: trained transformers generalize to unseen rules, achieving near-perfect deterministic rollouts and <0.005 nats KL divergence from Bayes-optimal predictor on stochastic rules. Attention patterns and probes align with predicted gather-and-match computation.

Conclusion: Spatial induction heads provide a mechanistic account of in-context learning in multidimensional settings. The gather-and-match circuit is a viable model for how transformers overcome the routing problem in serialized multidimensional data, with strong alignment between theoretical predictions and empirical observations in trained models.

Abstract: Induction heads provide a mechanistic account of in-context learning in sequential data, but existing theory largely assumes that the context relevant to a prediction forms a contiguous block. In multidimensional data, serialization breaks this assumption by scattering spatial neighbors across distant positions in the token sequence. We study how transformers overcome this routing problem in multidimensional stochastic and deterministic cellular automata, where each trajectory is generated by an unknown local rule and presented as a flattened sequence without an explicit coordinate-based spatial inductive bias. We introduce spatial induction heads, two-layer gather-and-match circuits in which the first layer reconstructs the relevant spatial neighborhood and the second matches the resulting configuration against earlier occurrences. We give two explicit realizations of the gather and show that the positional dimension required for spatial routing depends only on the local neighborhood and spatial dimension, not on grid volume or trajectory horizon. We further construct a matching layer which implements Bayesian counting. The end-to-end circuit can approximate the Bayesian posterior arbitrarily closely for stochastic rules and can predict exactly for deterministic rules. Empirically, trained two-layer transformers generalize to unseen rules in one and two dimensional settings, achieving near-perfect deterministic rollouts and less than 0.005 nats KL from the Bayes-optimal predictor on stochastic rules. Attention patterns and layerwise probes align with the predicted gather-and-match computation, providing mechanistic evidence for spatial induction in trained transformers.

</details>


### [180] [Domain-informed Adaptive Sampling for Generalizable PINNs in Metal Additive Manufacturing via Conditional Flow Matching](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09126)
*Hyeonsu Lee,Jihoon Jeong*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces the first adaptive sampling strategy for Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) in metal additive manufacturing thermal modeling. The method uses a two-stage framework combining a conditional Flow Matching model with mixed sampling to generate process condition-aware collocation points, achieving 62.1% reduction in relative L2 error compared to state-of-the-art baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior PINN works in metal AM rely on manual, static collocation sampling strategies that lack scalability across different process conditions and have poor generalization capability. There was a need for a principled, adaptive sampling approach that can capture process-dependent heat dissipation regions.

Method: The authors developed a two-stage framework: (1) A conditional Flow Matching model that learns approximate high-residual distributions across different process conditions, and (2) A mixed sampling strategy combining this distribution with a domain-informed base distribution to generate adaptive collocation points for refining the PINN predictor.

Result: The proposed method achieves an average 62.1% reduction in relative L2 error under identical collocation budget compared to state-of-the-art PINN baselines. It successfully captures process-dependent heat dissipation regions that were previously overlooked in literature.

Conclusion: This is the first adaptive sampling strategy for PINNs in metal AM, contributing to enhanced generalization and broader applicability. The theoretical analysis through empirical risk minimization demonstrates that process condition-aware adaptive sampling is strictly more favorable than conventional static sampling for generalization.

Abstract: Accurate thermal modeling is essential in metal additive manufacturing (AM) for understanding the process-structure-property chain. Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) offer effective surrogate thermal modeling by minimizing physics-based residual losses at collocation points. However, prior works typically rely on manually-crafted, static collocation sampling strategies, which are neither principled nor scalable across process conditions, hindering their generalization capability. In this work, we provide theoretical analysis through empirical risk minimization, showing that process condition-aware adaptive sampling is strictly more favorable than conventional static sampling for generalization. Building on this insight, we propose an adaptive sampling strategy within a two-stage framework: (1) a conditional Flow Matching model that learns approximate high-residual distributions across different process conditions, and (2) a mixed sampling strategy combining this distribution with a domain-informed base distribution to generate adaptive collocation points for refining the PINN predictor. Experiments on metal AM numerical benchmarks demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art PINN baselines, achieving an average 62.1\% reduction in relative $L_2$ error under an identical collocation budget, by capturing process-dependent heat dissipation regions often overlooked in the literature. To the authors' knowledge, this is the first adaptive sampling strategy for PINNs in metal AM, contributing to the enhanced generalization and broader applicability.

</details>


### [181] [Directional Evidence Guided Search-Space Reduction for Exact DAG Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09136)
*Upala Junaida Islam,Abdelmonem Elrefaey,Rong Pan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: DECO is a non-parametric hybrid framework for learning DAGs from observational data that uses dependency and directional evidence to construct admissible parent sets before exact optimization, reducing the search space exponentially while maintaining competitive structure recovery performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Learning DAGs from observational data is challenging due to exponential growth in candidate parent-set configurations. Existing exact score-based methods require computationally intensive combinatorial search, while constraint-based methods become unreliable or computationally demanding as graph size and conditioning-set complexity increase.

Method: DECO extracts dependency and directional evidence from observational data to construct admissible parent sets prior to exact optimization. It eliminates empirically unsupported parent configurations while preserving flexibility for all plausible edge orientations, reducing the optimization search space without requiring a fixed parametric structural model.

Result: Theoretical analysis establishes an exponential reduction in the admissible parent-set configuration space and quantifies how bounded edge-level omission affects the probability of retaining the true parent structure. Experiments on benchmark Bayesian networks and synthetic discrete/continuous DAGs demonstrate substantial search-space reduction with competitive structure-recovery performance and favorable structural Hamming distance across many settings.

Conclusion: Directional evidence can provide an effective preprocessing mechanism for reducing the computational burden of exact DAG learning without requiring a fixed parametric structural model.

Abstract: Learning a directed acyclic graph (DAG) from observational data is a challenging combinatorial problem due to the exponential growth in the number of candidate parent-set configurations. Existing exact score-based methods often require computationally intensive combinatorial search, whereas constraint-based methods can become unreliable or computationally demanding as graph size and conditioning-set complexity increase. We develop a non-parametric hybrid framework, referred to as DECO (Directional Evidence-guided Configuration Optimization), that extracts dependency and directional evidence from observation data to construct admissible parent sets prior to exact optimization. It reduces the optimization search space by eliminating empirically unsupported parent configurations while preserving flexibility for all plausible edge orientations. Theoretical analysis establishes an exponential reduction in the admissible parent-set configuration space and quantifies how bounded edge-level omission affects the probability of retaining the true parent structure. Experiments on benchmark Bayesian networks and synthetic discrete and continuous DAGs demonstrate substantial search-space reduction while achieving competitive structure-recovery performance, with favorable structural Hamming distance across many evaluated settings. These results show that directional evidence can provide an effective preprocessing mechanism for reducing the computational burden of exact DAG learning without requiring a fixed parametric structural~model.

</details>


### [182] [A Cognitive-Aware QML-CRL Framework for Detecting Affinity and Romance-Investment Fraud](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09141)
*Bibhas Adhikari,Ramya Srinivasan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A hybrid quantum-classical framework that detects affinity and romance-investment fraud by modeling cognitive biases in manipulative conversations using parameterized quantum circuits with dedicated qubits for cognitive biases, a frame qubit for temporal sensitivity, and a narrative qubit for co-occurrence aggregation, trained jointly with a reinforcement-learning agent modeled as an optimal stopping problem.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Detect affinity and romance-investment fraud by modeling the cognitive biases present in manipulative conversations, which are central to this fraud class.

Method: Hybrid quantum-classical framework using: (1) dedicated qubits in a structured parameterized quantum circuit to carry cognitive biases, (2) a frame qubit that makes encoding sensitive to temporal order of manipulative reframing, (3) a narrative qubit that aggregates co-occurrence through a trainable entanglement layer, trained jointly with a classical reinforcement-learning agent that decides turn-by-turn whether to flag conversations, modeled as an optimal stopping problem.

Result: Model performance evaluated on synthetic conversations including hard negatives, legitimate but urgent, and legitimate but pushy sales conversations.

Conclusion: The proposed framework demonstrates a novel approach to fraud detection by combining quantum computing elements (cognitive bias qubits, temporal frame qubit, narrative aggregation qubit) with classical reinforcement learning to model manipulative conversation patterns and temporal dynamics.

Abstract: We present a hybrid quantum-classical framework that detects affinity and romance-investment fraud by modelling the cognitive biases in a manipulative conversation.
