In our proposed framework, cognitive biases central to this fraud class are carried by dedicated qubits in a structured parameterized quantum circuit, together with a frame qubit makes the encoding sensitive to the temporal order of manipulative reframing, and a narrative qubit that aggregates co-occurrence through a trainable entanglement layer. The circuit parameters are trained jointly with a classical reinforcement-learning agent that decides, turn by turn, whether to flag the conversation, modeled as an optimal stopping problem. We evaluate the model's performance on synthetic conversations that include hard negatives, legitimate but urgent, and legitimate but pushy sales conversations.

</details>


### [183] [Noise Your Prompt: Noising Conditioning Tokens in Continuous Diffusion Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09145)
*Justin Jung*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes a simple modification to continuous diffusion language model training: noise the conditioning prompt tokens during training instead of keeping them clean. This single-line change improves generalization on combinatorial reasoning tasks (Sudoku, N-Queens) and natural language generation in modest data regimes, but gains don't transfer to all NLP tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The standard practice in continuous diffusion language model literature is to fix conditioning prompt tokens clean during training. The authors question this practice and propose modifying it to improve model generalization, particularly for combinatorial reasoning tasks and natural language generation.

Method: The method involves a simple modification: also noise the conditioning prompt tokens during training. This is a single-line change to the training objective that requires no additional inference costs by default and provides flexibility of classifier-free guidance inspired guided sampling.

Result: The method achieves significant improvements: Sudoku Hard solve rate improved from 3.73% to 24.65%; 10x10 N-Queens coverage increased from 50.60% to 73.79%; modest improvements in Gigaword summarization; but gains do not transfer to all natural language tasks (e.g., open-ended dialogue generation).

Conclusion: Noising conditioning prompt tokens during training is a simple yet effective modification that improves generalization in combinatorial reasoning tasks and some NLP tasks. However, the benefits are task-dependent and don't generalize to all natural language generation scenarios.

Abstract: We revisit a standard accepted practice in the continuous diffusion language model
  literature of fixing conditioning prompt tokens clean during training.
  We make a very simple modification: also noise the conditioning prompt tokens during training.
  We demonstrate that under this modified training objective, we achieve better generalization
  in combinatorial reasoning tasks such as Sudoku and N-Queens, with the largest gains on harder variants
  ($3.73\% \to 24.65\%$ solve rate on Sudoku Hard), and increased diversity of generated solutions ($50.60\% \to 73.79\%$ coverage on
  10x10 N-Queens). We also show measurable improvements to natural language generation quality
  in modest dataset regimes with Gigaword summarization, but notably demonstrate that gains do not
  transfer to all natural language tasks (e.g open ended dialogue generation).
  Our method is a single line change to the training objective, requires no additional inference costs by default,
  and provides the flexibility of classifier-free guidance inspired guided sampling. Our
  \href{https://github.com/LateralIntelligence/noise-your-prompt} {code} is publicly available.

</details>


### [184] [Context-aware Attention-based Gaussian Mixture Models for Vehicular Trajectory Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09174)
*Arash Raftari,Babak Ebrahimi Soorchaei,Yaser P. Fallah*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CAA-GMM is a Context-Aware Attention-based Gaussian Mixture Model for multimodal, uncertainty-aware motion forecasting in autonomous driving. It uses Gaussian components to model diverse behavioral modes, with a lightweight attention mechanism encoding inter-agent interactions and contextual salience. The method achieves competitive/superior accuracy on nuScenes and Argoverse 2 datasets while maintaining low computational complexity and resilience to uncertainty.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reliable and interpretable trajectory prediction is critical for cooperative and autonomous driving in complex and uncertain environments. The need is to capture diverse behavioral modes while maintaining interpretability and computational efficiency.

Method: 1) Models future motion as a probabilistic mixture conditioned on scene context and agent dynamics
2) Uses interpretable Gaussian components to capture diverse behavioral modes
3) Lightweight attention mechanism adaptively encodes inter-agent interactions and contextual salience
4) Efficient fusion of rasterized environment cues and motion history in dense traffic scenes

Result: 1) Achieves competitive or superior accuracy compared with state-of-the-art raster-based baselines on nuScenes and Argoverse 2 datasets
2) Maintains low computational complexity
3) Ablation analyses confirm importance of attention module for robust contextual reasoning and predictive precision
4) Shows resilience to uncertainty under imperfect communication and perception conditions

Conclusion: CAA-GMM is an efficient and scalable solution for cooperative trajectory prediction in intelligent transportation systems, offering a good balance between accuracy, interpretability, and computational efficiency.

Abstract: Reliable and interpretable trajectory prediction is critical for cooperative and autonomous driving in complex and uncertain environments. This paper introduces a Context-Aware Attention-based Gaussian Mixture Model (CAA-GMM) for multimodal, uncertainty-aware motion forecasting. The proposed approach models future motion as a probabilistic mixture conditioned on both scene context and agent dynamics, capturing diverse behavioral modes with interpretable Gaussian components. A lightweight attention mechanism adaptively encodes inter-agent interactions and contextual salience, enabling efficient fusion of rasterized environment cues and motion history in dense traffic scenes. Comprehensive evaluations on the nuScenes and Argoverse 2 datasets demonstrate that CAA-GMM achieves competitive or superior accuracy compared with state-of-the-art raster-based baselines, while maintaining low computational complexity. Ablation analyses confirm the importance of the attention module for robust contextual reasoning and predictive precision. Furthermore, evaluations under imperfect communication and perception conditions highlight the framework's resilience to uncertainty, establishing CAA-GMM as an efficient and scalable solution for cooperative trajectory prediction in intelligent transportation systems.

</details>


### [185] [LayerRoPE: Dynamic Depth-wise Magnitude & Angular Superposition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09179)
*Shikhar Srivastava,Christopher Kanan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper challenges the conventional view that the growth of hidden state norms with depth in Transformers is a pathology. Instead, the authors propose that this growth encodes layer position information through the normalization weight γ, and leverage this insight to create LayerRoPE, which improves depth scaling, reduces compute requirements, and enhances training stability across various model architectures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The "curse of depth" - where hidden state norms grow exponentially with transformer depth - has been universally treated as a pathology to suppress. This paper takes the opposite view, questioning whether this growth might actually carry useful information rather than being merely detrimental.

Method: The authors analyzed 16 pre-trained LLMs across 9 families (dense, MoE, hybrid architectures; Pre-, Peri-, Post-Norm designs). They discovered that layer normalization weights γ encode depth position information. Based on this, they proposed LayerRoPE - an implicit positional encoding along the depth axis that replaces per-layer γ vectors with a single shared vector and depth-conditioned scalars.

Result: LayerRoPE achieves Pre-Norm's 1.3B loss with 3.4× less compute. It is the only approach showing strong convergence at 512 layers. It improves learning-rate sensitivity by 3-10× and transfers to looped latent models and Vision Transformers. Notably, it widens the residual stream rather than shrinking it.

Conclusion: Depth stability in Transformers requires depth-conditioned regulation of computational blocks, not suppression of the residual stream. The "curse of depth" is actually an emergent depth positional encoding that can be harnessed rather than eliminated.

Abstract: As data propagates through a Transformer, the norm of its hidden states grows by orders of magnitude with depth, a phenomenon framed as 'curse of depth' and nearly universally treated as a pathology to be suppressed. We take the opposite view. Across 16 pre-trained LLMs from 9 families, spanning dense, mixture-of-experts and hybrid architectures and Pre-, Peri- and Post-Norm designs, we find that this growth reflects an emergent depth-positional encoding, carried by the only learned per-layer gain on the residual stream, the normalization weight $γ$: with depth, $γ$ grows in magnitude and rotates in direction, jointly encoding the layer index. We make this depth-conditioned encoding explicit with LayerRoPE, an implicit analog of RoPE along the depth axis, which replaces all layerwise $γ$ vectors with a single shared vector and depth-conditioned scalars, at a net reduction in parameters and $<0.02\%$ change in FLOPs. Across a model ladder scaled up to $100$B+ tokens, LayerRoPE consistently outperforms Pre-, Post- and Peri-Norm and Layer-Norm Scaling, reaching Pre-Norm's 1.3B loss with $3.4\times$ less compute; LayerRoPE is the only approach that shows strong convergence and improves near monotonically as depth scales to 512 layers. It improves learning-rate sensitivity by $3$-$10\times$, and transfers naively to and consistently improves looped latent models and Vision Transformers. Inspecting its learned schedule inverts the prevailing premise: LayerRoPE does not shrink the residual stream but widens it, damping what each block reads while amplifying what it writes. Depth stability, our results suggest, calls not for suppressing the residual stream, but for depth-conditioned regulation of the computational blocks it feeds.

</details>


### [186] [Q-PACE: Dynamic Precision Allocation for Quantization-Aware Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09183)
*Alexandra Volkova,Matin Ansaripour,Erik Schultheis,Christoph H. Lampert,Dan Alistarh*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Q-PACE is a new approach for mixed-precision quantization-aware training of LLMs that uses a second-order sensitivity model to predict loss increase and dynamically reassign precision to layers during training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Aggressive quantization in quantization-aware training (QAT) degrades LLM performance, while mixed-precision training requires determining precision assignments for each layer. Existing methods lack efficient ways to determine optimal precision allocation.

Method: Q-PACE uses a second-order sensitivity model that predicts loss increase as a sum of quantization noise MSE weighted by per-layer curvature coefficients. These coefficients are periodically recomputed using perturbations across layers, enabling precision re-assignment during training. Experiments were conducted on LLMs up to 4B parameters with pretraining and supervised fine-tuning.

Result: Q-PACE consistently improves over existing mixed-precision training recipes and achieves comparable loss at substantially lower total memory budgets. Quantization sensitivity is highly predictable by depth and layer type and remains stable during training, allowing for infrequent and cheap recalibration.

Conclusion: Q-PACE provides an effective solution for mixed-precision quantization-aware training, enabling efficient LLM deployment with reduced memory costs while maintaining performance. The stability and predictability of quantization sensitivity across depth and layer type enables infrequent recalibration, making the approach practical for real-world deployment.

Abstract: Quantization-aware training (QAT) leverages lower-precision arithmetic to reduce the cost of LLM deployment, but aggressive quantization degrades final model performance. A common remedy is mixed-precision training, in which high precision is assigned to some of the layers to maintain performance while keeping the cost constrained. This approach then requires precision assignments for model layers during training. We provide a new approach, called Q-PACE, consisting of a second-order sensitivity model that predicts the loss increase as a sum of quantization noise MSE weighted by per-layer curvature coefficients. During training, we periodically re-compute these coefficients using perturbations across layers, and re-assign precision. Pretraining and supervised fine-tuning experiments on LLMs of up to 4B parameters show that Q-PACE consistently improves over existing mixed-precision training recipes, and achieves comparable loss at substantially lower total memory budgets. We further find that quantization sensitivity is highly predictable by depth and layer type, and its stability during training allows for infrequent, cheap recalibration.

</details>


### [187] [The Dichotomy Between Pattern Recognition and Step-by-Step Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09186)
*Amrut Nadgir,Pratik Chaudhari,Vijay Balasubramanian*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes that pattern recognition and step-by-step reasoning exist on a spectrum, where reasoning corresponds to next-token predictions depending on a small context (c tokens), while pattern recognition depends on a large context. The authors model reasoning traces as paths on a De Bruijn graph and show that the number of edges needed to learn is much smaller than the number of reasoning traces, enabling sample-efficient learning. They demonstrate that the frequency of "states" in reasoning traces determines c, and that moderate state density balances accuracy and robustness.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors aim to understand the relationship between pattern recognition and step-by-step reasoning in large language models (LLMs). They investigate why some LLMs can perform complex reasoning tasks step-by-step while others rely on pattern recognition, and what determines the sample efficiency of learning to reason.

Method: The authors use a theoretical framework based on De Bruijn graphs, where nodes represent c-length contexts and edges represent next-token transitions. They prove that the number of edges is vanishingly small compared to reasoning traces. They also conduct experiments fine-tuning Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct on equation solving and story question answering, and test Qwen3-14B and Qwen3-32B with restricted attention windows on GSM8K, MATH-500, and GPQA-Diamond.

Result: The number of training samples needed follows a power law in the number of edges, indicating sample-efficient learning. Frequent states (small c) lead to higher accuracy but greater fragility to perturbations. Large c models perform similarly to pattern recognition models. Moderate state density balances accuracy and robustness. Real-world data has De Bruijn structure: Qwen3 models retain over 75% accuracy with attention restricted to less than 15% of the full reasoning trace length.

Conclusion: Pattern recognition and step-by-step reasoning exist on a spectrum determined by context dependency (c). Learning to reason is sample-efficient because only edges in the De Bruijn graph need to be learned. The density of states in reasoning traces is crucial—moderate density balances accuracy and robustness. Real-world reasoning tasks have De Bruijn structure, enabling efficient reasoning with limited attention windows.

Abstract: We argue that pattern recognition and step-by-step reasoning are two ends of a spectrum. A large language model (LLM) learns to reason step-by-step when data is structured such that the next token depends on a small amount of preceding context. Inference in LLMs resembles pattern recognition when the next token depends on a large amount of preceding context. If the next token depends on only the $c$ most recent tokens, reasoning traces are paths on a De Bruijn graph whose nodes are $c$-length contexts and edges are next-token transitions between contexts. The set of reasoning traces of a task forms a directed acyclic subgraph of the De Bruijn graph. An LLM that has learned all edges of this subgraph can compose them to solve longer, unseen tasks, i.e., it reasons step-by-step. We prove that the number of edges is vanishingly small compared to the number of reasoning traces. Empirically, the number of training samples a transformer needs is a power law in the number of edges, so learning to reason step-by-step is sample efficient. We can induce De Bruijn structure in any task by maintaining a ``state'' that makes future reasoning independent of the past. The frequency of states in the reasoning trace determines $c$. We show, by fine-tuning Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct to solve equations and answer questions about stories, that frequent states (small $c$) result in higher accuracy but greater fragility to perturbations at test time. LLMs trained with a large $c$ are only as good as models that perform pattern recognition without reasoning. A moderate density of states balances accuracy and robustness. We show that real-world data has De Bruijn structure: Qwen3-14B and Qwen3-32B retain over 75% of their accuracy on GSM8K, MATH-500 and GPQA-Diamond when attention is restricted to a sliding window less than 15% as long as the full reasoning trace.

</details>


### [188] [Patient, Place, Prior (P$^3$): What Counts as Personalization in Medical World Models?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09194)
*Xingrui Gu,Hanxue Gu,Yuxiang Zhang,Yang Yang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces P³ (Patient, Place, Prior), an audit framework to evaluate whether longitudinal imaging forecasts truly benefit from patient-specific data versus population-level patterns. Additionally, Cancer JEPA is proposed - a one-step model forecasting breast MRI exams during neoadjuvant therapy using patient-conditioned reduced-rank regression with a lesion-constrained neural correction. The framework separates input use from actual patient-specific predictive value.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Longitudinal models can accurately forecast patient imaging states, but accuracy alone doesn't demonstrate that the patient's own trajectory drives predictions. A population-average forecast might work well but cannot establish a patient-specific world-model. The authors seek to audit whether forecasts genuinely benefit from patient-specific information beyond population-level patterns.

Method: The authors propose two innovations: (1) P³ audit framework with three questions - whether forecast benefits from patient's longitudinal history (Patient), patient-matched spatial support (Place), and gains value beyond population-average prediction under matched support (Prior); (2) Cancer JEPA model using frozen representations of future breast DCE-MRI exams during neoadjuvant therapy, combining patient-conditioned reduced-rank regression baseline with lesion-constrained neural correction trained via occlusion-based latent objective, enabling post-hoc P³ audit.

Result: In validation cohort, forecast error decreased when neural correction received patient's own history versus another patient's history, and when using patient-matched lesion occupancy maps versus substituted maps. However, the 95% confidence interval comparing patient history-derived correction to population-average neural correction includes zero, indicating no statistically significant patient-specific predictive value beyond population-level patterns.

Conclusion: The P³ framework successfully separates input use from evidence of patient-specific predictive value. While Cancer JEPA shows that patient history and lesion maps can reduce forecast error descriptively, the confidence interval including zero suggests the neural correction may not provide statistically significant patient-specific value beyond population-level patterns. The framework demonstrates the importance of auditing whether model components genuinely leverage patient-specific information.

Abstract: Longitudinal models forecast how a patient's imaging state evolves, but accuracy does not show whether the patient's observed trajectory drives the prediction. A population-average forecast may be useful but cannot establish a patient-specific world-model claim. We introduce Patient, Place, Prior (P$^3$), an audit asking whether a forecast benefits from the patient's longitudinal imaging history (Patient), benefits from patient-matched externally supplied spatial support (Place), and gains predictive value beyond a population-average prediction under matched support and context (Prior). We also propose Cancer JEPA, a one-step model that forecasts frozen representations of future breast dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI examinations during neoadjuvant therapy. It adds a lesion-constrained neural correction, trained with an occlusion-based latent objective, to a patient-conditioned low-complexity reduced-rank regression baseline. This factorization permits a post-hoc P$^3$ audit of the frozen model. In a validation cohort previously used in development, forecast error is lower when the neural correction receives the patient's history rather than another patient's and patient-matched lesion occupancy maps rather than substituted maps. However, the descriptive 95% interval comparing the correction computed from patient history with the population-average neural correction includes zero. P$^3$ thus separates input use from evidence of patient-specific predictive value beyond a population-level pattern.

</details>


### [189] [Exact Dynamics and Finite-Sample Trajectory Recovery of Linear Recursive Feature Machines](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09196)
*Andrew Cheng,Bobak T. Kiani,Yue M. Lu,Adityanarayanan Radhakrishnan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper studies linear Recursive Feature Machines (RFMs) for noisy multi-output regression. RFMs learn data representations by alternating between predictor fitting and feature updates using Average Gradient Outer Products (AGOP). The study extends the connection between linear RFM and iteratively reweighted least squares to ridge-regularized settings with noise. Key result: the learned feature matrix stays close to its infinite-data ideal with error decaying as O(√(d/n)) with high probability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The connection between AGOPs and feature learning in neural networks motivates studying linear RFMs as a simple setting to analyze how representations evolve during training. The goal is to understand the dynamics and statistics of linear RFM in a well-defined noisy regression setting.

Method: The authors analyze linear RFM in noisy multi-output regression with isotropic sub-Gaussian input data and low-rank teacher targets (dimension d). They extend the known RFM-IRLS connection from interpolating to ridge-regularized multi-output regression with noise.

Result: The learned feature matrix remains close to its infinite-data ideal counterpart at every iteration. For n samples, the error in the feature matrix decays as O(√(d/n)) with high probability.

Conclusion: The simple linear RFM model can effectively learn meaningful features, as demonstrated by experiments on real-world text and single-cell gene-expression data. The theoretical analysis provides convergence guarantees showing feature learning error scales with √(d/n).

Abstract: Recursive feature machines (RFMs) learn representations of data by alternating between fitting a predictor to a dataset and updating features of that predictor using the average gradient outer product (AGOP). Connections between AGOPs and feature learning in neural networks motivate linear RFMs as a simple setting for analyzing how representations evolve during training. Here, we study the dynamics and statistics of linear RFM in noisy multi-output regression with isotropic sub-Gaussian input data and targets generated by a low-rank teacher matrix of dimension $d$. We extend the known connection between linear RFM and iteratively reweighted least squares from the interpolating setting to ridge-regularized multi-output regression with noise. We show that the learned feature matrix remains close to its infinite-data ideal counterpart at every iteration. Namely, for $n$ samples, we show the error in the feature matrix decays as $O(\sqrt{d/n})$ with high probability. Experiments on real-world text and single-cell gene-expression data illustrate the features learned by this simple linear model.

</details>


### [190] [An Accuracy--Information Tradeoff for Loss-Difference Conditional Mutual Information](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09206)
*Hazar Yueksel*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper establishes that accuracy forces loss-difference conditional mutual information (ld-CMI) in addition to model-level information. For linear predictors with smooth convex losses (e.g., logistic loss) on product distributions, proper learners with small excess risk necessarily have ld-CMI of order n bits, even when generalization gaps are O(n^{-1/2}). This shows range-scaled ld-CMI bounds cannot vanish on these distributions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The research addresses a gap in understanding: while accuracy is known to force information into models, it was previously unknown whether accuracy also forces information into loss differences. The goal is to determine whether ld-CMI (which measures what loss differences reveal about training data) exhibits similar information bounds to standard CMI measures.

Method: The authors bound three moments of loss differences for linear predictors with smooth convex losses (nonzero slope at zero) and regularizers with power r ≥ 2 curvature/growth, on product distributions over scaled sign cubes. They analyze the worst-case ld-CMI for proper learners with bounded expected excess risk, considering both standard and noisy (Gaussian noise with std τ) settings.

Result: Key findings: (1) Every proper learner with expected excess risk ≤ ε at optimal sample size n ≍ ε^{-2+2/r} has worst-case ld-CMI of order n bits; (2) Under Gaussian noise, ld-CMI is Θ(n/(1+(τ/ε)^2)) bits; (3) Without regularizer, same result at n ≍ ε^{-2}; (4) Range-scaled ld-CMI bounds cannot vanish despite O(n^{-1/2}) generalization gaps; (5) Model-level information does not determine noisy loss-difference information; (6) Growth, slope, and dimension conditions (up to log) are necessary.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that accuracy forces ld-CMI just as it forces model-level information. The bounds are tight and necessary—the growth, slope, and dimension conditions (the last up to a logarithm) are all required. This establishes that information-theoretic generalization bounds using ld-CMI cannot be vanishingly small for these common learning setups, even when generalization error is small.

Abstract: Loss-difference conditional mutual information (ld-CMI) uses the smallest of the standard observations in the supersample hierarchy of generalization bounds: it measures what a learner's loss differences reveal about which candidate of each pair it was trained on. Accuracy is known to force information into the model; data processing does not carry such lower bounds to losses. We show, by bounding three moments of the loss differences, that accuracy also forces ld-CMI. For linear predictors with a smooth convex loss of nonzero slope at zero, such as the logistic loss, plus a regularizer whose curvature and growth are both of power $r\ge2$, on product distributions over a scaled sign cube in dimension at least linear in $n$, every proper learner with expected excess risk at most $\varepsilon$ on these distributions at the optimal sample size $n\asymp\varepsilon^{-2+2/r}$ has worst-case ld-CMI of order $n$ bits, and $Θ(n/(1+(τ/\varepsilon)^2))$ bits under Gaussian noise of standard deviation $τ$ on the loss differences. The same holds without a regularizer, at $n\asymp\varepsilon^{-2}$. Consequently, range-scaled ld-CMI bounds cannot vanish on these distributions, although every proper learner's generalization gap is $O(n^{-1/2})$. We also show that model-level information does not determine noisy loss-difference information, and that the growth, slope and dimension conditions are needed, the last up to a logarithm.

</details>


### [191] [CurveTQ: Rotation-Free Trellis Quantization of LLM Weights via Curvature-Weighted Search](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09212)
*Guanhua Ding,Zi Wang,Ruichao Li,Jack Liu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CurveTQ is a novel 2-bit weight quantizer for large language models that incorporates Hessian diagonal weights into the Viterbi search within coding blocks, eliminating the need for random orthogonal transforms. It achieves 1-3 points higher downstream accuracy than prior methods (QTIP and Proteus) while being faster due to no rotation needing to be undone.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing quantizers like QTIP and Proteus rotate weight matrices by random orthogonal transforms and use error feedback, but they only use the Hessian information between coding blocks, leaving within-block curvature information unused. Additionally, rotation and curvature-weighted native search are substitutes, so rotation can be eliminated.

Method: 1) Use diagonal of Hessian's LDL factorization as weights in Viterbi branch metric for curvature-aware search within each coding block; 2) Build CurveTQ trellis codec without rotation, using factored scale field for amplitude and closed-form quantile table for marginal shape; 3) Store start state per coding block to adapt to residuals from error feedback.

Result: CurveTQ achieves 1-3 points higher mean downstream accuracy than QTIP and Proteus on three 4-8B Instruct models, even after both baselines receive the start state optimization (which alone improves them by 1-3 points). It also performs well on a 35B mixture of experts model. Without rotation, CurveTQ is the fastest decoder at all tested batch sizes and bit widths.

Conclusion: Incorporating Hessian diagonal weights into the Viterbi search within coding blocks eliminates the need for random orthogonal transforms, achieving superior accuracy and speed compared to prior 2-bit quantizers. The start state per block is a simple but effective optimization that benefits all methods.

Abstract: The best two-bit weight quantizers for large language models, such as QTIP and Proteus, rotate each weight matrix by a random orthogonal transform, which must be undone at every decoding step, then encode it with a trellis or lattice code under a Euclidean search; the layer Hessian enters only through error feedback between coding blocks. We show that this leaves part of the Hessian unused. Error feedback turns the loss into a weighted sum of per-coordinate rounding errors whose weights, the diagonal of the Hessian's LDL factorization, existing quantizers compute but never read. We put these weights into the Viterbi branch metric, so the search follows the curvature within each coding block. This also explains the rotation: it removes this within-block variation, so weighting in the native basis and rotating are substitutes. On three models the weighted native search matches a full-dimension randomized Hadamard to within about one point of downstream accuracy, and weighting after the rotation gains little. Around this search we build CurveTQ, a trellis codec with no rotation, which handles the weights' amplitude and marginal shape with a factored scale field and a closed-form quantile table, and stores a start state per coding block so the trellis can adapt to the residual that error feedback carries into it. At two bits CurveTQ is 1-3 points higher in mean downstream accuracy than QTIP and Proteus on three 4-8B Instruct models, even after both are given our start state, which alone lifts either baseline by 1-3 points. It also leads on a 35B mixture of experts, to our knowledge the first trellis-coded result on such a model. With no rotation to undo, our decoder is the fastest of the three at all tested batch sizes and bit widths.

</details>


### [192] [Consistent Distribution Matching for Data-Free Diffusion Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09221)
*Yuxiang Fu,Qi Yan,Zike Wu,Yongxing Zhang,Purang Abolmaesumi,Lele Wang,Renjie Liao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Consistent Distribution Matching (CDM) is a simulation-free and data-free distillation method that accelerates diffusion and flow models by training a student network to learn from a frozen teacher, using only two models and optimizing one objective. It achieves FID of 2.04 at 1-NFE and 1.37 at 4-NFE on ImageNet 256×256 within 40 epochs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Flow and diffusion models suffer from slow inference due to computationally expensive numerical integration. Existing distillation methods require curated datasets, costly teacher rollouts, or auxiliary proxy networks, complicating training and scaling. The authors seek a simpler, more efficient distillation approach.

Method: The key insight is unifying sample generation and score estimation with one student network. The framework uses only a frozen teacher and a trainable student, optimizing one objective. The method is proven to indicate Wasserstein convergence of student flow-map pushforwards to teacher marginals.

Result: On ImageNet 256×256, CDM achieves FID of 2.04 with a single function evaluation (1-NFE) and 4-NFE FID of 1.37 within 40 epochs of training, surpassing state-of-the-art distillation baselines without data.

Conclusion: Consistent Distribution Matching provides an effective simulation-free and data-free distillation approach for accelerating diffusion and flow models, achieving superior performance with minimal computational overhead and simple training setup.

Abstract: Flow and diffusion models suffer from slow inference due to computationally expensive numerical integration. Distillation provides a promising way for a student model to learn from a teacher's dynamics, enabling one-step or few-step generation. However, existing methods often depend on curated distillation datasets, costly teacher rollouts, or auxiliary proxy networks, which complicate model training and scaling. In this work, we propose Consistent Distribution Matching, a simulation-free and data-free distillation method for accelerating diffusion and flow models while preserving strong generative capacity. Our key insight is to unify sample generation and score estimation with one student network. Thus, our framework uses only two models, a frozen teacher and a trainable student, and optimizes one objective. We prove that minimizing our objective indicates Wasserstein convergence of the student flow-map pushforwards to the teacher marginals. On ImageNet 256$\times$256, our method attains an FID of 2.04 with a single function evaluation (1-NFE) and a 4-NFE FID of 1.37 within 40 epochs of training, surpassing the state-of-the-art distillation baselines without data. Our code code and model are available at https://consistentdmd.github.io/.

</details>


### [193] [Conditional Accuracy Profiles: Diagnosing LLM Judges across Deployment Conditions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09229)
*Wenqi Li,Bin Liu,Mindi Ruan,Chuanbo Hu,Minglei Yin,Xin Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces Conditional Accuracy Profiling (CAP), a diagnostic framework that decomposes LLM-judge accuracy into eight conditions across content sensitivity, robustness, and rationale quality categories, revealing that aggregate accuracy hides critical profile differences that affect judge selection in deployment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM-judge evaluation relies solely on aggregate accuracy, which obscures the specific conditions under which judges succeed or fail. This prevents practitioners from selecting judges suited to their deployment context, as important failure modes (like sensitivity to omitted qualifications or position bias) remain hidden in overall accuracy numbers.

Method: CAP is a benchmark-agnostic framework that can be applied: (1) directly when benchmarks provide required annotations, (2) approximately through task-subset proxies, or (3) through controlled augmentation when perturbation pairs can be generated. The authors instantiated CAP on seven LLM judges across six pairwise judging benchmarks, including creating judgerEva-Standard, a controlled testbed supporting all eight conditions.

Result: Key findings: (1) On judgerEva's Hard-Constructed subset, judges most sensitive to omitted qualifications rank bottom three of seven by overall accuracy, showing omission sensitivity is not predicted by aggregate accuracy; (2) Position Robustness shows highest rank stability (mean Spearman ρ̄=0.87) but is most fragile under adversarial stress, showing largest mean accuracy drop; (3) The dominant degradation channel varies by judge, indicating different failure mechanisms.

Conclusion: Condition-level profiles provide a more actionable basis than aggregate accuracy for selecting LLM judges, as they reveal deployment-specific strengths and weaknesses that aggregate metrics obscure. This enables practitioners to choose judges aligned with their specific use cases rather than relying on single accuracy numbers.

Abstract: LLM-as-judge is now a standard tool for scalable evaluation, but judge performance is still often summarized by a single accuracy number. This aggregate view hides the deployment conditions under which a judge succeeds or fails. We introduce \textbf{Conditional Accuracy Profiling} (CAP), a post-hoc diagnostic framework that decomposes pairwise LLM-judge accuracy into eight conditions organized into content sensitivity, robustness, and rationale quality. CAP is benchmark-agnostic: it can be applied directly when a benchmark provides the required annotations, approximately through task-subset proxies, or through controlled augmentation when perturbation pairs can be generated. We instantiate CAP on seven LLM judges across six pairwise judging benchmarks, including \textsc{judgerEva-Standard}, a controlled testbed we created to support all eight conditions. CAP exposes profile differences hidden by aggregate accuracy: on \textsc{judgerEva}'s judge-independent Hard-Constructed subset, the two judges most sensitive to omitted qualifications rank in the bottom three of seven by overall accuracy, so omission sensitivity is not predicted by aggregate accuracy. Across benchmarks, Position Robustness shows the strongest rank stability (mean Spearman $\barρ{=}0.87$) but is itself fragile under JudgeBench-Pro adversarial stress, showing the largest mean accuracy drop among the shared conditions, though the dominant degradation channel varies by judge. Condition-level profiles provide a more actionable basis than aggregate accuracy for selecting LLM judges.

</details>


### [194] [Symmetry-Informed Causal Partial Identification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09230)
*Uzair Akbar,Zulfiqar Zaidi,Niki Kilbertus,Krikamol Muandet,Bo Dai*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces data symmetries (invariance under data transformations) as a new source of constraints to sharpen partial identification (PI) bounds in causal inference. Two approaches are proposed: a shape constraint on the causal function and a change of measure via data pre-processing. Both methods are shown theoretically and experimentally to produce tighter bounds.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Partial identification (PI) bounds are often too wide or vacuous in practice. While practitioners can encode domain knowledge as additional constraints, this approach is underutilized. The paper aims to exploit known data symmetries - invariance properties of causal effects under certain transformations - as a natural and previously underexplored source of constraints to make PI bounds more informative.

Method: The authors propose two approaches to operationalize data symmetries as constraints: (1) encoding symmetries as shape constraints on the causal function, and (2) using a change of measure against which PI is posed via simple data pre-processing. Both approaches are applied to two canonical PI models.

Result: Both proposed approaches are shown to sharpen PI bounds under two canonical PI models. The results are demonstrated both theoretically (for the population case) and experimentally (in finite-sample scenarios).

Conclusion: The framework establishes data symmetries as a natural, underutilized source of background knowledge for robust causal inference. This work provides a principled way to incorporate symmetry-based domain knowledge into partial identification analysis, making bounds more informative for policy decisions even when the causal effect is not fully identifiable.

Abstract: Partial identification (PI) entails estimating bounds on causal effects by encoding different assumptions on data generation as a constrained optimization problem. Such bounds can suffice to inform policy decisions even if the causal effect itself is not identifiable. Often vacuous in practice, practitioners seek to exhaustively encode domain knowledge as additional constraints to make the PI bounds more informative. We introduce known data symmetries -- invariance of the causal effect under certain data transformations -- as a new source of constraints to inform PI. We operationalize this as a shape constraint on the causal function, and via a change of measure against which PI is posed using simple data pre-processing. Both approaches are shown to sharpen bounds under two canonical PI models. This is shown both theoretically for the population case, and via experiments in the finite-sample case. More broadly, our framework establishes data symmetries as a natural, underutilized source of background knowledge for robust causal inference.

</details>


### [195] [An Informational Curse of Horizon in Goal-Conditioned Policy Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09247)
*John L. Zhou,Yuxuan Dong,Jonathan C. Kao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper identifies an "informational curse of horizon" in goal-conditioned policy learning, where longer goal relabeling horizons during training degrade policy generalization. The authors show that behavioral cloning (BC) policies suffer from severe horizon-dependent performance degradation even for nearby subgoals, while RL objectives are more robust. This is explained by decreased conditional mutual information between actions and hindsight-relabeled goals, and both BC and RL policies show shift in sensitivity from goal to state information. The authors propose distilling input Jacobians from short-horizon policies into long-horizon policies to improve performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The difficulty of learning goal-reaching policies is often attributed to a "curse of horizon" from bias accumulation in temporal-difference backups and noisy advantage estimates. This work identifies an additional "informational curse of horizon" where increasing the goal relabeling horizon can significantly reduce policy generalization and performance, even when evaluating on nearby subgoals.

Method: The authors conduct controlled experiments with oracle planners, decoupling goal horizons sampled during training from test-time horizons. They analyze the conditional mutual information between actions and hindsight-relabeled goals, measure input Jacobians to assess sensitivity to goal vs state information, and propose Jacobian distillation from short-horizon policies into long-horizon policies.

Result: Goal-conditioned BC policies suffer severe, training horizon-dependent performance degradation even when evaluated only on nearby subgoals. RL objectives mitigate this issue. Both BC and RL policies trained on longer-horizon goals exhibit shift in sensitivity from goal to state information. Distilling input Jacobians from short-horizon policies yields significant performance gains, especially in combinatorial manipulation tasks.

Conclusion: Goal relabeling horizon is an important consideration when learning generalist policies from offline data. The informational curse of horizon affects policy generalization, with BC being more susceptible than RL. Jacobian distillation offers a promising approach to improve long-horizon policy performance.

Abstract: The difficulty of learning goal-reaching policies is often attributed to a "curse of horizon" that manifests as bias accumulation in temporal-difference backups and noisy advantage estimates. In this work, we identify an additional informational curse of horizon in goal-conditioned policy learning, where increasing the goal relabeling horizon can significantly reduce policy generalization and performance. Through a series of controlled experiments with oracle planners, we decouple the goal horizons sampled during training from those that the policy is asked to reach at test time. Even when evaluated only on a sequence of nearby subgoals, goal-conditioned behavioral cloning (BC) policies suffer from severe, training horizon-dependent performance degradation that is mitigated by reinforcement learning (RL) objectives. We explain this phenomenon as a horizon-dependent decrease in the conditional mutual information between actions and hindsight-relabeled goals, and find empirically that both BC and RL policies trained on longer-horizon goals exhibit a shift in sensitivity from goal to state information, as measured by the policy's input Jacobians. Motivated by this observation, we find that distilling the input Jacobians of short-horizon policies into long-horizon policies yields significant performance gains, especially in combinatorial manipulation tasks. Taken together, our results highlight goal relabeling horizon as an important consideration when learning generalist policies from offline data.

</details>


### [196] [Efficient Best-of-N policy evaluation for inference-time alignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09250)
*Jonas Schweisthal,Yuxin Wang,Athiya Deviyani,Stefan Feuerriegel,Dennis Frauen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses the challenge of evaluating and selecting Best-of-N (BoN) policies under sample-only access, where response likelihoods are unavailable. The key insight is to use the order-statistic structure of BoN to express density ratios through score-rank probabilities estimable from samples. The authors develop a doubly robust estimator (BoN-DR) with valid asymptotic inference and two selection rules: one maximizing estimated policy value and another maximizing a lower confidence bound for no-harm guarantees.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Evaluating BoN policies from logged data is challenging under sample-only access because standard off-policy estimators require density ratios that depend on unavailable response likelihoods. Additionally, larger budgets can amplify errors in the score function and lead to reward overoptimization.

Method: 1. Exploit the order-statistic structure of BoN to express required density ratios through score-rank probabilities that are estimable from samples alone. 2. Develop a doubly robust estimator (BoN-DR) that efficiently reuses a shared auxiliary sample pool across candidate budgets. 3. Establish valid asymptotic inference under reward estimator misspecification and prove efficiency. 4. Derive two selection rules: (i) maximizing estimated policy value, and (ii) maximizing a lower confidence bound on improvement over the reference policy.

Result: The framework accurately estimates BoN policy values and selects effective sampling budgets across synthetic experiments and GSM8K with multiple reference and reward models. The lower confidence bound selection rule provides a no-harm guarantee by accounting for estimation uncertainty.

Conclusion: The proposed sample-only framework successfully enables evaluation and selection of BoN policies without access to response likelihoods. BoN-DR provides efficient estimation with valid asymptotic inference, and the selection rules effectively balance between maximizing policy value and minimizing risk of performance degradation.

Abstract: Best-of-N (BoN) is a common inference-time alignment method that selects the highest-scoring response among N samples from a reference model. Evaluating BoN policies from logged data is challenging under sample-only access because standard off-policy estimators require density ratios that depend on unavailable response likelihoods. In this paper, we propose a sample-only framework for evaluating and selecting BoN policies without access to these likelihoods. We show that the order-statistic structure of BoN allows the required density ratios to be expressed through score-rank probabilities that are estimable from samples alone. We then develop a doubly robust estimator of the BoN policy value (BoN-DR) that efficiently reuses a shared auxiliary sample pool across candidate budgets. We establish valid asymptotic inference even under reward estimator misspecification and prove the efficiency of our BoN-DR estimator. Since larger budgets can amplify errors in the score function and lead to reward overoptimization, we derive two selection rules: (i) maximizing the estimated policy value and (ii) maximizing a lower confidence bound on the improvement over the reference policy, which accounts for estimation uncertainty and provides a no-harm guarantee. Across synthetic experiments and GSM8K with multiple reference and reward models, our framework accurately estimates BoN policy values and selects effective sampling budgets.

</details>


### [197] [The Symbol of the Surrogate: Measuring Numerical Provenance in Neural PDE Solvers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09255)
*Ridham Patel*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Neural PDE surrogates trained on numerical solver outputs may imitate the solver's discretization errors rather than learn the true physical evolution. The authors propose an empirical Fourier-symbol diagnostic to distinguish fidelity to exact evolution from imitation of numerical schemes. Tests on linear advection, Fourier neural operators, and nonlinear Burgers dynamics reveal that surrogates reproduce training scheme errors, with differences exceeding 99.8% of predicted imitation levels.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard benchmarks cannot distinguish whether neural PDE surrogates fidelity to exact evolution or merely imitate the numerical scheme they were trained on, since both training and test data come from the same solver.

Method: The authors introduce an empirical Fourier-symbol diagnostic that probes a trained surrogate's linearized one-step operator with individual Fourier modes and compares it with both exact-evolution and training-scheme references. To address architectural spectral bias, they train identical networks on schemes with orthogonal dissipative and dispersive signatures.

Result: In linear advection, learned surrogates reproduce the training schemes' amplitude and phase errors, with twin-scheme difference reaching more than 99.8% of the analytically predicted full-imitation ceiling. This behavior persists for non-local Fourier neural operators and at the operator level for nonlinear Burgers dynamics.

Conclusion: Agreement with solver-generated test data does not establish fidelity to the exact evolution. Fourier-symbol measurements provide a direct diagnostic of numerical provenance, revealing whether surrogates learned the true physics or just imitated the numerical scheme.

Abstract: Neural PDE surrogates are trained on numerical solver outputs that contain both physical evolution and solver-specific discretization errors. Because surrogates are also evaluated against held-out trajectories from the same solver, standard benchmarks cannot distinguish fidelity to the exact evolution from imitation of the numerical scheme. We introduce an empirical Fourier-symbol diagnostic that probes a trained surrogate's linearized one-step operator with individual Fourier modes and compares it with both exact-evolution and training-scheme references. To address architectural spectral bias, we train identical networks on schemes with orthogonal dissipative and dispersive signatures and compare their learned operators. In linear advection, the learned surrogates reproduce the training schemes' amplitude and phase errors, with the twin-scheme difference reaching more than 99.8\% of the analytically predicted full-imitation ceiling. The same behavior occurs for a non-local Fourier neural operator and at the operator level for nonlinear Burgers dynamics. These results show that agreement with solver-generated test data does not by itself establish fidelity to the exact evolution. Fourier-symbol measurements provide a direct diagnostic of numerical provenance.

</details>


### [198] [Evaluating Trajectory Features for Routing Final-Layer Attention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09272)
*Yupeng Yao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether trajectory-based signals (hidden-state extrapolation error, curvature, error change) can improve attention routing in language models beyond baseline uncertainty measures. The study tests utility-supervised routers on 100 held-out PG-19 books but finds no positive gains after familywise correction, with parameter-matched fixed-projection controls outperforming trajectory routers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The research addresses whether attention routing can be improved by predicting the value of attention on the current prefix using trajectory-based signals. The authors evaluate whether hidden-state extrapolation error, curvature, and error change provide predictive power beyond simpler baselines like uncertainty, one-step displacement, position, and state projections.

Method: The study uses paired executions of the final attention layer to obtain signed next-token loss differences in frozen SmolLM3-3B-Base and Qwen3.5-4B-Base checkpoints. Utility-supervised routers are tested on 100 held-out PG-19 books at an identical causal 20 percent invocation quota. Multiple configurations are tested including actual selected-query execution and learned routers with various operation removals, feature locations, and scoring horizons.

Result: None of the six prespecified comparisons shows a positive gain after familywise correction. In Qwen3.5, a parameter-matched fixed-projection control lowers NLL by 0.00356 nats/token relative to the trajectory router (95% CI: 0.00218 to 0.00487). Secondary results show that performance depends on the operation removed, feature location, and scoring horizon; frozen thresholds drift substantially at longer horizons. Actual selected-query execution yields small long-sequence latency reductions with increased NLL, while learned routers remain slower during cached continuation.

Conclusion: The study identifies limits on the incremental value of trajectory summaries for attention routing. It separates allocation quality from measured inference benefit, suggesting that trajectory-based signals do not provide meaningful improvements over simpler baseline methods. The findings caution against assuming that trajectory-based routing signals will automatically translate into practical inference benefits.

Abstract: Attention routing requires a signal that predicts the value of attention on the current prefix. We evaluate whether hidden-state extrapolation error, curvature and error change improve this prediction beyond uncertainty, one-step displacement, position and state projections. Paired executions of the final attention layer supply signed next-token loss differences in frozen SmolLM3-3B-Base and Qwen3.5-4B-Base checkpoints. Utility-supervised routers are tested on 100 held-out PG-19 books at an identical causal 20 percent invocation quota. None of six prespecified comparisons shows a positive gain after familywise correction. In Qwen3.5, a parameter-matched fixed-projection control lowers NLL by 0.00356 nats/token relative to the trajectory router (95 percent interval 0.00218 to 0.00487). Secondary results depend on the operation removed, feature location and scoring horizon; frozen thresholds also drift substantially at longer horizons. Actual selected-query execution yields small long-sequence latency reductions with increased NLL, while learned routers remain slower during cached continuation. The study identifies limits on the incremental value of these trajectory summaries and separates allocation quality from measured inference benefit.

</details>


### [199] [Twist Flow for Inverse Problems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09281)
*Shiqin Zeng,Zijun Deng,Felix J. Herrmann*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper addresses a key limitation in Bayesian inverse problems: conditional generative models often produce samples that are observation-consistent but under-represent true posterior variability, especially in multimodal scenarios. The authors propose "joint twist-flow," an augmented flow-matching method that introduces a Gaussian likelihood-side coordinate (z_y) to couple generated samples with observation consistency while preserving variability in weakly constrained directions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Direct conditional generative models for inverse problems can encourage nearly deterministic mappings from observations to targets, causing generated samples to be observation-consistent but under-represent posterior variability. This leads to undercoverage, mode distortion, or artificial transitions between distinct feasible solutions, particularly when dealing with multimodal posterior distributions.

Method: The proposed method, joint twist-flow, uses an augmented flow-matching formulation that learns continuous transport from an augmented source state (z_x, y) to an augmented terminal state (x, z_y). Here, x is the target variable, y is the observation, z_x is the Gaussian reference coordinate for posterior sampling, and z_y is a Gaussian likelihood-side coordinate associated with the observation branch. Under Gaussian observation models, z_y corresponds to the normalized observation residual, which helps reduce likelihood-inconsistent variation while preserving variability in weakly constrained directions.

Result: On low-dimensional inverse problems with reference posterior samples, joint twist-flow better preserves multimodal posterior support compared to direct conditional-flow baselines. On image restoration and seismic subsurface velocity-model inversion tasks, the method shows increased posterior variability while maintaining observation consistency.

Conclusion: Joint twist-flow provides a principled approach to balancing observation consistency with posterior variability in Bayesian inverse problems. The introduction of the z_y coordinate acts as a coupling mechanism that ties generated samples to observation compatibility, effectively addressing the underrepresentation of posterior variability in existing conditional generative models.

Abstract: In Bayesian inverse problems, posterior sampling requires generating samples that are consistent with given observations while capturing the range of plausible solutions. Direct conditional generative models introduce latent noise to model this ambiguity, but paired inverse-problem training can still encourage an almost deterministic map from the observation to the target. As a result, generated samples may be observation-consistent while under-representing posterior variability, especially when the posterior is multimodal, leading to undercoverage, mode distortion, or artificial transitions between distinct feasible solutions. We propose joint twist-flow, an augmented flow-matching formulation that learns a continuous transport from the augmented source state $(z_x, y)$ to the augmented terminal state $(x, z_y)$. Here x is the target variable, $y$ is the observation, $z_x$ is the Gaussian reference coordinate for posterior sampling, and $z_y$ is a Gaussian likelihood-side coordinate associated with the observation branch. Under a Gaussian observation model, $z_y$ is motivated by the normalized observation residual associated with observation compatibility. Its role is not to replace uncertainty in $x$, but to couple generated samples of x to observation consistency, helping reduce likelihood-inconsistent variation while preserving variability in weakly constrained directions. We validate the method on low-dimensional inverse problems with reference posterior samples, where joint twist-flow better preserves multimodal posterior support than a direct conditional-flow baseline. We further evaluate the method on image restoration and seismic subsurface velocity-model inversion, showing increased posterior variability while maintaining observation consistency.

</details>


### [200] [Self-attention summary networks for subsurface velocity-model building from common-image gathers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09282)
*Shiqin Zeng,Yunlin Zeng,Abhinav Prakash Gahlot,Zijun Deng,Felix J. Herrmann*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A multiscale self-attention summary network learns compact embeddings from 3D Common-Image Gathers (CIGs) for probabilistic subsurface velocity inversion using flow-matching. The approach preserves offset-dependent kinematic structure while reducing background-velocity mismatch variability, improving posterior inference compared to direct conditioning on raw CIGs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Common-image gathers (CIGs) contain physically meaningful information about velocity-model errors through reflector focusing and residual moveout, but in conventional imaging workflows they are typically used only as diagnostic tools rather than being fully utilized for velocity inversion.

Method: The proposed method uses: (1) a multiscale self-attention summary network that maps high-dimensional 3D CIG volumes into compact conditioning embeddings, preserving offset-dependent kinematic structure and spatial coherence while reducing variability from background-velocity mismatch; (2) a flow-matching model that learns a transport from a Gaussian source distribution to the posterior distribution of plausible velocity fields, conditioned on these learned embeddings.

Result: Numerical experiments show that the proposed summary network improves posterior velocity inference compared to direct conditioning on raw CIGs. The multiscale attention design provides greater robustness to background-model mismatch, yielding more accurate posterior reconstructions and lower predictive uncertainty.

Conclusion: The multiscale self-attention summary network effectively compresses high-dimensional CIG data into informative embeddings that enhance probabilistic velocity inversion. This approach successfully addresses the underutilization of CIG information in conventional imaging workflows and provides more reliable velocity estimates with reduced uncertainty.

Abstract: Common-image gathers (CIGs) contain physically meaningful information about velocity-model errors through reflector focusing and residual moveout, but in conventional imaging workflows they are typically used only as diagnostic tools. In this work, we propose a multiscale self-attention summary network that maps high-dimensional 3D CIG volumes into compact conditioning embeddings for probabilistic subsurface velocity inversion. These learned embeddings preserve offset-dependent kinematic structure and spatial coherence while reducing variability caused by background-velocity mismatch. Conditioned on these summary embeddings, a flow-matching model learns a transport from a Gaussian source distribution to the posterior distribution of plausible velocity fields. Numerical experiments show that, compared with direct conditioning on raw CIGs, the proposed summary network improves posterior velocity inference. In particular, the multiscale attention design provides greater robustness to background-model mismatch, yielding more accurate posterior reconstructions and lower predictive uncertainty.

</details>


### [201] [LeCuration: A Tiny World Model as a Data Curation Multi-Tool](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09285)
*Mayank Sengupta,Nirmit Desai,Eric Song,Kunal Sawarkar*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes LeCuration, a data curation tool for physical AI applications in finite worlds (warehouses, video games). It uses LeWorldModel as a latent encoder/predictor with a diffusion transformer decoder, enabling anomaly detection, content clustering, and action-state consistency checking. The approach is demonstrated qualitatively on CS:GO gameplay data as a proof-of-concept.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Physical AI applications operate in finite worlds with limited physical laws. However, organizing, filtering, and curating data for these applications lacks systematic approaches. The authors aim to address this by building a model that understands the unique settings and physical laws of individual datasets to serve as a curation tool for larger downstream models.

Method: The authors propose LeCuration, a small world model built using LeWorldModel (LeWM) as the latent encoder and predictor, combined with a diffusion transformer (DiT) decoder to add visuals to autoregressive gameplay rollout. The model learns to auto-regressively predict game states, and its embeddings are used for two downstream tasks: (1) anomaly detection as a signal, and (2) content-based clustering heuristic.

Result: The embeddings from the model can serve as an anomaly detection signal and as a content-based clustering heuristic. Auto-regressively predicting the game state allows for qualitative checking of action-state consistency. The paper presents a qualitative proof-of-concept on CS:GO gameplay data, demonstrating the feasibility of the approach.

Conclusion: The proposed LeCuration approach shows promise as a data curation tool for physical AI in closed worlds. However, this work is a qualitative proof-of-concept without quantitative curation metrics or downstream training results. The authors identify quantitative evaluation and downstream training as the key next steps.

Abstract: Many applications of physical AI run within finite or closed physical worlds with a limited set of physical laws governing object behavior. Examples include robots working in a warehouse and agents moving around in a video game. In order to better organize, filter, and curate data for physical AI applications, we propose a new approach centered on the unique settings and physical laws of individual datasets. We train LeCuration, a small world model intended to serve as a data curation tool for a separate, larger downstream model. To build this model, we choose LeWorldModel (LeWM)as our latent encoder and predictor, adding a diffusion transformer (DiT) decoder to add visuals to autoregressive gameplay rollout. We find that the embeddings of this model can be used as an anomaly detection signal and as a content-based clustering heuristic, and that auto-regressively predicting the game state with this model allows us to qualitatively check for action-state consistency. This paper presents a qualitative, proof-of-concept case study on CS:GO gameplay data; we do not yet report quantitative curation metrics or downstream training results, which we identify as the key next step.

</details>


### [202] [Node-level Graph Neural Architecture Search Framework](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09297)
*Lintao Yanga,Sirui Lia,Yaqing Wang,Pietro Liò,Xu Shen,Baisong Liu,Chengbin Peng*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: N-GNAS (Node-Level Graph Neural Architecture Search) is a novel algorithm that automatically selects appropriate network architectures for different node subsets when updating features, addressing the limitation of uniform convolution operations in traditional GNNs. It incorporates contrastive learning loss to separate features from different categories.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional GNNs apply uniform convolution operations to all nodes regardless of their varying structural and feature characteristics, which undermines model performance and leads to over-smoothing issues as network depth increases.

Method: 1) Node-level architecture search that automatically chooses appropriate network architecture for each subset of nodes when updating node features; 2) Contrastive learning loss to separate sample features from different categories while keeping similar features together.

Result: Outperforms current leading GNAS techniques and traditional human-designed GNNs on eight datasets for node and graph classification. Achieves 78.26% accuracy on CiteSeer dataset.

Conclusion: N-GNAS successfully addresses the over-smoothing and uniform operation limitations of traditional GNNs through node-level architecture search and contrastive learning, demonstrating superior performance across multiple benchmark datasets.

Abstract: In recent years, Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) and architecture search frameworks have gained extensive application in non-Euclidean data processing, attributable to their superior capacity in managing unstructured data. Nevertheless, traditional approaches typically apply uniform convolution operations to all nodes, regardless of their varying structural and feature characteristics, which can undermine model performance and result in over-smoothing issues as the number of layers increases. To overcome this limitation, in this work, we propose a \textbf{N}ode-Level \textbf{G}raph \textbf{N}eural \textbf{A}rchitecture \textbf{S}earch (N-GNAS) algorithm. It can automatically choose an appropriate network architecture for each subset of nodes when updating node features. N-GNAS also introduces a contrastive learning loss to separate sample features from different categories and vice versa. In experiments conducted on eight datasets for node and graph classification, our methodology outperforms current leading GNAS techniques and traditional human-designed GNNs. For example, it achieves an accuracy rate of 78.26\% on the CiteSeer dataset.

</details>


### [203] [Kuration SDK: Addressing the Virtual2Real Gap via Data Curation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09305)
*Nirmit Desai,Eric Song,Mayank Sengupta,Tejal Bedmutha,Siri Reddy,Sahiti Dharmavaram,Kunal Sawarkar*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses the Virtual2Real gap in action-conditioned world models - the mismatch between visual similarity metrics (FVD, LPIPS, JEDi) and actual playability quality. The authors propose Kuration SDK, a physical AI data curation toolkit, as a solution to bridge this gap by enabling diagnostic analysis of datasets before training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing benchmarks for world models rely on visual similarity metrics that fail to capture action-semantic and physically-grounded quality. This leads to the Virtual2Real gap where models with similar visual metrics perform very differently in practice. The authors needed a better way to evaluate and curate training data for domain-agnostic action-conditioned world models.

Method: The authors trained diffusion world models on CounterStrike gameplay data and evaluated them using multiple metrics (FVD, LPIPS, JEDi). They developed the Kuration SDK tocurate raw gameplay data and measure various diagnostic properties to identify root causes of performance differences between models.

Result: They confirmed that qualitative playability does not correspond with standard visual similarity metrics. Using Kuration SDK, they uncovered the root cause of why two world models trained on identical data (same map, action, state distribution) behaved very differently despite having similar LPIPS and FVD scores.

Conclusion: Kuration SDK provides a more robust signal for world model development by enabling diagnostic analysis of datasets before training. It can uncover root causes of the Virtual2Real gap in specific datasets and accelerate development of sample-efficient training datasets. The SDK is being open-sourced.

Abstract: Benchmarks for measuring the quality of action-conditioned world models are still evolving and shifting away from visual similarity-based metrics to action-semantic and physically-grounded metrics. However, for domain and task-agnostic action-conditioned world model training, existing benchmarks provide a limited signal. By training and evaluating diffusion world models on CounterStrike gameplay data, we confirm that qualitative playability does not correspond with metrics such as FVD, LPIPS, and JEDi. We term this the Virtual2Real gap. We posit that, in lieu of reliable benchmarks, curating raw gameplay data and measuring a variety of diagnostic properties provides a more robust signal to bridge the gap, before the training even begins. We present several curation strategies and a general-purpose kit for physical AI data curation called Kuration SDK, which is being open-sourced with this paper. The SDK was instrumental in uncovering the root cause of the virtual2real gap in a specific case: why two world models trained on identical gameplay map, action and state distribution, behaved very differently when played in spite of having very similar LPIPS and FVD scores. Thus, Kuration SDK has the potential to uncover the root causes of Virtual2Real gap in specific datasets and accelerate development of sample-efficient training datasets.

</details>


### [204] [MovieSTAGE: Scene, Transition, and Global Encoding for Movie-fMRI ADHD Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09306)
*Boseong Kim,Haejun Chung,Ikbeom Jang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MovieSTAGE is a multiscale fMRI framework that combines scene-level, transition-level, and whole-movie functional connectivity to predict clinical phenotypes (ADHD case-control, subtypes, and three-class classification) from naturalistic movie watching, achieving AUROCs of 0.69-0.75.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing predictive models rely on whole-run FC or temporally generic representations that don't align with narrative events. This study aims to capture event-aligned brain dynamics from naturalistic movie watching to improve clinical classification.

Method: MovieSTAGE combines: (1) hypergraph-structured FC-profile organization within scenes, (2) unsigned FC-profile differences across adjacent scenes, and (3) whole-movie FC. Evaluated on 260 participants using 10 repetitions of stratified 5-fold cross-validation with out-of-fold predictions and bootstrap/permutation tests.

Result: Achieved AUROCs of 0.69 (case-control), 0.73 (ADHD-subtype), 0.75 (three-class) with balanced accuracies of 67.6%, 69.8%, and 58.3%. The full model outperformed all two-branch variants; HGNN scene encoder outperformed MLP, GAT, and BNT; human-annotated partition outperformed random/fixed-count controls.

Conclusion: Event-aligned scene and transition representations provide incremental predictive value when combined with whole-movie FC. Post-hoc analyses generated network-level hypotheses involving frontoparietal and default-mode systems.

Abstract: Naturalistic movie-fMRI provides a shared, temporally structured probe of brain dynamics, yet predictive models commonly rely on whole-run functional connectivity (FC) or temporally generic representations that are not aligned with narrative events. We introduce MovieSTAGE (Scene, Transition, and Global Encoding), a multiscale framework that combines hypergraph-structured FC-profile organization within scenes, unsigned FC-profile differences across adjacent scenes, and whole-movie FC. We evaluated 260 participants from the CMI-HBN Despicable Me cohort on case-control, ADHD-subtype, and three-class classification using 10 repetitions of stratified five-fold cross-validation, complete out-of-fold (OOF) predictions, and paired subject-cluster bootstrap and permutation tests. MovieSTAGE achieved AUROCs of 0.69, 0.73, and 0.75 and balanced accuracies of 67.6%, 69.8%, and 58.3%, respectively, yielding the highest mean point estimates among the evaluated methods. On the three-class task, the full model outperformed all two-branch variants, the HGNN scene encoder outperformed MLP, GAT, and BNT alternatives under matched settings, and the human-annotated partition outperformed duration-matched random and fixed-count GSBS controls. These controlled results support incremental predictive value from event-aligned scene and transition representations when combined with whole-movie FC in this cohort. Post-hoc model-derived analyses generated network-level hypotheses involving frontoparietal and default-mode systems.

</details>


### [205] [Denoising Blocks, Not Tokens: Efficient Compressed Continuous Diffusion with Branching Token Realization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09311)
*Xinsong Feng,Peng Du,Zhizhuo Yang,Daniel M. Bikel,Jiayun Wang,Haipeng Chen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: BLD (Branching Latent Diffusion) is a novel diffusion language model that compresses 1024-token sequences into 64 block latents (16x reduction) using branching token realization, where each latent is decoded by a parallel local AR branch. This approach achieves over 6x throughput improvement and 80x FLOPs reduction compared to prior methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Diffusion language models (DLMs) generate text through iterative parallel refinement, but current DLMs maintain one generative state per token, requiring every denoising step to process a state sequence as long as the output. This limits throughput gains from parallel generation. Continuous DLMs offer an additional degree of freedom: a single continuous state can represent multiple tokens, enabling diffusion on a much shorter latent sequence.

Method: BLD combines latent compression with branching token realization. It compresses a 1024-token sequence into 64 block latents (16x reduction). Each latent is decoded by a local autoregressive (AR) branch, with all branches running in parallel. To handle the difficulty of joint latent generation due to strong compression, BLD generates latents in groups, conditioning each group on previously generated latents.

Result: On end-to-end evaluation using the same GPU, BLD reduces generation FLOPs by more than 80x and increases throughput by more than 6x relative to the similarly sized ELF-L baseline. Compared with the AR baseline, BLD achieves more than 6x higher throughput and more than 4x lower latency. Despite the compression, BLD maintains competitive local fluency and diversity, although long-range coherence remains challenging.

Conclusion: Moving diffusion from token-level states to compressed latent sequences can substantially improve the efficiency of long-sequence generation.
