BLD demonstrates that latent compression combined with parallel branching decoding is a promising direction for efficient long-sequence text generation.

Abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) generate text through iterative parallel refinement, offering the potential for higher throughput than autoregressive (AR) decoding. However, most DLMs still maintain one generative state per token, so every denoising step processes a state sequence as long as the output sequence, limiting the throughput gains from parallel generation. Continuous DLMs provide an additional degree of freedom: a single continuous state can represent multiple tokens, allowing diffusion to operate on a much shorter latent sequence. We introduce \emph{Branching Latent Diffusion (BLD)}, which exploits this flexibility by compressing a 1024-token sequence into only 64 block latents, a $16\times$ reduction. BLD combines latent compression with \emph{branching token realization}, where each latent is decoded by a local AR branch and all branches run in parallel. Because strong compression makes joint latent generation difficult, BLD generates the latents in groups, conditioning each group on previously generated latents. In end-to-end evaluation on the same GPU, BLD reduces generation FLOPs by more than $80\times$ and increases throughput by more than $6\times$ relative to the similarly sized ELF-L baseline. Compared with the AR baseline, BLD achieves more than $6\times$ higher throughput and more than $4\times$ lower latency. Despite the compression, BLD maintains competitive local fluency and diversity, although long-range coherence remains challenging. Overall, BLD shows that moving diffusion from token-level states to compressed latent sequences can substantially improve the efficiency of long-sequence generation.

</details>


### [206] [Benign Overfitting under Heterogeneous Input Fusion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09340)
*Houzhen Liu,Xiaobo Xia*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper studies benign overfitting when combining (fusing) two statistically dependent input blocks in high-dimensional linear interpolation. The key finding is that marginal benignity does not guarantee fused benignity - the joint signal and spectral geometry created by input interaction determines whether fusion preserves or harms benign overfitting. Results differ qualitatively between regression and classification settings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While benign overfitting is well-studied for single high-dimensional inputs, its behavior under heterogeneous input fusion (combining dependent input blocks) remains unexplored. This is practically important as real-world data often involves fusing multiple correlated input sources.

Method: Analysis of minimum-norm linear interpolation under heterogeneous Gaussian design. For regression: asymptotic analysis of covariance certificates. For classification: analysis of one-sparse Gaussian classification with regularized estimators.

Result: Regression: Identified a "full-spectrum covariance certificate" that determines benign behavior - this certificate is preserved by any positive-semidefinite joint covariance consistent with marginals. However, outside this certified regime, two benign marginals can produce harmful fusion. Classification: Benignity depends on balance between surviving predictive signal and nuisance contamination; fusion can move these in opposite directions, making all marginal-to-joint benign/non-benign patterns attainable. The same fused input can have qualitatively different effects on regression vs classification.

Conclusion: Benign overfitting under heterogeneous fusion is determined by the joint signal and spectral geometry created by input interaction, not by marginal benignity alone. This challenges the intuition that "benign" inputs will always fuse benignly.

Abstract: Benign overfitting is extensively studied when learning from a single high-dimensional input, but its behavior under heterogeneous input fusion remains largely unexplored. We study this question for minimum-norm linear interpolation under a heterogeneous Gaussian design, comparing two statistically dependent input blocks with their fusion while holding the underlying population task fixed. For regression, we identify a full-spectrum covariance certificate whose asymptotic status is independent of the cutoff threshold and prove that it is preserved by every positive-semidefinite joint covariance consistent with the two marginals. This protection is sharp, yet it does not extend to all benign regression problems: outside the certified regime, two benign marginals can have a harmful fusion. For one-sparse Gaussian classification, benignity in the regular regime is characterized by the balance between surviving predictive signal and nuisance contamination. Fusion can move these two quantities in opposite directions, and within this model class every marginal-to-joint benign/non-benign pattern is attainable. We further show that the same fused input can have qualitatively different effects on regression and classification. These results establish that benign overfitting under heterogeneous fusion is determined by the joint signal and spectral geometry created by input interaction, rather than by marginal benignity alone.

</details>


### [207] [Shared Low-rank Basis Factorization for Data-free Mixture-of-Experts Compression](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09342)
*Tianxiao Cao,Jiahe Shao,Yuning Qiu,Kyohei Atarashi,Hisashi Kashima,Qibin Zhao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses storage and serving challenges in MoE LLMs by analyzing three compression families (pruning, merging, weight reconstruction) and proposing Shared Low-rank Basis Factorization (SLBF), a data-free weight reconstruction method that outperforms prior approaches across 5 MoE architectures (16B-122B parameters).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) large language models decouple capacity from compute through sparse routing, but their large parameter count creates significant storage and serving challenges. The authors aim to understand the theoretical limitations of existing compression methods and develop a better approach.

Method: The authors first derive structural error bounds for three MoE compression families: expert pruning, expert merging, and weight reconstruction. They prove that pruning and merging incur non-vanishing errors tied to routing and expert heterogeneity. Then they propose Shared Low-rank Basis Factorization (SLBF), a data-free weight reconstruction method using rank-k bases shared among experts, enabling richer cross-expert sharing. A post-hoc gauge fixing is applied to remove redundant parameters.

Result: SLBF consistently outperforms methods from all three compression families across five MoE architectures spanning 16B to 122B parameters.

Conclusion: Weight reconstruction (specifically SLBF) is superior to pruning and merging for MoE compression because it preserves expert structure and routing, avoiding the structural costs incurred by the other methods. The proposed SLBF achieves better performance through shared low-rank bases, faster convergence, and lower reconstruction error.

Abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) large language models decouple capacity from compute through sparse routing, but their large parameter count creates storage and serving challenges. We analyze three MoE compression families: expert pruning, expert merging, and weight reconstruction, and derive structural error bounds showing that pruning and merging can incur non-vanishing errors tied to routing and expert heterogeneity. In contrast, weight reconstruction avoids these structural costs by preserving expert structure and routing. Motivated by the analysis, we propose Shared Low-rank Basis Factorization (SLBF), a data-free weight reconstruction method that uses rank-$k$ bases shared among experts, enabling richer cross-expert sharing, faster convergence, and lower reconstruction error. A post-hoc gauge fixing removes redundant parameters at no representational cost. Across five MoE architectures spanning 16B to 122B parameters, SLBF consistently outperforms methods from all three compression families.

</details>


### [208] [Multimodal LLMs Can Learn to Read Brain Signals: A Vision--Language Model for Unified Multi-Task EEG Decoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09355)
*Parastoo Azizeddin,Omid Sharafi,Maryam M. Shanechi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: BraVista is a visual-language framework that converts multichannel EEG signals into structured images, enabling multi-task EEG decoding through instruction-conditioned vision-language models (VLMs) without requiring large-scale EEG-specific pretraining.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The key challenge is learning EEG representations that generalize across cognitive tasks, subjects, and recording conditions. While foundation models have improved EEG decoding, effectively interfacing neural signals with these models for multi-task learning across datasets remains an open question.

Method: BraVista encodes multichannel EEG signals as structured images and leverages continued post-training of a general-domain VLM, utilizing its visual and linguistic priors to adapt to neural signals without separate large-scale EEG pretraining. The approach was evaluated on four datasets spanning sleep staging, emotion recognition, cognitive workload classification, and abnormal EEG detection.

Result: BraVista showed strong performance across all four tasks. Key findings: (1) The choice of EEG-to-image representation is critical to performance; (2) Controlled perturbations showed gradual performance degradation under increasing noise, indicating the model relies on EEG-relevant information rather than superficial visual patterns.

Conclusion: Structured visual representations serve as an effective and scalable interface between neural signals and general-domain foundation models for unified multi-task EEG decoding, enabling cross-dataset generalization without EEG-specific pretraining.

Abstract: Learning EEG representations that generalize across cognitive tasks, subjects, and recording conditions remains a key challenge in electroencephalography (EEG) decoding. Recent advances in foundation models have improved EEG decoding performance, yet a fundamental open question remains: how to effectively interface neural signals with these models to enable multi-task learning across datasets. To investigate this question, we introduce BraVista, a visual-language framework that encodes multichannel EEG signals as structured images and enables multi-task learning through instruction-conditioned vision-language models (VLMs). Our approach relies on continued post-training of a general-domain VLM, leveraging its visual and linguistic priors to adapt to neural signals without a separate large-scale EEG-specific pretraining stage. We evaluate BraVista on four datasets spanning sleep staging, emotion recognition, cognitive workload classification, and abnormal EEG detection, showing strong performance across these tasks. Further analyses show that the choice of EEG-to-image representation is critical to performance. Moreover, through controlled perturbations of the EEG signal, we observe a gradual performance degradation under increasing noise, suggesting that the model relies on EEG-relevant information rather than superficial visual patterns. Together, these findings establish structured visual representations as an effective and scalable interface between neural signals and general-domain foundation models for unified multi-task EEG decoding.

</details>


### [209] [Global Exponential Convergence of Two-Layer Linear Network Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09356)
*Stephen Y Zhang,Gabriel Peyré*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proves global exponential (linear) convergence with explicit rates for wide two-layer linear networks trained with smooth Polyak-Lojasiewicz (PL) predictor losses. The analysis extends to deep linear ResNets and heavy-ball momentum settings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To establish global convergence guarantees with explicit rates for training linear neural networks, addressing the gap between practical success of neural networks and theoretical understanding of their optimization dynamics.

Method: The analysis uses gradient flow in factors that closes as a finite-dimensional Bures flow of the neuron law covariance. Mean-field conservation laws provide uniform spectral lower bounds on hidden preconditioning blocks under a spectral support gap condition on the initial covariance. For momentum, training dynamics close over positions and velocities via a lifted phase covariance.

Result: For initial covariance Σ₀ = σ²Id, the loss converges to the global minimum with linear rate at least 4σ²κ, where κ is the PL constant. This rate is stable under finite-width sampling. For heavy-ball momentum, linear convergence holds under explicit conditions on energy and damping, specifying a window of admissible dampings. The interval is nonempty for sufficiently large position scales with two-scale white initializations.

Conclusion: The theory provides a complete characterization of linear convergence for wide linear networks with PL losses, extending layerwise to deep linear ResNets. The explicit rate 4σ²κ and the conditions on momentum (energy, damping, position scale) give precise guidelines for achieving guaranteed convergence in practice.

Abstract: We prove global exponential (linear) convergence with an explicit rate in the rich scaling for wide two-layer linear networks trained with smooth Polyak-Lojasiewicz predictor losses. Gradient flow in the factors closes exactly in terms of a finite-dimensional Bures flow of the neuron law covariance, in which the predictor dynamics are preconditioned by hidden covariance blocks. Mean-field conservation laws provide uniform spectral lower bounds on the hidden preconditioning blocks when the initial covariance satisfies a spectral support gap condition. This condition encompasses positive definiteness while still allowing for singular initializations. For an initial covariance $Σ_0 = σ^2 \mathrm{Id}$, the loss converges to the global minimum with linear rate at least $4σ^2κ$, where $κ$ is the PL constant. We establish stability of this rate under finite-width sampling, as well as global convergence of factor gradient descent for an explicit stepsize interval depending on smoothness, the initial loss, and conserved spectral margins. Our argument extends layerwise to deep linear ResNets, subject to a residual-path bound. In the case of heavy-ball momentum, training dynamics close instead over positions and velocities in terms of a lifted phase covariance. Linear convergence holds under an explicit condition on the energy and damping, specifying a window of admissible dampings. For two-scale white initializations, this interval is nonempty for sufficiently large position scales, with a fixed initial loss gap and velocity covariance. Numerical experiments illustrate the covariance geometry and compare the predicted and observed rates.

</details>


### [210] [From Retrieval to Customer Context: Evaluating Frontier-Model Systems for Voice-of-Customer Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09375)
*Raviraja G,Viraj Bagal,Prabhath Chellingi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A customer context graph (CCG) that unifies customer, operational, and analytical objects as typed relationships significantly improves AI agents' ability to analyze customer feedback. Tested on 9,432 Cursor feedback records across 30 questions, the CCG-backed Agent scored 0.961 overall vs 0.710 for Deep Research Agent and 0.651 for Agentic RAG, with its largest advantage in analytical depth (0.967 vs 0.642).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Organizations increasingly use frontier language models to analyze customer feedback, but answer quality depends heavily on how feedback is organized and made available. Current approaches lack unified context connecting what customers say, why, who is affected, what action followed, and resolution status.

Method: Three approaches were compared on 9,432 public Cursor feedback records using 30 realistic product, incident, comparison, and metadata questions: (1) Agentic RAG, (2) Deep Research Agent, and (3) Customer Context Graph-backed Agent. Responses were jointly scored on three dimensions: answer quality (coverage and organization), analytical depth (specificity and decomposition), and evidence quality (citation support and traceability). A comparative rubric calibrated on 28 of 30 questions was used, with cited records sampled against claims and three dimensions weighted equally.

Result: The Customer Context Graph-backed Agent scored 0.961 overall, significantly outperforming Deep Research Agent (0.710) and Agentic RAG (0.651). It led on 27 of 30 paired questions (sign-test p < 10^(-5); strictly best on 26 of 30). Its largest advantage was analytical depth (0.967 vs 0.642), reflecting more specific, hierarchically developed findings with quantified themes and traceable evidence.

Conclusion: The customer context graph architecture, which models typed relationships connecting customer objects (feedback, conversations, users, accounts), operational objects (tickets, support agents, opportunities, competitors), and analytical/action objects (taxonomy concepts, evidence, insights, work items, outcomes), substantially improves AI agents' analytical capabilities for customer feedback analysis. The architecture can generalize to any feedback source beyond Cursor.

Abstract: Organizations increasingly use frontier language models to analyze customer feedback, but answer quality also depends on how that feedback is organized and made available. We define a \emph{customer context graph} as a unified model of customer and business context. Typed relationships connect customer objects (feedback, conversations, users, and accounts), operational objects (tickets, support agents, opportunities, and competitors), and analytical or action objects (taxonomy concepts, evidence, insights, work items, and outcomes). This lets an agent investigate not only what customers say, but why, who is affected, what action followed, who owns it, and whether it was resolved. For this experiment, the graph is populated from public Cursor feedback; the same architecture can support any type of feedback source. We compare Agentic RAG, a Deep Research Agent, and a Customer Context Graph-backed Agent on the same 9,432 public Cursor feedback records using 30 realistic product, incident, comparison, and metadata questions. Without exhaustive ground truth, we jointly score responses on answer quality (coverage and organization), analytical depth (specificity and decomposition), and evidence quality (citation support and traceability), using a comparative rubric calibrated on 28 of the 30 questions. We sample cited records against their claims and weight the three dimensions equally. Under this aligned rubric, the Customer Context Graph-backed Agent scores 0.961 overall, versus 0.710 for the Deep Research Agent and 0.651 for Agentic RAG, and leads the Deep Research Agent on 27 of 30 paired questions (sign-test p < 10^(-5); strictly best on 26 of 30). Its largest advantage is analytical depth (0.967 versus 0.642), reflecting more specific, hierarchically developed findings with quantified themes and traceable evidence...

</details>


### [211] [Noise, Denoise, Correct: MCMC Posterior Sampling with Diffusion Priors in Three Steps](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09407)
*So Takao,Gregory David Bellchambers,Luke Ye,Sanmitra Ghosh,Michalis Michaelides*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Diffusion Waltz is an MCMC method that enables exact posterior sampling for inverse problems with nonlinear, non-differentiable forward models by using SDEdit-style noising-denoising as proposals, corrected via Metropolis-Hastings, with gradient-free ensemble Kalman updates for observation injection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Pretrained diffusion models serve as powerful priors for inverse problems, but posterior sampling remains challenging when the forward model is nonlinear and non-differentiable, limiting practical applicability.

Method: The paper proposes Diffusion Waltz, an MCMC framework with two key innovations: (1) Using SDEdit-style noising-denoising as proposal distributions, corrected via Metropolis-Hastings for exact posterior sampling without requiring prior evaluation; (2) Injecting observations into the proposal using a gradient-free ensemble Kalman update to preserve exactness.

Result: On a non-differentiable Navier-Stokes initial condition recovery task, Diffusion Waltz outperforms existing baselines across different noise and nonlinearity regimes.

Conclusion: Diffusion Waltz enables exact posterior sampling for inverse problems with complex forward models, demonstrating superior performance over existing methods in challenging nonlinear and non-differentiable settings.

Abstract: Pretrained diffusion models are powerful priors for inverse problems, but posterior sampling under nonlinear, non-differentiable forward models remain hard. We introduce diffusion waltz, an MCMC method using SDEdit-style noising-denoising as a proposal, corrected via Metropolis-Hastings for exact posterior sampling without prior evaluation. We further propose injecting observations into the proposal while preserving exactness, using a gradient-free ensemble Kalman update. On a non-differentiable Navier-Stokes initial condition recovery task, diffusion waltz outperforms existing baselines across different noise and nonlinearity regimes.

</details>


### [212] [Stability and Diversity of Networked Self-Consuming Generative Ecosystems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09409)
*Xiukun Wei,Yang Zhang,Xueru Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces a theoretical framework for analyzing networked self-consuming generative models, where multiple AI models consume synthetic data from each other through complex interaction pathways represented as a directed weighted graph. The study addresses a gap in prior research, which only examined isolated models or simplified two-model interactions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The widespread deployment of generative AI makes it increasingly difficult to distinguish synthetic from real data, leading to synthetic data being incorporated into training pipelines of future model generations. This creates self-consuming training loops. Prior work only studied isolated models consuming their own data or simplified two-model interactions, leaving a gap in understanding complex multi-model interactions in real-world scenarios.

Method: The authors represent models as nodes in a directed, weighted graph where edge weights govern the flow of synthetic data among models. They analyze long-term behavior under retraining dynamics, establishing conditions for convergence and characterizing the resulting fixed points. The study examines how stability and diversity are shaped by each model's access to real data, cross-model data consumption, and the structure of the interaction graph.

Result: The paper establishes conditions for convergence and characterizes the resulting fixed points in networked self-consuming generative models. The analysis reveals how the system's long-term stability and diversity depend on three key factors: each model's access to real data, the extent of cross-model data consumption, and the structure of the interaction graph.

Conclusion: This work provides a foundational theoretical framework for understanding networked self-consuming generative models, offering insights into the long-term dynamics and stability of multi-model AI ecosystems where synthetic data flows through complex interaction pathways.

Abstract: The widespread deployment of generative AI has made it increasingly difficult to distinguish synthetic content from real data. Consequently, synthetic data is inevitably incorporated into the training pipelines of future model generations, forming a self-consuming training loop. Prior work has studied the effects of such recursive self-consuming training, but analyses have largely been limited to isolated models, where a model consumes only its own synthetic data, or to simplified interactions between two models. This paper takes a first step toward understanding networked self-consuming generative models, in which multiple models consume synthetic data generated by one another through complex interaction pathways. We introduce a theoretical framework representing models as nodes in a directed, weighted graph, with edge weights governing the flow of synthetic data among models. Using this framework, we analyze the long-term behavior of networked models under retraining dynamics, establishing conditions for convergence and characterizing the resulting fixed points. We further investigate how the system's long-term stability and diversity are shaped by each model's access to real data, cross-model data consumption, and the structure of the interaction graph.

</details>


### [213] [Shared Geometry As A Rosetta Stone: Cross-Modal Alignment Without Paired Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09411)
*Dominik Schnaus,Thomas Dagès,Daniel Cremers,Xi Wang,Phillip Isola*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper demonstrates that independently trained models across different modalities (e.g., text and images) can be aligned without any paired examples using a Wasserstein Procrustes method, challenging the assumption that large paired datasets are necessary for cross-modal alignment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multimodal representations enable zero-shot classification and retrieval, but aligning independently trained models typically requires large amounts of paired data. This research investigates whether paired examples are truly necessary, motivated by the Platonic Representation Hypothesis suggesting models may converge toward shared representation geometry.

Method: The proposed Wasserstein Procrustes method uses a coarse geometric initialization to align two disjoint embedding sets by estimating a single orthogonal map without seeing any pairs. The method leverages geometric alignment metrics to predict when alignment is possible.

Result: Paired examples are unnecessary for coarse cross-modal alignment. The method consistently aligns independently trained representations across datasets, modalities, and unimodal models. In the few-pair regime, it substantially outperforms existing methods while remaining competitive with pair-based methods. The resulting alignments enable text-to-image generation without paired examples.

Conclusion: Independently trained models often share enough geometry to establish cross-modal correspondence with little or no paired data, suggesting that large paired datasets may be unnecessary for cross-modal alignment tasks.

Abstract: Multimodal representations enable zero-shot classification and retrieval, but aligning independently trained models usually requires large amounts of paired data. Yet, the Platonic Representation Hypothesis suggests that models trained on different modalities may converge spontaneously toward a shared representation geometry. But then, do we even need paired examples for cross-modal alignment? Remarkably, we show that paired examples are unnecessary for coarse cross-modal alignment. Our simple Wasserstein Procrustes method with a coarse geometric initialization aligns two disjoint embedding sets by estimating a single orthogonal map without seeing any pairs. Across datasets, modalities, and unimodal models, we show that we can consistently align independently trained representations without pairs, and standard geometric alignment metrics accurately predict when this is possible. Nevertheless, we can naturally benefit from paired examples. In the very few-pair regime, our method substantially outperforms existing ones, while staying competitive with pair-based methods with more added examples. Finally, we demonstrate that the resulting alignments can enable text-to-image generation without paired examples. These results show that independently trained models often share enough geometry to establish cross-modal correspondence with little or no paired data.

</details>


### [214] [Self-Consuming Generative Models with Co-Evolving Human Preferences](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09415)
*Xiukun Wei,Tian Xie,Ding Zhu,Xueru Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper studies the long-term dynamics of generative models trained in self-consuming loops where users curate preferred samples. When training uses only user-curated synthetic data, initial biases are amplified leading to singleton equilibria. However, injecting reference data at sufficient rates creates a unique globally attracting equilibrium, enabling controlled steering of the system.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work assumes fixed user preferences, but in reality, exposure to model outputs gradually reshapes what users perceive as desirable, creating a feedback loop where model distributions and user preferences co-evolve. This paper takes a first step toward understanding these coupled dynamics.

Method: The authors analyze the mathematical dynamics of coupled model-user systems, examining equilibria under two scenarios: (1) training entirely on user-curated synthetic data, and (2) training with reference data injection. They then propose an algorithm for jointly selecting reference distribution and mixing weight.

Result: When training relies entirely on user-curated synthetic data, iterative curation amplifies initial biases and drives the system toward one of multiple singleton equilibria—where an instance with initial advantage eventually dominates. In contrast, injecting reference data at a sufficiently large rate fundamentally changes the dynamics, yielding a unique globally attracting equilibrium.

Conclusion: Injecting reference data can control long-term outcomes. The authors propose an efficient algorithm that jointly selects a reference distribution and its mixing weight to steer the coupled system toward equilibria that preserve desired attributes while minimizing data collection costs.

Abstract: Generative models are increasingly trained in self-consuming iterative loops, where users curate preferred samples from model-generated candidates and the curated samples are used to train future generations of the model. Prior work has largely assumed fixed user preferences, but in practice exposure to model outputs gradually reshapes what users perceive as desirable, creating a feedback loop in which model distributions and user preferences co-evolve. We take a first step toward understanding the long-term behavior of such coupled dynamics. We show that when training relies entirely on user-curated synthetic data, iterative curation amplifies initial biases and drives the system toward one of multiple singleton equilibria in which the instance holding an initial advantage eventually dominates. In contrast, injecting reference data into training at a sufficiently large rate fundamentally changes the dynamics and yields a unique globally attracting equilibrium. Building on this insight, we study how reference-data injection can be used to control long-term outcomes, and propose an efficient algorithm that jointly selects a reference distribution and its mixing weight to steer the coupled system toward equilibria that preserve desired attributes while minimizing data collection costs.

</details>


### [215] [What a Reporting Convention Hides: A Matched-Budget Audit of Quantum Natural Gradient with an Exactly Computed Metric](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09425)
*Lu Wei,Yufeng Wang,Haibin Ling*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper reveals flaws in how variational quantum optimizer comparisons are typically measured, demonstrating that common evaluation conventions can hide significant performance differences between Adam, SPSA, and QNG. The authors recommend charging every miss the full budget and reporting verdicts across multiple targets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Previous comparisons of variational quantum optimizers only time runs that reach a target loss or evaluate at a single target. These conventions could incorrectly decide whether an optimizer's costlier steps pay off, potentially biasing results.

Method: The authors measure how much each convention changes verdicts among Adam, SPSA, and QNG on initializations held out from the selection of settings. They compute the exact metric that preconditions QNG, price every step in circuit evaluations, and give every method the same budget. They compare linear pricing (simulator) versus quadratic pricing (assumed hardware) for the metric.

Result: In median pooled over circuit widths, cost families and a sweep of settings with common misses, SPSA needs more than twice Adam's evaluations to reach a loose target. Dropping censored runs that miss the target hides this gap. On the global-cost family with settings fixed for a strict target, QNG usually reaches the loose target after Adam but the strict target first. QNG's strict-target lead disappears when switching from linear simulator pricing to quadratic hardware count.

Conclusion: The authors recommend charging every miss the full budget and reporting verdicts across multiple targets to get a more accurate assessment of variational quantum optimizer performance.

Abstract: Several published comparisons of variational quantum optimizers time only runs that reach a target loss, or read the verdict at a single target. Either convention could decide whether an optimizer's costlier steps pay off. We measure how much each convention changes verdicts among Adam, simultaneous perturbation stochastic approximation (SPSA) and quantum natural gradient (QNG), on initializations held out from the selection of settings. We compute the exact metric that preconditions QNG, price every step in circuit evaluations and give every method the same budget. In a median pooled over circuit widths, cost families and a sweep of settings with common misses, SPSA needs more than twice Adam's evaluations to reach a loose target. Dropping the censored runs that miss the target hides this gap. On the global-cost family we hold fixed the settings selected for a strict target. QNG then usually reaches the loose target after Adam but the strict target first. QNG's strict-target lead disappears when the metric's simulator price, linear in the number of parameters, is replaced by an assumed hardware count quadratic in that number. We recommend charging every miss the budget and reporting verdicts across targets.

</details>


### [216] [An extended deep energy method for thermo-mechanical crack propagation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09433)
*Han Zhang,Mehrisadat Makki Alamdari,Babak Shahbodagh,Mohammad Vahab,Cosmin Anitescu,Timon Rabczuk,Elena Atroshchenko*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper presents an extended deep energy method for thermo-mechanical crack propagation, where a sharp polyline crack is modeled using two neural networks representing temperature and displacement fields. The networks receive crack information through a scalar embedding function that is discontinuous across the crack but smooth elsewhere, enabling fields to jump across the crack without regularization. The method uses Williams expansion with trainable amplitudes for displacement enrichment near the crack tip, and extracts stress intensity factors via the interaction integral method.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Previous neural energy solvers have been proposed for phase-field fracture and sharp cracks, but heat conduction on cracked domains combined with crack propagation under thermal stresses has not been addressed. This work aims to fill that gap by coupling transient heat conduction with crack growth under thermo-mechanical loading.

Method: Two neural networks represent temperature and displacement fields, receiving crack information through a scalar embedding function that is discontinuous across the crack but smooth elsewhere. Fields are obtained by minimizing an incremental conduction functional and thermoelastic potential energy in a staggered sequence. Monte Carlo integration uses points stratified over background elements, densified near the crack tip and redrawn during training. Stress intensity factors are extracted via the interaction integral with the area term of Wilson and Yu, validated by contour radius sweeps. Crack advances at maximum hoop stress angle when energy release rate reaches critical value at crack-tip temperature.

Result: The method shows excellent accuracy: on a stationary thermal edge crack, the extracted stress intensity factor agrees with published values to 0.11%; in a functionally graded shear test, initiation agrees with independent sharp-crack finite element solutions within one load step; on a notched cruciform specimen, crack paths follow published solutions under mechanical, thermal, and combined loading.

Conclusion: The proposed deep energy method successfully couples transient heat conduction with crack propagation in thermo-mechanical fracture problems, providing accurate stress intensity factor predictions and crack path trajectories across various loading conditions without requiring regularization length parameters.

Abstract: Thermo-mechanical fracture couples transient heat conduction on a cracked domain with a crack that grows as the temperature and the displacement evolve. Neural energy solvers have been proposed for phase-field fracture and later extended to represent a sharp crack through the network input, but heat conduction on the cracked domain and crack propagation under the resulting thermal stresses have not yet been treated together in these solvers. We present an extended deep energy method for thermo-mechanical crack propagation in which the crack remains a sharp polyline. Two networks represent the temperature and the displacement and receive the crack through a scalar embedding function, discontinuous across the crack and smooth elsewhere, so that both fields can jump across it without a regularization length, and the displacement is enriched near the tip by the Williams expansion with trainable amplitudes. The two fields are obtained by minimizing an incremental conduction functional and the thermoelastic potential energy in a staggered sequence, with Monte Carlo integration on points stratified over background elements, densified near the tip and redrawn during training. The stress intensity factors are extracted by the interaction integral with the area term of Wilson and Yu and checked by a sweep of the contour radius, and the crack advances at the maximum hoop stress angle when the energy release rate of the kink reaches the critical value at the crack-tip temperature. On a stationary thermal edge crack the extracted stress intensity factor agrees with the published value to 0.11%, in a functionally graded shear test initiation agrees with an independent sharp-crack finite element solution to within one load step, and on a notched cruciform specimen the crack paths follow the published solutions under mechanical, thermal and combined loading.

</details>


### [217] [GeoPrior-Mamba: Structured Process Priors with Mamba for Fine-Resolution XCO2 Reconstruction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09456)
*Zhao Meng,Yinan Cai,Siru Zhong,Juepeng Zheng,Haohuan Fu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: GeoPrior-Mamba introduces a novel framework that uses offline language models to construct structured process priors for reconstructing fine-resolution XCO2 fields from sparse OCO-2 satellite observations, achieving 0.81 ppm RMSE and 0.93 R2 by integrating domain knowledge about biospheric uptake, ecosystem respiration, and anthropogenic emissions into a multi-directional Mamba backbone.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing learning-based methods treat environmental covariates as ordinary numerical inputs and must learn heterogeneous source-sink relationships from sparse supervision. The paper addresses this limitation by using language models to organize relative process knowledge into deterministic prior tables before training, rather than using them for direct prediction.

Method: GeoPrior-Mamba uses a multi-directional Mamba framework with offline language-model-induced structured process priors. Language models are used to organize process knowledge for biospheric uptake, ecosystem respiration, and anthropogenic emissions into prior tables. These priors are spatially instantiated using geographic, ecological, emission-related, and seasonal information, then adaptively injected into the reconstruction backbone through a lightweight knowledge adapter.

Result: Using OCO-2 observations from 2018-2020, GeoPrior-Mamba achieves RMSE of 0.81 ppm and R2 of 0.93 on held-out observations. This represents a 48.2% RMSE reduction relative to CAMS background interpolation and 3.1% relative to Trans-XCO2 under the same evaluation protocol. Ablation experiments show measurable contribution from the knowledge-prior branch and substantially faster convergence than the knowledge-free Mamba backbone. Independent TCCON evaluation supports consistency with ground-based column CO2 measurements.

Conclusion: Language models can provide a practical mechanism for constructing structured process priors when globally consistent process-response representations are difficult to obtain directly, while remaining outside the numerical prediction loop. The approach demonstrates that domain knowledge from language models can be effectively integrated into deep learning frameworks for atmospheric reconstruction tasks.

Abstract: Reconstructing fine-resolution column-averaged dry-air CO2 (XCO2) fields from sparse satellite observations requires models to infer spatial structure that is only weakly constrained by direct measurements. Existing learning-based methods typically treat environmental covariates as ordinary numerical inputs and must therefore learn heterogeneous source-sink relationships largely from sparse supervision. We introduce GeoPrior-Mamba, a multi-directional Mamba framework augmented with offline language-model-induced structured process priors. Rather than using a language model to predict XCO2, we use it before training to organize relative process knowledge for biospheric uptake, ecosystem respiration, and anthropogenic emissions into deterministic prior tables. These priors are spatially instantiated using geographic, ecological, emission-related, and seasonal information and are adaptively injected into the reconstruction backbone through a lightweight knowledge adapter. Using OCO-2 observations from 2018-2020, GeoPrior-Mamba achieves an RMSE of 0.81 ppm and an R2 of 0.93 on held-out observations, reducing RMSE by 48.2% relative to CAMS background interpolation and by 3.1% relative to Trans-XCO2 under the same evaluation protocol. Ablation experiments show a measurable contribution from the knowledge-prior branch and substantially faster convergence than the knowledge-free Mamba backbone. Independent TCCON evaluation further supports the consistency of the reconstructed fields with ground-based column CO2 measurements. These results suggest that language models can provide a practical mechanism for constructing structured process priors when globally consistent process-response representations are difficult to obtain directly, while remaining outside the numerical prediction loop.

</details>


### [218] [DSReg: Provably Recovering Individual World Latents without Reconstruction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09457)
*Yujia Zheng,David Klindt,Randall Balestriero,Bernhard Schölkopf*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces DSReg (Dependency-Sparsity Regularization), a method that achieves provable recovery of individual world latents from Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) without reconstruction, decoder, or labels. The key condition is Structural Diversity—different latents leave distinct dependency footprints on observations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current latent variable recovery methods (nonlinear ICA, dictionary learning, causal representation learning) require anchors like reconstruction, auxiliary supervision, or distributional asymmetries. JEPAs, which lack these anchors, only identify latent state up to linear transformation, leaving individual latents mixed. This limits interpretability and downstream use of learned representations.

Method: The authors propose Structural Diversity as a condition where different latents leave distinct dependency footprints on observations. DSReg is then applied post hoc to any linearly identified representation (building on LeJEPA's linear identifiability) to recover individual world latents up to signed permutation, without reconstruction or decoder.

Result: DSReg achieves the first fully identifiable JEPA that recovers every world latent. It applies post hoc to pretrained checkpoints without loss over joint training. Structural Diversity is strictly weaker than all structural conditions of prior identifiable latent variable models. Experiments across synthetic regimes, world model probes, learned visual encoders, and external renderers show improved individual-latent recovery while preserving dense prediction.

Conclusion: Individual world latents can be provably recovered with no reconstruction, no decoder, and no labels under the Structural Diversity condition. This bridges the gap between anchored latent variable methods and unanchored methods like JEPAs, establishing a new standard for identifiable representation learning.

Abstract: Methods that recover individual latent variables of the world, from nonlinear ICA to dictionary learning and causal representation learning, anchor the latents to observations through reconstruction, auxiliary supervision, or distributional asymmetries such as non-Gaussianity. Methods without these anchors, including joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs), identify the latent state only up to a linear transformation, so individual latents remain mixed. We close this gap: individual world latents can be provably recovered with no reconstruction, no decoder, and no labels. The key condition is Structural Diversity: different latents leave distinct dependency footprints on observations, just as no two snowflakes are alike. Building on the linear identifiability that LeJEPA provides, we prove that under Structural Diversity, DSReg (Dependency-Sparsity Regularization) recovers individual world latents up to signed permutation, without reconstruction or a decoder. It applies post hoc to any linearly identified representation, reusing trained checkpoints at no loss over joint training, and establishes the first fully identifiable JEPA that recovers every world latent. Moreover, as a condition on dependency footprints, Structural Diversity is strictly weaker than all structural conditions of prior identifiable latent variable models. Across synthetic regimes, world model probes, learned visual encoders, and external renderers, DSReg preserves dense prediction while improving individual-latent recovery and downstream use with scales.

</details>


### [219] [When Should an In-Context Learner Expand Its Hypothesis Space?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09471)
*Weihan Li,Xinlei Chen,Junhao Wu,Tianshi Zheng*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper addresses when learning systems should expand to a richer model family rather than making local repairs. It introduces a Structural Revision Environment that allows exact Bayesian calculations and finds that revision is a value boundary (not an evidence threshold). Transformers trained in this environment learn this boundary from utility alone, while language models show a failure-sensitive signal in predictions but not in revision decisions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The core challenge is deciding whether prediction failures represent noise, exceptions, or need for structural change - a costly sequential decision. The harder step is determining when opening a richer family is worth its cost.

Method: The authors create a Structural Revision Environment that produces matched failures from each source, varies expansion price and horizon independently of evidence, and admits exact Bayesian calculations and normative one-shot decision solutions.

Result: Key findings: (1) Revision is a value boundary, not an evidence threshold - same history has different optimal actions under different prices/horizons; (2) The boundary is set by inputs a rule predicts and a repair cannot cover; (3) Belief in richer family crosses long before the decision; (4) Transformers reproduce this boundary from utility alone; (5) Language models have failure-sensitive signals not reflected in revision decisions; (6) Reasoning models weigh stated gain but don't estimate what expansion would buy; (7) Post-training moves prior and prediction sharpness but not the criterion.

Conclusion: The study reveals a fundamental distinction between prediction signals and revision decisions in neural networks. Language models carry useful failure signals but fail to weigh them properly against cost and horizon when making expansion decisions. The normative solution shows revision depends on value considerations, not just evidence strength.

Abstract: Learning systems adapt quickly inside a familiar family of models. The harder step comes earlier: deciding, from observations that could be noise, an exception, a change within the family or structure outside it, whether opening a richer family is worth its cost. We treat this as a costly sequential decision: prediction failure must be turned into structural evidence, evidence into a value of expansion, and value into action. The Structural Revision Environment produces matched failures from each source, varies the price of expansion and the remaining horizon independently of the evidence, and admits exact Bayesian calculations and an exact normative solution of the one-shot decision. Its solution shows that revision is a value boundary and not an evidence threshold: one history has different optimal actions under different prices, horizons and announced queries, the boundary between local repair and expansion is set by the inputs a rule predicts and a repair cannot cover, and belief in the richer family crosses long before the decision does. Transformers trained in the environment reproduce this boundary from utility alone. Language models of three post-training lineages carry a failure-sensitive signal in their predictions that is not reflected in their revision decisions, and given the gain of expanding they read it without weighing it against price and horizon. Three models allowed to reason weigh the stated gain in the reference's proportions and still do not turn the history into an estimate of what expansion would buy. Controlled post-training of the meta-trained learners moves the prior and the sharpness of predictions, and neither moves the criterion.

</details>


### [220] [MORA: Modeling Observed Changes for Drift-Robust Time-Series Anomaly Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09473)
*Xudong Mou,Tiejun Wang,Rui Wang,Hui Wang,Pin Liu,Tianyu Wo,Xudong Liu,Renyu Yang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MORA addresses temporal change disambiguation in time-series anomaly detection by using paired short- and long-term views to reconstruct the same local target. The reconstruction gap measures contextual support, and a data-dependent correction mechanism conservatively adjusts anomaly scores without requiring drift annotations or online adaptation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In non-stationary settings, distribution drift and true anomalies cause similar local changes, making it difficult to distinguish between abnormality and evolving context. Existing methods adapt to detected shifts or learn drift-insensitive representations but cannot resolve this ambiguity.

Method: MORA reconstructs the same local target from paired short- and long-term views. The reconstruction gap measures contextual support for a local deviation. A data-dependent correction mechanism conservatively adjusts the primary local anomaly score, where context can only reduce the score when it improves reconstruction of the same target.

Result: Experiments on four TSAD benchmarks show strong robustness to non-stationarity while preserving sensitivity to genuine anomalies.

Conclusion: MORA effectively disambiguates temporal changes by leveraging dual-view reconstruction without requiring drift annotations or online adaptation, offering a principled approach to distinguishing true anomalies from distribution drift.

Abstract: Time-series anomaly detection (TSAD) identifies deviations from patterns learned from historical data. In non-stationary settings, distribution drift and true anomalies can cause similar local changes, making it difficult to tell whether a deviation reflects abnormality or evolving context. Existing methods typically adapt to detected shifts or learn drift-insensitive representations, but do not resolve this ambiguity. We define this problem as \emph{temporal change disambiguation}: determining whether a local deviation is explained by broader temporal evolution. We introduce MORA, a drift-robust TSAD framework that reconstructs the same local target from paired short- and long-term views. The reconstruction gap measures contextual support for a local deviation, and a data-dependent correction mechanism conservatively adjusts the primary local anomaly score. Context can only reduce the score when it improves reconstruction of the same target. MORA needs neither drift annotations nor online adaptation. Experiments on four TSAD benchmarks show strong robustness to non-stationarity while preserving sensitivity to genuine anomalies.

</details>


### [221] [CHASE: Channel-Aligned Structure Exploitation for Geometry-Aware Model Engineering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09476)
*Wei Wang,Wei Jiang,Ziran Liu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CHASE (Channel-Aligned Structure Exploitation) leverages GSA (Geometric and Spectral Alignment) structural insights to design practical model operations including parameter-efficient finetuning (CORA), structured-pruning compensation (COEC), model merging (CORAM), multi-head attention optimization (CAGA), KV-cache compression (SAKV), and structured pruning (CAPS).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The structures identified by GSA (spectral concentration, physical-channel alignment, support structure, and singular basis changes) can be directly used to design methods for model modification, reconfiguration, and compression tasks.

Method: GSA characterizes trained networks through four aspects: spectral concentration, physical-channel alignment, support structure, and changes in singular bases. CHASE applies these structural insights across six applications: CORA (parameter-efficient finetuning), COEC (structured-pruning compensation), CORAM (model merging), CAGA (geometric shared-head construction for MHA-to-GQA conversion), SAKV (low-rank KV-cache compression via layer grouping), and CAPS (output neuron grouping with separate channel selection).

Result: CORA, COEC, and CORAM demonstrate GSA's effectiveness for adaptation, pruning compensation, and model merging. CAGA's geometric shared-head construction substantially improves MHA-to-GQA conversion. SAKV and CAPS outperform representative baselines for KV-cache compression and structured pruning.

Conclusion: The structural properties identified by GSA can be directly leveraged to design practical methods across a range of model operations, including finetuning, pruning, merging, attention optimization, and compression.

Abstract: Geometric and Spectral Alignment (GSA) characterizes trained networks through spectral concentration, physical-channel alignment, support structure, and changes in singular bases. In this paper, we propose CHASE (Channel-Aligned Structure Exploitation) to use these structures in practical model design. CHASE covers six applications across model modification, reconfiguration, and compression. CORA, COEC, and CORAM apply GSA to parameter-efficient finetuning, structured-pruning compensation, and model merging. We further develop three new methods. CAGA uses GSA to identify multi-head attention heads that can share a KV representation and constructs the shared key and value heads through geometric alignment and low-rank subspace extraction. SAKV uses GSA to determine which adjacent layers can share a low-rank KV-cache representation and the retained rank for each layer group. CAPS uses GSA spectral structure to group output neurons and selects retained input channels separately for each group. Results from CORA, COEC, and CORAM establish the effectiveness of GSA for adaptation, pruning compensation, and model merging. Experiments on CAGA show that geometric shared-head construction substantially improves MHA-to-GQA conversion, and SAKV and CAPS improve over representative baselines for KV-cache compression and structured pruning. These results show that the structures identified by GSA can be used directly to design methods for a range of model operations.

</details>


### [222] [Safe on Average, Unsafe in the Tail: When Is the Episodic-Cost Tail Controllable?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09508)
*Samuel Tetteh,Cody Fleming*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses a critical gap in safe reinforcement learning: standard methods only constrain expected episodic cost (mean), potentially leaving policies unsafe in worst-case episodes. The authors propose using CVaR₀.₁ (Conditional Value at Risk at 10%) to measure the episodic-cost tail and classify policies as "tail-safe" when this metric falls within the safety budget. They evaluate five standard algorithms on Safety-Gymnasium tasks to identify policies that are safe on average but unsafe in the tail, then study whether tail violations can be controlled while preserving return.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard safe RL methods impose constraints on expected episodic cost and report mean episodic cost, which fails to characterize how cost is distributed across episodes. A policy satisfying mean-cost criterion may remain unsafe in its worst episodes. This tail violation is not identified by current evaluation practices, and it's unclear whether such violations can be brought within budget while preserving return.

Method: 1. Use CVaR₀.₁ (average cost of worst 10% of episodes) to measure episodic-cost tail
2. Classify policy as tail-safe when CVaR₀.₁ is within safety budget
3. Evaluate five standard algorithms on three Safety-Gymnasium navigation tasks to identify tail-unsafe policies
4. Examine four constraint families on dense-hazard navigation
5. Assess tail control across four navigation and four locomotion tasks

Result: The paper identifies policies that are safe on average but unsafe in the tail, and studies whether tail violations can be controlled while preserving return. Results show that standard algorithms can fail tail-safety criteria while satisfying mean-cost constraints.

Conclusion: The paper establishes the importance of evaluating cost distributions beyond just mean cost, introduces CVaR₀.₁ as a meaningful tail-safety metric, and demonstrates the need for methods that control tail risk while preserving return in safe reinforcement learning.

Abstract: Safe reinforcement learning seeks policies that maximize return while satisfying constraints on cumulative cost. Most methods impose these constraints on expected episodic cost. Consequently, standard evaluations report mean episodic cost without characterizing how cost is distributed across episodes. A policy that satisfies the mean-cost criterion may therefore remain unsafe in its worst episodes. Mean-cost reporting neither identifies this tail violation nor shows whether it can be brought within budget while preserving return. In this work, we measure the episodic-cost tail using $\mathrm{CVaR}_{0.1}$, the average cost of the worst $10\%$ of episodes. We classify a policy as tail-safe when $\mathrm{CVaR}_{0.1}$ is within the safety budget. This allows us first to identify policies that are safe on average but unsafe in the tail and then to study whether their tail violations can be controlled while preserving return. To identify tail-unsafe policies, we evaluate five standard algorithms on three Safety-Gymnasium navigation tasks. We then examine four constraint families on dense-hazard navigation and assess tail control across four navigation and four locomotion tasks.

</details>


### [223] [Physics-Informed Neural Plasticity: PDE Solvers That Reshape Themselves](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09510)
*Chun-Wun Cheng,Bingcheng Hu,Angelica I. Aviles-Rivero*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces physics-informed neural plasticity, where neural PDE solvers dynamically adapt their representational structure during training rather than using fixed architectures. The proposed ReCAP method uses local enrichment, residual-directed splitting, gate-based pruning, and function-aware merging to redistribute computational capacity based on solution complexity. Achieves 10.7%-27.5% error reduction over 11 competing solvers on 5 challenging 3D/4D PDE benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional physics-informed neural PDE solvers have fixed representational structure throughout training, which is inefficient for PDEs with heterogeneous complexity across space-time. This causes insufficient capacity where physics is complex and redundant capacity where it's simple.

Method: ReCAP (Representation Capacity Adaptation for PDEs): A Gaussian-localized solver that dynamically redistributes capacity through (1) local enrichment, (2) residual-directed splitting, (3) gate-based pruning, and (4) function-aware merging. Uses responsibility-weighted error indicators and residual energy geometry to guide refinement decisions. Introduces quiet-child refinement to minimize disturbance when splitting by initializing new components via parent representation transport while controlling functional perturbation.

Result: Outperforms 11 physics-informed solvers on 5 challenging 3D and 4D PDE benchmarks. Achieves lowest relative L2 error on every problem, with 10.7%-27.5% error reduction relative to the strongest competing method.

Conclusion: Physics-informed solvers can learn not just their parameters but also how their representational capacity should be organized. The paradigm of neural plasticity - adapting the representation itself during optimization - provides a new direction for improving PDE solver accuracy and efficiency.

Abstract: Physics-informed neural PDE solvers adapt their parameters to satisfy governing equations, yet their representational structure typically remains fixed throughout training. This rigidity is poorly matched to PDE solutions with strongly heterogeneous complexity across space and space--time, leaving capacity insufficient where the physics is difficult and redundant where it is simple. We introduce physics-informed neural plasticity, a paradigm in which the representation itself reshapes during optimization in response to unresolved physics. We instantiate this principle with Representation Capacity Adaptation for PDEs (ReCAP), a Gaussian-localized solver that dynamically redistributes capacity through local enrichment, residual-directed splitting, gate-based pruning, and function-aware merging. ReCAP uses responsibility-weighted error indicators and the geometry of residual energy to determine where and how to refine. To limit the disturbance introduced by splitting, we introduce quiet-child refinement, which initializes new components by transporting the parent representation while controlling instantaneous functional perturbation. We further establish conditional a posteriori reliability and structural-stability guarantees linking localized physics residuals to solution error and stable refinement. Across five challenging 3D and 4D PDE benchmarks against 11 physics-informed solvers, ReCAP achieves the lowest relative $L^2$ error on every problem, reducing error by $10.7\%$--$27.5\%$ relative to the strongest competing result. These results suggest that physics-informed solvers need not merely learn their parameters---they can learn how their representational capacity should be organized.

</details>


### [224] [Differential Refresh Policies for Models Trained on Lagging Data Snapshots: From a Single-Age Equivalence Limit to an Optimal Per-Segment Allocation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09519)
*Amit Rajula*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper shows that adaptive staleness triggers for ML model retraining are operationally equivalent to simple uniform timers, and proposes differential segment refresh as the correct solution. Optimal refresh rates follow a square-root rule proportional to √(weight × change rate), achieving 8-29% improvement over uniform refresh.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Production ML models become stale immediately after training, but the common approach of using weighted staleness scores to trigger retraining is fundamentally flawed. The authors argue this is the "wrong lever" - the key insight is that any global staleness trigger is equivalent to a calibrated clock.

Method: The authors first prove a theoretical equivalence limit: any refresh trigger that is a static, strictly monotone function of a single global training-data age is operationally identical to a uniform age timer. They then solve the budget-allocation problem for differential segment refresh, deriving a closed-form optimal solution using Cauchy-Schwarz inequality. They validate through discrete-event simulation with real Poisson change events and 50% rate-estimation noise.

Result: In the frequent-refresh regime, each segment's optimal refresh rate is proportional to √(w_j × λ_j). The optimal policy never costs more than uniform timer and beats it by a "price of uniformity" term that is zero for homogeneous workloads and grows with heterogeneity. In simulation, optimal policy reduces weighted stale exposure by 8-29% relative to uniform timer, winning on 86-100% of seeds. A naive exposure-threshold policy does not improve, confirming it's the allocation that matters. The advantage survives 50% rate-estimation noise.

Conclusion: The leverage in model refresh is not a better staleness score but better action allocation. The key is differential refresh across segments with separable costs, not better global triggers. The "price of uniformity" quantifies the cost of not doing segment-specific allocation.

Abstract: Production machine-learning models are derived artifacts of time-bounded training snapshots: a deployed model is a materialized view over a training cut that ages the instant it is built. A common response is to replace the fixed retraining cadence with an adaptive trigger -- a weighted staleness score that retrains when accumulated source risk crosses a threshold. We show this is the wrong lever, and identify the right one. First, an equivalence limit: any refresh trigger that is a static, strictly monotone function of a single shared global training-data age is operationally equivalent to a calibrated uniform age timer, so a global staleness budget, however elaborately it weights segments, sources, and sensitivities, carries no scheduling information a clock does not. The limit also shows how to escape it: refresh segments differentially, giving each its own age and refresh interval, which is meaningful when refresh cost is separable across segments (incremental training or per-segment models). We solve the resulting budget-allocation problem. In the frequent-refresh regime each segment's optimal refresh rate is proportional to the square root of its risk $w_j λ_j$ (weight times change rate), and the optimal policy never costs more than the uniform timer, beating it by a closed-form Cauchy-Schwarz "price of uniformity" that is zero for homogeneous workloads and grows with heterogeneity. In a discrete-event simulation with real Poisson change events, the optimal policy lowers realized weighted stale exposure by 8-29% relative to the uniform timer at matched refresh budget, winning on 86-100% of seeds; a naive exposure-threshold policy does not, showing the allocation is what helps; and the advantage survives 50% rate-estimation noise. The leverage in model refresh is not a better score but a better action.

</details>


### [225] [Align Before You Combine: Reference Space Calibration for Supervision Without Ground Truth](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09525)
*Jackson Eshbaugh,Jorge Silveyra*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A calibration-first framework for generating supervision scores without ground-truth labels or shared annotation space. Uses synthetic ordinal reference space constructed from ordered calibration features to align otherwise incomparable scorer outputs before fusion.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To construct supervision scores when neither ground-truth labels nor a shared annotation space is available, addressing the challenge of aligning subset-specific scorers that produce incomparable outputs.

Method: Framework aligns subset-specific scorers using a synthetic ordinal reference space before fusion. The reference space is constructed from ordered calibration features representing the latent concept, providing a common scale. The calibration procedure is independent of the training set's empirical distribution.

Result: Consistently outperforms uncalibrated averaging across three benchmark datasets (Ames Housing, Breast Cancer Wisconsin, Wine Quality). Achieves higher primary-metric point estimates than the best individual scorer. Performance differences: <0.02 on Ames Housing, <0.01 on Breast Cancer Wisconsin and Wine Quality. After Bonferroni correction: significant differences for all three comparisons on Ames Housing and one on Breast Cancer Wisconsin. Using fewer calibration levels per feature can closely approximate higher-resolution results at lower computational cost.

Conclusion: The framework is a viable approach for constructing supervision scores when neither ground-truth labels nor a shared annotation space is available.

Abstract: We introduce a calibration-first framework that produces supervision scores without access to ground-truth labels or a shared annotation space. Our framework aligns subset-specific scorers using a synthetic ordinal reference space before fusion. This reference space is constructed from ordered calibration features that represent the latent concept, providing a common scale on which otherwise incomparable scorer outputs can be aligned. Because our calibration procedure uses the reference space rather than training samples, it is independent of the training set's empirical distribution. Across three benchmark datasets, our framework consistently outperforms uncalibrated averaging and achieves higher primary-metric point estimates on the evaluation metrics than the best individual scorer. Performance relative to sample-dependent baselines varies by domain, with absolute differences below 0.02 on Ames Housing and below 0.01 on Breast Cancer Wisconsin and Wine Quality. After Bonferroni correction, differences remain significant for all three comparisons on Ames Housing and one on Breast Cancer Wisconsin. Additionally, we show that using fewer calibration levels per feature can closely approximate higher-resolution results at substantially lower computational cost. Together, these results support our framework as a viable approach to construct supervision scores when neither ground-truth labels nor a shared annotation space is available.

</details>


### [226] [CircuitGate: Logic-Consistent Circuit-Level Functional Modeling for And-Inverter Graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09549)
*Qifan Zhang,Ruijie Li,Fangzhou Zhang,Qian Ma,Hui Li,Furui Zhan,Yongpeng Wang,Liying Hao,Shikai Guo*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CircuitGate is a function-aware representation learning framework for And-Inverter Graphs (AIGs) in EDA that advances from gate-level to circuit-level functional modeling. It explicitly encodes global primary-input support and models support-overlap-aware reconvergence, achieving up to 21.7% and 14.2% MAE reductions on equivalent-gate identification and signal-probability prediction tasks respectively.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing GNN-based AIG representation learning approaches rely on local gate-level message passing, which limits their ability to capture circuit-level functional context and makes learned representations sensitive to topology-specific patterns rather than functional dependencies.

Method: CircuitGate explicitly encodes global primary-input (PI) support, models support-overlap-aware reconvergence between fanins, and incorporates logic-inspired Boolean constraints to encourage functionally consistent representations. This advances from gate-level semantics to circuit-level functional modeling.

Result: CircuitGate achieves up to 21.7% MAE reduction on equivalent-gate identification and 14.2% MAE reduction on signal-probability prediction across ForgeEDA, EPFL, and ITC'99 benchmarks. It also demonstrates the best cross-dataset generalization in direct ForgeEDA-to-OpenABC transfer without fine-tuning.

Conclusion: Modeling circuit-level functional dependencies beyond local topology is effective for AIG representation learning, enabling robust representations that generalize across datasets and remain stable under functionality-preserving transformations.

Abstract: And-Inverter Graphs (AIGs) are fundamental representations for logic synthesis and verification in Electronic Design Automation (EDA). As structured representations of complex digital systems, AIGs require models to capture functional dependencies beyond local structure and remain robust to functionality-preserving transformations. In learning-based AIG representation, existing approaches are predominantly based on GNNs and rely on local gate-level message passing, limiting their ability to capture circuit-level functional context and making the learned representations sensitive to topology-specific patterns. Therefore, we propose CircuitGate, a function-aware AIG representation learning framework that advances from gate-level semantics to circuit-level functional modeling. CircuitGate explicitly encodes global primary-input (PI) support and models support-overlap-aware reconvergence between fanins, while incorporating logic-inspired Boolean constraints to encourage functionally consistent representations. We evaluate CircuitGate on the large-scale ForgeEDA benchmark and further validate it on the EPFL and ITC'99 benchmarks. Across equivalent-gate identification and signal-probability prediction tasks, CircuitGate consistently outperforms existing methods, achieving up to 21.7% and 14.2% reductions in MAE, respectively. Under direct ForgeEDA-to-OpenABC transfer without fine-tuning, CircuitGate also achieves the best equivalent-gate identification performance, demonstrating strong cross-dataset generalization. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of modeling circuit-level functional dependencies beyond local topology.

</details>


### [227] [A Framework for the Systematic Review of ML Assets in AI Registries](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09551)
*Alexandra González,Quim Motger,Xavier Franch,Silverio Martínez-Fernández*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes adapting systematic review methods from scientific literature to support structured retrieval, selection, and reuse of Machine Learning (ML) assets (models, datasets, benchmarks) in AI registries. The framework addresses the current ad hoc nature of ML asset selection by making it transparent, reproducible, and evidence-based.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern software systems increasingly rely on ML assets, but their selection lacks systematic retrieval methodologies comparable to traditional evidence synthesis. In practice, ML asset selection is often treated as a settled design decision with informal justification rather than a traceable, evidence-based, and updatable process.

Method: The authors analyze established systematic review practices from scientific literature and adapt their phases (planning, conducting, and documenting) to Artificial Intelligence (AI) registries. The framework treats ML assets as first-class units of analysis and integrates: (1) registry-aware search strategies, (2) cross-registry schema alignment, and (3) dependency-driven ML asset exploration.

Result: The paper conceptualizes ML asset retrieval as a systematic and reproducible process rather than an ad hoc activity, and proposes a framework for structured ML asset discovery that makes the selection process transparent and grounded in explicit evidence.

Conclusion: This work demonstrates how systematic review principles can be extended beyond scientific literature to support evidence synthesis over evolving AI registries, enabling better selection and reuse of ML assets in practice.

Abstract: Background: Modern software systems increasingly rely on Machine Learning (ML) assets (i.e., pre-trained models, datasets, benchmarks) for building, evaluating, and integrating ML-based systems. However, current exploration, selection and reuse practices of ML assets are not supported by systematic retrieval methodologies comparable to those used in traditional evidence synthesis. Consequently, in practice, ML asset selection is often presented as a settled design decision, supported by informal justification rather than a traceable, evidence-based, and updatable selection process. Aims: This paper explores how systematic review methods can support ML asset retrieval. In doing so, we aim to make their selection transparent and reproducible, grounded in explicit evidence, and ultimately better suited to its intended use. Method: We analyze established systematic review practices from scientific literature and adapt their phases (i.e., planning, conducting, and documenting) to Artificial Intelligence (AI) registries, treating ML assets as first-class units of analysis. The resulting framework integrates registry-aware search strategies, cross-registry schema alignment, and dependency-driven ML asset exploration. Results: We conceptualize ML asset retrieval as a systematic and reproducible process rather than an ad hoc activity, and propose a framework for structured ML asset discovery. \textbf{Conclusions:} This work illustrates how systematic review principles can be extended beyond scientific literature to support evidence synthesis over evolving AI registries.

</details>


### [228] [UniCSI Towards a Universal Wi-Fi CSI Encoder for Ubiquitous Human Sensing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09559)
*Daniel Eckhoff,Hua Kang,Zhitang Chen,Jie Chuai*

Main category: cs.LG
