TL;DR: UniCSI is a unified foundation architecture for Wi-Fi sensing that directly processes heterogeneous Channel State Information (CSI) from diverse device configurations (varying subcarrier counts, bandwidths, and frequency bands) without lossy pre-processing. It uses a physics-informed RF tokenizer to encode frequency channels based on fractional spectral position and a spectral aggregator to generate fixed-size spectral signatures from variable-length inputs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The fundamental obstacle in Wi-Fi sensing is that CSI is acquired under diverse device-specific configurations (different subcarrier counts, bandwidths, carrier bands), resulting in CSI tensors that vary in spectral resolution and shape. Existing standard architectures struggle with this heterogeneity and must use lossy pre-processing that compromises the underlying signal quality.

Method: UniCSI employs two core innovations: (1) A physics-informed RF tokenizer that encodes each frequency channel based on its fractional position within the physical spectrum rather than rigid array indices, preserving intrinsic spectral coherence and enabling frequency resolution-agnostic processing. (2) A spectral aggregator that distills variable-length channel sequences into a fixed-size spectral signature, decoupling feature dimensionality from physical subcarrier spacing.

Result: Extensive evaluations on 25 heterogeneous public datasets (14 to 2048 subcarriers, 20 to 160 MHz bandwidth, 2.4 and 5 GHz bands) demonstrate that native heterogeneous ingestion substantially improves cross-domain transfer under both supervised and self-supervised training schemes, particularly in regimes where fixed-grid architectures fail to generalize.

Conclusion: UniCSI successfully bridges the gap between heterogeneous CSI data and unified deep learning processing, preserving native waveform integrity while enabling seamless cross-domain transfer learning. The approach outperforms fixed-grid architectures, especially in generalization scenarios.

Abstract: Wi-Fi sensing promises to turn the everyday wireless signals that already surround us into ubiquitous sensors for human sensing. However, a fundamental obstacle is that CSI is acquired under diverse device-specific configurations, including different subcarrier counts, bandwidths, and carrier bands. Consequently, the resulting CSI tensors vary in both spectral resolution and tensor shape, making heterogeneous modeling challenging. Standard architectures struggle with such heterogeneity, forcing lossy pre-processing which compromises the underlying signal. To bridge this gap, we present UniCSI, a unified foundation architecture that directly operates on heterogeneous CSI while preserving the integrity of the native waveform. UniCSI hinges on two core innovations: (1) a physics-informed RF tokenizer that encodes each frequency channel based on its fractional position within the physical spectrum rather than rigid array indices. It preserves intrinsic spectral coherence and enables seamless, frequency resolution-agnostic processing across arbitrary sensing configurations. (2) a spectral aggregator that distills variable-length channel sequences into a fixed-size spectral signature, effectively decoupling the feature dimensionality from the physical subcarrier spacing. Extensive evaluations on a large-scale corpus of 25 heterogeneous public datasets, spanning 14 to 2048 subcarriers, 20 to 160 MHz bandwidth, and the 2.4 and 5 GHz bands, demonstrate that native heterogeneous ingestion substantially improves cross-domain transfer under both supervised and self-supervised training schemes, particularly in regimes where fixed-grid architectures fail to generalize.

</details>


### [229] [EvoSignal: LLM-Guided Evolutionary Design of Modular Traffic Signal Control Programs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09563)
*Leizhen Wang,Peibo Duan,Zhenlin Qin,Yancheng Ling,Jian Xu,Yue Wang,Hao Wang,Zhenliang Ma*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: EvoSignal is an LLM-guided evolutionary framework that automates the design of traffic signal control programs. It treats TSC as a modular program design problem, separating traffic feature extraction, local phase prioritization, and network-based priority adjustment. The framework evolves control programs starting from established strategies, using feedback on congestion and signal operation, without requiring online LLM inference during operation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing traffic signal control strategies require repeated manual design and adjustment to adapt to changing traffic demand and network conditions. While LLMs can automate this process, they leave decision rules embedded in black-box models and incur recurring inference costs and latency. There is a need for systematically exploring better control rules that are inspectable and transferable across networks.

Method: The paper formulates TSC as a modular program design problem and proposes EvoSignal. The modular representation separates: (1) traffic feature extraction, (2) local phase prioritization, and (3) optional network-based priority adjustment. Starting from several established strategies, EvoSignal improves programs through evolutionary algorithms guided by LLM, using feedback on congestion and signal operation. The resulting programs operate without online LLM inference.

Result: Simulation experiments across five scenarios on two real-world road networks show: (1) The selected default EvoSignal program reduces waiting time by 16.8-49.2% relative to the lowest waiting time achieved by 20 baselines (conventional, RL-based, and LLM-based) in each scenario. (2) A program prioritizing travel time and queue length outperforms all 20 baselines on all three metrics in the search scenario and remains among the top three on each metric when transferred to the other four scenarios.

Conclusion: The findings support automated design of inspectable control programs that transfer across evaluated road networks and traffic demands. The approach successfully creates effective TSC programs without online LLM inference costs, achieving superior performance across multiple metrics and scenarios.

Abstract: Effective traffic signal control (TSC) requires policies that respond to changing traffic demand and network conditions while meeting different control objectives. However, adapting existing strategies often involves repeated manual design and adjustment, making it difficult to systematically explore better control rules for a target network. Large language models (LLMs) can automate this process, but directly using them to select signal phases leaves decision rules embedded in black-box models and incurs recurring inference costs and latency. This paper formulates TSC as a modular program design problem and proposes EvoSignal, an LLM-guided evolutionary framework using traffic knowledge and performance feedback. The modular representation separates traffic feature extraction, local phase prioritization, and optional network-based priority adjustment. Starting from several established strategies, EvoSignal improves programs through feedback on congestion and signal operation, retaining strategies with different performance trade-offs. The resulting programs operate without online LLM inference. Simulation experiments across five scenarios on two real-world road networks show that the selected default EvoSignal program reduces waiting time by 16.8--49.2\% relative to the lowest waiting time achieved by the 20 conventional, reinforcement learning-based, and LLM-based baselines in each scenario. A program prioritizing travel time and queue length outperforms all 20 baselines on all three metrics in the search scenario and remains among the top three on each metric when transferred unchanged to the other four scenarios. These findings support automated design of inspectable control programs that transfer across the evaluated road networks and traffic demands.Code is available at https://github.com/georgewanglz2019/EvoSignal.

</details>


### [230] [Online Resource Allocation with an Endogenous Markov State: Fewer LP Solves Earn More](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09577)
*Zhaohua Chen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper studies finite-horizon online resource allocation with endogenous Markov states, where actions affect state transitions. It examines how often to re-solve the underlying optimization problem (LP) and shows that more frequent re-solving can actually perform worse (Ω(T) regret vs Θ(√T) for infrequent) under certain degeneracy conditions. A three-phase U-shaped policy is developed for unknown priors achieving O(1) or O(√T) regret depending on conditions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The key insight is to understand the regret behavior of different re-solving frequencies (frequent vs infrequent) in online resource allocation problems where the state evolution is endogenous (affected by actions). The paper challenges the intuition that more frequent optimization always leads to better performance.

Method: The analysis uses two LP frameworks: (1) transient fluid LP benchmark for upper bounds, and (2) stationary LP for randomized controls. Key regularity conditions: primal nondegeneracy and irreducibility of optimal induced kernel. For unknown priors, a three-phase U-shaped infrequent re-solving policy is developed coordinating learning and inventory correction.

Result: With known prior: O(1) regret under nondegeneracy/irreducibility for both approaches; Ω(T) regret for frequent re-solving vs Θ(√T) for infrequent under degeneracy. With unknown prior: O(1) regret (nondegeneracy) or O(√T) regret (degeneracy) when target class is known; linear regret unavoidable otherwise. Numerical experiments confirm infrequent schemes dominate.

Conclusion: Counterintuitively, more frequent optimization can be asymptotically worse. Infrequent re-solving schemes are more robust, especially under degenerate conditions. The work provides guidance on when frequent vs infrequent re-solving is appropriate and identifies key structural conditions (nondegeneracy, irreducibility) affecting regret rates.

Abstract: We study finite-horizon online resource allocation with i.i.d. requests and an endogenous Markov state on a finite state space: each action affects the transition of the state that governs future rewards and resource consumption. In this problem, a transient fluid LP benchmark upper bounds the expected reward of every nonanticipating policy, while a stationary LP supplies randomized state-dependent controls. We assume that the stationary LP has a unique optimum and identify primal nondegeneracy and irreducibility of the optimal induced kernel as important regularity conditions in this framework. With a known request prior, we show that, under nondegeneracy and irreducibility, both frequent and infrequent re-solving attain $O(1)$ regret. However, under a degenerate optimum, irreducibility yields the sharp worst-case $Θ(\sqrt{T})$ rate for infrequent re-solving, while frequent re-solving can incur $Ω(T)$ regret. Thus, more frequent optimization can perform asymptotically worse. With an unknown request prior, we develop a three-phase U-shaped infrequent re-solving policy that coordinates learning and inventory correction with $O(\log\log T)$ LP solves. When the optimal induced kernel is irreducible and the algorithm is given the optimal target state class and a constant-cost entrance policy, it attains $O(1)$ regret under nondegeneracy and $O(\sqrt{T})$ regret under degeneracy. Without the target-class information, linear minimax regret is unavoidable. Numerical experiments further illustrate the instability of round-by-round re-solving relative to epoch-wise infrequent re-solving, show that thresholding greatly mitigates its loss, and find that infrequent schemes remain dominant under both known and estimated priors.

</details>


### [231] [Collaborative Reasoning Distillation via Cross-Feedback and Coherent Curation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09587)
*Taehoon Kim,Seunggeun Cho,Dongsu Han*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CRD (Collaborative Reasoning Distillation) is a framework for distilling reasoning capabilities from large teacher models to smaller student models. It uses interactive cross-feedback between teachers, fine-grained step-wise quality assessment, and coherence-aware step stitching to train compact models via Reasoning Quality Optimization (RQO). The resulting CRD-4B model achieves 97.3% on MATH-500 and 70.3% on AIME'25 with only 50K training examples.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current approaches for reasoning in LLMs require massive computational budgets or fail to effectively distill reasoning to smaller models. Standard distillation methods rely on outcome-based rewards and cannot distinguish between sound reasoning and lucky guesses.

Method: CRD introduces three innovations: (1) interactive cross-feedback where teachers iteratively critique each other's reasoning, (2) fine-grained step-wise quality assessment capturing logical validity independent of final answers, and (3) coherence-aware step stitching that synthesizes complementary strengths. Students are trained via Reasoning Quality Optimization (RQO) with budget constraints.

Result: CRD-4B achieves 97.3% on MATH-500 and 70.3% on AIME'25, using only 50K training examples, which is up to 12 times smaller than datasets of comparable models.

Conclusion: The proposed CRD framework successfully enhances reasoning in compact models through collaborative teacher feedback and quality-aware training, achieving state-of-the-art results with significantly less training data.

Abstract: Reasoning capabilities are critical for advancing Large Language Models, yet current approaches either require massive computational budgets or struggle to effectively distill reasoning to smaller models. Standard distillation methods rely on outcome-based rewards, failing to distinguish between sound reasoning and lucky guesses. We propose Collaborative Reasoning Distillation (CRD), a framework that enhances reasoning in compact models through three innovations: (1) interactive cross-feedback where teachers iteratively critique each other's reasoning, (2) fine-grained step-wise quality assessment capturing logical validity independent of final answers, and (3) coherence-aware step stitching that synthesizes complementary strengths. Students are trained via Reasoning Quality Optimization (RQO) with budget constraints. Our model, CRD-4B, achieves 97.3% on MATH-500 and 70.3% on AIME'25, surpassing baselines while using only 50K training examples, up to 12 times smaller than the datasets of comparable models.

</details>


### [232] [COPC: Coupled Off-Policy Correction for Asynchronous LLM Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09597)
*Zicheng Hu,Zhijian Zhou,Xuan Zhang,Yuchen Liu,Cheng Chen,Yuan Li,Qi Gu,Yan Feng,Hongyan Hao,Chao Qu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses a fundamental limitation in asynchronous reinforcement learning for LLM post-training: the reliance on stale trajectories. The authors identify that existing methods only correct token-level policy mismatch but ignore "advantage staleness" - the bias in advantage estimates from behavior-policy continuations. They propose COPC (Coupled Off-Policy Correction), which jointly corrects both policy-side and advantage-side errors through coordinated token-level ratio masking and two-sided clipped-ratio weighting of TD residuals.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation stems from a key limitation in asynchronous RL for LLM post-training: while decoupling rollout generation from optimization accelerates training, it introduces "staleness" - the model trains on outdated trajectories. Prior work focused on correcting token-level policy mismatch (policy-side correction), but the authors identify that this is insufficient because advantage estimates also inherit mismatch from behavior-policy continuations, which they term "advantage staleness."

Method: The authors derive exact bias and variance decompositions for a general two-channel actor update, revealing nonseparable coupling between policy-weight and advantage-estimation errors. This theoretical analysis shows that the interaction induces multiplicative bias terms, while squared policy weights amplify advantage uncertainty in gradient variance. Based on this, they propose COPC (Coupled Off-Policy Correction), an actor-critic method that combines: (1) token-level ratio masking for policy-side correction, and (2) two-sided clipped-ratio weighting of TD residuals for both return and advantage estimation.

Result: COPC achieves the highest reported performance on tool-integrated mathematical reasoning and search tasks, outperforming the strongest reported asynchronous baseline in each setting. It offers a broad high-performing parameter region and improved training stability. In search tasks, COPC remains stable throughout training while most evaluated baselines collapse late in training. These gains persist at 64-step policy staleness. COPC adds minimal step-time overhead over asynchronous PPO and retains a 1.7× step-time speedup over synchronous PPO.

Conclusion: The paper demonstrates that policy-side correction alone is insufficient in asynchronous RL; advantage-side correction must be coordinated with policy-side correction. The proposed COPC method successfully addresses both sources of staleness through coupled corrections, achieving superior performance and stability compared to existing asynchronous baselines while maintaining computational efficiency.

Abstract: Asynchronous RL accelerates large language model post-training by decoupling rollout generation from optimization, but trains on stale trajectories. Existing methods primarily correct token-level policy mismatch through importance-ratio control in the actor objective. We show that this \emph{policy-side correction} alone is insufficient: advantage estimates also inherit mismatch from behavior-policy continuations, which we term \emph{advantage staleness}. We derive exact bias and variance decompositions for a general two-channel actor update, revealing nonseparable coupling between policy-weight and advantage-estimation errors: their interaction induces multiplicative bias terms, while squared policy weights amplify advantage uncertainty in gradient variance. This motivates the hypothesis that policy- and advantage-side correction should be coordinated. We introduce Coupled Off-Policy Correction (COPC), an actor--critic method combining token-level ratio masking with two-sided clipped-ratio weighting of TD residuals for return and advantage estimation. Joint parameter sweeps across staleness levels support this hypothesis: the effect of one correction parameter depends on, and can reverse with, the other. COPC achieves the highest reported performance on tool-integrated mathematical reasoning and search, outperforming the strongest reported asynchronous baseline in each setting. It also offers a broad high-performing parameter region and improved training stability. In search, COPC remains stable throughout training, while most evaluated asynchronous baselines collapse late in training. These gains persist at 64-step policy staleness. COPC adds minimal step-time overhead over asynchronous PPO and retains a $1.7\times$ step-time speedup over synchronous PPO.

</details>


### [233] [Lightweight and Versatile Learned Optimization by Recombination of Gradient History](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09604)
*Minyoung Choi,Dalta Imam Maulana,Wanyeong Jung*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A lightweight learned optimizer that uses gradient history represented as averages over disjoint time spans, with a 37k-parameter network achieving strong zero-shot generalization across unseen tasks including BERT, GPT, Vision Transformer, and graph models, with minimal FLOPs overhead (0.3%).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional learned optimizers often require large parameter counts and significant memory overhead for storing long gradient histories. This work aims to create a lightweight, versatile optimizer that can efficiently handle gradient history while maintaining low computational overhead and generalizing well to unseen tasks.

Method: The optimizer dynamically recombines gradient history represented as averages over disjoint time spans. It reduces the prediction space to one scalar coefficient per gradient average, which is shared across multiple parameters. Older gradients are progressively averaged to minimize memory cost while keeping their contributions independently accessible.

Result: The 37k-parameter network trained in 0.87 GPU-hours generalizes zero-shot to unseen tasks. Results include: 9.1% and 0.4% validation loss reduction on BERT-Tiny and GPT-Tiny respectively; 3.5 percentage points improvement in test accuracy over Adam on Vision Transformer; 2.7 percentage points average improvement across nine graph models; with FLOPs overhead as low as 0.3%.

Conclusion: The proposed learned optimizer achieves strong zero-shot generalization to unseen tasks with minimal computational overhead, demonstrating that a compact optimizer (37k parameters) can effectively replace hand-crafted optimizers like Adam across diverse domains including NLP, vision, and graph neural networks.

Abstract: This paper presents a lightweight and versatile learned optimizer that dynamically recombines gradient history, represented as averages over disjoint time spans. The optimizer reduces the prediction space to one scalar coefficient per gradient average, shared by multiple parameters. Progressively averaging older gradients minimizes memory cost of long history, while keeping their contributions independently accessible. A 37k-parameter network trained in 0.87 GPU-hours generalizes zero-shot to unseen tasks, lowering validation loss by 9.1% and 0.4% on BERT-Tiny and GPT-Tiny, and improving test accuracy over Adam by 3.5 %p on a Vision Transformer and by 2.7 %p on average across nine graph models, with FLOPs overhead as low as 0.3%.

</details>


### [234] [Decoupled Optimization for Teacher-Student Semi-Supervised Learning via a Pioneer Student](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09609)
*Haorong Han,Jidong Yuan,Chixuan Wei,Yongqi Sun*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper identifies two optimization pathologies in semi-supervised learning: (1) parameter coupling in Teacher-Student framework causing synchronization constraints and limited generalization, and (2) gradient imbalance between labeled/unlabeled losses leading to premature convergence. It proposes Pioneer Student (PiS), an auxiliary branch with independent parameter space that periodically transfers knowledge back to the main T-S model.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Semi-supervised learning relies on self-training (Teacher-Student framework) and joint optimization of labeled/unlabeled losses, but both mechanisms introduce distinct optimization pathologies that limit performance. The motivation is to address these fundamental limitations in SSL methods.

Method: The proposed Pioneer Student (PiS) is an auxiliary branch that operates in an independent parameter space from the Teacher-Student model. It periodically transfers accumulated knowledge back to the T-S model, addressing both parameter coupling and gradient imbalance issues.

Result: PiS is a universal plug-and-play module that consistently improves mainstream SSL methods across extensive experiments.

Conclusion: The Pioneer Student approach successfully addresses both optimization pathologies in SSL by using an independent parameter space and periodic knowledge transfer, providing a universal improvement to existing SSL methods.

Abstract: Semi-supervised learning (SSL) relies on two core mechanisms: self-training under the Teacher-Student (T-S) framework and joint optimization of labeled and unlabeled losses. Despite their effectiveness, we find both mechanisms introduce distinct optimization pathologies. First, parameter coupling enforces strict synchronization between teacher and student, where strong regularization on the student degrades the teacher's fitting ability, thereby limiting the permissible generalization intensity. Second, the imbalance in gradient update consistency between labeled and unlabeled losses drives the shared parameters to prematurely converge to labeled-dominated local minima, creating a bottleneck for global optimization. To address both issues, we propose the Pioneer Student (PiS), an auxiliary branch that operates in an independent parameter space and periodically transfers accumulated knowledge back to the T-S model. Extensive experiments show that PiS is a universal plug-and-play module that consistently improves mainstream SSL methods.

</details>


### [235] [Sequential Pretraining Favors Large Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09611)
*Mohnish Harwani,Yujia Zheng*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates why large neural networks learn capabilities that small models cannot acquire, proposing that this advantage stems from robustness to primacy bias (impaired learning from early data distributions) rather than learning more representative features. The authors introduce Exposure Therapy (ET), a regularization method that improves small models' performance on late training data distributions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large neural networks acquire capabilities that small models fail to learn. The authors investigate whether this stems from learning more representative features or from being more robust to adverse training effects, specifically defining and quantifying "primacy bias" as the impairment of later learning caused by early data distributions.

Method: The authors define and quantify primacy bias as the extent to which exposure to early data distributions impairs later learning. They compare small vs. overparameterized models' ability to allocate learning capacity efficiently across sequential data distributions. They then propose Exposure Therapy (ET), a simple regularization technique that promotes more efficient allocation of learning capacity during sequential pretraining.

Result: Small models inefficiently allocate learning capacity toward early distributions, while sufficiently overparameterized models are robust to this effect. ET improves foundation models' performance on late data distributions and overall capability in models up to the billion-parameter scale.

Conclusion: Some benefits of large foundation models arise from greater robustness to adverse training effects (primacy bias) rather than learning more representative features. Improved training algorithms like Exposure Therapy can recover some advantages in smaller models, particularly for learning late-distributed data such as code, mathematics, and reasoning.

Abstract: Large neural networks often acquire capabilities that small models fail to learn. Does this stem from large models learning more representative features, or from being more robust to unaccounted-for adverse effects introduced during training? We define and quantify one such adverse effect, primacy bias, as the extent to which exposure to early data distributions impairs later learning. We show that small models can allocate learning capacity inefficiently toward early distributions, whereas sufficiently overparameterized models are robust to this effect. This inefficiency is particularly consequential in pretraining, where foundation models often encounter heterogeneous data distributions sequentially rather than jointly. As a result, small foundation models can struggle to learn distributions encountered late in training, which is particularly harmful when later data emphasizes desirable capabilities such as code, mathematics, and reasoning. Motivated by these findings, we introduce Exposure Therapy (ET), a simple regularization that promotes more efficient allocation of learning capacity during sequential pretraining. We demonstrate that ET improves foundation models' performance on late data distributions as well as overall capability in models up to the billion-parameter scale. Overall, our results suggest that some benefits of large foundation models may arise from greater robustness to adverse training effects, rather than from learning more representative features, and that improved training algorithms can recover some of these advantages in smaller models.

</details>


### [236] [The Identifiability and Observability of Deep Normalized Attention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09620)
*Pranav Venkata Konda*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates which parameters of deep, unmasked, single-head attention mechanisms are determined by the input-output function. It focuses on real-analytic normalizers (including softmax) and proves a conjecture by Henry-Marchetti-Kohn, showing that the function generically determines effective scores and combined value maps up to signs induced by even normalizers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to understand the identifiability of attention mechanism parameters from input-output behavior. This is important for understanding what information can be extracted from transformer models and for theoretical analysis of attention mechanisms. The paper addresses a conjecture in the field and provides classification of exceptional cases where parameter identification fails.

Method: The methods used include: (1) real-analytic function theory for normalizers, (2) classification of exceptional fibers under explicit normalizer conditions, (3) Taylor expansion analysis for local identification, (4) Jacobian analysis near query/key collapse, and (5) high-precision numerical calculations to illustrate numerical sensitivity loss.

Result: Key results include: (1) proof of the real-analytic case of the Henry-Marchetti-Kohn conjecture including softmax, (2) classification of when collapse makes scores unobservable, (3) sharp Taylor orders for local identification, (4) complete native Jacobian decay spectrum computation, and (5) formula for contact order $2k3^{i-1}-1$ for layer $i$ with first nonconstant normalizer degree $k$, including exact multiplicities and kernel dimension.

Conclusion: The paper establishes theoretical foundations for parameter identification in attention mechanisms, showing that under certain conditions parameters are determinable from input-output functions while identifying exceptional cases where identification fails. It provides precise characterization of numerical sensitivity loss through Jacobian decay and contact order formulas.

Abstract: We study which parameters of deep, unmasked, single-head attention are determined by its input--output function. For known positive nonconstant real-analytic normalizers, the function generically determines the effective scores and combined value map up to the signs induced by even normalizers. This proves the real-analytic case of a conjecture of Henry--Marchetti--Kohn, including softmax. We then classify exceptional fibers under explicit normalizer conditions, identifying when collapse makes later scores unobservable, and establish sharp Taylor orders for local identification. Near simultaneous query/key collapse, we compute the complete native Jacobian decay spectrum on separating finite input banks. For common first nonconstant normalizer degree $k$, layer $i$ has contact order $2k3^{i-1}-1$, with exact multiplicities and kernel dimension. High-precision and automatic differentiation calculations illustrate the resulting loss of numerical sensitivity.

</details>


### [237] [When does a network's training history predict its future learning better than its current state? Evidence from a response probe and a forecasting screen](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09621)
*Martin Hofmann,Patrick Mäder*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper investigates whether the training history of a neural network provides predictive information about future learning that cannot be captured by measuring the network's current state alone. Using small multilayer perceptrons trained under various history regimes, the authors find that history-based predictions generally do not outperform current-state models, except during early training when the current state is not yet informative about the target.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To determine whether the training path of a neural network carries information about future learning that is missed by measurements of the current state alone. This relates to understanding loss of plasticity and critical periods in neural networks.

Method: Main study: 42 training histories on small MLPs, future learning measured at 4 checkpoints using a probe (network copy trained for 100 updates on a new task). The probe was validated through tests for function-preserving rescaling, repeatability (ICC 0.940), and re-initialization detection. Companion study: 1,560 synthetic regression runs testing prediction of final error.

Result: History state (≤4 dimensions) did not improve prediction over calibrated current state model (gain -21.4%, 90% CI [-91.9, 8.1]). In companion study, history models predicted final error better than validation error after 12 epochs (30.3% improvement) but were indistinguishable after 48 epochs.

Conclusion: Training history is only informative about future learning during early training phases when the current network state has not yet become informative about the target. Once the current state becomes predictive, history adds no additional value. This suggests the current state captures all relevant information once the network has learned sufficient structure.

Abstract: Networks that behave alike now can still learn differently when training continues. Work on loss of plasticity and critical periods shows that the path to a state shapes what follows; it does not show whether the path carries information that a measurement of the state itself misses. We ask when the training history of a network predicts its future learning better than its current state. In a main study, small multilayer perceptrons were trained under three history regimes (42 histories), and future learning was measured at four checkpoints by a short probe: a copy of the network trained for 100 updates on a new task. Before the prediction result was read, the protocol checked the probe. It responded monotonically to a function-preserving rescaling of hidden units, repeated measurements agreed (intraclass correlation 0.940, [0.903, 0.997], in the least reliable class, mean of three repeats), and a re-initialisation of units was visible directly after it but not 100 to 200 updates later. A history state of at most four dimensions did not improve on a calibrated model of the current state (gain -21.4%, 90% interval [-91.9, 8.1]; required in advance: 10%). A companion screen on 1,560 synthetic regression runs asked the same question for a target further away, the final error of the run. There, history models forecast better than the current validation error after 12 of up to 240 epochs (compact state 30.3%, [15.8, 39.4], a contextual comparison) and were not distinguishable from it after 48. In both studies the history was informative only while the current state was not yet informative about the target; this reading was formed after the results.

</details>


### [238] [When Rank Rises as LLMs Degrade](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09647)
*Zhaohui Geoffrey Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper challenges the common assumption that representation rank decreases when language models degrade during post-training. Through controlled experiments on Qwen3-0.6B, the authors show that different degradation modes (data duplication, learning-rate misconfiguration) affect spectral statistics (RankMe, covariance effective rank) in different and sometimes counterintuitive directions. They propose a two-sided multichannel monitoring approach but find that spectral monitoring cannot predict failure earlier than held-out loss and requires held-out healthy data for calibration.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Practitioners monitor LLM representation health using spectral statistics like RankMe, assuming rank falls when representations degrade. This paper investigates whether this assumption holds during LLM post-training, as misunderstanding the relationship between degradation and spectral metrics could lead to incorrect monitoring and failed deployments.

Method: Controlled study on Qwen3-0.6B with four degradation modes (including data duplication and learning-rate misconfiguration) and three random seeds. The authors examined RankMe (uncentred and centered), covariance effective rank, and k95 statistics. They tested a two-sided multichannel sequential monitor with separate calibration and test data in a pre-registered shared-prefix, leave-one-seed-out evaluation.

Result: Data duplication increased held-out loss by 75% relative to healthy while INCREASING both original and centered RankMe (by 13.5 pooled standard deviations). Covariance effective rank rose to nearly twice its healthy value. This represents "spectral dispersion" rather than collapse. Learning-rate misconfiguration lowered centered RankMe and k95, while uncentered RankMe was inconsistent. The monitoring approach detected all three damage regimes but never preceded held-out probe loss, and calibration with two seeds produced false alarms on the held-out healthy seed.

Conclusion: Spectral monitoring direction is regime-statistic dependent and cannot be fixed by recalibration alone. Different degradation modes affect spectral statistics differently (some increase rank, some decrease). Spectral monitoring can diagnose failure regimes but does not warn earlier than held-out loss, and validity claims require held-out healthy data. The authors distinguish between RankMe (normalizes singular values) and covariance effective rank (normalizes eigenvalues), which behave differently on raw intermediate-layer states.

Abstract: Post-training adapts language models in non-stationary environments. Practitioners monitor representation health with RankMe and related spectral statistics, often assuming that rank falls when representations degrade. We show that this assumption is unsafe for LLM post-training. In a controlled study of Qwen3-0.6B with four degradation modes and three seeds, data duplication worsens held-out loss by 75% relative to healthy while increasing both original and centred RankMe; the latter changes by 13.5 pooled standard deviations. Covariance effective rank rises to nearly twice its healthy value. This failure is spectral dispersion rather than collapse, so a one-sided monitor rates the worst checkpoint as the healthiest. By contrast, a learning-rate misconfiguration lowers centred RankMe and k95, while uncentred RankMe is inconsistent across seeds. Direction is therefore a property of the regime-statistic pair and cannot be fixed by recalibration alone. We also distinguish two often-conflated statistics: RankMe normalises singular values, whereas covariance effective rank normalises eigenvalues. On raw intermediate-layer states in the pretrained model, massive activations pin the latter near 1 out of dimension d while RankMe retains usable range. We then test a two-sided, multichannel sequential monitor with separate calibration and test data. In a pre-registered shared-prefix, leave-one-seed-out evaluation, it detects all three damage regimes in every fold 10 to 60 steps after the fork and separates dispersion from downward-rank damage by firing direction. However, it never precedes held-out probe loss, and calibration with two seeds produces false alarms on the held-out healthy seed. Spectral monitoring can diagnose failure regimes, but it does not warn earlier than held-out loss, and validity claims require held-out healthy data.

</details>


### [239] [Closed-Form Noise Calibration Against Membership Inference for Random-Allocation DP-SGD](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09651)
*Murat Bilgehan Ertan,Marten van Dijk*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper presents a one-line formula for bounding membership inference attack (MIA) accuracy on models trained with DP-SGD using random allocation. The formula provides interpretable, fast (microsecond) privacy guarantees using only M (steps per epoch), E (epochs), and σ (noise multiplier). It requires approximately half the noise of state-of-the-art closed-form bounds. An exact expression is also derived that needs 13-20% less noise than the formula in experiments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: DP-SGD protects training data by adding Gaussian noise to clipped gradients, but choosing the appropriate noise level requires expensive privacy accounting. Existing methods are computationally intensive or require conservative bounds. The authors aim to provide a fast, interpretable, and tight bound for membership inference attack accuracy under random allocation.

Method: The authors derive the bound using chi-square divergence between a Gaussian distribution and a Gaussian mixture that dominates random allocation. They also derive an exact expression for attack accuracy of these two distributions for numerical evaluation. The method relates MIA accuracy to the divergence between distributions of model outputs for member vs. non-member training data.

Result: The one-line formula gives attack accuracy ≤ ½ + ¼√((1 + (e^(1/σ²) - 1)/M)^E - 1). This bound needs at most ~half the noise of state-of-the-art closed-form bounds. The exact expression requires 13.0% to 20.2% less noise than the formula in experiments. The exact method is found in seconds and certified in minutes, while search-based accountants took longer or required at least 0.62% more noise. MIAs on trained models stay below the bound.

Conclusion: The proposed formula provides a fast, interpretable, and tight bound for privacy guarantees in DP-SGD with random allocation. The exact expression further reduces noise requirements while remaining computationally tractable. Both methods outperform existing privacy accountants in terms of noise efficiency and computation time, providing practical tools for privacy-preserving machine learning.

Abstract: DP-SGD protects training data by adding Gaussian noise to clipped gradients. The amount of noise is usually chosen by running a numerical privacy accountant inside a search. We study DP-SGD with random allocation, where each epoch uses every record once, at a randomly chosen step. For this setting we give a one-line formula that bounds the accuracy of every membership inference attack (MIA) on the trained model. With $M$ steps per epoch, $E$ epochs and noise multiplier $σ$, and with membership and non-membership equally likely a priori, the attack accuracy is at most $\frac12+\frac14\sqrt{(1+(e^{1/σ^2}-1)/M)^E-1}$. The formula comes from the chi-square divergence between a Gaussian distribution and a Gaussian mixture that dominates random allocation. It is interpretable and gives $σ$ in about a microsecond. Where applicable, our formula needs at most about half the noise of the state-of-the-art closed-form bound. To measure how close the bound is, we also derive an exact expression for the attack accuracy of these two distributions and evaluate it numerically. Calibrating to this exact expression requires $13.0\%$ to $20.2\%$ less noise than the formula in our main experiments, and since it is exact, no accountant that knows only $M$, $E$ and $σ$ can certify a smaller $σ$. In training, the resulting $σ$ outperforms the formula and matches a published accountant in test accuracy. It is found in seconds and certified in minutes, whereas every search we ran with that accountant took longer or returned at least $0.62\%$ more noise. We show that MIAs on the trained models stay below the bound.

</details>


### [240] [DSTNet: Dynamic Spectral Trajectory Network for Causal Multi-Horizon Financial Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09654)
*Aashish Bohra,Lokendra Vishwakarm*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: DSTNet is a novel wavelet-based financial forecasting model that uses a causal Dynamic Spectral Trajectory built from technical indicators with a Factorized Scale-Temporal Spectral Transformer fused with CNN-BiLSTM. It outperforms all competitors including random-walk persistence across 7 equity indices and gold for 1-10 day forecasts, achieving 0.7-4.5% improvement, though downstream allocation shows no equity-timing advantage.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current wavelet-based financial forecasters have three key limitations: (1) using transform only for denoising rather than full temporal analysis, (2) reducing data to a single spectral snapshot at forecast origin, and (3) using bilateral convolution that can read past the forecast origin, introducing look-ahead bias.

Method: DSTNet retains the recent evolution of filter-bank magnitudes as a causal Dynamic Spectral Trajectory, built from seven trailing technical indicators over a twenty-day lookback with a one-sided Morlet-derived filter bank and explicit burn-in for left-boundary transient. A Factorized Scale-Temporal Spectral Transformer attends along time and filter-bank axes separately, a learned gate fuses the spectral branch with a CNN-BiLSTM, and horizon-specific gates emit one, three, five, and ten day forecasts in a single pass.

Result: Under MAE and MAPE metrics, random-walk persistence is the strongest of ten fixed competitors in 29 of 32 series-horizon cells. DSTNet is the only model below persistence in every cell, with improvements of 0.7 to 0.9 percent at one day and 3.4 to 4.5 percent at ten days. At one day, paired testing favors DSTNet against weaker learned baselines but is inconclusive against persistence and the strongest learned forecasters.

Conclusion: DSTNet achieves superior forecasting accuracy over all competitors including the strong persistence benchmark across multiple horizons and assets. However, a downstream allocation diagnostic does not support an equity-timing advantage on any of the seven indices, suggesting the statistical forecasting gains may not translate to practical trading profitability.

Abstract: Wavelet-based financial forecasters typically use the transform only to denoise, or reduce it to a single spectral snapshot at the forecast origin, and the convolution that produces the coefficients is usually bilateral, so it can read past the forecast origin. DSTNet instead retains the recent evolution of filter-bank magnitudes as a causal Dynamic Spectral Trajectory, built from seven trailing technical indicators over a twenty-day lookback with a one-sided Morlet-derived filter bank and an explicit burn-in for the left-boundary transient. A factorized Scale-Temporal Spectral Transformer attends along the time and filter-bank axes separately, a learned gate fuses the spectral branch with a CNN-BiLSTM, and horizon-specific gates emit one, three, five, and ten day forecasts in a single pass. We evaluate seven equity indices and gold under a common expanding-window protocol and an untouched one-year hold-out, against nine learned baselines and a random-walk persistence benchmark. Under MAE and MAPE, persistence is the strongest of the ten fixed competitors in 29 of the 32 series-horizon cells and DSTNet is the only model below it in every cell, by 0.7 to 0.9 percent at one day and 3.4 to 4.5 percent at ten days. At one day, paired testing favours DSTNet against the weaker learned baselines but is inconclusive against persistence and the strongest learned forecasters. A downstream allocation diagnostic does not support an equity-timing advantage on any of the seven indices.

</details>


### [241] [Gauss-Newton Accuracy and Indefinite Hessians: Uniform Coexistence in Low-Cost Sets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09675)
*Kihun Rhee,Hanjoon Byun*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper analyzes the accuracy of Gauss-Newton curvature approximation in ridge-regularized nonlinear least squares. It establishes theoretical bounds on Hessian approximation error, proves coexistence of multiple curvature regimes, and provides a pointwise certificate for controlling Hessian corrections. The work shows that a single positive ridge cap works uniformly across perturbations, with neighborhoods that remain stable as ridge weight approaches zero.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The Gauss-Newton method is widely used for nonlinear least squares problems, but understanding the quality of its curvature approximation—especially under ridge regularization—remains incomplete. This work aims to establish precise error bounds for Gauss-Newton curvature and understand when this approximation remains reliable versus when it fails, which is crucial for optimization theory and practical algorithms.

Method: The analysis uses local regularity assumptions and persistence of level-set curvature magnitude along an exact-fit section. The authors employ a pointwise certificate approach based on the current prediction level set to control normal, mixed, and tangent parts of the Hessian correction. Structural analysis provides full Jacobian row rank results throughout low-cost sets.

Result: Key results include: (1) Uniform coexistence of two curvature regimes under stated conditions; (2) Global minimizers exist with relative Hessian error below (1+√2)/8 ≈ 0.4268; (3) A point exists with indefinite Hessian and relative error at least 15/8 = 1.875; (4) A single positive ridge cap works for all independent center and label perturbations in fixed neighborhoods; (5) These neighborhoods don't shrink as ridge weight approaches zero; (6) Sharp relative-error bounds are proven over the pointwise class.

Conclusion: The paper establishes a comprehensive theory of Gauss-Newton curvature accuracy in ridge-regularized nonlinear least squares. The key insight is that both reliable (low-error) and unreliable (high-error with indefinite Hessian) curvature regimes can coexist uniformly. The pointwise certificate provides a practical tool for assessing approximation quality, and the persistence of neighborhood sizes as ridge weight → 0 is particularly notable for practical implementation.

Abstract: We study the accuracy of Gauss-Newton curvature in ridge-regularized nonlinear least squares. Under local regularity and persistence of level-set curvature magnitude along an exact-fit section, we prove uniform coexistence of two curvature regimes. Global minimizers exist, and every global minimizer has relative Hessian error below $(1+\sqrt2)/8$, while the same low-cost set contains a point with an indefinite Hessian and relative error at least $15/8$. One positive ridge cap works for all independent center and label perturbations in fixed neighborhoods and every positive ridge weight up to the cap. These neighborhoods do not shrink as the ridge weight tends to zero. A pointwise certificate based on the current prediction level set controls the normal, mixed, and tangent parts of the Hessian correction. We prove a sharp relative-error bound over the stated pointwise class when the prediction map and ridge vary. Analytic examples describe the roles of output alignment, curvature orientation, and persistence. A separate structural result gives full Jacobian row rank throughout low-cost sets and exact interpolation near a rank-deficient reference.

</details>


### [242] [CERO: Where and When to Allocate Rollouts for RL Post-Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09679)
*Yiming Zong,Yige Wang,Xing Hu,Jiashuo Jiang,Zuo-Jun Max Shen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces CERO, an online primal-dual scheduler for coordinating finite rollout budgets across prompts in group-relative reinforcement learning. It adapts prompt selection, revisit frequency, and group generation count across training rounds, achieving state-of-the-art results on mathematical reasoning benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current adaptive rollout methods allocate fixed per-update budgets across prompts, but this doesn't optimize the finite rollout budget over the entire training horizon. The authors seek to coordinate how budget is spent across time to maximize cumulative prompt exposure utility.

Method: The problem is formulated using a concave surrogate utility of cumulative prompt exposure. CERO uses: (1) a compact Fenchel representation to linearize dependence on cumulative exposure; (2) projected online gradient descent for updating prompt-specific supporting slopes and shared budget price using reward-variation feedback and budget deviations. Each admitted prompt receives a fixed-size response group.

Result: Under matched training-response budgets, CERO attains the highest avg@16 macro-average on each of three backbones across five mathematical reasoning benchmarks. Mechanistic analyses link CERO's prompt choices to within-group reward contrast. Multi-seed ablations show gains from adaptive pacing over both uniform and preset spending schedules.

Conclusion: Adaptive budget pacing across the training horizon significantly outperforms fixed-rate and preset spending approaches. The method provides theoretical pathwise guarantees against fixed-rate and same-path time-varying benchmarks with explicit terms for proxy discrepancy and rate variation.

Abstract: Adaptive rollout methods for group-relative reinforcement learning typically allocate a fixed per-update budget across prompts. We instead study how to coordinate a finite rollout budget over the entire training horizon. We formulate this problem using a concave surrogate utility of cumulative prompt exposure and introduce CERO, an online primal dual scheduler for prompt admission and budget pacing. In our experiments, each admitted prompt receives a fixed-size response group. CERO instead adapts which prompts are selected, how often they are revisited across rounds, and how many groups are generated in each round. A compact Fenchel representation linearizes the dependence on cumulative exposure, while projected online gradient descent updates prompt-specific supporting slopes and a shared budget price using reward-variation feedback and budget deviations. We establish pathwise guarantees for the surrogate allocation objective against fixed-rate and same-path time-varying benchmarks, with explicit terms for proxy discrepancy and rate variation. Under matched training-response budgets, CERO attains the highest avg@16 macro-average on each of three backbones across five mathematical reasoning benchmarks. Mechanistic analyses link CERO's prompt choices to within-group reward contrast, while multi-seed ablations show gains from adaptive pacing over both uniform and preset spending schedules.

</details>


### [243] [Few-Shot Learning for Personalised Automated Pain Assessment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09692)
*Heinke Hihn,Ibrahim Eisawy,Patrick Thiam,Hans A. Kestler,Friedhelm Schwenker*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper evaluates Few-Shot Learning (FSL), a Meta-Learning approach, for personalized automated pain assessment to address inter-subject variability in pain perception. The method treats subject-level evaluation as a task-domain shift and uses support-conditioned few-shot adaptation to improve performance across three databases.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Pain perception varies substantially across individuals, making it difficult for population-based classifiers to generalize across all subjects. The need for personalized classifiers that can adapt to individual subjects is the primary motivation, as standard population-level models fail to account for this inter-subject variability.

Method: The study re-interprets the shift from population-level to subject-level evaluation as a task-domain shift (classes fixed, target subject changes). They evaluate Few-Shot Learning with k-shot conditioning on three datasets: BioVid Pain Database, SenseEmotion Database, and PainMonit Experimental Dataset (PMED). They use Leave-One-Subject-Out Cross-Validation protocol.

Result: BioVid: 85.75% (binary) / 35.49% (multi-class); SenseEmotion: 82.37% (binary) / 41.88% (multi-class); PMED: 90.47% (binary). With k-shot conditioning: 86.25%, 40.06%, 83.43%, 44.08%, and 91.25% respectively. Additional ablation experiments and personalisation effects were investigated.

Conclusion: Support-conditioned few-shot adaptation can improve average performance under inter-subject variability, suggesting FSL is a viable approach for personalizing automated pain assessment. The method shows improvements across all datasets and settings when using k-shot conditioning.

Abstract: Pain perception varies substantially across individuals, making it difficult for population-based classifiers to generalise across all subjects in a dataset. One way to account for subject variability is to train personalised classifiers. In this work, we evaluate Few-Shot Learning, a sub-area of Meta-Learning, as an approach to personalisation in automated pain assessment. We re-interpret the shift from population-level to subject-level evaluation as a task-domain shift, where the observed classes remain fixed but the target subject changes. We evaluate our method on the BioVid Pain Database, the SenseEmotion Database, and the PainMonit Experimental Dataset (PMED), reaching 85.75% and 35.49% accuracy on BioVid and 82.37% and 41.88% on SenseEmotion in the binary and multi-class settings under a Leave-One-Subject-Out CV protocol respectively, and 90.47% on PMED, for which only a binary benchmark exists. Using samples to implement k-shot conditioning, the accuracies can be improved to 86.25%, 40.06%, 83.43%, 44.08%, and 91.25%, respectively. To further evaluate the effects and robustness of our method, we provide additional ablation experiments and investigate the personalisation effects. Our results suggest that support-conditioned few-shot adaptation can improve average performance under inter-subject variability.

</details>


### [244] [Pretraining Shapes Spectral Structure: Architecture- and Strategy-Conditional Prediction of OOD Robustness in Foundation Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09709)
*Sangyoon Bae,Sk Miraj Ahmed,Shinjae Yoo,Jiook Cha*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper presents a method to predict out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization of foundation models using only pretrained weight statistics, without requiring any target data. The key insight is that OOD robustness is encoded in the spectral structure of pretrained weights, which is shaped by both architecture and pretraining strategy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors address a critical gap in ML practice: currently, determining whether a foundation model will generalize OOD requires target domain data, which doesn't exist before a target domain is defined. Existing diagnostics either need source/target data or fail to distinguish robust from fragile models. The motivation is to enable OOD robustness assessment at model-selection time, before committing resources to any target domain.

Method: The authors prove that OOD accuracy gap is bounded by source representation concentration. They compute a statistic from pretrained weights as a proxy for this concentration. The key insight is that the direction of this proxy reverses between architecture families, so it's operationalized within "cells" - combinations of (architecture X strategy). They validate across 116 models spanning 7 modalities, and perform external validation on EEG, genomic, and protein data.

Result: Two main results: (1) Pooled across all 116 models, a single statistic ranks OOD robustness weakly because opposite-direction cells cancel out. (2) Within a cell, the selected statistic orders 92% of model pairs by OOD robustness in-sample. The prediction direction held for all external validation cases (EEG, genomic, protein). Applying this diagnostic at model selection narrows the OOD gap by 24% while retaining 87.5% of in-distribution accuracy.

Conclusion: OOD robustness can be predicted from pretrained weight statistics alone, enabling model selection before target data exists. The method works within architecture-strategy combinations ("cells"), and the direction is consistent within each cell. This makes OOD robustness checkable at model-selection time, potentially saving significant computational resources. The authors open-source their diagnostic for practitioners.

Abstract: Can we determine whether a foundation model will generalize out-of-distribution (OOD) before any target data is available? Existing diagnostics require source or target data, which rules them out before a target domain exists. Those that use the weights alone apply one statistic to every architecture, and do not separate robust models from fragile ones. We show the answer is encoded in the spectral structure of pretrained weights. Two forces shape that structure. Architecture determines how information is stored in weight matrices. Pretraining strategy determines what is rewarded. Together they set a spectral geometry that governs OOD robustness. We prove that the OOD accuracy gap is bounded by how tightly the source representations concentrate. A statistic computed from the pretrained weights alone serves as a proxy for that concentration. The direction of that proxy reverses between architecture families. We operationalize it: the direction is stable within one (architecture X strategy) combination, the finest grouping we test, which we call a cell. Pooled over 116 models spanning 7 modalities, a single statistic ranks OOD robustness weakly, because cells of opposite direction cancel. Within a cell, the statistic selected for it orders 92% of model pairs by OOD robustness in-sample. The selection does not leak the target: for each model family outside the matrix we logged the cell, metric and sign before running its OOD evaluation, and the predicted direction held in every case: EEG, genomic and protein. Acting on spectral concentration narrows the OOD gap by 24% at 87.5% ID retention. The diagnostic operates on released weights alone, so OOD robustness becomes checkable at model-selection time, before data or compute is committed to a target domain.

</details>


### [245] [EC-EarthFlow: Probabilistic emulation of daily transient global climate model simulations with flow matching](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09715)
*Kirien Whan,Nikolaj T. Mücke,Karin van der Wiel*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: EC-EarthFlow is a generative flow matching model that emulates climate simulations from EC-Earth3 at significantly lower computational cost, predicting day-ahead temperature fields from previous observations and annual mean temperature.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Climate models like EC-Earth3 are computationally expensive, limiting their use for many applications. This paper aims to develop a faster emulator that can reproduce key climate characteristics while being much more computationally efficient.

Method: Flow matching model trained on EC-Earth3 transient simulations (1950-2166, SSP2-4.5). Uses auto-regressive prediction with rollout periods ranging from one month to an extended season. Input features include previous days' temperature and annual mean temperature.

Result: EC-EarthFlow successfully reproduces daily variability, spatial patterns, annual cycle, and long-term trend from EC-Earth3 at substantially lower computational cost. The model remains stable for long inference periods and learns physical relationships simulated in EC-Earth3.

Conclusion: Flow matching provides an effective approach for emulating physical climate models, offering a promising alternative for applications requiring rapid climate simulations while maintaining fidelity to the underlying physics.

Abstract: We introduce EC-EarthFlow, a generative flow matching model that emulates simulations from the physical climate model EC-Earth3. The model is trained on transient simulations from EC-Earth3 (1950-2166, SSP2-4.5) to predict the day ahead temperature field from the previous days temperature as well as annual mean temperature. Predictions are made auto-regressively with rollout periods of between a month and an extended season. Using only this variable of interest, we are able to reproduce the daily variability, spatial patterns, annual cycle and long-term trend from EC-Earth3 at a substantially lower computational cost than the physical model. We demonstrate that EC-EarthFlow is stable for long inference periods, and that it can learn the physical relationships as simulated in EC-Earth3.

</details>


### [246] [SoftSEEPS improves ML-based precipitation forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09752)
*Jost Arndt,Utku Isil,Noelia Otero,Rodrigo Almeida,Wojciech Samek,Jackie Ma*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A differentiable approximation of the SEEPS score called SoftSEEPS is developed to enable direct ML-based precipitation forecasting. Tested on IMERG dataset using a decoder on latent space of pre-trained low-resolution model, the approach shows marginal trade-offs when combined with RMSE in a joint objective.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The standard SEEPS (Spatial Ensemble Equitable Threat Score) is non-differentiable, preventing end-to-end training of machine learning models for precipitation forecasting. This limitation motivated the development of a differentiable proxy (SoftSEEPS) to enable direct optimization of precipitation forecasts.

Method: SoftSEEPS was developed as a differentiable approximation of the SEEPS score. The method was tested on the IMERG dataset at 0.1-degree resolution by training a decoder for precipitation on the latent space of a pre-trained low-resolution forecasting model. A joint objective combining SoftSEEPS and RMSE was used for training.

Result: The combination of SoftSEEPS and RMSE in a joint objective is possible with marginal trade-offs in either metric, indicating the approach can optimize both scores simultaneously without significant performance loss.

Conclusion: SoftSEEPS provides a practical solution for training ML models to directly forecast precipitation by enabling gradient-based optimization. The method successfully balances SEEPS and RMSE objectives on the IMERG dataset.

Abstract: In this paper we have developed a differentiable approximation of the well-known SEEPS score, which we name SoftSEEPS. This allows the training of a Machine Learning model to forecast precipitation directly. We test SoftSEEPS on the IMERG dataset (0.1 degree resolution) by training a decoder for precipitation on the latent space of a pre-trained low-resolution forecasting model. Combining SoftSEEPS and RMSE in a joint objective is possible with marginal trade-offs in either metric.

</details>


### [247] [EntroPrefill: Renyi-Guided Context Pruning with Conditional Stability Guarantees for Retrieval-Augmented Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09757)
*Inbasekaran S*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: EntroPrefill is a theoretical framework for mid-prefill pruning in transformer models, using Renyi entropy-guided mechanisms with explicit constraints on discarded attention mass. It provides quantitative bounds on token removal feasibility and formal guarantees, but defers experimental validation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current attention concentration approaches in mid-prefill pruning do not certify that discarded context is truly dispensable. The authors seek a more rigorous approach that couples entropy-based guidance with explicit constraints on discarded attention mass to ensure pruning safety.

Method: The paper proposes: (1) A Renyi-guided proposal mechanism for token removal, (2) Sink-isolated regularized head pooling for grouped-query attention, (3) Mixture-to-head deletion envelope for computing upper bounds on token removal, (4) Finite-sample observer guarantees valid under adaptive pruning layer selection, (5) Conditional transformer perturbation bounds with explicit Lipschitz constants, (6) Systems analysis distinguishing query-head unions, physical page allocation, and KV-transfer payload.

Result: The paper establishes: (1) A computable upper bound on feasible token removal, (2) A finite-sample observer guarantee for adaptive pruning, (3) A conditional transformer perturbation bound with sufficient Lipschitz constants, (4) A first-token decision-margin corollary, (5) A counterexample showing limitations of shallow observations, (6) Arithmetic break-even condition for pruning. No experimental results are reported.

Conclusion: This theoretical work defines EntroPrefill procedure, its assumptions, and formal limits. The authors provide rigorous bounds and guarantees but acknowledge that experiments validating assumptions, approximation tightness, and end-to-end resource trade-offs are reserved for future work.

Abstract: Mid-prefill pruning can reduce the sequence processed by deeper transformer layers, but attention concentration alone does not certify that discarded context is dispensable. We formulate EntroPrefill as a Renyi-guided proposal mechanism coupled to explicit constraints on discarded attention mass. Sink-isolated, regularized head pooling respects grouped-query attention while exposing a quantitative trade-off between specialization and worst-head coverage. We derive a mixture-to-head deletion envelope, a computable upper bound on feasible token removal, and a finite-sample observer guarantee that remains valid when the pruning layer is selected adaptively. We then establish a conditional transformer perturbation bound with explicit sufficient Lipschitz constants and a first-token decision-margin corollary. A counterexample shows why shallow observations alone cannot imply an unconditional future-output guarantee. The systems analysis distinguishes query-head unions, physical page allocation, and KV-transfer payload, and gives an arithmetic break-even condition for pruning. This manuscript is theoretical in scope: it defines the procedure, its assumptions, and its formal limits, but does not report measured acceleration or task-accuracy preservation. Experiments are reserved for subsequent validation of the assumptions, approximation tightness, and end-to-end resource trade-offs.

</details>


### [248] [Unrolled Flow Models for Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09759)
*Faissal Izermine,Hanru Bai,Oscar Davis,T. Konstantin Rusch*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether flow matching models can improve reasoning through additional integration steps. The authors prove theoretically that flow-based two-layer Transformers can solve graph reachability, identify a limitation in standard flow language models (independent supervision at each time point), and propose solutions including latent rollout training over random subintervals, spherical retraction of latent states, and parameter-free selection scores for multiple rollouts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Flow matching enables fast language generation with few steps, but it remains unclear whether additional integration steps can improve reasoning capabilities. Standard flow language models fail to benefit from additional steps on reasoning tasks, suggesting a fundamental limitation in how these models are trained.

Method: The authors theoretically prove that flow models parameterized by two-layer Transformers can solve graph reachability (with required integration steps increasing with target distance). To address the limitation of standard flow models, they propose: (1) training through the model's own latent rollout over random subintervals of [0,1], decoding only at the endpoint; (2) retracting latent states onto a sphere to stabilize dynamics for longer rollouts; (3) sampling multiple rollouts with a parameter-free selection score.

Result: On ProsQA, accuracy raised to 97% and performance improved with additional integration steps. For longer reasoning tasks (Sudoku, Maze), spherical retraction yielded substantial gains over baselines with 3x more parameters. Multiple rollouts further improved performance, though reliable selection remained challenging for longer answers.

Conclusion: This work establishes a theoretical basis for reasoning with flow models and demonstrates that rollout training, stable latent dynamics, and rollout selection help realize reasoning capabilities in practice. The approach successfully enables flow models to benefit from additional integration steps for reasoning tasks.

Abstract: Flow matching enables language generation in few steps, but whether additional integration steps improve reasoning remains unclear. We prove that a flow parameterized by a two-layer Transformer can solve graph reachability, with the required number of integration steps increasing with the target's distance from the root. Yet, standard flow language models can fail to benefit from additional steps on reasoning tasks. We attribute this limitation to objectives that supervise each time point independently, without explicitly training successive steps to build on one another. To address this, we instead train through the model's own latent rollout over a randomly sampled subinterval of [0, 1], decoding only at the endpoint. On ProsQA, this raises accuracy to 97% and enables performance to improve with additional integration steps. For the longer rollouts required by reasoning tasks such as Sudoku and Maze, retracting the latent state onto a sphere stabilizes the dynamics and yields substantial gains over baselines with more than three times as many parameters. Sampling multiple rollouts further improves performance when paired with a parameter-free selection score, although reliable selection remains challenging for longer answers. Together, these results establish a theoretical basis for reasoning with flows and show how rollout training, stable latent dynamics, and rollout selection help realize this capacity in practice.

</details>


### [249] [Leaner Transformers Can Easily Learn to Cluster](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09760)
*Charlotte Park,Kenneth L. Clarkson,Lior Horesh,Takuya Ito,Parikshit Ram*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper presents a smaller transformer that executes Lloyd's k-means clustering algorithm with reduced embedding size (d + ⌈log₂k⌉ compared to d+k), trains these transformers to learn clustering algorithms from task distributions, and analyzes their convergence, generalization, and failure cases.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work required embedding size d+k with attention projection matrices of size (d+k)². This work aims to create a more efficient transformer that can still exactly perform Lloyd's algorithm while being smaller and more expressively efficient.

Method: 1) Design a smaller transformer with embedding size d_emb = (d + ⌈log₂k⌉) that can execute Lloyd's algorithm exactly; 2) Train transformers on distributions of clustering tasks using stochastic gradient descent; 3) Theoretically characterize convergence and in-distribution generalization; 4) Empirically validate the theoretical findings; 5) Probe the general clustering abilities to understand success and failure cases.

Result: The authors achieved a more efficient transformer with reduced embedding size, successfully trained transformers to learn clustering algorithms, and characterized factors affecting convergence and generalization. They also identified situations where the learned algorithms succeed and fail.

Conclusion: Transformers can learn to execute Lloyd's k-means clustering algorithm through in-context learning with improved efficiency. The work provides theoretical guarantees for convergence and generalization, while also revealing limitations of learned clustering algorithms through empirical analysis.

Abstract: Transformers have in-context learning capabilities, where some known learning algorithms can be executed in the forward pass through the model. Recent work shows that transformers can exactly perform Lloyd's algorithm for $k$-means clustering with $n$ points in $d$ dimensions with an embedding size $d_{\textsf{emb}} = d+k$ (thus, requiring attention projection matrices of size $(d+k)^2$). In this work, we build upon this result in the following ways: First, we present an equally expressive but smaller transformer that executes Lloyd's algorithm with embedding size $d_{\textsf{emb}} = (d + \lceil \log_2 k \rceil)$. Next, we train these transformers to learn the clustering algorithms given a distribution of clustering tasks, and theoretically characterize and empirically validate the factors affecting the convergence and in-distribution generalization of learning algorithms based on stochastic gradients. Finally, we probe the general clustering abilities of these learned algorithms (in the form of transformers), and try to understand situations where they succeed and fail.

</details>


### [250] [Beyond Policy Support: Interaction Constrained Offline Reinforcement Learning for Autonomous Driving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09763)
*Mahmoud Selim,Cristina Cipriani,Karl Henrik Johansson*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses distribution shift in offline reinforcement learning for autonomous driving, introducing Interaction Distribution Shift (IDS) - where ego trajectories may be supported marginally but not jointly with surrounding-agent behavior. The proposed ICDP framework uses contrastive density-ratio estimation to control interaction-level distribution shift without requiring explicit joint-density modeling or rollouts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Offline RL enables policy improvement from fixed datasets without online exploration, ideal for safety-critical domains. However, existing approaches only control distribution shift in the policy's own action space. In interactive driving scenarios, a candidate ego trajectory may appear well-supported under marginal behavior distribution but be poorly supported when jointly considered with surrounding-agent behavior observed in logged interactions - this degradation is termed Interaction Distribution Shift (IDS).

Method: The paper proposes Interaction-Constrained Drive Policy (ICDP), which: 1) Starts from the joint data distribution over ego and surrounding-agent futures; 2) Decomposes joint-support degradation into ego-support component and residual interaction-support component; 3) Recovers the interaction-support component through contrastive density-ratio estimation, isolating interaction compatibility without explicit joint-density modeling, surrounding-agent prediction, or rollouts in reactive simulators/learned world models.

Result: Closed-loop evaluations on nuPlan, Interplan and real-world truck experiments show that ICDP suppresses high-value yet interaction-unsupported trajectory selections and improves performance in interaction-critical driving scenarios.

Conclusion: ICDP effectively controls interaction-level distribution shift in offline RL for autonomous driving, achieving improved performance in interaction-critical scenarios without requiring reactive simulators or learned world models during policy optimization.

Abstract: Offline reinforcement learning enables reward-driven policy improvement from fixed datasets without requiring online exploration, making it particularly attractive in safety-critical domains.
