A central challenge, however, is distribution shift: policy optimization may favor actions that are weakly supported by the offline data, rendering value estimates unreliable. Existing approaches primarily control this shift in the policy's own action space. In interactive environments such as autonomous driving, this can be insufficient: a candidate ego trajectory may remain well supported under the marginal behavior distribution while being poorly supported jointly with the surrounding-agent behavior observed in the logged interaction. We refer to this degradation in interaction support as \emph{interaction distribution shift} (IDS), and introduce \emph{Interaction-Constrained Drive Policy} (ICDP), an offline reinforcement learning framework that explicitly controls interaction-level distribution shift. Starting from the joint data distribution over ego and surrounding-agent futures, we show that joint-support degradation decomposes exactly into an ego-support component and a residual interaction-support component. We recover the latter through contrastive density-ratio estimation, isolating interaction compatibility without explicit joint-density modeling, surrounding-agent prediction, or rollouts in reactive simulators or learned world models during policy optimization. Closed-loop evaluations on nuPlan, Interplan and real-world truck experiments show that ICDP suppresses high-value yet interaction-unsupported trajectory selections and improves performance in interaction-critical driving scenarios. Project webpage: https://mahmoud-selim.github.io/ICDP/

</details>

### [251] [Adaptive Workflow Intelligence: A Cognitive Architecture for Context-Driven Enterprise Automation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08793)
*Sreedevi Pandiyath Viswambaran*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AWI introduces a four-layer PCAR (Perception-Cognition-Action-Reflection) cognitive architecture for enterprise agents that combines hybrid reasoning with reflective memory and feedback-driven adaptation to handle non-stationary conditions, evolving policies, and delayed operational feedback in enterprise workflows.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enterprise systems rely on automated workflows but current AI-driven solutions are brittle under non-stationary conditions, evolving policies, and delayed operational feedback. Existing solutions like reinforcement learning and LLM agents lack persistent reflection mechanisms and straightforward integration with policy-constrained enterprise operations.

Method: AWI uses a four-layer PCAR loop architecture treating reflection as a mechanism for continuous policy refinement. It combines hybrid reasoning with reflective memory and feedback-driven adaptation. Evaluation is conducted in a simulated enterprise decision workflow with delayed outcomes and controlled regime shift (drift-and-delay stress test).

Result: Guardrail-constrained adaptive approaches recover more rapidly than static automation while maintaining policy compliance. AWI's reflective components modestly reduce behavioral oscillation and feedback variance, illustrating the stability-agility trade-off introduced by reflective policy adaptation.

Conclusion: The PCAR architecture with reflective components provides a promising approach for enterprise agents to balance stability and agility under environmental drift and operational constraints, though benefits are modest and the stability-agility trade-off remains a key challenge.

Abstract: Enterprise systems increasingly rely on automated workflows, yet many AI-driven solutions remain brittle under non-stationary conditions, evolving policies, and delayed operational feedback. While reinforcement learning and large language model (LLM) agents offer partial adaptability, they do not by themselves provide persistent reflection mechanisms or straightforward integration with policy-constrained enterprise operations. This paper introduces Adaptive Workflow Intelligence (AWI), a cognitive architecture for context-driven enterprise agents organized around a four-layer Perception-Cognition-Action-Reflection (PCAR) loop. AWI treats reflection as a mechanism for continuous policy refinement and combines hybrid reasoning with reflective memory and feedback-driven adaptation to support decision making under environmental drift and operational constraints. We evaluate AWI in a simulated enterprise decision workflow characterized by delayed outcomes and a controlled regime shift. In a drift-and-delay stress test, guardrail-constrained adaptive approaches recover more rapidly than static automation while maintaining policy compliance. Within this setting, AWI's reflective components modestly reduce behavioral oscillation and feedback variance, illustrating the stability-agility trade-off introduced by reflective policy adaptation.

</details>


### [252] [Humanity's Sixth Sense: Benchmarking Intuitive Visual Reasoning in Multimodal Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08966)
*Xingang Guo,Jing Gu,Brian Jang,Renxiong Wang,Utkarsh Tyagi,Daniel Quigley,Steven Li,David Yan,Daniel Yue Zhang,Darvin Yi,Forrest Huang,HiJae Kim,Tianyi Zhang,Jared Lichtarge,Jihua Huang,Le Xue,Manan Tomar,Qiuyi Richard Zhang,Ruofei Yu,Seth Neel,Yaning Hu,Marcella Valentine,Xinzhe Jiang,Daniel Evans,Chenguang Wang,Dustin Tran,Tong Zhao,Yinfei Yang,Yunzhong He*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: HSS (Humanity's Sixth Sense) is a new benchmark designed to evaluate multimodal large language models' ability to perform intuitive visual reasoning—the rapid, zero-shot inference of implicit temporal, spatial, social, and abstract information from images and videos that humans do effortlessly.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing visual benchmarks focus either on deliberate expert-level analysis (academic/mathematical domains) or low-level perception, leaving the intuitive reasoning that humans perform daily largely untested. This gap is critical because intuitive visual reasoning is essential for MLLMs deployed alongside people in everyday navigation and social interactions.

Method: HSS comprises diverse image and video inputs organized under a structured taxonomy. Each item is paired with human-written prompts probing implicit information (temporal, spatial, social, and abstract structures) that people infer at a glance. The benchmark tests frontier MLLMs and also explores agentic setups with dynamic visual manipulation.

Result: Human participants achieve 93.1% accuracy, while the strongest model (GPT-6-astra) achieves only 53.6% even at maximum reasoning effort. Agentic setups with dynamic visual manipulation narrow but do not close the gap.

Conclusion: Current MLLMs, despite excelling in many complex tasks requiring advanced perception and knowledge, still struggle significantly on intuitive visual reasoning tasks that are trivial for humans. HSS establishes intuitive visual reasoning as a measurable axis and highlights a capability that scaling on current benchmarks has not yet developed.

Abstract: Humans perceive far more in a scene than what is explicitly depicted: a single glance captures past causes and future trajectories; a quick peek determines if a vehicle can fit between two parked cars; a few seconds of video reveals who holds authority in a room; and a fleeting clip highlights subtle abstract patterns like unwritten rules or hidden labels. This capacity reflects a form of humanity's sixth sense: an intuitive reasoning mechanism that recovers implicit information beyond raw sensory perception. Crucially, this rapid, zero-shot visual intuition underpins everyday navigation and social interaction, making it a vital capability for Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) deployed alongside people. Existing visual benchmarks, however, target either deliberate expert-level analysis in academic and mathematical domains or low-level perception, leaving the intuitive reasoning that people perform largely untested. To bridge this gap, we introduce Humanity's Sixth Sense (HSS), a benchmark for intuitive visual reasoning. HSS spans diverse image and video inputs, organizes items under a structured taxonomy, and pairs each with human-written prompts probing the implicit temporal, spatial, social, and abstract structure that people infer at a glance. Frontier MLLMs fall short of human performance: participants reach 93.1% accuracy, while the strongest model, GPT-6-astra, reaches only 53.6% even at maximum reasoning effort. Despite excelling in many complex tasks that require advanced perception and knowledge, current models still struggle significantly on these visual tasks that are intuitive for humans. We further explore agentic setup that apply dynamic visual manipulation to HSS, which narrows but does not close the gap. HSS establishes intuitive visual reasoning as a measurable axis and directs attention to a capability that scaling on current benchmarks has so far left behind.

</details>


### [253] [Accelerating Floating-Point Satisfiability Solving via Gradient Normalization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08808)
*Yuanzhuo Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: GradSAT is a novel SMT solver that combines optimization-based solving with Multi-Task Learning (MTL) to overcome gradient domination, where difficult clauses hijack optimization and trap solvers in local minima. It uses dynamic gradient normalization (GradNorm) to balance gradients across clauses and implements a two-stage hybrid pipeline: GPU-accelerated continuous relaxation followed by bit-precise local search.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: SMT solvers over Quantifier-Free Floating-Point (QF_FP) are foundational to software verification, program analysis, and compiler testing. However, optimization-based SMT solvers are fundamentally bottlenecked by gradient domination—a phenomenon where a small subset of difficult clauses hijacks the optimization trajectory, preventing the solver from satisfying the broader formula and trapping it in local minima.

Method: GradSAT reformulates the constraint satisfaction process by treating each SMT clause as an independent MTL task. It applies dynamic gradient normalization (GradNorm) to actively balance gradient magnitudes across all clauses at runtime, systematically penalizing dominant gradients and accelerating lagging clauses for uniform convergence. The implementation uses a two-stage hybrid pipeline: (1) a GPU-accelerated PyTorch backend with symbolic compilation and operator fusion for continuous relaxation, and (2) a bit-precise local search engine for rigorous exact assignment resolution.

Result: GradSAT stabilizes continuous search dynamics, mitigates the brittleness of prior gradient-based solvers, and provides a robust, highly parallelizable architecture for complex constraint solving.

Conclusion: By bridging optimization-based SMT solving with Multi-Task Learning and dynamic gradient normalization, GradSAT successfully overcomes gradient domination and enables more reliable and efficient constraint solving for software verification and program analysis applications.

Abstract: Satisfiability Modulo Theories (SMT) solvers are foundational to software verification, program analysis, and compiler testing, particularly over the theory of Quantifier-Free Floating-Point (QF_FP). While recent optimization-based SMT solvers have successfully applied gradient descent to continuous relaxations of logical formulas, they are fundamentally bottlenecked by gradient domination, a phenomenon where a small subset of difficult clauses hijacks the optimization trajectory, preventing the solver from satisfying the broader formula and trapping it in local minima.
  To overcome this, we present GradSAT, a novel framework that bridges optimization-based SMT solving with Multi-Task Learning (MTL). GradSAT reformulates the constraint satisfaction process by treating each SMT clause as an independent MTL task. By applying dynamic gradient normalization (GradNorm), GradSAT actively balances the gradient magnitudes across all clauses at runtime, systematically penalizing dominant gradients and accelerating lagging clauses to ensure uniform convergence. GradSAT implements this through a highly optimized, two-stage hybrid pipeline. First, a GPU-accelerated PyTorch backend leveraging symbolic compilation and operator fusion navigates the continuous relaxation to a high-quality basin. Second, the candidate assignment is handed off to a bit-precise local search engine to rapidly resolve the exact, rigorous assignment. By stabilizing the continuous search dynamics, GradSAT mitigates the brittleness of prior gradient-based solvers and provides a robust, highly parallelizable architecture for complex constraint solving.

</details>


### [254] [Route-Verify-Vote: Procedure-Conditioned Self-Consistency for Mixed-Domain Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08814)
*Xinchen Xiao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces Route-Verify-Vote (RRV), a framework for procedure-conditioned self-consistency that enables language models to perform compositional generalization across mixed domains without parameter updates. The system uses domain-specific reasoning procedures, verification against constraints, and adaptive sampling to achieve 79.4% accuracy on the SCoRE 2026 benchmark, ranking second among participants.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Compositional generalization remains a key challenge for language models—combining familiar reasoning operations in unfamiliar ways. The SCoRE 2026 benchmark tests this ability across three mixed domains absent from training, requiring models to identify the complete set of correct options for each question. This work addresses the need for inference-time computation allocation methods that can handle mixed-domain reasoning without fine-tuning.

Method: The RVV framework consists of three components: (1) Route uses domain labels to select appropriate reasoning procedures that guide constraint representation and application; (2) Verify prompts the model to assess each option against those constraints; (3) Vote aggregates complete answer sets and allocates additional samples to questions with small vote-count margins between competing answer sets. The system uses 16 sampled answer sets per question with adaptive allocation based on disagreement.

Result: On the SCoRE 2026 official test set: voting over 16 sampled answer sets achieves 74.6% exact-set accuracy; adaptive RVV reaches 77.3%; combining models on selected domain routes raises accuracy to 79.4%. The final system ranked second among participating systems.

Conclusion: Domain-specific reasoning procedures combined with answer-set disagreement provide effective tools for allocating inference-time computation in mixed-domain compositional reasoning. The success of adaptive sampling and model combination suggests that leveraging domain knowledge and multiple model perspectives significantly improves compositional generalization without requiring parameter updates.

Abstract: Compositional generalization remains challenging when language models must combine familiar reasoning operations in unfamiliar ways. The Scenario-Based Commonsense Reasoning Evaluation (SCoRE) 2026 tests this ability on three mixed domains absent from training and requires models to identify the complete set of correct options for each question.
  We introduce Route-Verify-Vote (RVV), a framework for procedure-conditioned self-consistency that uses language models without parameter updates. Route uses the provided domain label to select a reasoning procedure that guides the model in representing and applying the relevant constraints. Verify prompts the model to assess each option against those constraints. Vote aggregates complete answer sets and allocates additional samples to questions with a small vote-count margin between the two most frequent sets. Samples for each question follow the same domain-specific procedure.
  On the official test set, voting over 16 sampled answer sets per question achieves an exact-set accuracy of 74.6%. Adaptive RVV reaches 77.3%, and combining models on selected domain routes raises accuracy to 79.4%. The final system ranked second among participating systems. These results support domain-specific reasoning procedures and answer-set disagreement as useful tools for allocating inference-time computation in mixed-domain reasoning.

</details>


### [255] [An Empirical Study of Agent Skills' Downstream Utility](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08875)
*Yu Cheng,Dehai Zhao,Zhongxin Liu,Qing Huang,Zhenchang Xing,Xiaoxue Ren*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper empirically studies how Agent Skills (procedural guidance packages) affect task performance across different configurations. Analyzing 87 SkillsBench tasks with 37,596 marketplace candidates, the study finds that the same Skills can help or hurt performance depending on execution configuration, and that relevance rankings often miss better candidates. The authors derive 17 authoring practices and show that structured Skill organization (Dependency DAG) outperforms simple use order.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The research addresses a critical gap in understanding why relevant Skills don't always improve task performance. While existing studies characterize Skill content and evaluate downstream performance, they provide limited explanation of how utility depends on content, execution configuration, and multi-Skill organization. The motivation is to understand these relationships to guide better Skill development and deployment.

Method: The study conducted an empirical analysis on 87 SkillsBench tasks, defining downstream utility as pass-rate difference from No-Skill baseline. They compared the same Skills across nine configurations, examined alternative published Skills and organizations under three selected configurations, and retrieved marketplace candidates from a curated corpus of 37,596 Skills. LLM-assisted analysis examined content, execution traces, and final artifacts, followed by author review to relate provided support to actual use and task outcomes.

Result: Key findings include: (1) Same Skills help some configurations and hurt others on 36.78% of tasks; (2) Recommended procedures can become execution burdens; (3) Relevance rankings overlook more useful candidates; (4) Reranking by support for required operations raises first-choice pass rates by 4.35-5.80 percentage points; (5) 17 authoring practices were derived linking procedures to recovery, preservation of task requirements, and artifact checks; (6) Stage Plan and Dependency DAG outperform use order alone, with DAG's benefits concentrated in tasks supplied with five or six Skills.

Conclusion: The findings provide concrete guidance for developers: (1) Assess usable operation support rather than relying on relevance rankings; (2) Allow procedure adaptation while preserving task requirements; (3) Make artifact dependencies explicit when organizing Skills. The study demonstrates that proper Skill organization and content alignment with execution configuration are critical for improving task performance, and that structured approaches like Dependency DAGs significantly outperform simple ordering.

Abstract: Agent Skills package procedural guidance and resources for reuse, but a relevant Skill does not necessarily improve task performance. Existing studies characterize Skill content and evaluate downstream performance, yet provide limited explanations of how utility depends on content, execution configuration, and multi-Skill organization. We conduct an empirical study on 87 SkillsBench tasks, defining downstream utility as the pass-rate difference from No-Skill on the same tasks under the same model--harness configuration. We compare the same Skills across nine configurations, then examine alternative published Skills and organizations of fixed Skill sets under three selected configurations. We retrieve marketplace candidates from a curated corpus of 37,596 Skills. LLM-assisted analysis of content, execution traces, and final artifacts, followed by author review, relates provided support to actual use and task outcomes. The same Skills help some configurations and hurt others on 36.78\% of tasks, with trajectories showing that recommended procedures can become an execution burden. Relevance rankings overlook more useful candidates. Within the evaluated candidate sets, reranking by support for required operations raises first-choice pass rates by 4.35--5.80 percentage points across the three configurations. We derive 17 authoring practices linking executable procedures to recovery, preservation of task requirements, and checks on final artifacts. Stage Plan and Dependency DAG outperform use order alone, with DAG's additional benefits concentrated in tasks supplied with five or six Skills. These findings guide developers to assess usable operation support, allow procedure adaptation while preserving task requirements, and make artifact dependencies explicit when organizing Skills.

</details>


### [256] [How Could AI Eliminate Humanity? A Failure-Mode Analysis of Civilizational Risk](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08878)
*Mikołaj Sienicki,Krzysztof Sienicki*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper develops a comprehensive failure-mode framework for analyzing how advanced AI could cause human extinction, civilizational collapse, or permanent disempowerment—without requiring AI consciousness, hostility, or intentional harm.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation appears to be addressing a critical gap in AI safety research: moving beyond simplistic "AI goes rogue" scenarios to identify multiple realistic pathways through which advanced AI systems could cause catastrophic outcomes. The authors aim to provide a systematic, non-operational framework that identifies causal conditions and defensive research priorities.

Method: The paper employs a conceptual framework analysis approach, identifying distinct failure pathways (autonomous misalignment, harmful human use, organizational failure, competitive deployment) and analyzing how severity factors (capability, autonomy, external access, persistence, institutional safeguards, recovery capacity) interact to determine catastrophic risk levels.

Result: The framework identifies four major failure pathways and six key severity factors. The central insight is that catastrophic AI risk can emerge even from well-intentioned AI systems through various mechanisms, not requiring malicious intent or consciousness. The analysis identifies empirically tractable intermediate quantities and defensive research questions.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that catastrophic AI risk is a multi-faceted problem requiring analysis across multiple pathways. The non-operational approach aims to inform defensive research and policy without providing harmful instructions, emphasizing the importance of institutional safeguards and preserving recovery capacity.

Abstract: This article develops a failure-mode framework for analyzing how advanced artificial intelligence could contribute to human extinction, irreversible civilizational collapse, or permanent human disempowerment. The central thesis is that catastrophic AI risk does not require consciousness, hostility, or an explicit intention to harm humanity. Instead, risk may arise through several distinct but interacting pathways, including autonomous misalignment, harmful human use, organizational failure, and competitive deployment. The severity of these pathways depends on factors such as capability, autonomy, external access, persistence, institutional safeguards, and the preservation of recovery capacity. The analysis is deliberately non-operational: it identifies causal conditions, empirically tractable intermediate quantities, and defensive research questions rather than procedures for causing harm.

</details>


### [257] [Humanize: Judgement Engineering for Agentic Coding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08900)
*Sihao Liu,Ligeng Zhu,Zijian Zhang,Dongyun Zou,Zhengyang Zhang,Changye Li,Song Bian,Song Han,Tony Nowatzki*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Humanize is a multi-agent orchestration workflow for agentic coding that uses "judgement engineering" - explicit, mechanically enforced decisions at boundaries between planning, implementation, review, and learning. It involves human approval of plan contracts, builder agents implementing in rounds, and reviewer agents from another vendor deciding completion, with 72 deterministic mechanical gates routing work between roles.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Agentic coding makes code generation cheap, but reliable completion remains difficult: the agent that writes the code is a weak judge of whether it is done.

Method: Multi-agent orchestration with judgment engineering: A human approves a plan contract, a builder agent implements in rounds, and a reviewer agent from another vendor decides completion. Deterministic hooks (not a model) route work between roles and enforce 72 mechanical gates. Viewed as a Markov chain over repository states, alternating builder and reviewer samples jointly from two models, so a defect survives only if both miss it.

Result: Over 68 versions in 108 days, Humanize gathered 1,468 GitHub stars. Applications include: 567-file gem5 build-system migration under upstream review; Kernel Design Agents (top three in all three Full-Agent tracks of MLSys 2026 FlashInfer contest); Humanize Olympiad Agents (HOA) achieving full scores in IOI 2026, IMO 2026, IPhO 2026, IBO 2024, 418.5/437 in IChO 2026 gold-medal); 672/672 on PutnamBench; and first place (251/303) on Lean-Eval's leaderboard. 118 public postmortems show independent review catches unsupported builder claims, but stopping remains a key weakness - two thirds of rounds occurred after implementation was accepted.

Conclusion: Independent review catches unsupported builder claims, but stopping remains a key weakness. Evidence is observational, not a controlled comparison of workflows.

Abstract: Agentic coding makes code generation cheap, but reliable completion remains difficult: the agent that writes the code is a weak judge of whether it is done.
  We present Humanize, a multi-agent orchestration workflow for agentic coding built around judgement engineering: explicit, mechanically enforced decisions at the boundaries between planning, implementation, review, and learning. A human approves a plan contract, a builder agent implements it in rounds, and a reviewer agent from another vendor decides completion; deterministic hooks, not a model, route work between these roles and enforce 72 mechanical gates. Viewed as a Markov chain over repository states, alternating builder and reviewer samples jointly from two models, so a defect survives only if both miss it. We study Humanize through its deployment, 118 public postmortems of real loops, and its applications. Over 68 versions in 108 days, it gathered 1,468 GitHub stars.
  Applications include a 567-file gem5 build-system migration under upstream review; Kernel Design Agents, which extend the loop with a kernel knowledge base and profiling feedback and placed in the top three of all three Full-Agent tracks of the MLSys 2026 FlashInfer contest; and, through Humanize Olympiad Agents (HOA), full scores in IOI 2026, IMO 2026, IPhO 2026, and IBO 2024, 418.5/437 in IChO 2026 (gold-medal). Humanize also achieves 672/672 on PutnamBench and ranks first (251/303) on Lean-Eval's leaderboard even competiting with professional mathematicians. The postmortems show that independent review catches unsupported builder claims, but stopping remains a key weakness. In reports that separate rounds by phase, two thirds of rounds occurred after implementation was accepted. This evidence is observational, not a controlled comparison of workflows.

</details>


### [258] [Sequential Probabilistic Uncertainty Estimation for Parallel Multi-Agent Reasoning Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08901)
*Tunyu Zhang,Zihao Zhao,Yusong Zhao,Haizhou Shi,Zhuohang Li,Haoxian Chen,Hao Wang,Dimitris N. Metaxas*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SAUCE is a training-free uncertainty estimator for LLM-based multi-agent systems that models uncertainty as sequential inference over latent system-level belief, aggregating round-level agreement and generation-uncertainty signals through filtering-style updates.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While LLM-based multi-agent systems have shown strong reasoning performance through agent interaction, uncertainty estimation for such systems remains underexplored. The reliability of a MAS depends not only on individual generations but also on how agents interact and evolve across rounds, requiring a novel approach to uncertainty quantification.

Method: SAUCE formulates MAS uncertainty as sequential inference over a latent system-level belief. It aggregates round-level agreement and generation-uncertainty signals through a filtering-style update mechanism, requiring no additional training.

Result: SAUCE was evaluated across five backbones, five benchmarks, and two MAS protocols. It demonstrated improvements in misclassification detection, selective prediction, and calibration compared to various uncertainty estimation baselines including standard log-likelihood-based methods and MAS-specific estimators.

Conclusion: SAUCE provides a lightweight, training-free solution for uncertainty estimation in parallel multi-agent reasoning systems, effectively capturing both individual agent uncertainty and collective system behavior across rounds.

Abstract: LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) have attracted growing attention for improving reasoning through interaction among multiple agents. In this work, we focus on parallel multi-agent reasoning systems, where several agents solve the same problem over multiple rounds and aggregate their outputs into a final answer. Despite their strong reasoning performance, uncertainty estimation for such systems remains underexplored: the reliability of a MAS depends not only on individual generations, but also on how agents interact and evolve across rounds. We propose SAUCE (Sequential Agent Uncertainty through Consensus Evolution), a lightweight, training-free uncertainty estimator that formulates MAS uncertainty as sequential inference over a latent system-level belief. SAUCE aggregates round-level agreement and generation-uncertainty signals through a filtering-style update. Across five backbones, five benchmarks, and two MAS protocols, SAUCE improves misclassification detection, selective prediction, and calibration over a broad set of uncertainty estimation baselines, including standard log-likelihood-based methods and MAS-specific estimators.

</details>


### [259] [Agent Plasticity: Measuring Self-Improvement Through Experience](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08902)
*Harman Singh,Anton Bakhtin,Rulin Shao,Gabriel Synnaeve,Ilia Kulikov,Rob Fergus,Sanjeev Arora,Kurt Keutzer,Jason Weston,Anuj Mahajan,Anirudh Goyal*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces metrics to evaluate self-improving AI agents, including "agent plasticity" (efficiency of converting experience into future performance gains). The study finds that frontier models exhibit vastly different improvement trajectories - some achieve substantial gains while others degrade or stagnate - and that the best final performance doesn't necessarily come from the most efficiently improving agent.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing AI evaluations measure static capabilities at a fixed point in time rather than how effectively agents learn and improve through experience. There was a need to evaluate three key aspects: whether performance generalizes beyond training interactions, how efficiently new capabilities are acquired, and where self-improvement breaks down.

Method: The study uses a controlled setting where agents amortize past experience into reusable artifacts inherited by future instances. Performance is measured on both training and held-out environment interactions at each checkpoint, while accounting for learning costs. Multiple environments and frontier models were compared.

Result: Frontier models show sharply different improvement trajectories despite comparable learning opportunities. Some achieve substantial persistent gains while others remain near or below initial performance. Training gains often transfer only partially to out-of-distribution conditions. Agents with low plasticity fail to reuse relevant artifacts, while more plastic agents may still fail due to artifact quality, generalization, or application limitations.

Conclusion: Evaluating self-improving agents requires measuring not only what they can do, but how effectively they become better through experience. The concept of "agent plasticity" provides a framework for assessing learning efficiency in AI systems.

Abstract: AI agents increasingly operate in environments where they can diagnose failures and improve through experience, yet existing evaluations largely measure what an agent can do at a fixed point in time rather than how effectively it learns. Evaluating self-improvement requires answering three questions: does future performance improve and generalize beyond the interactions that enabled learning; how efficiently are new capabilities acquired; and where does the self-improvement process break down? To answer these questions, we study self-improvement in a controlled setting where agents amortize past experience into reusable artifacts that are inherited by future instances. At each checkpoint, we measure performance on training and held-out environment interactions while accounting for learning cost. We introduce agent plasticity, the efficiency with which an agent converts experience into gains in future held-out performance. Across multiple environments, frontier models exhibit sharply different improvement trajectories despite comparable opportunities to learn. Some achieve substantial and persistent gains, while others remain near or below their initial performance, and gains within the training regime often transfer only partially to out-of-distribution conditions. Endpoint capability and acquisition efficiency also diverge: the agent that ultimately performs best need not be the one that improves most efficiently. Tracing failures through the improvement loop further reveals different candidate bottlenecks. Agents with low plasticity often fail to reuse relevant artifacts, whereas more plastic agents may still fail despite reusing relevant artifacts, pointing to limitations in artifact quality, generalization, or application. Evaluating self-improving agents requires measuring not only what they can do, but how effectively they become better through experience.

</details>


### [260] [AdaGuard: Enhancing Safety and Policy Compliance with Reasoning-Enabled LLM-As-A-Judge Guardrails](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08923)
*Melissa Kazemi Rad,Sihui Dai,Isha Slavin,Kushal Chawla,Mann Patel,Jian Ni,William M. Campbell,Stephen Rawls,Sambit Sahu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AdaGuard is an adaptive LLM-as-a-Judge framework for enterprise generative AI safety that dynamically enforces policies and allocates reasoning resources, rivaling larger models while balancing latency and transparency requirements.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current guardrail solutions are rigid, relying on fixed policy sets with limited transparency or reasoning flexibility. Enterprise applications need mechanisms that can accommodate diverse risk postures, evolving policies, and varying latency constraints.

Method: AdaGuard is built using supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (GRPO). It dynamically infers the complexity of input-policy pairs to switch between high-speed black-box inference and explainable, reasoning-enabled moderation.

Result: AdaGuard can generalize to user-defined safety and compliance policies at runtime without frequent model updates. It rivals other guardrail and frontier models several times its size. Its auto-reasoning mode recovers the accuracy of always-on reasoning at a fraction of the latency.

Conclusion: AdaGuard provides a flexible, efficient solution for enterprise AI safety that balances stringent latency requirements with actionable transparency through adaptive reasoning-budget allocation.

Abstract: Enterprise generative AI applications require robust safety mechanisms that can accommodate diverse risk postures, evolving policies, and varying latency constraints. Current guardrail solutions often suffer from rigidity, relying on fixed policy sets and offering limited transparency or reasoning flexibility. We present Adaguard, an adaptive LLM-as-a-Judge framework designed to address these challenges through dynamic policy enforcement and adaptive reasoning-budget allocation. Built using supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (GRPO), AdaGuard generalizes to user-defined safety and compliance policies at runtime without requiring frequent model updates. A core innovation of our approach is the ability to dynamically infer the complexity of input-policy pairs, allowing the model to switch between high-speed black-box inference and explainable, reasoning-enabled moderation. This flexibility enables developers to balance stringent latency requirements with the need for actionable transparency. This adaptive capability allows AdaGuard to rival other guardrail and frontier models several times its size, while its auto-reasoning mode recovers the accuracy of always-on reasoning at a fraction of the latency

</details>


### [261] [Can AI Agents Make Open-Ended Scientific Discovery? Evidence from Station](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08927)
*Wenyu Du,Stephen Chung*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether AI agents can autonomously perform open-ended scientific discovery (without well-defined metrics) using a novel environment called Station. The study finds that Station with Supervisor mechanism and Meta Reflection achieves 62.7% rediscover rate of original findings, significantly outperforming Codex Multiagent-v2 (15.4%) and AI Scientist-v2 (14.4-20.6%). Some discoveries also match real-world research published after the knowledge cutoff.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Recent AI systems excel at scientific discovery with well-defined metrics, but their ability to autonomously tackle open-ended scientific discovery (without clear metrics) remains unknown. This is a critical question for understanding AI's potential in truly autonomous scientific research.

Method: 1) Built Station, an open-world multi-agent environment simulating a scientific ecosystem; 2) Augmented Station with two mechanisms: Supervisor mechanism (encourages persistent exploration) and periodic Meta Reflection; 3) Constructed open-ended tasks from 3 ICLR oral papers, giving agents the research question but withholding results and web access; 4) Measured rediscover rate of original findings partitioned into individual criteria; 5) Conducted ablation studies and behavioral analysis; 6) Evaluated on two tasks without oracle papers.

Result: Station rediscovers 62.7% of criteria on average, compared with 15.4% for Codex Multiagent-v2 and 14.4-20.6% for AI Scientist-v2. Ablation shows the two mechanisms together improve research coverage and continuity. On open-ended tasks without oracle papers, some agent discoveries match real-world findings reported after the knowledge cutoff date.

Conclusion: A suitable environment (Station with Supervisor and Meta Reflection mechanisms) can enable AI agents to autonomously make meaningful progress in open-ended scientific discovery, suggesting potential for AI to contribute to genuine scientific research without human-defined success metrics.

Abstract: Recent AI systems have made rapid progress in scientific discovery when given well-defined metrics, but whether they can autonomously undertake open-ended scientific discovery remains unclear. We investigate AI's ability to tackle open-ended tasks in Station, an open-world environment in which multiple agents simulate a scientific ecosystem. To tackle challenges specific to open-ended tasks, we propose augmenting Station with two mechanisms: a Supervisor mechanism and periodic Meta Reflection, which encourage persistent exploration even when intermediate metrics are lacking. We construct open-ended tasks from three recent oral papers presented at ICLR. We give agents the main research question studied in each paper while withholding the paper's results and disabling web access. We then measure how many of the original findings-partitioned into individual criteria-agents rediscover. We find that Station rediscovers 62.7% of the criteria on average, compared with 15.4% for Codex Multiagent-v2 and 14.4-20.6% for AI Scientist-v2. Ablation and behavioral analyses indicate that adding the two mechanisms together improves research coverage and continuity. We further evaluate Station on two open-ended tasks without oracle papers and find that some of the discoveries made by the agents closely match discoveries reported by researchers after the knowledge cutoff date. Together, these results indicate that a suitable environment can enable agents to autonomously make meaningful progress in open-ended scientific discovery.

</details>


### [262] [Socio-Foundation: A Model for Generalizable Individual Behavior Simulation via Hierarchical Capability Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08967)
*Liang Wang,Wenxuan Xie,Xinyi Mou,Yixin Luo,Zhongyu Wei*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Socio-Foundation is a specialized LLM for individual behavior simulation that addresses persona flattening and task fragmentation issues through a three-stage training pipeline, organizing capabilities into the FONTS taxonomy (persona fidelity, outcome realization, behavioral naturalness, trajectory coherence, and social grounding).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: General-purpose LLMs flatten distinct personas when simulating individual behavior, while task-specific tuning suffers from fragmentation and poor generalization. There was a need for a unified framework to preserve persona traits while adapting to dynamic social contexts.

Method: The approach involves: (1) Organizing individual simulation into the FONTS Taxonomy with five capability dimensions; (2) Curating a standardized training corpus of ~10 million instances across 14 datasets; (3) Using a three-stage pipeline: DAPO for learning task experts, off-policy distillation for consolidating capability experts, and multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) for unification; (4) Evaluating with IndiEval comprising 29 metrics across FONTS dimensions.

Result: Socio-Foundation outperforms its Qwen3-8B base by 11.0 points and approaches frontier models like GLM-5.2. Ablations and out-of-distribution evaluations demonstrate effectiveness and generalization.

Conclusion: The FONTS taxonomy provides a comprehensive framework for evaluating individual simulation capabilities. The three-stage decoupled training approach successfully integrates specialization with integration, achieving strong performance while maintaining generalization across different scenarios.

Abstract: Simulating individual behavior requires large language models (LLMs) to preserve persona traits while adapting to dynamic social contexts. However, general-purpose LLMs often flatten distinct personas, while task-specific tuning suffers from fragmentation and generalization. To overcome these challenges, we organize individual simulation into the \textbf{FONTS Taxonomy}, comprising five complementary capability dimensions: \emph{persona fidelity} (\textbf{F}), \emph{outcome realization} (\textbf{O}), \emph{behavioral naturalness} (\textbf{N}), \emph{trajectory coherence} (\textbf{T}), and \emph{social grounding} (\textbf{S}). Grounded in this taxonomy, we curate a standardized training corpus library of approximately 10 million instances across 14 representative datasets and present \textbf{Socio-Foundation}. Socio-Foundation decouples specialization from integration via a three-stage pipeline: learning task experts via DAPO, consolidating them into capability experts via off-policy distillation, and unifying them via multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD). We also establish \textbf{IndiEval}, consolidating 29 metrics across the FONTS dimensions. Experiments show that Socio-Foundation outperforms its \textit{Qwen3-8B} base by 11.0 points and approaches frontier models such as \textit{GLM-5.2}, with ablations and out-of-distribution evaluations further demonstrating the effectiveness and generalization of our model.

</details>


### [263] [Verify Less, Evolve More: Training Idea-Level Critics for Verification-Efficient ML Evolving Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08993)
*Jiamu Bai,Lizhu Zhang,Xin Yu,Yanhong Wu,Zellux Wang,Serena Li,Weiwei Li,Zhuokai Zhao,Lingzhou Xue,Kiwan Maeng,Xiangjun Fan,Bo Peng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper addresses the computational bottleneck in AI-for-Machine-Learning (AI4ML) agents by developing specialized idea-level critic models that predict whether proposed ML modifications will improve solutions. These critics screen ideas before costly empirical verification, enabling more efficient agent evolution.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In AI4ML, empirical verification (model training/evaluation) is computationally expensive, limiting the speed and scale of agent evolution. While frontier models exist, they provide limited gains as idea selectors. Verification efficiency remains under-explored.

Method: The approach involves training specialized idea-level critic models through: (1) Supervised fine-tuning on high-quality critiques synthesized by Gemini-3.1-Pro, followed by (2) GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) to further improve predictive accuracy. These critics predict whether ML modifications will improve current solutions.

Result: Critic models outperform Gemini-3.1-Pro in static idea evaluation. Gains extend to agent inference, continual learning, and policy training. During inference-time evolution, better final solution quality is achieved under the same verification budget. During policy training, critics serve as learned reward models, reserving empirical verification for uncertain cases and enabling substantially more policy updates with the same resources.

Conclusion: Idea-level critic models help ML agents discover better solutions and learn stronger proposal policies under limited verification budgets, effectively addressing the computational bottleneck in AI4ML agent evolution.

Abstract: As large language models become more powerful, self-evolving agents are able to tackle challenging tasks including AI for machine learning (AI4ML). In AI4ML, while empirical verification is available, it often requires computationally costly model training and evaluation, limiting the speed and scale of agent evolution. Yet verification efficiency remains under-explored, and frontier models provide only limited gains when used directly as idea selectors. We address this gap with specialized idea-level critic models that predict whether a proposed ML modification will improve upon the current solution, allowing agents to screen ideas and concentrate verification resources on the most promising candidates. We train the critic models through supervised fine-tuning on high-quality critiques synthesized by Gemini-3.1-Pro, followed by GRPO to further improve their predictive accuracy. Empirically, our critic models outperform Gemini-3.1-Pro in static idea evaluation, and these gains extend to agent inference, continual learning, and policy training. During inference-time evolution, they improve final solution quality under the same verification budget by selecting more promising ideas, with further gains from continual learning. During policy training, they serve as learned reward models, reserving empirical verification for uncertain cases and enabling substantially more policy updates with the same verification resources. Together, these results show that idea-level critic models help ML agents discover better solutions and learn stronger proposal policies under limited verification budgets.

</details>


### [264] [How Fragile Is On-Device Language Model Safety? Localizing Safety-Critical Parameters for Sparse Fault Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09000)
*Muhammad Zeeshan Karamat,Christiana Chamon Garcia*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether safety-sensitive behavior in LLaMA-2-7B-Chat is concentrated in a sparse subset of parameters, enabling targeted fault analysis for on-device SLMs. Using two complementary localization methods (low-rank subspace analysis and parameter-level importance filtering), the authors find highly non-uniform safety sensitivity, with MLP down_proj being the primary safety-sensitive component.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As small language models are increasingly deployed on resource-constrained and on-device platforms (including agentic systems), the integrity of locally stored model parameters becomes a critical safety concern. Understanding where safety-critical behavior resides in the model parameter space could enable targeted protection strategies.

Method: Two complementary localization methods were employed: (1) low-rank safety-associated subspace analysis to identify safety-relevant parameter directions, and (2) parameter-level safety-utility importance filtering to assess individual parameter contributions to safety vs. utility.

Result: The study reveals highly non-uniform safety sensitivity across the network. The MLP down_proj consistently emerges as the prominent safety-sensitive component, while o_proj provides a smaller contribution. By modifying only 0.19% of model weights in down_proj, the authors achieved 53% Basic ASR (Adversarial Success Rate) and 56% GCG ASR, while tinyBenchmarks accuracy remained at 51.6% (vs. 52.2% baseline).

Conclusion: Safety-sensitive behavior is concentrated in a sparse subset of parameters (primarily down_proj), creating a reduced fault surface for targeted analysis. This motivates targeted fault analysis and selective integrity protection for language models deployed in resource-constrained, on-device, and agentic settings.

Abstract: As small language models (SLMs) are increasingly deployed on resource-constrained and on-device platforms, including as components of agentic systems, the integrity of locally stored model parameters becomes an important safety concern. We investigate whether safety-sensitive behavior in LLaMA-2-7B-Chat is concentrated within a sparse subset of parameters, creating a reduced fault surface for targeted analysis. We study two complementary localization methods: low-rank safety-associated subspace analysis and parameter-level safety--utility importance filtering. Both approaches reveal highly non-uniform safety sensitivity across the network, with the MLP down_proj consistently emerging as a prominent safety-sensitive component and o_proj providing a smaller contribution. Using parameter-level localization, modifying only 0.19% of model weights in down_proj yields 53% Basic ASR and 56% GCG ASR, while tinyBenchmarks accuracy remains at 51.6% compared with a 52.2% unmodified baseline. These results motivate targeted fault analysis and selective integrity protection for language models deployed in resource-constrained, on-device, and agentic settings.

</details>


### [265] [Learning to Report Unsafe Tasks in a Multi-Agent Game](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09002)
*Avyay M. Casheekar,Hariganesh Tangirala*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper investigates multi-agent systems where agents can report unsafe work, which may reduce their own reward by stopping a task. The authors study how audit mechanisms can incentivize reporting without causing teams to learn silence. They provide theoretical analysis of policy gradients and audit conditions, and demonstrate empirically that separating co-witnesses significantly reduces unsafe task completion compared to shared policies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The core problem is that when agents share rewards for completed tasks, reporting unsafe work can be personally costly (by stopping a task and reducing the reporter's share). While audits can theoretically make reporting optimal, they don't prevent training from teaching a "silent team" to not report. This creates a fundamental tension in multi-agent safety systems.

Method: The authors model this as a game where k witnesses can each stop a task by reporting. They analyze the expected-reward derivative with respect to silence probability, comparing universal silence vs universal reporting. They derive audit conditions sufficient for exact policy-gradient updates to reach universal reporting. They then train PPO policies on 24 witness graphs, comparing fully shared networks versus separated co-witnesses under various audit conditions.

Result: Theoretical results show that at universal silence, the expected-reward derivative counts each task's benefit k times (for k witnesses), while universal reporting counts it once. The cheapest audits meeting the condition cost exactly k times more for full sharing than for one policy per role. Empirically, separating co-witnesses reduces unsafe completion by 33.59 percentage points (95% CI: 21.03-45.13). Only 9 of 48 runs achieve <1% unsafe completion while retaining ≥90% legitimate completion. A fully shared network with independent action draws meets neither threshold in any run, but achieves both with a common draw.

Conclusion: The paper demonstrates a fundamental tension between audit costs and policy sharing in multi-agent safety systems. Separating co-witnesses into distinct policies significantly improves safety outcomes compared to shared policies. The findings suggest that architectural choices (policy sharing vs separation) have major implications for safety in multi-agent systems, and that common action draws can unexpectedly improve performance under audits.

Abstract: When agents share a reward for completed tasks, reporting unsafe work can reduce the reporter's reward by stopping a task. Audits can make reporting optimal without ensuring that further training teaches a silent team to report. We study this learning problem in a game where any witness can stop a task by reporting. With $k$ witnesses per task sharing a policy and drawing independently, the expected-reward derivative with respect to their shared silence probability counts each task's benefit $k$ times at universal silence. The comparison with universal reporting counts it once. For arbitrary policy groups, we give an audit condition sufficient for exact policy-gradient updates to reach universal reporting and, apart from boundary cases, necessary near universal silence. In a balanced family, the cheapest audits meeting the condition with prescribed positive margins cost exactly $k$ times as much for full sharing as for one policy per role. We train PPO policies on 24 witness graphs from learned silence. Separating co-witnesses reduces unsafe completion by 33.59 percentage points compared with shuffled groups of the same sizes under the same audits (95% graph-bootstrap interval: 21.03-45.13). Only 9 of 48 witness-group runs achieve below 1% unsafe completion while retaining at least 90% legitimate completion. At the same audit budget, a fully shared network meets both thresholds in none of 48 runs with independent action draws and all 48 with a common draw.

</details>


### [266] [Sigma-Hunter: A Domain-Specific Language Model for Threat Hunting and Detection Engineering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09007)
*Kemal Davaslioglu,Sastry Kompella*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Sigma-Hunter is a domain-adapted LLM designed to assist detection engineers in generating valid Sigma rules for threat hunting. Built by fine-tuning 7B Mistral and Phi-4 models on 7,663 examples derived from 3,635 validated Sigma rules, it outperforms general-purpose LLMs in producing semantically correct detection rules while running locally in disconnected environments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Detection engineers need to convert threat reports, forensic observations, and hunt hypotheses into precise, testable Sigma rules. General-purpose LLMs often produce invalid YAML, incorrect log sources, unsupported fields, or overly broad detection logic, making them unsuitable for this specialized task.

Method: The authors built an instruction-tuning dataset from 3,635 validated open-source Sigma rules, expanded into 7,663 question-answer and analyst-reasoning examples. They fine-tuned a 7B Mistral model and a Phi-4 model using LoRA. The dataset was split at the rule level (not the expanded example level) to prevent data leakage across train, validation, and test partitions. Evaluation covered syntax validity, approximate field consistency, and semantic judgment of detection logic, completeness, selectivity, and log-source alignment.

Result: Sigma-Hunter-Mistral achieved an overall score of 8.17, outperforming the strongest general-purpose baseline (7.88) and untuned Mistral (4.61). The study found that domain adaptation enables a compact 7B model to perform competitively with larger general-purpose models, and that syntactic validity is a weak proxy for semantic rule quality—many baselines produce well-formed YAML but with weak detection logic.

Conclusion: Domain adaptation through instruction tuning on validated Sigma rules significantly improves LLM performance on structured detection engineering tasks. A compact 7B model can rival larger general-purpose models when properly fine-tuned. The work highlights that syntactic correctness alone does not guarantee rule quality, necessitating holistic evaluation of detection logic. The adapted models run locally, addressing operational needs in disconnected environments.

Abstract: Detection engineers must translate threat reports, forensic observations, and hunt hypotheses into precise, testable rules. General-purpose large language models (LLMs) can draft such rules, but often produce invalid YAML, incorrect log sources, unsupported fields, or overly broad detection logic. This paper presents \emph{Sigma-Hunter}, a domain-adapted LLM for analyst-assistive Sigma rule generation and threat hunting. We build an instruction-tuning dataset from 3,635 validated open-source Sigma rules, expanded into 7,663 question-answer and analyst-reasoning examples. Each source rule is assigned to a single train, validation, or test partition before this expansion, so no rule leaks across splits. We fine-tune a 7B Mistral model and a Phi-4 model with LoRA and score held-out rule generations on syntax, approximate field consistency, and a semantic judgment of detection logic, completeness, selectivity, and log-source alignment. Sigma-Hunter-Mistral scores 8.17 overall, against 7.88 for the strongest general-purpose baseline and 4.61 for untuned Mistral. Two findings stand out: domain adaptation enables a compact 7B model to perform competitively with larger general-purpose models on this structured task, and syntactic validity is a weak proxy for semantic rule quality, as several baselines emit well-formed YAML carrying weak detection logic. The adapted models run locally, which suits detection engineering in disconnected environments where analysts cannot reach hosted model services.

</details>


### [267] [Finding Blind Spots in AppWorld and WorkArena Task Verifiers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09142)
*Richard Abrich*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper audits execution-based task verifiers in AppWorld and WorkArena benchmarks using source-informed mutation tests. The audit reveals that AppWorld verifiers accept incorrect task variants (6/15 constructed effects), and WorkArena verifiers incorrectly accept 21/23 extra-field candidates with confirmed nondefault persisted values. The main audit does not modify shipped checkers, and findings represent selected cases rather than population rate estimates.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to audit shipped task verifiers in AppWorld and WorkArena benchmarks to check if they correctly validate whether AI agents succeeded at their assigned tasks. Execution-based verifiers are crucial for evaluating agent performance, so their correctness is essential.

Method: The authors use source-informed mutation tests to audit the verifiers. In AppWorld, they duplicate non-idempotent writes to create extra records while preserving checked field values. In WorkArena, they prospectively rerun 23 extra-field candidates with independent Table API readback to confirm persisted values. Each increment is specified before its own cells are scored.

Result: In AppWorld: Verifier accepts all three task variants from two of five eligible generators (6/15 constructed effects). A cardinality patch makes all six cells fail while preserving valid controls. In WorkArena: 21 of 23 extra-field candidates show nondefault persisted values but all 23 receive PASS. Two requested strings are aliases of stored defaults. The 21 confirmed wrong effects span three form templates. In intent-swap grids, checkers return no PASS on 2,689 off-diagonal executions (57 WorkArena cells use session-scoped evidence; 2,632 lack classified rejection causes).

Conclusion: The audit reveals significant flaws in both AppWorld and WorkArena verifiers. Selected cases confirm wrong effects under the audit protocol, but these do not estimate population rates. The main audit never modifies shipped checkers. Zero-PASS families are reported separately. The paper includes a supplement with construction grammar, evidence, content-bound stage lineage, and count reproducer.

Abstract: Execution-based task verifiers decide whether an agent succeeded. We audit shipped AppWorld and WorkArena verifiers with source-informed mutation tests. The main audit never modifies a shipped checker.
  In AppWorld, duplicating a non-idempotent write creates an extra record while preserving every checked field value. The verifier accepts all three task variants from two of five eligible generators: 6/15 constructed effects. A cardinality patch applied to checker copies after the census makes all six cells fail while preserving valid controls.
  In WorkArena, we prospectively rerun 23 extra-field candidates selected for earlier checker-PASS outcomes. Independent Table API readback confirms nondefault persisted values in 21, while all 23 receive PASS. Two requested strings are aliases of stored defaults. The 21 confirmed wrong effects span three form templates. These selected cases confirm wrong effects under the audit's protocol; they do not estimate a population rate.
  No other construction produces an independently confirmed false accept. Other checker-PASS cases are effect-correct degeneracies. We report zero-PASS families separately because retained evidence differs. In fixed intent-swap grids, the checkers return no PASS on 2,689 off-diagonal executions. This is a rejection census: 57 WorkArena cells use session-scoped evidence; the other 2,632 lack classified rejection causes and independent target ground truth.
  Each increment is specified before its own cells are scored. A supplement accompanies the OpenReview submission with the construction grammar, evidence, content-bound stage lineage and count reproducer.

</details>


### [268] [Whose Memory Is It? Scope-Aware Commit Rules for Long-Term LLM Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09008)
*Hongyu Gu,Xinchang Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CASK addresses a critical flaw in LLM agent memory systems where reasoning deliberations (tentative plans, simulated tool results, rejected beliefs) get stored as facts because the context validating them is lost. The solution preserves "discourse ownership" signals through causally anchored scoping keys rather than internal coordinates.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Persistent memory in LLM agents converts reasoning into durable records, but this process detaches intermediate propositions from their valid context (world, branch, or speaker). This turns temporary reasoning artifacts into false facts - a critical reliability issue for agent systems.

Method: CASK (Causally Anchored Scoping Keys) - a commit rule that preserves discourse ownership signals by tracking stable relations rather than internal coordinates. Distinguishes between shared-world facts (durable memory) and provisional content (temporary scope).

Result: CASK improves memory admission accuracy and prevents provisional content from contaminating later answers while complementing runtime provenance. Allows agents to explore more possibilities without granting intermediate sentences authority over future behavior.

Conclusion: The paper demonstrates that: (1) LLMs already carry causally active ownership signals internally, (2) storing internal coordinates is unreliable due to representation instability, (3) preserving stable relations is a more robust approach. CASK creates a commit boundary that enables safer exploration in agent deliberation.

Abstract: Persistent memory allows an LLM agent to carry experience across conversations, but it also turns a local reasoning mistake into a durable one. During deliberation, an agent may consider a plan, simulate a tool result, report another speaker's belief, and then reject all of them. If memory retains only the resulting sentences, those once-useful possibilities can later return as facts. The record is neither fabricated nor irrelevant; it has simply been detached from the context in which it was valid. We identify this missing context as \emph{discourse ownership}: the world, branch, or speaker that licenses a proposition. Our first finding is counterintuitive. Language models already carry a causally active signal for ownership, yet conventional memory interfaces discard it when they convert reasoning into records. We introduce CASK (Causally Anchored Scoping Keys), a commit rule that preserves this signal so that shared-world facts enter durable memory while provisional content remains available only within its original scope. Our second finding is that the most obvious way to preserve the signal---storing the discovered internal coordinates---is unreliable because equivalent representations need not keep the same coordinates. CASK instead preserves the stable relations that express ownership. Controlled long-conversation conflicts and tool-agent traces show that this design improves memory admission and prevents provisional content from contaminating later answers while complementing runtime provenance. The resulting commit boundary lets agents explore more possibilities without granting every intermediate sentence authority over future behavior.

</details>


### [269] [SpecGuard: Proving a Task Is Broken Before the Agent Cheats](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09159)
*Param Biyani,Krishnamurthy Dvijotham*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SpecGuard is a system that detects and formally certifies conflicts between task intent and tests in autonomous coding agents. It autoformalizes task descriptions and tests into Lean 4 specifications, then uses the Lean kernel to verify whether any implementation could satisfy both, providing a pre-execution safety check against reward-hacking.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The risk of dangerous agent behavior from misspecified tasks (where tests conflict with actual intent) is critical. Prior work shows agents rarely flag these conflicts and instead cheat (edit tests, hard-code outputs), which can cause real damage. There was a need for independently verifiable evidence of conflicts before agents act.

Method: SpecGuard takes only the task description and codebase, autoformalizes the intended behavior into a Lean 4 specification, formalizes tests independently, and uses the Lean kernel to check whether any implementation could satisfy both formalizations. When no implementation can satisfy both, it produces a machine-checked certificate.

Result: On conflicted SWE-bench tasks, SpecGuard detects up to 72.8% of conflicts and formally certifies up to 51.1%, with a nearly five-fold lower conflict miss rate than model-based judgment.

Conclusion: SpecGuard provides a pre-execution safety check that identifies reward-hacking opportunities through formal certification of task-level conflicts before any agent behavior is observed, outperforming model-based approaches.

Abstract: As autonomous coding agents get increasingly deployed, the risk that accidental or adversarially injected misspecifications in tasks lead to dangerous agent behavior is critical to address. Prior work has shown that agents given such tasks rarely flag the conflict and instead cheat, editing tests or hard-coding expected outputs, and the actions taken to cheat can cause real damage, such as deleting a security defense to make a corrupted test pass. It remains unclear whether such conflicts can be established with independently verifiable evidence before the agent acts. We present SpecGuard, which detects and formally certifies these conflicts between task intent and tests. Given only the task description and codebase, SpecGuard autoformalizes the intended behaviour into a Lean 4 specification. The tests are formalized independently, and the Lean kernel checks whether any implementation could satisfy both formalizations, producing a machine-checked certificate when none can. On conflicted SWE-bench tasks, SpecGuard detects up to 72.8% of conflicts and formally certifies up to 51.1%, with a nearly five-fold lower conflict miss rate than model-based judgment. SpecGuard provides a pre-execution safety check that identifies reward-hacking opportunities through formal certification of task-level conflicts, before any agent behavior is observed. Our code is available at https://github.com/prmbiy/specguard.

</details>


### [270] [Enabling Dynamic Computation in Looped LMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09013)
*Aayush Mishra,Arnau Padrés Masdemont,Victor Conchello Vendrell,Jordi Ros Giralt,Arash Behboodi,Fabio Valerio Massoli*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper addresses inefficiencies in Looped Language Models (LMs), specifically Ouro models that fail to deliver dynamic computation savings due to KV-cache requirements per loop iteration and static early-exit mechanisms. The authors propose a "best-available" KV caching strategy, training awareness of this strategy, and a fix to the early-exit prior for heterogeneous depth processing based on token difficulty.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: State-of-the-art open Looped LMs (Ouro models) with dynamic computation capability do not realize it in practice because: (1) each loop iteration requires its own level of KV-cache, necessitating all loop computations; (2) the early-exit prior is enforced equally on all tokens, resulting in static lower-depth processing regardless of token difficulty.

Method: Three key contributions: (1) A simple "best-available" KV caching strategy that works out-of-the-box; (2) Training looped LMs with awareness about the KV caching strategy to improve performance and efficiency; (3) A small fix to the early-exit prior enforcement objective that enables tokens to exit at truly heterogeneous depths based on effort.

Result: The approach achieves up to 30% reduction in FLOPs and KV memory while retaining full-depth performance, demonstrating the true flexibility of Looped LMs. Findings are validated on Ouro models and smaller looped LMs pre-trained from scratch.

Conclusion: The proposed KV caching strategy creates a new frontier in the performance vs depth space. Training with awareness of this strategy improves both performance and efficiency. The fix to early-exit prior enables truly heterogeneous depth exit based on token effort, realizing the dynamic computation promise of Looped LMs.

Abstract: Looped LMs are parameter efficient and promise dynamic computation (saving memory and FLOPs on easy tokens). However, state-of-the-art open Looped LMs trained with this dynamic computation capability (Ouro models) do not realize it in practice as each loop iteration (depth) requires its own level of KV-cache, necessitating all loop computations. Moreover, Ouro's early-exit prior is enforced on each token equally, which results in static lower-depth like processing of all tokens regardless of difficulty. In this work, we propose a simple "best-available" KV caching strategy that works out-of-the-box, creating a new frontier in the performance vs depth space. Our approach enables up to 30% reduction in FLOPs and KV memory while retaining full-depth performance, showing the true flexibility of Looped LMs. Furthermore, training looped LMs with awareness about this KV caching strategy improves performance and efficiency. Finally, we apply a small but effective fix to the early-exit prior enforcement objective that makes tokens exit at truly heterogeneous depths based on effort. Our findings are validated on Ouro models as well as smaller looped LMs pre-trained from scratch.

</details>


### [271] [PAIR: Bridging Perception and Action in Vision-Language-Action Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09016)
*Kaixi Feng,Guoheng Sun,Ang li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: PAIR introduces a bridge representation between perception and action spaces in continuous-action VLA models. It uses a Masked Action Autoencoder to encode expert actions into Action Latent Tokens, and a Bridge Module to align task-relevant visual-language features with these tokens. This creates Bridge Tokens that provide an action-ready starting point for Action Expert refinement, improving VLA performance on manipulation tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current continuous-action VLAs leave the transition from visual/language representations to action generation implicit, supervising it mainly through final action-prediction loss. This lacks an explicit interface between perception and action spaces, potentially limiting performance on complex manipulation tasks.

Method: PAIR employs three key components: (1) A Masked Action Autoencoder that encodes expert action chunks into horizon-aligned Action Latent Tokens; (2) A Bridge Module that extracts task-relevant features from current visual-language representations; (3) An alignment mechanism that forms Bridge Tokens by aligning Bridge Module features with Action Latent Tokens, preserving task information while capturing expert action structure. Bridge Tokens are projected into action-token space and injected into initial Action Tokens as a starting point for Action Expert refinement. At inference, the autoencoder is removed and Bridge Tokens are generated from current observation and instruction alone.

Result: On LIBERO-Plus, PAIR raises VLA-Adapter's success rate from 59.1% to 64.2%. On CALVIN ABC-D, it increases VLA-Adapter's average completed sequence length from 4.42 to 4.53. Across seven real-world tasks, PAIR raises OpenVLA-OFT's success rate from 51.4% to 65.0%. Representation analyses confirm Bridge Tokens retain task information while making continuous-action information accessible before Action Expert refinement.

Conclusion: A shared intermediate representation (Bridge Tokens) serves as a useful interface between perception and action in continuous-action VLAs, enabling meaningful alignment between task-relevant features and action space structure, leading to consistent improvements across simulation and real-world benchmarks.

Abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models map visual observations and language instructions to continuous robot actions. This task requires a transition from representations that describe the scene and instruction to representations that support action generation. Many continuous-action VLAs leave this transition implicit and supervise it mainly through the final action-prediction loss. We introduce PAIR, a framework that learns a shared perception-action representation between these two spaces. During training, a Masked Action Autoencoder encodes expert action chunks into horizon-aligned Action Latent Tokens. A Bridge Module extracts task-relevant features from the current visual-language representations. PAIR aligns these features with the Action Latent Tokens to form Bridge Tokens that preserve task information and capture the structure of expert actions. The Bridge Tokens are then projected into the action-token space and injected into the initial Action Tokens, providing an action-ready starting point for Action Expert refinement. At inference, the autoencoder is removed, and the Bridge Tokens are generated only from the current observation and instruction. Experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and CALVIN ABC-D show gains for the evaluated OpenVLA-OFT and VLA-Adapter models. On LIBERO-Plus, PAIR raises VLA-Adapter's success rate from 59.1% to 64.2%. On CALVIN, it increases VLA-Adapter's average completed sequence length from 4.42 to 4.53. Across seven real-world tasks, PAIR raises OpenVLA-OFT's success rate from 51.4% to 65.0%. Representation analyses show that Bridge Tokens retain task information while making continuous-action information accessible before Action Expert refinement. These results support a shared intermediate representation as a useful interface between perception and action in continuous-action VLAs.

</details>


### [272] [Cost-Efficient Theorem Proving via Agent Orchestration in Program Verification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09681)
*Shuangjie Yao,Nikolaus Holzer,Mark Paul Santolucito,Baishakhi Ray,Suman Jana,Dongdong She*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CoCo-Prover is a cost-efficient program verification system that uses metalevel decision-making to optimize the proof search process. It combines two-level proof graphs (AND/OR hypergraphs within declarations and lemma-dependency graphs across declarations) with an agentic router that orchestrates specialist agents to maximize the success-vs-cost frontier in formal program verification.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing theorem provers optimize only for pass rates without considering cost efficiency, yet real software verification involves hundreds of interdependent proof obligations. The key insight is that at scale, what matters is not whether one theorem can be proved, but how many can be proved economically.

Method: CoCo-Prover uses two-level proof graphs: (1) AND/OR proof hypergraph within each declaration, and (2) lemma-dependency graph across declarations. It makes two decisions at each step: (1) which open goals to select (via topological pass over proof graphs), and (2) which actions to purchase on these goals. Action choice uses an agentic router that treats bounded specialist invocations as separately priced, best-effort computations, matching heterogeneous specialist agents with configurations under evolved routing rules.

Result: On five Lean 4 program verification benchmarks (function-level CLEVER, VERINA, AlgoVeri, and repository-level NTP4VC, Vero), CoCo-Prover achieves the best solve rate on every benchmark (up to 100% on two benchmarks). It reduces cost by up to 30.9% compared to the strongest baseline with the strongest LLM.
