Conclusion: CoCo-Prover demonstrates that cost-efficient program proving is achievable through metalevel decision-making under cost constraints, achieving superior success-vs-cost tradeoffs compared to frontier coding agents and state-of-the-art LLM-based provers.

Abstract: Program verification establishes software correctness through machine-checkable proofs constructed in theorem provers. It's a guarantee especially valuable for code generated by large language models (LLMs), which is fluent but carries no assurance of correctness. Almost all existing provers, however, pursue pass rates alone at whatever sampling or search budget it takes, and overlook the success-vs-cost frontier; yet real software often carries hundreds of interdependent proof obligations, so what matters at scale is not whether one theorem can be proved, but how many can be proved economically. We introduce CoCo-Prover, which formalizes cost-efficient program proving as metalevel decision-making under cost, grounded on two-level proof graphs: an AND/OR proof hypergraph within each declaration is joined to a lemma-dependency graph across declarations; and at each step, it answers two questions: which open goals to select, and which actions to purchase on these goals. Selection stays symbolic as a topological pass over the proof graphs. Action choice is agent orchestration via metalevel decision-making: an agentic router treats every bounded specialist invocation as a separately priced, best-effort computation, matching heterogeneous specialist agents together with configurations, under evolved routing rules as evidence accumulates. On five program verification benchmarks in Lean 4 including function-level CLEVER, VERINA, and AlgoVeri, and repository-level NTP4VC and Vero, we show that CoCo-Prover achieves a better success-vs-cost frontier than baselines including frontier coding agents and state-of-the-art LLM-based provers: it achieves the best solve rate on every benchmark and up to 100% on two benchmarks. It also reduces cost by up to 30.9% compared to the strongest baseline with the strongest LLM in our evaluation.

</details>


### [273] [Not Every Call Needs a Frontier Model: Per-Call-Site Evaluation of Small Language Models in a Deployed Agentic Home-Automation System](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09021)
*Panagiotis Kasnesis,Christos Chatzigeorgiou,Lazaros Toumanidis,Amalia Contiero Syropoulou*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper evaluates 9 LLM models (0.8B to frontier) across 5 call sites in a home automation framework (Wactorz), finding that model capabilities vary by site, larger models aren't uniformly better, and best local models match hosted models at 4/5 sites, with code generation being the key differentiator.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current agentic systems use a single model (chosen for the hardest call site) across all sites, despite varying difficulty by an order of magnitude. This work investigates whether this is necessary and whether smaller local models can match hosted models at easier sites.

Method: Evaluated 9 models across 5 call sites (intent routing, action classification, device grounding, multi-agent planning, code generation) using unmodified production prompts on two real Home Assistant installations (280 cases, 2520 scored calls).

Result: Model capabilities are not uniformly ordered; larger models are not uniformly better. One 4B model is worse than its 2B sibling at grounded actuation. Best local model matches hosted models at 4/5 sites (only code generation separates them). Safety failures observed: Gemma4 E2B actuates on 87.2% of requests for devices the site doesn't own. Routing each site to its best local model achieves 91.8% vs 95.4% for hosted. Live deployment with only generative sites matches full deployment (39/43) for 28% of the spend.

Conclusion: Selective deployment using local models is viable: routing each call site to its best local model is cost-effective, and hosting only generative sites matches full hosting performance at 28% cost. Model selection should be site-specific rather than one-size-fits-all.

Abstract: An agentic system issues several structurally different kinds of LLM calls. It routes intent, classifies actions, grounds language in a device registry, plans multi-agent pipelines and writes the Python code those pipelines run. The difficulty of these call sites varies by an order of magnitude, yet in practice a single model, chosen for the hardest site, serves all of them. In this work, we evaluate 9 models from 0.8B to a frontier hosted model across the five call sites of a deployed open-source home-automation framework (Wactorz), using its unmodified production prompts and two real Home Assistant installations (280 cases, 2520 scored calls). We find that capability is not ordered the same way at every site, and that larger models are not uniformly better: one 4B model is worse than its 2B sibling at grounded actuation. Paired testing shows the best local model to be statistically indistinguishable from both hosted models at four of five sites. Only code generation separates them, against a small hosted model (p = 0.039) as well as a frontier one (p = 0.002). Aggregate accuracy also hides a safety failure specific to actuation, where small models resolve the accuracy/refusal trade-off in degenerate ways: one model (Gemma4 E2B) actuates on 87.2% of requests for devices the site does not own, while another refuses every request it receives. Routing each site to its best local model reaches 91.8% against 95.4% at no per-call cost. In a live deployment judged by a user, hosting only the two generative sites matches hosting everything (39/43 against 39/43) for 28% of the spend, and the actuation gap the benchmark predicted appears as exactly one case in twenty-six. Benchmark, harness and all records are released at https://github.com/waldiez/slm-callsite-eval.

</details>


### [274] [Agentic AI-Assisted Modeling for Production Scheduling: Assessment in Constraint Programming](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.10184)
*Ángel Sánchez-Fernández,Javier Pernas-Álvarez,Diego Crespo-Pereira*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This study investigates whether general-purpose LLMs, orchestrated as agents without task-specific training, can formulate and implement constraint programming models from natural-language problem descriptions for production scheduling. The researchers compared single-agent and multi-agent architectures with a Model Context Protocol server against a direct LLM baseline across six industry-oriented scheduling problems using three different LLMs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Developing optimization models for production scheduling requires substantial expert effort. Existing research has two limitations: (1) specialized automated modeling approaches for MIP rely on dedicated training or problem-specific architectures limiting industrial deployment, and (2) agentic AI for operational decision support assumes the optimization model already exists. This study bridges both directions by assessing if general-purpose LLMs can formulate and implement constraint programming models from natural language without task-specific training.

Method: The researchers integrated single-agent and multi-agent architectures with a Model Context Protocol server that provides context-aware retrieval of solver documentation to mitigate hallucinations during implementation. They compared both architectures with a direct LLM baseline on six industry-oriented problems covering flow-shop, job-shop, flexible job-shop, and resource-constrained warehouse scheduling. The study used three LLMs and assessed modeling accuracy, execution success, latency, and token consumption.

Result: Formulation is largely within reach of current LLMs, while implementation is the main barrier. The multi-agent workflow significantly improved results: the share of scripts that run correctly as generated increased from 14.8% (direct LLM) to 59.3% (multi-agent), reaching 80.6% on the four less complex problems. However, tightly coupled intralogistics models remain an open challenge.

Conclusion: General-purpose LLMs orchestrated as agents can successfully formulate constraint programming models from natural language descriptions for production scheduling, but implementation remains the primary challenge. The multi-agent architecture with Model Context Protocol server substantially outperforms direct LLM calls, though complex intralogistics scheduling problems still pose significant difficulties for current LLM technology.

Abstract: Developing optimization models for production scheduling requires substantial expert effort. Research on large language models (LLMs) has followed two directions: specialized approaches for automated modeling, mostly for mixed-integer linear programming, which often rely on dedicated training or problem-specific architectures that limit industrial deployment; and agentic artificial intelligence for operational decision support, which generally assumes that the optimization model already exists. This study bridges both directions by assessing whether general-purpose LLMs, orchestrated as agents without task-specific training, can formulate and implement constraint programming models from natural-language problem descriptions. Singleagent and multi-agent architectures are integrated with a Model Context Protocol server that provides context-aware retrieval of solver documentation to mitigate hallucinations during implementation. Both are compared with a direct LLM baseline on six industry-oriented problems covering flow-shop, job-shop, flexible job-shop and resource-constrained warehouse scheduling, using three LLMs and assessing modeling accuracy, execution success, latency and token consumption. Formulation proves largely within reach of current LLMs, whereas implementation is the main barrier. The multi-agent workflow raises the share of scripts that run correctly as generated from 14.8% with a direct LLM call to 59.3%, reaching 80.6% on the four less complex problems, while tightly coupled intralogistics models remain an open challenge.

</details>


### [275] [BEACON-SP: Ontology-Grounded GraphRAG Framework for Clinical Suicide Risk Assessment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09026)
*Kemal Davaslioglu,Nathan Conger,Sastry Kompella,Yalin E. Sagduyu,Nathaniel D. Bastian*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: BEACON-SP is an ontology-grounded GraphRAG framework for clinician decision support in suicide prevention, combining patient knowledge graphs with ontology-guided retrieval to enable multi-hop reasoning across diagnoses, medications, risk factors, and temporal relationships.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Effective suicide risk assessment requires integrating heterogeneous clinical, behavioral, social, and temporal evidence from multiple sources, which traditional retrieval methods may not adequately address.

Method: The framework integrates Three-Step Theory, Integrated Motivational-Volitional Model, and Suicide Social Determinants of Health Ontology into a unified suicide prevention ontology. Ontology-grounded patient knowledge graphs were constructed and evaluated against a vector-based RAG baseline using a 1,500-query benchmark spanning 15 clinical categories and 100 patients.

Result: BEACON-SP improved completeness, clinical relevance, and evidence grounding compared to the baseline, with small gains in factual accuracy. In paired criterion-level comparisons, GraphRAG was preferred in 76.4% of cases.

Conclusion: Ontology-guided GraphRAG demonstrates potential for providing structured, contextualized patient evidence for clinical decision support in behavioral health settings.

Abstract: We present BEACON-SP, an ontology-grounded Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation (GraphRAG) framework for clinician-facing decision support in behavioral health settings such as suicide prevention, where effective assessment requires integrating heterogeneous clinical, behavioral, social, and temporal evidence. BEACON-SP combines patient knowledge graphs with ontology-guided retrieval to support multi-hop reasoning across diagnoses, medications, risk and protective factors, life events, and temporal relationships. The framework is enabled by a comprehensive suicide prevention ontology that integrates the Three-Step Theory, the Integrated Motivational-Volitional Model, and the Suicide Social Determinants of Health Ontology into a unified representation of patient risk factors. We construct ontology-grounded patient knowledge graphs and evaluate BEACON-SP for clinician-facing question answering. Compared with a vector-based retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) baseline on a 1,500-query benchmark spanning 15 clinical categories and 100 patients, BEACON-SP improves completeness, clinical relevance, and evidence grounding under a corrected comparative evaluation protocol, with a small gain on factual accuracy. In paired criterion-level comparisons, GraphRAG is preferred in 76.4% of cases. These results demonstrate the potential of ontology-guided GraphRAG to provide structured, contextualized patient evidence for clinical decision support.

</details>


### [276] [OOM-RL II: Reality Is an Oracle, Not a Debugger Provenance-Constrained Diagnosis in Continually Evolving Agent-Engineered Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.10256)
*Kun Liu,Liqun Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper examines the "outcome-diagnosis gap" in production ML systems, using a quantitative trading system case study over one year. It argues that knowing an outcome occurred is distinct from knowing which procedure produced it or why, and proposes a prospective production-binding protocol to address this issue. The case shows that while the trading account outperformed a broad market index, annual alpha was not statistically distinguishable from zero under retrospective specification.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to address a fundamental problem in production ML systems: the inability to establish which evolving procedure produced a given outcome or why. This distinction matters critically in production systems where code, configuration, and artifacts change continuously while external feedback accumulates. The authors use a real-world quantitative trading system as their case study to illustrate this problem.

Method: The authors conduct a retrospective case study of a human-directed, agent-engineered quantitative trading system over one year. They examine engineering records documenting changes during the episode, analyze the distinction between outcome evidence, evaluated-object identity, and causal explanation, and organize archive-relative claim identifiability into an evidence hierarchy.

Result: The trading account gained and outperformed a broad market index, but annual alpha was not statistically distinguishable from zero under the main retrospective specification. Retrospectively selected subperiods showed adverse relative performance and conditional candidate-level weakness. The archive could not establish a common frozen instance or a unique cause, demonstrating the outcome-diagnosis gap in practice.

Conclusion: The authors conclude that external feedback constrains outcome claims while provenance and additional identification structure determine the resolution of diagnosis. They propose a prospective production-binding protocol to resolve the outcome-diagnosis gap, though this protocol is proposed rather than prospectively validated. The key contribution is distinguishing frozen instances, pre-specified adaptive procedures, and ad-hoc development, and organizing archive-relative claim identifiability into an evidence hierarchy.

Abstract: Reality may establish that an outcome occurred without identifying which evolving procedure produced it or why. This distinction matters in production ML systems whose code, configuration, and artifacts change while external feedback accumulates. We examine it in a human-directed, agent-engineered quantitative trading system, using oracle to mean an external source of realized outcomes rather than a complete correctness specification. Across one year, the account gained and outperformed a broad market index, while annual alpha was not statistically distinguishable from zero under the main retrospective specification. Retrospectively selected subperiods include adverse relative performance and conditional candidate-level weakness under declared approximate references. Engineering records document changes during the episode, and complete recommendation-to-runtime binding is unavailable. The archive does not establish a common frozen instance or a unique cause. The case motivates an outcome--diagnosis gap: outcome evidence, evaluated-object identity, and causal explanation support distinct claims. We distinguish frozen instances, pre-specified adaptive procedures, and ad-hoc development; organize archive-relative claim identifiability and an evidence hierarchy; and propose a prospective production-binding protocol. An illustrative compatible-history example shows how factual binding can resolve a recommendation's referent without supplying its counterfactual effect. The protocol is proposed rather than prospectively validated. External feedback constrains outcome claims, while provenance and additional identification structure determine the resolution of diagnosis.

</details>


### [277] [Shared-Roadmap Generation and Evaluator for Multi-Agent Path Planning Using Heterogeneous Graph Neural Network](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09034)
*Brandon Ho,Nikola Rogers,Seung-Kyum Choi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes a heterogeneous Graph Neural Network (GNN) framework for automated generation and evaluation of shared multi-agent roadmaps in continuous environments. The model represents waypoints, agent locations, and task locations as distinct nodes in a heterogeneous graph, learning to identify critical points and prune redundant elements.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional roadmap generation methods (lattice grids, sampling-based approaches) face a trade-off between graph density and the likelihood of finding feasible, high-quality solutions for multi-agent path planning (MAPP).

Method: A scalable heterogeneous GNN framework that: (1) represents waypoints, agent locations, and task locations as distinct node types in a heterogeneous graph; (2) trains on occupation density maps aggregated from expert solver trajectories; (3) learns to identify critical points of interest and prune redundant nodes/edges; (4) produces compact, coordination-aware roadmaps invariant to task permutations.

Result: The framework achieves at least 40% reduction in both runtime and graph size for dense roadmaps, while potentially finding better solutions and reducing planning effort.

Conclusion: The proposed GNN-based approach effectively generates compact, coordination-aware multi-agent roadmaps that are reusable for pick-and-delivery tasks, offering significant improvements in planning efficiency through intelligent graph pruning based on learned occupancy patterns.

Abstract: Multi-agent path planning (MAPP) in continuous environments often relies on roadmaps to balance safety and search efficiency. However, traditional roadmap generation methods, such as lattice grids or standard sampling-based approaches, frequently face a trade-off between graph density and the likelihood of finding feasible, high-quality solutions. In this paper, we propose a scalable heterogeneous Graph Neural Network (GNN) framework for the automated generation and evaluation of shared multi-agent roadmaps. Our model covers the representation of waypoints, agent locations, and task locations as distinct nodes in a heterogeneous graph, allowing it to reason over global connectivity and inter-agent interactions. By training on occupation density maps aggregated and collected from expert solver trajectories, the GNN learns to identify critical points of interest and prune redundant nodes and edges. This process produces a compact, coordination-aware roadmap that is invariant to task permutations and is reusable for multi-agent pick and delivery tasks. Experimental results demonstrate that our framework can reduce planning effort and can potentially find better solutions, reaching at least 40% reduction in runtime and in graph size for dense roadmaps.

</details>


### [278] [When the Governor Becomes the Disturbance: Control-Generated Disturbance and Cost-Aware Backoff in Governed Tool-Using Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09037)
*Veronique Ziegler*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper studies how supervisory governors can interfere with tool-using agents in a controlled file-recovery environment. The authors show that increased regulatory intensity triggers tool failures, which a cost-blind governor can turn into persistent blocking that prevents task completion. They propose a backoff rule that reduces intervention probability using a moving average of known induced events, which improves task completion rates compared to a fixed weak governor. Experiments on a hand-coded stochastic-policy agent and a Gemini 2.5 Flash model (576 episodes across 6 tasks) demonstrate that adaptive backoff reduces blocking and improves success rates, with intermediate backoff strength performing best.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The research is motivated by the concern that supervisory governors (regulatory mechanisms) can interfere with the tool-using agents they regulate, potentially causing persistent blocking that prevents task completion. This is a problem in AI systems where regulatory oversight may inadvertently harm performance.

Method: The study uses a controlled file-recovery environment where regulatory intensity triggers experimentally imposed tool failures. The authors compare two governors: (1) a cost-blind governor that turns failures into persistent blocking, and (2) a backoff rule that reduces intervention probability using a moving average of known induced events. Experiments are conducted on a hand-coded stochastic-policy agent and a Gemini 2.5 Flash model across 576 episodes and 6 tasks, testing different backoff strengths.

Result: The failure pattern appears under both result replacement and execution of corrupted tool arguments. Adaptive backoff improves completion relative to a fixed weak governor with matched intervention frequency. In the Gemini 2.5 Flash experiment, backoff reduces blocking and improves completion, with intermediate backoff strength achieving the highest aggregate success.

Conclusion: The results identify an interaction between intervention cost and persistent action blocking, and suggest that adaptive backoff is a possible mitigation. However, the cost mechanisms are imposed and directly observable to the backoff rule, so applicability beyond this controlled environment remains an empirical question.

Abstract: Supervisory governors can interfere with the tool-using agents they regulate. We study this possibility in a controlled file-recovery environment where increases in regulatory intensity trigger experimentally imposed tool failures. A cost-blind governor can turn these failures into persistent blocking that prevents task completion. We compare this governor with a backoff rule that reduces intervention probability using a moving average of known induced events. On a hand-coded stochastic-policy agent, the failure pattern appears under both result replacement and execution of corrupted tool arguments. For the persistent policy, adaptive backoff improves completion relative to a fixed weak governor with approximately matched intervention frequency. A Gemini 2.5 Flash experiment comprising 576 episodes across 6 tasks also shows reduced blocking and improved completion under backoff; among the tested settings, intermediate backoff strength achieves the highest observed aggregate success. These results identify an interaction between intervention cost and persistent action blocking, together with a possible mitigation. The cost mechanisms are imposed and their induced events are directly observable to the backoff rule; applicability beyond this controlled environment remains an empirical question.

</details>


### [279] [Before They Can Solve: Predicting Post-Training Coding-Agent Performance from Base Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.10478)
*Tan Yu,Alexander Bukharin,Khushi Bhardwaj,Jennifer Williams,Zirui Liu,Jonathan Lingjie Li,Soumye Singhal,Joseph Jennings,Sanjeev Satheesh,Yash Jain,Ashish Vaswani,Venkat Krishna Srinivasan,Matthew Papakipos,Hyunwoo Kim,Jian Zhang,Oleksii Kuchaiev,Markus Kliegl,Mostofa Patwary,Mohammad Shoeybi,Bryan Catanzaro,Jonathan Cohen,Jiantao Jiao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes methods to predict which base model checkpoints are worth expensive agentic post-training, by using successful post-trained agent trajectories as lookahead signals. The key innovation is identifying the "decisive step" (first step that flips a task from failing to passing) and building three evaluation screens that don't require the base model to drive the harness from cold start.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: End-to-end pass@K is poorly suited for agentic coding because base checkpoints often fail to produce well-formed tool invocations needed to complete multi-step tasks. Single-shot tasks avoid this but don't capture the core capability of maintaining coherent state over many tool-using steps as repositories evolve.

Method: 1) Replay successful post-trained trajectories and identify the "decisive step" - the first step whose cumulative patch passes tests. 2) Build three screens at this step: (i) Decisive-Action BPB measuring probability mass on certified action, (ii) Patch MCQ testing checkpoint's choice between certified action and verifier-rejected alternatives, (iii) prefix-conditioned pass@K evaluating support for functionally-correct generations.

Result: Across ten pairs of public base and post-trained models, all three screens rank the cohort in close agreement with post-trained SWE-bench Verified pass@1.

Conclusion: The proposed methods can evaluate base models for agentic coding tasks using only a benchmark's successful trajectories and verifier, enabling future agentic coding benchmarks to serve as base-model evaluations without requiring the base model to independently solve tasks.

Abstract: How can we predict which base checkpoint is worth an expensive round of agentic post-training? End-to-end pass@$K$ tests whether successful behavior already appears in a base model's distribution, but it is a poor fit for agentic coding: many base checkpoints cannot reliably produce the well-formed tool invocation required to complete a task end-to-end. Single-shot or short-horizon tasks avoid these tool-calling failures by collapsing a multi-step interaction into a fixed prompt and a single patch, but they sidestep the core capability we care about: maintaining coherent state over many tool-using steps as the repository evolves. To bridge this gap, we treat successful post-trained agent trajectories as a lookahead signal of base-model potential. Replaying each trajectory and rerunning tests after every code-changing step identifies the decisive step: the first step whose cumulative patch flips the repository from failing to passing, certifying that the recorded action solves the task given the prior context. Motivated by a coverage principle for agentic traces, we build three screens at this step that do not require a base checkpoint to drive the harness from a cold start: (i) Decisive-Action BPB (bits per byte) measures the probability mass on the certified action, (ii) Patch MCQ tests the checkpoint's choice between that action and alternatives rejected by the same verifier, and (iii) prefix-conditioned pass@$K$ evaluates support for functionally-correct generations and credits any continuation that the tests accept. Across ten pairs of public base and post-trained models, all three screens rank the cohort in close agreement with post-trained SWE-bench Verified pass@$1$. As our methods need only a benchmark's successful trajectories and its verifier, they can be applied to turn future agentic coding benchmarks into base-model evaluations.

</details>


### [280] [From High Recall to High Utility: Dataset-Adaptive Post-Processing of LLM-Generated Customer Intents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09039)
*Mahesh Viswanathan,Joan Rossello,Leticia Fernandes,Paul Mutawe*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A dataset-adaptive post-processing architecture for Customer Intent Extraction (CIE) that transforms high-recall LLM outputs into stable, reusable intent units through standardization, deduplication, clustering, and constrained language-model aggregation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: High-recall LLM extraction from heterogeneous enterprise data produces outputs that are duplicated, uneven in granularity, semantically overlapping, or too numerous for downstream use.

Method: A multi-stage pipeline: (1) source-specific preprocessing to isolate evidence from multimodal plans, operational records, and structured data; (2) standardization and deduplication; (3) embedding computation in shared semantic vector space; (4) adaptive clustering with strategy selection; (5) cluster-level keyword extraction for explainability; (6) singleton reassignment using embedding and keyword similarity agreement; (7) constrained language-model aggregation producing one concise intent per cluster.

Result: A semantic reduction layer that converts high-recall LLM outputs into reusable enterprise intelligence with retained provenance, clustering, embedding, and generation metadata.

Conclusion: The architecture enables two downstream applications: (1) Machine-Generated Intents - inferring likely objectives for customers lacking direct evidence from similar peer profiles; (2) Intent-guided semantic retrieval and mapping - using stable intents as queries to map customer intents to business outcomes.

Abstract: Large language models can extract useful signals from heterogeneous enterprise data, but high-recall extraction often produces outputs that are duplicated, uneven in granularity, semantically overlapping, or too numerous for downstream systems and human reviewers to use effectively. We present a dataset-adaptive post-processing architecture developed for Customer Intent Extraction (CIE), where unstructured customer language is transformed into stable, traceable intent units. The approach separates recall-oriented extraction from utility-oriented reduction. Source-specific preprocessing first isolates evidence from multimodal plans, sparse operational records, and structured opportunity data. Candidate intents are then standardized and deduplicated, optionally enriched with metadata for embedding computation, represented in a shared semantic vector space, and grouped using a clustering strategy selected according to the candidate set's characteristics. Cluster-level keywords provide an explainability layer, while singleton reassignment requires agreement between embedding and keyword similarity. Finally, constrained language-model aggregation produces one concise intent per cluster without introducing unsupported concepts, and the resulting unit retains provenance, clustering, embedding, and generation metadata. This treats post-processing not as cosmetic cleanup, but as a semantic reduction layer converting high-recall LLM outputs into reusable enterprise intelligence. We also describe two downstream applications: Machine-Generated Intents, which infer likely objectives for customers lacking direct evidence from peer customers with similar profiles, and intent-guided semantic retrieval and mapping, which uses the stable intent as a query against a downstream decision space, illustrated here by mapping customer intents to business outcomes.

</details>


### [281] [Justice After Identity: Large Language Models and the View from Everywhere](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09053)
*W. Russell Neuman*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper explores whether Large Language Models (LLMs) could serve as an "integrative original position" - a computational approximation of Rawls' philosophical thought experiment for determining principles of justice. The authors investigate whether LLMs, which encode diverse human identities but lack singular social positions, could provide fairer moral judgments than humans, and whether humans would accept AI advice on fairness issues.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to address the challenge of achieving common justice and fairness judgments in human societies, which are inevitably shaped by self-interests, social positions, and cultural backgrounds. While Rawls' "original position" aims to overcome these limitations, critics question whether humans can truly suspend their identities. The authors propose that LLMs, lacking singular identities but encoding diverse human perspectives, might offer a novel computational approach to fairness judgments.

Method: The authors conducted experiments comparing human judgments with those of base models and frontier/fine-tuned models on classic moral dilemmas. They systematically varied identity relationships and applied Rawlsian constraints on identity to test how different agents (humans, base LLMs, fine-tuned LLMs) judge fairness across various scenarios.

Result: The abstract does not provide specific quantitative results but indicates the authors present comparative data on how humans versus different LLM configurations judge moral dilemmas under varying identity conditions and Rawlsian constraints.

Conclusion: The authors conclude by speculating on whether humans would actually accept thoughtful advice from advanced AI systems regarding fairness and justice, even if AI could provide more impartial judgments. They suggest AI may play a positive role interacting with human judgment rather than replacing it entirely, but acknowledge people are unlikely to hand over complete agentic control to computational systems.

Abstract: The search for a common view of justice and fairness has challenged human collective activity, as our diverging judgments are unavoidably shaped by the self-interests of social position, personal benefit, cultural inheritance, and historical circumstance. John Rawls famously attempted to overcome this limitation through popularizing a philosophical tradition known by the phrase "the original position" - a thought experiment by which people select principles of justice without knowing the identities or advantages they will possess. Critics, however, have long questioned whether people can meaningfully suspend their social identities and suppress morally relevant forms of lived experience. Artificial intelligence engaged to calculate algorithmic and agentic fairness introduces a novel possibility. LLMs have no singular class, race, gender, nationality, or biography, yet their parameters encode linguistic representations of a vast range of human identities and moral traditions. Perhaps the ethical judgments of LLMs could approximate an integrative original position - a "view from everywhere" generated not by excluding social identities but by computationally incorporating their diversity.It is unlikely that humankind will "hand over the keys" to computational systems by simply delegating complete agentic control of distributive and procedural collective processes. But AI may play a role, perhaps a positive one, interacting with individual and collective human judgment as we often confront increasingly polarized views on what is fair and just. We present data comparing human, base model, and frontier/fine-tuned model judgments about classic moral dilemmas while systematically varying identity relationships and Rawlsian constraints on identity. We conclude by speculating whether, if advanced AI systems provide humans with thoughtful advice, humans would actually be likely to accept it.

</details>


### [282] [Epistemic Uncertainty-Aware Defect Detection for Quality Control in Medical Device Manufacturing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09057)
*Raham A. Butt,Marco Romanelli,Roche C. de Guzman*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper investigates using epistemic uncertainty to improve reliability of automated defect detection in medical device manufacturing. A rejection strategy that abstains from predictions with high epistemic uncertainty is proposed. On 266,170 FDA MAUDE device reports, 10% abstention reduces classification error by 48%, while 70% coverage yields near-perfect accuracy. On synthetic benchmarks, 9% abstention reduces risk up to 63%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To improve reliability of automated defect detection in medical device manufacturing by addressing errors arising from epistemic uncertainty in decision models, particularly in high-stakes applications where incorrect predictions could have serious consequences.

Method: A machine learning framework operating on heterogeneous manufacturing and device-report data represented with Knowledge Graphs. A principled rejection strategy abstains from predictions whose estimated epistemic uncertainty exceeds a specified threshold. Evaluated on synthetic benchmarks and real-world FDA MAUDE device reports (266,170 reports).

Result: On real-world FDA MAUDE data: 10% abstention rate reduces classification error by 48%; approximately 70% coverage yields near-perfect accuracy on retained samples. On synthetic manufacturing benchmarks: abstaining on 9% of decisions reduces risk up to 63% compared to standard no-abstention approach.

Conclusion: Abstaining from predictions with high epistemic uncertainty provides a practical tool for controlling reliability of ML-based defect detection in high-stakes medical device manufacturing, identifying cases requiring additional inspection rather than issuing potentially harmful predictions.

Abstract: Objective: We investigate whether accounting for epistemic uncertainty can improve the reliability of automated defect detection in medical device manufacturing. Methods: We consider a machine learning framework that operates on heterogeneous manufacturing and device-report data represented with Knowledge Graphs. To mitigate errors arising from uncertainty in the decision model, we analyze a principled rejection strategy to abstain from predictions whose estimated epistemic uncertainty exceeds a specified threshold. We evaluate the approach using standard synthetic benchmarks and real-world medical device report data. Results: The theoretical results establish the validity of the method characterizing the regimes under which it is expected to be effective. Empirically, the rejection strategy enables explicit control of coverage, that is, the proportion of samples for which the model issues predictions, while improving performance on the retained samples. On 266,170 real-world FDA MAUDE device reports, a 10% abstention rate reduces classification error by 48%, and more aggressive rejection (approximately 70% coverage) yields near-perfect accuracy on the retained samples. On standard synthetic manufacturing benchmarks, abstaining on 9% of the decisions, our approach reduces the risk up to 63% compared with the standard no-abstention approach. Conclusions: Abstaining from predictions with high epistemic uncertainty can provide a practical tool for controlling the reliability of machine learning-based defect detection, especially in high-stakes medical device manufacturing applications. Significance: Uncertainty-aware defect detection may support safer and more reliable quality assurance in medical device manufacturing by identifying cases that require additional inspection rather than issuing potentially harmful predictions.

</details>


### [283] [RippleCP: Measuring Counterfactual Checkpoint Advantage in Coding Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09088)
*Mayur Akewar,Ravi Ranjan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper addresses the problem of determining which checkpoints in agent systems are worth saving. The authors propose "counterfactual checkpoint advantage" - measuring the recovery cost reduction when checkpointing vs skipping a candidate state. By driving both paths to the same failure and recovering both, they find checkpointing saves 49.4s/task, but with two distinct regimes: first checkpoint yields 0.64 conversion (100.0s saved on 156.5s work), while the second yields -0.03 conversion (-1.1s). The key insight is that recovery is re-derivation, not replay, so preserved work ≠ saved work, and classical elapsed-work rules misprice checkpoints.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Agent checkpoint systems exist to decide what state is recovery-relevant, how to snapshot it, and whether rollback is admissible. However, none of them decide which safe boundaries they expose are worth materializing (saving). This creates a gap in checkpoint optimization.

Method: The authors formulate the problem as counterfactual checkpoint advantage - the reduction in future recovery cost obtained by checkpointing a candidate rather than skipping it. They measure this by driving two parallel branches: a CP (checkpoint) branch and a SKIP branch, both reaching the same logical failure, then recovering both under matched model, tool, verifier, and stopping conditions. Experiments were conducted on 12 SWE-bench Verified tasks with 106 real recovery branches.

Result: Checkpointing saves 49.4 seconds per task on average. The results reveal two distinct regimes separated by two orders of magnitude: (1) First checkpoint returns 100.0s savings on 156.5s of protected work (conversion rate 0.64); (2) Second checkpoint (one step later) returns -1.1s on 41.8s (conversion rate -0.03), meaning it actually costs time. The paper shows recovery is re-derivation rather than replay, so preserved work is a poor proxy for saved work, and the classical elapsed-work rule misprices the second checkpoint by its full nominal cost.

Conclusion: The authors identify where checkpoint placement can pay off and establish the criteria a placement policy must meet. The key insight is that checkpoint value depends on re-derivation cost, not preserved work, and simple elapsed-time rules fail to capture this nuance. Future placement policies should consider the counterfactual advantage metric rather than classical work-based rules.

Abstract: Agent checkpoint systems decide what state is recovery-relevant, how to snapshot it, and whether rollback is admissible. None decides which of the safe boundaries they expose are worth materializing. We formulate this as counterfactual checkpoint advantage, the reduction in future recovery cost obtained by checkpointing a candidate rather than skipping it, and measure it by driving a CP branch and a SKIP branch to the same logical failure and recovering both under matched model, tool, verifier, and stopping conditions. On a frozen pilot of 12 SWE-bench Verified tasks and 106 real recovery branches, checkpointing saves 49.4 s per task, and that figure resolves into two regimes two orders of magnitude apart. The first checkpoint returns 100.0 s on 156.5 s of protected work, a conversion of 0.64; a second one step later returns-1.1 s on 41.8 s, a conversion of -0.03. Recovery is a re-derivation rather than a replay, so preserved work is a poor guide to saved work, and the classical elapsed-work rule misprices the second checkpoint by its full nominal cost. We identify where placement can pay, and set the bar a placement policy must clear.

</details>


### [284] [Constraint Tree Exploration for Learning from Language Feedback](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09107)
*Shaoang Li,Daniel R. Jiang,Jian Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper addresses the problem of learning from natural-language feedback in interactive settings, where misinterpreting feedback can cause agents to incorrectly eliminate valid solutions. The authors model user intent as latent constraints and propose TRACE, a tree-based algorithm that tests constraint refinements through action generation. The algorithm has two modes: falsification (detecting contradictions) and identification (naming violated constraints). TRACE-Identification achieves 73-86% success rates on RecMovie compared to 42-48% for baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: When agents receive natural-language feedback explaining why an action failed (e.g., "you can't do X because Y"), misinterpreting this feedback can lead them to incorrectly rule out valid solutions. This is a fundamental problem in interactive learning systems where users provide feedback in natural language.

Method: The paper models user intent as latent constraints over an action space and formulates learning as pure exploration over feasible regions. TRACE organizes candidate constraints in a tree structure and tests refinements by generating actions that satisfy proposed constraints. The algorithm commits to refinements only when feedback doesn't contradict over repeated tests. Two modes: (i) Falsification - detects contradictions to current constraint set; (ii) Identification - can additionally name violated constraints.

Result: Theoretical results: TRACE-Falsification achieves high-probability coverage bounds dependent on H (candidate class size). TRACE-Identification replaces this dependence with K/p_ext where K is number of latent constraints and p_ext bounds probability of extracting missing true constraints. Empirical results: On RecMovie task, TRACE-Identification achieves 73% and 86% final-output success under 20 and 60 output caps, compared to at most 42% and 48% for prompting baselines. Identity-corruption experiments show robustness when falsification detector remains reliable.

Conclusion: TRACE provides a principled approach to learning from language feedback by distinguishing between falsification and identification modes. The identification mode offers better sample complexity (replacing H dependence with K/p_ext). Empirically, TRACE significantly outperforms baselines on language-feedback tasks, with particular improvements in constrained optimization scenarios. The approach is robust to certain types of feedback corruption when the falsification detector is reliable.

Abstract: Natural-language feedback in interactive learning often explains why an action failed by pointing to violated requirements. Misinterpreting this feedback can lead an agent to rule out valid solutions. We study this setting by modeling user intent as latent constraints over an action space and formulating learning from language feedback as pure exploration over feasible regions. We introduce TRACE, an algorithm that organizes candidate constraints in a tree and tests each proposed refinement by generating actions that satisfy it. TRACE commits to the refinement only if the resulting feedback does not contradict it over repeated tests. We distinguish two ways of using the same feedback: (i) falsification, which detects contradictions to the constraint set currently being tested, and (ii) identification, which may additionally name a violated constraint. We prove high-probability coverage bounds with dependence on the candidate class size $H$ for TRACE-Falsification. With reliable identification, TRACE-Identification can replace this dependence by $K/p_{\mathrm{ext}}$, where $K$ is the number of latent constraints and $p_{\mathrm{ext}}$ lower-bounds the probability of extracting a missing true constraint from informative feedback. We evaluate TRACE across six language-feedback tasks. On RecMovie, TRACE-Identification achieves 73% and 86% final-output success under caps of 20 and 60 evaluated outputs, compared with at most 42% and 48% for the evaluated prompting baselines given the same feedback and output caps. Controlled identity-corruption experiments further show greater robustness than direct accumulation when the falsification detector remains reliable.

</details>


### [285] [GeoNatureAgent (GNA): A Framework and Benchmark for Pre-Production Evaluation of Tool-Using Agents on Geospatial and Environmental Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09112)
*Gabriel Diaz-Ireland,Diego Prieto-Herráez,Mario García Peces,Javier Velázquez,Benjamin Zaitchik,Devika Jain*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: GeoNatureAgent (GNA) is a framework for pre-production evaluation of tool-using LLM agents in geospatial workflows, featuring a 16-tool MCP server and 103-task benchmark tested against 9 LLMs. Claude Sonnet 4 achieves highest capability (61.7%), while DeepSeek V3.2 offers best cost-accuracy tradeoff at 11.3x lower cost than Claude.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Before deploying tool-using LLM agents in environmental and geospatial workflows, teams need evidence that agents reliably select right operations against real APIs. Current benchmarks lack standardized tool layers, task suites, and deterministic scorers.

Method: Evaluation framework with fixed 16-tool geospatial interface published as MCP server; 103-task benchmark (93 main tasks across 18 categories + 10-task comparison expansion); tested against open geospatial API serving three environmental indicators across Spain and Portugal; evaluated 9 LLMs under three temperature-1.0 seeds; assessed capability and per-case cost as orthogonal axes.

Result: Claude Sonnet 4 achieves highest capability (61.7% ± 0.7% on all 103 tasks; 60.8% on main suite), followed by DeepSeek V3.2 (57.9%), no other model exceeds 53%. DeepSeek V3.2 offers 93% of Claude's capability at 11.3x lower list-price cost. Under strict all-checks scoring, best model sits 24-36 points below 85-97% on general GIS benchmarks; per-check partial credit for top four models reaches 86-90%.

Conclusion: Open-weight models dominate cost-accuracy Pareto frontier. The gap between strict scoring and general-purpose benchmarks reflects scoring strictness rather than task difficulty alone. Framework is extensible - swapping tool executors and task suite enables equivalent benchmarks for any geospatial domain.

Abstract: Before tool-using LLM agents are deployed in environmental and geospatial workflows, teams need evidence that an agent reliably selects the right operations against real APIs. We introduce GeoNatureAgent (GNA), a framework for pre-production evaluation of tool-using agents: a fixed sixteen-tool geospatial interface published as a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, so the agent under test is the only variable, scored against an identical tool layer, task suite, and deterministic scorer. Its flagship instance is a 103-task benchmark (a 93-task main suite across 18 categories plus a ten-task comparison expansion) evaluated against an open, self-hostable geospatial API serving three environmental indicators across Spain and Portugal. We evaluate nine LLMs under three temperature-1.0 seeds, reporting capability and per-case cost as orthogonal axes. (1) Claude Sonnet 4 achieves the highest capability (61.7% +/- 0.7% on all 103 tasks; 60.8% on the main suite), followed closely by DeepSeek V3.2 (57.9%), while no other model exceeds 53%; (2) the cost-accuracy Pareto frontier is mostly open-weight, with DeepSeek V3.2 offering 93% of Claude's capability at 11.3x lower list-price cost; (3) under strict all-checks scoring the best model sits 24-36 points below the 85-97% reported on general-purpose GIS benchmarks, whereas per-check partial credit for the top four models (86-90%) is comparable, so much of that gap reflects scoring strictness rather than task difficulty alone. The MCP server, evaluation harness, benchmark, and API are publicly available; swapping the tool executors and task suite instantiates an equivalent benchmark for any geospatial domain.

</details>


### [286] [From Uncertainty to Action: Learning to Steer LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09115)
*Hanwen Li,Jinhao Duan,Guanhua Zhu,Junchi Lu,Bo Shen,Chenxi Yuan,Kaidi Xu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper addresses the problem of when and how to steer (correct) LLM agents during execution. The authors create a large dataset of counterfactual continuations (SOT) and find that while uncertainty can identify failing trajectories, no single signal reliably identifies where steering helps. They propose VoS (Value of Steering), a trajectory-level monitor that learns from SOT when steering is valuable, achieving improvements in all 12 experimental settings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to determine whether uncertainty can guide the decisions of when and how to correct an LLM agent. Currently, uncertainty is commonly used to decide when to correct, but it remains unclear whether it can effectively guide these steering decisions - specifically where to steer and which mechanism to use.

Method: The authors: (1) Steer agent trajectories separately at every non-terminal step using four different mechanisms; (2) Run each continuation to completion; (3) Create a Stepwise Outcome Table (SOT) with ~82,000 counterfactual continuations from 1,864 trajectories across three benchmarks and two agents; (4) Propose VoS (Value of Steering), a trajectory-level monitor that can be used offline or online, which learns from SOT the value of steering at each step and decides where to steer using a harm-budgeted trigger.

Result: Key findings: (1) Uncertainty can identify failing trajectories but no single signal reliably locates the step at which steering helps; (2) VoS improves on unmodified execution in all 12 settings (benchmark × agent × offline/online) by 7.8 points on average; (3) VoS outperforms the strongest of five existing uncertainty-triggered methods in 11 out of 12 settings, by 2.9 points on average; (4) Ablations show that training on measured outcomes and a tight harm budget are both essential.

Conclusion: The conclusion is that uncertainty alone is insufficient for effective agent steering; instead, a learned trajectory-level monitor (VoS) that estimates the value of steering at each step is more effective. The harm-budgeted trigger successfully limits the fraction of successful trajectories disturbed while improving overall performance. This represents a paradigm shift from uncertainty-based to value-based steering decisions.

Abstract: Steering an LLM agent means deciding whether to correct it, at which step, and with which mechanism. Uncertainty is often used to decide when to correct an agent, but whether it can guide these decisions remains unclear. We steer agent trajectories separately at every non-terminal step with each of four mechanisms and run each continuation to completion. The resulting stepwise outcome table (SOT) holds about 82,000 counterfactual continuations of 1,864 trajectories from three benchmarks and two agents. It shows that uncertainty can identify failing trajectories, but that no single signal reliably locates the step at which steering helps. We therefore propose VoS (Value of Steering), a trajectory-level monitor, offline or online, that learns from SOT the value of steering at each step and decides where to steer by it. A harm-budgeted trigger decides whether to steer, limiting the fraction of successful trajectories that VoS disturbs. VoS improves on unmodified execution in all 12 settings of benchmark, agent, and offline or online use, by 7.8 points on average, and outperforms the strongest of five existing uncertainty-triggered methods in 11, by 2.9 points on average. Ablations show that training on measured outcomes and a tight harm budget are both essential.

</details>


### [287] [Which Buildings Are Artificial Intelligence-Ready? A Measurement-Based Assessment Framework for AI Question Answering and Actuation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09119)
*Wooyoung Jung*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes a framework to quantify building readiness for agentic AI systems by measuring two "ceilings" based on a building's knowledge graph: answerable-readiness (operational questions data could answer) and actuation-readiness (control actions exposed). The study evaluates a reference AI agent on simulated and real buildings, finding that missing data, not AI capability, typically limits readiness (median answerable ceiling of 0.16 across 37 real buildings).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Agentic AI systems are increasingly becoming interfaces to buildings for answering questions and controlling operations, but there has been no systematic method to assess whether a building is ready for such AI integration. This gap needed to be addressed to enable proper evaluation and retrofit planning.

Method: The study proposes a framework with two components: (1) A building's knowledge graph establishing two ceilings - answerable-readiness ceiling (share of operational questions data could answer) and actuation-readiness ceiling (share of control actions exposed); (2) A reference AI agent's accuracy evaluation on a fixed set of questions to measure realized ceiling. The framework was tested on a simulated office building and 37 public real-building graphs.

Result: In the simulated office, the agent realized 0.62 of a 0.64 answerable ceiling, indicating that missing data, not AI limitations, primarily restrict readiness (except for naming fault causes). Across 37 real buildings, the median answerable ceiling was only 0.16, and in 15 of 45 cases, unlinked sensors lowered the ceiling.

Conclusion: The framework transforms the question "is this building AI-ready?" into an auditable, ranked retrofit question. This enables building operators to systematically assess AI readiness and prioritize necessary upgrades to enable effective AI integration.

Abstract: Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) systems are becoming the interface to buildings, answering questions and controlling operations, but a building's readiness for them has not been systematically assessed. This study proposes a framework to quantify it. First, a building's knowledge graph sets two ceilings. The answerable-readiness ceiling is the share of operational questions its data could answer, and the actuation-readiness ceiling is the share of control actions it exposes. Second, a reference AI agent's accuracy on a fixed set of these questions shows how much of the ceilings is realized. On a simulated office, the agent realizes 0.62 of a 0.64 answerable ceiling, so missing data, not the AI, limit readiness, except in naming a fault's cause. Across 37 public real-building graphs, the median answerable ceiling is 0.16, and in 15 of 45, unlinked sensors lower it. The framework turns "is this building AI-ready?" into an auditable, ranked retrofit question.

</details>


### [288] [CADFather: Autonomous CAD Reconstruction through Coordinated Tool Use](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09127)
*Gennadiy Savrasov,Maksim Elistratov,Nikita Gavrilov,Albert Garifullin,Oleg Pavlov,Soslan Kabisov,Vladimir Frolov,Anton Konushin,Andrey Kuznetsov,Dmitrii Zhemchuzhnikov*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CADFather is an autonomous agentic system that coordinates multiple tools (vision-language assistant, CAD operation proposal tools, numerical optimization) to reconstruct editable parametric CAD programs from 3D meshes, without requiring additional training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reconstructing editable CAD models from 3D shapes remains challenging because no single method works well across different part geometries and reconstruction stages. Existing methods can propose CAD operations but lack flexibility and robustness.

Method: CADFather uses a vision-language assistant that inspects renders of target and intermediate reconstructions to make decisions: which CAD programs to extend, which tools to invoke, how many proposals to generate, and when to finish. It combines learned and algorithmic tools for proposing CAD operations, with numerical optimization for parameter refinement. The system maintains alternative candidate programs and preserves the best valid result.

Result: Evaluated on DeepCAD, Fusion360, MCB test sets, CADENA-Bench, CADBench, and BenchCAD. Shows reconstruction quality and execution validity across multiple benchmarks. Also analyzes computational cost and quality trade-offs.

Conclusion: CADFather demonstrates that coordinating complementary tools via an autonomous agent can successfully reconstruct parametric CAD programs from 3D meshes using pretrained models without additional training, offering a flexible approach to CAD reconstruction.

Abstract: Reconstructing an editable CAD model from a 3D shape remains a challenging engineering task. Existing methods can propose CAD operations, but no single source of proposals works equally well across different part geometries and stages of reconstruction. We introduce CADFather, an autonomous agentic system that coordinates complementary tools to recover parametric CAD programs from 3D meshes. A vision-language assistant inspects renders of the target and intermediate reconstructions, then decides which candidate CAD programs to extend, which tools to invoke, how many proposals to generate, and when to finish. Learned and algorithmic tools propose CAD operations, while numerical optimization refines the parameters of existing programs. Proposed or refined programs are executed and evaluated to provide feedback for subsequent decisions. The agent maintains alternative candidate programs for each target part and preserves the best valid result throughout reconstruction. CADFather uses pretrained generation and assistant models without additional training. We evaluate reconstruction quality and execution validity on the full DeepCAD, Fusion360, and MCB test sets, as well as on CADENA-Bench, CADBench, and BenchCAD. We additionally analyze computational cost and the trade-off between cost and reconstruction quality.

</details>


### [289] [Breaking the Space Barrier and its Application to Language Model Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09139)
*Arip Asadulaev*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper addresses the problem of enforcing structured output (JSON, tool calls) from language models using automata. The authors leverage a rare property of the format-enforcing automaton: from any state, each token leads along exactly one path. They apply complexity theory results about graphs with few paths to achieve space-efficient format verification, beating Savitch's theorem. The practical implementations demonstrate significant improvements: 1.2-1.3x faster extraction, 3MB vs 1.5GB grammar size, and 2.5x faster tool-calling agents.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Language models increasingly need to produce structured output (JSON with schemas, typed tool calls). Current methods use automata to enforce format by forbidding invalid tokens, but this approach faces memory/scalability issues. The authors seek to solve an open theoretical problem about verifying graphs with few paths while achieving practical efficiency gains.

Method: The authors establish theoretical results showing that deciding whether a graph with few paths connects two points can be done with O(log²n / log log n) space (below Savitch's O(log²n)). They then apply these constructions to build an inference engine that: writes format-forced text without running the model, recomputes masks on GPU without tables, uses small stacks for recursive formats, maintains validity under token limits, and decodes independent fields in parallel.

Result: The theoretical result settles an open question about space complexity for graphs with few paths (classes ReachUL, LOGDCFL, C=L, SC2). Practically, on a 16GB Apple M2 Pro with Qwen3.5-2B and 4B against MLX with llguidance: schema-constrained extraction is 1.2-1.3x faster with same answers; grammar costs 3MB vs up to 1.5GB; one server holds 16 grammars where tables run out of memory; 16 tool-calling agents finish 2.5x faster.

Conclusion: The paper bridges automata theory and complexity theory with practical systems work. By exploiting the unique property of format-enforcing automata (deterministic token paths), the authors achieve both theoretical advances (sub-Savitch space complexity) and practical improvements (faster extraction, smaller grammar size, better scalability). The approach enables efficient structured output generation from language models on consumer hardware.

Abstract: Language models are more and more often asked for structured output: JSON that follows a schema, or a tool call with typed arguments. A small machine, an automaton, enforces the format by forbidding the tokens that would break it. We observe that this machine has a rare property: from any of its states, each token leads along exactly one path. Graphs in which only a few paths join any two points are a classical object of complexity theory, and our theoretical result settles an open question about them: one can decide whether such a graph connects two points while verifying that it really has few paths, with very little memory. Precisely, the problem lies in the classes ReachUL, LOGDCFL, C=L and SC2, and needs only O(log2 n/ log log n) space, below the classical O(log2 n) of Savitch's theorem. The constructions behind the proofs become an inference engine: text the format forces is written without running the model, the mask is recomputed on the GPU without any table, recursive formats use a small stack, every output stays valid under a token limit, and independent fields are decoded in parallel and verified. On one 16 GB Apple M2 Pro with Qwen3.5-2B and 4B, against MLX with llguidance, the standard setup for this hardware, schema-constrained extraction finishes 1.2- 1.3x sooner with the same answers, a grammar costs 3 MB instead of up to 1.5 GB, one server holds sixteen grammars where tables run out of memory, and sixteen tool-calling agents finish 2.5x sooner.

</details>


### [290] [DIVA: Dual-Space Intent-Aware Visual Attenuation for Vision-Language-Action Policies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09144)
*Kaixi Feng,Guoheng Sun,Ziyao Wang,Yexiao He,Zheyu Shen,Ang Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DIVA introduces a dual-space intent-aware visual attenuation module for vision-language-action (VLA) policies. It addresses the lack of explicit mechanism to regulate visual token influence by combining task intent with visual evidence to estimate patch-wise relevance anchors, applied in two complementary spaces: reweighting before backbone entry and attenuating within the backbone.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies use dense visual patch tokens but lack explicit mechanisms to regulate how strongly different visual tokens influence policy computation. This limits their ability to focus on task-relevant visual information and be robust to task-irrelevant visual perturbations.

Method: DIVA uses an anchor-then-attenuate design combining high-level task intent with low-level visual evidence to estimate patch-wise relevance anchors. It applies these anchors in two complementary spaces: (1) reweighting projected visual tokens before backbone entry, and (2) persistently attenuating low-relevance visual states within the backbone. The method preserves full visual token sequence and requires no external grounding supervision.

Result: On LIBERO benchmark, DIVA improves OpenVLA-OFT from 96.6% to 98.0% average success rate and raises zero-shot LIBERO-Plus score from 69.6 to 72.6. Real-world experiments demonstrate consistent gains under task-irrelevant visual perturbations.

Conclusion: DIVA effectively enhances VLA policy performance and robustness through intent-aware visual attenuation, achieving state-of-the-art results on LIBERO and demonstrating generalization to real-world scenarios with visual perturbations.

Abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies typically feed dense visual patch tokens into a language-action backbone, preserving scene context but offering no explicit mechanism to regulate how strongly different visual tokens influence policy computation. We introduce DIVA, a Dual-Space Intent-Aware Visual Attenuation module with an anchor-then-attenuate design. DIVA combines high-level task intent with low-level visual evidence to estimate patch-wise relevance anchors, then applies them in two complementary spaces: it reweights projected visual tokens before backbone entry and persistently attenuates low-relevance visual states within the backbone. DIVA preserves the full visual token sequence and requires no external grounding supervision. On LIBERO, DIVA improves OpenVLA-OFT from 96.6% to 98.0% average success and raises its zero-shot LIBERO-Plus score from 69.6 to 72.6. Real-world experiments further show consistent gains under task-irrelevant visual perturbations, supporting the robustness of intent-aware visual attenuation beyond simulation.

</details>


### [291] [Frozen Models, Evolving Expertise: Model-Agnostic Learning from Deployment Experience for Multimodal Medical AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09146)
*Yexiao He,Yucheng Tang,Pengfei Guo,Yufan He,Andriy Myronenko,Can Zhao,Ang Li,Daguang Xu,Dong Yang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A model-agnostic framework enabling frozen LLMs and VLMs to learn from deployment experience through external expertise (Skill, Knowledge Memory, Multimodal Knowledge Base) without fine-tuning, validated across 6 benchmarks with 4 base models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs and VLMs are frozen after deployment and cannot learn from solved cases. This is problematic in medicine where clinical evidence, guidelines, and therapies evolve. Fine-tuning requires model weight access and training; parameter-free methods have limitations like overfitting validation sets, lacking domain knowledge, or losing visual details.

Method: Three-component framework: (1) Skill guides reasoning and tool use, (2) Knowledge Memory stores reliable facts from earlier cases or external evidence, (3) Multimodal Knowledge Base retains visual examples and relates retrieved cases to current images. Validation strategy keeps updates only if they improve new cases without degrading earlier performance.

Result: Up to 34.2% performance improvement over base model on medical tasks across six benchmarks (clinical diagnosis, workflows, medical reasoning, visual reasoning). Generalizes to unseen cases, transfers to other models without optimization, and works in non-medical domains.

Conclusion: The proposed framework successfully enables frozen LLMs/VLMs to learn from deployment experience without retraining, addressing limitations of fine-tuning and existing parameter-free methods. It achieves significant performance gains while maintaining model-agnostic transferability.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs) are usually frozen after deployment, so they do not learn from the cases they solve. This is especially concerning in medicine, where new clinical evidence, updated guidelines, and new therapies can change established practice. Fine-tuning can update the model, but it requires access to model weights and additional training. Parameter-free methods avoid training, but they may overfit a fixed validation set, lack reliable domain knowledge, or lose visual details by saving experience only as text. To address these limitations, we present a model-agnostic framework that allows frozen LLMs and VLMs to learn from deployment experience through three forms of external expertise: a Skill that guides reasoning and tool use, a Knowledge Memory that stores reliable facts supported by earlier cases or trusted external evidence, and a Multimodal Knowledge Base that keeps visual examples and guides the model to relate each retrieved case to the current image. Instead of relying on a fixed validation set, a validation strategy keeps an update only if it helps on new cases without degrading performance on earlier ones. Across six benchmarks covering clinical diagnosis, clinical workflows, medical reasoning, and medical and non-medical visual reasoning, and with four open-weight and closed-source base models, our framework improves performance during online deployment by up to 34.2% over the base model on medical tasks, generalizes to unseen cases, transfers to other models without further optimization, and works in non-medical domains.

</details>


### [292] [Training Language Models To Be Coherent Decision-Makers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09164)
*Khurram Yamin,Xavier Fernandes,Paul Koch,Bryan Wilder,Eric Horvitz*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether language models can learn decision-making procedures from supervised fine-tuning, including preserving beliefs, applying utilities, and recognizing missing information. Using 20 datasets, the study shows that targeted fine-tuning improves coherent decision-making and transfers across domains and framings, with models learning to identify when actions cannot be justified due to missing information.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reliable decision-making requires more than accurate prediction: models must preserve beliefs, apply relevant utilities, and recognize when decision-relevant information is missing. The authors investigate whether language models can learn this decision procedure from supervised fine-tuning and generalize it across domains and varying natural-language expressions.

Method: Across 20 datasets, the researchers elicit probabilities of outcomes, then vary only utilities and framing while holding evidence fixed. Models are trained to preserve elicited beliefs while selecting actions that maximize expected utility. Evaluation includes transfer to unseen domains, held-out framings, different payoff structures, and incomplete-information settings where required utilities are withheld.

Result: Targeted fine-tuning substantially improves coherent decision-making. Learning transfers across domains and framings to unobserved situations. Models trained for decidability learn to identify when action cannot be justified based on missing information. A routed system considering recognition of decision completeness and utility-sensitive decision execution shows value.

Conclusion: Language models can learn decision procedures from supervised fine-tuning and generalize them across domains and framings. The key insight is that models can learn to recognize incomplete information and refrain from making unjustified decisions, which is crucial for reliable decision-making in practice.

Abstract: Reliable decision-making requires more than accurate prediction: a model must preserve its beliefs, apply the relevant utilities, and recognize when the information needed to justify an action is missing. We study whether language models can learn this decision procedure from supervised fine-tuning and generalize it across domains and differing natural-language expressions of the decision challenge. Across 20 datasets, we explore challenges of belief instability and decision-making errors by first eliciting probabilities of outcomes and then varying only the utilities and the framing of the decision problems, while holding the evidence fixed. We train models to preserve elicited beliefs while selecting the action that maximizes expected utility, and evaluate transfer to unseen application domains, held-out framings, and different classes of payoff structures. We further introduce incomplete-information settings in which required utilities are withheld and replaced with irrelevant text, testing whether models can distinguish missing decision-relevant information from merely additional context. We find that targeted fine-tuning substantially improves coherent decision-making and that in many situations, learning transfers across domains and framings to situations unobserved during training. Further, models trained for decidability learn to identify when action cannot be justified based on missing information. Finally, we show the value of a routed system that considers separately the recognition of decision completeness and utility-sensitive decision execution.

</details>


### [293] [From Probabilities to Decisions: Search and Multi-Teacher Distillation with Jev](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09188)
*Mohamad Yazan Sadoun,Sarah Sharif,Yaser Mike Banad*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper studies probability-only models (System One models) through a model called Jev. In bullet chess, combining Jev's judgments with Stockfish search achieves 2200+ Lichess rating. Using Jev as a teaching partner with Qwen3-32B outperforms using Qwen alone by 9.6 Elo. In passage reranking, Jev alone trains a competitive reranker in 21 minutes vs 5.1 GPU-hours for Qwen, with minimal gains from adding Qwen.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The research investigates how probability-only models that return calibrated probabilities without generating text can be effectively utilized under tight time constraints. The authors explore whether such models can be useful partners for LLMs in decision-making tasks.

Method: Two tasks were conducted: (1) Bullet chess: Jev's judgments were distilled into a compact evaluator running at every position, combined with Stockfish search and an opening book/endgame tablebases. (2) Passage reranking: Training rerankers using Jev's labels alone vs Qwen's labels vs combined labels, measuring labeling budget efficiency.

Result: In chess, averaging both Jev and Qwen labels beats spending entire budget on Qwen alone by 9.6 Elo (95% CI: 4.3-14.9), with gains replicating on fresh openings. Jev is the strongest partner for Qwen among tested models. In passage reranking, Jev alone trains a reranker equal to Qwen's from 21 min API calls vs 5.1 GPU-hours, with adding Qwen providing only marginal gains (few thousandths).

Conclusion: Probability-only models can be valuable: search provides lookahead, distillation makes judgment cheap enough for per-position evaluation, and an LLM partner pays off in chess. The key insight is that combining a fast probability model with an LLM leverages the strengths of both - speed and quality.

Abstract: Probability-only models, which TypeSafe calls System One models, return calibrated probabilities for fixed choices in milliseconds and generate no text. We study one such model, Jev, through two tasks that require decisions under tight constraints. In bullet chess, a bot that places Jev's judgment inside Stockfish search alongside an opening book and endgame tablebases climbs above a 2200 Lichess bullet rating against other bots. Live model calls are too slow for search, so we distill pairwise judgments into a compact evaluator that runs at every position. We then ask how best to spend a fixed labeling budget when an LLM, Qwen3-32B, is available as a second teacher. In chess, averaging both judges' labels beats spending the whole budget on Qwen alone by 9.6 Elo (95% interval 4.3 to 14.9), and the gain replicates on fresh openings; a second answer from the same judge is no substitute, and Jev is the strongest partner for Qwen among the models tested. In passage reranking, Jev's labels alone train a reranker that scores as high as Qwen's, from 21 minutes of API calls instead of 5.1 GPU-hours, and adding Qwen gains at most a few thousandths in ranking quality. Search supplies the lookahead, distillation makes the judgment cheap enough to use at every position, and an LLM partner pays off in chess.

</details>
