### [294] [Bookkeeping, Composition, or Unreachable Gold? Reading MemoryAgentBench's Conflict-Resolution Scores Against a Frozen Last-Write Resolver](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09193)
*Egor Pakhomov,Erik Nijkamp*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper evaluates a simple rule-based approach (newest statement wins) on MemoryAgentBench's Conflict Resolution split, which measures selective forgetting in memory systems. The rule achieves 80.25% accuracy, but 67 items require accessing overwritten statements. Testing shows models perform well on rule-solvable items (84.7%, 82.6%) but poorly on the 67 items requiring overwritten data (10.4%, 11.9%).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors investigate whether a simple rule-based resolver can serve as a baseline for measuring selective forgetting in memory agents. They note that the benchmark's official metric aggregates scores, but argue the per-item split is the meaningful unit of analysis.

Method: The authors execute the benchmark's own rule (newest statement about a fact wins) as a zero-learning resolver frozen on one of four fact lists. They tested two long-context models and a BM25 agent (one retained run per item), comparing performance on items the rule solves versus the 67 problematic items requiring overwritten statements.

Result: The rule-based approach answers 80.25% of questions (74.5% on held-out lists). Of the remaining items, 67 have gold answers that the last-write graph cannot reach but overwritten statements would (e.g., "capital of India is Grosseto" overwritten by "New Delhi"). These 67 items constitute a third of the 262K multi-hop questions. Two long-context models scored 84.7% and 82.6% on rule-solvable items but only 10.4% and 11.9% on the 67 items. The BM25 agent scored 41.6% vs 6.0% respectively.

Conclusion: The failures represent a reachability split (needing to access overwritten statements) plus a small parser-scope residual. The authors argue that per-item split, not aggregate, is the proper unit for measuring performance on this benchmark. The simple rule-based approach serves as a strong baseline that current models struggle to exceed on the 67 items requiring overwritten memory access.

Abstract: MemoryAgentBench's Conflict Resolution split is read as measuring "selective forgetting". We execute the benchmark's own rule - the newest statement about a fact wins - as a zero-learning resolver frozen on one of the four fact lists. Under the official metric the rule answers 80.25% of the questions (74.5% on the three held-out lists). Of the rest, 67 items have a released gold that the last-write graph cannot reach but overwritten statements would ("The capital of India is New Delhi." superseded by "The capital of India is Grosseto."; gold New Delhi); such items are a third of the multi-hop questions at 262K. Two long-context models and our pre-registered approximate re-implementation of the benchmark's BM25 agent, one retained run per item and outcomes only, score 84.7%, 82.6% and 41.6% on the items the rule solves against 10.4%, 11.9% and 6.0% on those 67. The failures are a reachability split plus a small parser-scope residual; the per-item split, not the aggregate, is the unit at which a score here can be read.

</details>


### [295] [FreeEvolve: Learning to Evolve Beyond Fixed Loops](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09197)
*Lecheng Kong,Like Hui,Nikos Kanakaris,Prithwish Jana,Sahika Genc,Narayanan Sadagopan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: FREEEVOLVE automates the optimization process of language model agent design by using meta-evolution to learn and improve the evolution skill itself. Instead of relying on fixed search loops, the system learns from experience which candidates to pursue and when to stop, achieving 13.6 point improvement on average across benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current agent evolvers automate the design of prompts, skills and workflows for language model agents, but the optimization process itself (how candidates are evaluated, which are kept, when to stop) is still hand-designed. This limits adaptability and requires manual engineering for each new environment.

Method: FREEEVOLVE uses an environment that specifies goals, target agent, evaluator, data and resource limits. Within these constraints, the evolver autonomously decides what to test, how much evidence to collect, which candidates to pursue, and when to stop. These decisions follow an editable evolution skill that is improved through meta-evolution by scoring each candidate skill on the fresh target agent it produces.

Result: On tau3-bench, ARC-AGI-2, ARC-AGI-3 and Terminal-Bench 2.1, FREEEVOLVE improves the primary held-out metric by 13.6 points on average and matches or exceeds hand-designed evolvers. Meta-evolved skills add 6.9 points over the seed skill on fresh target agents, demonstrating transferability across environments.

Conclusion: The optimization process for agent evolution can be learned from experience rather than engineered in advance. The learned process keeps improving with experience, and meta-evolved skills transfer across different environments, showing the viability of automating the optimizer design itself.

Abstract: Agent evolvers automate the design of the prompts, skills and workflows around language model agents, yet the optimization process they follow is still designed by hand: a fixed search loop decides how candidates are evaluated, which are kept and when the search stops. We propose FREEEVOLVE, which automates this process as well. An environment specifies the goal, target agent, evaluator, data and resource limits; within these limits, the evolver itself decides what to test, how much evidence to collect, which candidates to pursue and when to stop. These decisions follow an editable evolution skill, which we improve through meta-evolution by scoring each candidate skill on the fresh target agent it produces. The optimization process thus becomes a capability learned from experience rather than a loop engineered in advance. On tau3-bench, ARC-AGI-2, ARC-AGI-3 and Terminal-Bench 2.1, FREEEVOLVE controls the evolution campaign by itself, yet improves the primary held-out metric by 13.6 points on average and matches or exceeds hand-designed evolvers. The learned process keeps improving with experience: meta-evolved skills add 6.9 points over the seed skill on fresh target agents, demonstrating transferability across environments.

</details>


### [296] [Few Bits, One Law: Toward W2A4KV2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09202)
*Kai Yi,Tarek Elgamal,Sruthikesh Surineni,Vignesh Vivekraja,Soumyadeep Ghosh,Steven Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CanonQ is a unified quantization-aware training framework for extreme low-bit LLM compression that addresses the challenge of jointly quantizing weights, activations, and KV caches. It separates source canonicalization (using fixed rotations and energy normalization to map heterogeneous tensors to canonical coordinates) from task-aware adaptation (joint training to handle coupled quantization errors). The framework uses frozen Gaussian-reference codebooks reusable across layers and models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Extreme low-bit LLM compression is challenging when weights, activations, and KV caches are quantized together because: (1) their distributions differ, and (2) quantization errors interact throughout the network. Prior methods lack a unified approach to handle these heterogeneous tensor types and their coupled errors.

Method: CanonQ uses a two-stage approach: (1) Source canonicalization - fixed rotations and energy normalization map heterogeneous tensor sources to canonical coordinates, enabling frozen Gaussian-reference codebooks to be reused across layers and models; (2) Joint training adapts the network to the coupled errors of weight, activation, and KV cache quantization within a common scalar/vector interface. The method includes theoretical bounds on frozen-codebook transfer error and local task loss, and derives an exact normalization-aware straight-through Jacobian linking quantization distortion to gradient bias.

Result: Under joint W2A4KV2 compression across LLaMA3-1B/3B/8B: CanonQ achieves up to 14.28x lower WikiText-2 perplexity and up to 57.9% higher mean zero-shot accuracy than prior state-of-the-art. On instruction-tuned MobileLLM-Pro-1B at W2A16KV16: 41.7% relative improvement in HumanEval pass@1 and 39.1% improvement in GSM8K exact match over the strongest baseline. Benefits extend to Qwen3-1.7B, code generation, and mathematical reasoning tasks.

Conclusion: CanonQ successfully addresses the challenges of joint weight, activation, and KV cache quantization through canonicalization and task-aware adaptation. It demonstrates significant improvements in perplexity and zero-shot accuracy across multiple model sizes and architectures, establishing a new state-of-the-art for extreme low-bit LLM compression.

Abstract: Extreme low-bit LLM compression is most challenging when weights, activations, and KV caches are quantized together: their distributions differ, and quantization errors interact throughout the network. We introduce CanonQ, a unified quantization-aware training framework that addresses these challenges by separating source canonicalization from task-aware adaptation. Fixed rotations and energy normalization map heterogeneous tensor sources to canonical coordinates, enabling frozen Gaussian-reference codebooks to be reused across layers and models. Joint training then adapts the network to the coupled errors of weight, activation, and cache quantization within a common scalar/vector interface. We bound frozen-codebook transfer error and local task loss, and derive an exact normalization-aware straight-through Jacobian that links quantization distortion to gradient bias. The strongest gains arise under joint W2A4KV2 compression: across LLaMA3-1B/3B/8B, CanonQ-Omni achieves up to 14.28x lower WikiText-2 perplexity and up to 57.9% higher mean zero-shot accuracy than prior state-of-the-art and representative quantization baselines. The benefits extend to Qwen3-1.7B, code generation, and mathematical reasoning: on instruction-tuned MobileLLM-Pro-1B at W2A16KV16, CanonQ achieves relative improvements of 41.7% in HumanEval pass@1 and 39.1% in GSM8K exact match over the strongest evaluated quantization baseline.

</details>


### [297] [AGAR: a reinforcement learning substrate for LLM program evolution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09215)
*Haoran Li,Zengle Ge,Xiaomin Yuan,Yui Lo,Haoxin Li,Songlin Zhou,Qianhui Liu,Jiahua Ying,Yuanhang Liu,Mingju Chen,Annan Li,Jianmin Wu,Dawei Yin,Dou Shen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AGAR formalizes program evolution as a Markov decision process where the action is the modular prefix the model is conditioned on, rather than the emitted program. This allows standard RL components (credit assignment, value estimation, exploration, memory) to attach to distinct components, enabling auditable mechanism transfer without gradient training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current program evolution systems rely on five hand-tuned constants: parent selection, mutation strength, diversity maintenance, memory, and scalar scoring. These lack explicit credit assignment and cannot identify which parts of a program earned the score. The obstacle is that program evolution is not typically formalized as a decision process.

Method: The paper formalizes program evolution as an MDP where the action is the modular prefix the language model is conditioned on, rather than the program itself. This allows credit assignment, value estimation, adaptive exploration, and experience memory to attach to distinct components. AGAR enables any estimator to be replaced or switched off without changing the controller, making transfers auditable one mechanism at a time, with no gradient training of the backend model.

Result: Across 19 tasks, two backends, and three seeds under one harness, AGAR improves on the stronger of two published baselines on most tasks, with gains concentrated in the competitive-programming family.

Conclusion: The formalization yields a checkable reading of prior work: these systems are implicitly zero-discount, not by choice, but because fitness is exogenous to an individual rather than a return over successors, leaving a discount factor nothing to act on.

Abstract: Given a task and an evaluator, a language model can rewrite a candidate program while a search loop decides which rewrites survive, offering a practical route to algorithm discovery. But that loop is governed by five constants set by hand: which parent to select, how hard to mutate, how to keep diversity, what to remember, and a scalar score that never says which part of the program earned it. Reinforcement learning already has an estimator for each. The obstacle is that program evolution is not usually written down as a decision process. We formalize it as a Markov decision process whose action is the modular prefix the model is conditioned on, rather than the program it emits. Credit assignment, value estimation, adaptive exploration, and experience memory can then attach to distinct components. AGAR (Algorithm Generation As RL) provides the resulting substrate: any estimator can be replaced or switched off without changing the controller, making the transfer auditable one mechanism at a time, with no gradient training of the backend model. Across 19 tasks, two backends, and three seeds under one harness, AGAR improves on the stronger of two published baselines on most tasks, with gains concentrated in the competitive-programming family. The formalization also yields a checkable reading of prior work: these systems are implicitly zero-discount, not by choice, but because fitness is exogenous to an individual rather than a return over successors, leaving a discount factor nothing to act on.

</details>


### [298] [RLDISCOVER: LLM-driven co-evolution of reinforcement learning algorithms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09218)
*Haoran Li,Zengle Ge,Xiaomin Yuan,Yui Lo,Songlin Zhou,Jiahua Ying,Haoxin Li,Qianhui Liu,Yuanhang Liu,Jiaqun Liu,Guokai Chen,Mingju Chen,Ruinan Wang,Annan Li,Jianmin Wu,Dawei Yin,Dou Shen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: RLDiscover is a framework for self-evolving model-free deep RL algorithms using LLM-guided program evolution. It addresses two key obstacles: scaling joint search over coupled algorithmic components and costly candidate evaluation. The framework employs Progressive Co-Evolution to transition from isolated to joint component evolution, and Progressive Probabilistic Evaluation to balance search breadth with evaluation fidelity through staged training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-guided program evolution has enabled discoveries in mathematics and computational optimization, raising the prospect of RL algorithms that self-evolve to improve learning. However, two obstacles impede this: (1) joint search over coupled algorithmic components is difficult to scale—simultaneous changes can disrupt learning while isolated changes overlook dependencies; (2) evaluating candidate algorithms requires costly training with fitness uncertainty across random seeds.

Method: Two key innovations: (1) Progressive Co-Evolution advances from targeted component edits to joint evolution, addressing the scalability challenge of searching over coupled components; (2) Progressive Probabilistic Evaluation balances search breadth and evaluation fidelity through staged training and repeated evaluation, reducing computational cost while maintaining reliability.

Result: Experiments across SAC, PPO, and DQN on four benchmark suites show substantial improvements. Per-family median gains of 32%-84%, with peak return ratio of ~363x over near-zero baseline. Includes transitions from failed learning to successful task completion. Improvements persist when starting from stronger open-source implementations. On measured SAC locomotion runs, evaluation uses ~1/15th the compute of full evaluation. Independent searches repeatedly discover interpretable combinations: adaptive robust losses, progress-dependent value targets, and running statistics. Selected programs transfer to unseen tasks.

Conclusion: Self-evolution can discover interpretable algorithms that improve how agents learn. This points toward a broader role for self-evolution in AI: discovering interpretable algorithms that improve learning across tasks, with reusable components that transfer to unseen problems.

Abstract: LLM-guided program evolution has enabled discoveries in mathematics and computational optimization, raising the prospect of reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms that self-evolve to improve how agents learn. However, realizing this prospect faces two obstacles. Joint search over coupled algorithmic components is difficult to scale: simultaneous changes can disrupt learning, while isolated changes overlook their dependencies. Evaluating candidate algorithms also requires costly training, with fitness remaining uncertain across random seeds. We introduce RLDiscover, a framework for the self-evolution of model-free deep RL algorithms. Progressive Co-Evolution advances from targeted component edits to joint evolution, while Progressive Probabilistic Evaluation balances search breadth and evaluation fidelity through staged training and repeated evaluation. Experiments across SAC, PPO, and DQN on four benchmark suites show substantial improvements in mean return, with per-family median gains of 32%-84% and a peak return ratio of approximately 363x over a near-zero baseline. These gains include transitions from failed learning to successful task completion, and improvements persist when evolution starts from stronger open-source implementations. On measured SAC locomotion runs, evaluation uses approximately one-fifteenth the estimated compute required to fully evaluate the same candidate pool. Remarkably, independent searches repeatedly discover interpretable combinations of adaptive robust losses, progress-dependent value targets, and running statistics, with selected programs transferring to unseen tasks. These findings point toward a broader role for self-evolution in AI: discovering interpretable algorithms that improve how agents learn.

</details>


### [299] [CM-DPO: Constraint-Margin Direct Preference Optimization for LLM Planning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09219)
*Rabimba Karanjai,Qun Gu,Hemanth Hegadehalli Madhavarao,Wenhuan Sun,Xiaojiao Yu,Suryabhan Singh Hada,Libin N. George,Uma Kona,Richard Williamson,Linsey Pang,Prakhar Mehrotra*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CM-DPO replaces DPO's binary preference signal with a continuous margin from a deterministic symbolic verifier, scaled by violation severity. Uses lexicographic objective to separate hard/soft constraints. With SynPlan-R data generation (DCCG + RT-MED), achieves 89.2% pass rate and 93.4% solve rate, matching multi-agent systems at 13x lower latency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: DPO treats all constraint violations equally (no severity scaling) and is susceptible to length/style bias when preference pairs come from different model families.

Method: Constraint-Margin DPO (CM-DPO): replaces binary preference with continuous margin from deterministic symbolic verifier scaled by violation severity; uses lexicographic objective to ensure hard constraints are never traded off against preferences. Data generation via procedurally generated constraint profiles (DCCG) and minimal-edit distillation from reasoning teacher (RT-MED) within SynPlan-R framework.

Result: 89.2% pass rate and 93.4% solve rate on TravelPlanner, NaturalPlan, and out-of-distribution PlanBench; matches multi-agent systems at 13x lower latency; outperforms GPT-4o by 9.2 points on unseen Blocksworld.

Conclusion: CM-DPO effectively addresses DPO's equal-violation treatment and bias issues through continuous margin signals and lexicographic optimization. An 8B model fine-tuned with CM-DPO achieves state-of-the-art planning performance with significantly lower latency than multi-agent systems.

Abstract: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) treats all constraint violations equally: a $1 budget overshoot and a $1,000 overshoot induce the same training signal. It is also susceptible to length and style bias when preference pairs come from different model families. We introduce Constraint-Margin DPO (CM-DPO), which replaces DPO's binary preference signal with a continuous margin derived from a deterministic symbolic verifier and scaled by violation severity. Hard and soft constraints are separated through a lexicographic objective, ensuring hard constraints are never traded off against preferences. To supply CM-DPO with bias-reduced training pairs, we generate preference data through procedurally generated constraint profiles (DCCG) and minimal-edit distillation from a reasoning teacher (RT-MED), within a framework we call SynPlan-R. On TravelPlanner, NaturalPlan, and out-of-distribution PlanBench, an 8B model fine-tuned with CM-DPO achieves 89.2% pass rate and 93.4% solve rate, matching multi-agent systems at 13x lower latency while outperforming GPT-4o on unseen Blocksworld by 9.2 points.

</details>


### [300] [Trajectory Abstraction for the Science of Language Agent Behavior](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09237)
*Tianqiang Yan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes a hierarchical framework for discovering generalizable behavioral hypotheses in language agent research. It introduces a recursive procedure that measures events, tests relation stability, constructs motif variables, and validates abstractions through intervention experiments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The research problem addresses the need for behavioral variables that support hypotheses across different tasks and models in language agent studies. Existing approaches lack a systematic way to discover generalizable behavioral hypotheses.

Method: The method involves: (1) measuring role- and phase-indexed events, (2) proposing temporally constrained relations and testing their stability across conditions, (3) constructing episode-level motif variables from selected relations, and (4) repeating the analysis recursively. The framework includes explicit measurement functions connecting abstraction levels to original trajectories, uses observations and randomized protocol experiments, and employs comparisons between intervention realizations to determine whether abstractions should be retained, refined, or restricted.

Result: Theoretical results include: a finite-depth bound for accepted reductions, identification of protocol effects on fixed abstractions, characterization of realization disagreement and composition of abstraction error, and a finite-sample test for projected intervention consistency. Constructed examples illustrate motif construction and abstraction refinement.

Conclusion: The formulation distinguishes this experimental approach from semantic taxonomies, qualitative theory induction, and behavior-model recovery. It provides a proposed research procedure for discovering generalizable behavioral hypotheses, with literature-relative novelty assessed separately from model-relative surprise.

Abstract: Scientific studies of language agents need behavioral variables that support hypotheses across tasks and models. We formulate this research problem as learning and testing a hierarchy of trajectory abstractions. A concrete recursive procedure first measures role- and phase-indexed events, proposes temporally constrained relations, and tests their stability across conditions. It then constructs episode-level motif variables from selected relations and repeats the analysis on those variables. Explicit measurement functions connect every abstraction level to the original trajectories. Observations and randomized protocol experiments assess the resulting hypotheses, while comparisons between intervention realizations determine whether an abstraction should be retained, refined, or restricted. We derive a finite-depth bound for accepted reductions, identify protocol effects on fixed abstractions, and characterize realization disagreement and composition of abstraction error. A finite-sample test makes projected intervention consistency operational, and constructed examples illustrate motif construction and abstraction refinement. The formulation distinguishes this experimental approach from semantic taxonomies, qualitative theory induction, and behavior-model recovery. It specifies a proposed research procedure for discovering generalizable behavioral hypotheses, with literature-relative novelty assessed separately from model-relative surprise.

</details>


### [301] [The Winner's Curse in LLM Self-Improvement Loops: Selection Noise, Lock-in, and Acceptance Rules](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09239)
*Litao Hu,Yutong Tang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper studies measurement bias in LLM self-improvement systems, where models iteratively rewrite their own instructions and select improvements based on evaluation scores. The key finding is that selection-set scores substantially overestimate held-out performance (by 13-20 points with 16 selection items), revealing a "winner's curse" effect that persists even with separate validation sets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Self-improving LLM systems select modifications based on evaluation scores, but evaluation on small sets introduces measurement noise. The winners of such selection processes tend to be overestimated due to correlated errors—a statistical phenomenon known as winner's curse. The authors investigate how this bias manifests in practice and whether it can be corrected.

Method: The authors conducted multiple empirical studies: (1) Qwen models rewriting their own instructions with candidates scored on 600 held-out items; (2) a pre-registered study with varying selection set sizes (16 vs 256 items); (3) testing different acceptance rules against greedy acceptance; (4) using separate 64-item validation sets to debias. They compared selection-set scores against held-out accuracy across different datasets (TREC, GSM8K) and optimization methods (GEPA, MIPROv2).

Result: Key findings: (1) Most proposals after the first are harmful; (2) Winner' s curse causes substantial overstatement of true performance—13-20 points with 16 selection items, 1-5 points with 256; (3) Gains on selection set exceed held-out gains in both instruction refinement and automated tuning (GEPA, MIPROv2); (4) Using a separate 64-item validation set removes average bias but individual estimates remain off by ~6 points; (5) No tested acceptance rule beat greedy acceptance overall.

Conclusion: Self-improvement systems suffer from significant selection bias that inflates reported gains. The authors recommend that self-improvement studies should always report held-out gains with uncertainty estimates rather than relying solely on selection-set scores. This bias is a fundamental issue in iterative LLM optimization and affects both human-written and automatically tuned instructions.

Abstract: Self-improving LLM systems propose changes to themselves and keep those that score better on a small evaluation set. We treat this keep-if-better step as selection under measurement noise, model the correlated errors of the candidates in a single decision, and study empirically what happens when the evaluation set is reused. In runs where Qwen models rewrite their own instructions and every candidate is also scored on 600 held-out items, most proposals after the first are harmful, and the model gives the size of the winner's curse of a generation's best candidate. With a prior from a separate pilot, it matches the average overstatement of first-generation commits in native loops, though not setting by setting. In a pre-registered study, the final selection-set score of greedy loops exceeded held-out accuracy by 13 to 20 points with 16 selection items and by 1 to 5 points with 256. Held-out gains grew with the selection set on TREC but not on GSM8K, and the tested acceptance rules did not beat greedy acceptance over whole runs. Gains measured on the selection set also exceeded held-out gains when a current model refined a competent instruction, and in the validation scores of GEPA and MIPROv2. Scoring the starting and the current instruction on 64 items never used for selection removes the average bias of a loop's reported gain, but single estimates remain off by about 6 points. Self-improvement studies should report held-out gains with their uncertainty.

</details>


### [302] [We Query, Therefore We Compute: On Oracle Computation beyond the Machine, with an Application to Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09243)
*Kefan Liu,Fengning Ou,Yelin Luo,Jingdi Lei*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper constructs an abstract machine that unifies two forms of agentic systems (Workflows and Agents) by combining an LLM (treated as an Oracle) with a two-stack pushdown automaton (the Priestess). The machine uses autoregressive stack growth to model agent context, and introduces symmetry breakings to differentiate between Workflow and Agent placements. The construction is realized through ArchNights, an extended RISC-V ISA and Linux-style OS, enabling agentic systems to be designed like computer systems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work on agentic systems borrows OS abstractions (scheduling, caching, isolation) piecemeal without common ground, and the unified view of Workflows and Agents is limited. The authors seek a formal foundation that unifies both forms of agentic systems and enables shared invariants and bounds.

Method: The authors extend a two-stack pushdown automaton with an Oracle instruction that hands the Oracle a whole stack as its query and appends the answer to that same stack. This creates two synchronized computations: the Oracle's (LLM) and the Priestess (Turing-complete). Two symmetry breakings (S in storage, T in transitions) differentiate Agent from Workflow placements. For autoregressive Oracles, the computations synchronize at answer boundaries, enabling modeling of caching and scheduling analysis.

Result: The abstract machine provides a unified foundation for agentic systems, with the ArchNights implementation (extended RISC-V ISA + Linux-style OS) demonstrating realizability. The approach enables formal analysis of caching and scheduling through synchronization, and establishes that while no universal guarantee fixes which content crosses between computations, the boundary itself can be fixed.

Conclusion: With a formal foundation established and a unified view of Workflows and Agents, future work can share invariants and bounds under specific conditions. Agentic systems can now be designed with the same rigor as computer systems, with ArchNights-SE running on gem5 as a concrete implementation that becomes agentic when running an LLM as the Oracle.

Abstract: Agentic systems use large language models (LLMs) to carry out concrete tasks. Prior work often borrows abstractions such as scheduling, caching or isolation piecemeal from operating systems, so the mechanisms it builds share little common ground, and the shared view of the two forms of agentic system, Workflows and Agents, is limited. We construct an abstract machine that provides both.
  We treat the LLM as an Oracle and extend a two-stack pushdown automaton with one instruction, which hands the Oracle a whole stack as its query and appends the answer to that same stack. The machine thus performs two computations, the Oracle's and a Turing-complete one that we call the Priestess. A stack that the program only appends to grows autoregressively, as an agent's context does. Two symmetry breakings, S in storage and T in transitions, make a Priestess program the operating system of the programs the Oracle runs, and produce the Agent and the Workflow as the two placements of a task's program.
  For internally autoregressive Oracles, the two computations synchronize at the end of every answer under certain conditions, and through that synchronization we model caching and analyse scheduling. No guarantee that holds for every Oracle can fix which content crosses between the two computations, but such a guarantee does fix the boundary itself.
  The construction V fits the machine to a von Neumann computer. To show that it is realizable, we propose ArchNights, an extended RISC-V ISA and a Linux-style operating system implementing the machine by design. ArchNights-SE runs on gem5 as a computer system, becomes an agentic system when it runs an LLM as the Oracle, and will be open source.
  Agentic systems can then be designed as computer systems are. With a foundation built and a unified view, future work can share invariants and bounds, each with its conditions.

</details>


### [303] [RT-Safe: Benchmarking Agent Safety in Real-Time Embodied Environment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09294)
*Tianruo Rose Xu,Jiawei Ren,Yichi Yang,Zhaoxu Zheng,Lianhui Qin*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: RT-SAFE is a simulated urban benchmark for evaluating embodied-agent safety under real-time constraints. The study reveals that while Vision-Language Models (VLMs) achieve high task completion rates (91-94%), real-time execution increases collisions by 12.3x, with only 0.7% of episodes completing safely in the hardest setting. Standard task success metrics mask substantial safety failures, and decision latency itself becomes a source of physical risk.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As AI agents move from digital to physical environments, embodied safety becomes critical—failures can cause human injury and hardware damage. Beyond selecting safe actions, embodied agents must operate under real-time constraints: the physical world does not pause during inference. An action safe at observation time may become unsafe before execution, making decision latency a potential source of physical risk.

Method: RT-SAFE combines navigation tasks with moving actors, environmental hazards, and traffic rules, allowing the world to evolve throughout inference and action execution. Eight VLMs were evaluated across static and real-time settings, with the world continuing to evolve during inference and action execution. The benchmark also tested offline RL training for safety improvements.

Result: Across eight VLMs, agents achieve high task completion (91.3% static, 94.1% real-time) yet almost never complete safely: only 0.7% of episodes finish without a safety event in the hardest setting. Real-time execution increases collisions by 12.3x compared to static evaluation. RT-SAFE can support offline RL training, substantially reducing collision rates while achieving strong task completion.

Conclusion: Standard task success metrics can mask substantial safety failures. Decision latency itself can become a source of physical risk in embodied agents. The benchmark demonstrates that safety and task completion must be jointly evaluated, and that RT-SAFE can support training approaches that improve safety without sacrificing performance.

Abstract: Rapid progress in AI agents has brought growing attention to agent safety, with extensive evaluation focused on digital environments. As agents move into the physical world, embodied safety becomes increasingly important: failures can cause human injury and costly hardware damage. Beyond selecting safe actions, embodied agents must also operate under real-time constraints: the physical world does not pause while an agent reasons. As pedestrians move and vehicles approach during inference, an action that appears safe at observation time may become unsafe before execution. Real-time embodied safety therefore depends on both decision quality and decision latency. We introduce RT-SAFE, a simulated urban benchmark for evaluating embodied-agent safety under real-time constraints. RT-SAFE combines navigation tasks with moving actors, environmental hazards, and traffic rules, while allowing the world to evolve throughout inference and action execution. Across eight VLMs, agents achieve high task completion yet almost never complete safely: in the hardest setting, only 0.7% of episodes finish without a safety event. More strikingly, matched static and real-time evaluations yield task completion rates of 91.3% and 94.1%, respectively, while real-time execution increases collisions by $12.3\times$. These results reveal that standard task success can mask substantial safety failures, and that decision latency itself can become a source of physical risk. Finally, we show that RT-SAFE can support offline RL training and substantially reduce collision rates while achieving strong task completion.

</details>


### [304] [The AI Evaluation Ecosystem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09296)
*Yash Dave,Sang T. Truong,Serena Wang,Sanmi Koyejo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper develops a simulation architecture combining rule-based market dynamics with LLM-driven strategic actors to study AI evaluation ecosystems. The model represents benchmarks, consumer needs, and provider capabilities as vectors in a six-dimensional capability space (reasoning, coding, knowledge, safety, communication, agentic). Applied to benchmark holdout design, the study finds that shifting from public to private holdout benchmarks generally narrows the gap between benchmark scores and user satisfaction but can widen it depending on scoring credit allocation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI evaluation significantly influences decisions of model providers, users, funders, and regulators. However, the design choices in benchmarks are not adequately contextualized within the dynamics of this ecosystem. The researchers aim to address this gap by creating a simulation framework that can explore how benchmark design choices affect the broader AI ecosystem.

Method: The study develops a Generative Agent-Based Modeling (GABM) simulation that combines rule-based market dynamics with LLM-driven strategic actors. Benchmarks, consumer needs, and provider capabilities are modeled as vectors over a six-dimensional capability space (reasoning, coding, knowledge, safety, communication, agentic), with structural information partitions across actors. The framework is stress-tested using the V&V framework of Sargent (2013) and GABM-specific evidence criteria.

Result: Moving from public benchmarks to private holdout benchmarks shrinks the gap between benchmark scores and user satisfaction on most benchmarks but widens it on a few, depending on where holdout weights shift scoring credit. The simulation serves as a hypothesis-generating sandbox for studying how evaluator and policy choices reshape the ecosystem.

Conclusion: The simulation architecture provides a valuable tool for understanding the complex dynamics of AI evaluation ecosystems. It demonstrates that benchmark design choices have significant and nuanced impacts on the relationship between benchmark performance and user satisfaction. The framework can be extended to study various evaluator and policy choices and their effects on the AI ecosystem.

Abstract: AI evaluation shapes the decisions of model providers, users, funders, and regulators. We argue that designing valid benchmarks requires contextualizing design choices in the dynamics of this ecosystem of actors. We develop a simulation architecture that combines rule-based market dynamics with LLM-driven strategic actors, building on advances in Generative Agent-Based Modeling (GABM). We model benchmarks, consumer needs, and provider capabilities as vectors over a six-dimensional capability space (reasoning, coding, knowledge, safety, communication, agentic), with structural information partitions across actors. As a case study, we apply this stylized simulation to explore benchmark holdout design. We find that moving from public benchmarks to private holdout benchmarks shrinks the gap between benchmark scores and user satisfaction on most benchmarks but widens it on a few, depending on where holdout weights shift scoring credit. We stress-test our findings at both the instrument and case-study level, drawing on the V&V framework of Sargent (2013) and GABM-specific evidence criteria. Beyond holdout design, our simulation is a hypothesis-generating sandbox for studying how evaluator and policy choices, in turn, reshape the ecosystem.

</details>


### [305] [SearchWorld: Spatial Value-Grounded Imagination for UAV Object Search via World Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09335)
*Yatai Ji,Zhengqiu Zhu,Yong Zhao,Yue Hu,Fanglong Yao,Chen Gao,Pengfei Zhu,Quanjun Yin*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SearchWorld is a recurrent state-space world model for autonomous UAV object search in urban environments. It combines explicit spatial memory (BEV exploration and obstacle memory) with value-guided imagination to enable prospective planning rather than reactive behavior. The model uses a cognition-action network that leverages learned spatial value priors for imagined rollouts without requiring a separate critic.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Urban UAV object search faces challenges of partial observability, large search areas, narrow egocentric views, dense 3D geometry, and open-world instructions requiring target identification among distractors. Existing methods use explicit maps or memory but remain largely reactive, reasoning over past observations without predicting future states. Image-generating world models incur high inference latency, while latent world models struggle with spatially grounded planning.

Method: SearchWorld maintains BEV (Bird's Eye View) exploration and obstacle memory, and decodes a task-aware spatial value layer to guide search. A cognition-action network uses this learned spatial value prior to improve policy through imagined rollouts, without training a separate scalar critic. Training progresses in three stages: world-model learning, expert imitation, and imagination-based exploration refinement.

Result: On UAV-ON benchmark, SearchWorld improves success rate to 23.8% (vs 19.5% for the strongest published agent), raises oracle success to 35.5%, and remains robust on unseen scenes with 19.9% success rate.

Conclusion: By grounding imagination in explicit spatial representations, SearchWorld enables UAV agents to plan prospectively rather than react. The combination of spatial memory with value-guided imagination addresses the partial observability challenge in urban UAV search tasks.

Abstract: Autonomous unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) object search involves a closed loop of perception, decision-making, and action under partial observability. Urban environments pose several challenges: large search areas and narrow egocentric views limit coverage, dense 3D geometry constrains safe motion, and open-world instructions require identifying a specific target among distractors. Many existing methods mitigate partial observability through explicit maps or memory representations, yet remain largely reactive, reasoning over past observations without explicitly predicting future states. World models enable prospective reasoning through imagined rollouts. However, image-generating world models can incur high inference latency, while spatially grounded planning remains challenging for latent world models. We propose SearchWorld, a recurrent state-space world model that connects explicit spatial memory with value-guided imagination. The model maintains BEV exploration and obstacle memory and decodes a task-aware spatial value layer to guide search. A cognition-action network uses this learned spatial value prior to improve the policy through imagined rollouts, without training a separate scalar critic. Training progresses from world-model learning to expert imitation and imagination-based exploration refinement. On UAV-ON, SearchWorld improves the success rate to 23.8% (19.5% for the strongest published agent) and raises oracle success to 35.5%, while remaining robust on unseen scenes (19.9% success rate). By grounding imagination in explicit spatial representations, SearchWorld enables UAV agents to plan prospectively rather than react.

</details>


### [306] [Relevance Is Not Sufficiency: What Actually Closes the Evidence Gap in Long-Term Memory QA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09348)
*Yufeng Li,Shuxin Li,Zhenhua Xu,Junxian Li,Peng Zeng,Sheng Yao,Changting Lin,Gaolei Li,Ran Bi,Meng Han*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper addresses the problem of memory retrieval in LLM agents that interact across multiple sessions. Existing systems rank memories by relevance but fail to ensure sufficient coverage of jointly needed facts. The authors propose Budgeted Flat Reconstruction (BFR), which uses Formal Concept Analysis (FCA-MS) to decompose questions into information requirements and iteratively retrieves complementary records until budget exhaustion.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing memory systems rank records by lexical or embedding relevance, but the top-ranked memories can each be relevant while jointly omitting a complementary fact that the answer requires, especially for multi-session and temporal questions. The authors draw on the distinction between relevance and sufficiency in legal evidence scholarship to recast memory retrieval as constructing a sufficient memory set rather than just a relevant one.

Method: The authors introduce: (1) a blinded LLM judgment over the retrieved set, with Gold Hit and Turn Hit as evidence-coverage proxies; (2) Budgeted Flat Reconstruction (BFR) in two stages - first applying Formal Concept Analysis for Memory Selection (FCA-MS) to decompose the question into information requirements and select a compact candidate subset that jointly covers them, then repeatedly acquiring unseen records through deeper text search or complementary entity and session views, stopping when the budget is exhausted.

Result: Experiments on LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S show that BFR outperforms same-store adaptations of recent agent-memory systems in both answer quality and evidence coverage. On LongMemEval-S, it raises judged accuracy from 72.4% to 82.2% and Turn Hit to 91.4%.

Conclusion: The proposed BFR method effectively addresses the sufficiency problem in memory retrieval for multi-session LLM agents by ensuring joint coverage of information requirements rather than just individual relevance. The use of FCA-MS for decomposing questions and iterative complementary retrieval proves effective in improving both answer quality and evidence coverage.

Abstract: LLM agents that interact with a user across many sessions accumulate histories that exceed their context window, so they store past interactions in an external memory and answer each question from a small set of retrieved records. Existing memory systems rank records by lexical or embedding relevance, yet the top-ranked memories can each be relevant while jointly omitting a complementary fact that the answer requires, especially for multi-session and temporal questions.
  Drawing on the distinction between relevance and sufficiency in legal evidence scholarship, we recast memory retrieval as constructing a sufficient memory set.
  To operationalize this view, we introduce a blinded LLM judgment over the retrieved set, together with Gold Hit and Turn Hit as evidence-coverage proxies. We then propose Budgeted Flat Reconstruction (BFR), which builds sufficient sets over a fixed flat memory store in two stages. Specifically, we first apply Formal Concept Analysis for Memory Selection (FCA-MS) to decompose the question into information requirements and select a compact candidate subset that jointly covers them. Then, we repeatedly acquire unseen records through deeper text search or complementary entity and session views, stopping when the budget is exhausted.
  Experiments on LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S show that BFR outperforms same-store adaptations of recent agent-memory systems in both answer quality and evidence coverage. Specifically, on LongMemEval-S it raises judged accuracy from 72.4% to 82.2% and Turn Hit to 91.4%.

</details>


### [307] [TopoGraphRAG-Bench: Evaluating Multimodal GraphRAG on Layout-Grounded Evidence Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09360)
*Ruochi Li,Jianzhe Lin,Haoxuan Zhang,Haihua Chen,Junhua Ding,Edward Gehringer,Yang Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: TOPOGRAPHRAG-BENCH is a layout-grounded benchmark for evaluating multimodal evidence reasoning in GraphRAG systems. It comprises 2,024 questions over 201 visually rich documents with three controlled evidence topologies (single-hop, bridge-chain, multi-source synthesis). The benchmark includes counterfactual validation to ensure question quality and evaluates text-only GraphRAG, page-level visual retrieval, and multimodal GraphRAG systems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Real-world documents distribute evidence across text, tables, figures, and captions with complex page layouts. Existing GraphRAG evaluations are text-centered, while multimodal benchmarks assess cross-modal retrieval without evaluating evidence topology recovery. This gap motivates the need for a benchmark that assesses how well systems recover the evidence topology connecting heterogeneous evidence units.

Method: Built a benchmark with 2,024 questions over 201 long, visually rich documents. Questions were constructed bottom-up from text, figure, and table evidence units under three controlled topologies: single-hop retrieval, bridge-chain reasoning, and multi-source synthesis. Applied counterfactual validation for shortcut resistance, modality necessity, and evidence necessity. Evaluated three system types using retrieval, generation, and topology-aware reasoning metrics.

Result: Multimodal GraphRAG systems achieve the strongest overall performance but still fail when visual-textual evidence alignment or multi-unit composition is incomplete. Text-only GraphRAG struggles when key dependencies are grounded in figures or tables. Page-level visual retrieval lacks fine-grained structure needed for topology recovery.

Conclusion: GraphRAG systems must move beyond text-derived entity relation graphs to explicitly model document layouts, cross-modal evidence alignment, and the reasoning roles of evidence units. Code and data are available at https://richardlrc.github.io/TopoGraphRAG-Bench/.

Abstract: Real-world documents distribute evidence across text, tables, figures, and captions within complex page layouts. Answering complex questions over such documents therefore requires more than retrieving relevant passages: systems must recover the evidence topology that connects heterogeneous evidence units. Existing GraphRAG evaluations remain largely text-centered, while multimodal document RAG benchmarks assess cross-modal retrieval and generation without directly evaluating recovery of the intended evidence topology. We introduce TOPOGRAPHRAG-BENCH, a layout-grounded benchmark for multimodal evidence reasoning in GraphRAG, comprising 2,024 questions over 201 long, visually rich documents. Questions are constructed bottom-up from text, figure, and table evidence units under three controlled topologies: single-hop retrieval, bridge-chain reasoning, and multi-source synthesis. To ensure that questions preserve their intended structure, we apply counterfactual validation for shortcut resistance, modality necessity, and evidence necessity. We evaluate text-only GraphRAG, page-level visual retrieval, and multimodal GraphRAG systems using retrieval, generation, and topology-aware reasoning metrics. Multimodal GraphRAG systems achieve the strongest overall performance, but still fail when visual-textual evidence alignment or multi-unit composition is incomplete. Text-only GraphRAG struggles when key dependencies are grounded in figures or tables, while page-level visual retrieval lacks the fine-grained structure needed for topology recovery. These findings motivate GraphRAG systems that move beyond text-derived entity relation graphs to explicitly model document layouts, cross-modal evidence alignment, and the reasoning roles of evidence units. Code and data are available at https://richardlrc.github.io/TopoGraphRAG-Bench/.

</details>


### [308] [DUDA-Bench: Benchmarking LLM Agents on Multimodal Data-Driven Urban Diagnosis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09374)
*Yizhi Song,Hang Ni,Weijia Zhang,Hao Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DUDA-Bench is a hierarchical benchmark formalizing data-driven urban diagnosis as multi-stage agent workflows, comprising 86 atomic and 22 workflow tasks across 12 cities and 5 urban problem types. Evaluations reveal substantial gaps between isolated analytical competence and end-to-end diagnosis.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Urban diagnosis currently relies on labor-intensive, case-specific expert workflows that limit scalability and reuse, motivating the exploration of agent-based execution to automate and scale urban problem identification and analysis.

Method: The study introduces DUDA-Bench with hierarchical and interactive benchmark design, comprising 86 atomic and 22 workflow tasks spanning four analytical stages, using multimodal data from 12 cities covering five urban problem types. Seven backbone models and five agent systems were evaluated.

Result: A substantial gap exists between isolated analytical competence and end-to-end diagnosis. System benefits vary across backbones. Unresolved evidence gaps propagate across stages, while successful recovery involves revising assumptions and actions using feedback. Key limitations include coordinating analytical capabilities across stages, particularly adaptive planning, evidence integration, and verification.

Conclusion: DUDA-Bench provides a framework for translating expert analytical workflows into hierarchical agent tasks and process-aware evaluation, supporting systematic assessment of end-to-end analytical capabilities. Limitations in coordinating analytical capabilities across stages are highlighted, particularly adaptive planning, evidence integration, and verification.

Abstract: Urban diagnosis integrates heterogeneous observations to identify urban problems, localize affected areas, and investigate contributing factors, informing evidence-based urban planning and management. However, its reliance on labor-intensive, case-specific expert workflows limits scalability and reuse, motivating the exploration of agent-based execution. To evaluate this capability, we introduce DUDA-Bench, a hierarchical and interactive benchmark that formalizes data-driven urban diagnosis as a multi-stage agent workflow. It comprises 86 atomic and 22 workflow tasks spanning four analytical stages, grounded in multimodal data from 12 cities covering five urban problem types. Evaluations of seven backbone models and five agent systems reveal a substantial gap between isolated analytical competence and end-to-end diagnosis, with system benefits varying across backbones. Trajectory analysis shows that unresolved evidence gaps propagate across stages, while successful recovery involves revising assumptions and actions using feedback. These findings highlight limitations in coordinating analytical capabilities across stages, particularly adaptive planning, evidence integration, and verification. More broadly, DUDA-Bench provides a framework for translating expert analytical workflows into hierarchical agent tasks and process-aware evaluation, supporting systematic assessment of end-to-end analytical capabilities.

</details>


### [309] [From Plausible Hierarchies to Useful Taxonomies: Evaluating Agentic Harnesses on Customer Feedback](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09377)
*Prabhath Chellingi,Raviraja G,Viraj Bagal*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper addresses a critical gap in AI taxonomy evaluation: current checks only validate individual nodes (names, descriptions, hierarchy) but fail to assess whether the entire taxonomy is actually useful for production. The authors introduce two new evaluation approaches—structural discriminators and team partitionability—and demonstrate that taxonomies passing generic checks can still be fundamentally flawed.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors observed that modern agentic harnesses can easily generate plausible-looking taxonomies, but existing evaluation methods only check individual nodes in isolation. This leads to taxonomies that "look correct" but fail operationally—leaf nodes that just restate ancestor names, records that span multiple top-level categories, and poor team ownership potential. The motivation is to move beyond surface-level plausibility to meaningful whole-tree evaluation.

Method: The authors built six taxonomies over two proprietary customer feedback corpora (1,940 and 5,000 records): for each corpus, they created a production reference taxonomy and two repeated runs using the same harness with identical inputs. They then applied: (1) generic naming and structure checks that each taxonomy passed, (2) a product-coverage check that actually preferred the generated trees, (3) structural discriminator metrics to test if tree shape was learned from data vs. imposed by the generator, and (4) team partitionability metrics to test whether branches split feedback into groups teams can own.

Result: All six generated taxonomies passed every generic naming and structure check, and the product-coverage check even preferred the generated trees over the references. However, the deeper analysis revealed severe problems: at least 97.7% of leaf names in generated trees merely restated an ancestor's name (compared to 13.9% and 2.9% in the reference taxonomies). In one generated tree, 75% of records fell under multiple top-level categories. Trees rated equally correct by generic checks differed by 27 percentage points in cross-branch leakage, and only one of the two generated trees beat a random split for team partitionability.

Conclusion: Surface plausibility is an insufficient measure of taxonomy quality. The paper demonstrates that evaluation must measure the whole tree as well as each node, using metrics like structural discriminators (to detect if shape was learned vs. imposed) and team partitionability (to test if branches enable meaningful team ownership). The authors recommend that taxonomy evaluation should include both node-level and whole-tree metrics to ensure production usefulness.

Abstract: Taxonomies are the symbolic representations through which AI systems organize evidence, aggregate patterns, and answer questions over large document collections. Over customer feedback, the category tree decides how every record is counted and routed, which problems get seen, and which team owns them. Agentic harnesses now make it easy to generate a plausible-looking hierarchy, and such trees are checked today with generic, individually scoped checks: each name fits its description, sits under the right parent, and stays distinct from its siblings. We ask a more operational question: when is a generated hierarchy actually useful as a production taxonomy? We build six taxonomies over two proprietary feedback corpora (1,940 and 5,000 records): for each corpus, a production reference and two repeated runs of the same harness under identical inputs. All six pass every generic naming and structure check, and a deeper product-coverage check even prefers the generated trees. Yet in every generated tree at least 97.7% of leaf names merely restate an ancestor's name (13.9% and 2.9% in the references), and in one, three of every four records fall under multiple top-level categories. We introduce two families of whole-tree metrics: structural discriminators test whether a tree's shape was learned from the data or imposed by its generator; team partitionability tests whether branches split feedback into groups teams can own. Trees the generic checks rate as equally correct differ by 27 percentage points in cross-branch leakage, and only one of the two beats a random split. Surface plausibility is an insufficient measure of taxonomy quality: evaluation must measure the whole tree as well as each node.

</details>


### [310] [Let the Library Speak: Self-Advertised Method Selection for Formal Proving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09401)
*Xiaopeng Yuan,Suijin Wang,Yanli Wang,Haibo Jin,Peng Kuang,Jerry Wang,Lijun Yu,Haohan Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper addresses a key limitation in LLM-based formal theorem provers: retrieved methods may be relevant but not applicable. The authors propose "self-advertisement" where models generate problem-specific proposals stating target, action, and required conditions before ranking. They validate this on Putnam and IMO ProofBench benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM formal provers can retrieve relevant lemmas but relevance alone doesn't indicate whether a mathematical method can actually be applied. Methods with similar relevance may differ substantially in their applicability (prerequisites, target, action, obligations). This creates a need for applicability-aware method selection.

Method: The authors formulate this as an applicability-aware method-selection problem and introduce self-advertisement: before ranking candidates, a model generates a problem-specific proposal for each method stating what part of the goal it targets, what action it would take, and what conditions it requires. They organize 82 reusable methods from Putnam 2000-2014 as "Method Contracts" - pairing applicability descriptions with Mathlib anchors, checked examples/scaffold, and expected proof obligations. Vague or unsupported proposals are demoted, yielding a ranked shortlist with inspectable claims.

Result: Self-advertisement achieves 95.0% hit@5 on Putnam 2015-2025 (vs 84.2% for strongest reranker) and 91.7% on IMO ProofBench (vs 88.3%). Results indicate improved coverage of annotated methods in retrieved shortlists, particularly on Putnam.

Conclusion: Self-advertisement significantly improves method selection in LLM-based formal provers by incorporating applicability reasoning. The approach substantially outperforms baseline reranking methods on both Putnam and IMO ProofBench benchmarks, demonstrating the value of generating problem-specific applicability proposals before ranking.

Abstract: LLM-based formal provers can retrieve relevant lemmas and prior proofs, but relevance alone does not say whether a mathematical method can be used on the current theorem. A method has prerequisites, a target, an intended action, and obligations that its use leaves to prove. Methods that look equally related to a theorem may therefore differ substantially in whether they offer a plausible next step. We formulate this as an applicability-aware method-selection problem and introduce self-advertisement: before candidates are ranked, a model generates a problem-specific proposal for each one, stating what part of the goal it targets, what action it would take, and what conditions that action requires. We organize 82 reusable methods from Putnam 2000-2014 as Method Contracts, which pair applicability descriptions with Mathlib anchors, a checked example or scaffold, and expected proof obligations. A single batched call elicits proposals across the library; vague or unsupported proposals are demoted, yielding a ranked shortlist accompanied by inspectable claims about each candidate's use. We analyze when similarity-based representations cannot distinguish methods with different applicability, how errors in applicability estimates affect shortlist quality, and what a checked scaffold guarantees under its stated assumptions. Against lexical, embedding, and embedding-plus-LLM reranking baselines, self-advertisement achieves 95.0% hit@5 on Putnam 2015-2025, compared with 84.2% for the strongest reranker. On IMO ProofBench, it achieves 91.7% compared with 88.3%. These results indicate improved coverage of annotated methods in the retrieved shortlists, particularly on Putnam.

</details>


### [311] [Efficient Reasoning with Flow Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09416)
*Hanru Bai,Faissal Izermine,Oscar Davis,T. Konstantin Rusch*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper investigates how continuous representations in Flow Language Models (FLMs) benefit reasoning compared to discrete diffusion models. The key insight is that FLMs maintain information about multiple candidate solutions in a superposition state throughout denoising, allowing evidence to accumulate before committing to a discrete answer. Experiments on maze planning and Sudoku tasks show FLMs achieve higher accuracy than discrete diffusion baselines at matched model sizes with fewer denoising steps, and can achieve comparable accuracy with 36.5% fewer parameters.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand why continuous representations in FLMs might be more efficient for reasoning tasks than discrete diffusion models, which rely on categorical states between denoising steps.

Method: Theoretical analysis from a superposition perspective combined with intermediate-state intervention experiments. Comparisons between FLMs and discrete diffusion models (MDLM) on maze planning (Maze15) and Sudoku tasks, measuring solution accuracy under matched denoising steps.

Result: FLMs achieve greater reasoning efficiency in the few-step regime: higher sequence accuracy than discrete diffusion at matched model sizes and small denoising steps. On Maze15, FLM reaches 95% accuracy at 64 denoising steps with 36.5% fewer parameters than MDLM.

Conclusion: Continuous state spaces in FLMs allow evidence for multiple candidates to persist and inform subsequent reasoning before producing a discrete answer. This makes continuous representations a promising foundation for reasoning models requiring fewer refinement steps.

Abstract: Flow Language Models (FLMs) have emerged as a continuous-state alternative to discrete diffusion language models, yet the role of their continuous representations in reasoning remains unclear. We investigate this question by comparing the reasoning efficiency of FLMs and discrete diffusion models, measured by solution accuracy under matched denoising steps. Unlike discrete diffusion, which passes categorical states between denoising steps, FLMs evolve a continuous sequence representation throughout denoising and decodes it into discrete tokens only at the end. Our theoretical analysis shows, from a superposition perspective, how information retained in these continuous states can benefit reasoning. Intermediate-state interventions provide further empirical support for this theoretical account, showing that removing information about alternative candidates reduces subsequent solution recovery. Together, these findings show that FLMs allow evidence for multiple candidates to persist and inform subsequent reasoning before a discrete answer is produced. Furthermore, our experiments on maze planning and Sudoku tasks show that FLMs achieve greater reasoning efficiency in the few-step regime: FLMs achieves higher sequence accuracy than discrete diffusion baselines at matched model sizes and small denoising steps. On maze planning tasks, FLMs can also achieve comparable accuracy with smaller models. For example, on Maze15, FLM reaches the 95\% accuracy target at 64 denoising steps with 36.5\% fewer parameters than MDLM. These findings point to continuous state spaces as a promising foundation for reasoning models that require fewer refinement steps.

</details>


### [312] [RSI-Forge: From Research Papers to Environments for Recursive Self-Improvement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09426)
*Renxiong Wang,Darvin Yi,Abril Herrlein,Anas Mahmoud,Advait Gosai,Lisiman Hua,MohammadHossein Rezaei,Xingang Guo,Anisha Gunjal,Utkarsh Tyagi,David J. Lee,Minglai Yang,Haris Riaz,Chenguang Wang,Huaxiu Yao,Daniel Yue Zhang,Aakash Sabharwal,Tong Zhao,Yunzhong He*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: RSI-Forge is a multi-agent pipeline that automatically transforms published papers into executable research environments for self-improving agents, creating 210 environments across 18 fields with automated evaluators.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Environment construction for recursive self-improvement currently depends on domain experts, limiting scale and disciplinary coverage. There is a need for scalable approaches to create challenging research environments with reliable evaluation.

Method: Three coordinating agents (construction, reproduction, review) turn papers into executable tasks with automated evaluators. Each paper's method is independently reimplemented to establish baseline scores. Four models were evaluated over 3 successive attempts on 120 environments, with each attempt inheriting prior code and notes while model weights remained fixed.

Result: 210 environments across 18 fields created, including 90 reviewed by independent human experts. At least one model improves after the first attempt in 84% of environments. Models outperform reproduced paper methods in 68 of 120 environments. 95% of successful attempts involve work beyond parameter tuning. Lower-scoring models explore less, accept smaller gains, and rely more heavily on development set tuning.

Conclusion: RSI-Forge provides a scalable approach to constructing research environments for training and evaluating self-improving agents, demonstrating that models can improve upon baseline methods and that meaningful improvement typically requires more than parameter tuning.

Abstract: Environments are the foundation of recursive self-improvement: they provide the problems agents work on and the feedback used to evaluate progress. Yet constructing challenging research environments with reliable evaluation still depends on domain experts, limiting their scale and disciplinary coverage. We introduce RSI-Forge, a multi-agent pipeline that turns published papers into executable environments for self-improvement. Three agents coordinate construction, reproduction, and review to produce tasks with automated evaluators; each paper's method is independently reimplemented to establish a baseline score. We present 210 environments across 18 fields, including 90 reviewed by independent human domain experts. Both experts and agent judges give high ratings to the potential for improving the provided starting solutions and the evaluators' ability to distinguish solution quality, whereas experts are more critical of shortcut resistance, faithfulness to the source paper, and whether a single idea can exhaust a task. To validate their use for repeated improvement, we evaluate four models over 3 successive attempts on 120 environments, with each attempt inheriting prior code and notes while model weights remain fixed. At least one model improves after the first attempt in 84% of environments. Models also outperform the reproduced paper methods in 68 of the 120 environments, demonstrating room for gains beyond these baselines. Transcript analysis identifies work beyond parameter tuning in 95% of these successful attempts. Analysis of the resulting trajectories shows that models scoring lower on these tasks explore less, more often accept gains smaller than the reported standard error, and rely more heavily on tuning to the development set. RSI-Forge provides a scalable approach to constructing research environments for training and evaluating self-improving agents.

</details>


### [313] [LLM-Enabled UAV Dispatch: A System-Level Survey and Taxonomy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09466)
*Xiao Han,Aoyang Quan,Xiangyu Zhao,Xiangjie Kong,Guojiang Shen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This survey examines how Large Language Models (LLMs) can be integrated into Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) dispatch systems as a cross-layer semantic orchestration layer. It proposes a unified taxonomy of four dispatch paradigms (pipeline, global assignment, decentralized agentic, and divide-and-conquer) and analyzes LLM roles in semantic parsing, planning, solver orchestration, multi-agent coordination, and safety assessment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current UAV dispatch relies on isolated path planning and optimization-driven resource allocation. The field is moving toward system-level coordination requiring semantic reasoning and LLM-based interfaces. Existing approaches treat LLMs as standalone add-ons, lacking a unified framework for integrating LLMs as semantic orchestration layers connecting human instructions, external solvers, and distributed control modules.

Method: This survey provides a system-level taxonomy and design perspective through: (1) Conceptualizing LLMs as cross-layer semantic orchestration rather than standalone add-ons; (2) Organizing literature into four representative dispatch paradigms with analysis of decision logic, system structure, control flow, and LLM roles; (3) Examining LLM support for semantic parsing, retrieval-grounded planning, solver orchestration, local agent reasoning, multi-agent coordination, safety assessment, and human-facing explanation; (4) Discussing implications for scalability, robustness, coordination burden, and verification requirements.

Result: The paper presents a comprehensive taxonomy of four dispatch paradigms: pipeline dispatch, global assignment dispatch, decentralized agentic dispatch, and divide-and-conquer dispatch. For each paradigm, the analysis covers decision logic, system structure, control flow, representative methods, and potential LLM roles. The survey identifies key LLM functions: semantic parsing, retrieval-grounded planning, solver orchestration, local agent reasoning, multi-agent coordination, safety assessment, and human-facing explanation.

Conclusion: The survey establishes a system-level taxonomy and design perspective for integrating LLMs into safety-critical UAV dispatch systems. It identifies open challenges including latency-aware reasoning, grounding reliability, physical feasibility guarantees, edge deployment, privacy protection, and distributed consistency. This work provides a foundational framework for future research in LLM-enabled UAV coordination.

Abstract: Unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) dispatch is beginning to move beyond isolated path planning and optimization-driven resource allocation toward system-level coordination supported by semantic reasoning and LLM-based interfaces. This survey provides a unified characterization of LLM-enabled UAV dispatch systems that bridges semantic intent, symbolic decision-making, and physical UAV execution. Rather than treating LLMs as standalone add-ons, we conceptualize them as a cross-layer semantic orchestration layer connecting human instructions, external solvers, and distributed control modules. We organize the literature into four representative dispatch paradigms: pipeline dispatch, global assignment dispatch, decentralized agentic dispatch, and divide-and-conquer dispatch. For each paradigm, we analyze its decision logic, system structure, control flow, representative methods, and potential LLM roles. We further examine how LLMs support semantic parsing, retrieval-grounded planning, solver orchestration, local agent reasoning, multi-agent coordination, safety assessment, and human-facing explanation. We discuss the implications of these paradigms for scalability, robustness, coordination burden, and verification requirements, and identify open challenges including latency-aware reasoning, grounding reliability, physical feasibility guarantees, edge deployment, privacy protection, and distributed consistency. This survey provides a system-level taxonomy and design perspective for integrating LLMs into safety-critical UAV dispatch systems.

</details>


### [314] [MIMESIS: Learning User Simulators as Training Environments for Interactive Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09484)
*Hoang Phan,Dat Huynh,Andrey Zhmoginov,Qi Zeng,Wancen Mu,Yue Cao,Shengjie Bi,Yun He,Changdae Oh,Deren Lei*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MIMESIS is a purpose-built user simulator for training interactive language agents, using explicit reasoning supervision and 13 realistic behavioral patterns. It outperforms frontier models on behavioral fidelity and Turing distance metrics. Combined with a novel training method called Coached On-Policy Self-Distillation (CSD), it enables better agent generalization across multiple environments and user simulators.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Training interactive language agents requires rich user interactions, but collecting human feedback is expensive and difficult to scale. Existing agent-training frameworks rely on off-the-shelf assistant LLMs as simulators, which are too cooperative, explicit, and behaviorally homogeneous compared with real users.

Method: 1) MIMESIS: A 9B parameter user simulator trained on human conversations with explicit reasoning supervision and 13 realistic behavioral patterns derived from real user interactions. 2) Multi-turn reinforcement learning: Train agent by interacting with frozen MIMESIS simulator. 3) CSD (Coached On-Policy Self-Distillation): Uses simulator-generated reasoning traces and utterances as feedback; a coach converts this into concise coaching notes providing dense token-level supervision beyond sparse task rewards.

Result: - MIMESIS achieves SOUL-Index of 65.7, surpassing strongest frontier model
- Improves behavioral fidelity by 13.4 points and reduces Turing distance by 3.6 points vs Claude-Opus-5
- Training with MIMESIS yields better agent performance than GPT-5.5 across 8 environments
- Demonstrates stronger generalization to new user simulators
- CSD yields further gains across all 9 evaluation user models

Conclusion: MIMESIS, combined with CSD training, provides a scalable and effective solution for training interactive language agents. The purpose-built simulator with realistic behavioral patterns and dense feedback mechanism enables better agent performance and generalization compared to using off-the-shelf assistant LLMs as user simulators.

Abstract: Training and evaluating interactive language agents typically requires rich user interactions, yet collecting human feedback is expensive and difficult to scale. Simulated users offer a scalable alternative, but they must both resemble real user behavior and provide useful learning experiences for agents. In contrast, most agent-training frameworks rely on off-the-shelf assistant LLMs, whose helpfulness can make them overly cooperative, explicit, and behaviorally homogeneous compared with real users. We introduce MIMESIS, a purpose-built user simulator trained on human conversations with explicit reasoning supervision and 13 realistic behavioral patterns derived from real user interactions. Empirically, our 9B model achieves a SOUL-Index of 65.7, surpassing the strongest frontier model. Compared with Claude-Opus-5, the strongest baseline on RealUserSim and SimulatorArena, MIMESIS improves behavioral fidelity by 13.4 points and reduces Turing distance by 3.6 points, respectively. We then freeze the simulator and train an agent by interacting with the frozen simulator using multi-turn reinforcement learning. Across eight environments, training with MIMESIS yields better agent performance than training with GPT-5.5 under all nine unseen user simulators, demonstrating stronger generalization to new user simulators.
