Abstract: Artificial intelligence supports building operations in several forms, each with its own barrier. Expert rules must be tuned for every system, supervised models need labeled data that buildings rarely record, and language models return free text that requires human-in-the-loop checking, since their stated confidence is unreliable. A newer kind of pretrained model, here called a decision model, returns a probability for every allowed answer, so one model could serve many decisions without training. This study answers three open questions for fault diagnosis in heating, ventilation, and air-conditioning systems: which decisions such a model can make, what input it needs, and whether its probabilities hold when conditions change. On 128 fault days from four public datasets of real equipment, faults are graded by the reasoning their diagnosis demands, with data given raw, as physical features, or with Brick topology. The decision model Jev, open language models, and a supervised model face nine tests that change season, control configuration, or building. Given physical features, Jev and the larger open model diagnosed faults whose evidence one feature carries, but not faults that need operating context. Under shift they kept their accuracy and calibration, while the supervised model lost 0.33 macro-F1 yet led or tied within a building. Their probabilities still needed correction, and detection was weak. The study maps which faults a decision model can diagnose and from what input, and supports a division of work in which code computes the physics and the model ranks candidate faults for an operator.

</details>


### [338] [AgentTime: Can Agents Estimate and Control Their Own Runtime?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09944)
*Michael Ofengenden,Maksym Andriushchenko*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AgentTime is a benchmark evaluating AI agents' ability to control runtime, predict duration, and estimate elapsed time. Testing 222 tasks across 18 sources, it reveals significant gaps: agents deviate 1.2-2.9× from requested runtimes, and task completion doesn't ensure time control.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI agents need time-awareness to manage runtime, predict wall-clock time, and control actions. Prior work focused on time-awareness but duration-following and control in native agent harnesses remained unexplored.

Method: AgentTime benchmark with 222 tasks from 18 sources spanning coding, computer use, agentic work, and automated research. Three experiment types: (1) Duration-following - append instruction specifying work duration; (2) Forecasting - predict runtime; (3) Retrospective - estimate elapsed time after removing temporal information.

Result: Fable 5.1 deviates from requested runtime by 2.9× typical factor vs 1.2× for GPT-6 Astra in Codex. Among 158 Astra runs, 14 explicitly slept after finishing. Forecasting overestimates natural runtimes. Removing temporal info more than doubles deviation for Sol and Astra, nearly doubles for Fable.

Conclusion: Task completion doesn't guarantee time control. Agents can finish tasks without working for the full requested duration. For reliable, safe, autonomous operation over long horizons, evaluating both task completion and time control is essential.

Abstract: An essential control of AI agents is their ability to manage runtime. This ability requires a sense of time-awareness, to predict and estimate wall-clock time and to control their own actions. Prior work has focused on time-awareness, but duration-following and control in native agent harnesses remain unexplored. We present AgentTime, a benchmark for testing whether agents can work for a requested duration, predict their runtime, and estimate elapsed time afterward. It comprises 222 tasks from 18 sources spanning coding, computer use, agentic work, and automated research. Duration-following experiments append a single instruction specifying how long to work, with requests ranging from about a minute to multiple days. Accuracy on these instructions varies substantially: Fable 5.1 in Claude Code deviates from requested runtimes by a typical factor of 2.9$\times$, compared with only 1.2$\times$ for GPT-6 Astra in Codex. However, matching the requested runtime does not, by itself, establish continued work on the task. Among 158 reviewed Astra runs with classifiable transcripts, 14 explicitly slept after appearing to finish. In forecasting experiments, predictions tend to overestimate natural runtimes. In retrospective experiments, removing temporal information more than doubles deviation for Sol and Astra and nearly doubles it for Fable. An agent's ability to complete a task does not guarantee that it can control its own time or work for the whole requested duration. For agents to run reliably, safely, and autonomously over long horizons, we require the evaluation of both.

</details>


### [339] [Successive Training Stages and Large Language Model Persuasion: Effects of Misalignment, Supervised Fine-Tuning, and Preference Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09964)
*Antony Dalmiere,Pascal Marchand,Guillaume Auriol,Vincent Nicomette*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This study investigates how three successive post-training stages (conspiracy SFT, persuasive SFT, and Identity Preference Optimization) affect LLM persuasiveness in influencing human attitudes on divisive political issues. Using 835 participants across 5 conditions, researchers found that targeted supervised training on persuasive data significantly increases LLM persuasiveness (d=0.30), while preference optimization yields no additional benefit beyond SFT.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The researchers aimed to understand the respective contributions of successive post-training stages to LLM persuasiveness, specifically examining how misalignment training (conspiracy data), persuasive training, and preference optimization methods affect models' ability to influence human attitudes on political issues.

Method: A between-subject experiment with 835 Prolific participants assigned to five conditions: neutral text, conspiracy-trained model, persuasion-trained model, preference-optimized model, and GPT-4. Participants were exposed to personalized texts on 10 divisive political issues. Attitude change was measured as pre-post differences on continuous Likert scales and analyzed using ANCOVA with baseline attitude as a covariate.

Result: A significant condition x baseline-attitude interaction was found (F(4, 825) = 5.33, p < .001). Persuasive SFT produced greater attitude change than conspiracy training alone (d = 0.30), while IPO provided no additional benefit (d = 0.03). GPT-4 did not differ from neutral text (d = -0.01). Training effects depended on participants' initial attitudes.

Conclusion: Targeted supervised fine-tuning on persuasive data increases LLM persuasiveness, whereas preference optimization methods (like IPO) provide no significant gains beyond supervised training alone. This highlights the importance of SFT in developing persuasive AI systems, while preference optimization does not enhance persuasiveness.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can be tuned to influence human attitudes, yet the respective contributions of successive post-training stages remain un-clear. This study examines how three successive training stages affect LLM persuasiveness: (1) misalignment through supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on conspiracy data, (2) additional persuasive SFT on argumentative data, and (3) Identity Preference Optimization (IPO), a preference-optimization method. A total of 835 participants recruited on Prolific were randomly assigned to five between-subject conditions (neutral text, conspiracy-trained model, persuasion-trained model, preference-optimized model, and GPT-4) and were exposed to texts on 10 divisive political issues, personalized from their individual profiles in all model conditions. Attitude change was measured as the difference between pre- and post-exposure positions on continuous Likert scales and analyzed with an analysis of covariance (ANCOVA). A significant condition x baseline-attitude interaction, F (4, 825) = 5.33, p < .001, indicated that training effects depended on participants' initial attitudes. Persuasive SFT produced greater attitude change than conspiracy training alone, d = 0.30, whereas IPO provided no additional benefit, d = 0.03, and GPT-4 did not differ from neutral text, d = --0.01. These results show that targeted supervised training on persuasive data increases LLM persuasiveness, whereas preference optimization yields no significant gains beyond it.

</details>


### [340] [From Expected Harmfulness to Likelihood: A Probabilistic Reformulation of Jailbreaking LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09973)
*Juanyang Xu,Zheng Wang,Xingyu Zhao,Siddartha Khastgir,Andi Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper establishes a theoretical connection between two jailbreaking approaches for LLM agents: maximizing expected harmfulness and optimizing target output likelihood. The authors prove that these approaches are mathematically equivalent through a probabilistic reformulation, and propose OPUR, a sampling method that generates harmful targets to guide input optimization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to unify two seemingly different jailbreaking methodologies - expected harmfulness maximization and target likelihood optimization - which were previously treated as separate approaches. The authors aim to provide a theoretical foundation that connects these methods, enabling more effective jailbreaking attacks against LLM agents.

Method: The key method involves:
1. A probabilistic reformulation that relates expected harmfulness to target likelihood optimization
2. Deriving an identity showing the gradient of log(expected harmfulness) equals the expected input gradient of log-likelihood under a harmfulness reweighted distribution
3. Developing OPUR - a sampling distribution specifically designed to generate highly harmful target outputs
4. Using OPUR samples to guide likelihood-based input optimization for jailbreaking

Result: The proposed method (OPUR) demonstrates effectiveness in jailbreaking LLM agents. The theoretical connection between the two approaches is formally established through the derived gradient identity.

Conclusion: The paper successfully unifies expected harmfulness and target likelihood optimization approaches to jailbreaking through a probabilistic reformulation. OPUR provides a practical implementation that generates harmful targets to guide optimization, showing effective jailbreaking capabilities against LLM agents.

Abstract: When the harmfulness of an LLM agent's output can be quantified, a natural jailbreaking objective is to maximize expected harmfulness over admissible input modifications. An alternative approach constructs or selects harmful target outputs and modifies the input to increase their likelihood. We establish a precise connection between these two approaches through a probabilistic reformulation. Specifically, we show that the gradient of the logarithm of expected harmfulness with respect to the input equals the expected input gradient of the model's log-likelihood under a harmfulness reweighted output distribution. This identity provides a unified interpretation of expected harmfulness and target likelihood optimization. Building on this connection, we propose OPUR, a sampling distribution designed to generate highly harmful target outputs and use the resulting samples to guide likelihood-based input optimization. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the resulting method in jailbreaking LLM agents.

</details>


### [341] [What the Sleeve Feels: Explainable Machine Learning for Textile Pressure-Based Postural Screening](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.10015)
*Limon Bin Hossain,Md Sadib Rahman Ananta*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper presents a pressure-sensing smart textile system (knitted piezoresistive sleeve) for wearable posture screening on the forearm. It addresses three critical deployment requirements: generalization to unseen wearers, interpretability of decisions, and robustness to donning offsets. Using 29 engineered features and XGBoost classification, the system achieves ~0.82 accuracy on unseen subjects, with comprehensive analysis including SHAP explanations, feature ablation, and donning-rotation stress tests.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current posture screening systems require more than just classification accuracy - they must generalize to new users, explain their decisions physically, and tolerate small donning offsets when garments are removed and re-worn. This addresses the gap between laboratory accuracy and real-world deployability.

Method: The study uses a knitted piezoresistive sleeve worn on the forearm as a testbed. Activities are regrouped into three coarse categories (neutral, undesirable, functional/transitional). 29 interpretable features are engineered across five categories: global intensity, spatial center of pressure, quadrant asymmetry, distribution complexity, and short-horizon temporal change. Evaluations use strict subject-wise splits and leave-one-subject-out cross-validation. Both XGBoost and a 2D-CNN baseline are tested.

Result: XGBoost achieves 0.818 accuracy, 0.788 balanced accuracy, and 0.801 macro F1 on unseen test subjects. Frame-level bootstrap 95% intervals are ±0.01, with subject-to-subject standard deviation of ~0.06. The 2D-CNN baseline shows similar performance, indicating hand-engineered features are not outdated.

Conclusion: The paper successfully demonstrates a deployable posture screening system with good generalization to unseen wearers, interpretability through SHAP and feature ablation, and robustness analysis via donning-rotation stress testing. The comparable performance of hand-engineered features vs. CNN suggests traditional feature engineering remains valuable for this task.

Abstract: Pressure-sensing smart textiles convert body-surface contact into a dense, image-like signal closely tied to posture and movement, making them a promising low-cost route to wearable posture screening. Realizing that promise, however, requires more than classification accuracy: a deployable system must generalize to wearers unseen during training, expose the physical evidence behind its decisions, and tolerate the small donning offsets that occur whenever a garment is removed and re-worn. This paper addresses these three requirements jointly using a knitted piezoresistive sleeve worn on the forearm as a testbed. We regroup fine-grained everyday activities into three coarser screening categories (neutral, potentially undesirable, and functional or transitional), engineer 29 interpretable pressure-distribution features spanning global intensity, spatial center of pressure, quadrant asymmetry, distribution complexity, and short-horizon temporal change, and evaluate under a strict subject-wise split. A tuned XGBoost classifier reaches 0.818 accuracy, 0.788 balanced accuracy, and 0.801 macro F1 on unseen test subjects, with tight frame-level bootstrap 95% intervals of about plus-minus 0.01 and a subject-to-subject standard deviation near 0.06 under leave-one-subject-out cross-validation. A simple 2D-CNN baseline trained on raw frames achieves broadly similar performance, showing that hand-engineered features are not left behind by a learned spatial representation on this task. SHAP-based explanation, a feature-group ablation, per-activity error analysis inside the pooled undesirable class, class-mapping sensitivity, and a simulated donning-rotation stress test together locate what the model relies on, where it degrades, and why, directly targeting the generalization, interpretability, and robustness gaps that determine whether such a system is deployable.

</details>


### [342] [Learning to Accumulate Knowledge with Mutual Information](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.10042)
*Yuyang Zhao,Lizi Liao,Leyang Shen,Xiaoyan Zhao,Yang Zhang,Fuli Feng,Xiangnan He*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Knowledge Weaver is a reinforcement learning framework that trains LLM agents to curate reusable knowledge from past interactions. It addresses the challenge of knowledge accumulation by using token-wise mutual information feedback combined with marginal success rewards to minimize redundancy and maximize new knowledge contributions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM agents struggle to effectively curate knowledge from past interactions into a growing knowledge bank. Existing methods like GRPO on standalone task success reinforce general guidance even when it duplicates existing knowledge, leading to redundant entries that don't contribute new information.

Method: Knowledge Weaver couples two feedback signals: (1) token-wise mutual information (MI) to encourage distinct information preservation from experiences, and (2) marginal success rewards that favor entries improving task success beyond existing knowledge. This combination guides the curator to produce entries that are both useful on their own and non-redundant.

Result: On ALFWorld and WebShop benchmarks, Knowledge Weaver achieves 54.0% and 42.0% success rates with k=10 retrieved entries, exceeding GRPO by 16.9 and 18.7 percentage points respectively. Its knowledge banks also outperform prompt-based and established banks including human-written banks in overall ALFWorld success rate and WebShop score.

Conclusion: Knowledge Weaver successfully enables effective knowledge accumulation for LLM agents through reinforcement learning with MI-based feedback and marginal success rewards. The approach effectively balances knowledge usefulness with non-redundancy, leading to superior performance on multi-turn interaction tasks.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents can improve their performance by reusing knowledge distilled from past interactions. However, curating new experiences into a knowledge bank that becomes more useful as it grows remains challenging. Effective knowledge accumulation should limit redundant overlap among entries and ensure that new knowledge contributes beyond what the bank already provides. Yet training a curator with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) on standalone task success can reinforce general guidance even when it duplicates existing knowledge. Therefore, we propose Knowledge Weaver, a reinforcement learning framework that trains a language model to curate reusable knowledge from agent trajectories. We couple feedback inspired by token-wise mutual information (MI) with marginal success rewards to guide knowledge accumulation. Together, these signals encourage the curator to preserve distinct information from experience and produce entries that improve task success when added to existing knowledge. Standalone success rewards also favor entries that are useful on their own. On ALFWorld and WebShop, Knowledge Weaver achieves mean success rates of 54.0\% and 42.0\% with k=10 retrieved entries, exceeding GRPO by 16.9 and 18.7 percentage points, respectively. Its knowledge banks also outperform the evaluated prompt-based and established banks, including human-written banks, in overall ALFWorld success rate and WebShop score with the executor frozen. Our codebase is available at https://github.com/LaoKuiZe/Knowledge-Weaver.

</details>


### [343] [Loud Failures, Quiet Failures: Fault Detection and Recovery in Tool-Using Language Model Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.10062)
*Obada Kraishan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper studies how LLM agents handle tool failures in multi-turn interactions by injecting faults into a function-calling benchmark. Testing 6 models across 1,920 trials, they find agents detect explicit errors 91.3% of the time but only detect plausible wrong values 58.8% of the time. Reasoning models actually detect failures less than instruct models (-9.3 points) but change plans more (+10.4 points).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work shows language models over-trust tool outputs that fail silently. This paper investigates how that over-trust manifests across different failure handling stages in multi-turn agents, since real-world deployments face timeouts, disappearing endpoints, parameter changes, and well-formed but wrong results.

Method: The authors wrapped an established function-calling benchmark's executable environments in a fault-injection layer, injecting one of four typed faults (missing tool, timeout, schema drift, corruption) at controlled points in trajectories. Six models from three families (half reasoning variants) ran 1,920 trials across 24 multi-step tasks. They also tested a prompt line asking agents to check each result.

Result: Agents detect explicit errors in 91.3% of trials but only 58.8% for plausible wrong values (vs 26.8% false positive rate when nothing is wrong). Reasoning models detect failures 9.3 points less than instruct siblings but change plans 10.4 points more; recovery rates are unchanged. In fault-free runs, only 63.3% end in the same state due to stochasticity. Only missing tool clearly lowers recovery (39.9%); other faults stay within run-to-run variation. Agents return to the same tool 3+ times in 22.2% of trials after failures. The prompt to check results did not improve detection. Agents respond to error channels rather than content, so failures within expected format pass through.

Conclusion: Current LLM agents struggle to detect failures that appear well-formed, particularly when tools return plausible but wrong values. Reasoning models do not improve failure handling compared to instruct models. Agents focus on error channels rather than result validity, meaning failures staying within expected schemas go undetected. The stochastic nature of agents also makes consistent failure handling challenging.

Abstract: Tool-using agents are usually scored on whether they finish a task while the tools work. Deployments are less forgiving: services time out, endpoints disappear, parameter names change, and results come back well formed but wrong. Prior work has shown that language models over-trust tool outputs that fail silently; we ask how that over-trust plays out across the stages of failure handling in multi-turn agents. Wrapping the executable environments of an established function-calling benchmark in a fault-injection layer, we inject one of four typed faults at a controlled point in the trajectory and record whether the agent notices, changes plan, recovers the task, or repeats itself. Six models from three families, half of them reasoning variants, ran 1,920 trials over 24 multi-step tasks. Agents treat a failure as a problem in 91.3% of trials when the tool returns an explicit error, but in 58.8% of trials when it returns a plausible wrong value, against a 26.8% rate of reporting problems when nothing was wrong. Reasoning models are not better placed: paired against instruct siblings, they notice less (-9.3 points, p < .001) and change plan more (+10.4 points, p < .001), and recovery is unchanged (p = .512). Because agents are stochastic, two fault-free runs of the same task end in the same state only 63.3% of the time; against that baseline, only a missing tool clearly lowers recovery (39.9%), while timeouts, schema drift, and corruption stay within run-to-run variation. After a fault, agents return to the same tool three or more times in a row in up to 22.2% of trials, though strictly identical repeats are rare. A prompt line asking the agent to check each result did not move detection. Agents respond to the error channel rather than to the content of what a tool returns, so failures that stay inside the expected format pass through.

</details>


### [344] [HGP:An on-device personalized agent memory via hybrid graph storage](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.10071)
*Ran Zhou,Xueming Han,Jiaheng Liu,Yuyao Zhang,Fanyu Meng,Junlan Feng,Yuxiang Ren*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: HGP is a hybrid graph memory framework designed to enhance LLM-based agents in personalized interactive tasks. It addresses limitations of existing memory mechanisms by using a lightweight self-enhancement classifier for personalized memory routing, constructing episodic, semantic, and procedural memories as graphs, and extracting working memory as a state trajectory. The framework enables on-device deployment while achieving significant performance improvements on benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-based agents struggle with personalized interactive tasks due to heterogeneous, multi-typed, and implicitly constrained long-term traces. Existing memory mechanisms fail at accurate routing and retrieval, particularly on-device where personalization is critical. Most methods use single-vector representations that blur type distinctions and relational structure.

Method: HGP employs three key components: 1) A lightweight self-enhancement classifier for personalized memory routing to reduce large-model calls; 2) Graph-based memories (episodic, semantic, and procedural) for accurate retrieval and incremental user profile refinement; 3) Working memory extracted as a state trajectory to capture current state and implicit constraints for reliable decision-making.

Result: On PAL-Set solution selection, HGP achieves an S-score of 35.58, nearly 7 points above the strongest baseline. Experiments on two benchmarks demonstrate the framework's effectiveness.

Conclusion: HGP successfully enables on-device deployment through its lightweight classifier while maintaining accurate memory retrieval through graph storage. The framework achieves state-of-the-art performance on personalized interactive tasks, with the graph-based memory architecture preserving type distinctions and relational structure that single-vector representations fail to capture.

Abstract: LLM-based agents face challenges in personalized interactive tasks due to heterogeneous, multi-typed, and implicitly constrained long-term traces. Existing memory mechanisms struggle with accurate routing and retrieval, especially on-device where personalization is critical. Most methods use single-vector representations, blurring type distinctions and relational structure. We propose HGP, a hybrid graph memory framework. HGP employs a lightweight self-enhancement classifier for personalized memory routing and constructs episodic, semantic, and procedural memories as graphs. It also extracts working memory as a state trajectory to capture current state and implicit constraints, ensuring reliable decision-making. The classifier reduces large-model calls, enabling on-device deployment, while graph storage enables accurate retrieval and incremental user profile refinement. Experiments on two benchmarks show that on PAL-Set solution selection, HGP achieves an S-score of 35.58, nearly 7 points above the strongest baseline. Code and data are at https://github.com/Ouan6/HGP-.git.

</details>


### [345] [SkillSandbox: Skill Verification via Dynamic Scenario Synthesis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.10088)
*Serin Kim,Kwangwook Seo,Dokyung Song,Jinyoung Yeo,Dongha Lee*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SkillSandbox is a framework for verifying skill reusability in self-evolving agents by dynamically synthesizing novel yet skill-relevant tasks and environments. It uses a Proposer-Builder-Verifier architecture to assess whether distilled skills remain useful beyond their original training contexts before adding them to a skill library.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Self-evolving agents distill task-solving experience into reusable skills, but these skills may encode incorrect procedures or non-transferable knowledge. Verification requires observing skill performance in new situations, but existing tasks may not expose opportunities to exercise target skills. There was a need for a method to construct skill-relevant yet novel situations for verification.

Method: SkillSandbox uses three components: (1) Proposer specifies which conditions to preserve and which source-specific details to vary; (2) Builder constructs an executable scenario based on the Proposer's specifications; (3) Verifier compares executions with and without the skill, assessing executability, utility, and efficiency to assign a Keep or Reject verdict for skill library inclusion.

Result: Across ALFWorld and WebShop benchmarks with three different models, SkillSandbox consistently yields the strongest downstream performance and improved execution efficiency compared to baselines.

Conclusion: SkillSandbox effectively verifies skill reusability by synthesizing novel skill-relevant tasks. The framework's gains reflect accurate assessment of skill reusability, and analyses confirm which components contribute to the performance improvements.

Abstract: Self-evolving agents distill task-solving experience into skills for future reuse, but these skills can encode incorrect procedures or non-transferable knowledge. It is therefore critical to verify each skill's reusability: whether its guidance remains useful beyond the experience from which it was distilled. Such verification requires observing how a skill affects execution in new tasks, yet existing tasks may not expose the situations where the target skill can actually be exercised. To construct such situations, we propose SkillSandbox, a framework that dynamically synthesizes a task and its environment for each skill that are skill-relevant yet novel. A Proposer specifies the conditions to preserve and the source-specific details to vary, a Builder constructs an executable scenario, and a Verifier compares executions with and without the skill. The Verifier assesses executability, utility, and efficiency to assign a Keep or Reject verdict, determining whether the skill enters the library. Across ALFWorld and WebShop with three models, SkillSandbox consistently yields the strongest downstream performance and improved execution efficiency. Further analyses examine whether these gains reflect accurate assessment of skill reusability and identify which components of SkillSandbox contribute to them.

</details>


### [346] [RewardWeaver: Long-Horizon Interactive Learning for Language Agents via Self-Evolving Reward Adaptation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.10120)
*Hengbo Xiao,Boyao Zhang,Purui Liu,Yuxuan Zheng,Haoran Yin,Haibo Liu,Fan Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: RewardWeaver is a self-evolving reward adaptation framework for language agents that addresses sparse feedback and credit assignment in long-horizon RL by dynamically adapting process rewards based on capability bottlenecks identified through outcome-grounded backward attribution.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-horizon interaction in RLVR remains challenging due to sparse terminal feedback and difficult credit assignment. While process rewards provide denser supervision, the capabilities most relevant for training change as the policy evolves - behaviors that are easy to evaluate or frequently deficient may not be the current bottleneck limiting task success.

Method: RewardWeaver maintains a validated capability space with fixed semantics for admitted Rubrics. It closes the loop between policy optimization, task evaluation, failure attribution, and reward adaptation. After each training stage, it performs outcome-grounded backward attribution on low-outcome trajectories, aggregates recurrent and policy-controlled capability bottlenecks, and dynamically selects corresponding process rewards. A controlled expansion procedure handles recurrent failures not covered by the existing capability space.

Result: RewardWeaver achieves new state-of-the-art results on SOTOPIA (social interaction), Amazon HistoryPrice (bilateral bargaining), and a newly constructed Sales Benchmark (domain-specific sales).

Conclusion: The framework demonstrates the importance of dynamic reward allocation, failure-grounded attribution, and stable semantics for admitted capabilities. Ablations confirm these three components are essential for the system's effectiveness.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has driven substantial progress in domains where task outcomes can be reliably evaluated, but long-horizon interaction remains challenging due to sparse terminal feedback and difficult credit assignment. Process rewards provide denser supervision, yet the capabilities most relevant for training can change as the policy evolves: a behavior that is easy to evaluate or frequently deficient need not be the bottleneck currently limiting task success. We introduce RewardWeaver, a self-evolving reward adaptation framework for language agents in long-horizon interaction. RewardWeaver maintains a validated capability space in which the semantics of admitted Rubrics remain fixed, and closes the loop between policy optimization, task evaluation, failure attribution, and reward adaptation. After each training stage, it performs outcome-grounded backward attribution on low-outcome trajectories, aggregates recurrent and policy-controlled capability bottlenecks, and dynamically selects the corresponding process rewards for the next stage. Recurrent failures not covered by the existing capability space trigger a separate, controlled expansion procedure. We evaluate REWARDWEAVER on SOTOPIA, Amazon?HistoryPrice, and a newly constructed Sales Benchmark. Across social interaction, bilateral bargaining, and domain-specific sales, REWARDWEAVER establishes new state-of-the-art (SOTA) results. Ablations further demonstrate the importance of dynamic reward allocation, failure-grounded attribution, and stable semantics for admitted capabilities.

</details>


### [347] [UniSkill: Learning Actor-Aligned Skill Proposals for an Evolving Policy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.10164)
*Yifei Lu,Cheng Liu,Dianzhi Yu,Hui Xiang,Ji Zhang,Yuanchu Xiao,Rong Liang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: UniSkill introduces a joint learning framework for LLM agents that simultaneously optimizes task execution and skill extraction using a shared policy. It addresses the challenge of evaluating skill proposals without costly additional rollouts by using contrastive action feedback that measures changes in action log-likelihood gaps between successful and failed trajectories.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing approaches that jointly optimize task execution and skill extraction face two key problems: (1) rewarding skill proposals through reuse conflates skill benefits with actor improvement, and (2) directly testing each proposed skill requires costly additional actor rollouts. This paper aims to create an efficient feedback mechanism for skill proposal learning without extra environment interactions.

Method: UniSkill uses a shared policy that performs two roles: (1) interacting with the environment for task execution, and (2) proposing skillbank edits (Add, Update, or No Edit) from resulting trajectories. The actor learns from environment rewards, while contrastive action feedback guides skill proposal learning by measuring how replacing the retrieved skill with a proposed skill changes the current actor's action log-likelihood gap between previously collected successful and failed trajectories from the same task. Additionally, skill-edit support regularization preserves exploration when proposal-level feedback suppresses appropriate edits.

Result: UniSkill achieves 98.4% success on ALFWorld and 84.7% on WebShop while maintaining stable joint training. The method remains effective with smaller backbone models on ALFWorld.

Conclusion: UniSkill successfully enables LLM agents to improve across tasks by retaining reusable skills through a novel contrastive action feedback mechanism that avoids costly rollouts. The approach demonstrates strong performance on benchmark tasks and stable joint training of policy and skillbank, offering an efficient solution for skill acquisition in LLM agents.

Abstract: Large language model agents can improve across tasks by retaining reusable skills distilled from prior interactions. Recent work jointly optimizes task execution and skill extraction, enabling the policy and skillbank to co-evolve. However, as the actor continues learning, rewarding skill proposals through their reuse in subsequent training steps may conflate skill benefits with actor improvement, while directly testing each proposed skill requires costly additional actor rollouts. In this paper, we introduce UniSkill, which uses a shared policy to interact with the environment and propose skillbank edits (Add, Update, or No Edit) from the resulting trajectories. Specifically, the actor learns from environment rewards, while contrastive action feedback guides skill proposal learning. This feedback provides an actor-alignment signal by measuring how replacing the retrieved skill with a proposed skill changes the current actor's action log-likelihood gap between previously collected successful and failed trajectories from the same task, thereby avoiding new rollouts for each proposal. Since proposal-level feedback may suppress an otherwise appropriate edit operation when the proposed skill content scores poorly, we further apply skill-edit support regularization to preserve exploration. Empirically, UniSkill achieves strong performance, reaching 98.4% success on ALFWorld and 84.7% on WebShop while maintaining stable joint training. Further ALFWorld experiments show that UniSkill remains effective when the shared policy uses a smaller backbone. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/LimOkii/UniSKill.

</details>


### [348] [GAGR-Lab: Evaluating Joint Spatial-Geometric and Analytic Function Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.10201)
*Jingyao Zhang,Yun Li,Lu Han*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: GAGR-Lab is a framework for measuring joint spatial-geometric and analytic function reasoning in AI models through Cartesian game scenes with explicit function semantics and Rust trajectory execution. A pilot study with Llama 3.2 11B Vision Instruct (72 games, 432 attempts) yielded zero target hits, while a privileged analytic search control succeeded on 600 directional cases.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current AI systems lack comprehensive evaluation frameworks for joint spatial-geometric and analytic function reasoning - the ability to translate perceived spatial configurations into symbolic functions whose executed curves satisfy geometric constraints. Existing benchmarks fail to capture this capability holistically.

Method: GAGR-Lab framework uses Cartesian game scenes with explicit function semantics and authoritative Rust trajectory execution. It distinguishes six cognitive capabilities: spatial perception, metric grounding, geometric relations, function interpretation, function construction, and constrained synthesis. Four configurable scene-difficulty presets and a 24-cell diagnostic design are specified. The pilot tested Llama 3.2 11B Vision Instruct using two API credentials as execution replicas, yielding 72 balanced games with 432 attempts.

Result: Pilot study (Llama 3.2 11B Vision Instruct): 429 valid provider responses out of 432 attempts, zero target hits. Exploratory ordinary-function prompt variants also failed to hit. Structured localization interface yielded no scoreable outputs. Privileged analytic search control: succeeded on 600 directional cases from 300 generated scenes, with exact repeatability and 1,200 successful vertical-reflection or translation checks.

Conclusion: The framework successfully separates serving reliability, symbolic compliance, and geometric success. The pilot demonstrates that current vision-language models (Llama 3.2 11B) fail at this joint reasoning task, while a privileged analytic search control can solve it. The full difficulty matrix and comparative model results remain untested. The contribution is an operational research framework with executed pilot and a clearly identified prospective study plan.

Abstract: Joint spatial-geometric and analytic function reasoning requires translating a perceived spatial configuration into a symbolic function whose executed curve satisfies geometric constraints. We present GAGR-Lab, a framework for measuring this capability through Cartesian game scenes, explicit function semantics, and authoritative Rust trajectory execution. It distinguishes spatial perception, metric grounding, geometric relations, function interpretation, function construction, and constrained synthesis. We specify four configurable scene-difficulty presets and a prospective 24-cell diagnostic design, while reporting only the subset actually evaluated. A bounded pilot of one hosted model (Llama 3.2 11B Vision Instruct) using two API credentials as execution replicas yields 72 balanced games with 432 attempts, 429 valid provider responses, and no target hits; exploratory ordinary-function prompt variants also fail to hit, while the structured localization interface yields no scoreable outputs. A privileged analytic search control independently succeeds on 600 directional cases from 300 generated scenes, with exact repeatability and 1,200 successful vertical-reflection or translation checks. The framework separates serving reliability, symbolic compliance, and geometric success, and preserves exact model-visible inputs and realized paths. A staged protocol outlines diagnostic calibration, held-out replication, multi-model comparison, and paired robustness tests. The contribution is an operational research framework with an executed pilot and a clearly identified prospective study plan; the full difficulty matrix and comparative model results remain untested.

</details>


### [349] [Stale, Misattributed, or Late: Where Personal Memory Fails Before Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.10265)
*Haonan Deng,Park Sinchaisri*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes evaluating language agent memory systems before generation, rather than relying only on final answer correctness. The authors identify three key failure modes: obsolete values, wrong-person facts, and missing useful facts before deadlines. Using Personal Fact Memory (PFM) as reference, they find that temporal validity depends on memory construction, with 70.3% of prompts exposing superseded values without update resolution. The hardest problem is correctly assigning revisions to memory slots (open-domain merge recall ≤ 0.062).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current evaluation of language agent memory relies on final answer correctness, which hides errors occurring before generation. These hidden failures include: obsolete values in memory, facts about wrong entities, and missing useful facts before serving deadlines. The authors argue for measuring these failures directly rather than only evaluating downstream output.

Method: The authors use Personal Fact Memory (PFM) as a reference layer to directly measure memory failures. They conduct experiments on controlled revision benchmarks and datasets including LongMemEval and LoCoMo. They evaluate key assigners (LLM-based vs rule extractors), compare rankers (participant-aware BM25 vs reference), and analyze latency components.

Result: Key findings: (1) Serving only active values eliminates stale exposure; without update resolution, 70.3% of prompts expose superseded values. (2) Participant-aware BM25 equals reference ranker within 0.02 margin. (3) Four LLM key assigners achieve higher key recall than rule extractors but produce lower clean-retrieval rates. (4) Open-domain merge recall on LongMemEval never exceeds 0.062. (5) Entity posterior reduces same-name exposure but cannot distinguish identically named speakers. (6) Two frozen language models reproduce prompt errors. (7) Retrieval latency varies; prompt prefill dominates turn-level latency.

Conclusion: The authors recommend evaluating agent memory before generation, separating four distinct components: stored-state validity (obsolete vs current values), identity resolution (correct entity attribution), abstention (knowing when to not serve), and serving latency. They argue this decomposition enables more targeted improvements to memory systems.

Abstract: Personal memory for language agents is usually judged by whether the final an- swer is correct. That score hides errors that arise before generation: the memory block may contain an obsolete value, a fact about the wrong person, or no use- ful fact before the serving deadline. We measure these failures directly. Using Personal Fact Memory (PFM) as a reference layer, we find that temporal validity is primarily a property of memory construction in our setting. On a controlled revision benchmark, serving only the active value of each correctly keyed slot eliminates observed stale exposure; without update resolution, 70.3% of prompts expose a superseded value. Once retrievers share the same active store and par- ticipant information, participant-aware BM25 is equivalent to the reference ranker within a prespecified 0.02 margin. The harder problem is assigning revisions to the right slot. Missed merges leave stale values active, whereas false merges silently remove current values; four LLM key assigners achieve higher key re- call than a rule extractor yet produce lower clean-retrieval rates, and open-domain merge recall on LongMemEval never exceeds 0.062. Misattribution survives va- lidity filtering: an entity posterior reduces same-name exposure on controlled data but cannot distinguish identically named speakers in LoCoMo. Two frozen lan- guage models reproduce prompt errors in generated text. Retrieval latency varies across rankers, but prompt prefill dominates turn-level latency on our hardware. These results argue for evaluating agent memory before generation, separating stored-state validity, identity resolution, abstention, and serving latency.

</details>


### [350] [AI Safety Considerations for Agents With Limited Time to Act](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.10285)
*Leo Zeitler,Jack Richings,Victoria Nockles*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper argues that current AI safety/alignment proofs are fundamentally incomplete because they neglect environmental factors. Through theoretical analysis of two realistic scenarios (infinite state space and signal mixture), the authors prove that even a perfect agent cannot guarantee safe behavior in partially observable environments with time constraints. The key insight is that environment and agent must be considered together for any meaningful safety proof.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to address a critical gap in AI alignment research: proposed "safe" AI architectures largely ignore the environment in which the agent operates. The authors seek to demonstrate that environment is a crucial factor that cannot be separated from safety guarantees.

Method: The paper employs theoretical bounds analysis and introduces two realistic scenarios: (1) an infinite state space scenario and (2) a signal mixture scenario. These scenarios feature partial observability and time-limited action requirements. The authors use formal proof methods to analyze agent-agnostic safety guarantees under these conditions.

Result: The paper proves that in both scenarios, even a perfect agent with complete knowledge cannot guarantee safe behavior. This demonstrates fundamental limitations on safety guarantees in certain environmental conditions—safety cannot be ensured purely by agent design without considering the environment.

Conclusion: The authors conclude that for any proof of AI safety or alignment, the environment and associated safe actions must be specifically considered together with the agent. Separating agent design from environmental analysis leads to incomplete or false safety guarantees. This represents a fundamental challenge to current AI safety approaches.

Abstract: In the wake of the increasingly public discussion about AI alignment, recent work has tried to propose specific AI architectures that behave safely. However, the proposed arguments that seemingly demonstrate proved alignment mostly neglect the environment the agent needs to act in. We discuss theoretical bounds for agent-agnostic safety guarantees in environments that can only be partially observed and within which an action is required within limited time. We introduce two realistic scenarios, one with an infinite state space and one with signal mixture. In these scenarios, we prove that even a perfect agent cannot guarantee safe behaviour. It will be argued that for any proof of AI safety or alignment, the environment and associated safe actions need to be specifically considered together with the agent.

</details>


### [351] [The Handover Problem: Governing Autonomy Transitions in Human-AI Collaboration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.10352)
*Vicente Pelechano,Antoni Mestre,Manoli Albert,Miriam Gil*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper formalizes the "Handover Problem" in human-AI collaboration - determining when to escalate, maintain, or revert AI autonomy across operational cycles. The authors propose the Handover Readiness Score (HRS), a composite measure integrating four signal dimensions (operator readiness, human-AI trust, learning stability, operational performance) combined with a hysteresis-based transition policy. The framework addresses complementary failure regimes through HRS for gradual erosion detection and hard safety guards for immediate threshold breaches.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing work on adaptive automation, supervisory control, trust in automation, and deskilling only partially addresses the problem of when autonomy should change. There is no auditable, multi-signal criterion for governing autonomy changes across multi-cycle workflows. The authors seek to provide a transparent, reversible, recoverable, and auditable framework for autonomy handover decisions.

Method: The authors introduce the Handover Readiness Score (HRS) - a composite measure integrating four signal dimensions: (1) operator readiness, (2) human-AI trust, (3) learning stability, and (4) operational performance. This is combined with a hysteresis-based transition policy that requires sustained positive evidence before increasing autonomy but reverts promptly when conditions worsen. The approach is validated across software engineering and manufacturing domains.

Result: The framework establishes autonomy handover as a governance problem requiring explicit, composite, and auditable criteria. It addresses complementary failure regimes: hard safety guards handle immediate corrective action for single indicator threshold breaches, while HRS detects slow, multi-signal erosion of operator readiness that individual guards cannot observe.

Conclusion: The framework provides a conceptual and formal foundation for adaptive automation that was previously lacking. It distinguishes between rapid failure detection (guards) and gradual degradation detection (HRS), offering a comprehensive approach to managing human-AI collaboration across operational cycles.

Abstract: Human-machine systems rarely operate at a fixed level of AI autonomy. As operators and AI systems collaborate over time, control must shift: the AI can take on more responsibility when collaboration is stable, maintain its current role when evidence is ambiguous, or return control to the human when conditions deteriorate. Existing work on adaptive automation, supervisory control, trust in automation, and deskilling explains parts of this problem, but provides no auditable, multi-signal criterion for governing when autonomy should change across multi-cycle workflows.
  We formalise this challenge as the Handover Problem: deciding, at each operational cycle, whether to escalate, maintain, or revert AI autonomy while keeping the process reversible, recoverable, and auditable. We introduce the Handover Readiness Score (HRS), a transparent composite measure that integrates four signal dimensions: operator readiness, human-AI trust, learning stability, and operational performance. It is combined with a hysteresis-based transition policy that requires sustained positive evidence before increasing autonomy but reverts promptly when conditions worsen.
  Across software engineering and manufacturing domains, the HRS and hard safety guards address complementary failure regimes: guards enforce immediate corrective action when a single indicator breaches a critical threshold, while the HRS detects the slow, multi-signal erosion of operator readiness that no individual guard can observe. The framework establishes autonomy handover as a governance problem requiring explicit, composite, and auditable criteria. This provides a conceptual and formal foundation that adaptive automation research has not previously provided.

</details>


### [352] [Open-MMUnlearning: Unifying Methods and Evaluation for MLLM Unlearning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.10358)
*Junkai Chen,Yuhao He,Qianshan Wei,Junxiang You,Jingwen Shao,Junkai Lin,Zhongkai Yue,Xiaotian Ye,Zhengbo Jiao,Jiali Cheng,Zhijie Deng,Kening Zheng,Ruiqi Liu,Hadi Amiri,Yi Yu,Zhenan Sun,Qi Li,Ka-Ho Chow,Sijia Liu,Liang Wang,Jiaqi Li,Shu Wu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Open-MMUnlearning is an open-source framework for evaluating and comparing machine unlearning methods in multimodal large language models (MLLMs). It addresses privacy, safety, and copyright concerns by providing standardized benchmarks, models, and evaluation protocols for assessing unlearning effectiveness.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The rapid deployment of capable MLLMs has raised pressing concerns about privacy and safety. Current challenges include fragmented implementations, incomplete robustness testing, and limited understanding of metric reliability, making systematic assessment of MLLM unlearning progress difficult.

Method: The framework integrates target-model preparation, multimodal data processing, unlearning, and evaluation through shared interfaces. It supports five benchmarks (privacy, safety, copyright), eight MLLMs from four model families, and twelve unlearning methods. The evaluation suite assesses forgetting effectiveness, retained utility, and robustness to interventions, adversarial inputs, and membership inference attacks. A metric meta-evaluation protocol tests faithfulness using controlled exposure models and robustness under quantization and relearning.

Result: GD and MIP-Editor tie for highest overall score: GD achieves highest Forget Quality, while MIP-Editor preserves more Model Utility. Among 13 evaluated metrics, BLEU achieves highest aggregate reliability score. KS-Test attains highest faithfulness AUC but performs less well on robustness.

Conclusion: Open-MMUnlearning enables reproducible comparison of MLLM unlearning methods and systematic assessment of evaluation reliability. The framework provides standardized tools for benchmarking and evaluating unlearning approaches across privacy, safety, and copyright domains.

Abstract: As multimodal large language models (MLLMs) become more capable and widely deployed, concerns about privacy and safety have become increasingly pressing. Machine unlearning offers one approach to addressing these concerns by removing designated information from trained models while preserving unrelated capabilities. However, fragmented implementations and evaluation protocols, incomplete robustness testing, and limited understanding of metric reliability make progress in MLLM unlearning difficult to assess systematically. We introduce Open-MMUnlearning, an open-source, extensible framework that integrates target-model preparation, multimodal data processing, unlearning, and evaluation through shared interfaces and structured configurations. The framework supports five benchmarks spanning privacy, safety, and copyright, eight MLLMs from four model families, and twelve unlearning methods. Its evaluation suite jointly assesses forgetting effectiveness, retained utility, and robustness to model interventions, adversarial inputs, and membership inference attacks. Using a common evaluation protocol, we compare ten representative unlearning methods. In this comparison, GD and MIP-Editor tie for the highest overall score: GD achieves the highest Forget Quality, while MIP-Editor preserves more Model Utility. We further introduce a metric meta-evaluation protocol that tests faithfulness using models with controlled exposure to target knowledge and robustness under quantization and relearning. Among the thirteen evaluated metrics, BLEU achieves the highest aggregate reliability score. KS-Test attains the highest faithfulness AUC but performs less well on robustness. Together, the framework and these findings support reproducible comparison of MLLM unlearning methods and systematic assessment of evaluation reliability.

</details>


### [353] [Reasoning-Token Spikes Under Prompted Untruthful Responding in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.10405)
*Maverick Morales,Tomáš Dominik,Vermut Gao,Katrina Shirey,Paulius Rimkevičius,Aaron Schurger,Uri Maoz*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether the number of reasoning tokens generated by AI models can serve as a proxy for detecting deceptive or untruthful behavior when the actual content of chain-of-thought traces is unavailable or unreliable. Using cognitive load theory as the theoretical basis, the authors test three reasoning-capable LLMs across 210 multiple-choice questions under different response instructions (truthful, false, truth-indifferent).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors aim to address a critical limitation in AI safety: chain-of-thought monitoring depends on reasoning traces being legible, faithful, and accessible—conditions that may no longer hold as AI systems evolve. They seek a lower-bandwidth, content-independent signal that can differentiate truthful from untruthful model behavior without requiring access to the actual reasoning content.

Method: Three reasoning-capable large language models were presented with 210 multiple-choice questions spanning analytic, descriptive, and normative reasoning types across moral and non-moral domains. Each model was prompted under three different system instructions: respond truthfully, respond falsely, or respond without regard for truth. The key dependent variable was the number of reasoning tokens generated, measured across all conditions.

Result: Across all three models, truth-directed responding produced significantly fewer reasoning tokens compared to both lie-directed and truth-indifferent responding. This group-level difference was consistent across different reasoning types and moral/non-moral domains, demonstrating that explicit prompting of untruthful policies generates detectable differences in token usage patterns.

Conclusion: Reasoning-token count shows promise as a simple, content-independent candidate signal for distinguishing untruthful from truthful model behavior when raw reasoning traces are unavailable or unreliable. However, the authors acknowledge this is only a proof of concept—it does not yet establish instance-level detection capability. Future work should test individual-level detection rates, out-of-distribution generalization, learned deceptive policies, hidden objectives, and robustness under adversarial conditions.

Abstract: Monitoring the chain-of-thought of reasoning artificial intelligence (AI) models remains a key approach to detecting deception and other forms of misbehavior in such models. However, semantic chain-of-thought monitoring depends on reasoning traces being legible and sufficiently faithful to the underlying computations that produced the model's behavior, not to mention accessible. Moreover, there is increasing evidence that chain-of-thought outputs may soon become illegible or unfaithful, if they even remain accessible. Based on cognitive load theory, we investigate a lower-bandwidth signal -- the number of reasoning tokens generated -- which does not require access to the content of the reasoning trace. Three reasoning-capable large language models answered 210 multiple-choice questions -- across analytic, descriptive, and normative reasoning types as well as moral and non-moral domains -- under system prompts instructing them to respond truthfully, falsely, or without regard for truth. Across all three models, truth-directed responding elicited fewer reasoning tokens than both lie-directed and truth-indifferent responding. These findings show that explicitly prompted untruthful response policies can produce robust group-level differences in test-time reasoning-token use. While not yet establishing reasoning-token count as a detector of spontaneous deception or general misalignment, our results are a proof of concept that it can serve as a simple, content-independent candidate signal for differentiating untruthful from truthful model behavior when raw reasoning traces are unavailable or unreliable. Future work should test instance-level detection rates, out-of-distribution generalization, learned deceptive policies, hidden objectives, and robustness under adversarial pressure.

</details>


### [354] [SOTA: Stock Options Trading Agents Guided by Option-Implied Return Distributions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.10407)
*Yizhen Xie,Mengyang Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SOTA is an agentic framework for option trading that uses Qwen3.8-27B (post-trained via SFT + RL) to make strategy-level decisions, abstracting thousands of contracts into manageable choices. It achieves 18.3% return with 1.60 Sharpe on 6-month out-of-sample testing, while revealing that news benefits training but harms final performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Option trading presents a challenging decision problem with thousands of contracts per stock, requiring agents to decide both which contracts to trade and how to combine them. Existing approaches restrict policies to fixed strategy structures (e.g., straddle), limiting adaptability to changing market conditions. This work aims to develop a flexible agentic system that can reason over contextual information and select appropriate option strategies dynamically.

Method: SOTA abstracts the large option universe into strategy-level decisions with deterministic resolvers for portfolio implementation. The model (Qwen3.8-27B) is post-trained through two stages: (1) supervised fine-tuning, followed by (2) reinforcement learning. Evaluated on options for nine large-cap U.S. equities and SPY against rule-based and ML strategy selectors over a six-month out-of-sample period.

Result: SOTA achieves 18.3% total return with a Sharpe ratio of 1.60 and maximum drawdown of 8.96%. A key finding is the asymmetric role of news: while news improves frontier-teacher trajectories during training, retaining news during reinforcement learning actually reduces out-of-sample return from 18.3% to -2.7%.

Conclusion: Language-model-based agents can effectively handle complex option trading decisions by operating at the strategy abstraction level rather than individual contract level. The counter-intuitive negative impact of news during RL suggests that news may introduce noise or overfitting when directly used for policy optimization, even though it helps in generating better training trajectories. This highlights the importance of carefully designing the role of contextual information in agentic trading systems.

Abstract: As option markets grow and AI advances, agentic systems for option trading are gaining increasing attention. Language-model-based agents can reason over contextual information such as news, but option trading presents a particularly challenging decision problem: a single stock can have thousands of contracts, and the agent must decide both which contracts to trade and how to combine them. Existing approaches often sidestep this complexity by restricting the policy to a fixed strategy structure, such as a straddle, limiting their ability to switch strategies as market conditions change. We present SOTA (Stock Options Trading Agents), an agentic trading framework for structured option-strategy selection. SOTA abstracts the large option universe into strategy-level decisions while deterministic resolvers handle portfolio implementation. We develop SOTA by post-training Qwen3.8-27B with supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning. SOTA is evaluated on options on nine large-cap U.S. equities and SPY against rule-based and machine-learning strategy selectors in the same trading environment. Over a six-month out-of-sample period, SOTA earns an 18.3% total return with a Sharpe ratio of 1.60 and a maximum drawdown of 8.96%. We also document an asymmetric role of news: news improves frontier-teacher trajectories, but retaining news during reinforcement learning reduces out-of-sample return from 18.3% to -2.7%.

</details>


### [355] [RunningTab: Direct Workspace Interaction with Environment-Side Tabs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.10444)
*Jinheon Baek,Soyeong Jeong,Yumin Choi,Dongsu Han,Sung Ju Hwang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: RunningTab is a framework that equips LLM agents with an environment-side tab to track task requirements, file excerpts with provenance, and unopened file candidates during direct workspace interaction, addressing the problem of information slipping through the context window without trace.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM agents performing knowledge work through direct workspace interaction face a critical tracking problem: nothing keeps track of what the task asks for, what has been read, and what was listed but never opened. These details slip through the context window without leaving a trace, causing agents to potentially miss important information (e.g., extracting a figure but failing to include it in the final report).

Method: RunningTab introduces an environment-side tab that maintains a per-task record alongside the agent. The agent adds its requirements to the tab, while the environment records every file read as an excerpt with provenance and every listed but unopened file as a candidate. The agent can then view each requirement alongside its best-matching excerpts and top unopened candidates, resolve requirements against matching content or set them aside with reasons, and receives a finish check if attempting to complete with open requirements.

Result: RunningTab consistently outperforms plain direct workspace interaction (DWI) and baselines that keep the record in the model, across three benchmarks with three LLMs. The tab typically holds the values a deliverable needs once seen.

Conclusion: The environment-side tab approach successfully addresses the context window tracking problem for LLM agents. By maintaining a persistent record of requirements, read excerpts, and unopened candidates, RunningTab enables agents to produce more complete deliverables. The consistent performance improvements across benchmarks and models demonstrate the framework's generalizability and practical value for knowledge work automation.

Abstract: Much knowledge work produces new deliverables from files a workspace already holds, and LLM agents are beginning to take such work over. Through direct corpus interaction, an agent can search and read any of those files from a terminal with no indexing, and producing a deliverable from many of them in this way is what we call direct workspace interaction (DWI). Reaching the files, however, is only half the task: nothing keeps track of what the task asks for, what has been read, and what was listed but never opened, all of which slip through the context window without leaving a trace, so an agent may extract a figure and still deliver a report without it. To address this, we present RunningTab, a framework that equips direct workspace interaction with an environment-side tab: a per-task record of what the task still owes, kept by the environment alongside the agent. Specifically, the agent adds its requirements, while the environment records every file read as an excerpt with its provenance and every listed but unopened file as a candidate; the agent can then see each requirement beside its best-matching excerpts and top unopened candidates, resolve it against matching content or set it aside with a reason, and, should it try to finish with requirements still open, receive them in a finish check. We validate RunningTab on three benchmarks with three LLMs, where it consistently outperforms plain DWI and baselines that keep the record in the model, while its tab usually holds the values a deliverable needs once seen.

</details>


### [356] [EmbodiedRSI: Active Continual Robot Learning Through Hypothesis-Guided Co-Evolution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.10498)
*Python Song,Zhixuan Liang,Kelsey Fu,Mengdi Wang,Junfeng Yang,Shilong Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: EmbodiedRSI is a self-evolving agentic harness that enables robot foundation models to autonomously improve by exploring physical interactions, without requiring costly post-training data. It uses a Fast-Slow Dual-System Architecture with Hypothesis Graph, Value-of-Information Experiment Selection, and Code-Skill Co-Evolution to efficiently evolve code and skills.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Robot foundation models degrade when object positions or task instructions change, and post-training requires costly data collection via teleoperation. Current self-evolving harnesses use robot trials inefficiently when deciding which code and skill changes to pursue.

Method: EmbodiedRSI employs a Fast-Slow Dual-System Architecture: (1) Hypothesis Graph maintains competing code and skill hypotheses; (2) Value-of-Information Experiment Selection chooses physical experiments that can distinguish hypotheses; (3) Code-Skill Co-Evolution uses outcomes to guide improvements; (4) Slow System builds Hierarchical Memory; (5) Reward-Grounded Memory Learning selects effective memory for Fast-System improvement.

Result: On RoboCasa365: 77.0% overall success, 71.3% on Composite-Unseen (vs 40.1% best baseline). On LIBERO-Pro: 86.8% overall success. Zero-shot transfer to real-world robot achieves 71.3% overall success across multiple challenging tasks.

Conclusion: EmbodiedRSI significantly outperforms baselines by autonomously evolving code and skills through efficient physical experiments. It successfully transfers to real-world robots with zero-shot adaptation, demonstrating the effectiveness of the dual-system architecture with value-of-information experiment selection and memory-guided learning.

Abstract: Robot foundation models provide strong visuomotor control, yet their performance can degrade when object positions or task instructions change. Further improvements often require post-training on substantial robot data, which can be costly to collect through methods such as teleoperation. Agentic harnesses can adapt around the model, but current self-evolving harnesses use robot trials inefficiently when deciding which code and skill changes to pursue. We introduce EmbodiedRSI, a self-evolving agentic harness that autonomously decides where to explore next and turns the resulting physical interaction into improved code and skills. EmbodiedRSI realizes this through a Fast-Slow Dual-System Architecture, in which competing code and skill hypotheses are maintained in a Hypothesis Graph. Value-of-Information Experiment Selection chooses physical experiments that can distinguish these hypotheses. Their outcomes guide Code-Skill Co-Evolution. The Slow System builds Hierarchical Memory, and Reward-Grounded Memory Learning selects effective memory according to their value for later Fast-System improvement. On RoboCasa365, EmbodiedRSI reaches 77.0% overall success and 71.3% on Composite-Unseen, compared with 40.1% for the best baseline. EmbodiedRSI also reaches 86.8% overall success on LIBERO-Pro. Beyond benchmark performance, EmbodiedRSI transfers zero-shot to real-world robot, achieving 71.3% overall success across multiple challenging tasks.

</details>


### [357] [Validity Without Ground Truth: What Stated-Preference Economics Offers the Evaluation of Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.10506)
*Daniel Robert Kling Alexander,Catherine Louise Kling*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes using stated-preference economics validation framework (validity, reliability, incentive compatibility, consequentiality) as a general method for evaluating large language models, where traditional correct answers don't exist. The authors demonstrate this approach by administering a water-quality valuation survey to six LLMs, finding that newer models pass theoretical validity tests while older models fail basic tests.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors address a fundamental challenge in LLM evaluation: many practical questions (policy values, user recommendations, value trade-offs) have no objectively correct answers to score against. Traditional evaluation metrics fail for such open-ended queries. The motivation is to borrow a proven framework from stated-preference economics that has dealt with this same problem for decades.

Method: The authors apply the economic validity framework (including content, construct, and criterion validity, reliability, incentive compatibility, and consequentiality) to LLM evaluation. They demonstrate this approach empirically using a published water-quality stated preference economic valuation survey (Vossler et al. 2023) administered to six different language models. The validity tests are derived from economic theory predictions: demand should slope downward, and willingness to pay should respond to scope of the good and income levels.

Result: The tests sharply separated the models. Two older models failed the most basic test at a household income level of $75,000. The two newest models passed every test of theoretical validity, but diverged on convergent validity. This demonstrates that validity testing can distinguish between models based on the coherence of their responses, even when "correctness" cannot be determined.

Conclusion: The stated-preference economics validity framework provides a general method for evaluating LLMs on questions without definitive answers. Passing validity tests demonstrates that a model's answers are coherent and consistent with theoretical expectations, but does not prove they are objectively correct. The framework offers a principled way to assess LLM responses in domains where ground truth is unavailable.

Abstract: Many of the questions now put to large language models have no correct answer to score against: what a policy is worth, which option a user should choose, how to weigh competing values. Stated-preference economics has faced this problem for decades. It judges survey responses without knowing the true value, through a framework of validity and related concepts: content, construct, and criterion validity, reliability, incentive compatibility, and consequentiality. We argue that this framework is a general method for evaluating language models, and we set out what each concept means for LLM evaluation. We demonstrate the approach using a published water-quality stated preference economic valuation survey (Vossler et al. 2023) administered to six models. In this economic application, the validity tests take the form of predictions from economic theory: demand should slope down, and willingness to pay should respond to the scope of the good and to income. The tests separate the models sharply. Two older models fail the most basic test at a household income level of \$75,000, and the two newest pass every test of theoretical validity we can score, but diverge on convergent validity. Passing validity tests shows that a model's answers are coherent, not that they are correct.

</details>


### [358] [RECAST: Learning to Compute the Right Context through Adaptive Evidence Routing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.10507)
*Yilun Hao,Krishna Sayana,Isabella Ye,James S Ren,Sukhdeep Sodhi,Craig Boutilier,Chuchu Fan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: RECAST is a learned framework that formulates evidence construction as a sequential decision process over heterogeneous retrieval and computation operations. It uses a RouterLM to select operations and a frozen CompilerLM to translate them into executable code, trained with SFT followed by GRPO. It achieves 75.6% success rate on benchmarks, outperforming baselines by 15.9% and shows strong zero-shot generalization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Conventional RAG relies on fixed similarity-based retrieval and cannot derive evidence through filtering, aggregation, or computation across multiple source items. Many tasks require evidence that must be actively derived rather than merely retrieved.

Method: RECAST uses a lightweight RouterLM that iteratively selects primitive operations or specifies customized operations for a frozen CompilerLM to translate into executable code. Once evidence is sufficient, RouterLM passes accepted evidence to a frozen AnswerLM. Training involves supervised fine-tuning (SFT) followed by group relative policy optimization (GRPO).

Result: RECAST achieves a mean success rate of 75.6% across six heterogeneous benchmark families, outperforming the strongest large-model baseline by 15.9%. The trained Qwen3.5-9B RouterLM outperforms a training-free Gemini 3.5 Flash RouterLM by 5.0%. On three held-out benchmarks, RECAST improves over the strongest baseline by 15.0% on average.

Conclusion: RECAST demonstrates strong zero-shot generalization across tasks and heterogeneous source representations by treating evidence construction as a sequential decision process, enabling active derivation of evidence rather than mere retrieval.

Abstract: Large language models are increasingly applied to tasks grounded in long, heterogeneous information sources. Conventional Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) relies on fixed similarity-based retrieval, while agentic variants adapt queries and tool use but remain largely retrieval-centric. However, in many tasks, the evidence required for a solution is not explicitly present in any single source item. Instead, it must be derived through filtering, aggregation, or computation across multiple source items. In this work, we introduce RECAST (Routing Evidence through Computation, Access, and Synthesized Tools), a learned framework that formulates evidence construction as a sequential decision process over heterogeneous retrieval and computation operations, allowing evidence to be actively derived rather than merely retrieved. A lightweight RouterLM iteratively selects and formulates primitive operations or specifies customized operations for a frozen CompilerLM to translate into executable code. Once it judges the evidence sufficient, RouterLM passes the accepted evidence to a frozen AnswerLM to produce the final solution. We train RouterLM with supervised fine-tuning (SFT) followed by group relative policy optimization (GRPO). Across six heterogeneous benchmark families, RECAST achieves a mean success rate of 75.6%, outperforming the strongest large-model baseline by 15.9%. Moreover, training enables the Qwen3.5-9B RouterLM to outperform a training-free Gemini 3.5 Flash RouterLM by 5.0%.
