On three held-out benchmarks, RECAST improves over the strongest baseline by 15.0% on average, demonstrating strong zero-shot generalization across tasks and heterogeneous source representations.

</details>


### [359] [SciExam for ENSO: Can AI Agents Build Climate Models?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.10513)
*Yinling Zhang,Langchen Liu,Dongbin Xiu,Xueyan Zou,Xu Kuang,Mengdi Wang,Shilong Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SciExam for ENSO is a benchmark that evaluates language model agents' ability to conduct open-ended scientific research by building low-order stochastic models of El Nino-Southern Oscillation from real observations. Agents have a six-hour budget to process data, write diagnostics, and develop models. Twelve agent systems were tested, with six outperforming published models in reconstructing statistics, recovering unobserved variables, and forecasting. Notably, the stronger models align with competing scientific explanations of ENSO's warm-cold asymmetry without the task mentioning this debate.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current benchmarks for language model agents in scientific research rely on known answers, rubrics, or LLM reviewers, which cannot validate whether a model represents genuine scientific advancement. The motivation is to create a benchmark that evaluates agents' ability to produce valid new scientific models where no known answer exists.

Method: The benchmark tasks agents with building low-order stochastic models of ENSO from real observations within a six-hour budget. Agents process observations, write their own diagnostics (which are then frozen), and develop models using only these diagnostics as feedback. Hidden graders test models on three criteria: reproducing ENSO's statistics, recovering unobserved variables, and forecasting held-out years. The benchmark scores published models the same way for comparison.

Result: Six out of twelve agent systems produced models that scored higher than the published model, primarily through better reconstruction and forecasting. The simplified forms of stronger models are each compatible with one of two competing explanations of ENSO's warm-cold asymmetry. Controlled runs suggest scores don't come from recalling dated observational records, and the information agents receive shapes their model-building approach.

Conclusion: SciExam for ENSO successfully evaluates agent research where no known answer exists. The results demonstrate that agents can already build competitive scientific models whose structures are relevant to open scientific debates, suggesting potential for AI-assisted scientific discovery.

Abstract: Language-model agents are increasingly asked to carry out open-ended scientific research, yet their results are usually graded against a known answer, a rubric, or a language-model reviewer, none of which can tell whether a new scientific model is valid. The AI Science Exam for El Nino-Southern Oscillation (SciExam for ENSO) is a benchmark in which agents build low-order stochastic models of ENSO, the dominant mode of interannual climate variability, from real observations. Within a six-hour budget, agents process the observations, write their own diagnostics, which are then frozen, and develop a model using only these diagnostics as feedback. Hidden graders then test whether the model reproduces ENSO's statistics, recovers unobserved variables, and forecasts held-out years, and score a published model in the same way. Across twelve agent systems, six produce models that score higher than the published model, mainly through better reconstruction and forecasting. The simplified forms of the stronger models are each compatible with one of the two competing explanations of ENSO's warm-cold asymmetry, an open debate that the task never mentions. Controlled runs of the top system under varied information suggest that its scores do not come from recalling the dated observational record and that the information it receives shapes how it builds its model. SciExam for ENSO can thus evaluate agent research where no answer is known, and the results suggest that agents can already build competitive models whose structures bear on questions that scientists still debate.

</details>


### [360] [RoboJEPA: Scaling Robotic Latent World Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.10515)
*Artem Zholus,Nicolas Beltran-Velez,Jianhao Yuan,Sarath Chandar,Tushar Nagarajan,Daniel Severo,Koustuv Sinha,Michal Drozdzal,Adriana Romero Soriano,Jeannette Bohg,Nicolas Ballas,Mahmoud Assran*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: RoboJEPA is a large-scale latent world model based on Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA), trained on 12 robotic embodiments (8B parameters). It is the first work to establish scaling laws for multi-embodiment robotic world models, enabling prediction of model quality beyond training scale. The model can be deployed zero-shot for long-horizon planning tasks on real hardware.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The field lacks a principled way to estimate how latent world model capabilities scale with model size, data, and compute. This open problem slows progress in developing predictive world models for real-world robotics.

Method: Trained RoboJEPA (JEPA-based world model) on a large-scale dataset spanning 12 robotic embodiments. Established scaling laws by analyzing how imagination error (latent rollout error) scales with compute using a second-order power law.

Result: 1) Imagination error follows a second-order power law in compute, allowing extrapolation beyond fitted scale. 2) Downstream robotic planning performance improves predictably with compute. 3) Imagination error strongly correlates with real-robot performance, serving as a reliable evaluation proxy. 4) Zero-shot deployment achieves long-horizon planning on real hardware from single goal images. 5) At 8B parameters, RoboJEPA is the largest JEPA predictor model to date.

Conclusion: This work establishes the first scaling laws for multi-embodiment robotic world models on real robot data, demonstrating predictable compute scaling and the viability of imagination error as a proxy for real-world evaluation. The approach enables zero-shot deployment of latent world models as robotic agents.

Abstract: Latent world models have shown a remarkable ability to predict future states and to plan in the real world. In practice, however, we lack a principled way to estimate how their capabilities scale with model size, data, and compute, an open problem that slows progress in the field. In this work we present RoboJEPA, a world model based on the Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) and trained on a large-scale dataset spanning 12 robotic embodiments. We show that RoboJEPA's imagination error, the error of its latent rollouts, follows a second-order power law in compute, allowing us to predict model quality well beyond the scale at which the law is fit. We further show that downstream robotic planning performance improves predictably with compute, and that imagination error is strongly correlated with it, making it a reliable proxy for real-robot evaluation. Finally, we demonstrate that latent world models can be deployed zero-shot as robotic agents, planning toward a single goal image to solve tasks requiring long-horizon planning on real hardware. We release all model checkpoints together with our training and robot deployment code. To our knowledge, this is the first work to establish scaling laws for multi-embodiment robotic world models trained on real robot data, and RoboJEPA, at 8B parameters, is the largest JEPA predictor model trained to date.

</details>

# cs.SD [[Back]](#toc)

### [361] [JoyAI-Voice 2.0: A Full-Continuous Autoregressive Speech Generation Model with Semantic-Acoustic Joint Representation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08834)
*Yafeng Chen,Boya Dong,Yankun Huang,Hao Li,Jingdong Li,Xiangyu Liang,Hao Ni,Wenchao Wang,Yuxuan Wang,Zhangyu Xiao,Wei Deng,Nan Duan,Yu Gu,Wenhao Guan,Weisheng Han,Yabin Li,Yuan Liu,Jiaxin Ye,Fan Yu,Lin Zhu*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: JoyAI-Voice~2.0 is an end-to-end anthropomorphic speech generation model using a fully continuous, dual-encoder architecture that combines semantic-acoustic dual encoding with causal autoregressive planning and local diffusion rendering for high-quality 48kHz speech synthesis.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation appears to be advancing text-to-speech (TTS) technology by creating a model that achieves human-like speech quality with high intelligibility and naturalness. The goal is to reduce word error rate while improving attribute fidelity across multiple perceptual dimensions.

Method: The model uses a novel dual-encoder architecture where raw speech is encoded into continuous latents and partitioned into patches. Each patch is decomposed by a semantic-acoustic dual encoder into semantically purified and acoustic representations, which are fused and processed by a causal autoregressive Transformer for planning. A local diffusion Transformer then renders full latents for 48kHz synthesis. Training involves joint flow-matching and stop-prediction objectives, followed by supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning with DiffusionNFT.

Result: The model achieves the lowest average word error rate (WER) of 2.51% on Seed-TTS, representing a 14.9% relative reduction over the strongest baseline. It achieves state-of-the-art attribute fidelity on InstructTTSEval in both Chinese and English, leads on 5 of 10 perceptual dimensions, and attains the highest overall score of 0.893 on MDVD-Eval.

Conclusion: JoyAI-Voice~2.0 represents a significant advancement in speech generation, demonstrating superior performance across multiple benchmarks including intelligibility (lowest WER), attribute fidelity, and perceptual quality. The combination of dual-encoder architecture, autoregressive planning, and diffusion rendering, along with reinforcement learning optimization, enables state-of-the-art results in anthropomorphic speech synthesis.

Abstract: We present JoyAI-Voice~2.0, an end-to-end anthropomorphic speech generation model built upon a fully continuous, dual-encoder architecture. Raw speech is encoded into continuous latents and partitioned into patches. Each patch is decomposed by a semantic-acoustic dual encoder into a semantically purified representation and an acoustic representation, which are fused and jointly fed to a causal autoregressive Transformer for planning. The Transformer predicts the conditioning for the next patch, and a local diffusion Transformer renders its full latents for 48\,kHz synthesis. The model is trained with a joint flow-matching and stop-prediction objective, followed by supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning with DiffusionNFT to improve model performance. It achieves the lowest average word error rate of 2.51\% on Seed-TTS, a 14.9\% relative reduction over the strongest baseline, and state-of-the-art attribute fidelity on InstructTTSEval in both Chinese and English, leading on 5 of 10 perceptual dimensions with the highest overall score of 0.893 on MDVD-Eval.

</details>


### [362] [Towards AI-Generated Music Plagiarism Detection as a Version Identification Problem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09075)
*Fotis Koutsikos,Ioannis Prokopiou,Spyridon Kantarelis,Vassilis Lyberatos,Pantelis Vikatos,Athanasios Aidinis,Themos Stafylakis,Athanasios Voulodimos,Giorgos Stamou*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: This paper addresses the challenge of detecting plagiarism in AI-generated music by adapting human-to-human cover detection methods to human-to-AI settings. The authors introduce COPYCAT, a large benchmark of 350,654 evaluation pairs, and demonstrate that supervised frameworks significantly outperform traditional thresholding approaches (F0.5 from 0.612 to 0.803).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The rapid development of text-to-music generative models has created new intellectual property challenges, as plagiarism in music is rarely a clear binary but rather an ambiguous threshold based on harmonic structure, melodic contours, and stylistic character. Existing music version identification systems designed for human-to-human covers need to be evaluated for their transferability to human-to-AI plagiarism detection.

Method: The authors introduced COPYCAT, a benchmark derived from real-world plagiarism cases augmented through generative re-synthesis and DSP obfuscations. They tested state-of-the-art music version identification architectures by comparing scalar distance thresholding against a supervised framework leveraging coordinate-wise embedding shifts.

Result: Scalar distance thresholding collapses under generative re-synthesis, while the supervised framework recovers the dispersed plagiarism signal, improving F0.5 from 0.612 to 0.803—a significant improvement of 31.2%.

Conclusion: The transfer of music version identification architectures from human-to-human cover detection to human-to-AI plagiarism is feasible with supervised learning approaches. The supervised framework effectively handles the challenges posed by generative re-synthesis, making it a viable solution for detecting AI-generated music plagiarism.

Abstract: The rapid expansion of text-to-music generative models challenges traditional paradigms of music creation and intellectual property. Plagiarism in this context is rarely an absolute mathematical binary, but an ambiguous threshold negotiated over harmonic structure, melodic contours, or overall perceived stylistic character. In this work, we test the transferability of state-of-the-art music version identification architectures from the human-to-human cover domain to the human-to-AI plagiarism setting. To evaluate this task, we introduce COPYCAT, a benchmark derived from real-world plagiarism cases and extended through generative re-synthesis and digital signal processing obfuscations, yielding 350,654 evaluation pairs. We show that scalar distance thresholding collapses under generative re-synthesis, while a supervised framework leveraging coordinate-wise embedding shifts recovers the dispersed plagiarism signal, raising overall $F_{0.5}$ from $0.612$ to $0.803$.

</details>


### [363] [SwinDS-BWE: A Parameter-Efficient Swin-1D Lattice Generator with Decision-Science Discriminators for Speech Bandwidth Extension](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09189)
*Tarikul Islam Tamiti,Sajid Fardin Dipto,Luke Baja-Ricketts,David Vergano,Anomadarshi Barua*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: SwinDS-BWE is a decision-science-inspired bandwidth extension model that uses Swin Transformers with lattice-style cross-stream interaction for efficient locality-aware modeling, reducing generator size from 33M to 17M. It incorporates three novel lightweight discriminators (CVaR, Chance-Constraint HF, and Multi-Criteria Utility) to achieve superior performance with a 30x smaller discriminator (1.36M vs 42.3M) on English and French datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to address the limitations of prior AP-BWE models, specifically the large generator size (33M parameters) and the need for large discriminators (42.3M) to achieve high fidelity. The authors aim to reduce model size while maintaining or improving performance by incorporating decision-science-inspired approaches.

Method: The method involves two main contributions: (1) Swin Transformers with lattice-style cross-stream interaction for efficient locality-aware modeling with linear-in-sequence per-window attention; (2) Three novel lightweight discriminators - CVaR discriminator for tail-pooling worst HF segments, Chance-Constraint HF discriminator with differentiable barrier for penalizing excessive HF energy, and Multi-Criteria Utility discriminator for learning convex style weights over spectral criteria.

Result: SwinDS-BWE surpasses prior AP-BWE with 30x smaller discriminator (1.36M vs 42.3M parameters) and achieves higher fidelity on English and French datasets. The generator size is reduced by 50% (from 33M to 17M).

Conclusion: Decision-science-inspired critics can effectively supervise bandwidth extension tasks, enabling significant reduction in discriminator size while improving or maintaining fidelity. This demonstrates the value of incorporating decision-science concepts into audio enhancement models.

Abstract: We propose SwinDS-BWE, a decision-science-inspired bandwidth extension (BWE) model with two coupled contributions: (1) Swin Transformers with lattice-style cross-stream interaction yield locality-aware modeling with linear-in-sequence per-window attention cost and reduce the prior AP-BWE generator size 0.5x from 33M to 17M. (2) Three novel lightweight decision-science-inspired discriminators augment AP-BWE's performance: a CVaR discriminator tail-pools activations to emphasize worst high-frequency (HF) segments, a Chance-Constraint HF discriminator penalizes excessive HF energy via a differentiable barrier, and a Multi-Criteria Utility discriminator learns convex style weights over spectral criteria. SwinDS-BWE surpasses prior AP-BWE with a 30x smaller discriminator (42.3M vs. 1.36M) and higher fidelity on English and French datasets. This work shows that decision-science-inspired critics can supervise BWE to reduce discriminator size.

</details>


### [364] [BanglaBox: A Phonetically-Balanced Corpus and Data-Efficient Foundation-Model Adaptation for Bangla Text-to-Speech with Zero-Shot Voice Cloning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09211)
*Emtiaz Uddin Ahmed,Araf Mahmud,Sajib Hossain,Tarikul Islam Tamiti,Sajid Fardin Dipto,Anomadarshi Barua*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: This paper presents a recipe for adapting English-pretrained autoregressive TTS foundation models to Bangladeshi Bangla, an underrepresented language. The authors contribute a phonetically/gender-balanced corpus, three fine-tuning modifications (tokenizer extension, text normalization, prompt-masked dual-loss), and a comprehensive evaluation protocol (BanglaEval). Their system BanglaBox achieves near-natural naturalness and outperforms baselines while using 7x less training data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing Bangla TTS corpora are small and single-speaker, and no open zero-shot voice-cloning system exists for the Bangladeshi register. This limits accessibility for Bangla speakers.

Method: The authors developed: (1) A two-tier Bangladeshi Bangla corpus balanced via tiered Jensen-Shannon divergence over conjunct clusters (juktakkhor); (2) Three fine-tuning changes: merge-consistent tokenizer extension, Bangla text normalization, and prompt-masked dual-loss objective. Evaluation uses Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Bonferroni correction over native-speaker ratings.

Result: BanglaBox achieves near-natural Naturalness, outperforms commercial and open-source baselines on Naturalness, Speaker Similarity, and Clarity, and reaches speaker similarity comparable to prior few-shot results while using approximately 7x less Bangla fine-tuning audio. Validated on stress sets, public BnTTS benchmarks, and naturally occurring Bangla.

Conclusion: The proposed recipe successfully adapts English-pretrained TTS models to underrepresented languages while preserving zero-shot cloning capabilities. All artifacts are released publicly.

Abstract: We present a recipe for adapting English-pretrained autoregressive TTS foundation models to underrepresented languages, demonstrated on Bangladeshi Bangla. Existing Bangla TTS corpora are small and single-speaker, and to our knowledge no open zero-shot voice-cloning system is available for the Bangladeshi register. We contribute a phonetically- and gender-balanced two-tier Bangladeshi Bangla corpus balanced via a tiered Jensen-Shannon divergence objective over conjunct clusters (juktakkhor), together with three fine-tuning changes: a merge-consistent tokenizer extension, Bangla text normalization, and a prompt-masked dual-loss objective. These changes preserve zero-shot cloning across the language switch. Our BanglaEval protocol applies Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Bonferroni correction over native-speaker ratings. BanglaBox attains near-natural Naturalness, outperforms commercial and open-source baselines on Naturalness, Speaker Similarity, and Clarity, and reaches speaker similarity comparable to prior few-shot results while using approximately 7x less Bangla fine-tuning audio. We further validate the recipe beyond our own test split using a seven-category stress set of difficult real-world text, the public BnTTS evaluation benchmarks, and naturally occurring Bangla that no language model wrote. All artifacts, including the corpus, weights, code, and complete evaluation materials, are released publicly and unconditionally.

</details>


### [365] [Lyapunov-Inspired LyRIC Activation and GLARE Attention in Chaos-Guided State Space Modeling for EMG-To-Speech (ETS) Synthesis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09225)
*Sajid Fardin Dipto,Tarikul Islam Tamiti,Luke Baja-Ricketts,David Vergano,Anomadarshi Barua*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: This paper introduces the first chaos-inspired approach to Electromyography-to-Speech (ETS) synthesis, proposing a novel Lyapunov-derived activation function (LyRIC) and two chaotic loss functions (Lyapunov Exponent Regularization and Multi-Scale Detrended Fluctuation Analysis) to capture the deterministic chaos of human phonation. The system also includes a novel GLAME encoder combining Mamba state-space modeling with GLARE attention, achieving 4.69x improvement in STOI and 2.08x improvement in LSD with 73.49% fewer parameters.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior ETS synthesis works treat the system as a standard non-linear problem and rely on parameter-heavy transformers that over-smooth natural acoustic dynamics. No prior work has studied the chaotic behavior of ETS synthesis, despite it being a non-linear, chaotic dynamical system. This work aims to explicitly capture the deterministic chaos of human phonation to improve synthesis quality while reducing model complexity.

Method: The paper proposes: (1) LyRIC - a Lyapunov-derived activation function, (2) Lyapunov Exponent Regularization - a loss function to preserve chaotic dynamics, (3) Multi-Scale Detrended Fluctuation Analysis (DFA) - another loss function for multi-scale temporal correlations, and (4) GLAME encoder - combining global Mamba state-space modeling with localized GLARE attention. Evaluation uses English and Mandarin datasets in a multilingual, multi-speaker setup at frame-level.

Result: The proposed system achieves: STOI (Short-Time Objective Intelligibility) of 0.61 vs. 0.13 baseline (4.69x improvement), LSD (Log-Spectral Distance) of 1.08 vs. 2.25 baseline (2.08x improvement), with only 14.34M parameters vs. 54.10M baseline (73.49% reduction).

Conclusion: This is the first work demonstrating that integrating non-linear chaotic physics into neural networks yields superior yet compact inductive biases for real-time ETS synthesis. The chaos-inspired approach successfully captures the deterministic chaos of human phonation, establishing a new baseline for ETS synthesis with significantly improved quality and efficiency.

Abstract: Electromyography-to-Speech (ETS) synthesis is typically a non-linear, chaotic dynamical system. However, no prior work has studied the chaotic behavior of ETS synthesis to date. Yet, prior works strictly rely on standard reconstruction metrics with parameter-heavy transformers that systematically over-smooth natural acoustic dynamics. To close this gap, for the first time, we propose a chaos-inspired Lyapunov-derived activation function (LyRIC) with two novel chaotic loss functions, Lyapunov Exponent Regularization and Multi-Scale Detrended Fluctuation Analysis, to explicitly capture the deterministic chaos of human phonation. In addition, we introduce a compressed novel encoder, GLAME, which synergizes global Mamba state-space modeling with localized GLARE attention. We comprehensively perform frame-level acoustic evaluation in a multilingual and multi-speaker setup using English and Mandarin datasets. The proposed system outperforms the established baseline with a 4.69x increase in objective intelligibility (STOI: 0.61 vs. 0.13) and a 2.08x improvement in spectral reconstruction (LSD: 1.08 vs. 2.25). Importantly, this improvement is achieved with 73.49% fewer parameters (14.34M vs. 54.10M), establishing a new baseline for ETS synthesis. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work demonstrating that integrating non-linear chaotic physics into neural networks yields superior yet compact inductive biases for real-time ETS synthesis.

</details>


### [366] [A multi-scenario EEG dataset for auditory attention decoding in naturalistic multi-talker environments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09539)
*Shu Peng,Rui Liu,Yufei Zhang,Wenlong You,Zhige Chen,Jiachen Xi,Qiyuan Sun,Yan Liu,Kay Chen Tan,Jibin Wu*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: The SoundBubble-EEG dataset is a new high-density 128-channel EEG resource with 25+ hours of recordings from 30 participants, designed to study auditory attention in realistic multi-speaker scenarios (restaurant, home TV, meeting) rather than idealized laboratory paradigms.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current EEG datasets for Auditory Attention Decoding (AAD) use oversimplified single-competing-talker paradigms that fail to capture the acoustic, spatial, and semantic complexity of everyday communication. There is a need for ecologically valid datasets to advance neuro-steered hearing technologies.

Method: The dataset comprises 128-channel EEG recordings from 30 participants totaling over 25 hours. Participants were tasked with selectively attending to a "target speaker group" (sound bubble) while competing "distractor bubbles" played simultaneously across three realistic scenarios: restaurant, home TV viewing, and meeting discussion.

Result: A high-density EEG dataset capturing multi-talker speech comprehension in realistic acoustic environments with semantic variability, enabling investigation of neural speech tracking and cross-scenario generalization.

Conclusion: The SoundBubble-EEG dataset bridges the gap between constrained laboratory protocols and real-world auditory scenes, providing a benchmark for AAD algorithms under realistic conditions and supporting the development of neuro-steered hearing technologies.

Abstract: Understanding how the brain selectively follows relevant speech amid competing voices is a central challenge in auditory neuroscience and a key step toward neuro-steered hearing technologies. However, most open-source Electroencephalography (EEG) datasets for Auditory Attention Decoding (AAD) use idealized single-competing-talker paradigms that oversimplify the acoustic, spatial, and semantic structure of everyday communication. To capture this ecological complexity, we introduce the SoundBubble-EEG dataset: a high-density 128-channel EEG resource comprising more than 25 hours of recordings from 30 participants. The paradigm requires listeners to selectively attend to a dynamic target speaker group, a designated "sound bubble", amid competing multi-speaker distractor bubbles across three realistic scenarios: a restaurant, a home TV viewing, and a meeting discussion. By bridging the gap between constrained laboratory protocols and real-world auditory scenes, this dataset enables investigations of multi-talker speech comprehension, neural speech tracking, and cross-scenario generalization. It also provides a benchmark for AAD algorithms under realistic acoustic and semantic variability and may support auditory neuroscience and the development of neuro-steered hearing technologies.

</details>


### [367] [Tracing Inputs, Verifying Outputs: Validating Attribution in Music Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09637)
*Taejun Kim,Wonil Kim,Jongmin Jung,Hyeongseok Wi,Sangeun Kum,Keunhyoung Luke Kim,Taehyoung Kim,Dongjoo Moon,Seungsoon Park,Taewan Kim,Virginie Berger,Juhan Nam,Jongpil Lee*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: This paper presents input-based attribution methods to verify which audio sources contributed to AI-generated music outputs. The system uses an audio-only conditioned generator (MixAudio) combined with a memorization detection model (musicDNA) to trace input contributions and detect unauthorized training data reproduction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The challenge of verifying music attribution in AI-generated outputs and identifying whether specific audio sources shaped the generated content, while also detecting any unauthorized memorization of training data not supplied as inputs.

Method: The approach conditions generation solely on audio without text input, then traces inputs behind each output and establishes their musical effect. MixAudio generates stems based on prompt audio (controlling timbre) and context audio (controlling harmony). Memorization is audited using musicDNA, a musical version identification model.

Result: In prompt adherence tests and controlled input swaps, generated stems follow the prompt audio in timbre and context audio in harmony. The musicDNA model achieves higher precision and recall than other tested memorization detectors on human-judged cases within the flagged pool, with few reproductions found outside the input records.

Conclusion: Input records and output analysis provide complementary evidence for attribution, enabling rights-holder reporting and compensation as the AI music economy develops.

Abstract: How can we verify whose music contributed to an AI-generated output? This paper demonstrates how input-based attribution can provide verifiable evidence of which audio sources were used in a generation and whether they shaped the output. To do so, we condition the generation solely on audio without any text input, then trace the inputs behind each output, and establish their musical effect. In prompt adherence tests and controlled input swaps, the stems generated by our generator, MixAudio, follow the prompt audio in timbre and the context audio in harmony. Yet these outputs may still reproduce training data not supplied as inputs. We therefore audit memorization with our musical version identification model, musicDNA, and find few reproductions outside the input records. On human-judged cases within the flagged pool, it achieves higher precision and recall than the other tested memorization detectors. The two evaluations suggest that input records and output analysis provide complementary evidence for attribution, on which rights-holder reporting and compensation can draw as the AI music economy takes shape. Audio examples are available at https://neutune.github.io/attr2027demo/

</details>


### [368] [Backdooring Acoustic Foundation Models for Physically Realizable Triggers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09819)
*Zebin Yun,Eyal Ronen,Mahmood Sharif*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: This paper introduces the Foundation Acoustic model Backdoor (FAB) attack, demonstrating that state-of-the-art Acoustic Foundation Models (AFMs) are vulnerable to backdoor attacks. The attack uses physically realizable, task-agnostic triggers (e.g., background sirens) that work without synchronization and survive fine-tuning, posing significant security risks to downstream acoustic applications.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While Acoustic Foundation Models have democratized acoustic applications (speech recognition, speaker verification, etc.), the security of AFM-based applications remains underexplored. This work addresses this critical gap by investigating backdoor vulnerabilities in AFMs under practical attack settings.

Method: The FAB attack operates with minimal adversary assumptions (no access to pre-training data). It uses task-agnostic, physically realizable, inconspicuous, and sync-free triggers (such as background sirens). The attack was evaluated using two leading AFMs, nine downstream tasks, and four different triggers. The researchers tested effectiveness against established defenses and both digital and physical domains.

Result: FAB preserves benign performance while successfully inducing backdoors that survive fine-tuning and cause significant degradation across diverse downstream tasks. The attack is effective against established defenses and works in both digital and physical domains. Only extensive end-to-end fine-tuning can mitigate FAB, but this defense is resource-intensive and task-specific.

Conclusion: Acoustic Foundation Models face critical security risks from backdoor attacks. The FAB attack demonstrates practical vulnerabilities that survive standard defenses and fine-tuning. Advanced defenses specifically designed for AFMs are urgently needed. The work highlights the need for security considerations in the development and deployment of foundation models for acoustic applications.

Abstract: Acoustic foundation models (AFMs) have democratized acoustic applications, enabling powerful models for tasks ranging from speech recognition to speaker verification with minimal resources. However, the security of applications based on AFMs remains largely underexplored. Our work addresses this gap by proposing the Foundation Acoustic model Backdoor (FAB) attack, demonstrating that state-of-the-art AFMs are susceptible to backdooring under practical settings. Despite making minimal assumptions about adversary capabilities (e.g., no access to pre-training data), we show that FAB preserves benign performance while inducing backdoors that survive fine-tuning and cause significant degradation across diverse downstream tasks when activated. Notably, FAB utilizes task-agnostic, physically realizable, inconspicuous, and sync-free triggers (e.g., a background siren). We evaluate FAB using two leading AFMs, nine downstream tasks, and four different triggers. We further demonstrate its effectiveness against established defenses and across both digital and physical domains. While extensive end-to-end fine-tuning can mitigate FAB, such a defense is resource-intensive and task-specific. Our work highlights critical risks to AFMs and calls for advanced defenses.

</details>


### [369] [A Study on Improving Multi-class Audio Source Separation Via Decoupled CLAP Query Optimization and an Automated Data Engine](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.10025)
*Amirhossein Hajavi,Hanhee Lee,Pushya Jain,Sky Qiao,Emmanuel Ko,Yuanhao Yu,Irina Kezele*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: This paper addresses challenges in adapting language-queried audio source separation (LASS) models to specific sound classes by proposing an automated data curation engine and a two-stage CLAP control signal optimization process. The approach shows improved performance through both objective and subjective evaluations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Adapting LASS models to application-specific sound classes is challenging due to noisy training data and limited semantic coverage of CLAP-based control signals. Current approaches lack effective methods for data refinement and semantic control optimization.

Method: The framework consists of two components: (1) an automated data engine for training-data curation to address noisy data, and (2) a two-stage optimization process for class-specific CLAP control signals to improve semantic coverage. Evaluations were conducted across seven sound classes (objective) and with 17 participants (subjective).

Result: Data refinement and control signal optimization consistently improve source separation performance. The model trained with optimized control signals demonstrates perceptual improvements over baseline and commercial models.

Conclusion: The proposed framework successfully addresses LASS model adaptation challenges through automated data curation and control signal optimization, achieving both objective and subjective improvements in audio source separation quality.

Abstract: Language-queried audio source separation (LASS) enables extracting any sound source using natural language. However, adapting LASS models to application-specific sound classes is challenging due to noisy training data and limited semantic coverage of the CLAP-based control signals. We propose a framework comprised of an automated data engine for training-data curation and a two-stage optimization process for class-specific CLAP control signals. Our objective evaluations across seven sound classes show that data refinement and control signal optimization consistently improve source separation performance. Subjective evaluation with 17 participants further demonstrates perceptual improvements of the model trained with optimized control signals over baseline and similar commercial models.

</details>


### [370] [CARES: A Controlled Synthetic Benchmark of Speaker Reactions to Sound](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.10208)
*Marcel Gibier,Thomas Thebaud,Olivier Boëffard,Jean-François Bonastre*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: This paper introduces CARES, a corpus of 10,000 two-speaker audio scenes with ground truth annotations based on a novel definition of sound salience (when speakers audibly react to sounds). Six audio-language models are benchmarked on scene identification, sound tagging, and reaction classification tasks, revealing that while models can detect sounds, they fail to capture speaker reactions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The core challenge in automatic audio scene description is determining which elements to include in a text description, since not all audio events can be captured. Annotator disagreement makes ground truth definition difficult, and existing approaches lack a principled way to define sound salience.

Method: The authors define sound salience using a simple rule: a sound is salient when a speaker audibly reacts to it. They create a controlled set of scenarios to establish ground truth and use a language model to generate dialogues. The resulting corpus, CARES, contains 10,000 two-speaker scenes. Six audio-language models are then benchmarked on three tasks: scene identification, sound tagging, and reaction classification.

Result: The benchmark results show that audio-language models can detect sounds in the scenes but consistently fail to capture how speakers react to those sounds. Models perform reasonably on identifying scenes and tagging sounds present, but struggle significantly with reaction classification.

Conclusion: Current audio-language models can perceive auditory events but lack the ability to understand the contextual and behavioral aspects of audio scenes—specifically, how speakers react to sounds. This represents a fundamental gap in audio scene understanding that requires further research.

Abstract: Automatic audio scene description turns a recording into a text account of a situation. One difficulty is deciding which elements of the audio should be kept, since a description cannot include them all. Annotators disagree about this, making a ground truth hard to obtain. In this work, we first define the ground truth, then generate the data. We focus on audio events and define sound salience with a simple rule: a sound is salient when a speaker audibly reacts to it. For scale and variety, a controlled set of scenarios fixes the ground truth, and a language model writes the dialogues. The resulting corpus, CARES, contains 10,000 two-speaker scenes. We then benchmark six audio-language models on three tasks: identifying the scene, tagging the sounds present, and classifying reactions. We show that these models hear the sounds but miss how the speakers react to them.

</details>


### [371] [CrossEdit: Cross-Modal Training Enables Rich Audio-Visual Editing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.10264)
*William Chen,Prem Seetharaman,Ke Chen,Oriol Nieto,Kevin Duarte,Siddharth Srinivasan Iyer,Mamshad Nayeem Rizve,Zhiwen Cao,Shinji Watanabe,Yuanjun Xiong,Jianming Zhang,Zeyu Jin,Justin Salamon*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: CrossEdit is a unified omni-modal editing model for images, audio, and video that performs audiovisual movie scene edits zero-shot through cross-modal transfer. It uses procedurally generated audio editing pairs and self-supervised AV masked reconstruction to learn instruction-following that generalizes across modalities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multimedia editing requires interpreting complex, compositional instructions and modifying only desired elements across modalities - a capability largely beyond existing systems. Current approaches are limited to simple, single-attribute edits within one modality because diverse, high-quality editing pairs are hard to obtain, especially for cross-modal tasks where aligned audiovisual data is scarce.

Method: 1) Exploit the additive nature of acoustic signals to procedurally generate large-scale audio editing pairs with compositional instructions; 2) Fine-tune on this synthetic data and self-supervised AV masked reconstruction; 3) Use a targeted set of curated cross-modal tasks; 4) This induces instruction-following that transfers zero-shot to unseen modality and instruction combinations.

Result: Improved performance on zero-shot AV movie scene editing, while maintaining or improving performance on lip-synced speech editing and standard image, video, and audio editing benchmarks.

Conclusion: Complex instruction-following, once learned in any modality, can generalize to others. The proposed techniques successfully enable cross-modal transfer for instruction-following in multimedia editing, with a new benchmark (CrossEditBench) and metric (AV-FES) for evaluation.

Abstract: Multimedia editing requires generative models to interpret complex, compositional instructions and modify only the desired elements across modalities, a capability largely beyond existing systems. Current approaches are typically limited to simple, single-attribute edits within one modality, since diverse, high-quality editing pairs are hard to obtain, especially for cross-modal tasks where aligned audiovisual (AV) data is scarce. We present CrossEdit, a unified omni-modal editing model for images, audio, and video that performs AV movie scene edits zero-shot through cross-modal transfer. Our key observation is that complex instruction-following, once learned in any modality, generalizes to others. We exploit the additive nature of acoustic signals to procedurally generate large-scale audio editing pairs with compositional instructions, and show that fine-tuning on this synthetic data and self-supervised AV masked reconstruction, alongside a targeted set of curated cross-modal tasks, induces instruction-following that transfers zero-shot to unseen modality and instruction combinations. To evaluate this capability, we release CrossEditBench, a human-annotated benchmark of AV edits on movie scenes, and propose AV-FES, a metric that jointly scores instruction following and consistency. We show that our proposed techniques improve performance on zero-shot AV movie scene editing, while maintaining or improving performance on lip-synced speech editing and standard image, video, and audio editing benchmarks. Demos are available at https://wanchichen.github.io/crossedit/.

</details>


### [372] [MIRA: A Musical Intent Refinement Agent for Aligning Text-to-Music Generation with User Intent](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.10355)
*Zekai Liu,Zhilin Wang,Xuzheng He,Yu Cheng,Yang Yang*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: This paper addresses the gap between text-to-music generation quality and user intent alignment by proposing a rubric-based evaluation framework (MuRA-Bench) and an iterative refinement agent (MIRA) that uses tree search to improve prompt revisions for better intent matching.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current text-to-music evaluation relies on global text-audio relevance scores that fail to capture implicit user intent and mask specific requirement failures (instrumentation, structure, rhythm, mood progression). This limits diagnostic feedback and improvement.

Method: 1) Formulate intent alignment as satisfying per-request rubrics with independently verifiable items. 2) Create MuRA-Bench benchmark from real-world platform requests curated by music experts. 3) Develop MIRA agent with: intent grounding into rubrics, bounded-budget prompt revision search, iterative generation-verification loop, and trajectory-aware tree search for feedback.

Result: MIRA improves intent alignment across open-source and commercial backends. An open-source generator using MIRA achieves performance comparable to representative commercial systems (Suno and Mureka).

Conclusion: Rubric-based evaluation enables diagnostic assessment by intent source and musical dimension. MIRA's test-time agent approach successfully bridges the intent alignment gap, making open-source generators competitive with commercial systems through iterative prompt refinement.

Abstract: Text-to-music systems produce increasingly convincing audio, yet evaluation reveals little about whether the result matches user intent. A global text-audio relevance score can overlook the implicit intent in underspecified prompts and mask failures in specific requirements, such as instrumentation, structure, rhythm, or mood progression. To bridge this gap, we formulate text-to-music intent alignment as satisfying a per-request rubric of independently verifiable items covering both a request's explicit requirements and its implied musical intent. Scoring items individually makes evaluation diagnostic by intent source and musical dimension, rather than a single opaque score. We instantiate this as MuRA-Bench, a benchmark of real-world platform requests curated by music experts. We further propose MIRA (Musical Intent Refinement Agent), a test-time agent that first grounds a request's intent into rubrics, then searches over prompt revisions for a black-box generator under a bounded budget, iteratively generating music, verifying it against the rubrics, and using this feedback to guide a trajectory-aware tree search. Experiments across open-source and commercial backends show that MIRA improves intent alignment, enabling an open-source generator to achieve performance comparable to representative commercial systems (e.g. Suno and Mureka). Project page: https://mirareview.github.io/.

</details>


### [373] [Steerspeech: Activation Steering For Emotion Control In Generated Speech](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.10415)
*Afsara Benazir,Darius Pétermann,Felix Xiaozhu Lin,Salar Rahili*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: SteerSpeech is a lightweight activation-steering framework that enables inference-time emotion control in pretrained TTS models by injecting steering vectors into hidden activations. It uses low-rank transforms trained with a multi-expert objective and a two-pass generation-and-replay pipeline with straight-through estimation to optimize through discrete speech tokens.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Pretrained TTS models can generate expressive speech, but reliable inference-time emotion control remains challenging. Existing approaches (prompts, reference audio) offer coarse/inconsistent control, while specialized conditioning and model adaptation require costly training.

Method: 1) Train lightweight low-rank transforms for each target emotion using a multi-expert objective that: encourages monotonic emotion control, preserves speaker identity and linguistic content, constrains steering drift, and keeps the TTS backbone frozen.
2) Introduce a two-pass generation-and-replay pipeline using straight-through estimator to backpropagate expert supervision through sampled discrete speech tokens.
3) At inference, optimize target-emotion steering direction with respective transform and inject into base TTS model.

Result: Evaluations with Qwen3-TTS across seen, unseen, and accented speakers show: 1) Stronger continuous emotion control with limited speaker/content degradation; 2) 1.08x-7.12x baseline target-emotion scores; 3) Subjectively, 78.1%-96.8% intensity preference and 1.43x-1.46x speaker-identity preservation at high steering strengths.

Conclusion: SteerSpeech achieves effective emotion control in pretrained TTS models with minimal degradation to speaker identity and linguistic content, offering a lightweight alternative to costly model adaptation or specialized conditioning approaches.

Abstract: Pretrained text-to-speech (TTS) models can generate expressive speech, but reliable inference-time emotion control remains challenging: prompts and reference audio offer coarse, inconsistent control, whereas specialized conditioning and model adaptation require costly training. We present SteerSpeech, a lightweight activation-steering framework that controls emotion by injecting steering vectors into hidden activations. For each target emotion we train a lightweight low-rank transform, using a multi-expert objective that encourages monotonic emotion control while preserving speaker identity and linguistic content, constraining steering drift, and keeping the TTS backbone frozen. To optimize through discrete speech tokens, we introduce a two-pass generation-and-replay pipeline using a straight-through estimator to backpropagate expert supervision through sampled tokens. At inference, a target-emotion steering direction is optimized with its respective transform and injected into the base TTS model. Objective and subjective evaluations with Qwen3-TTS across seen, unseen, and accented speakers show stronger continuous emotion control with limited speaker and content degradation. SteerSpeech achieves 1.08x-7.12x baseline target-emotion scores and for a representative emotion subjectively, it receives 78.1%-96.8% intensity preference and 1.43x-1.46x speaker-identity preservation at high steering strengths.

</details>


### [374] [Unsupervised Maneuver-Aware Acoustic Fault Detection for Autonomous Drones](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.10517)
*Ali M Ali,Ziyi Tang,Nurdaulet Nazarbay,Hashim A. Hashim*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: A maneuver-aware acoustic fault detection framework for autonomous drones that uses Noise2Noise-inspired denoising combined with maneuver-conditioned reconstruction in an unsupervised learning paradigm, requiring only nominal flight data for training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Collecting labeled faulty-flight data for drone health monitoring is difficult and potentially unsafe. Additionally, acoustic signals are affected by environmental noise and maneuver-dependent aerodynamic effects, complicating fault detection.

Method: Two-stage architecture: (1) Noise2Noise-inspired denoising model to attenuate stochastic noise while preserving fault-relevant structures; (2) Maneuver-Conditioned Convolutional AutoEncoder (maneuver-CCAE) trained with maneuver labels (drone type, flight direction) to model nominal acoustic behavior. Fault detection uses reconstruction error as anomaly score.

Result: The maneuver-aware conditioning raised AUC from the unconditioned baseline to the full model. Deployed on NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano Super with ROS2, achieving ~20ms latency per audio segment using TensorRT FP16.

Conclusion: Maneuver-dependent modeling is critical for acoustic fault detection. The framework achieves real-time viability for onboard UAV health monitoring with low latency.

Abstract: This paper presents a maneuver-aware acoustic fault detection framework for autonomous drones that integrates Noise2Noise-inspired deep learning denoising with maneuver-conditioned reconstruction. A key practical constraint motivating this work is that labeled faulty-flight data are difficult and potentially unsafe to collect; the proposed framework therefore follows an unsupervised learning paradigm in which only nominal flight recordings are required for training. In flight environments, acoustic signals acquired from unmanned aerial vehicles are subject to variability arising both from environmental noise and from structured, maneuver-dependent aerodynamic effects. To address these challenges simultaneously, a two-stage learning architecture is developed. In the first stage, a Noise2Noise-inspired denoising model attenuates stochastic acoustic noise while preserving fault-relevant spectral-temporal structures, without requiring clean reference signals. In the second stage, a maneuver-Conditioned Convolutional AutoEncoder (maneuver-CCAE) is trained using maneuver-related labels including drone type and flight direction to model nominal acoustic behavior under varying operating conditions. Fault detection is subsequently performed using reconstruction error as an anomaly score. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed maneuver-aware conditioning raises the area under the ROC curve (AUC) from $\AUCaeOnly$ (unconditioned baseline) to $\AUCfull$ (full model), validating the critical role of maneuver-dependent modeling. The complete framework is deployed on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano Super embedded platform within a ROS2 pipeline, achieving an end-to-end fault detection latency of approximately $20\,\text{ms}$ per audio segment with a TensorRT half-precision (FP16) backend, confirming real-time viability for onboard UAV health monitoring.

</details>


<div id='cs.GR'></div>

### [375] [Physics-based Sphere Packing for Lagrangian Mesh Morphing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08880)
*Jiong Lin,Hod Lipson*

Main category: cs.GR

TL;DR: JamTet is a physics-based sphere-packing framework for volumetric meshing and morphing in differentiable simulation and computational design. It combines octree-hierarchical packing with constrained Delaunay tetrahedralization, preserves interior-node identities during morphing, and integrates with a differentiable JAX simulator for gradient-based shape optimization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Fixed-connectivity meshes degrade under large morphs, while remeshing from scratch discards node correspondence. A new volumetric mesh representation is needed that can maintain element quality and node identity during shape optimization.

Method: The method has three main components: (1) GPU-parallel mesher combining octree-hierarchical packing with constrained Delaunay tetrahedralization; (2) Lagrangian mesh morphing that preserves interior-node identities by re-equilibrating spheres within changing shapes and rebuilding boundary/connectivity; (3) Differentiable GPU simulator in JAX with mass-spring edges and volumetric Neo-Hookean term, integrated with mesh morphing.

Result: The mesher produces more uniform element volumes than TetGen and fTetWild. The morphing method remains inversion-free where fixed-connectivity and TetSphere meshes invert. In soft-robot design experiments, interior-node gradients improve swimming fitness by 0.73-1.07 over surface-only variants, while voxelized versions yield 32-63% lower fitness.

Conclusion: Sphere packing is established as a practical volumetric mesh representation for gradient-based shape optimization, enabling interior-node gradients that significantly improve design outcomes compared to surface-only or voxelized approaches.

Abstract: This paper studies tetrahedral meshes as the body representation for differentiable simulation and computational design. Fixed-connectivity meshes degrade under large morphs, while remeshing from scratch discards node correspondence. We present JamTet, a physics-based sphere-packing framework for volumetric meshing and morphing. We contribute (i) a GPU-parallel mesher combining octree-hierarchical packing with constrained Delaunay tetrahedralization, producing more uniform element volumes than TetGen and fTetWild; (ii) Lagrangian mesh morphing that preserves interior-node identities by re-equilibrating the same spheres within changing shapes and rebuilding the boundary and connectivity, remaining inversion-free where fixed-connectivity and TetSphere meshes invert; and (iii) a differentiable GPU simulator in JAX, with mass-spring edges and a volumetric Neo-Hookean term, integrated with mesh morphing in a design pipeline. In soft-robot morphology design experiments, interior-node gradients improve swimming fitness by 0.73-1.07 over a matched surface-only variant, while voxelized versions of the same designs yield 32-63% lower fitness. These results establish sphere packing as a practical volumetric mesh representation for gradient-based shape optimization. Code and media: under review.

</details>


### [376] [emg2face: Expressive Facial Animation with High-Density Surface EMG](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09304)
*Ganidhu Abey,Wendy Greening,Ashika Kamboj,Leonhard Helminger,Abhijeet Ghosh,Karel Petranek,Sergio Orts Escolano,Dinesh K. Pai*

Main category: cs.GR

TL;DR: This paper presents a non-optical facial motion capture method using high-density surface electromyography (HD-sEMG) that can work with VR headsets and addresses privacy concerns of traditional optical methods. The system uses 64 EMG channels to predict 383 expression blendshapes via a deep neural network, enabling real-time expression transfer to various characters.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional optical face capture methods fail when faces are occluded by head-mounted devices (HMDs) like VR headsets, raise privacy concerns, and require bulky head-mounted rigs. There is a need for a non-optical alternative that can capture facial movements through occlusion and without privacy issues.

Method: The study used 64-channel HD-sEMG (32 channels on forehead, 32 on face side) recorded at 2048 Hz, synchronized with MediaPipe's 478 facial landmarks using analog audio bursts. A deep neural network with spatial encoders and dilated TCN was trained to predict 383 expression blendshapes from EMG signals at 100 Hz. The GNM head model (253 identity + 383 expression blendshapes) was fitted to landmarks using a staged fitting method. Experiments involved 25 participants.

Result: The trained network can predict expression blendshapes solely from HD-sEMG recordings at 100 Hz. The output integrates with standard real-time blendshape animation pipelines, enabling direct expression transfer to various human faces and non-human characters.

Conclusion: HD-sEMG provides a viable non-optical alternative for facial motion capture that works through VR headset occlusion, addresses privacy concerns, and enables real-time expression transfer to diverse characters without optical sensors.

Abstract: Facial movements convey subtle and important information that is critical for human social communication. Optical methods for face capture are difficult or impossible to use when the face is occluded by head-mounted devices (HMDs), such as VR headsets. Even with a clear line of sight, such methods raise privacy concerns and require head-mounted capture rigs that offset cameras and lighting from the face. We show that high-density surface electromyography (HD-sEMG) provides a viable non-optical alternative that addresses these challenges.
  We measured 64 EMG channels, using two textile EMG grids, with 32 from the forehead (typically occluded by an HMD) and 32 from the side of the face. EMG data were digitized at 2048 Hz and filtered. Facial movements were simultaneously recorded and used to estimate 478 3D facial landmarks using MediaPipe's Face Landmarker. A major challenge in such multimodal recordings is synchronizing EMG and video data, which have different sampling frequencies and independent clocks. We developed a novel synchronization method using analog audio bursts that is capable of sub-millisecond synchronization. We also developed a staged fitting method that fits a recent high-resolution parametric head model (GNM), with 253 identity blendshapes and 383 expression blendshapes, to the MediaPipe landmarks as participants performed different facial expressions.
  We trained a deep neural network comprising per-grid spatial encoders followed by a dilated temporal convolutional network (TCN) to predict blendshape parameters from HD-sEMG signals at 100 Hz. Once trained, the network can predict expression blendshapes solely from HD-sEMG recordings. The output can be rendered using standard real-time blendshape animation methods. We demonstrate the methods using recordings from 25 participants, and direct expression transfer to a variety of human faces and non-human characters.

</details>


### [377] [ScribbleEdit: A Benchmark for Scribble-Only Image Editing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09382)
*Jie Ren,Hao Kang,Kai Guo,Yiding Yang,Bo Liu,Liming Jiang,Qing Yan,Zichuan Liu,Yizhi Song,Yue Xing,Hui Liu,Xin Lu*

Main category: cs.GR

TL;DR: Summary generation failed


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Motivation analysis unavailable

Method: Method extraction failed

Result: Result analysis unavailable

Conclusion: Conclusion extraction failed

Abstract: Scribble-based interaction provides a lightweight and intuitive way for users to specify image editing intents in interactive editing tools. However, current image editing models based on VLMs or LLMs struggle to understand and execute edits based solely on scribble inputs. To systematically study this problem, we construct a new benchmark, ScribbleEdit, that evaluates the ability of image editing models to perform image editing conditioned on scribbles. This task requires both a deep understanding of the intention of the scribble and an accurate interpretation of its spatial information. In ScribbleEdit, we design an automated data construction pipeline and introduce a dedicated evaluation protocol that explicitly measures intention alignment. Our analysis reveals that existing VLM/LLM-based editing models fail to accurately capture scribble intentions. To guide future progress on scribble-only image editing, we propose a simple yet effective soft-token baseline, which enhances the model's understanding of scribble semantics and outperforms standard image editing models on our benchmark. Our evaluation and baseline together provide a concrete foundation for assessing and improving the scribble-driven image editing.

</details>


### [378] [Simulation Methods for Multiphysics Phenomena in Visual Computing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09822)
*Fabian Löschner,Stefan Rhys Jeske,José Antonio Fernández-Fernández,Jan Bender*

Main category: cs.GR

TL;DR: This paper provides comprehensive course notes on multiphysics simulation methods for computer graphics, covering mathematical foundations, algorithms for various materials (rigid/deformable bodies, fluids, granular materials), coupling strategies, software frameworks, and emerging ML-based trends.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Physics simulation is essential for computer graphics applications (games, VR, visual effects, computational design), and the field has grown rapidly with numerous techniques developed for physically-based modeling and animation.

Method: The paper presents an in-depth introduction through detailed mathematical derivations for each method, discussing how different materials and coupling strategies integrate into the unified formulation. It also surveys existing software frameworks.

Result: The paper covers the most widely used approaches in the computer graphics community, including rigid bodies, deformable bodies, fluids, granular materials, and their interactions, along with software tools for multiphysics modeling.

Conclusion: The paper concludes by highlighting emerging trends in physics-based animation, particularly machine learning-based methods that have gained popularity in recent years.

Abstract: Physics simulation is a cornerstone of many computer graphics applications, ranging from video games and virtual reality to visual effects and computational design. The number of techniques for physically-based modeling and animation has thus skyrocketed over the past few decades, facilitating the simulation of a wide variety of materials and physical phenomena. These course notes provide an in-depth introduction to multiphysics simulation methods for computer graphics, covering the mathematical foundations, key algorithms, and practical considerations behind the most widely used approaches. We focus on methods developed by the computer graphics community for simulating various physical phenomena and materials -- including rigid and deformable bodies, fluids, and granular materials -- as well as the interactions between them. For each method, we present the underlying mathematical framework with detailed derivations and discuss how different materials and coupling strategies fit into the formulation. A selection of software frameworks that offer out-of-the-box multiphysics modeling capabilities is also presented. Finally, we touch on emerging trends in physics-based animation, including machine learning-based methods which have become increasingly popular in recent years.

</details>


### [379] [DynaConTalk: Wavelet-Constrained Diffusion for Long-Form and Controllable Holistic Co-Speech 3D Motion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09846)
*Yifei Zhu,Yangyang Cai,Mingyi Shi,Miao Cheng,Lin Gu,Taku Komura,Yoshifumi Kitamura*

Main category: cs.GR

TL;DR: DynaConTalk is a wavelet-constrained diffusion framework for long-form and controllable holistic co-speech motion generation. It operates in stationary wavelet transform (SWT) coefficient space to separate coarse posture, gesture strokes, and fine expressive details, addressing the averaging problem in traditional holistic co-speech animation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Holistic co-speech animation suffers from two main problems: (1) averaging in motion representation where slow body posture, mid-frequency gesture strokes, and fast hand/facial details are entangled, producing low-variance over-smoothed motion; (2) dominance of dense rhythmic/acoustic cues over sparse content-specific information under fixed multimodal fusion.

Method: The framework uses several key components: (1) Stationary wavelet transform (SWT) to separate motion into temporally aligned bands; (2) Dynamic gating network preserving HuBERT and speaker identity while selectively adding rhythm, mel, and transcript features through motion-state- and noise-aware residual gates; (3) Attention pooling and learned depth routing for complementary conditions to each denoising stage; (4) Frame-resolution rhythm path for precise timing; (5) Signed proposal-consensus update to reconcile conditions with evolving motion state; (6) Matched-noise constraint injection for history continuation and keypose repair; (7) Separate body-hand and facial denoisers with inverse SWT and pose-driven root regressor.

Result: The experiments evaluate generation quality, facial accuracy, temporal continuity, and controllable editing. The paper provides code, models, and an interactive editing interface.

Conclusion: DynaConTalk successfully addresses the averaging problem in holistic co-speech animation by using wavelet-based decomposition to separate different motion frequencies, enabling long-form generation with controllable editing capabilities while preserving both rhythmic coherence and content-specific information.

Abstract: Holistic co-speech animation is prone to averaging in both motion representation and speech conditioning. In coordinate-space diffusion, slow body posture, mid-frequency gesture strokes, and fast hand or facial details are entangled in one prediction target, often producing low-variance, over-smoothed motion. Meanwhile, dense rhythmic and acoustic cues can dominate sparse content-specific information under fixed multimodal fusion. We present DynaConTalk, a wavelet-constrained diffusion framework for long-form and controllable holistic co-speech motion generation. Diffusion operates in stationary wavelet transform (SWT) coefficient space, whose temporally aligned bands separate coarse posture evolution, gesture strokes, and fine expressive details. Our dynamic gating network preserves HuBERT and speaker identity as a base and selectively adds rhythm, mel, and transcript features through motion-state- and noise-aware residual gates. Attention pooling and learned depth routing deliver complementary conditions to each denoising stage, while a frame-resolution rhythm path preserves precise timing. A signed proposal-consensus update then reconciles these conditions with the evolving motion state. Matched-noise constraint injection uses the same sampling interface for history continuation and localized keypose repair, and extends to reference-guided control. Separate body-hand and facial denoisers, followed by inverse SWT and a pose-driven root regressor, produce holistic motion. Experiments evaluate generation quality, facial accuracy, temporal continuity, and controllable editing. Code, models, and the interactive editing interface are available at https://github.com/zhuyifeiabcd1/DynaConTalk.

</details>


### [380] [TRACK: Telemetry-Based Racing Analysis and Coaching Kit in Sim Racing Games](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.10061)
*Efe Çangırılı,Murat Kurt*

Main category: cs.GR

TL;DR: TRACK is a framework for analyzing sim racing driving performance by representing recording sessions as 4D fingerprints (speed, braking, strategy, consistency) and grouping them using unsupervised clustering, with normalization against a reinforcement learning reference agent.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To analyze driving performance in sim racing and profile individual driver behavior without restricting to preset labels or scoring systems, creating an analytical foundation for personalized improvement suggestion systems.

Method: Represent each recording session as a compact geometry in a 4-dimensional behavioral space (speed, braking, strategy, consistency), group fingerprints by similarity using unsupervised clustering, calibrate clustering results against null models, and normalize metrics against a reinforcement-learning reference agent.

Result: Corner types differ along a behavioral dimension not used to define them; when car changes, only speed and consistency carry over; repeatability not shown for braking or strategy measures; cluster separation becomes less distinct with wider telemetry range; results are preliminary with small sample size.

Conclusion: The framework provides an analytical foundation for personalized improvement suggestions but with significant limitations: small sample size, cross-car results change with broader sample definition, and grouping on braking/strategy dimensions cannot treat cars as interchangeable until repeatability is demonstrated.

Abstract: This paper presents TRACK (Telemetry-Based Racing Analysis and Coaching Kit), which is a framework for analyzing driving performance in sim racing and profiling how individual drivers behave behind the wheel. We report this framework together with its limitations: we calibrate each clustering result against a null, and when one does not separate from chance, we say so. Instead of restricting ourselves to scoring drivers or sorting them into preset labels, we represent each recording session as a compact geometry in a four-dimensional behavioral space (speed, braking, strategy, and consistency), and we group these fingerprints by their similarity using unsupervised clustering. Over time, we have developed and refined this framework on the open Assetto Corsa Gym (ACGym) dataset. Our study suggests that corner types differ along a behavioral dimension that was not used to define them. It also suggests that when the car changes, only speed and consistency carry over in the restricted population, while repeatability could not be shown there for any of the braking or strategy measures. Cluster separation becomes less distinct as the range of available telemetry widens. Until that repeatability is shown, grouping on the braking and strategy dimensions cannot treat the car as interchangeable, which divides an already small sample into smaller cells. It is also not clear whether a driver's grouping carries over from one corner type to the next. We also normalize each metric against a reinforcement-learning reference agent. The reference does not depend on the sample, so the scale does not shift when the sample does. We intend these results as an analytical foundation for a personalized improvement suggestion system. The sample is small. The cross-car result changes when the sample is defined more broadly. These outcomes are preliminary.

</details>

### [381] [MemoCare: An Interactive Multimodal Mobile System for Automated Cognitive Screening](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.10448)
*Duy-Cat Can,Mau Minh Phuc Le,Tuan-Khoa Hoang,Hai-Dang Nguyen,Trung-Hieu Do,Dang Minh Ly,Minh-Duc Nguyen,Nghia TT Hoang,Linh-Trung Nguyen,Huy-Hieu Pham,Huong Ha,Binh T. Nguyen,Oliver Y. Chén*

Main category: cs.MM

TL;DR: MemoCare is a React Native mobile application that provides automated multimodal cognitive screening in English and Vietnamese, integrating speech transcription, spatial orientation via GPS, touchscreen interaction tasks, and visuoconstruction drawing assessment using a three-model CNN consensus approach.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation appears to be addressing the need for accessible, automated cognitive screening tools that can be deployed in various settings, potentially to assist clinicians in detecting cognitive impairment through multiple assessment modalities combined into a single mobile system.

Method: The system uses Google Speech-to-Text for transcription with local rule-based scoring, GPS coordinates for spatial orientation matching, touchscreen event recording for interaction tasks, and a three-model CNN consensus for drawing task interpretation. Validation included software testing (151 test cases), spatial regression (48 coordinate cases), and a locked 71-image test set for the drawing module using ShuffleNetV2 x1.5. Clinician evaluation involved four co-authors rating the end-to-end workflow across eight criteria.

Result: Software tests passed 151/151 cases; spatial regression passed 48/48 cases; the drawing module achieved 91.33% mean balanced accuracy and 78.87% exact three-criterion accuracy on the test set. Clinician ratings yielded a pooled median of 4/5 across eight criteria with item-level medians of 3-4.5.

Conclusion: MemoCare demonstrates a viable multimodal cognitive screening system with strong performance across automated scoring components and positive clinician evaluation, suggesting potential for practical deployment in cognitive assessment workflows.

Abstract: MemoCare is an interactive mobile system for automated multimodal cognitive screening. A React Native application combines spoken responses, temporal and spatial orientation, touchscreen actions, and visuoconstruction in complete English and Vietnamese workflows. Speech is transcribed by Google Speech-to-Text and scored locally with deterministic task-specific natural language processing rules; GPS coordinates are resolved by the MemoCare spatial module before answer matching; touch tasks are scored from interaction events; and the drawing task uses a three-model convolutional neural network consensus with separate visual interpretation. Software tests pass 151/151 predefined cases across speech/language, spatial-answer, and touch-interaction scoring, while spatial regression passes 48/48 four-country coordinate-resolution cases. For the drawing module, validation-selected ShuffleNetV2 x1.5 achieved 91.33% mean balanced accuracy and 78.87% exact three-criterion accuracy on a locked 71-image test set. Four clinician co-authors additionally inspected the end-to-end workflow, yielding a pooled median rating of 4/5 across eight criteria, with item-level medians ranging from 3 to 4.5. At MMM, attendees can directly try a shortened multimodal screening workflow and inspect automatic item-level and total scoring.

</details>
